notes.explains: White opens with the Nimzowitsch-Larsen, b3. The classical reply is to occupy the centre at once — e5.
He develops, and the knight to f3 attacks our pawn on e5.
Rather than defend it, we push the pawn forward to e4.
This is a well-known, fully legitimate theoretical line — and a very complex one. White's hypermodern idea is to tempt our pawns forward now so he can attack them later.
We don't capture the knight — instead the queen comes to f6 to chase it. It may look like we're pinning ourselves...
...but because his bishop was hanging, the knight was forced to run specifically to c4.
And we reposition the queen to g6.
He's blitzing his moves out, shuffling the same knight again and again in the opening.
There's no reason to be intimidated by an opponent who flouts opening principles — you simply obey them yourself. The knight comes to f6.
He plays g3. The way to punish this kind of play is precisely to follow opening principles to the letter.
What have we not done yet? Completed development, and fully occupied the centre with pawns. So d5, building a big central pawn chain.
He fianchettoes with the bishop to g2. Now all that remains is to bring our pieces out.
We develop the bishop to e6 first, reinforcing the centre.
He castles. This is the instructive moment: we could keep developing or castle long — but notice White has completely neglected his queenside development.
Even though we're not fully developed either, we're ready to start attacking — so h5, aiming to pry open the h-file.
He answers with h4, but that only softens his kingside further.
Now we castle long, completing our development — and mark that pawn on g3; sacrifices are in the air.
He lunges with a4 — very creative, but not objectively sound.
The refutation is patience: don't panic, finish developing, and only attack once you're ready. The bishop swings to d6.
He plays the king to h2, walking right into it. We're eyeing a knight check on g4 — though he can capture the knight.
But that's the point: the knight checks on g4, and after he takes, we recapture with the pawn, ripping open the h-file — exactly what we wanted.
Now we threaten to grab his pawn, and he's forced to drop the king back toward g1.
That retreat was his only serious move; instead he lets us capture on h4 with check.
But don't rush the capture — first the bishop steps to e5, out of the sticky spot it was in.
Now we take on h4 with check, and head for a beautiful little finale.
This is what happens when you shamelessly violate opening principles. After the king to g1, there's a lovely way to finish.
The queen swings to h6...
...sacrificing the rook.
Despite being a whole rook down, Black's pressure on the kingside is absolutely overwhelming.
We're threatening mate; his only way to stave it off is the rook to e1.
But after g3, all of our pieces come pouring in.
If he tries e3, we can simply take the rook, winning the material back...
...or play the bishop to g4. The position is overflowing with mating ideas — completely crushing, which is why he resigned.
The plan with black is solid, positional chess, and nothing is more solid than a Queen's-Gambit structure — meet the pawn on d4 with d5 and build from there.

White fianchettoes with g3, steering the bishop to the long diagonal. It isn't a dangerous line and there's nothing special to answer it with — the recipe is simply to develop the pieces to good squares.
notes.teaches: Against a quiet fianchetto, just develop soundly rather than reaching for a refutation.

notes.explains: Nf6 continues the plain development plan, guarding d5 and readying the rest of the army. Think of it as a war: pieces left on their home squares win nothing, they have to be marched to active posts before any attack is possible.
Bh3 offers to trade the fianchettoed bishop off, and it illustrates the whole drawback of that setup — the bishop leaves home only to swap itself, and the holes it was covering stay behind.
Accepting is right: taking the bishop hands White weak light squares around his king that the traded bishop was supposed to guard.
notes.teaches: Trade off a fianchettoed bishop and the color-complex it defended turns permanently weak.

notes.explains: A very favorable swap. White has nothing in the centre and now an awkwardly placed knight on h3 — and note it well, that knight is undefended, so ideas that hit it become real resources later.
notes.teaches: Log every undefended enemy piece the moment it appears; it seeds forks and tempo-gaining moves.

notes.explains: There's no reason not to stake a claim of our own with c5 — almost a Queen's Gambit with colors reversed, prodding the d4-pawn to declare itself.
notes.plans: If White takes on c5, recapture and take over the centre exactly as White does in the Queen's Gambit Accepted.

notes.explains: Be3 is clumsy — it props up the centre pawn but ties the bishop to its defense, and White still isn't generating anything.
Taking on d4 would only help White centralize his bishop, so refuse the trade and develop the knight to c6, keeping the pressure and again inviting him to release the tension by taking on c5.
notes.teaches: Don't resolve a central tension when the recapture activates your opponent's worst piece.

notes.explains: c3 shores up the centre but is another slow move — White keeps developing incoherently while our pieces flow out naturally.
e5 is available to prise the centre open, but the solid choice is e6 — keep the centre closed on purpose and outplay him in the quieter structure.
notes.teaches: You don't have to open the position just because you can; choose the structure you understand best.

notes.explains: White takes on c5 — which was the real point of Be3, tying himself to that pawn.
Ng4 is the move: it hits the bishop and threatens to wreck White's structure, and its second point is that if the bishop steps away, we take on c5 and regain the pawn in fine shape.
notes.teaches: A knight leap that attacks a defender AND unpins the recapture does two jobs at once.

notes.explains: White answers with Bg5. In these structures with a pawn on c5, White also has the pawn break b4 as a resource to remember.
f6 kicks the bishop and gains the crucial tempo. Never play f6 — except exactly when it comes with a threat like this.
notes.teaches: f6 is fine when it hits a piece with tempo; it's bad when it only weakens your own king.

notes.explains: The point of moving with tempo is that when the bishop is forced to shift, we can take on c5 immediately. e5 is tempting here but held back on purpose.

The drawback of e5 is that it would weaken the light squares f5 and e6 and undermine the d5-pawn — so in the name of solidity we take on c5 instead, keeping the centre firm and the light squares covered.
notes.teaches: Weigh the squares a pawn push abandons before you play it, not after.

notes.explains: b4 attacks the bishop; keep it on the strong diagonal with Bb6 rather than let White chase it to a worse square.
Keep the knight near the centre with the reroute rather than the rim — linked knights are healthy, and from here the knight can later swing to c4.
notes.teaches: Knights belong toward the centre and love to be linked; the rim starves them of squares.

notes.explains: By shoving the b-pawn White only manufactures weaknesses — his own pawn is now backward, and he's developing without any coherent plan while his position starts to crack.
notes.teaches: Wing pawn lunges without development leave backward pawns and holes behind them.

notes.explains: Now think in terms of targets. White's knights sit miserably on the rim, and there are two clear plans — one on the queenside, one on the kingside.

The biggest queenside target is the pawn on c3, so rook to c8 takes the semi-open file. If he defends with a rook, that rook is nailed to the pawn — the weakness ties his pieces down, which matters more than the pawn itself, because he can't reallocate his forces while we can.
notes.teaches: A weak pawn's value is often the defenders it pins in place, not the material.

notes.explains: The kingside target is the h3-knight. A maneuver as old as the hills — bring the queen to h5 — gathers the pieces on that wing, attacks the knight, and builds real mating potential.
notes.plans: Swing the queen to h5 to pile onto the h3-knight and open a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Qh5 completes the plan and White has essentially one move, Kg2, to prop up the knight. Look at the bishop on f4 — its retreat is blocked by the queen, and the knight on e5 eyes the c4 jump to hit the queen before a central break, though for now the knight on a3 is contesting that very c4 square.
notes.teaches: Before committing to a jump like Nc4, check which enemy piece already guards the landing square.

notes.explains: We open with the king's pawn and Black declares the French.
We take the full center with the d-pawn — the invitation the French always accepts.
Black strikes at our center with d5. This is the defining tension of the French: the pawn on e4 has to decide its fate.
We choose the Advance — lock the chain and take the space. The pawn on e5 cramps Black's kingside and hands us a long-term spatial edge; the whole game will be about who breaks the chain first.
teaches: Advance = space + a fixed pawn chain

notes.explains: Instead of the near-universal c5, Black tries the rare b6, planning to reroute the light-squared bishop to a6 and trade off the French's famously bad bishop before it gets buried behind the chain.
Here's the clever touch: the quiet c3 first. It looks like nothing, but it lays a trap for the immediate a6 trade — and the reason is worth pausing on.
Black finds the correct reply, tucking the queen to d7 rather than grabbing the trade at once.
We develop the bishop to d3, its best diagonal in the Advance — aimed straight at Black's kingside where our space advantage will tell.
Black carries out the plan with the bishop to a6, offering to swap off the light-squared bishops.

The key decision — and the move most players get wrong. Not the natural Nf3 but the knight to e2, because it leaves the f-pawn unobstructed. That is the whole strategic key to the Advance: once we castle we want the thematic f4-f5 break to storm the kingside, and a knight on f3 would block it. From here the plan writes itself. Black concedes the light-squared bishops but loses tempi doing it; when he lunges with h5 he only hands us a weak square on g5 that we'd occupy with the dark-squared bishop — and we don't rush h4 ourselves, we wait for Black to push it and then freeze it with h3, since a pawn that comes to h4 becomes a target once our knight reroutes to g3 and later f3. On the queenside we play the advanced-French idea a3 and b4 to force the c-pawn to commit, prying open the c-file to double rooks, with a prophylactic h3 to deny Ng4. Then the classic finish: having won the queenside, we swing the queen to the kingside and play on both wings at once, where Black is most exposed.
teaches: Ne2 keeps the f-pawn free for f4
provoke h4 then fix it with h3
plans: double on the c-file, then attack the king

notes.explains: We take the white pieces and open with the king's pawn; Black answers symmetrically with e5, a reply we haven't met in a while. Into it we've been alternating two systems — the Vienna and the Four Knights Scotch — and today we steer for the Scotch.
The king's knight develops to f3, the first step into the Four Knights.
Black brings a knight to c6, and we mirror with the queen's knight to c3. Both sides simply develop the knights first; once Black adds the knight to f6, we're set to break in the centre.
Black plays the last knight to f6, and now the point of the system: d4, striking the e5-pawn with every piece already developed.

Instead of resolving the centre, Black steps the bishop to b4 — a rare sideline here that we've almost never faced, and a touch passive. The main road would have been the capture on d4, we retake with the knight, and only then the bishop to b4. This is playable, but it leaves White a small edge.

We must not grab with the pawn: after taking on e5 the knight springs to e4 and hits our c3-knight. Instead we push d5, seizing space and locking the centre. Black sometimes steers into this very structure with the black pieces, because it forces White to close up and gives the second player something to play for — though positionally Black is simply more cramped.
Black swings the knight from c6 to e7, heading for g6.

We develop the bishop to d3, defending e4 and drawing the sting from any jump to e4 — with that square covered, the knight can no longer hit our c3-knight with tempo. And we're untroubled by a capture on c3.
Black bolsters the centre with d6. We're not afraid of the trade on c3: yes, it damages our pawns, but in return we get the bishop pair and the chance to buttress the centre with c4.
We castle kingside. We could also slip in h3 to discourage the bishop coming to g4, but that pin is toothless here — Black's pieces are too passive to make anything of it.
Black captures on c3. Had he tried the bishop to g4 instead, we'd have answered h3 to chase it back, and could even have followed with g4.
We recapture with the b-pawn, accepting the doubled c-pawns in exchange for the bishop pair and a broad centre.

Black lands the knight on g6 — the correct setup in this closed centre. And that's the lesson of these positions: when the centre is locked, the worth of any single move drops. Move orders turn flexible; what matters is reaching the right setup and the right plan, not the exact sequence.
We begin with h3, denying the bishop the g4-square. In a closed position the emphasis shifts from the individual move to the overall aim.
Black castles. Another strong move for us is c4, reinforcing the d5-pawn.
We play c4, cementing d5 and hinting at a future c5 break.
Black plays b6, holding the queenside confidently. We simply keep developing.

The bishop to g5 would catch the eye, but Black just plays h6 and shoos it away — so we settle for the bishop to e3, completing our development. Now we can turn to the side where we hold the edge: the kingside. On the queenside we'll never get in c5; on the kingside we have more force gathered.
Black centralizes the queen to e7. Our development is done, and the extra pieces sit on the kingside — that's where the game will be decided, and we have several promising ideas there.
We tuck the king to h2 — a quiet move with a double purpose that will show itself: it is at once prophylactic and aggressive.
Black lunges the knight to h5, aiming for f4. Now the point of the king move surfaces: it is prophylaxis against exactly this, and our reply is g3.

We meet it with g3. This is only safe because the king stands on h2 — otherwise the h3-pawn could fall to a sacrifice; with the king there, that door is shut. And why did Black go to h5 at all? He is angling for f5, but it fails tactically: after f5 we take, the bishop retakes, we take again, the rook recaptures, and g4 at the very end forks the rook and the knight. There is a hidden cost to the knight sitting on h5 too — our queen x-rays it straight through our own f3-knight, so we can lift that knight, which we wanted to do anyway to prepare f4, and chase the h5-knight back to f6, gaining a tempo on our own plan.

Black retreats the knight to f6. With the knight back, we press on — but carefully. Play the knight to d2 now and the queen comes to d7, forcing g4; and g4 fatally weakens the f4-square, killing the very break we're preparing.
So we play the knight back to g1, preemptively: it guards h3 and clears the path to prepare f4. We're not ready to play f4 just yet.

Black plays the knight to d7 — pre-moved, so he never saw the queen-to-d7 resource. But committing to a plan doesn't mean closing your eyes: you must read how the opponent's move reshapes the position. And f4 still carries a serious flaw — after f4, the capture on f4, and g-takes-f4, Black strikes back with f5, and once the centre opens our e3-bishop falls under the queen's x-ray, so taking on f5 walks into tactics that leave our king badly exposed. Piling another defender on f4 with the knight to e2 isn't the cure; the cure is to shield the bishop first — but there's no time, because after the queen to d2 the knight swings to c5 and the break fails anyway, since capturing on f4 leaves our e4-pawn hanging.

So we change tack — shelve f4 for now and open a second front with h4. It doesn't come from nowhere: the g3-pawn supports the advance. Worried about the sacrifice on h4? The knight takes, g-takes, queen-takes-h4 with check, and we simply slide the king to g2 — and here the knight on g1 earns its keep, guarding h3, so once Black's d7-knight moves there's no check on h3. The upside of h4: the straightforward h5 next, shoving the g6-knight to the rim; the knight on g1 is freed and the h3-pawn stops being a worry — the queen can still reach h3, but no longer with a capture — and we may win the g5-square as an outpost for the bishop.

Black jumps the knight to c5. A healthy positional move for us either way — and we haven't wholly abandoned f4, though with the pawn heading to h5 it's far less likely: once h5 is in, an f4 break would only gut our own king, so we'd allow it only under perfect circumstances. Black is playing this very well.
We push h5. This can hardly hurt — and it looks like the knight is more or less forced to h8, buried on the edge.

Instead Black finds the knight to f4 — I'll admit I missed it. Does it work? The lines run deep: it holds tactically to a draw by perpetual, but it doesn't win. And crucially we don't have to take it — we can capture on c5 first, which may be the real solution.
We take on c5 first with the bishop. Now the queen to h4 is not mate, because the g3-pawn covers that square.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn on c5. There was a very specific reason to take on c5 first.
Now g-takes-f4 works — though it's razor-thin, move-for-move calculation where you get it exactly right or lose ground.
Black checks with the queen on h4.

We step the king to g2. The looming idea is the queen to f3 — a genuinely frightening move; there may be a hidden win for Black I can't see, but move-for-move I believe we hold. Behind these choices sit the details: if the bishop comes to g4 now, we take on e5, and the bishop to h3 only looks like it traps the queen — our knight swings in, takes the bishop and defends the queen at once; and if Black tries a perpetual with the queen to g5 and back to h4, that same knight blocks on h3.
A Trompowsky — the bishop to g5 — met at once by the knight to e4, hitting the bishop.
He avoids the little trick, and the position is still basically equal.
The bishop to d3 is a nice move. The idea I'm weighing is to take on f3 and follow with e5.
Taking on f3 — very risky, but the only way to play for a win here is to take on real risk.
He recaptures, and now e5, striking at the centre — the risk we have to accept to win.
He takes on e5 — that surprised me. Now the bishop to b5 and rook to c6 are strong for him, and I have to recapture with the knight. I underestimated that.
I think I can get away with c6.
He's eyeing a tactic here — the bishop into h7 — but it's not the end of the game.
I'd forgotten this trick — the bishop takes on h7 with check, the classic sacrifice — though it's still complicated.
The queens come off, which isn't what I want to see.
I still had f5 available.
We have White and open the pawn to e4, met by e5.
The knight to f3.
Black develops the knight to c6. We could play many things here — the Scotch, the Italian.
Let's play the Scotch — in fact the Scotch Gambit, with the pawn to d4.
Black captures on d4. The Scotch Gambit is a cross between a Scotch and an Italian.
The bishop to c4 — an opening that slips through the cracks. A great alternative if you play the Evans Gambit: super dangerous at this level, played by grandmasters, a completely legitimate weapon.
Black plays the pawn to d6. There are a bunch of traps here that bring quick wins, and d6 leads to a slightly worse but solid position — a good way to sidestep the traps.

Black recaptures with the knight on d4, giving back the pawn to open the diagonal for the bishop. We have a very nice position — better central control, a bishop on c4 like a good Scotch, and the sacrificed pawn recovered.
Black develops the knight to f6. Now, should we fear a capture on d4 that puts our queen in the centre?
The knight to c3 — and no, no fear: Black has no second knight to bring to c6, so the queen would sit perfectly well placed on d4.
Black plays the bishop to e7 — a Philidor-like, very solid setup, the d6-pawn restraining our e4. Don't lunge at Black's throat here.
We castle — nurture the advantage, bring the pieces out, and enjoy the space and well-placed pieces.

Black castles — and it's trickier than it looks. The pawn to f4 is premature with the queen undeveloped. The bishop to e3 or g5 look natural, but both allow tactics: the bishop to e3 runs into the knight to g4, and the center-fork trick — the knight takes e4, then the pawn to d5 recovers the piece with mass trades we don't want.
So the bishop to b3 — it permanently takes the center-fork trick away, tucking the bishop onto a defended square, out of the pawn's reach.
We take the white pieces and steer for the Glek System.
Black's knight comes to f6 and we answer with the knight to c3, heading into the Four Knights.
We fianchetto with g3 — the move that defines the Glek.
Black chooses the bishop to e7.
Black plays d6 — a modest, passive setup: nothing outright wrong with it, but it lets us do whatever we like.
We castle.

Black develops the bishop to e6, which tempts d4 — but in the Glek be careful with that push. Not because Black might trade everything on d4 (that suits us fine), but because of ...Bg4: even at the cost of a tempo it hangs the d4-pawn and can force us to close with d5, betraying the whole spirit of the system. Ducking it by taking on e5 is a dull move that invites mass exchanges.
So instead of an immediate d4 we play h3, keeping our options open and preparing d4 under better circumstances (the quiet d3 is also available).
Black replies h6 — and now d4 will work.
We push d4. It works like a charm: it threatens a fork and all but forces Black to release the tension.
Black captures on d4 and we recapture with the knight.
The knights come off on d4 and our queen recaptures, landing us a very pleasant position — but we mustn't forget the h3-pawn.
Black centralizes the queen to d7.
We step the king to h2 to defend h3. Careful here: many players castle queenside instead and simply hang the a7-pawn — a mistake I've seen again and again.

Black lunges h5, trying for a kingside attack — but knowing the system, you see it isn't one: Black threatens nothing. To ...h4 we simply push g4, and a sac like ...Bxg4 is futile — the position is too passive, there aren't enough attackers, and our king is far too safe.
Notice the bishop on e6 has run out of squares — so f4 comes naturally, grabbing space and setting a very nasty threat.
Black plays c5. And yes, White's plan is genuinely hard to meet: as long as we deny the bishop its escape, f5 is a monstrous threat.
That tells us where the queen belongs — d3, guarding the c4-square and discouraging ...b5 (which wasn't dangerous anyway, since e5 would answer it).
Black plays g6 — but it doesn't stop f5.
We play f5. The game is effectively over — after the coming exchanges the e6-bishop is trapped.
Black takes with the g-pawn on f5.
We recapture with the e-pawn on f5 — the bishop is trapped and our position fully open.
Black tries c4, but it changes nothing. We could lift the queen to f3, but simpler is to capture on e6.
We take on e6, hitting the queen on d7.
Black recaptures on e6. Now reposition the queen toward f3 — but note, with the king on h2 under an x-ray, keep an eye on a sudden ...Ng4 check; in the right setting it can be very nasty.
Here the check would be harmless — our king just steps to g1 — but there's no reason to invite it. Instead the queen goes to f5, more to the point, and now the queen trade can't be avoided.
Black castles long. There's no reason for us to capture on e6 ourselves — it would only repair Black's pawns and help build a central chain.
So instead we play the bishop to g5, hitting the knight — this should win further material, since after a queen trade on f5 and the rook recapture the pin tells.
Black tries the knight to g4 with check, but we simply take it — the g1-square is free.
We capture on g4.
Black checks on g4 and we tuck the king to g1.
Black recaptures the bishop on g5.
We don't need the queen — we just take the bishop back on g5, staying up two minor pieces. Always watch the a7–g1 diagonal, but with no checks there our king is perfectly safe.
Black tucks the king to b8. We're up two pieces — time to bring a rook to the centre.
The rook swings to e1, heading for the seventh rank — and the capture on f7 is coming. It's over.
Black plays the queen to d7.
We plant the rook on e7.
Black's queen retreats to c8.
Simpler than taking on b7 is to double on f7.
Black pushes d5.
We take on b7 with check, winning the queen and mopping up everything loose.
The queens come off, we recapture with check, and the bishop check on d5 opens the hunt for the king.
A check on f6 herds the king forward.
The king walks to c5. Chasing the very fastest mate here is fiddly.
So don't agonize over the quickest path — just keep checking and the mate arrives. We check on c6.
The king steps to d4 and the knight checks from b5 — Black walks right into it.

The king goes to e5 and the queen delivers mate on e6. The takeaway on the Glek: you don't have to prevent ...Bg4 in general — if Black plays it, h3 and then g4 just shove the bishop to a passive square. It's ONLY when you intend d4 that stopping ...Bg4 matters, because d4 ...Bg4 forces the closed, King's-Indian-like structure you don't want from a Glek. If you'd rather not bother with h3 or d4 at all, the quiet d3 setup is fine — it just doesn't squeeze the most from the position. Against this passive setup White simply does everything he wants: fianchetto, seize the centre, and Black stays paralysed until he can free himself with ...d5.
The beauty of the King's Indian is one setup against everything — an English can transpose to a Queen's-Pawn game, but with this system you don't have to care.
notes.teaches: A universal setup buys you move-order immunity; you learn one plan instead of ten.

notes.explains: Unlike the Queen's Gambit Declined or the Slav, you never rewire your own move order depending on whether White chooses c4, d4, or Nf3 — the same moves work against all of it.
Complete the fianchetto with Bg7; the bishop takes up its long-diagonal post and the kingside is ready to castle.
We answer the big centre with d6. White's most testing plan from here is the fianchetto with g3 and Ng2 — the Botvinnik setup.

Be2 doesn't fit White's structure. With the pawn on d4 this would be a mainline King's Indian; the pawn on d3 instead is a real positional downgrade, because it hands us the d4 square as a stronghold. So don't reflexively play e5 here — think flexibly about what the structure actually wants.
notes.teaches: A pawn on d3 instead of d4 gifts the opponent d4 as an outpost; don't play the automatic move, play the structure.

notes.explains: Against this semi-Botvinnik setup, c5 fits better than e5 — it steers into a Dragon-Sicilian formation and stakes a direct claim to d4.
notes.plans: Follow with Nc6 to pile onto d4 and clamp the square.

notes.explains: White drifts with Bd2; there's really no fight for d4 to speak of — we simply occupy and control it. A bloodless war.
Nc6 completes the clamp. The battle for the key central square is over before it started.
White shuffles fairly randomly, which doesn't disturb our development at all — we just keep bringing pieces out.

h4 flips White from quiet play to hunting the king, but positionally he isn't equipped to do real kingside damage. Still, there's no reason to let him play h5 and rip open the h-file — and the instructive point is that the popular answer here is wrong.
notes.teaches: Don't allow the opponent a free rook-file opening just because the attack looks toothless.

notes.explains: h5 is the accurate reply, not h6 — it clamps the g4 square and denies White the break, whereas h6 carries drawbacks we'd rather avoid.
notes.teaches: Meeting a wing pawn thrust by fixing it with your own pawn can be stronger than inviting the exchange.

notes.explains: With the g4 square locked down, it's very hard for White to prise our kingside open at all.
Nd4 plants the knight on the dream square and starts angling to win the bishop pair.
White simply hands over the bishop pair. A hidden bonus of Nd4 was that it took the g4 break away — if White plays g4 anyway, we take the bishop and recapture on g4 with our structure fully intact.
notes.teaches: A well-placed knight can quietly veto a pawn break before it's played.

notes.explains: A good exercise: pause and list the factors giving Black the edge, then try to guess the engine's number. The honest assessment here is around minus one and a half, maybe closer to minus two.
We're close to positionally winning, so we keep the dark-squared bishop rather than trade it, retreat it to safety, and plan to chase the knight from the centre at our leisure with e6.
notes.plans: Nudge the centralized knight back with e6 once we're ready.

notes.explains: After Nf3, think flexibly — don't just grab on e2 because that was the earlier plan; the position has changed and asks a new question.
notes.teaches: A plan formed three moves ago isn't binding; re-evaluate every time the board shifts.

notes.explains: We meet the queen-pawn setup with the knight to f6; White stakes out c4 and d4, and we're heading into a King's Indian.
We fianchetto with g6, and White develops the knight to f3.
The bishop lands on g7, and White goes for the fianchetto too with g3 — one of the most respected tries against the King's Indian.
We reply with the classical d6.
White completes the fianchetto, the bishop settling on g2.
We castle, and White castles.
We pick the classical setup — the queen's knight to d7. Easy to learn, easy to understand, and what I play in my serious blitz.
White develops the bishop to g5, eyeing our knight — though the e7-pawn means it's no real pin.
The knight to d7 is at least as common as the knight to c6 here — c6 invites d5 with tempo, and d7 sidesteps that.
And the whole idea of the d7-knight is to prepare the e5 break.
So the bishop to g5 shows up — common at the lower levels, but not really threatening, since it isn't hitting anything it can win on f6.
We ask the bishop the polite question with h6.
White hands over the bishop pair, capturing on f6.
We recapture on f6 with the knight — flexibility. With White's dark-squared bishop gone, White brings the other knight to c3.
We carve open the long diagonal with c5.
White clamps the centre with d5 — now it's a Benoni structure, and that long diagonal is beautiful.
The bishop comes to f5, preparing the knight to e4 — a very standard maneuver.
White plays the knight to d2 to stop e4. It's a good move, but if White ever pushes e4, that d2-knight is left without a clear home.
We play a6, planning to drop the bishop calmly back to d7.
White grabs the centre with e4, and the bishop retreats to d7, ready for the classic Benoni break, b5.
White reroutes with the knight to f3, preparing to counter-strike with e5.
We stop it with the knight to g4, heading for the e5 outpost.
White pokes with h3, and the knight lands on e5, going for a trade.
White takes on e5, and we recapture with the bishop, capturing on e5 — this bishop is our main asset.
White lunges g4, doing nothing at all against our real plan of b5.
We push b5. Some would grab dark squares with g5 here, but that would be a serious mistake.
White takes on b5, and we recapture with the a-pawn, capturing on b5.
White brings the queen to d2, hitting the h6-pawn.
Rather than g5, we keep piling on with b4.
White retreats the knight to e2.
The bishop swings to b5 — indirectly defending h6, since grabbing that pawn would now achieve nothing.
White lifts the rook to e1, reinforcing the threat.
We tuck the bishop back to g7, which also stops f4 coming with tempo.
White plants the knight on f4. Back to the queenside: c4 is tempting, but it would drop the b4-pawn.
So we prepare it and beef up the queenside with the queen to a5.
White throws in h4.
Now we step on the gas with c4.
White pushes h5.
We could close the kingside with g5, but there's no need yet — instead we play c3.
White captures on c3.
The greedy move is to grab material, but we recapture on c3 with the b-pawn — very much in the King's Indian spirit.
White drops the queen to c2.
Now we shut the kingside with g5 so our king never gets pried open.
White reroutes the knight to d3. Time for the final stage on the queenside.
There's the quiet bishop to a4, but the Soviet way is the queen to a4, offering the trade.
White takes, and we recapture with the rook, capturing on a4 — the queen trade itself is our weapon, and White's position collapses.
White scrambles the knight back to c1.
The passed pawn marches to c2.
White tries the knight to b3, but the rook on a1 is now trapped.
We collect the exchange, capturing on a1 with the bishop.
White recaptures on a1 with the rook.
We bring the other rook in — to a8, not c8 — forcing White's knight back to c1.
White's rook retreats to c1, and we snatch the pawn, capturing on a2 with the rook — the rook to b4 and b1 was cleanest, but this wins too.
White's king steps to h2.
We swing the back rook down to a3, doubling on the third rank.
White tries the knight to d4, and the bishop comes to d3, guarding the c2-pawn.
White lurches the knight to b5 — a serious inaccuracy.
We simply capture on b5 with the bishop; White has blundered the knight.
White plays f3.
The bishop returns to d3.
White's king wanders to g3, and we plant a rook on a1.
White grabs the c-pawn, and we recapture with the bishop, capturing on c2 — up two full rooks now.
White's king shuffles to f2.
We double the rooks again, the back one to a2.
White's king goes back to g3, and the bishop snaps the pawn, capturing on e4.
White tries the bishop to h3.
We finish it — the rook captures on f3, checkmate. A classic, smooth King's Indian win.
The pawn to e4, c5 — a Sicilian.
The knight to f3 — a Najdorf?
d6. We've mostly been playing the Accelerated Dragon, but lately we've experimented with the Najdorf.
d4 — the Open Sicilian.
We take on d4.
The knight takes d4, the knight to f6. After the knight to c3 we have several moves: g6 is the traditional Dragon —
— the knight to c6 is the Rauzer or Classical Sicilian, there's e6, and there's e5 —
— e5 isn't great, but the Najdorf holds a special place in Sicilian players' hearts: a6. The most immediate idea is to cover the b5-square, stopping the knight from going to b5.
The bishop to e2 — one of the most popular responses to the Najdorf, considered among White's quietest options; quiet in the proper context, not boring.
e6 leads to the Scheveningen structure, but I've always been an e5 player. If you don't play the Najdorf and this move doesn't seem weird to you, then you're doing something wrong.

Why does the knight to b3 look like a big positional mistake, when it's the theoretical move? Because e5 weakens d6 and correspondingly the d5-square. This is precisely why I don't recommend the Najdorf to beginners — you have to earn the right to violate these basic rules by knowing them first; practice violating them too early and you build a rotten foundation. There isn't one single reason Black gets away with e5 — it's a very complex network of reasons.

First, we develop and get our king out of the centre — the bishop to e6 is possible, but the main move is the bishop to e7, preparing to castle as early as possible, and the c8-bishop might later fianchetto to b7. The first of the reasons d5 isn't the end of the world: Black has a lot of pieces to contest d5 —

— you can put the bishop to e6, and the knight on f6 is supported by its brother on d7, so two pieces directly and one indirectly control d5, making it incredibly hard for White to plant and hold a knight there in practice, with Black's pieces clustered on the kingside.

That's reason one why the weakness of d5 isn't as devastating as it looks. Reason two: Black has counterplay on both sides of the board, one source being the b-pawn advance to b4 — though games have been lost by letting a knight sit on d5 all game; I once mishandled it and lost. Now we deploy the bishop to e6, adding another protector to d5; the queen to d3 is a legitimate try. Against the bishop to g5, the knight to d7 is correct — it's very hard to dislodge the f6-knight, and if he takes we retake — and all four minors are clustered, ready for queenside operations. He drops the knight, a blunder, and I take it, up a piece; part of the benefit of playing what most people don't is that unfamiliar positions cause blunders. We keep making Najdorf moves: the rook to c8, a typical Sicilian move pressuring the knight, sometimes with an exchange sac on c3; h6 to tickle the bishop and make luft. The bishop drops to d2, x-raying the queen, so we move the queen — since our rook is on the c-file, the queen to c7, queen and rook on the c-file, very common in the Najdorf. What does doubling do when the knight isn't hanging? Pressure — the knight can't move because pieces fall behind it. Then b5, expanding on the queenside and making an outpost on c4 for a knight, bishop or queen, and the queen gets access to b7 to pressure e4. The ultimate goal is d5, prepared flexibly: not the knight to b6, which with b3 played has no c4 prospects, but the queen to b7 — flexible, a standalone good move pressuring e4 and threatening the knight to c5. Then the knight to c5, the knight takes c4 winning the pawn, and d5 in the best version. On the recapture on e4, we trade queens to simplify while up a piece, since he can't move the queen without dropping the bishop; the knight takes d4 pins us, but White can't exploit it because d5 supports the knight next move — the queen takes e4 is great. He gives up the bishop, two pieces down, and resigns. The knight to a5 was the decisive blunder.
The pawn to e4, e5 — traditional, old-school, and we play very solid.
The knight to f3, the knight to c6.
The Italian. At this rating there's the knight to f6 and the bishop to c5, the two main moves.
The Fried Liver is a little questionable for a beginner without the theory, so my recommendation is to stick with the bishop to c5 — less tricky, easier to learn.
c3 is the main move.
We go the knight to f6, and White has d4 or d3 — d3 is what the big guns play.
d4 is the old main line, the traditional move —
— leading to an extremely theoretical line.
The pawns come off on d4. Now, very importantly, we don't drop our bishop back —
— that would let White dominate the centre; we give the important check on b4, a tempo to either capture the pawn or strike back with d5.

The bishop to d2. The main continuation isn't the knight takes c4 — that's what we'll play — the main move is the bishop takes d2 with check, the knight recaptures, and d5 striking the centre; that's my game against Sevian from the US Championship, a colorless position. A narrower, more interesting move is the knight takes e4 —
— it looks very scary to grab the pawn, but if you know the theory you get away with it; not well known even among people who play the Italian.
The knight to c3 is already a very bad reaction — it lets us off scot-free and gives us a favorable trade. What should we take?

Take the bishop, clearly. He pre-moves the knight takes d2, and now another decision: castle to complete development, or take on d4 for another pawn. Much of it is intuitive — quickly look for forks; I don't see anything nasty after the knight takes d4, since White is so passive.
He didn't defend it —
The knight takes d4.

For instance, if there were a queen here, the knight to e4 would be very nasty, hitting the queen and pressuring the knight. Now we choose our bishop move carefully — a lot of people would play the bishop to c5, but why is that, though totally fine, a little inaccurate?
Because of the knight to e4, winning a tempo; the bishop to b6 lets the other knight get to d5 with a lot of activity. Let's take c3 —
— simplify, up two pawns. Where does the knight go? Doesn't really matter — the knight to c6, e6, or even the counter-attack d5.

Let's play the simplest, the knight to c6 — no need to spend a lot of time; people overly obsess over basic decisions, spend five minutes, and get into time pressure. Always know which decisions are likely to matter.
This is clearly in the less-important category.
He's given us the chance to go d5, so we'll play d5 and then get the bishop out with e6, maybe the queen to f6 hitting the pawn on c3.
I like developing the bishop to e6. Not every piece needs to be climbing Mount Everest —
— the bishop defends d5 and f7, doing a perfectly fine job on e6. The bishop to f5 would appeal to more people —
The knight to f3. Now I'd get this queen off its initial square with the queen to f6 —
— activating it, and bringing the rooks to the centre next is a good idea.
The rook to b1 — the queen takes c3 forces us to calculate; the queen takes it, the rook takes b7 —

— I honestly don't see the need to calculate it. How to defend the pawn? b6 — generally you play it against the rook to b1 to blunt the rook, biting on granite. The drawback: it weakens the light squares and, more specifically, the knight becomes undefended. If your king were on e8, it'd be dangerous, but here the knight has a good spot on a5 to jump to, and later c4.
We answer the king's pawn with the Sicilian.
White pins the queen's knight with the bishop to b5 — the Rossolimo, effectively a Ruy Lopez cast against the Sicilian.
teaches: Rossolimo = Ruy ideas vs the Sicilian

notes.explains: As an Accelerated Dragon player we stay consistent and fianchetto with g6 anyway — the bishop belongs on the long diagonal whether or not White ever takes on c6.
White swaps on c6, and the recapture is a real decision.

We take with the d-pawn, not the b-pawn. Recapturing toward the center looks natural, but taking with the d-pawn opens the d-file for our rooks and frees the light-squared bishop — activity over a tidy pawn mass.
teaches: dxc6: open the d-file, free the bishop

notes.explains: Now the pawn to e5 clamps the center and grabs kingside space, freezing White's structure before he can expand.
The knight belongs on e7 for two reasons: it keeps the e5-pawn from hanging, and it leaves the a-pawn free so we can strike with a5 later. It blocks the bishop only for a moment.
teaches: Ne7 guards e5 and prepares a5

notes.explains: White plays c3, but he isn't actually threatening d4 yet — a bit of simple counting shows the center holds, and even if he pushed d4 it would only open our long-diagonal bishop.
teaches: count before you fear a break

notes.explains: The pawn on d3 is weak, and that's our target. There are two ways to pressure a fixed weakness: the brute-force pawn lever with c4 or the bishop swinging to a6, and doubling rooks on the d-file. We aim to do both.
teaches: two ways to hit a backward pawn

notes.explains: The bishop reaches a6, bearing down the diagonal at the weak pawn — the first half of the plan.
f6 here is fine, despite the old rule against it — White simply has no pieces to exploit the weakened square, so it's a safe, temporary loosening.
teaches: a rule is not a law: f6 when it can't be punished

notes.explains: The queen to d7 links up with a rook to d8 — piling every piece we can onto the d3 weakness. Win that pawn and his position caves.
We kick the knight off its active post with b5.
The knight slinks back to a3, buried and passive; it did block our light-squared bishop, but a knight on the rim is a fair trade for that.
teaches: a rim knight is a poor blockader

notes.explains: Now b4 is finally right. A move earlier it would have run into a nasty queen check on b3; with that resource gone we push it.
teaches: timing a pawn break around a check

notes.explains: White reroutes to c2, which removes the b3-check idea for good — so b4 is safe and pairs perfectly with a rook to d8.
teaches: the enemy piece that leaves cues your break

notes.explains: Rook to d8 — but the f-rook, not the a-rook. The a8-rook stays home to babysit the a7-pawn, which can hang later.
teaches: choose which rook by what it must still guard

notes.explains: With the push to d4 the whole battle now revolves around that pawn.
We double on the d-file, rook to d7, stacking the pressure exactly where White is weakest.
The pawn to c4 walls the knight in — his knight on a3 is now buried alive with no way out, effectively leaving us a piece up in the fight for the d-file.
teaches: bury the rim knight with c4

notes.explains: We answer his regrouping in kind, rerouting our own knight to d6 — a superb square eyeing c4 and e4 and reinforcing the pressure.
a6 cements the bishop on a light square defended by a pawn, so it can never be harassed off the diagonal.
teaches: support your bishop with a pawn

notes.explains: The knight steps to f7, unmasking the rook so it bears straight down the file.
When White releases the tension we recapture with the f-pawn, not the knight — taking with the knight would have surrendered the d4-square, and control of d4 is the whole point of the position.
teaches: recapture to keep your key square

notes.explains: The rook drops onto d3 — a dream outpost deep in White's camp, jamming his pieces and paralyzing the position.
We swing the bishop around toward h6 to bring the last piece into the attack.
h5 leans on the knight, and c5 slams the door on White's dark-squared bishop, leaving it stranded on b6 with no scope — squeezing from both wings at once.
teaches: lock out a bishop to leave it dead

notes.explains: Now the exchange sacrifice: give up the rook, because in return we get a monster.
teaches: sac the exchange for a runner

notes.explains: The rook comes off for a beast of a passed pawn on d3, buried in White's position and worth far more than the material given.
teaches: a protected passer can outweigh a rook

notes.explains: We take Black and answer the king's pawn with e5 — back to our roots.
We develop the knight to c6.
White plays d4 — the Scotch.
We capture on d4.
White recaptures with the knight — the pure Scotch.
We choose the bishop to c5 — still theoretical, but more manageable than the chaos of the ...Nf6 lines.
White develops the bishop to e3.
The main move: the queen to f6, piling pressure on the d4-knight.
We take White. Today is a defensive lesson — we're going to sacrifice a knight on purpose and show how to fight on when down material.
We develop the knight to c3, a Three Knights setup.
Black develops the bishop to c5. Our plan: sacrifice the knight — but not just yet.
We develop the bishop to c4.
Black plays d6.
Here's the sacrifice — the knight takes on e5, giving up the piece for at least a pawn.
Black recaptures, dxe5. Objectively we're a piece down and lost — but development isn't finished, so the plan is to complete it and make Black work for the win.
We play d3, part of finishing development — castle next, then start thinking in earnest.
Black plays the queen to f6, going for mate — and honestly that's encouraging: this walks into our hands.
We castle, defending f2. The trouble with the queen on f6 is that it invites a later knight to d5.

Black guards the square with the knight to e7. Now, the best defensive moves both improve your position and set a trap. The bishop to e3 is logical — if Black trades, we retake with the f-pawn and hit f7 from two sources. But there's something sharper: after the bishop to b3, Black plays ...Bb6 and comes to regret it.
We want f4 to prise open the f-file for chances — so first the king steps to h1, the classic preparation.
Black castles, and we're ready for f4.
We push f4, opening the file and stirring real intrigue on the kingside — the first progress in our counterplay.
Black captures on f4.
We must recapture with the bishop. Taking with the rook tempts you — it hits the queen — but attacking the queen isn't automatically good: the rook on f4 would be badly placed.
Black plays the queen to g6. Remember we're only a piece down — win three pawns for it and material is level.
So we take on c7 with the bishop, snapping off a pawn — pawns like that don't lie by the roadside.
Black pins with the bishop to g4. We must move the queen — to d2, or the interesting e1 to drag it toward the kingside.
The queen goes to d2. I avoid e1 because it runs into the knight rerouting to d4, and we want c2 guarded; from d2 the queen can also swing to f4 later.
Black jumps the knight to d4 — but it no longer carries a threat and hands us a free tempo.
We play the cryptic bishop to e5, pressing the knight on d4 — hoping Black obliges with the knight from e7 to c6.
Black finds the queen to h5 instead — a different, even stronger way of hitting our e5-bishop.
We drop the bishop back to g3 — where it was headed anyway, off the awkward c7-square and out of tactical trouble.
Black plays the knight to g6. My trick failed — yet it half-worked, because moving that knight has the same effect I was after.
Here's why I wanted that knight off e7: it guarded d5. Now we plant the knight on d5 and start building central pressure.
We were eyeing c3 next — but Black finds the knight to e2, a really nasty shot I missed. The bishop to f2 would defend, but ...Bd6 keeps the pressure; our emergency resource is the queen to e1.
So the queen to e1, forced — Black is playing superbly; that knight leap completely escaped me.
The knight takes on g3 with check — it was a mating threat — and we recapture with the queen. The trade actually helps us: Black has thinned his own attack, and now h3 is coming.
Black brings a rook to d8, setting a threat. We have two pawns for the piece — consolidate and we hold real chances.
The threat was ...Bd6, skewering the queen with mate to follow — so h3 must come at once, blunting it; if Black tries ...Bd6 anyway, we simply take the bishop on g4.
Black retreats the bishop to e6. Our sole trump is the central pawn mass Black doesn't have, so we must expand there.
We play c3, preparing to roll the centre with d4 and later e4–e5.
Black plays the bishop to d6. We're in deep trouble — ...Qe5 next is a serious problem.
We try the queen to f2 — a long shot, hoping to bait a sacrifice on h3.
Black takes the bait, sacrificing on h3.
We recapture, gxh3 — and I can't quite see where Black's mate is.
Black checks on h3, our king goes to g1 — and ...Nh4 is a bolt from the blue, threatening ...Nf3 with check and a mating net.

But there may be a defence. The knight lands on h4 threatening ...Nf3, which works only by pulling our queen off f2 — so we sidestep the queen. And here c3 pays off: a bishop to c5 now would allow d4, so if ...Nf3 comes we take it with the rook and keep control of h2. Black has a perpetual for a draw if he wants it — I'd gladly take that; what would truly worry me is a slow strengthening move like ...Re8.
e4, the knight to f6, and White throws the queen out to h5 — a famous early sortie. We answer with c5, striking at the centre and offering the pawn.
The queen takes c5. Obviously
the knight grabs on e4 — we've traded our c-pawn for his e-pawn, but the real point is that White has developed nothing but his queen.
Where White puts the queen matters — if it dropped back to e3 we'd hit it with d5. He keeps it on h5, and the knight to c6 and later b5 are our ideas.
We develop with the knight to c6. You might ask, what if White chases it with d3? So be it — the knight just goes back; we've lost nothing by developing.
The bishop to c4, obviously threatening mate on f7, so we have to be careful — don't play d6, which doesn't defend the f7-pawn.
There are two good moves here; the one more consistent with our strategy is e6, which blunts the bishop.
If I were White I'd continue with the knight to c3 or c3. There's a clear drawback to e6 —
— but it's true in many positions that it's fine to tuck a piece back to d7 temporarily; it won't change the assessment. We play d5, striking at the bishop and grabbing the centre.
The bishop to b5, and we develop the bishop to c5. We break the pin naturally, so we don't really need the bishop to d7 or a6 — we can just keep developing.
Is the queen to b6 ever an idea? Generally yes, it's a good move in many positions, especially here — but
castling is more flexible right now: we keep our options open and unpin the knight.
And remember the queen to b6 would threaten the bishop, but White's f2-pawn is well defended, so that's not the whole story.
The knight to d4 — the queen drops back, we take his bishop, but then he takes our knight; what do we actually gain? Let me think it through.
The knight to d4 might even be the more accurate try — I'm not certain; the queen to a5 was a perfectly legitimate alternative that worked much the same. He plays the knight to a3.

The knight takes f3 with check. These opponents do find good moves — the bishop to c4, the queen back to f3, the bishop to b5, and the knight to h3 was the only move defending the pawn — but then it falls apart anyway.
We open with e4, and Black springs the Alekhine, the knight to f6.
We go for maximum space, chasing the knight with e5.
The knight jumps in to d5.
We build the big centre with d4 — heading for the Four Pawns Attack.
Black strikes at our centre with d6.
We keep grabbing space with c4, kicking the knight again.
The knight retreats to b6. The classical main line is to take on d6, but there's a far more ambitious road.
The Four Pawns Attack — f4, propping up e5. It's central domination, and if White doesn't know it, White can get crushed in five moves.
Black strikes first, capturing on e5.
We recapture on e5 with the f-pawn — a giant centre, but we've fallen behind in development.
Black develops the knight to c6. The automatic knight-to-f3 here is a serious inaccuracy because of the bishop to g4.
Rather than c5, which would gift the d5 outpost, we defend the centre with the bishop to e3.
Black develops the bishop to f5.
We develop the knight to c3, so a later knight-to-b4 can be met with the rook to c1.
Black lines the queen up on d7.
Now that we're developed, the knight to f3 is safe — the bishop-g4 pin no longer bites.
Black pins the f3-knight with the bishop to g4 anyway.
Black castles queenside instead of grabbing the pawn.
The engine's idea — c5. With Black castled queenside, giving up d5 is worth it: c5 clamps down and jump-starts our own attack.
Black posts the knight on d5.
We take on d5.
Black recaptures with the queen, capturing on d5.
Artemis-style — the king to f2, guarding the bishop, connecting the rooks, and preparing the queen to a4.
Black solidifies with e6.
The queen to a4 is tempting, but first we tickle with h3 — so if the bishop ever comes to h5, we have g4 in our pocket.
The bishop drops instead to f5, a little unexpected.
Out comes the queen to a4, and Black answers with the queen to e4, eyeing our c5-pawn.
We sidestep the queen to a3, Black slots the queen into c2, and we push b4, insisting on the attack.
Black tucks the bishop to e7, and we roll on with b5.
The knight is forced back to b8 — so we can simply grab the a7-pawn.
We snatch the pawn, capturing on a7 with the queen.
Black tries the bishop to d3 — less of a problem than it looks.
We defend by bringing the h-rook over to e1.
Black grabs back, capturing on b5 with the bishop. It's tremendously complex — you just roll with the chaos.
Better than trading queens: the a-rook swings to b1.
Black finds a brilliant resource — the queen to a4, defending the bishop and offering the trade.
We have to take, and Black recaptures with the bishop, capturing on a4 — into an endgame.
We reroute — the knight to d2, aiming for c4 and a5.
Black plays f6. That b7-pawn is a long-term weakness with the file open.
The knight to c4 — if Black takes on e5 we take back with the knight, so we both eye a5 and guard e5.
The bishop returns to c6. Now knight-to-a5 no longer works — it would drop the e5-pawn.
We don't want the centre to collapse, so we target the bishop and offer a trade with the bishop to f3.
Black takes, capturing on e5 — but now b7 loses its last defender.
We take back with the knight, capturing on e5.
Black lifts the h-rook to f8 — but that leaves the e6-pawn weak.
We step the king to g3, breaking the pin.
Black takes on f3, and we recapture with the knight, capturing on f3 — no isolated pawns.
The knight comes out to c6 — and the rook stops covering e6.
We drop the bishop back to f2, building pressure on e6 and planning to double rooks on the e-file.
Black defends with the rook to f6, and we centralise our rook to e4. About equal — this will be a grind.
Black slides the rook to d5, and we double up with the rook to e1.
Black's king walks to d7, and our king tucks back to h2, freeing the bishop's diagonal.
Black plays h6, and we reposition the bishop to g3 — d4 still has its two defenders.
Black expands with g5, and we plant the bishop on e5, offering a trade to shift that f6-rook.
Black goes for it, capturing on e5 with the knight.
We recapture with the knight, capturing on e5 with check — and the king must leave d7, weakening e6.
The king steps to d8.
The knight swings back to g4, hitting the rook and preparing to capture on e6.
Black defends with the rook to g6. Grabbing e6 now gets murky, so we play patiently.
We take the open f-file with the rook to f1, continuing to probe.
Black pushes h5. Our plan is to make inroads with a rook to f7.
We don't want the rook reaching f6, so we drop the knight back to e3 with tempo.
Black covers with the rook to d7 — now the rook to f7 runs into a bishop-d6 check, so we reroute.
The rook goes to b1, back to the old plan of hitting b7.
The king shuffles to c8.
We reroute the knight to c4, and Black lunges g4.
The knight lands on e5 — pressure, pressure, pressure.
And finally a blunder — Black pushes g3 with check.
We step the king to g1.
Black missed the fork, playing the rook to f6 and expecting knight-to-a5.
There's the fork — the knight takes, capturing on d7.
Black recaptures with the king on d7.
Rather than grab another pawn, we play the rook to f1, offering the trade and preparing to infiltrate on f7.
Black sidesteps the rook to g6.
We reach the seventh rank with the rook to f7.
The king retreats to e8.
The other rook joins on h7.
Black pushes h4.
We don't want the rook coming to f6 and f2, so we cover with the rook to f4, planning to double on the seventh.
Black tries the bishop to g5, and we swing the rook to f3, snuffing out counterplay Soviet-schoolboy style.
Black blocks with the bishop to f6 — we may have to concede the d4-pawn.
We suck it up and play the rook to f4, heading for f7.
Black returns the bishop to g5, and we double on the seventh with the rook to f7 — totally winning; it's just one pawn.
Black checks with the bishop to e3, and our king steps to f1. We're going to take on c7 and threaten mate.
Black grabs the pawn, capturing on d4, and we take on c7 with the rook — threatening mate on c8.
Black checks with the rook to f6.
We march the king toward the centre — king to e2, staying clear of any mating net.
Black tries the bishop to e5, and we finish it — the rook to c8, checkmate. Tough game, but we're over 2100.
We take White and meet the Sicilian — today we play normal theory, then deliberately sacrifice a piece and show how to fight back from a lost position.
We open the Alapin with c3.
We strike with d4.
The c-pawns come off on d4.
Black plays e6.
We develop the knight to c3 — though the bishop to g5 would have been a fine chance to hang it; now Black just plays ...Nf6.
Black pins with the bishop to b4 — and here's our chance: we play the bishop to g5.
We play the bishop to g5 — a believable blunder, and at least it develops a piece. The comedy would be if Black declined it.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We even offer the bishop to a6 — all but begging Black to win material; it's oddly hard to give a piece away.
Black takes on c3 with check.
We recapture, bxc3.

Black wins our bishop, the pawn recapturing on a6 — the sacrifice is complete, and we've even traded off another pair of minors, making it harder on ourselves. Now the recovery begins, a full piece down. First, know this: ...e5 does not win the knight back — after ...h6, the bishop to h4, ...g5 unpins, and if the bishop drops to g3 the knight is free. Basic, but essential.
So we play e5 — in a situation like this it's a genuine attempt to complicate the game.

Black plays h6. It slightly weakens his structure, but down a piece a small weakness isn't enough — we need something concrete. The idea is to take on f6: after ...hxg5 we push to g7, and even after ...Rg8 we defend the g7-pawn indirectly with the queen to h5 — if the rook grabs g7, the queen forks on h8. Recovery rarely comes in a single move: build tension and sow doubt.
We capture on f6.
Black wins our bishop, recapturing on g5.

We push to g7 and set the queen toward h5, sowing doubt. This game is really about recovery technique when you're lost, and the principles are these. Complicate — pose your opponent decision after decision, because decisions breed fatigue and doubt. Keep your pieces active — bring the rook in with h4 rather than a timid g3, and ask the "Shankland question": what happens if you just do it anyway, developing and ignoring a pawn? Defend key pawns by developing, not by a passive king move — a rook to d3 both guards c3 and prepares to lift to g3. Manoeuvre the knight toward a dream square like d6, via f7. Use a break like d5 not only to lure the bishop off b7 but to open lines and strip away defenders. And once you win material back, convert with a passed pawn — push it hard while the opponent is passive, escort it with a rook cutting off the king, and finish with the ladder-mate technique, bringing your own king up to guard the checking square so the rooks can deliver mate. Even dead lost, purposeful, problem-posing play saves a remarkable number of games.
We go for the kill with e4, and Black answers with the Scandinavian, d5.
We take, and Black recaptures early with the queen, capturing on d5.
We hit the queen with the knight to c3.
The queen retreats to a5.
Now the special setup — g3, preparing to fianchetto. It looks tame, but it gets dangerous fast.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We fianchetto the bishop to g2, planning a modest d3 and a specific attacking idea.
Black develops the bishop to g4.
We put the knight on e2, not f3 — the knight to f3 would block our own fianchettoed bishop.
Black plays the typical c6, making a little home for the queen.
A useful no-brainer — h3, so that g4 is available later to unpin.
The bishop slides back to h5.
We castle.
Black develops the knight to d7.
We play the modest d3, opening the fianchettoed bishop.
Black castles queenside — which actually makes our plan five times stronger. Long castling here is very risky.
We hit immediately with b4 — if Black takes, the b-file opens straight onto the king.
Black declines and drops the queen to c7.
We push on with b5.
Black closes with c5.
We keep the storm rolling with a4, planning a5 and b6.
Black plays b6 — but that just creates a hook.
We absolutely play a5, prying open the king.
Black plays e6.
No rush to take b6 — first we develop the bishop to f4, connecting the rooks.
Black tries the bishop to d6 — tempting, but there's a trick.
We take on d6, and Black recaptures with the queen, capturing on d6 — move order matters here.
Now we take, capturing on b6 — and Black is in huge trouble.
Black recaptures with the knight, capturing on b6 — but that opens the a-file, which is deadly.
We grab, capturing on a7 with the rook, and the queen will join the attack via a1.
Black defends with the rook to d7. Already devastating.
The queen is the supporting actress — so rather than rush her out, we keep the rook alive with a6, pinning the knight.
Black blocks with the knight to d5.
We remove it — the knight takes, and Black recaptures with the pawn, capturing on d5 — killing the knight-to-b4 idea.
First we insert g4.
The bishop retreats to g6.
Now the queen finally comes to a1 — dictating from behind, with the attack coming from all sides.
Black shuffles the rook to b7.
The knight jumps to c3, threatening to take on d5. The queen on a1 supports the knight, the rook, and an a5 leap.
Black covers with the rook back to d8.
We win material, capturing on d5 with the knight.
The king steps to b8.
The fastest path — we take, capturing on b6 with the knight, so the a6-rook can swing to a8.
Black recaptures with the queen, capturing on b6 — the most resilient try.
We take back, capturing on b6 with the rook.
Black recaptures, capturing on b6 — and now we check on a8.
The queen swings to a2, the king runs to c7, and the queen to a7 with check wins the rook and the game. Long castling — dangerous, over and over.
We've seen e3 before, and the response is d5. This looks like a Hippo setup — g3, e3, then b3 and d3.
Against all of these flank defences, the best plan is to occupy the centre — e5.
The effective anti-Hippo setup starts with the knight to f6...
...and then c6, which I really like — it builds a pawn chain so his fianchettoed bishop bites on granite.
That pawn triangle, just like in the London, gives the bishop a home on d6.
You might ask where the queen's knight goes now that c6 is taken — the answer is d7.
The knight to d7 — heading, ultimately, toward the kingside to feed an attack. Not c5, where it would walk into d4 and do nothing.
The knight reroutes, f8 then g6 — Ruy Lopez style.
What is that knight doing? It sits on the kingside — so future sacrifices are in the air, and it makes the h5-then-h4 storm much more effective.
Since we're attacking on the kingside, close the centre — e4. If he plays c4 it achieves nothing; the pawn on d5 is very well protected.
A common misconception is that we must develop the bishop. We don't — it's perfectly happy on c8, and we'll bring it out only when we need it. Play h5; we're going for the king.
c4 accomplishes nothing.
The pawn on d5 is well protected, so h4 — we're already on the verge of delivering mate. That's how fast this is.

Recapture on d5. His knight to c3 accomplishes nothing. Now be careful how we open the kingside — hxg3 is double-edged, since after fxg3 he opens the f-file for his rook, so we need a follow-up. Don't hurry: the tempting knight to e4 hits h2, but it's wrong — it gives up the pawn on d5, and if d5 falls, the e4-pawn goes with it.
One prophylactic move first — the bishop to e6. It defends the pawn on d5 and clears the way for a future knight to g4. These are exactly the quiet moves people hate to play when they're attacking.
If he's angling for the knight to b5, we can always retreat the bishop to b8. Now the time has come to open fire on the kingside.
hxg3, and the knight to g4.

Notice his bishop is overloaded — defending both d5 and the knight. He grabs on d5, but I'd planned for this: his knight is now hanging, and if we move ours with tempo, he'll have two loose pieces at once.
Not taking on f3 — that just drops the knight. The knight takes on h2, hitting the rook: if it moves, we win the other knight. It isn't fully clear-cut, since his knight can return to c3.
He finds the knight to f4, also a good move.
We take the rook.
Now we're up the exchange, and still attacking.
Trade on f4 to remove his knight.

He recaptures, and we've converted the attack into material — an extra exchange. Now the technique: f5 is one way, but it allows d5, opening his bishop's diagonal, so this must be handled very carefully.
f5 — defending the e4-pawn, which feels like the most important pawn on the board.
It also shuts his bishop out of the game. He answers d5 — he's good.
We retreat the bishop to f7.
He takes on g7 — the question I was weighing is whether that pawn is worth giving up.
And it is worth it — because we keep the e4-pawn, which is enormous.
The bishop to h6 is a mistake — a losing move. Whenever the king on g1 is this weak, be hyper-aware of every route to it, on both wings — and the f2-square is the sensitive one.
The bishop to c5 with check is guarded, but the queen to b6 with check forces his king onto the h-file — and there sits his undefended bishop on h6. We swing the rook to h8 and collect it.
My technique here was a touch sloppy — the bishop to d4 was not actually so clear.
The rook to g6 doesn't trap the bishop, because of bishop g5. The rook to h8 is better — it pins.

Convert as fast as possible: his knight on h2 is very vulnerable, so double on the h-file — walk the king to e7 and bring the other rook to h8. We're not afraid of him grabbing on c4; he's out of pieces and our king is safe in the centre. And there's even a forced mate: once his queen leaves e2 and the bishop is gone from g2, the f2-square lights up — take on h2, swing the rook to the h-file, and after the block, crash into f2.
Against the Modern, we want a sound positional line rather than a sharp theoretical race.
c3 is the quiet, strong choice: the pawns on c3, d4, and e4 lock into a chain so the fianchettoed g7-bishop bites on granite.
notes.teaches: A c3-d4-e4 chain neutralizes the long-diagonal bishop before it ever gets going.

notes.explains: The bishop tucks into d3, where it defends the e4-pawn while the pawn chain looks after d4 — every unit covers the next.
notes.teaches: Build a self-supporting structure: pawns hold one square, a piece holds the other.

notes.explains: We could play h3 to rule out a pin with Bg4, but Bg5 is the more aggressive continuation, provoking a decision.
With e5 the game sharpens — the idea is exd4 followed by g5 and g4, chasing the f3-knight off the defense of the d-pawn.
notes.plans: Meet the coming ...g5-g4 by resolving the centre before the knight is kicked.

notes.explains: So we take on e5, keeping the h4-bishop passive rather than letting Black free it with the pawn break.
After the trades the question is the queen's-knight: Nd2 would drop the d3-bishop to Qxd3, so that square is off-limits.
notes.teaches: Before choosing a developing square, check that it doesn't undefend a piece behind it.

notes.explains: Na3 looks ugly, but it's only a transit stop — the knight is bad on a3 for exactly one move, then it reroutes to its ideal square c4.
notes.teaches: A knight on the rim is fine if the rim is a layover, not a destination.

notes.explains: Nc4 leans on e5. You might ask why, since the queen guards the pawn — but pressure isn't only about winning material; it ties the defender down.
notes.teaches: Attacking a defended point still pays: it pins the guard in place.

notes.explains: f4 is risky and does loosen our king, but the logic is clean: if Black takes, we push e5 and win the pinned f6-knight; if he plays g5, we take the knight with tempo on the queen. Even the Qc5-check has an answer — an interposition that hits the queen — which is exactly the resource f4 was counting on. Remember the three ways to meet a check: capture the checker, move the king, or block.
notes.teaches: The three replies to a check are capture, king-move, and interpose — the block is the one people forget.

notes.explains: Now recapturing with the pawn is tempting because it hits the f6-knight, but a move isn't good just because it makes a threat: Black slides the knight to d7, and the e5-pawn, hit three times, simply falls.
notes.teaches: A move that only creates a threat can still be bad if the threat is easily met and leaves a weakness.

notes.explains: So Nxe5 instead — it makes no threat, but it banks the extra pawn cleanly and keeps our structure sound.
notes.teaches: The unflashy recapture that keeps the material and the structure beats the noisy one that gives them back.

notes.explains: Two ideas carry the position. First, sidestep the coming Rd8 pin with Qe2 before it lands — even at the cost of the usual 'defend with the least valuable piece' rule. Second, prepare slowly and attack fast: overprotect the centre first, and once Black's king is loose, look immediately for captures near it — that's how a shot like Nxf7 appears.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is weak, start your search with captures on its doorstep.

notes.explains: Black meets the king's pawn with the Scandinavian, challenging our center at once.
We develop the knight to c3 with tempo, hitting the queen on d5 and gaining a free move.
teaches: develop with tempo against the early queen

notes.explains: The queen tucks to d6 — a modern, fully respectable branch of the Scandinavian — and we seize the full center with d4.
teaches: Qd6 is a legitimate modern line

notes.explains: Nothing exotic is needed: we simply develop and control the center, and let Black prove his setup.
Black leans on the d4-pawn and eyes the pin with the bishop to g4 — the classic pressure we have to answer.
So we play the mildly ugly but effective h3, taking the g4-square away from the bishop before the pin can happen.
Threat handled, we develop actively — the bishop to c4, raking toward f7 and supporting a future d5 break.
The bishop to g5 is the active square; parking it on e3 would be a touch too passive here.
More quiet prophylaxis: a4 denies Black the b5 push with tempo and the queenside fianchetto that follows — the kind of preventive move you see constantly at master level.
teaches: a4 stops b5 before it starts

notes.explains: The idea behind the retreat: reroute the knight to e2, then to g3, which frees us to play c3 and secure d4 permanently. A backward-looking move can be exactly right.
plans: Ne2-g3 then c3 to cement d4

notes.explains: The queen to b4 looks intimidating, but the grab on b2 is simply unthinkable — so there's nothing real behind it.
teaches: a scary-looking sortie with no bite

notes.explains: b3 solves everything at once: no worry about the capture on b2, and if the knight harasses from a5 our bishop just drops to d3 and aims at the king.
The queen on b4 is stranded in no man's land now; we can trade on e7 or tuck the bishop back to d2, both comfortable.
The rook to e1 x-rays the black queen down the file, quietly discouraging the e5 freeing break.
teaches: x-ray pressure to prevent a break

notes.explains: The knight to g3 completes that x-ray idea, both pieces trained on the e-file.
The knight jumps into e4, a superb central post, and White is now clearly the more comfortable side.
The knight swings to c5 and we begin piling onto the queenside.
b6 shoves the knight but leaves lasting holes on the queenside — weaknesses we intend to make him pay for later.
Rather than grab anything, we reroute the knight back to d3, heading for e5. It looks mysterious, but it's pure piece-optimization — hunting the best central square for every piece.
teaches: maneuver to your best squares before striking

notes.explains: The knight settles on e5, the commanding outpost, while keeping the other knight free so the queen can reach the kingside for an attack.
The bishop drops to d3, trained once again on Black's king.
f6 only makes Black more passive and, above all, weakens the e6-pawn — the new target.
We bring the knight back to g4 with tempo: the e6-pawn is falling and the black queen is running out of squares.
teaches: retreat with tempo to win the weakness

notes.explains: The rook swings to e4 to collect the pawn — once e6 goes, the whole position caves.
The trap springs: the black queen has no squares. A pawn to g3 will hem it in, the rook on e6 covers d6, and the knight guards the rest — so the queen has to be given up for two pieces.
teaches: net the queen by taking its last squares

notes.explains: That's why the rook went to e6 — not just to take the pawn but to deny the queen its escape to d6. With both knights loose, we move one with a threat to win material, pin the defender with the bishop to c4, and route the knight via g5 to e6 to crash through on g7.
teaches: deny the escape square, then collect

notes.explains: d4, the knight to f6 — let's play some positional d4 openings this game.
c4 — we could play a London or Trompowsky, but let's play the main line. g6 — either the King's Indian or the Grünfeld.
The knight to c3 — a King's Indian.
The bishop to g7.
e4 — against the King's Indian.
He castles.
Black can get checkmated really easily — so we play f3.
d6. The point of f3 is threefold: it reinforces the e4-pawn, it prepares a later pawn storm with g4, and it prevents the knight from coming to g4 —
— which is important, because we now develop the bishop to e3.

e5. The ideal Sämisch scenario: close the centre, play the queen to d2, castle long, and checkmate Sicilian-style on the kingside with the bishop to h6, h4, h5, and the pawn takes g6. Black has to stop us in that order, which isn't as easy as it seems. e5 is the old-school main line.
We go d5, closing down the centre — the first step.
c6 is indeed the correct move.
Now we aim at step two — tuck our king away with the queen to d2. We'll take on c6.
The bishop to d7 is very awkward — it deprives the knight of its natural developing square; I'm not sure what he's trying to do.
Now obviously we castle long, completing the second stage of our plan.
b5 — his heart's in the right place, trying to attack the queenside, but the wheels are going to come off. We can play the pawn takes b5, that's fine, but there's an even better version —

— the d-pawn takes c6, which exposes a very weak pawn on d6, and we'll take b5 in a very good version. Aren't we opening the centre I said to keep closed? Circumstances have changed — he gave us a pawn, and the great thing about the Sämisch is that it's structurally healthy —

— so opening the centre doesn't expose us; we're perfectly developed and our centre is in good hands. What do we take the pawn with? Tricky — a lot of you will be tempted to take with the pawn to carry a threat, but you should take with the knight.
The knight takes b5 — taking with the pawn opens the c-file only he benefits from, and lets him play the knight to d4. This is definitely the best move.
Now we're attacking d6 with three pieces — the rook, the queen, and the knight. a5 — he keeps trying to attack, but he's grasping at straws.
Time to reap the harvest — take the pawn with the queen, swooping in and paralyzing him; if he moves the bishop, we trade queens, up two pawns. The knight takes d6 was also possible.
The knight to b4 is a good try, attacking the a2-pawn — no need to give that pawn away.

The simplest is a3, chasing the knight away with tempo; the king to b1 is also good prophylaxis, but a3 comes with tempo. Our king is perfectly safe on c1. After he moves the knight, the bishop to g5 is coming — the bishop on d7 is defended by queen and knight, and the bishop to g5 pins the knight and threatens to win the bishop by taking it.
The only way to defend is to move his bishop, which allows the queen trade. The knight to c6 —
— and the bishop to g5, very reasonable.
The rook to c8 — he's not effectively doing anything against our threat.
Why did we play the bishop to g5? To take on f6, and then the bishop on d7 is toast.

The bishop takes f6 wins a piece, and now he plays the queen to b6. It's a dangerous period — we're still quite undeveloped, our whole kingside is at home, so it's like we won a lottery ticket but we're in a war zone and need to escape before we can cash it in. Identify the threats: the rook to d8, and the bishop to g5 with check disattaching our king from the rook, which would make the rook to d8 a devastating pin.
