We can't cover d8, but the queen to d2 takes the sting out of both — keep the queen close to the king, don't abandon it. If the knight to d4, we just take it; c4 is well defended. Then the bishop to d3, to stop him opening his bishop with the d3 pawn-sac, and we consolidate. After a check, the king to b1, a move we wanted anyway; then, against an Alekhine's-gun triple on the b-file, the king to a1 is prophylaxis so a rook can come to b1 — a1 over a2, since the queen could later come to b3 with check. Now, it's the Sämisch, so we attack: h5, ripping open the h-file, and the rook to b1; the rook takes b2, we recapture, and the queen takes a3 with check is a paper tiger — the rook to a2 ends it. He tries the rook to b3, and now the king to a2, then a4. We play f4 to lock his bishop, then e5, eyeing a bishop sacrifice on g6 to rip open his king — I've verified he has zero queenside threats, so think concretely, not by how scary it looks. e5 threatens the sac on g6, or f5 as a battering ram to open the king; take on g6, and the queen to f5, or checks on f7 or h7, lead to mate; the bishop to e4 rerouting to d5 also opens the diagonal. Then the queen to d7 with check, and the king hunt begins — don't rush the first check you see, like the rook to f1 with check; map the king's escape, e8-d8-c7, and prevent it. Give a check on h8, the king goes to e7, and now every square is covered — the bishop covers e6, the pawn covers d6, the rook covers the eighth rank — and one more check is checkmate.
We open e4, Black replies e5, and we head for our Four Knights Scotch.
The knight goes to f3.
Black develops to c6. A bonus of this system: you needn't learn a separate line against the Petrov — the knight to c3 covers it, saving work.
We face the Nimzowitsch Defence, the knight to c6. In most cases this move has little independent value — meaning it just transposes into another opening.
d4 would give an independent game, but the knight to f3 is easier — Black usually plays e5, and we're back into familiar territory.
I'm in the mood for the Belgrade Gambit — let's see how it holds up at this level.
We take White; Black meets our king's pawn with ...e5.
Let's diversify from the Italian — the knight to f3.
Black plays d6 — the Philidor.
Against the Philidor we strike with d4. It's strong because ...d6 has left Black undeveloped and boxed in his own bishop.
Black takes on d4.
We recapture with the knight on d4. Those concessions mean we open the centre to exploit them.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We simply develop the knight to c3 — no need to rush the d4-knight; once he trades it off, our queen will be perfectly safe.
Black trades on d4 and we recapture with the queen — safe, because with no knight left on b8 there's no ...c-pawn or ...Nb8 tempo to chase it.
Black develops the bishop to d7. A caution: ...c5 to hit the queen is a classic mistake here — attacking the queen isn't automatically a good thing.
We continue with the bishop to c4, pressuring f7. The queen needs no move; we're happy to provoke ...c5, which would permanently weaken the d5-square.
Black develops the knight to e7; we castle.
Black attacks the queen with the knight to c6.
We tuck the queen back to d1 — Qd5 would walk into ...Be6, Qd3 into ...Ne5, and we don't want to give up our bishop. Sometimes you retreat, and it costs nothing when your pieces are this active.
Black develops the bishop to e7.
We swing the knight to the d5 outpost — a beautiful square. We could take the bishop at our leisure, but the knight is so strong we'd rather make him be the one to take it.
Black castles.
We grab more central space with f4 — not necessarily what I'd play myself, but a lesson in how to attack.
Black plays the bishop to e6. Development isn't finished — a good moment to maneuver.
The bishop looks awkward on d2, but it's a maneuver heading for the long diagonal — not b3, which would weaken it.
Black lunges the knight to a5, hitting our bishop.
We snap off the knight, the bishop landing on a5.
Black plays b6, attacking the bishop.
We slot the bishop onto c3 — the long diagonal we were aiming for all along — a clean piece up.
Black hits our knight with c6.
Rather than move the attacked knight, we set threats — the queen to d4, forming a battery with the bishop down the long diagonal toward g7.
Black grabs the knight, a pawn recapturing on d5 — but that opens the long diagonal straight to g7.
The queen crashes into g7 — checkmate.
We take on d5.
The knight to f6.
The line goes: a check on b5 —

— a developing move that forces a piece to appear on d7, which severs the connection between the black queen and the pawn on d5. There are two approaches: you could cling to d5 with the bishop takes d7, the queen recaptures, and c4 — many less-experienced players gravitate there, but after c6 Black gets massive positional compensation for the pawn.
So my coach's move is to drop the bishop back to e2 —
— giving away the d-pawn —
— and now you occupy the centre with d4, a slight advantage in an easy position. The whole point of the bishop to b5 and back was just to force Black's bishop onto d7.
Why force it — isn't it good for Black to develop a piece? Not quite: the bishop on d7 is very awkward, cutting the queen off from the centre and blocking that square.
— pushing c4 and then driving the pawn to d5 for a firmer central presence. I think we should go c4 and counter-attack the knight.

The knight to f6 — he's still playing instantly, probably some obscure theory. The d-pawn taking c5 isn't stupid: not to win a pawn but to gain tempi — the queen to a5 with check is one tempo, taking on c5 another, then the bishop to e3 and complete development with the knight to f3.
So I like the look of the d-pawn taking c5, but d5 is what we initially planned, so let's stick to our guns and play d5.

e6. Most people's instinct is the knight to c3 and to meet the trade with the pawn recapture, but when that chain turns into an isolated pawn, the d5-pawn becomes more a liability than a strength. A more prudent approach is to take on e6 — anticlimactic, since we're giving away our centre, but concretely: if the f-pawn recaptures, it ruins Black's structure; if the bishop, we trade queens and force Black's king to the awkward d8-square, castling queenside with check as fuel for our development.

White has a very small but stable endgame edge, and we haven't had many endgames, so I wanted an excuse. The f-pawn recapture is bad — Black is saddled with a permanent weakness on e6, and his kingside is no longer as safe. Now we just develop in any order.
We do want to protect the d4-square so Black can't quickly establish a knight there — we do that with the knight to f3 — but let's start with the knight to c3, it doesn't matter.
Now we'll play the knight to f3, gaining a little time.
The knight to f3.
And now we'll castle.
We castle.

He castles. Now we should think — this bishop can go to at least four spots: b3, f4, g5, or the queenside fianchetto with b3 and the bishop to e2. Black's annoying idea is to push e5 and establish a knight outpost on d4 — a risk we need to fight.
With d6, Nf6, and the trades on d4 we've steered into a Najdorf — the most theory-heavy of the Sicilians.
a6 is the move that defines the Najdorf; it's the whole point of the setup.
notes.teaches: In the Najdorf, a6 fights for b5 and gives the king a future haven on c7.

notes.explains: We don't need to commit the e-pawn yet, so just develop — Nc6 — and wait for White to declare himself.
e5 here simply hands over a pawn without real compensation.
We take with Nxe5, inviting the further trade — because even though the queens come off and we lose castling rights, White can't exploit it.
notes.teaches: Losing castling isn't fatal when the opponent is undeveloped and the king has a safe square waiting.

notes.explains: The king recaptures and looks exposed, but two things save us: White is poorly developed, and the king has a ready-made home. It can simply walk to c7.

Now the point of a6 shines: it covers b5 while the f6-knight covers d5, so together they seal the light squares around the king's future home on c7. First, though, we must be ready to defend the e5-pawn once White castles and swings a rook to e1.
notes.teaches: a6 plus a knight on f6 blankets b5 and d5 — the light squares a king on c7 needs covered.

notes.explains: Order matters: e6 first, because it opens the path for the bishop to d6, which will shield the e5-pawn against Rook-e1 pressure.
notes.teaches: Sequence your development so each move enables the defensive resource the next one needs.

notes.explains: Kc7 parks the king on its ideal, unassailable square. Now a rook to e1 is comfortably met by Bd6.
White's f4 hopes we take, so he can come out with a bishop-check and spoil things on c7. Instead we trade on our own terms: Bd6 invites White to take on e5 rather than the other way around.
notes.teaches: Don't capture into your opponent's plan — set up the position so he has to make the trade you want.

notes.explains: After the recapture the bishop sits beautifully in the centre, and every further trade helps us since we're the one up a pawn.
notes.teaches: When you're up material, trades bring you closer to a won endgame — welcome them.

notes.explains: Ne4 looks scary because Nxe4 runs into the zwischenzug Bxf7-check before White recaptures on e4. But ask the real question — does White actually threaten anything right now? He doesn't, so we just carry on developing.
notes.teaches: Before reacting to a scary move, define its concrete threat; often there isn't one.

notes.explains: So Bd7, the only clean developing move, connecting the rooks — the bishop can always reach the long diagonal later via c6.
Recapturing with the pawn, gxf6, over keeping the structure pretty — the open g-file is worth more here.
notes.teaches: A doubled-pawn recapture that opens a file for attack can beat the 'healthy' structure.

notes.explains: The idea behind gxf6 is a slow endgame attack: the g-file plus the light bishop rerouting to c6 build a lasting threat against the g2-pawn — not mate, but relentless pressure.
notes.plans: Reroute the bishop to c6, double on the g-file, and grind the g2-pawn.

notes.explains: No rush — Bc6 first. If White tries Bf4, it doesn't work: we take and push f5.
This is the Scandinavian/Caro-Kann pawn formation, and it's far better than it looks because every pawn defends the next. Its one real drawback is that the h7-pawn is isolated.
notes.teaches: The f5-e6 pawn chain is self-supporting; only the isolated rook-pawn is a genuine weakness.

notes.explains: Activate the rooks starting with Rad8. With only one open file on the board, seizing it usually converts straight into material.
notes.teaches: Own the only open file and material tends to follow.

notes.explains: A neat endgame subtlety: the natural doubling with Rg8 and Rg2 fails to Rh4, which guards the h2-pawn and keeps the king safe — so don't rush the second rook to the seventh.
notes.teaches: Calculate the 'obvious' rook lift; a quiet defensive rook shift can refute it.

notes.explains: Why allow any counterplay when we can just snap off on b2 instead? There is no need to force the second rook in.
Under checks, tuck the king to b8 — in this endgame the rooks do the work, not the king, so keep it out of the checking lanes.
notes.teaches: In rook endings, hide the king from checks rather than marching it into activity.

notes.explains: Simplest is to trade one pair of rooks and immediately plant the other on the open file, hitting the weak queenside pawns.
To win the b4-pawn by force, attack it from behind: Rd4 lets Rb1 defend, but starting with a check and swinging to b2 pins it down — a pawn attacked from behind can't be defended.
notes.teaches: Attack a passed or weak pawn from behind so no rook can shield it.

notes.explains: Rely on calculation, not vague technique: use the central-kingside pawn majority to deflect White's rook off the back rank, then collect the a-pawn and make new passers.
notes.plans: Roll the kingside majority to deflect the defending rook, then win the a-pawn.

notes.explains: The best way to defend a pawn is with another pawn — f6 props up the chain rather than tying a rook to defense.
notes.teaches: Defend with a pawn before you defend with a piece; it frees your pieces to attack.

notes.explains: A Russian-school endgame idea worth filing away: pin the pawn laterally along the rank, then bring up your own pawn to win the f3-pawn — commonly missed even at a high level.
notes.teaches: Freeze an enemy pawn with a rook on its rank, then attack it with a pawn.

notes.explains: This looks like a deep-freeze where one pawn holds two, but it isn't — b6 is a breakthrough. After axb6, the a-pawn runs; it's a sacrifice that costs us nothing.
notes.teaches: A pawn breakthrough sacrifices one pawn to clear the path for another to queen.

notes.explains: In the queen-versus-pawn finish, win by zugzwang: force White to shove the h-pawn into a lost race. Kb7 is the elegant key — it makes White dig his own grave.
notes.teaches: Queen-vs-pawn endings are won by zugzwang that separates the king from its pawn.

notes.explains: We take on d5.

The knight to f6 — a poor man's Scandi; technically it's in the Portuguese Gambit family, but White isn't supposed to keep the extra pawn. Why not simply c4? Because Black responds with c6, and after we either transpose to the Panov Caro-Kann or take greedily with the d-pawn, Black gets massive central control, a stronghold on d4, and White has a terrible light-squared bishop biting on c4 — tremendous compensation for the pawn.

So the line my coach taught me years ago — easy to learn, cool, and demonstrating positional principles: a check on b5. It's weird that our first move is with a bishop, but it develops with tempo, and if Black plays c6 now, we play the d-pawn takes c6, and since we haven't pushed to c4, c6 makes no sense for him. Black covers the check with the knight to d7 or —

— the bishop to d7, which most people play. Is that bishop well placed? Absolutely not — it deprives the b8-knight of a square, cuts the queen off from the centre, and stands in the middle of everything, so we should leave it there. That's the idea: provoking a move that ends up counterproductive. You might reason we should play the bishop back to c4 to defend the pawn, but the bishop to c4 allows the bishop to g4, hitting the queen — and f3 isn't a move you want in the opening, and we might not keep the extra pawn on d5.
So not the queen to e2 or a4, which give Black a way out by letting him trade off that awkward piece on d7 — we physically move the bishop to e2 to stop the bishop to g4.
The idea is to stop the bishop to g4, and the reason we move the bishop at all is so that after a move like a4, Black doesn't rid himself of that awkward piece by agreeing to the bishop trade —
— and then taking on d5, say with the queen. The queen to e2 does prevent the immediate bishop takes b5, which would be a fork, but after the queen to e2 Black just plays the knight takes d5 —

So we prevent that and grab the centre at the same time. You'd be right that c4 is coming — it won't be taken away from us — to push the knight from d5, giving us nice development and better central control, a small but stable advantage. Start with a simple developing move, the knight to f3, then castle, and only then c4. Conversely, that gives Black the extra option of the bishop to d6, intending to meet c4 with the knight to f4.

But we'll find a way around it. c5 is a good move — Black contests the centre and forces our hand. I said castle next, but the opportune moment has come to play c4, meeting Black in the centre instead of giving free rein, knocking the knight out immediately; if we castle instead, Black takes on d4 and plays the knight to c6, and by the time we play c4 it might be less effective.

If the knight to b4, we just play a3, not dangerous — though in some Alekhine and Scandi lines, with the light-squared bishop on f5, the knight to b4 is unpleasant, threatening a fork. Black plays the knight to f6. We can play the knight to c3 or castle. d5 might look appealing to create a passer, but it's totally innocuous — Black can trade, and an isolated passer this early is a liability, blockaded by the dark-squared bishop on d6. So instead of rushing forward, keep the tension with the knight to c3, and if the pawns trade we recapture with the knight, not the queen, which walks right into the knight to c6.

The knight to c6. Now d5 makes perfect sense — a tempo move hitting the knight, and, most importantly, denying Black the time to play the bishop to d6. We can prevent the bishop to d6 with the bishop to f4, a move we want anyway, because the bishop to d6 is the only way to blockade the passer; after the bishop to f4, the bishop to e7, d6, the bishop is almost trapped, and the passer becomes a great asset. g4 blunders a pawn, since we have two attackers on d4, so Black panics and blunders. The bishop to b4 is good; I don't like d6 here, since it doesn't gain a tempo and runs into the queen to b6 forcing a queen trade that leaves the pawn unguarded with the knight to e4 — too concrete — so we just castle, not a3. Like the e4-b6 game, we don't chase the bishop; we take the sting out of the pin by castling, and we want Black to take on c3 himself, losing a tempo compared to a3, and a3 would also take the a3-square from our dark-squared bishop, which gets a nice post there after the b-pawn recaptures. Then we develop the dark-squared bishop to g5 — this pin is underrated and very dangerous with Black castled kingside, the queen pressuring the knight, and the knight to g4 a huge threat; the bishop to e7 to escape the pin fails to d5 and d6. h6 — we can trade with the bishop takes f6, but it's early to trade queens when up a pawn, unlike up a piece where a queen trade helps simplify, so we keep the tension with the bishop to h4; if g5, that's amazing to provoke, weakening the knight and the king. The bishop to b7 walks into our idea, and the passer ends up deciding the game. The tricky bishop to c6 sets up an x-ray against the queen and precludes the take on c7, so we answer with the rook to d1, which protects the queen and the pawn at once and ends it, renewing the threat and keeping the bishop trapped. The queen to c6 is the most-popular-wrong-answer — we've won a minor piece and will trade queens soon. There's an elegant combination to win a second piece: the bishop takes f6, since the queen can't recapture, forcing the g-pawn to recapture, which opens the g-file for the queen to g3 with check — but not immediately, since the king goes to h8, so first the rook to d1 x-raying the queen, and if the bishop moves, the queen to g3 wins the queen; order of operations matters, since the rook to d1 first then the bishop takes f6 lets the queen recapture. The knight to e4 is terrible, since Black takes it hitting our queen. The rook to c7 — heavy pieces are bad defenders, and the bishop on d7 is on life support, so the knight to b5 plays itself; if he takes, the queen to g3 with check wins the queen and the rook. Let's finish in style: the queen to g3 with check, a discovery against the queen, we take the queen, and then take the rook, which has lost its support.
Black chooses the Caro-Kann, preparing to challenge our center with d5.
We take the full center with d4.
But Black shirks the principled d5 for a passive d6 — a hybrid that hands us the center for free.
teaches: a passive setup concedes the center

notes.explains: No need for anything clever — we just develop and let the extra space work for us.
Keep it old-school: knights before bishops. The knight comes to f3 rather than grabbing more center with f4.

Black has spent the opening shuffling pawns and only now develops a piece to b7. Against passive play the recipe is fixed: pry the center open so our better-placed pieces can infiltrate — otherwise he consolidates and escapes.
teaches: open the center against a passive setup

notes.explains: The d5 hammer is the move — not e5, which he'd meet with d5 and slam the door. We smash the center open and, crucially, keep it open.
teaches: choose the lever that keeps the center open

notes.explains: Black tries to shut it again with the pawn to e5. The plan now is to push f4, contest that pawn, and open the e-file — the main artery to his king.
teaches: the e-file as the road to the king

notes.explains: But a knight blocks the f-pawn, so first we reroute it to d2 — not a random square: from there it heads to c4 to hit the b6-pawn.
Going straight to c4 would have let him kick the knight with b5 — so patience first.
a4 handcuffs that pawn preemptively — like a surgeon, we stop b5 before it can happen.
Now the knight lands on c4 unopposed, sandwiched into a fine square eyeing b6 and e5.
His position is riddled with holes, and f5 is the juiciest — we plant a bishop on it.
To open the e-file we first prepare it, bringing the rook to e1 so f4 comes with full force.
a5 carves out an outpost on b6 for the knight — every pawn move here has a piece behind it.
We recapture with the knight, not the rook — the knight comes with a threat on the bishop and gains its own outpost.
The rook lifts to a4, aiming to swing to c4 and chase the queen — rooks get activated too, not just minor pieces.
We can't swing to c4 yet — the knight hangs — so the queen drops to a1 to defend it first, then the rook is free.
teaches: support the piece before the maneuver

notes.explains: Plan complete. The pawn was sacrificed, not blundered — given up deliberately to blow the center open, which was the whole idea from the start.
teaches: a sacrifice is a purchase, not a loss

notes.explains: The knight jumps into the c6 outpost, deep in his position and impossible to dislodge.
We play it traditional — e5.
White plays the knight to c3 — this could still become a Vienna.
We develop the knight to f6.
It's the Four Knights — the knight to f3.
We bring out the knight to c6.
And the Four Knights Scotch with d4 — rare to face; this is what I play myself.
We take, capturing on d4.
White recaptures with the knight, capturing on d4. The main reply here is the bishop to b4.
But I like the bishop to c5 — just as natural, very reputable, only less well-known than the bishop to b4.
White takes, capturing on c6.
We recapture with the b-pawn, capturing on c6 — not the d-pawn, which would allow a queen trade and cost us castling.
White develops the bishop to g5 — nothing special, and e5 is no real threat yet.
We castle — if White ever pushes e5, we pin it with the rook to e8.
White develops the bishop to e2. Now e5 becomes a possibility, so we deal with it.
We throw in h6 — for a specific reason.
The bishop keeps the pin from h4.
We play d6, shutting the door on e5 for good.
White castles.
The rook comes to e8 — old school. And with h6 in, we can later win the e4-pawn with g5.
Very old school — the bishop to f3.
Now g5. King safety is the most important thing, but pushing pawns in front of your king doesn't automatically get you mated — let me show you.
The bishop retreats to g3.
We push g4, kicking the bishop and planning to snag the e4-pawn.
White lunges e5 — unexpected, and not great; it hands us a very nice endgame.
That opens the diagonal onto c6, so we take the bishop, capturing on f3.
White takes back, capturing on f6.
We play it safe and remove it, the queen capturing on f6 — no pawn left on f6 for a back-rank trick.
White grabs d6, and we recapture with the queen, capturing on d6 — heading for that good endgame, and we'll trade queens.
White recaptures on f3 — White's kingside pawns are wrecked, while our queenside stays compact.
We develop the bishop to f5, stopping the knight from landing on e4.
White jumps the knight to e4 anyway.
We take, capturing on e4 with the bishop.
White recaptures with the pawn, and we take on e4 with the rook — now we own the e-file too.
White contests with the rook to e1.
We don't trade — we double up with the a-rook to e8, keeping the file on our terms.
White's king steps to f1.
In an endgame the king is the priority — we march it up with the king to g7.
White trades a pair of rooks on e4, and we recapture, capturing on e4 — improving while White simplifies.
White offers the last rook trade with the rook to e1.
We take, capturing on e1 with check.
White recaptures with the king on e1.
An instructive moment — White wants c3 to bury our bishop, so we seize the centre first with the bishop to d4.
White plays c3.
We reroute — the bishop to e5, staying central. If White tries f4, it only pushes a pawn onto a dark square.
White's king comes to e2 — which lets us head into a pawn endgame, and up a pawn it should be winning.
We trade, the bishop capturing on g3.
White recaptures with the h-pawn on g3 — our structure is ragged, but I like our chances.
Top priority — the king to f6, marching toward the centre.
White's king hurries up to f3.
We centralise further, the king to e5. The plan is c5, then d5 and d4, making a passed pawn.
The moment White's king heads to g4, we begin creating that passer.
There we go — c5.
e4, c5, the knight to f3, the knight to c6.
The bishop to b5 — the Rossolimo.
He plays e6 —
we castle short,
and Black develops with the knight to e7. Here I go with a recommendation from a well-known one-e4 course of a couple of years back —
this is where I learned the move. By popularity, the most common move here is the rook to e1, by a large margin, followed by
We're going Black in a King's Indian — the knight to f6.
White stakes out c4, and we fianchetto with g6.
White fianchettos too with g3, and our bishop lands on g7.
White completes it, the bishop to g2.
We play the classical d6, White develops the knight to f3, and we castle.
White castles. At this level, expect the fianchetto — a supposedly steady edge, but Black has real ways to fight for equality.
I'll play my old over-the-board line — the traditional King's Indian, the queen's knight to d7, preparing e5.
White pushes d5 — premature, the cart before the horse; now our King's Indian bishop is happy and the d5-pawn can be chipped away.
Since c6 here would drop a pawn, we route the knight to b6 — unusual in the King's Indian, but here White can't play b3.
White develops the knight to d2 — the c1-bishop stays locked in, and b3 is still off the table.
We develop the bishop to d7, preparing c6 and fighting for the centre.
White plays the rook to b1. We could force a draw with the bishop to f5, but that piece often ends up misplaced.
We prefer a5, stopping b4 and daring White into the blundering b3.
White grabs the centre with e4.
We continue the plan with c6, with e6 to follow to press d5.
White plays b3.
We keep poking the queenside chain with a4 — if b4, then we take on d5.
White develops the bishop to b2 — playing well, not budging.
Now we play e5, shutting down that bishop and reaching the traditional King's Indian centre.
White plays b4, wanting to push on to c5.
We shove our own pawn to a3, making a little escape window for the knight.
White reroutes the bishop to c3.
We exploit it at once — the knight to a4 with tempo, hitting the bishop.
The bishop tucks into a1.
We take at the most inconvenient moment for White, capturing on d5.
White recaptures, capturing on d5 — but White's pieces are shoved back, and new squares open for our minor pieces either way.
Our bishop grabs the lovely b5 square.
White plays the rook to e1. Now it's pure King's Indian, with the c-file ours.
A mysterious-looking move — the knight to g4.
White lifts the rook to b3. The point of g4: White's light bishop guards f1, so we set up on f2.
We swing the queen to b6 — White can't defend f2 without losing at least the exchange.
Note that h3 there is met by the knight capturing on f2, then the queen to b6 with check — I'll show the follow-up.
White is simply busted here — pure King's Indian minutiae.
White tries the rook to e3.
We just grab the rook while we can, capturing on e3.
White recaptures, capturing on e3 — and our other knight can leap into b2.
The knight jumps to b2 — the a3-pawn was hanging; the real point is to force off White's dark-squared bishop.
White plays the queen to b3.
We occupy the c-file with the rook to c8 — no rush to trap the queen.
White takes, capturing on b2.
We recapture with the pawn, capturing on b2.
White grabs the pawn back, capturing on b2 — but with our opponent's dark bishop gone, we optimise our own.
The bishop swings to h6 — a very King's Indian idea.
White drops the rook to e1. The c2 square looks juicy, and we keep an eye on the a-file.
A sexy retreat — the queen to a7, using every inch of the queenside.
White's paralysed — the rook to a1, at our mercy.
Simplification is the order of the day — the queen to a3; trading queens actually shortens the game.
White's queen goes to b1, crumbling on all sides.
The niftier way is the bishop to e2 — luring the knight off d2 so we check on c1 and win the queen.
White tries the bishop to h3. Now we threaten to take on f3, and the rook can come to c3.
Time to collect — the bishop takes, capturing on f3.
White takes a rook, capturing on c8.
We take back, capturing on c8 — faster than grabbing the knight.
White's queen retreats to e1.
Simplest is simplification — the bishop takes, capturing on d2.
White recaptures, and we grab a free pawn, the bishop capturing on e4, making room for our queen.
White plays the rook to e1, and we swing the queen to f3, toward the king.
White takes the bishop, and we recapture with the queen, capturing on e4 — a short, sweet kingside attack.
White throws up f3.
We check with the queen to d4.
White trades queens, and we recapture with the pawn, capturing on d4.
White's king comes to f2, and our rook infiltrates to c2 with check.
The king steps to e1, and our passed pawn rolls to d3.
A big game against a very strong player. The pawn to e4, c6 — a Caro-Kann.
Black takes on e4.

We recapture with the f-pawn, and Kusha responds with one of the most reputable lines against the Fantasy — the e5 variation; the point is that the d-pawn taking e5 runs into the queen to h4 with check.
So it's important to proceed with the knight to f3 — this is theory —

— and the bishop to g4, the recommendation in quite a few books, incredibly solid. White has many reactions; the main move is the bishop to c4, threatening the bishop takes f7 and the knight takes e5. After it Black plays the knight to d7 to cover e5, White castles, Black plays the knight to f6. There's another move I analyzed — c3 — but what worries me is Black grabbing the pawn.
The bishop takes f3, the queen takes f3, the pawn takes d4, and I'm hunting for compensation. Let's play the bishop to c4 and stick to what I know is fine.
The knight to d7 — I'm definitely out of my league theory-wise here.
We should probably castle and keep developing.
The knight to f6 — this is the line. If White plays d5, Black responds with the bishop takes f3 and recaptures the pawn on e5.
So we support the d4-pawn, because Black is constantly threatening the pawn takes d4 — the move is c3.

The bishop to h5. Kusha knows this line very well; let's try to take him out of theory. We can play the bishop to g5 and then the knight to d2, or the knight to d2 immediately — but that blocks the c1-bishop, so I lean toward developing the bishop first. We can also play the queen to e1 to get out of the pin.

I like the queen to e1 — flexible, solidifying the centre, taking the sting out of the pawn takes d4. If Black develops the bishop to d6, a typical idea is the knight to h4 and f5, with the queen swinging to g3. The Fantasy is an attacking, tactical weapon — we want to play for the kingside attack.

I really like the queen to e1 — a dangerous move. The bishop takes f3 — a big move; Kusha gives up the important light-squared bishop, an integral defender, without which f7 becomes weak, and our bishop is now uncontested. How to recapture? Not a given — the g-pawn recapture solidifies e4, opens the g-file, and prepares f4 to knock out e5; a serious alternative, since Black hasn't finished kingside development.
But I'm not in an overly adventurous mood — I prefer the conventional rook takes f3.
The bishop to d6 — Kusha pre-moves it.

The bishop to g5, the queen to f2, and if the knight takes e4 we snap off f7 and the king is in huge trouble. This is a bit flimsy, but it's the Fantasy — and potentially very rewarding: with the centre, if we complete development we're better, but if the centre collapses we're in huge trouble.

The queen to c7 — I didn't expect it, but it's reasonable; maybe he wants to castle queenside. Why not the knight to d2? We must reckon with the pawn takes d4 and the bishop takes h2 with check — but that's a worthy pawn to sacrifice, since the pawn takes d4 is a massive concession giving us a juicy centre.
The knight to d2 is essentially a no-brainer — I'm more than willing to part with a corner pawn for full control of the centre. The rook to f8.

He's telegraphing queenside castling; the point of the rook to f8 is to defend f7. We can't prevent castling, but we can prepare. I have an idea combining tactics and positional play: the bishop from c4 to d3 — I know I said the bishop is crucial there, but circumstances have changed; f7 is no longer a weakness —

— especially since Black is going to castle queenside, so protecting the centre matters more. The knight wants the c4-square more than the bishop; the knight to c4 comes with greater effect. After he castles and puts a rook on e8, our e4-pawn is nicely protected, freeing the knight for c4, pressuring the bishop and the e5-pawn; I'll happily take that bishop for two bishops against two knights. Pawn storms are slow, cumbersome, and generally overrated.
In opposite-side castling, a lot of people indiscriminately go b4, a4, b5 — that's not the only way.

You can also play with your pieces — the knight from d2 to c4. We're still sacrificing the h2-pawn; if he takes d4 and the bishop takes h2, nothing has changed — we'll still have a monster centre, and Black will have logistical problems getting the bishop back out.
The caveman attack has its time and place, but not every position. The rook to e8 — a great move. Let me think in silence.

The queen to g3 — its intention is to prevent the pawn takes d4. Didn't I want to encourage that? This is a dynamic position — things change every move: now the pawn takes d4 is an x-ray against my queen, with the knight takes c4 and f5 ideas, so it's a bigger enemy. The queen to g3 sits on a good square and stops the pawn takes d4, because the knight takes d6 wins the bishop with check. If the knight to h5, the queen tucks away on h3, x-raying the knight on d7. I'm starting to get control, though there's a lot of work to do.

The knight to g8. Notice the work of the bishop on d3 — a purely defensive piece, and defensive pieces are underrated: it guards the pawn on e4 so I needn't worry. Kusha probably wants f6 or f5. The tempting rook to f1 runs into f6, so maybe drop the bishop from g5.

The bishop to e3 — I like it a lot, because it solidifies the centre and attacks the g7-pawn. The bishop has done its job on g5; now it's time for a more defensive posture. Now g7 is hanging — that's our first threat.

g6 is a pretty significant weakness we can try to exploit later; Black's position is starting to show cracks. f5 isn't a threat — we can take the bishop, but no hurry, though maybe there is, or the bishop drops back to e7. One idea: the rook to f1 inducing f6, then take the bishop and reposition it to c4, or move the queen to h3, or launch the pawn storm — a4 is tempting, grabbing queenside space.
Let's start by doubling — the rook to f1 — and speed up a little; Kusha is a very fast player.

f6. I have an idea — the queen to h3, attacking h7 and x-raying the knight; the knight is protecting e5 and f6, so the queen to h3 strains those pawns, and that may lead to an unexpected tactic. I wanted the pawn to sit on f6 first, to restrict the knight.
I want to vary our openings — instead of the Queen's Gambit Declined I've leaned on, let's play the Baltic.

The Baltic is the bishop to f5 — the whole point is to develop this bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain before playing e6. The critical try is queen b3, which develops the queen and hits b7. The key is not to panic: pretend nothing is hanging and just develop rapidly. In the Baltic you throw caution to the wind — you sacrifice the b7-pawn for initiative against the queen, and you bank on quick development and opening the centre early.
The rationale for the Baltic is simple: you want a Queen's Gambit Declined, but without burying the bishop behind the pawn chain. Positionally it's a very sound idea.
We meet the king's pawn with c6 — the Caro-Kann.
White claims the full centre with d4.
We strike back at the centre with d5 — the heart of the Caro-Kann.
White pushes past with e5 — the Advance Variation, locking the centre and banking on space.

Here's the whole reason the Caro exists: unlike the French, we get to develop this light-squared bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain, to f5, before we ever shut it in with e6 — and that's exactly what we've done. White answers with f4, grabbing more central space, but it's not a good move: it curbs the development of White's own light bishop and it weakens his king.
The proper reply is e6 — White has over-committed his pawns while lagging in development.

White develops the bishop to d3. Since this is our first Advance Caro, here's the rationale. The centre is CLOSED, and a closed centre is built of pawn chains — our black pawns form one chain, and d4 with e5 is White's chain. The side with more levers, more ability to attack and undermine the OTHER side's chain, is the side holding the initiative — and the whole point of the Caro is that Black is that side. White's compensation is space; those two things balance out. And right now we don't want to surrender this prime parking spot on f5 so easily — we trade it on OUR terms.
Trading on our own terms means: when this bishop comes off, we want to replace it with a KNIGHT. So the typical move is the knight to h6 — and if White takes on f5, we recapture with the knight.
White develops the knight to f3. Why do we want our knight to reach f5? To pressure d4. So the question becomes how we keep piling onto that pawn.
We play c5 — hitting the base of White's pawn chain, and at the same time opening the c6 square for our knight.
White trades, capturing on f5.
We recapture with the knight, capturing on f5 — and now we have TWO attackers bearing on the d4 pawn.
White castles. Now we could grab d4 at once, but to play it cleanly there's a subtlety worth a second — and note White can also take on c5, which we'll deal with.

Rather than snatch d4 immediately, we play the knight to c6 first — the more flexible move, since we want it on the board regardless. The queen to b6 is also possible, but we hold it in reserve: if White plays c3, THEN the queen to b6 becomes strong.
White plays c3, showing his intent to prop up d4.

Now the clean way is to take on d4 first and then play the queen to b6, winning the pawn — and in a real game that's what I'd do. But I want to show a beautiful idea, so I play the queen to b6 first, hoping he grabs a pawn.
White plays b3, refusing to walk into it.
He won't allow the trick, so we simply take, capturing on d4 — there's a lot to unpack in this Advance.

White recaptures, capturing on d4. This is a critical pawn: it's the link that breaks up his chain, and with two of our pieces attacking it against a single defender, it's falling — and his whole position starts to crumble.
The knight from c6 takes, capturing on d4 — we've won the pawn and reached the decisive stage: up material, with a protected passed pawn on d5.
White plays the king to h1 — a good move, sidestepping a discovered-check threat.
We ask what we haven't done yet, and develop with the bishop to c5 — a great move. The h5 push was also good, but we save it; g4 would have been White's best, though I don't expect it.
White takes our knight, capturing on d4 — a mistake; now he collapses. The only question is what we recapture with.
We recapture with the bishop, capturing on d4 — the right choice. White's rook is now in trouble, and the game is essentially over: he's losing it.

White finds g4. Here's a common trap — tunnel vision. After a move like the bishop to d4, many players automatically snatch the rook on a1. But look wider: taking on a1 gives up our knight, so White gets a knight back for the rook — a real chunk of material. So we do NOT grab the rook immediately.

And not the knight to e3 either — White just takes it, and then our bishop, which we've assigned the vital task of winning the rook, gets distracted defending. Instead we simply drop the knight back to e7. The point isn't to activate it; we're after far greener pastures — the rook. White's best is the knight to c3, cutting his losses to just the knight.
White does find the knight to c3, and we take it, capturing on c3 — good defence, but we're winning the rook.
White saves the rook to b1. Now — White's king is very weak: the move g4 has opened a direct avenue toward it.

We exploit that avenue with d4 — a move doing several jobs at once: it shelters our bishop on c3, advances our passed pawn, and prepares the queen to c6, setting up a discovered check. It also opens the path for our e7-knight to reroute via d5 and even into e3 when we're ready.
We have Black against a strong player — White opens the pawn to d4 and we answer the knight to f6.
White pushes the pawn to d5 — unusual, and played in bullet by some strong grandmasters. It's not terrible, but only good if White follows it up very carefully.
We play the pawn to g6 — our response doesn't change, a King's Indian setup.
White builds the pawn chain with c4.
The bishop to g7, the fianchetto.
White develops the knight to f3.
We castle — the kingside is developed, and now we get down to punishing White's overextension in the centre.
White plays the bishop to e3 — a slightly odd move that locks in the f1-bishop. White's c4-and-d5 chain aims to cramp us, so we want to break it.
The pawn to c6 — the basic idea, using our own pawn to break the chain. I prefer c6 to e6: it opens an avenue for our queen, and if White takes on c6 we recapture and develop.
White plays the knight to d2.
We capture on d5, and White switches into bullet mode with the queen to c2.
We keep developing with the knight to c6.

White plays the knight to d4, offering a trade. The default from beginner level on is to keep the tension — only trade with a good reason — and here I dislike taking, because it lets White's bishop reposition to contest ours and ease his kingside development.

The knight to d4 threatens nothing, so we develop with the pawn to d6, and White reroutes the knight to b3. Now the decisive central invasion begins — I'm focused on the centre, where White has a failing pawn structure.
We take on d4 first — modifying the move order so White can't reply with a knight capture on c6 that gains a tempo for the defence.
White recaptures on d4, and we play the pawn to e5.
White's bishop is chased back to e3 — then the pawn to d4 drives in a nasty wedge.
But before that, we throw in the bishop to f5 with tempo — not playing automatically; this move has zero downside and a major upside.
White plays the queen to d2, and now we don't play d4 at all, since it might allow the bishop to h6.
Instead we take on c4 — far more efficient, winning another pawn, and White is suffocating without any kingside development.

White plays the knight to a5. It hangs by a single thread — if we could kick the queen off the diagonal we'd win it, but the knight to e4 runs into the queen to b4, a dead end. So look at the interference tactic.
The pawn to c3 — the interference tactic. It's a deep move: after the queen takes it, we hunt the knight and induce further concessions.
White captures on c3.
The knight to d5 — hitting the queen and preparing to cash in. If the queen drops back, we take the bishop and White can't recapture with the queen.
White plays the queen to b3, blundering the knight.
The point would have been to induce horrific, fatal damage to White's pawn structure.
Through a strange move order we've reached a Jobava London, and the whole game turns on one idea: trading the dark bishops to expose White's centre.
After d5 and Nc3 it's a Jobava London — and Nc3 carries a hidden cost: it makes the pawn on d4 chronically weak, which becomes our target.
notes.teaches: Nc3 in a Queen's-Pawn setup weakens d4; pressure it with c5.

notes.explains: White opens with the flank move g3, so we grab the center at once with e5 — a reverse Modern where we get the big pawn share.
teaches: answer a flank opening by taking the center

notes.explains: White heads for the Hippopotamus, fianchettoing on both wings and conceding the center entirely.

The key move: c6. It's aimed at the fianchettoed light-squared bishop, disarming it by leaving it to bite on granite against a fixed pawn wall — a London-flavored idea, with the bishop coming to d6 next.
teaches: blunt the fianchettoed bishop with a pawn wall

notes.explains: The bishop to d6 props up the e5-pawn; a later f4 holds no real danger for us here.
White's knight to f3 is already a slight inaccuracy — in the Hippo it belongs on e2, precisely so this doesn't happen.
teaches: the Hippo knight belongs on e2

notes.explains: And here's why: the pawn to e4 clamps the light squares, seizing space the fianchettoed bishop can no longer contest.
White's knight to e5 is dubious — we're not winning outright, but Black is now solidly the better side.
The harmonious answer is the queen to e7 — natural development that leaves the intruding knight with no squares, so White must lash out with f4 or d4, both weakening.
teaches: improve a piece while trapping his

notes.explains: An instructive moment: we do NOT capture en passant here. Taking would do the dark-squared bishop and the f3-square a real favor — and our pawn on e4 is exactly what clamps f3 shut. The clamp is worth more than the trade.
teaches: don’t relieve his bad bishop or free f3

notes.explains: The right way to remove the knight is clinical, not the capture on e5 that would hand over our good bishop — the queen's knight comes to d7 to swap it off instead.
teaches: trade off cleanly, keep your good bishop

notes.explains: We take White; Black answers our king's pawn with ...e5.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black develops ...Nc6; we develop the knight to c3.
Black plays the aggressive ...f5.
We strike back with d4.
Black takes on e4.
We grab on e5 with the knight.
Black develops ...Nf6.
We pin with the bishop to g5.
Black pins with ...Bb4.
We develop the bishop to c4.
Black takes our knight, capturing on c3 with check.
We recapture with the b-pawn.
Black pushes d5.
We retreat the bishop to b3.
Black castles.
We castle.
Black plays the queen to e8.
We take on f6.
Black recaptures with the rook; we grab on d5 with check.
Black's king steps to h8.
We snatch on e4.
Black takes our knight on e5.
We recapture with the d-pawn.
Black lifts the rook to h6.
We play f4.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
We play the queen to e2.
Black plays the rook to d8.
We push f5.
Black retreats the bishop to f7; we push the passed pawn to e6.
Black plays the bishop to h5.
We push g4, hitting the bishop.
Black plays ...Qe7; we take on h5 with the g-pawn.
Black checks with ...Qg5.
We block with the queen to g2.
Black grabs on h5.
We centralize the rook to e1.
Black plays the rook to f6.
We reroute the bishop to d3.
Black plays the queen to h6.
We grab on b7 with the queen.
Black plays g6.
We take on c7.
Black plays the rook to g8.
We centralize the queen to e5.
Black takes on f5 with check; we step the king to h1.
Black plays the queen to g7.
We play the rook to g1.
Black checks with ...Qb7; we block with the bishop to e4.
Black retreats the queen to e7.
We take on g8 with check.
Black recaptures with the king; we check again with the rook on g1.
Black's king steps to f8.
We check with the queen on b8.
Black blocks with ...Qe8.
We play the rook to g7; Black takes with the king; and we take on e8, winning the queen.
We have White, open with the pawn to e4, and get e5.
The knight to f3, aiming for a normal open game.
Black strikes with the pawn to d5 — the Elephant Gambit. It's a more serious line than it's often credited: if White misplays it, Black gets a genuine initiative out of the opening.
The best line by most grandmasters' verdict — the knight takes e5. Capturing on d5 is also fine; there are several roads to an edge.
We're Black against the knight to f3. We go the knight to f6.
d4. Let's play
d5 — I want to play d5.
This is what's called the Colle System — White plays e3, a very peaceful, quiet line.
Black has many ways to respond, but there's one line people don't really talk about — the bishop to d7.
Something people don't talk about. I was going to play the bishop to g4 — I guess
we'll just do it now, the bishop to g4. It's not the
end of the world — it just lost a tempo. And c4.

Let's go e6, basically playing a Queen's Gambit structure, except with the bishop outside the pawn chain. The problem with my loss of a tempo is that it gave him a chance to develop, with the queen coming to b3. Now this b7-pawn is hanging. The move you often want to avoid is b6 — it creates a lot of weaknesses on that side, look at the c6-square and the light squares b6 weakens, and White has the very nasty knight to e5; if that knight reaches e5 we come under real pressure. So logically, since b6 and g5 are a problem, I'll make a move that may look like a blunder: just take the knight on f3. The queen takes b7 is often possible in such positions, but here it's not as good as it looks — after the queen grabs b7, the knight to d7 is the usual move, but we can actually snatch the pawn on g2 with that same bishop, which is why he didn't go for it. Now, we want to have some fun — we don't want to play like a coward. I'm proposing that we sacrifice. What am I noticing? White's king won't be safe on the kingside, and it's very far from castling queenside; and here's the funny thing — if White takes on b7, that does our bidding for us, because if White then castles queenside, the open b-file gives us very nice play. So we pretend there's no threat and develop as normal. In such positions we rarely put the knight on c6, because we want the c5 pawn lever, so we develop the knight to d7 anyway — objectively probably unsound, but I've had a lot of success sacking b7 like this. What should we recapture with? Both pieces make sense: taking with the pawn preserves the structure; taking with the knight keeps the centre looser and more open, which I like — provocative chess, trying to get him to play e4 and weaken the centre. It's a Grünfeld-style approach where we don't occupy the centre with pawns, planning c5 at some point. Do we play g6? We might, but I don't think we need to — we can just get the bishop out to d6. Then e4, which I think is a mistake. Now the most energetic move — not the knight to f4, that blunders the knight — the knight to g4. We're not threatening to capture the bishop, but there's a hidden threat; we want to play as aggressively as possible, because White is extremely underdeveloped, and the way to exploit a development lead is to open the centre. We could play e5, but that gives the queen pressure on f7 — better to play c5. Then a3, and the knight drops back to c6, increasing the pressure on d4; the knight to d4 is coming and it's unstoppable, these knights are pouring out. e4 walked right into what we wanted, and c5 and a3 is also a mistake — this knight wants to be on c6, then on d4. d5 isn't dangerous; the knight to d4, and now the queen has to keep control of c2, so it goes back, and we grab the pawn, weakening his centre even further — this is close to losing for White. The queen to h4 is a move to keep in mind, but it does nothing yet. Taking on d5 makes sense — weaken his centre and open the e-file, and later we can put a rook to e8. If I were White I'd seriously consider not recapturing, but he recaptures. This is an instructive moment: people get tempted to do something immediate, but the best approach is to complete your development — nothing good happens when only one piece is developed; that knight is great, but without the other pieces and a safe king it's hard to do what we want. So the bishop to d6 — this requires patience — then castle, and only then start thinking about concrete actions. Do we defend that knight, or allow White to capture it on d4? The answer is no, we don't need to defend it — let him take it — because this bishop is the only thing standing in the way of us dominating the e-file; if White takes on d4 twice, we simply put a rook to e8, and this knight on d7 can jump to c5 and perhaps to b3 later. We're essentially replacing one advantage with another — transforming your advantage is one of the hardest things to master, because visually you look at the knight and want to preserve it. Now, which piece to activate? The bishop to e5 would block the e-file — no; the rook to c8 allows the knight to e4; so the knight to c5, threatening the knight to b3, and taking the sting out of a potential g4 — the knight is excellently placed on c5 even if we never reach b3. We certainly don't play the knight to b3 now, because that blunders checkmate in one; we don't have many ways to meet that mate threat, but f6 is perfectly acceptable — it blunts the queen and creates a stronghold on e5. The bishop to f8 was possible, but why overload the bishop? The queen to d1, and White's king is basically busted. When you're attacking, take free material that lies by the side of the road, so if the attack fizzles you still have something to fall back on — the bishop is coming back to e5, a great square, so we grab a pawn along the way first. White is defending well and making it hard, but now the material is equal and he has nothing to show for it, and our pieces are beautifully placed. The only piece we haven't activated is the queen — reverse-engineer where it belongs: the queen to b6 isn't as good because of b4; I want the queen on the kingside where everything is abandoned, so the queen to d7, heading for h3. We could also play f5, opening the path to h4 — equally good. King to f1. Before the queen goes to h3, I'll start with the bishop to f4 — you'll understand the idea soon — then the queen to h3, and if I've calculated correctly we're winning. I actually missed one detail and got a bit bamboozled; rather than take the bishop and try to mate, it's better just to restore the material balance and win positionally. Snag another pawn — now we're up a pawn, and Black is still winning pretty handily. One detail: if White ever captures on f6 with the queen, trying to use the pin, we have a trick — we can 'blunder' the f6-pawn and play the queen takes g2, taking the rook with check so the queen is no longer pinned. Then g4, an excellent move — we take it; the rook to c8 was actually bad, there was an insane idea White had there. Then the bishop to d6. We could take and take on e4, but then the queen to b3 wins our bishop — so instead we drop the bishop back to e6 and blockade with the rook to e8, trying to win the pawn; or the bishop to e7, getting it out of the danger zone. I like blockading the passed pawn so nothing can happen with promotion. Then the bishop to c4 — be careful: although it's not possible right now, a move like the queen to d3 would be dangerous, and the queen to a4 is the same concept, because if we move our bishop he pins our queen and wins. So we defend the bishop with the queen and sidestep the pin: the queen to d6 — better than the queen to e7, because now we have the idea of mating him on d1 if the queen ever loses control of that square. The king to f8 is interesting, but the king to h8 is much safer, and the queen to f7 here is a very common blunder that misses the mate. e5 seems to be panic — we take the pawn, up a ton, and it's winning. King to g1. Remember the queen to f7 is a real threat, so the queen has done its job on d6 — we keep the bishop protected and cover f7 with the queen to e7. Then a6, accomplishing our main plan, and White can resign, because the bishop is actually trapped: the bishop to a4, b5, and White loses not only the bishop but the pawn too. A good game, very well played by our opponent, who climbed back
Against the knight to f3, play the same setup — it's so likely to transpose into a d4 opening. It could be an independent King's Indian Attack, but here it transposes.
We answer with g6.
g6 is the gateway to both the Grünfeld and the King's Indian.
He chooses the fianchetto setup, and to start we complete our kingside development.
Castle short — and here's the main crossroads. d6 is what a King's Indian player chooses; d5 is the Grünfeld move, and that's what we're playing.
d5, reaching a completely symmetrical position.
He plays the main line, c4 — a very theoretical line, impressive to see at this level. Another major crossroads, with two main moves.

The top-GM choice is the Slav-style c6, but the more testing line at club level — the one I played against Kramnik — is to take on c4. c6 leads to dull, often symmetric positions that draw at the highest level.
The King's Indian is theoretically demanding because White has a huge spread of systems, all of roughly equal value — so don't just learn the classical main line and assume you're covered.
notes.teaches: Against a broad opening, prepare across every system, not only the one with 'main line' in its name.

notes.explains: The setup is the same against everything: g6, Bg7, d6, castle, and let White declare which system he's chosen.
Black meets the king-pawn with c5, the Sicilian.
Black develops the knight to f6, immediately poking the e4-pawn and inviting White to commit the centre.
Black lashes out with f5, gaining a tempo on the e4-knight but committing the pawns and leaving lasting holes on the light squares around the king.
teaches: A ...f5 thrust wins a tempo but weakens the king\u2019s light squares

notes.explains: The knight drops back to c3, and Black's knight sorties to b4, eyeing the tender c2 and d3 squares.
White reaches for the fianchetto with g3 — the bishop will rake the long light diagonal, exactly where Black just created weaknesses.
teaches: Fianchetto toward the squares the opponent weakened

notes.explains: Black strikes the centre with d5, and the pawn can be taken in passing.
White captures en passant on d6.
After the recapture White completes the fianchetto, the bishop settling on g2 and glaring down the long diagonal.
Both sides castle and the middlegame battle lines are drawn.
Black claims space with e5, building a broad pawn front.
White keeps it flexible with a small centre on d3, a King's-Indian-in-reverse setup behind the fianchetto.
White reroutes the knight to d2, heading for the fine c4 and e4 squares in front of Black's pawns.
teaches: Reroute a knight toward the outpost in front of the enemy pawns

notes.explains: The light-squared bishops come off, and after the trade White grabs the c4-pawn, opening files toward Black's queenside.
Black pushes e4, ramming the centre and asking White how to meet the advance.
White answers f3, levering directly against the e4-pawn to break Black's front open.
teaches: Lever an advanced enemy pawn with f3 to open lines

notes.explains: White breaks through on e4 and emerges a pawn up with the freer position — the engine reads it as a clear edge for White, the sharp opening having gone White's way.
A flurry of captures peels the queens off the board, White carrying that healthy edge into the middlegame.
White plays c3 to slam the door on the d4-square — Black's knights are the real problem here, and denying them the central outpost is job one.
teaches: Deny active knights their central outpost with a pawn

notes.explains: Black's knights swarm into the centre, one landing on e5 beside White's on d5 — active, annoying pieces that keep the defense on its toes.
Here the thread slips: the rook to d1 lets the edge evaporate, the engine snapping all the way back to dead level. A single loose move under pressure can hand back everything the opening earned.
teaches: One careless move can surrender a whole game\u2019s advantage

notes.explains: The knight leaps in with a check on f3, forking into White's camp and grabbing back material.
The pieces come off in a burst of trades, and the game simplifies toward a sharp minor-piece ending.
Black grabs a loose queenside pawn and edges a pawn ahead — now it's White defending a knight-and-rook ending, a pawn down but holdable.
teaches: A pawn-down knight ending is often a fortress if the pieces are active

notes.explains: The knights and rooks dance through checks and probes; with active pieces and few pawns, White keeps the balance and the position stays a fight.
teaches: Activity, not material count, decides these light endings
plans: Keep the knight and rook active
Trade into a drawable pawn-down ending

notes.explains: We take Black and answer the king's pawn with the Sicilian.
White develops the knight to f3.
We develop the knight to c6.
White plays the bishop to b5 — the Rossolimo.
We reply g6 — the natural choice if you play the accelerated dragon against the Open Sicilian.
White castles.
We complete the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
White plays the rook to e1, keeping maximum flexibility.
We play the surprising ...e5 — it blocks the bishop and leaves holes, yet it's the heart of Black's Rossolimo setup, since it clamps d4 and hands the knight the e7-square.
White develops the knight to c3.
We link the knights with ...Nge7 and prepare ...d6 — our pawns on c5 and e5 combining to lock down d4 so White can never play the break.
White plays d3 — a touch cramped without the d4 break.
We play d6, deliberately holding off on castling — the closed centre means our king is safe in the middle for now.
White plays the bishop to g5.
We kick it with f6 — normally unthinkable, but with the centre closed it's perfectly safe.
The bishop retreats to e3.
We develop the bishop to e6, covering the a2–g8 diagonal that ...f6 just weakened.
White plays the queen to d2.
We castle kingside at last.
White offers the trade with the bishop to h6.
We play the bishop to g4 — the plan is to take on f3, wreck White's kingside, then land our own knight on d4 with a fork, the queen eyeing h3.
White trades on g7.
We recapture with the king.
White defends the f3-knight with the rook to e3 — but rook and knight now sit on forkable squares.
We plant the knight on d4.
White takes it.
We recapture with the pawn, hitting the rook on e3.
White dodges with the rook to g3.
We capture on c3, removing the knight — and the pawn simultaneously attacks the queen.
White recaptures on c3; we're a clean piece up for a pawn.
We're White. d4, and e6 — a very commonly misunderstood move. Black allows a transition to the French, but if you don't play e4 yourself, there's no need to transition to the French.
Because maybe your opponent does play the French against c4 — so if you're a d4 player who wants main lines, you just play c4 anyway; there's no reason not to.
He plays d6 — already very weird, d6 and e6. Just like in e4 openings, you handle this exactly the same way: occupy
part of the centre, then develop your pieces quickly. A couple of ways to proceed — we could play e4 for more centre, or just develop the knights; let's play the knight to c3 and test the waters.
The bishop to e7 — very passive. Nothing horrible about it, just tremendously passive.
So I'd propose e4, building a three-pawn centre — we're trying to punish him.

But there's always a balance between controlling the centre with pawns and developing your pieces. We could toe the line with f4 — I'd probably play f4 in one of my own games — but for players in this range I recommend mastering that balance rather than pushing the envelope: it's much better to keep your

pieces developed and your centre well protected than to go crazy occupying the centre with five or six pawns and get overextended. So let's not reinvent the wheel — the knight to f3, developing casually.

He keeps playing very weird moves. How to continue? Let's develop as unoriginally as possible, putting pieces on reasonable squares. I'd prefer the bishop to d3 — because I don't yet know where the dark-squared bishop belongs; if he plays the knight to f6, that bishop might want to jump to g5, so we delay it until he shows his cards. But the light-squared bishop we don't need to delay, and I prefer d3 over e2 because
on d3 it supports the e4-pawn, and if we later play e5 you can imagine it aiming at the h7-pawn — a lot of potential energy.
Now we castle.
I'll play that move pretty quickly.

We need to be very patient against these setups. If we strike too early — some of you want d5 — d5 looks good, but after e5 it just lets him close the centre. You often get only one try to punish, so be well prepared for it; don't strike willy-nilly and prematurely.
What move gears us up for the centre opening? The rook to e1 — it not only helps prepare e5, but if we play d5 and the centre

opens up, the rook is going to be well poised. He plays g5, and now the time has come to step on the gas — he keeps abandoning his development, and if we do nothing he plays g4 and the opportunity train leaves the station. Two realistic ways to break through: d5 or e5. d5 isn't great, because he can play e5. Who can explain why e5 — provoking d5 — is a better version for White than us playing d5 and letting him play e5?
It's an instructive difference. I'll play e5 now because of the time situation, and I anticipate d5. We keep the centre pawns and block the development of the knight
on g8 — it can't go to f6, which is very significant — and we open up more of the position. After d5, c-takes-d5, we open the c-file, and this structure
The real issue here is that this is insufficient compensation — that's the core of the problem, and I probably should have captured earlier.
I need to find a very accurate move here, or I'm simply lost.
He somehow defends everything, so the rook to d4 — I really don't think I have a choice.
Now I get to trap the knight.
After the rook to b3 the knight is suddenly trapped — the rook to d1 next seals it. In the rook-to-d4 line his knight to c5 intercepted the bishop, but here the rook simply comes to d1 and it works.
Fix his pawn on a dark square, so that we can attack it with our bishop.
Infiltrating makes sense — the rook to d3, the king to f2, and then go for the direct attack on g7.
The rook to c7 is simpler, though everything is winning by now.
Against the Modern we run the 150 Attack: Be3, the queen to d2, and a quick h4 — the order of h4 barely matters as long as it goes in.
h4 gains kingside space and probes; whether it comes now or a move later is fine.
Black wants his bishop on b7, so we play f3 first — reinforcing e4 so that when the bishop arrives it isn't hitting a loose pawn.
notes.teaches: Pre-defend the pawn a fianchettoed bishop will target, before the bishop gets there.

notes.explains: A menu for the light bishop: Bd3 severs contact with d4 and invites c5; castling instead ups our control of the d-file and discourages c5 — but there's a sharper third idea.
notes.teaches: Each bishop square trades a different concession; know what each one invites before you choose.

notes.explains: That third idea is Bh3, leaning on e6. It isn't a move we must follow up immediately — the point is that from here on White threatens a sacrifice there, and Black has to reckon with it every move.
notes.teaches: Building pressure on a point forces the defender to spend resources on it, weakening him elsewhere.

notes.explains: Nf4 plants the knight on its ideal square, piling more pressure onto e6 — and notice we haven't castled: the king is perfectly safe in the centre while we prioritize the attack.
notes.teaches: Don't castle on reflex; if your king is safe, keep developing the attack instead.

notes.explains: His Nf8 is the only real defense — it guards e6, so taking there twice just trades our attackers off.
So we castle — patient, no forced sacrifices, simply completing development and increasing the pressure.
notes.teaches: When the pressure is building on its own, finish developing rather than forcing the issue.

notes.explains: And then a healthy waiting move, Kb1 — good chess procrastination: improve the king's safety and let the opponent commit first.
notes.teaches: A prophylactic king-tuck like Kb1 is a useful waiting move that never wastes a tempo.

notes.explains: When he gives up his dark-squared bishop, the dark squares around his king turn permanently weak — that's the concession we'll exploit.
notes.teaches: Trading off the king's-side bishop leaves a dark-square hole complex behind it.

notes.explains: The knight is attacked, and we can't defend the pawn directly, so reroute the knight toward the centre where it stays relevant — and now the plan is to prise the position open to reach those weak dark squares.
notes.teaches: When the opponent surrenders a key defender, open lines to cash in the squares it guarded.

notes.explains: Careful with e5 or d5 — he answers each by pushing the other pawn past. There's a third way to crack it open.
Two clean levers: f4-f5, or c3 hitting the b4-pawn — either one opens the door without letting him seal the centre.
notes.teaches: When the natural break is neutralized, look for a flank pawn lever that opens a file instead.

notes.explains: Recapture with cxd3 — it opens the c-file for our rook and, as a bonus, shores up the e-pawn.
notes.teaches: Choose the recapture that opens a file for you while simultaneously fixing your own structure.

notes.explains: The c-file is beautiful; we don't even need to occupy it, but the rook belongs there all the same.
notes.plans: Post a rook on the open c-file to pressure c7.

notes.explains: The other rook belongs on the f-file, because once f5 lands we crash straight through his position.
notes.plans: Double toward the f-file to power the f5 break.

notes.explains: f5 is the hammer — the break the whole setup was built around.
After the exchanges, don't rush the recapture: take with the rook, sacrificing the exchange to keep the light bishop as the main attacker — his king is caught in the crossfire.
notes.teaches: Give up the exchange to preserve the piece that actually delivers the attack.

notes.explains: Follow the attack: Bf4 leans on the c7-pawn, coordinating with the rook already on the c-file.
notes.plans: Combine bishop and c-file rook against c7.

notes.explains: Now the knight on h7 is a loose piece, defended only by a rook — so attack that rook with the piece we just improved.
notes.teaches: Undefended-except-by-one pieces fall when you hit their single defender.

notes.explains: Be5 improves the bishop and hits the rook; then ask which squares just opened — Qg5 and Rc6 arrive, and the knight is lost into mate.
We open with the queen's pawn, looking for a solid, structured game.
The fianchetto — this could be a King's Indian or a Grünfeld.

Black commits to the Grünfeld with d5 — the ultimate hypermodern opening. It concedes the center on purpose, then swarms it with pieces. You rarely see it below master level because it demands staggering memorization; it's one of the hardest openings to learn.
The natural e4 kicks the knight and builds the broad pawn center Black has invited us to build.

There's the hypermodern bargain: Black lets us plant pawns on d4 and c3 and fianchettoes, planning to strike with c5, the knight to c6, and the bishop to g4 — giving up the center only to assault it as fast as possible.
teaches: Black concedes then attacks the center

notes.explains: Here's my sideline that sidesteps the theoretical ocean — the bishop check on b5. Practically it's hard for Black to equalize against it.
The point is simpler than it looks: induce c6, then tuck the bishop back to a4. It delays Black's freeing c5, slices through the position, and can later drop to b3 to eye f7.

The knight goes to e2, not f3 — f3 would walk into the g4 pin, while e2 keeps f3 in reserve to shoo the bishop and, above all, lends another defender to the d4-pawn for the coming c5 and Nc6 pressure.
teaches: Ne2 keeps f3 available and guards d4

notes.explains: We roll out the Alapin — e4, and Black answers with the Sicilian, c5.
The Alapin move: c3, preparing to build a big centre with d4.
Black develops the knight to f6, hitting e4, so we shove it away with e5.
The knight jumps in to d5.
Here the traditional move is d4, but the newer idea — the one I like at this level — is the knight to f3 first.
Black plays d6, striking at our e5 pawn.
Now the modern idea from the Alapin course — a check on b5. To feel its power you need one very important tactic in this line.
Black blocks with the bishop to d7 — the most popular response, and exactly what we wanted to provoke.
We drop the bishop back to c4. The point: if the knight retreats to b6, hitting the bishop, we have a trick.
Black plays the natural knight to b6, attacking our bishop — and now the trick.

We sacrifice — the bishop takes on f7 with check, and the king must recapture on f7. Most people follow with the knight to g5, but here that's WRONG: the king to g8 is a dead end, and the queen to b3 isn't mate because Black blocks with c4.

The key is to start with e6, check. If you play the knight to g5 first, e6 lets the bishop retreat to e8. So e6 first: if Black takes with the king, it's forced mate with the knight to g5, the king driven into the open; if Black takes with the bishop, the knight to g5 wins the piece back with a slight edge.
This isn't a forced win, just a small edge — and Black takes with the bishop, capturing on e6.
Now the knight to g5, check.

Black's king steps to f6 — this is supposed to be losing. I'm nearly certain it's the queen to f3. Calculating: if the king takes the knight, then h4, the king to g6, h5, the king to h6 forced, then d4 with a discovery — but the king can escape to g7. Instead, after h4 and the king to the side, the queen to e3 is mate. d4 would let Black save the bishop to d5 and make our queen harder to activate.
So the queen to f3, check — I still remember this is the move.
Black takes the knight, capturing on g5 — if I've calculated right, it's forced mate.
h4, check.
The king to h6 — and what Black forgot is the queen-f4 idea.
The queen to f4, check — and it's mate, with just a pawn, the queen and the rook. A thirteen-move game, all theory, and Black resigns.
We have White, and after the pawn to e4 comes e5. My recommendation against this is a blend of two openings — the Four Knights Scotch and the Vienna — but today Black is heading for the Philidor.

The knight to f3. The Four Knights Scotch is criminally under-studied below 2000, and far from the boring reputation it carries — but that's a talk for another day, because we're about to face the Philidor.
Black plays the pawn to d6 — the Philidor. It has a shoddy reputation, deservedly, but you still have to know how to meet it; the game won't win itself.

But I like starting with the bishop to c4 — incredibly tricky, and it sets an immediate trap: Philidor players are disconcerted when White doesn't play d4. I learned this from a Kasparov game; unlike his d3 Italian route, we'll follow up with d4.
Black develops the bishop to e7.
First we finish queenside development with the knight to c3, then we castle or play d4. The move order barely matters, as long as d4 arrives in good time.
Black develops the knight to f6.
This is as good a moment as any — the pawn to d4, opening the centre.
Black captures on d4 — still theory.
We recapture, the knight taking on d4.

Black castles — and now beware the universal center fork trick: the knight takes e4, then the pawn to d5 forks two of our minor pieces. It's not fatal — dropping the bishop to d3 keeps the bishop pair, three minors against three — but trading our e4-pawn for Black's d6-pawn is a bad deal: it opens Black's bishop and our whole edge rests on superior central control. We avoid it not with f3, which is weakening and we're not castled, but simply by moving the bishop.

The bishop to b3 — not d3, because if we wanted d3 why go to c4 at all? We developed to c4 to stay on this diagonal. The pawn there may look loose for a move or two, but we can defend it many ways after castling, and Black can't attack it effectively.

Black plays the pawn to a6, preparing to expand with b5. A reminder: don't reflexively meet a6 with a4 — sometimes you want to invite b5 and then answer with a4, shattering the chain. But here allowing b5 lets Black meet a4 with the pawn to c5, chasing the knight, then c4, locking our bishop out in a very concrete, tactical struggle.
And I'm not in the mood for something that concrete this early — so the pawn to a4, the direct prophylactic that stops b5. The pawn to a3 was possible, but a4 is the cleaner prevention.
Black develops the bishop to d7.
We continue with castling — unafraid of c5.
Black develops the knight to c6.
So we keep improving as if nothing's happening — the rook to e1, a good general move to make before committing the bishop.
Black captures, the knight taking on d4.
We recapture with the queen.

Black centralizes the bishop to c6. White is clearly better — better pieces, better centre — but Black is rock-solid with no weaknesses, and it's hard to make progress against a position with no weaknesses. Be patient and methodical, and don't imagine you're winning just because you have more space. Now, where to put the bishop? The bishop to g5 looks natural, but...
I dislike the bishop to g5 because Black moves the knight and offers a bishop trade — and trades favour the cramped side, plus Black's e7-bishop is a dud. So the bishop goes to f4 instead.

Black plays the knight to d7 — a fine Philidor move, preparing both c5 and the bishop to f6; our bishop bites on granite, but at least our rooks are coordinated. So I'll preemptively move the queen off d4, or the bishop to f6 would come with tempo.
The queen to d2 — a prudent prophylactic that also prevents the bishop to g5 offering a dark-squared trade. With our space edge, we want to keep pieces on.

Black plays the knight to e5. A kingside attack — the rook lift to e3 and g3 — is tempting, but hard: Black has defenders and the knight can return to g6 to cover the g-file. Better to play in the centre, where our superiority is greatest, with a natural move that forces Black to part with a bishop.
The knight to d5 — it makes no concession, just piles on central pressure and forces Black to give up one of the bishops.
Black captures, the bishop taking on d5. This is different from avoiding trades earlier — here we remove Black's strongest piece, the well-centralized bishop, and gain the bishop pair.
We recapture with the bishop, hitting b7 — not with the pawn, which would leave our bishop complaining about its own structure.
We open with e4, and Black chooses the French Defense, e6.
We take the centre with d4.
Black challenges it with d5 — the heart of the French.
We push past into the Advance, e5, grabbing space.
Black strikes at the base of the chain with c5 — standard fare. Most players now automatically prop the chain with c3, entering heavy theory.

But my recommendation slips through the cracks — the Nimzowitsch French: the knight to f3, developing as if nothing's wrong, letting Black wreck our pawn chain by taking on d4. It seems utterly counter-intuitive to allow that, even to sacrifice the d4 pawn, which is what we'll do.

Black develops the knight to c6. We keep developing as though Black exerts no pressure on d4.
