One common beginner mistake here is the bishop to b5 — not because it drops a piece, since after a queen-a5 check there's the knight to c3, but conceptually: the bishop on b5 is a paper tiger, and Black just blocks with the bishop to d7.

The best square for our bishop is d3, for several reasons. With a pawn on d4 like this, placing the bishop behind it is good practice: if Black castles kingside — the likeliest direction — we'll have a Greek-gift sacrifice ready.
Now — doesn't Black just have c4, hitting the bishop?

They do, and we retreat the bishop to e2 — but we've PROVOKED c4, and with the centre relatively closed we can afford to move the same piece twice. What did provoking c4 achieve? It took the pressure off d4 — our chain is safe now — so we can focus on completing kingside development.

Black's queenside pawns look imposing, and b5 is actually a good move — but Black has bitten off more than she can chew, pushing all those pawns without piece support. We'll use OUR pawns, a very typical idea, to break down the whole chain.
We pressure both the c4 and b5 pawns at once: b3 hits c4, and we'll follow with a4 — classic pawn play to demolish Black's chain as fast as possible.
Black plays the queen to b6.
We don't even castle first — we play a4 at once, and Black is under serious fire on the queenside. One key tactical detail: a6 is futile here.
The bishop to a6 is powerful — our opponent tries to shield the chain with the minor pieces, but they're just not good at keeping a pawn chain intact.
Which pawn first? Normally you start at the base — a takes b5, capturing on b5, removing the linchpin.
Black recaptures, capturing on b5. Now step two: take on c4, opening the centre and leaving a major weakness there.
We play b takes c4, capturing on c4 — consecutive and to the point.
Black takes, capturing on c4, and gets a massive weakness there.
We complete the trade, capturing on c4.

And after d takes c4, capturing on c4, we've achieved exactly what we set out to do — a long-term, permanent weakness on c4. Step three has two parts: complete development and solidify our own chain. The solidifying move every French-with-White player knows is c3. Not the knight to c3 — the knight goes to d2 here, because the ultimate plan is to harass and win the c4 pawn. I like to castle kingside first, getting the king clear with no nasty checks on b4, then play c3.
So we castle first — safe, since Black has no good way to hit d4; the rook to d8 is likely at this level — then we follow with c3.

Instead Black plays f6. Note the knight can't take on e5 — our f3-knight guards it. Black tries to open the centre, but that's counterproductive when you're behind in development. This is a great moment for flexibility: our whole c3-then-knight-d2 scheme is set aside, because f6 changes everything. Who benefits when the centre opens? The better-developed side with fewer weaknesses — clearly us.
So we welcome it — e takes f6, capturing on f6: you want to open the centre? Thank you very much.

Black recaptures with the knight, capturing on f6 — and now the e-file opens onto a massive weakness on e6. Two weaknesses in Black's camp: the new one on e6 and the old one on c4. Put them together and you get the classy move, the queen to e2, hitting both pawns at once. A good alternative is simply the rook to e1 — e6 is the juicy pawn; win it and we mate soon. After the queen to e2, though, there's the nasty knight takes d4: knight takes d4, knight takes d4, queen takes d4, we grab e6 with check, Black plays the bishop to e7, and I'm not sure White has a crystal-clear finish.

So the more controlled move is the rook to e1, leaving the queen guarding d4. It's incredibly hard for Black to defend e6, and Black's lack of development costs her — a developed f8-bishop would let her castle.
Black just doesn't have time to develop. The king to f7 tries to defend e6, but it's futile — the king is a poor defender in these positions.
There's a rip move — the simple fork on g5, knocking the king back. The game's far from over, though: we've won a pawn but our queenside is still undeveloped, so we need accuracy.

I'm expecting the king to g8, but our opponent plays fast and walks straight into the pin with the king to e7 — a terrible move. How do we punish it most clinically? The knight takes c6 is tempting, to set up a discovery, but it gives Black life.
The knight takes c6 lets the king slip via f7 back to g8. Better is to take on e6 with the rook, capturing on e6 — the check is a nice byproduct; what matters is the pin against the knight on c6.
The king to d7 — and now we can pre-move d5, ending the game: it wins the pinned knight on c6, and once that minor piece falls the king is hunted down.
So d5 is the game-winning move — we'll win without even using our back-rank knight or bishop, that's how powerful our existing pieces are.
The game's totally over — we take the knight next move, the knight can't move because the queen is pinned, and it's mate in three.
d takes c6, capturing on c6 with check — and importantly the pawn defends our rook. After the king to c7, the mating move is the bishop to f4.
The king to c7 — Black technically has the bishop to d6, which is why it's mate in three.
We bring the bishop out with a devastating check, the bishop to f4 — no moratorium on developing the queenside pieces.
Black blocks with the bishop to d6.
The queen takes d6, capturing on d6 — checkmate. Straightforward attacking chess, and the power of this French line at any level up to 2300.
This is a worthy opening — either as your primary weapon or as a secondary one when you tire of e4. d4, d5, the knight to c3, and the knight to f6,

and the bishop to f4 — the Jobava London. A bit of history: the sequence first appears in the database in 1882 and is sometimes called the Mason variation; it was revived and developed heavily in the mid-2000s, and much of the modern understanding of the line comes from that work.

There are several replies here — a6; e6, the most common online; the bishop to f5, which our opponent played; c5; and e4, a sharp recent innovation, where before people played e3. The knight to c6 is one appeal of this line at a lower level, because after the knight to b5 White is not simply winning — that's a misconception — but you can win quickly if Black doesn't find the only way to stop the knight taking c7, which is e5, intercepting the diagonal; and here you're supposed to take with the bishop. There's one idea worth knowing that recurs in the Jobava
Against a strong opponent we bring out our real weapon — the Ruy Lopez. We open e4, Black meets e5, and the knight develops to f3.
Black develops to c6 and we pin with the bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez.
Black plays d6 — the Steinitz Variation. It's fine, and doesn't change our approach; note that ...d6 sets up a pin of its own.
To exploit that pin we open the centre. The Ruy offers two roads — c3 preparing d4, or the immediate d4, which is perfectly good; after ...exd4 we recapture with the knight.
Black defends with the bishop to d7.
Now a hard-to-grasp move: we capture on c6. You'd think the whole point was to keep that bishop, but there's a deeper idea here.

We are pressing and keeping the pin — White stands better. There is a buffet of captures, and the e5-point is not going anywhere: Black will not take on d4 himself, as it disastrously opens the e-file, so we can round that pawn up in due course, with Black's queenside wrecked and our pieces active. But careful: a mindless bishop to e3 allows ...Rb8 hitting b2, and fianchettoing with b3 weakens the dark squares.
Black develops the knight to f6. Played right, this eventually forces Black to release the centre by taking on d4.
We castle. If Black grabs on e4, he opens the e-file — and once his bishop lands on e4 we get a big initiative.
Black takes on e4.
We recapture on e4 with the knight.
Black recaptures with the bishop on e4. How do we hit it while improving?
The rook to e1 — we can reclaim the e5-pawn later, no hurry; the rook attacks down the file and adds a pin.

We are pressing and keeping the pin — White stands better. There is a buffet of captures, and that central point is not going anywhere: Black will not take on d4 himself, as it disastrously opens the e-file, so we can round up the pawn in due course, with Black's queenside wrecked and our pieces active. But careful: a mindless bishop to e3 allows ...Rb8 hitting b2, and fianchettoing with b3 weakens the dark squares.
Another King's Indian — since we've spent so long talking about it, we might as well play it.
He plays the main line.
I'll play an interesting line I like myself — take on d4.
In effect we've reached the Maroczy structure from the last game — but with one key difference.
Our pawn is on c7 instead of e7, and that gives us a direct line of fire at the e4-pawn. The question is what breakthrough to prepare.
The typical idea is c6, aiming for the c5 break — the combative main line; the knight to c6 is also possible.
He plays the king to h1 — the best move, prophylaxis.
The plan is the knight to h5 — no surprise to anyone who watched the previous King's Indian game.
This opens ideas like the queen to h4 — and note, his bishop is now on a square where it's undefended, and our rook on e8 x-rays it.
Combine those two ideas: f5, planning to drive the pawn to f4 — which builds a stronghold for the knight on g3.
He's stopped f4 — so ask the Sam Shankland question: can we play it anyway?
Yes we can — because if he captures, we recapture, and he's forced to shed a tempo with the knight.
The typical move: centralise the bishop on e5, a fine central outpost.
And there's a sacrifice we're beginning to eye — one we can apply right now.
It's not d5 anymore — he's clamped that down — it's the knight to g3, with check.
It looks like we should just grab the rook on f1 — and against another grandmaster I would. But here we're going for mate: the queen to h4.
He defends with the bishop to d4 — a really good move.
So we take the exchange, not forfeiting the opportunity.
We've won the exchange — and now the key principle: the number one cause of disaster after winning material is forgetting to keep applying basic principles, like continuing your development.
His best try here would be c5, but he doesn't find it.
He trades pieces, which only cements our pawn structure.
To consolidate: develop the knight and bring a rook to d8 — the question is whether we can do both, or first have to defend the pawn.
The knight to d7 — and we can always smoke his queen out with the queen to e7 next.
He goes pawn-hunting with the queen to c7.
A good move — and I offer the queen trade with the queen to d8.
Against the queen to b7 I'd planned to trade queens with the queen to b6.
The knight to c5 — nothing has happened to the idea from the previous game: we threaten a check on d2 that would win his knight.
He doesn't seem aware he's down the exchange. We double the rooks on d8, and a5 will stop him chasing our knight away.
a5 — even in an endgame, the typical middlegame ideas still apply.
Now bring our king into the picture.
And begin the kingside attack — play it as if it's a middlegame, because the same ideas apply.
A textbook King's Indian position — the pawn on c6 guarding d5.
Push the pawn — it breaks through, and it opens a path for our king to march all the way to g3, Russian-school style.
Instead g3. Doesn't that lock the position in White's favour? No — keep your eye on the g2-pawn.
The tempting move doesn't work — let's find a more methodical way to apply pressure on that pawn.
Reroute a piece that has already done its job on its square — that's flexibility of thinking. People get almost emotionally attached to a piece's placement, but once its work is done, move it on.
Always look at the undefended pieces and the x-rays. The bishop to h3, textbook style, forces the pawn forward — then we win the knight and promote, or force him to give up his bishop for the pawn.
Now his knight is lost — we send our knight forward with a check, or simply promote; the game is over.
The King's Indian looks wrong — you hand White the whole centre — but that's the point: you cede it in pawns to attack it later with your pieces from a distance. That's the hypermodern idea.
notes.teaches: Hypermodern openings surrender the pawn centre on purpose, then bombard it with pieces.

notes.explains: e5 is the main move, striking straight at the d4-pawn. It doesn't lose a pawn, and the point is to open the centre so our pieces can get at e4.
The simplest way to lean on e4 is Re8, putting the rook behind the pawn on the open file.
notes.teaches: Attack a central pawn with the simplest tool — a rook on the file it stands on.

notes.explains: f3 is a general weakening move, and here's the concrete flaw: it leaves the bishop on e3 undefended. If we can lever the e4-pawn out of the way, that loose bishop turns into a target.
notes.teaches: Every f3 push weakens something — log the pieces it leaves undefended.

notes.explains: We can't play d5 at once, so prepare it with c6 — this is main-line theory, and if White doesn't know exactly how to handle it he's in serious trouble.
notes.plans: Follow up with the d5 break to blast open the centre.

notes.explains: d5 goes in anyway — even with the bishop defended the whole centre is flimsy, and the pawn break cracks it open.
White's e5 just drops a pawn; Rxe5 grabs it and hands us exactly what we wanted — the open e-file.
Keep developing with Nc6; if he takes, we recapture with the pawn and shore up our passed pawn on d5.
notes.teaches: Recapture toward the centre to reinforce your advanced pawn.

notes.explains: By the book we develop the bishop — not Bf5, which allows Nxf5, but Bd7. Not every piece needs an active job; some just connect the rooks and sit quietly, and that's fine.
notes.teaches: A modestly-placed developing move that connects the rooks beats a flashy square that hangs.

notes.explains: Now the metal detector goes off: Nxd4. The knight is defended by the queen, but taking drags the queen onto d4 — a square x-rayed by our bishop on g7. That x-ray is the seed of a discovered attack.
notes.teaches: Lure the queen onto a square your bishop already x-rays, then tear the cover off.

notes.explains: Get the most from it: Nh5 makes contact with the f4-bishop before we cash in.
Bxc3 is the winning stroke — it chops off the only defender of the bishop on e2, and that undefended piece falls next move. We're up a clean piece.
notes.teaches: Win a piece by removing the single defender of a loosely-guarded target.

notes.explains: This is the beauty of the King's Indian: White makes one inaccurate move and the game is simply over.

The key vocabulary: a type-one piece is defended by nothing, a type-two by a single piece — never a pawn — and the queen counts as undefended always, because it must flee any attacker. Harp on those loose pieces and the tactics find themselves.
notes.teaches: Scan for type-one and type-two pieces every move; they are where combinations live.

notes.explains: So the bishop goes to c6, not b5 — c6 is defended by a pawn, and a piece is only truly safe when a pawn guards it.
notes.teaches: A piece is genuinely secure only when a pawn, not another piece, defends it.

notes.explains: Bring the sad, out-of-play rook into the game and build Alekhine's gun — tripling the heavy pieces along the file.
notes.plans: Triple queen and rooks on the file for a crushing battery.

notes.explains: And catalog the opponent's weaknesses like a librarian — h4 was one, and the queen is tied to it, so we simply collect it with check.
notes.teaches: Keep a running list of enemy weaknesses; the winning move is usually already on it.

notes.explains: We have Black against a strong opponent and play a very conceptual opening — the Caro-Kann, answering the king's-pawn with the pawn to c6.
White plays the pawn to d4 and we meet it with d5.
White captures on d5.
We recapture with the c-pawn — the Exchange Caro-Kann.

White develops the bishop to d3 — the Exchange, one of the most reputable lines: very solid and London-like, with the bishop on d3, the pawn to c3, and the other bishop to f4. Black's setups all revolve around finding a home for the light-squared bishop, which, as in the French, often struggles for a good square — and if White plays h3, its development gets badly restricted.
So the soundest choice is the knight to f6 first, rather than the natural knight to c6 — and if White plays c3, we develop the bishop before it can be shut in.
White plays the pawn to h3, restricting our bishop — so we revert to a different plan.
We develop the other knight to c6. And if White plays c3, we have an interesting line that gives Black a very active game.
White plays the pawn to c3. The principal reply is the pawn to e5 — punishing White for not developing the king's knight early enough.
The pawn to e5 — this is real theory, not spitballing. It most likely leads to an isolated queen's pawn structure for us on d5.
White captures on e5, and we get the IQP structure — a good chance to talk about handling the isolated queen's pawn.
We recapture with the knight on e5.
White plays the knight to f3 — the best line. Now we decide what to capture.

The plan, step by step. The bishop pair is worth keeping active, so we take the light-squared bishop — the knight takes d3 with check, and the queen recaptures. Now the dark-squared bishop: e7 is too passive and c5 runs into the check on b5 that provokes the awkward knight to d7, so the right square is d6 — safe and eyeing the kingside. In an IQP position, whoever controls the square in front of the isolated pawn is better, and that's White on d4 — but our compensation is the bishop pair in an open position with fine coordination. If White plays the bishop to g5, we answer the pawn to h6, sacrificing the IQP for an open game and the two bishops. After the trade on f6 we recapture toward the centre — never with the g-pawn, which would wreck our structure. Then the rook swings to d8, an x-ray on the queen forcing it off the centre, and since White's queenside is undeveloped we pour on the initiative: the bishop to f5, ignoring the b7-pawn, chasing the queen around — the queen has almost no squares, and there's a recurring bishop-h2 back-rank motif because we still control the luft square even after White's h3. The deepest idea is the bishop to c2 setting up the retreat bishop to d6 to trap the queen. When we finally win the extra piece, we convert cleanly: simplify with a rook trade, force the queens off with the queen to e6 while keeping the bishop attacking the knight, then the deep freeze — the pawn to b5 to freeze White's queenside pawns so the dark-squared bishop can pick them off, trade the light bishop for the knight, and mop up.
We stay with the Sicilian.
White tries the bishop to c4, and its main flaw against the Sicilian is that e6 can blunt it entirely at any moment — we don't even have to hurry.
We develop the knight to c6 first; e6 stays in our pocket for later.
We bring out this knight to f6 rather than the other — developing the far knight first could invite an annoying e5. No rush.
teaches: develop the right knight to deny e5

notes.explains: Now e6 does its job: it blunts the bishop, and it clears the way for d5, killing two birds — because opening the center is especially good now that White has committed to f3.
teaches: e6 then d5 to open the center

notes.explains: d5 strikes the center open — the punishment for that early f3.
Development doesn't have to be a volcano of activity — a plain, effective bishop to d7 is fine, and it stops White from taking on c6 and wrecking our structure.
We recapture with the bishop to keep our pawns healthy.
Out of the pin, the spicier move is the queen to b6 — it hits the b2-pawn and, crucially, it eyes the long diagonal that White weakened the moment he played f3.
Now the breakthrough: c4. It looks mysterious but it's the direct punishment for f3 — blasting open the diagonal straight at White's king.
teaches: the c4 lever to open the diagonal

notes.explains: The pin with the bishop to b4 wins material — it attacks the c3-knight, which has only a pawn to defend it, and we can pile more pressure on with d-pawn support.
teaches: pin and pile onto the undefended knight

notes.explains: Black hands over the knight with check — a total disaster for White.
With the king stuck on e2, we recapture and head straight for the finish.
The king marooned on e2 should immediately scream long castle — bringing the rook to the d-file with the enemy king trapped in the center.
After the king shuffles we open every file and diagonal we can — the point of taking on c4 isn't to level the pawns, it's to tear more lines open.
teaches: open lines, don’t count pawns, when attacking

notes.explains: We take the queen and infiltrate — simple, direct, and the rest is history.
White opens with the pawn to d4, and we answer the knight to f6. It's been ages since we faced d4 — and this becomes a Trompowsky.
The bishop to g5 — the Trompowsky, one of the non-c4 sidelines. The London system has largely eclipsed it in popularity these days.

The standard reply is the knight to e4, challenging the bishop at once. Nimzo-Indian or Queen's Gambit players might prefer the pawn to e6, but the knight jump is the principled try and worth learning.
White plays the bishop to f4 — the main response, keeping the bishop and stepping out of the knight's way.
White has three real tries here: the aggressive pawn to h4 sideline popularized by English players like Hodgson, the retreat to e3, and the main bishop to f4.
We open d4, Black replies ...d5, and we develop the knight to c3.
Black plays e6 — the French.
We enter the French proper with e4.
Black plays ...Nd7 — a small but significant mistake, leaving the d5-pawn underdefended.
We take on d5.
Black recaptures on d5.
We grab the free pawn, the knight landing on d5.
Black develops with ...Ngf6.
Already a pawn up, we simplify — trading on f6 with check.
Black recaptures with the queen.
We develop the knight to f3, a clean pawn up in the centre.
Black develops the bishop to d6.
We choose the bishop on d3, not b5 — a pin there is easily broken by ...c6, which would be a healthy move for Black anyway.
Black castles.
We castle.
Black plays h6.
We play c3 — supporting d4 and preparing the Bc2 then Qd3 battery.
Black strikes with c5.
Our d4-pawn is well protected, so we ignore the poke and continue with the bishop to c2.
Black plays c4, trying to stop Qd3.
We undermine that pawn with b3 — the textbook method.
Black holds with b5.
We take on c4, softening it up.
Black recaptures on c4 — but the pawn is now weak.
We swing the bishop to e4, completing the battery that threatens mate on h7; Black defends with ...Nb6, we bring the queen to c2 behind the bishop, and Black must cover with ...Qg6.
We reposition the queen to b3; Black grabs our bishop with ...Qxe4; we return to c2 offering the trade, and the queens come off on c2 — leaving us up material.
The pawn to e4, e5. The King's Gambit has been around since the 16th century — essentially forever.
f4 — as long as chess has existed in Europe, so has the King's Gambit.
He takes on f4, the knight to f3 — d6 is the second most popular move; I played d4.
And g5, of course, to keep the pawn, otherwise this makes no sense — the bishop to c4 is actually rare; h4 is the main line.

— a sacrifice line: h4, g4, and the knight to g5, which Morozevich played and is interesting but probably unsound; the real move is the knight back to g1, since you've softened f4 enough to undevelop the knight, justified if you take the pawn in the end. I was out of book, so I played the natural bishop to c4 — nothing particularly wrong with it. If Black had played g4, I fully intended to sacrifice the knight and castle, a variety of the Muzio Gambit — the spirit stays sound because of how many pieces White develops and how weak Black's king is; practically, if Black doesn't know the theory, this is dangerous.
We're Black — e5. And ladies and gentlemen, let's hope for the Stafford.
The knight to f3 — there's nothing wrong with playing a guilty-pleasure opening once in a while.
The knight to f6 — let's see how the Stafford holds up at an 1800 level.
The knight takes e5 — let's see if these guys know the refutation.
The knight to c6 — the Stafford.
The knight takes c6.
The d-pawn recaptures — this is the Stafford Gambit; everybody should know what it is.
d3 — let's see if he falls into one of the traps. How should Black continue?
We want the bishop to c5, aiming at the f2-pawn — this creates a very wide range of tricks.
The bishop to e3 by our opponent takes a little of the sting out — it's accurate, though as I remember not the best move.
The reason it's not best is obvious: he weakens his kingside. After the bishop trade —

— look how nasty: he creates all these weaknesses on his kingside, which we exploit through targeted play and rapid development. The key word is rapid — if he plays the bishop to e2 and castles, the flame of the Stafford initiative is extinguished.
The knight takes e4 doesn't work here — we play the knight to g4, going straight after the e3-pawn; we don't let him consolidate. How can we pile up the pressure on it?
The queen to f3. Don't fall into queen-attacks-queen syndrome — don't play g5 just because it hits the queen; if you pose a threat, make sure it's meaningful. This one is —
— it forces the king up. Now, as many of you spot, if the knight were gone from g4 we'd have a pin —
— so the knight takes h2 comes to mind. In a classical game I'd play it — and it's too cool to pass up, so the knight takes h2.
The rook takes h2 — and he blunders the queen.
I can't believe he just thought and then did that.
Should we take the queen, or is there a slightly more accurate move?
Let's just castle — the queen's not going anywhere.
The king to f2. Don't forget to take the queen, though —
— he actually escaped the pin, so don't forget to take the queen when the time comes.

The g-pawn recaptures. A clear application of 'strike while the iron is hot' — after winning material, your opponent often blunders more, less attentive to tactics. What tactical detail do we watch here? This rook — tactical observation 101.
The rook is unprotected. Is anything else undefended? The queen to e5 forms a classic triangle —
— a fork: not only do we win b2, we're going to take all the other queenside pawns.
Give me that, and that, and that — our king is perfectly safe, the game is over.

Assuming the rook to b1, and wanting to win efficiently, which pawn do we take? We can take c2 then a2 — could a case be made for a2 immediately? Yes, both create a passed pawn, but there's a subtle reason: if we play the queen takes c2, he walks the king to g3, opening his rook's defence and the queen x-ray.
So when we push the a-pawn, he might get his rook into the defence. Largely irrelevant — we're totally winning — but keeping the c-pawn alive walls his rook off from its defence.
That pawn on c2 sections the rook off from its defence, like plexiglas. Now —
— should we defend the a-pawn? No — push it. a4, a3 —
— and the game is over.
The knight to c4.
a3 — trying to make him give up the knight for the pawn. I hope he takes c7, because there's a very sexy winning continuation. And a big shout out to Eric Rosen, the king of the Stafford.
The bishop to h3. The queen takes c4 is the fancy move I mentioned, but it's not a good idea — the queen takes c4, the pawn takes c4, and a2 gets a little too fancy.

Be very careful — look at the whole board. Can he prevent the a-pawn queening? The rook to h1, and we'd only be up the exchange, starting over. When in doubt, go for the simplest continuation — the queen to a1 followed by a2 ends it, unless he plays the bishop to f5. Don't pre-move a2; stay vigilant of counterplay to the very end.
He plays the rook takes c7.
No threats, so a2. What here? The queen to d1 with check —
— the queen to d1 with check, and then the a-pawn queens.
d4, the knight to f6. We've been alternating between e4 and d4 — a chance to learn new positions, which can be exciting.
c4 — main-line d4 and c4.
g6 — a Grünfeld or a King's Indian.
The knight to c3, sticking to the main line.
Most people at this level don't play the Grünfeld — and indeed.
Black plays the King's Indian; our move is e4, the main line.
d6 — we reach the first tabia, a big branching point almost every King's Indian passes through, with ten or fifteen viable lines from here.
The line I recommend — underrated, poorly studied, one most King's Indian players pass by — is the Averbakh, named after Yuri Averbakh, and it starts with the bishop to e2.
Black castles.
The bishop to g5 — not just development, but a prophylactic move.
What does the bishop to g5 discourage? e5.

The bishop to e3 — preserving pressure on the h6-pawn, with the queen to d2 to follow, and h6 as a hook for a pawn storm. It's not automatic to castle kingside in the King's Indian; keeping the king in the centre, which is so well protected, lets you storm with g4, h4 and g5 straight at Black's king.
The downside of the bishop to e3 is that e5 becomes possible — but it's not the end of the world, just a typical King's Indian move. Why the bishop to e3 for the semi-Averbakh —

— because inducing h6 helps White; that pawn on h6 rather than h7 typically favors us. Now we close the centre with d5 — the whole point: closing it unties our hands for kingside action, since we no longer divert resources to hold the centre.

a5 — a typical King's Indian move preventing b4, usually followed by the knight maneuver to c5 via d7 or a6, pressuring e4. Another branching point; in the spirit of the Averbakh we go straight for Black's throat with a move that looks like a coffee-house move but is often the engine's top choice —
— not h4, though that's possible, but directly g4.
The knight to a6. Do we need to stop the knight from reaching c5? No — as I just explained, it's fine —
— because we protect e4 with f3. So we continue the kingside campaign with h4, launching the second pawn. Why not g5 immediately? That was also very good, I agree —

— but the added benefit of h4 is that after g5 and the h-pawn takes g5, we recapture with the h-pawn and open the h-file. The knight to d7. Now a pleasant choice: h5, and Black closes with g5, which actually helps us — f5 becomes a gaping weakness and a coveted outpost for our knight. Or the queen to d2, but after the king to h7 it's hard to open the kingside; the knight to d7 was smart, so it's the classic situation where if we play g5 Black plays h5, and if we play h5 Black plays g5.
So we switch from tactics to positional play and play h5, inducing g5, then aim to bring the g1-knight around to f5 —
— which sounds very hard, but there's a typical maneuver in these positions.
The knight to f3, exploiting the temporary fact that the knight on d7 blocks the bishop —
The knight to f6 — as predicted, Black moves off d7. In fact White has superiority on both flanks.
The knight to d2 — serving both purposes; then the knight to f1 and g3. Note the g4-pawn is very well protected.

The knight to c5, and now that our knight is off g1 we can play f3 very safely — not interfering with the knight's path from f1 to g3. Note the queen to c2 would have been a blunder, taking our eye off the g4-pawn; there's a strict order of operations. And we're not worried about king safety as long as the centre stays closed.
c6 — Black does everything right, but weakening f5 means Black is worse for the rest of the game. Do we take on c6 or on c5? No and no —
— White's job is to keep the centre closed. c6 and the trade on d5 don't open it much, so we continue routing the knight to g3.
The pawn takes d5 — an interesting moment. We recapture with the c-pawn to keep the structure symmetrical; you consider the e-pawn recapture only when you control e4 —

— but the flaw here is that Black could advance e4, opening the centre and reopening the dark-squared bishop, the last thing we want. So the c-pawn takes. The c-file opens, but our queenside is perfectly defended; why not recapture with the knight —
— because the knight on c3 is important: it discourages b5, defends e4, protects d5 and guards b5. The bishop to d7.
The bishop to d7 doesn't threaten b5 yet — we have two defenders there. So finally, after about seven moves, we land the knight on g3. Long-term, our top goal is a specific minor-piece trade.

Not the dark-squared bishops — that Black bishop is terrible, a big pawn — the light-squared bishops: trade them and we land an uncontested knight on the f5-square, which just terrorizes Black. The queen to b6 hits b2; we must defend it.

Not b3 — that creates a queenside hook, allows a4 and loosens the knight on c3. We play the queen to d2 — harmonious, connecting the rooks and defending the bishop. Watch for the bishop takes g5, a frequently missed tactic: after the h-pawn takes g5, h6 can lead to a quick mate; Black defends with the knight to h7. Also, a nice square for the king is g2 — out of the way when the queenside opens.
On f2 the king is still susceptible to long-term tactics on g4 and c4. The rook to c8 — we can start walking the king toward g2.

The king to f2 — routed this way to keep the rooks connected, so we could bring a rook in urgently without the king to g2. We forfeit the bishop takes g5 for now. Why not castle? We can, but I want to keep the bishop takes g5 alive by leaving the rook on h1 — in closed positions you keep tactical possibilities open to keep the opponent on edge.
a4. Black wants a3, inducing b3, which loosens the knight on c3 with a rook on c8 and ideas like the queen to b4. There's a nice way to take the sting out of a3 —

— if Black plays a3 we meet it with b4, pinning the knight on c5; but playing a3 ourselves leaves a hole on b3, and after a3 Black has the knight to b3 hitting the queen. So the subtle rook to b1, planning to answer a3 with b4.

The rook to b1 protects b4. The queen to a5 — Black shows keen King's Indian knowledge, but now we're almost ready for the bishop takes g5. Let's calculate: the bishop takes g5, the h-pawn takes g5, h6, and after the bishop to h8 the problem is that if we take on g5 with check the king hides on h7; so we need to open the h-file for the other rook to jump to h1 — meaning after the bishop to h8 we play h7, forcing the knight to take on h7, and there's a critical move.

The bishop takes g5 — I briefly checked the knight takes e4 with check and made sure Black has no shenanigans with the knight takes c4; the counterplay comes too late, since the queen to a5 shows Black wants to push to b4, and there isn't time.
The h-pawn takes g5 — we're already checkmating the black king.
The h-pawn takes g5, and of course h6.
h6, the bishop to h8.
h7 with check. Why not the queen takes g5 —
The knight takes h7, and the rook takes h7 — without this move the whole combination would fall apart.
The king takes on h7. The necessary component of the entire combination was actually putting our king on f2. What's the best move now? Not the rook to h1 —

— because Black plays the king to g6 and defends g5. So instead the queen takes g5, cutting the king off the g-file, and next we swing the rook to h1 with mate. Black's only try is the bishop to g7 to block g8, but then the rook to h1 forces the king back to g8, and the winning move is the knight to h5.
We're playing Black. d4 — let's deviate a little from the Queen's Gambit and play the knight to f6; I'm feeling a bit more adventurous.
e3 — a Colle setup.
Here it makes sense to play d5 and transpose to a Queen's-Pawn structure.
c3 — a traditional Colle setup. There are two ways for White: f4 for the reverse Stonewall, or the bishop to d3 for the Colle — but
Now we can play the bishop to f5, and in the event of the bishop to d3, that bishop trade favours

Black — the whole point of the Colle is to preserve the light-squared bishop, not to trade it. We don't have to rush with the bishop taking d3; there's a nice positional move some of you might not see intuitively. Many of you are thinking of the bishop to g6, but there's another way to keep the tension and offer a change of pawn structure that I really like —
not g6 but e6. That's the move I enjoy here, and in the event of a trade we get this massive structure.
The bishop takes f5 — I'm glad he took.

e-takes-f5, and now I can explain what to do in this structure. The queen to d3 is a good move, and we need to be careful tactically for one move: if we play g6, those with a sharp eye see the queen to b5 with check, hitting the king and the pawn — same after the knight to e4, there's the queen to b5 with check — so we play the queen to d7 to defend both at once. We need to stay careful for a couple of moves, because the knight is coming to e5. You could play the knight to c6, but if you remember, I don't like blocking the c-pawn in Queen's-Pawn openings, so I much prefer the bishop to d6; and if g5, we just take it and play g4 — not a good trade for White. He castles; we also castle; then we play the rook to e8, to prevent g5 and clamp down even further on the centre. This is the whole zen of our strategy: it's hard for White to free himself. Good players know how to handle these positions with White, but in the fourteen-, fifteen-hundred range people aren't very good at dealing with being cramped. The bishop to a3 is White's idea — one of the best against this setup. What do we do now? Several improving moves: the rook to e8, centralising the knight on e4, or c5 at some point — but I actually prefer to put the pawn on c6, because c5 defeats the purpose: opening the centre goes against what we're trying to do and gives the opponent breathing room. So I like either the rook to e8 or the knight to e4, but the most flexible is the rook to e8. g6 isn't bad, but it's not necessary — our queen defends the pawn just fine. Is the knight to e4 still good? Absolutely, because if he takes it, we recapture with a fork; then we play c6 to protect the d5-pawn. And where does the queenside knight go? The position is closed, so no rush — for instance after c6 we can go the knight to a6 and back to c7, a route you've seen before. So c6, reinforcing the d5-pawn. The other approach: the queen has done its job on d7 and now looks awkward there, so we move it aside and open the d7-square for the knight — more palatable to me than the knight to a6. Where to move the queen? The primary point is to free d7 for the knight, but if you're moving it anyway, accomplish something else too — White's king isn't the safest piece and White is very passive, so an attack could be a way to play. So I like the queen to e6 — the queen to e7 is also fine, but I like e6 because the queen can swing to h6, a queen lift; not saying we will, but we might. Which brings up an important point: playing positionally doesn't mean you can't attack — you can do both, and transition to a king attack at the right moment. c4 — I think that's what we do now; we've fully improved, so what are we waiting for? Time for the queen lift, the queen to h6. We're not worried about the trade opening the c-file, because we have all the c-file squares well protected — his queen can't infiltrate. This closes things down even further and unties our hands for kingside action, and winter is coming for his king. g5 might run into g3; he plays g3 anyway. When you're attacking like this, think in terms of drawbacks — the drawback of g3 is that it weakens h3. Can we exploit it? Yes: we can put the queen coming to h3, and then bring the knight to g4, creating a situation where White is totally helpless, with one flimsy knight over on f3 saving him from death; there are also ideas of sacrificing on g3, though it's not as appetising here. Multiple approaches — we could lift the rook to h6 — but the best is the knight to f6 and the knight to g4. Why the queen to h3 first, rather than the knight to f6 immediately? Because White can sometimes play h4 and keep our queen out of h3. So we continue with the knight to f6, we see it does nothing, and White's position totally collapses. We could play the knight to g4 anyway, giving up f5 — but the f5-pawn is totally unimportant here. These situations with the queen coming to h3 and the knight landing on g4 are important to understand tactically: our objective is to distract the knight from f3, and only a knight can do that — the knight to g5. Our opponent plays resiliently — the knight to g1 makes it harder — but it was already over. Be flexible: one objective is removing that knight from f3, but there's also a brute-force approach, crashing through by overloading the h2-pawn. There's an idea with the rook to e6, the knight sitting on g5: if the queen takes f5, the simplest win is the knight takes f3, the knight recaptures, and then, noticing the alignment of the queen and knight, the knight to f6 wins the knight and mates; and if he doesn't take on f5, we play the rook to h6 and the knight takes h2 — and there's one cool idea, the knight takes h2, the knight recaptures, and it's mate; I've seen cases where people drop the knight back to f3, and then there's a cool tactic with the queen to h1.
Our first 2000-rated opponent — and I'll play the c3 Sicilian, the Alapin, which I've recommended in this rating range for a while.
He plays d6, which isn't the best line against it — it lets us take control of the centre.
He hits the e4-pawn, so we defend it with the bishop to d3 — and there are subtleties to watch for, particularly if he plays the knight to c6.
The knight to f3 defends d4. His bishop to g4 here would look intimidating...
...but instead he plays the very passive e6.
Two ways to continue here: open the centre with dxc5, which makes a lot of sense, or play flexibly with the bishop to g5.

Let's develop by the book — the knight to d2. That's the downside of the Alapin: you can't route this knight to c3. But it's fine here, and it buttresses the e4-pawn. We're clearly better, with a nice pawn centre.
He plays e5. Now a lot of people struggle with the decision between capturing and pushing.
Taking on e5 would open the position to his benefit and let him attack our bishop — so d5, keeping the centre closed. Our space advantage should, in theory, tell against him.
There's a tactical detail here I failed to anticipate — let's see if he finds it.
He does — the knight takes on d5. I'd missed this move.
But that's the beauty of being positionally better — you can blunder a pawn and still be fine. He's opened the d-file, so the question is how to pressure the pawn on d6.
The knight to c4 — no disaster, still a good position, but I did just make an instructive mistake.
We win the pawn back on d6; roughly equal. And if he pushes d5, we take, and his e5-pawn hangs — we're eyeing that pawn too.
His knight on b4 is a nice counterweight. His best was the queen to b6, preparing a rook to d8; the queen to c7 is not the most accurate.

Our knight was the vulnerable piece — so rather than use the get-out-of-jail rook to c1 to activate the rook, we've evacuated it to b5. Chess is all about priorities, and the top priority was getting that knight out.
Now our knight is safely out and defended — something we couldn't do a move ago.
He's forgotten the pawn is hanging — the knight takes on e5, and we're up a pawn. Sometimes chess is about resisting the by-the-book move and prioritising.
If he grabs on a2 he'll lose material.
We retreat the knight to c3 — an even safer square.

The rook to d8 — and we must be careful, because the queen to e1 walks into a fork. So the queen goes to a4 instead, active and pressuring his knights. When he tries the queen to c5 it doesn't actually attack our knight, because his knight on b4 would hang. That b4-knight is what cramps us, so e3 compels the trade — and with us a pawn up, trades are good, plus it removes his strongest piece. Then the finishing trick: with his queen in contact with the rook, we swing a rook to d8, and he can't defend it without a back-rank mate or giving up the rook; the queen to f5 finishes with mate to follow.
d4, the knight to f6 — we've got to play a King's Indian, since this may be our last game.
The knight to c3 — what I've played my whole life.
The bishop to g7.
d6 — it's about time we paid homage to it from the Black side.

f3 — one of my top recommendations for White, the Sämisch, named after Friedrich Sämisch, who developed a lot of systems connected with f3; the Nimzo-Indian f3 is also called the Sämisch. Against it, Black has a gazillion viable continuations.
Most lines start by castling; it's automatic. White generally plays the bishop to e3, though the knight to e2 also transposes. The point of f3 is twofold — first, to safeguard e4 —

— and, in many cases, to prepare the kingside pawn storm with g4; the drawback is you can't use f3 for the knight, so the knight goes to e2. I want to play an old line I grew up on, played prolifically by Kasparov; nothing's inherently wrong with it — Black is worse only if White is incredibly accurate. Nowadays King's Indian players mostly play the Benoni with c5, considered objectively best, or the Panov —
— the Panov with the knight to c6 and a6. But the old move is e5, the traditional way to play the King's Indian; a lot of people think you can't play e5 against the Sämisch — not true at all.
e5 is totally viable and frequently slips through the cracks; one drawback is that White has the pawn takes e5 —
— which takes all the fun out of the game, but you've got to learn to play these types of positions too.
The queens come off on d8 — an endgame, a version of the Exchange Variation.

The knight to d5. I'll confess I'm not a specialist here — probably my first time. The knight takes d5 isn't forced: White recaptures with the c-pawn, and a pawn on d5 greatly hampers our queenside, controlling c6 and e6; the traditional treatment is the knight to c5, take, then c6 to remove the pawn, but the e2-knight slides to c3, and taking on d5 just replaces the pawn with a bloodthirsty knight. So the knight on d5 isn't that scary — it's attacking c7, which we must defend, and we can't play c6, since the knight jumps into c7 and traps the rook.

In the King's Indian, the queen's knight's traditional developing square is a6, so the knight to a6, protecting the pawn from the side. If the bishop to g5, we must play the rook to d6, getting out of the pin and protecting the f6-knight. Long-term, Black is favored: with pawns on c4 and e4, White has traded off d4 and accepted a gaping weakness there; most central squares are Black's, and once we get the knight off d5, we control d4, d3 and e3 — the whole central complex is weak, currently masked by that imposing d5-knight. Play c6 to chase it, get White to trade on f6, and Black is solidly better.

Our opponent is correctly taking his time. The bishop to g5, the rook to d6 — a very important resource, otherwise we lose an exchange. Note that sometimes giving up an exchange isn't the end of the world — the knight to c5 doesn't lose on the spot —

— since after the bishop takes the rook, the knight can jump into e3; but it's all moot, because the rook to d6 is perfectly sufficient. This isn't just heading toward a draw — the resulting endgame is full of life and playable for a Black advantage; White isn't worse if very accurate, but most players relinquish the initiative and fall prey to the plan of grabbing the key central squares.
The knight to c3. The fundamental asymmetry: we haven't pushed our pawn to c5, which is why Black is positionally better.

c6 — we exploit the reserved possibility of pushing to c6, controlling d5; White can't exercise the same control over the mirrored square, d4, which is why White is often in a lot of trouble. The knight to e7 with check and the knight takes c8 is possible, but our c8-bishop isn't an integral piece — the heavy lifting is done by the a6-knight, which will head for d4 via the knight to c7 or c5 and e6.

We're not blindly closing our eyes and playing three moves — we'll do other things depending on our opponent. And from an opening-rules perspective, White has spent a gazillion moves with this knight.

He's taken the bishop and gotten the bishop pair, but his f1-bishop isn't impressive, just staring at the pawn. If White could push c5, that'd be a total game-changer. The knight to b4 has merit — probably our next move if permitted; if I play c5 we take with the knight, which is partly why we put the knight on a6, to prevent c5. White's best, and it's not easy, is the bishop from g5 to e3, restricting the a6-knight and preparing c5, which opens the f1-bishop —

— because if we don't move the a6-knight away, it gets captured, ruining our structure, and getting the other knight to d4 becomes a cumbersome four-move process. Against all of White's ways to prepare c5, we have an important retreating move to prevent it. The bishop to e2 is the game continuation. The tempting knight to b4 is a bit of a dead end — after the rook to c1 we have the knight to d3 check, but we don't want to trade this knight unless for something on d4. Since White hasn't prepared c5, no rush. An interesting idea, though it fails concretely, is the knight from f6 to d7, covering c5 once more and opening the bishop to support a knight heading for d4.

Our king's knight was a little awkward where it stood, disrupting our coordination and needing babysitting, so the knight to d7 lends maximum energy to the knights — now both can access d4. A dream would be to trade the dark-squared bishops, making d4 ours forever, but it's not so easy; the bishop to f6 just encourages the bishop to e3, so don't assume your opponent makes the trades you want. And f5 isn't an idea here —

— because when you consider f5, always ask who benefits from the position opening: generally not the side controlling the central squares. We want it closed, to single-mindedly focus on that square. g4 accomplishes little, actually weakening f4, so I'm already considering an arrangement with one knight toward f4 and the other toward d4, far in the future. My instinct is the knight to c5; the knight to b4 is significantly sexier now that our other knight is ready to support with the knight to c5, and it might be the most efficient path to d4, since after the rook to c1 the other knight jumps to c5, threatening a fork on d3 and using d3 as a transit point to f4, the square White just weakened.

There's one complication I can't quite make work, so maybe the mundane knight to c5 — but I'll follow my intuition; g4 can't be wrong. After the rook to c1, the knight to d3 with check — but knights are more valuable than bishops here, since the centre is closed; think of a knight as a Phillips screwdriver getting into the small spaces a bishop can't.
You're flossing the board a little. He can castle. The point of the knight to b4 isn't the fork — we're not expecting White to miss it — but to use b4 as a transit point toward f4.

Our opponent is disallowed d4. Let's proceed with the knight to c5, threatening a fork again, planning to drop back to e6 and finally get a knight to d4 — the first big step toward winning, though you can't win such positions in three moves; you do it step by step and celebrate the small victories.

What makes d4 important? It comes down to square control — a knight in the centre controls eight squares, a knight in the corner only two; a knight reaching d4 just lords over the whole position. The knight to d3 tempts, but after the rook to d1 we'd pin ourselves —

— and we couldn't double rooks, since the bishop controls that square. So the knight back to e6, which comes with tempo, attacking the bishop, forcing it off g5, and making possible the future doubling of rooks on the d-file.
We have White and open the pawn to e4, met by e6 — the French Defence.
We play the pawn to e5 — the Steinitz Variation — and I'm a big fan of following up with the knight to f3.
The knight to f3. Black pre-moves the bishop to d7 expecting the pawn to c3 — but we're not going to play c3.
The traditional bishop to d3. The whole point of the Steinitz is that we leave the pawn on d4 and never play c3, conserving that tempo.
We castle — making all the normal French moves except c3.
Black captures on d4. The entire system revolves around the e5-pawn — we over-protect it with everything we have, and recover d4 later by rerouting the knight from d2 to b3.
But first the bishop to f4 to over-protect e5, so we needn't worry about it. Against the queen to b6, don't play b3 — we want that square for our knight — and don't reflexively defend b2 either.

The knight to d2, without defending b2. If Black takes on b2, the rook to b1 opens the file, and with Black so undeveloped that's disaster for him — no calculation needed. So the plan is the knight to b3 and the rook to e1.
Black plays the knight to b4 — a good move, but it doesn't change our approach; we're in no rush to grab the d4-pawn.
The knight to b3. In this system it's fine to give up the light-squared bishop — not ideal, but survivable — and Black keeps neglecting his kingside, which could get costly.
After the capture on d3, the queen recapture loses to the bishop to b5, so we take with the c-pawn — which we'd want anyway, since it opens the c-file for a rook.
Black plays the rook to c8. I wouldn't rush to take on d4 — that pawn isn't going anywhere. Better to contest the c-file first with the rook to c1 and capture d4 at our leisure.
The rook to c1, and Black plays the knight to e7. Now it's a good moment to take on d4 — but which knight? We take with the f-knight, so the b3-knight can later jump into c5 with queenside pressure.
The f-knight takes d4, and Black recaptures with the knight to c6. I'm also thinking of dropping the bishop back to e3.

The bishop to e3. A kingside plan to consider: pushing the pawn to f4 and f5. We're x-raying the queen with a fine position and central control — and if Black takes on e5, we have a cool discovery with the knight to c6.
Black plays the queen to a6, threatening to take on c5 — we need to react.
We take on c6. The pawn to f4 was possible too, but taking is simplest — these positions always offer three or four roughly equal options.
The point of g4 and then h4 in this Jobava setup is the coming h5 — it hunts down the light-squared bishop on g6, which is running short of squares.
notes.teaches: The g4-h4-h5 pawn thrust is a standard way to trap a bishop that comes to g6.

notes.explains: After the trade the bishop on g6 is snared — a free piece is falling into our lap.
f3 slams the door: it kicks the bishop off e4, and with no safe retreat the piece is simply lost.
notes.teaches: Kick a trapped piece with a pawn to collect it when it has no escape square.

notes.explains: Our patented Sicilian again.
White lunges with f4 — a legitimate but slightly dubious try, because it invites an immediate central strike.
We punish it with d5 at once. This is precisely why the Grand Prix Attack is supposed to start with the knight to c3 — to stop this very move. Skip it, and d5 is the refutation.
After the capture we do NOT slide into a Scandinavian with the queen — that would throw away the whole point of d5.
teaches: don’t recapture with the queen here

notes.explains: Instead the knight to f6. White can't just hold the extra pawn with c4, because e6 undermines it and Black gets tremendous positional compensation — in fact the better game.
So we safely recapture on d5, and here the queen would sit far more securely than in a normal Scandinavian — White has no second knight to hit it from c3.
teaches: the point: no Nc3 available to harass the queen

notes.explains: The f4-pawn hangs, but grabbing it isn't the spirit of the line. The prudent move is to drop the knight back to b6 — after which a later c4 nearly traps the bishop and forces an awkward check. And we're glad to keep White's dark-squared bishop terrible, hemmed in by its own f4-pawn.
teaches: don’t contort for a pawn you want left on the board

notes.explains: The knight to b6 is the practical choice, forcing the bishop to decide. That f4-pawn is actually in our favor — it dries up White's kingside and buries his bishop — and we own the d4-square, which is the whole job of the c5-pawn.
teaches: a cramping enemy pawn can be your asset

notes.explains: Out comes the sacrifice on f7 — not entirely stupid, but just as clearly unsound. These are exactly the tries people struggle to refute, so let's do it cleanly.

We take, and the refutation is castling by hand. Since the king has moved we build the shelter from scratch — clear the bishop, swing a rook to f8, tuck the king to g8. Short term, the f3-knight eyes e5, but any knight check we simply answer by stepping the king to g8; we only avoid the blunder of the bishop to g4.
plans: develop the kingside, then Rf8 and Kg8

notes.explains: g6 is the classy move — get the kingside out so the king feels safe. There's no rush to develop the other knight yet.
teaches: safety first when up a piece

notes.explains: The bishop to g7, and even a knight check we'd meet calmly, because White is simply out of attackers — the c1-bishop is buried and the c3-knight has no prospects. Next comes the rook to f8 and the manual castling is complete.
teaches: count the attackers — the defense holds

notes.explains: White has to throw in f5 to keep any hope alive; its point is to rip open the file. Taking with the bishop plays into his hands — it runs into g4 and a crushing double check. If we capture, we capture with the pawn.
teaches: open-file sac: capture with the pawn, not the bishop

notes.explains: So we take with the pawn — the principled choice. Don't fear ghosts: if there's no forced mate, an uncomfortable-looking king is nothing to be afraid of.
teaches: no forced mate means no reason to panic

notes.explains: g4 just loses on the spot — pure trickery — so of course we don't take it.
We follow through with the rook to f8: castling by hand is complete, and the win won't be far behind.
e4, and the knight to f6 — let's play an Alekhine, a generally underrated opening at this level.
Unfortunately our opponent plays the knight to c3, sidestepping the main line with e5.
Here there are two choices. e5 transposes into the Vienna, but if you want to play like a genuine Alekhine player, you play d5 and transpose into a favorable version
of the Scandinavian. If you're a genuine Alekhine
player, you go for this position. e-takes-d5, and the knight recaptures on d5.
The bishop to c4 would let the knight drop back to b6 with tempo; instead he takes on d5.
The queen recaptures on d5.

The knight to f3. This doesn't seem too impressive — it's a kind of Scandinavian, but White can't play the knight to c3, because that knight is gone, so the queen is quite safe in the centre. Black has many ways to develop: more positionally with g6 and the bishop to g7, or, if we want to play ambitiously, we can aim to castle long, developing the queenside pieces as quickly as possible.
So the bishop comes to g4 and the knight will come to c6, and then we castle queenside. We can start with the bishop to g4,
just to try to induce the bishop to e2. Now, the knight to c6.
And then we castle queenside. Black has a very nice position, because we can also play e5 to
control more of the centre. There's an upside and a downside to e5 here. We could go more modestly with e6 and then the bishop to d6 to hit the h2-pawn.
But given that White has positioned his pawn passively with d3, e5 makes a lot of sense — grabbing as much space in the centre as possible.
The bishop to e3.
Now, the king to b8 — though a moment too early it would walk into a strange tactic, the knight capturing on e5. So I want the king to b8 at some
We open e4, and Black replies e5.
The knight to f3, hitting e5.
Black defends with the knight to c6.
We develop the knight to c3, heading for a Four Knights or Glek system.
Black plays the bishop to c5 — a sideline.
Our opponent takes it back — the knight returns to b1, the bishop to f8 — so we're back to the earlier position.
We develop the knight to c3 again.
And the bishop to c5 again — a sideline, and not a good one: not conceptually bad, but tactically flawed.
If you've spent time around these e5 openings you should already sense why the bishop to c5 is a serious inaccuracy — the center fork trick: the knight takes on e5, capturing on e5.
Black recaptures, capturing on e5 — there's a lot going on here.
We play the Caro-Kann. e4, c6.
The knight to f3, d5.

e5 — we've met this line at several junctures before. There are several ways to tackle it; the Caro-Kann response is the bishop to f5. But funnily, against the bishop to f5 there's a very nasty knight to d4, which I'll cover after the game — so it's worth switching up the move
order here to stop the knight to d4, by making a move we often make in the Caro-Kann anyway — c5. Trust me, the knight to d4 is the super-nasty idea he may have.
The bishop to b5 with check — not a dangerous move; we can cover it a variety of ways.

There's no reason not to play the knight to c6 and develop normally. He'll probably take it — a lot of people at this level still fall in love with doubling our pawns, but I don't fear that structure.

We save a tempo, he's moved his bishop twice, and I like the two bishops and that his e5-pawn is weak — I'm not worried about the bishop taking c6 in the slightest. The knight to c3. In what order do we develop? e6 is fine but would block the c8-bishop, so we turn to that bishop first. The bishop to f5 is possible, but be flexible in development and always consider whether there's something better —
and here you notice the bishop to g4 exists, which I think is quite a bit more active.
h3, and the bishop to h5, keeping the pin alive. g4,
the bishop to g6.

He goes d4 — he's created a lot of weaknesses on his kingside, and now d4. He's not playing this badly, and he's hoping for c-takes-d4, because then he plays the knight takes d4 and piles up on our knight on c6.
How should we respond to d4? Just e6 — a super-typical Caro-Kann move,
preparing to recapture with the bishop, trading on our own terms. The bishop to g5 is not dangerous; the knee-jerk reaction for most people is the bishop to e7 here,
but I think there's a better move — the queen to b6, which is just very nasty.

Because we're applying pressure on the pawn and on the bishop, and there's a sense in which White is already close to collapsing. When he played g4, out of the corner of my eye I made a note to check a move: the knight on f3 no longer has a defender, and the d4-pawn is also very poorly defended — it would be nice for White to have a pawn on c3, as he usually does here. He plays the queen to d2. You might be

saying, wait, I have three attackers and only two defenders on d4 — why can't I just take? The complicating factor is the pin. So we play the bishop to e4, attacking the knight; if he takes the bishop, I recapture with the pawn, the knight is dislodged, and his bishop will also be
undefended if he takes on e4. The queen to e3 defends the knight but doesn't solve the underlying issue — and actually, looking again, we have something even better.
Let me look a bit more carefully — what can we do here?
A fork — but that's a bit of a misleading
If you wanted to play the most precise way — he just resigns — we can take either knight; I'd take the knight on f3.
Recapturing toward the centre with the pawn is the point here — it heals the structure. The doubled pawns are gone, and we're left with a clean, healthy pawn front instead of a crippled one.

There's a tactical shot lurking in this position: if the queen grabs the pawn on d5, the position explodes into real complications. It's the kind of central capture that looks greedy but changes the whole character of the fight.
Black sets up the Leningrad Dutch on autopilot — d6, castle, Nc6, a rook to the e-file — solid, well-trodden development.
e6 is perfectly acceptable, though d5 with tempo — chasing the bishop off c4 — would have been the more forcing choice.
notes.teaches: Prefer the developing move that comes with a tempo-gaining threat when one is available.

notes.explains: Black answers with g6 — the Modern Defense. It's uncommon and, crucially, makes no claim on the center at all.
So we take the invitation and occupy the center with our pawns.
Black fianchettoes — the bishop to the long diagonal — a hypermodern idea: hand over the center, then pressure it from a distance.
teaches: hypermodern: attack the center from afar

notes.explains: We develop with our pawns in mind — the bishop to e3, reinforcing d4 so a knight to c6 won't win it.
To the rescue comes the corner pawn: a4 stops Black's queenside expansion with b5 before it can grab space.
f3 looks like it violates principle, but it does two jobs: it denies the knight the g4 jump that would dislodge our e3-bishop, and it further braces the center.
teaches: f3 stops Ng4 and props the center

notes.explains: Now the attacking scheme: the queen to d2, so we can bring the bishop to h6 and trade off Black's fianchetto bishop — the guardian of the dark squares around his king.
teaches: Qd2 and Bh6 to trade the fianchetto bishop

notes.explains: Black strikes back correctly in the center with e5 — distraction. Note we can't grab with the bishop to h6 yet: the trade would cost us the d4-pawn.
teaches: a central break answers a wing attack

notes.explains: So first we brace d4 again with the knight to e2 — not its dream square, blocking our own bishop, but priorities: the king attack comes first.
teaches: accept a small concession for the main plan

notes.explains: Black takes and we recapture with the knight, centralizing it on d4.
Black keeps distracting with d5 — sensible play, striking in the center to pull us off the kingside plan.
We keep the center closed with e5, refusing to take on d5 — opening it would expose our own king and make us regret f3.
teaches: keep the center shut to keep your king safe

notes.explains: Instead of defending the e5-pawn, we push it to e6 — a shot: if Black takes, the knight recaptures with a fork on the queen and rook. And even the forced capture on f7 only helps us, tearing away a pawn shielding his king.
teaches: e6 push: the fork or the shattered shelter

notes.explains: We capture on f7 — eliminating one of the pawns that form his kingside foundation, exactly what we want before an attack.
Black recaptures with the rook, and now the e-file is open — with our own king still on it, we need to move it.
So we castle long. It looks odd to castle where we pushed the a-pawn, but the a4-pawn is protected and there's no quick attack — don't let a knee-jerk assumption stop the right move.
teaches: question the assumption: long castling is safe here

notes.explains: The knight is hit, so we drop it back to b3 with tempo — now two pieces bear on the c5-pawn.
The knight goes to c5 — active, and keeping the pressure on the weak d5-pawn, unlike a retreat to d4 which would drop that pressure.
teaches: pick the square that keeps the pressure

notes.explains: The knight lands on e4 — a square the d5-pawn supposedly guards, but that pawn is pinned and can't capture, so the knight sits there safely, ready to help win d5.

With the knight centralized we look for the fork by default — the knight to g5 hits bishop and rook. It won't win a piece, but it erodes Black's grip on d5, and clears the way for our bishop to c4 later.
We take on d5 with the knight, planting it in the middle and dominating the center.
Black tries an interception tactic — the knight to d3, forcing something onto that square to cut our defense of the d5-knight. In effect it's just a trade of pieces, nothing more.
We take with the bishop, not the pawn, so our knight keeps its protection.
After the dust settles we're two pawns up with a monster knight on d5 and beautiful control of the center — conceding our light-squared bishop was worth it. Now discovered-check ideas are in the air.
teaches: stay flexible — the plan can change

notes.explains: The bishop is Black's only working piece, the gatekeeper of his king. With the queen no longer on d2 we can't play Bh6, but the bishop to d4 contests it — trade it and his king is defenseless.
He'll play e4 for sure — he plays it nearly every game — and you respond with e5.
Then he almost always plays the knight to f3, so that's to be expected.
And you respond with the knight to c6. He plays the same opening every single time,
so we can actually prepare for him. He plays what's called the Scotch — the move d4.
We take White and open d4; Black replies with the knight to f6.
We claim space with c4.
Black fianchettoes with g6.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black completes the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
We build the big centre with e4.
Black plays d6 — a true King's Indian.
We develop the bishop to e2.
Black castles.
We pin the knight with the bishop to g5.
Black develops the knight to d7.
We launch the h4 pawn storm.
Black plays h6.
We drop the bishop back to e3.
Black strikes with ...e5.
We close with d5 — a King's-Indian pawn chain.
Black plays b6.
We bring the queen to d2.
Black tucks the king to h7.
We roll g4, storming the kingside.
Black plays the knight to c5.
We buttress with f3.
Black expands with a5.
We develop the knight to h3.
Black plays the rook to h8.
We push g5, prying open lines.
Black retreats the knight to g8.
We push h5.
Black takes our knight, capturing on h3.
We recapture with the rook.
Black takes on h5.
We castle queenside.
Black's king wanders to g6.
We bring the rook to g1.
Black returns the king to h7.
We grab on h5 with the rook.
Black develops the knight to e7.
We open with f4.
Black takes on f4.
We take on c5.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn; we grab on f4 with the queen.
Propping the centre with c3 comes at a cost — it concedes the light squares. Once the pawns commit like this, those holes don't come back, and the opponent gets a lasting square to work with.
The d4 break is the idea here — striking in the centre when the opponent has no comfortable way to meet it. That's the lever that turns a passive setup into an initiative.
Pushing d5 and following with c4 is the structural plan, clamping down on space. It's a committal choice — these locked structures cut both ways, but the space grab is the point.
The game opens with d4, g6, e4, and the bishop to g7 — a Modern Defense heading toward a Caro-Kann Gurgenidze structure.
We develop the knight to c3, and Black plays c6.
After c6 we choose the bishop to e3.
Black plays d5, and we build the pawn chain with f3.
The most popular move here is d takes e4, capturing on e4 — which I don't think is correct, but you'll face it very often.
We recapture, capturing on e4 with the f-pawn, and Black often counter-strikes in the centre with e5 — but after e5 Black is clearly worse.
We take on e5, capturing on e5, and generally Black trades queens here.
If Black instead takes on e5 right away with the bishop, capturing on e5, that's an even worse version.
You trade queens on your own terms — the queen takes d8 with check.
The king recaptures on d8, and you get your knight out with an overwhelming development advantage.
The knight to f3.
Black retreats the bishop to g7.
Just look — the bishop to c4, castle queenside, it's already plus three; this is out of the question for Black. So most of the time Black takes the queen and White recaptures.
I've had this position against Hikaru several times. The bishop takes e5 is a mistake — it walks right into the knight to f3, ten games in the database, and Black is in massive trouble.
The bishop to g7...
...the bishop comes out to c4, with tactics galore on all sides of the board.
After something like the knight to d7, White castles — look at the pressure on the f-file; Black can't get the pieces out at all.
The knight to f6 walks into e5.
...the knight to g4, and then the bishop to d4 — that's how the game continued.
The bishop to d4...
Actually White didn't play e5 in the game — this position is utterly lost for Black. If Black plays the knight takes e5...
...you play the knight takes e5, then the bishop to e5 — spot the killer blow.
It's a trick question — be careful here.
The trick: the rook to e1 is NOT the best move.

Black defends the knight with f6; White is still winning, but more accurate is the bishop takes f7 with check — simple tactics: takes, takes, the rook to g8, and White ends the game with the rook to e1, winning all of Black's pieces. If Black plays the king to e7, it's literally checkmate.
The pawn to e4, d5 — the Scandinavian.
We take on d5.
The queen recaptures — multiple options in the Scandinavian.
The knight to c3 — d4 is far less common but also good; everybody plays the knight to c3, so that's what we do.
The queen to a5. I want to teach you an uncommon setup that'll surprise people — most play d4, some the trappy b4 — but I'll play a move that makes a lot of you roll your eyes —
— g3, preparing to fianchetto; it's an easy system, heavy on good positional principles.
c6, the bishop to g2. Once you fianchetto, the knight comes to e2 so as not to obstruct the bishop. It might seem the bishop is biting on granite —
— but the second component of this setup is where this bishop, assuming the game goes along normal lines, becomes a very good piece.
The knight to e2 — White has a plan that involves breaking down the c-pawn and getting this bishop to operate at full potential.
e5, and we castle — just the normal developing moves, d3, nothing much to say; once development is complete I'll show the main plan.

The bishop to b4 isn't great — usually people play e6; I'm less familiar with e5, which could let us play d4 and challenge the centre. The bishop to b4 walks right into a move we'd have played anyway.
a3 — a natural reaction to the bishop to b4; e5 was a bit loosey-goosey. a3 doesn't threaten to take the bishop —
— but he takes anyway. Neither the b-pawn nor the d-pawn recapture is worth ruining our pawn structure —
— we take with the knight. Now, what are we preparing with a3? Ask it that way and you should see the plan —
— the plan is to push the b-pawn to b5, a classic minority attack of sorts, getting this bishop to fire on all cylinders. The bishop to g4.
We don't want f3, and definitely not the bishop to f3 — we want the queen to e1, and later chase the bishop away with h3.
If Black castles, are we in a huge rush to play b4? No — knowing your plan doesn't mean carrying it out immediately; it's fine to complete development first and carry out the plan when you're ready.

You could play b4, but I like the more patient d3; don't reveal your hand too soon, especially when there's no way to stop b4 — c5 would be horrendous and does our work for us. Maybe we'll want the bishop to g5 first, for a kingside attack.
Black's best here is the knight from b8 to d7, completing development. I don't want the bishop to d2 — it's counterproductive, because it helps Black's queen get away from a5.

That defeats part of the purpose of b4, which is that it's a move with tempo. So now we play b4, which also opens a very attractive developing square on b2 for the bishop — a double fianchetto — pressuring the e5-pawn. The knight on c3 will eventually move; don't hesitate to put a piece on a square another of your pieces covers.

The knight will go to e4, or maybe stay; the bishop has a lot of potential energy. The queen to a6 is very strange — trying to prevent b5, but this queen goes offside, and we reinforce b5 with a later a4.

Why not kick the bishop with h3? Fine, but the bishop isn't truly bothering me on g4; I'll throw it in to force a decision, though I wouldn't in a classical game, since it lets the bishop reposition. When Black's bishop lands on f5, watch for e4 later — we have a queen on e1 and an x-ray — though e4 isn't immediately possible, with four defenders against three attackers.
It's very hard for Black to reinforce that square, because the queen is so out of the game it can't easily get to e7.
The bishop to h5 is something I like to see; now let's complete development with the bishop to b2.
White opens d4, and we play the King's Indian move-order, the knight to f6.
The knight to f3.
We fianchetto with g6, heading for a King's Indian — my real opening repertoire at this stage.
The knight to c3 — the entry to the Jobava London or Barry system.
The bishop to f4, and we've transposed into the Jobava London — the old name is the Barry system, specifically the setup against g6.
We complete our fianchetto, the bishop to g7 — all standard fare.
White plays e3.
We complete kingside development with castling.

White plays the bishop to e2 — a quieter, tamer, more positional treatment. There's a sharp, tactical way to play the Jobava London, connected with an early pawn push, but here White is playing it strategically and quietly.
Black has a million ways to disarm the Barry. I'll play solidly — starting with c6, shoring up the centre and in some lines preparing the queen to b6.
And White does play h4, combining two ideas: the bishop to e2 lulled us into a false sense of security, and now suddenly the h4 attack.
Very dangerous. The typical response is h5, stopping White's h-pawn.
The knight to e5, in some lines preparing a quick g4.

We have to get this knight off the board ASAP, so the knight to d7 is standard — otherwise White plays g4 and crashes through, and we could get mated. If White plays g4, my plan is the knight takes e5, d takes e5, the knight takes g4 — in time to eliminate the g-pawn while keeping the kingside intact.

Jobava players like to keep the tension with a move like the queen to d2. Once White plays h4, it's clear that in almost every case White castles queenside — so we're heading for an opposite-side-castling position with attacks on both wings. f3 is a very good move, preparing g4; our opponent is showing fantastic knowledge of the system's ideas.
We could play the queen to b6 hitting b2, or the queen to a5, but I'll implement a creative idea — we take on e5, capturing on e5.
White recaptures, capturing on e5. One drawback of f3 is that it weakens e3 — that pawn is now a target.

I'll play the unconventional bishop to h6 — within the framework of attacking the weak e3 pawn it makes sense. Players find it awkward to move the bishop off its fianchetto spot, but here it works, especially because if White pushes e4, he'll struggle to castle queenside, since our bishop will be holding c1. So e4 is way over-ambitious.
If White plays the queen to d2 — the standard defence of the pawn — then our bishop exerts nasty long-term pressure on this diagonal. Now we prepare for White most likely castling queenside next.

If White castles queenside, we'd want a queenside attack — so preemptively, b5 might discourage it. It's like a lead-off in baseball, stepping off the base ready for the pitch. If White doesn't castle queenside, b5 costs nothing and grabs space; if White does, we've gained a tempo, our attack already started. And every tempo is crucial in opposite-side castling, since White will try to get g4 going.

White takes their time with the bishop to d3, a nice move — I assume preparing to meet things with the knight to e2, a high-level idea. Our options: drop the knight back to d7 to trade off that annoying bishop; or something tactical like c5 for pandemonium; or b4, the knight to e2, then c5, staking a big central claim; or the knight to d7, the bishop to f4, the bishop to g7 to prepare e5.
The knight-d7, bishop-f4 trade looks sterile, so let's go crazy — b4, chasing the knight and forcing a decision.
The knight to e2.
And the follow-up, c5.
Why start with b4? First, to expand on the queenside; second, we were threatening c4, which would trap the bishop. White plays c3.
