White's treating this like a London. We take, capturing on c3, to fully discourage White from castling queenside.
White recaptures, capturing on c3. We've opened the queenside and prevented queenside castling, which would now be madness with the b-file open — very easy to reach White's king.
Now the second idea — the knight back to d7 — to open the centre. Why? Because White's king is stuck in the middle.
White can castle kingside, but then the h4 pawn becomes a major liability; queenside castling is easy to punish; and if White stays in the centre and we open it, we get to the king.
So we drop the bishop back to its fianchetto square, g7, preparing e5 — which would blast open the centre and open the bishop's diagonal, with very positive consequences.

The rook to d1 — clearly our opponent sees the idea and discourages e5. Do we push anyway? If e5, d takes e5, knight takes e5, there's the weird bishop-e4, and our d5 pawn crumbles a bit — so maybe prepare one more move.
We play the bishop to b7 — which seems silly in isolation, biting on granite, but after e5 and the trade it makes sure the d5 pawn isn't a soft target for White's heavy pieces on the d-file.
g4 — now things really heat up, and I'll likely go quiet as it gets tactical. After take, take on h5, we push e5, feeling good for Black.
We take, capturing on g4 — starting with e5 first would allow g takes h5, which feels scary and could get us mated, so this order first.
White recaptures, capturing on g4. I'm not ruling out getting mated, but with accurate play I hope not.
Now e5, opening the centre and striking at White's well-protected d4 pawn — things really heat up.
The bishop to g3. Time's fine — four minutes, plenty. We force another decision.
We could snap off a pawn, but I go with my gut — the rook to e8, keeping the tension and preparing e takes d4, putting the rook in an x-ray with the king.
White castles kingside, abandoning the mating ambitions for king safety — probably the right call. I underestimated that move.
The knight to f6 — actually the immediate knight to f6 is a smart alternative, with tactics behind it I'll explain after the game.
g5 — most people eye the bishop takes e5. What if White just snaps the pawn? The knight to g4 or the knight to h5 make sense.
Let's go knight to g4, going after the e3 pawn. Maybe the knight to h5 and the queen to d7 was better, but too late now.
The knight to g4 is probably a mistake, but not so bad. White plays the bishop to b5.
We could take on d4, but why not calmly bring the rook up to e7, also solidifying the very valuable f7 pawn?
White takes the pawn, capturing on c5. Now we'd love to win it back.

We can win it back with the queen — the queen to c8 makes most sense, with more tactics behind it: if White pushes c6, after the trade White can't take on d5, because we'd pick up the e3 pawn with a fork. That's why I didn't play the rook to c8.

White pushes c6, we take with the queen, White takes with the bishop, and we recapture, capturing on c6 with the bishop — and once we collect the c5 pawn we'll have an intact centre, excellent coordination with both bishops fianchettoed, and White's pawns terribly weak.
White plays c6 and the bishop to f2 — but we're very close to winning; he wants to take on d5.

Let's solidify — the rook to d8, protecting d5 and bringing the rook into play. I expect e4, then we double on the d-file and blast through the centre. Black is borderline winning, strategically, given how many weaknesses White has.
The knight to g3. If I keep my clock under control, we're going to win.
e4 — not sure it's best, but it opens our bishop and creates strongholds for our knight, which can circle back to e5.
The rook to c1.
The knight to e5 — very juicy squares, and the queen can drive in on the light squares too.
White's starting to crumble. The knight to f3 — an outpost, also hitting the h4 pawn.
White plays the queen to e2.
We capture, taking on h4 with check — not just for the free pawn, but because now the g5 pawn is a huge weakness.
The king to h3 — and I see a mating net forming around it.
We don't need the complications — we simply go back to f3.
The rook to h1 — I'm not worried about anything on the h-file; there's no attack.

We check with the bishop to d7 — the g5 pawn isn't going anywhere, so we go for the kill — the king goes to g2, and the bishop repositions to e6, heading for g4 to set up a discovered attack on White's queen.
The king to f1, and the bishop to g4 — with our other bishop coming to e5 to press the knight, and if needed our king can escape through the centre.
The bishop to e5 — White's resistance is ending, because after the rook to g1 there's a check on h3 that wins. We're not taking the rook and blundering our queen.
We give the check, the bishop to h3 — let's be accurate; I see at least two ways to win.

Two wins: the knight back to h4, or, more accurate, the bishop takes g3 and then the queen to h1 and the rook. As I've said, when finishing an attack, don't fixate on mate — often you use the king's weakness as a springboard to winning decisive material. So I'll cover the h-file with the rook to b7 heading for b2, or, which I like, the king to g7 — one rook to the h-file, the other to the b-file, division of labour, and mate materialises. White literally can't move because of this knight.
Against Owen's b6 we start with d4 — an incredibly effective system that drains the fun out of this offbeat opening.

Nc3 defends e4 naturally, and here's the first fork: the lazy Nf3 sleepwalks into trouble, because Black's whole idea is Bb4, pinning the knight and piling onto the e4-pawn until careless players simply drop it.
notes.teaches: Against ...b6/...Bb4 setups, don't develop on autopilot — the target is the e4 pawn behind the pin.

notes.explains: The antidote is Bd3, shoring up e4 before the pin can bite.
notes.teaches: Pre-reinforce the pawn the coming pin will attack.

notes.explains: After Bb4 comes the crux — Ne2, not a3. It connects the knights, so Bxc3 loses its sting and the b4-bishop is neutered, and we never have to weaken ourselves with f3.
notes.teaches: Ne2 defuses a ...Bb4 pin by connecting the knights, without the concession a3 or f3 would make.

notes.explains: The pawn to e4, e5.
The knight to f3.
The knight to f6.

The knight to c3 — not the Belgrade Gambit, not the Four Knights Scotch, but an opening I've played and analyzed for about two years: an incredibly underrated, dangerous weapon that flies under the radar. It's the Glek System, named after Igor Glek.
The knight to c6. A lot of Black players don't study this, so they misplace their pieces, and you seriously contend for an advantage.
g3 — the fianchetto of the bishop in a king-pawn game.
The bishop to c5.
The bishop to g2.
d6 — the most popular reply if you actually check the database; most people who don't know what to do with Black develop in exactly this manner.
The first step in the Glek is to finish kingside development with d3 — stage one, flexible, delaying castling a touch.
h6 is a move Black often defaults to; we weren't intending the bishop to g5 anyway, but it's a healthy enough move.
Now we castle —

— and Black castles. Stage two. There's a branching point: one plan is the bishop to e3, which the engine dislikes but I've scored with online; the way Glek intended is a King's-Indian-style setup preparing the f2-f4 strike — h3, the king to h2 to unpin the f-pawn, the knight back to d2, then push f4.

The bishop-to-e3 plan poses Black the dilemma of trading bishops, and with the semi-open f-file White gets serious attacking chances connected to the knight transfer to h5. I want to play the main line here as an introduction to the system.
h3 — healthy and non-committal. Black plays a5, crossing the t's and dotting the i's; with our next move we already choose between the bishop to e3 and the king to h2.

The king to h2. Rather than meeting a4 with a4, in blitz I like to allow a4 and stop the pawn with a3 — or even allow a3, met calmly by b3 — and keep preparing f4. The whole Zen of this opening is that f4 push. A byproduct of the king to h2: the h3-pawn is now safely protected, so if Black builds the classic bishop-and-queen battery we don't lose a tempo defending it.

The knight to e7 — unconventional; not bad, but it changes how we handle the position, and it relinquishes Black's grip on the d4-square. Because we've played h3 and the king to h2, we're still uncommitted — we could even revert to the bishop to e3. One thematic try is to strike with d4 ourselves, as any Ruy player would look for: after d4 the pawns come off, and thanks to our e4-pawn we keep slightly superior central control, a minuscule edge. The other candidate is the knight to d2 following the plan with f4; after it Black may reroute the knight to g6, we push f4, Black trades, and there's a move to be aware of — the knight from g6 to h4, hitting our g2-bishop; we don't want to give that bishop up, so we'd drop it back to h1, which looks a little flimsy. The knight to h4 for us is possible too, then the knight to g6, then the knight to f5. The knight to g1 is also playable — it keeps the bishop's diagonal open but is more passive and undevelops the knight, and after it Black might counter-strike with d5. A hard call between d4 and the knight to d2.
Let's play by the textbook — the knight to d2 — and see if Mr. Glek knew what he was talking about.
We take White and face the Sicilian.
We play f4 — the Grand Prix Attack.
Black strikes back with d5.
We take on d5.
Black develops ...Nf6, attacking the d5-pawn.
We check on b5.
Black blocks with the bishop to d7.
We take on d7 with check.
Black recaptures with the queen.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black regains the pawn with the knight.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We play d3.
Black plays e6.
We castle.
Black develops the bishop to e7.
We plant the knight on e5.
Black takes our knight on e5.
We recapture with the f-pawn.
Black castles.
We swing the queen to f3.
Black plays ...Nb4.
We lift the rook to f2.
Black retreats the knight to c6.
We develop the bishop to f4.
Black pushes c4.
We play the rook to d1.
Black develops the bishop to c5.
We offer a trade with the bishop to e3.
Black grabs on e5 with the knight.
We play the queen to e4.
Black takes our bishop on e3.
We recapture with the queen.
Black plays ...Ng4.
We return the queen to e4.
Black takes our rook, capturing on f2.
We recapture with the king.
Black takes on d3.
We recapture with the rook.
Black plays the queen to c7.
We play g3.
Black doubles rooks with ...Rad8.
We play b3.
Black takes our rook on d3.
We recapture with the queen; Black plays the rook to d8.
We play the queen to e3.
Black plays the rook to c8.
We jump the knight to b5.
Black grabs on c2 with check.
We walk the king to f3.
Black checks with ...Qf5.
We block with the queen to f4.
Black takes the knight, capturing on b5.
We wave the pawn by with d5, heading into Benoni/Benko territory.
Black offers the Benko Gambit — b5, giving up a pawn for lasting queenside pressure down the half-open a- and b-files.
teaches: the Benko pawn sac for queenside files

notes.explains: Instead of the topical capture we play an old Soviet sideline — the knight to d2. Little-known, but it has teeth.
Here's the point: we meet the capture on c4 with e4, almost reversing the gambit — sacrificing a pawn ourselves, but only temporarily, since we'll win it straight back.
We recapture on c4 with the bishop — it has to be the bishop, or the pawn on e4 hangs. White holds a small but stable edge.
Black sets up the Benko-Benoni structure with the fianchetto to g7. There's a standard plan here — Black's knight rerouting through g4 to e5 — so we'll want to restrain it.
h3 restrains that knight from g4. We can't rush the bishop to b2 yet — b3 right now runs into the Nxc4 tactic — so first we prepare it.
teaches: prepare the fianchetto around the Nxc4 trick

notes.explains: The rook to e1 is one of those moves that's almost always useful — quietly improving while we sort out the bishop's route.

Now the whole middlegame plan. Our overarching aim is to fix on the d6-pawn and lean on Black's center as a whole. We finally want the dark-squared bishop on b2 — reached either through a rook to b1, then b3, then bishop to b2, or the creative rook-swing to a3 and into the center. Then it's a division of labor: one rook hammers d6 while the other lifts to g3 against the king. Squeeze both wings, and the position cracks with a mating tactic on the kingside.
teaches: squeeze d6 and the king at once
division of labor between the rooks
plans: one rook on d6, one lifted to g3

notes.explains: e4, the knight to c6 — the Nimzowitsch Defense; the Alekhine would be the knight to f6. We play the knight to f3.
This is a completely different opening, and it definitely is underrated.

d4 is the principled way to meet it, and now Black has d5 — a line I find incredibly annoying for White. I don't like playing it, because it's a form of the Scandinavian where Black often quickly castles long. There's a lot of theory, White's supposed to be better, but I never know how to play it, and White can literally get crushed here, because this pawn comes under fire and e5 is coming — not a good line to play in blitz.

Another move for Black is e5 — this one is a little more innocuous; I can just take on e5, or play d5, but even in that closed centre the knight reroutes to g6 and it can be hard to play with White. So I wouldn't give people what they

This g5 lunge shows up constantly at this level — it's meant to intimidate. But the right question is: what did it weaken? Immediately the f5 square becomes a permanent hole. So the plan writes itself — steer a knight toward g3 or e3 to occupy it.
Even without a bishop to chase, the point stands: routing the knight this way is all about earning access to that f5 square. The square is the target, not any single piece.
Now the strange-looking move — the knight pulls all the way back. The end goal is simple even if the route is odd: land a knight on f5. Everything is bent toward reaching that square.
Two goals sit behind this: first, get the knight to f5; second, prise the position open, because the opponent has moved nothing but pawns. Undeveloped pieces are an invitation to open lines.
The knight steps to e3, and the earlier retreat starts to make sense — that quiet regrouping was clearing the runway for this.
Here's the puzzle: a knight dragged all the way home. Why? The hint is that it's there to support one specific pawn thrust — the piece isn't parked, it's loading a lever.
That lever is h3 — the move the retreat was preparing all along. It's the break that cracks the kingside open.
Aren't knights on the rim grim? Usually — but this one has a future, with g5 waiting for it. And the deeper win is that the position has been forced open while the opponent is still asleep.
Opening lines against such a lagging development is decisive. And the second goal lands too — the other knight is on its way to that f5 outpost.

If the outpost knight gets taken, the pawn recaptures, chases the defending knight, and can even ram down to f6. Normally you want to recapture an outpost with a piece — but there are exceptions, and this is shaping into one.

The exception is justified by how badly the opponent is developed — the whole aim is to keep the flames roaring and the position wide open. From here the search shifts to the kill, and there's already a fork in the air against a loose, undefended pawn.

It's an undefended pawn we're already making contact with, so we simply round it up. Grabbing material like this is usually greedy, but total development dominance earns the right — and it rips open the h-file, a road that could lead all the way to the king.

That pawn thrust looks menacing but folds easily — no need to defend, just push past it. The check that follows is harmless because it traps the opponent's own knight, forcing it to shuffle back and lose more time.

Now the heavy pieces join: the queen swings over to x-ray the king, the bishop develops and long castling links the rooks — full development, at last, all pointed at the enemy king. The attack itself is a knight leaping to g5, hitting f7 and threatening mate; goad the dark-square concessions, and the open h-file becomes the highway for a hook-mate finish. The opponent's whole campaign was bluff — there were never any attackers behind it.
White plays d4, and we develop the knight to f6, keeping our options open.
White grabs space with c4, and we fianchetto with g6 — heading for a Grünfeld this time rather than the King's Indian.
The knight to c3. The Grünfeld, unlike the King's Indian, meets this with d5, not d6.

We strike in the centre with d5 — the Grünfeld, universally regarded as one of the best objective defenses to d4. Nobody has found an advantage against it anywhere; the downside is just the out-of-this-world amount of theory to play it professionally.
The bishop to f4 is a legitimate try. The Grünfeld's idea is simple: we grab central control by combining the King's Indian fianchetto with a proactive d5, instead of letting White build with e4.
We don't take the c4 pawn — that's not the point. The point is rapid development so we can attack White's centre; it's a hypermodern opening. So the bishop goes to g7, and c6 is unnecessary.
We're perfectly happy to recapture on d5 with the knight. White takes, capturing on d5.
The knight takes, capturing on d5.

The bishop to g3 is correct. What makes the Grünfeld both fun and hard is constant tactical alertness — these centralized pieces are integral to Black's central strategy, and unlike the King's Indian, where you play the long game, here you assault White's centre directly, with moves like c5 and the knight to c6. White can lose quickly if he doesn't develop precisely. So between c5 and the knight to c6, which harasses the centre more effectively?

It's c5 — the knight to c6 can be met by e3, forming a pawn chain, but c5 is very strong: if White simply takes with d takes c5, we play the knight takes c3, and after trading queens he loses a piece, because he can't recapture the bishop takes c3 with check between the king and rook. If instead e3, after the trade he gets an isolated queen pawn and we blockade the square in front of it — phenomenal for Black.
He should probably take the knight first, then the pawn — but he takes the pawn, capturing on c5. Unless I miscalculated, we're in great shape.
The knight takes, capturing on c3 — this basically wins the game.
He miscalculated something — maybe he thought he had a check — but the queen takes d8 with check, and we simply recapture on d8. A nice introduction to the Grünfeld.
He takes, capturing on c3 — making things worse, but people familiar with an opening still don't always handle it well at this level.
We take, capturing on c3 with check — and at this point it's already over.

The king to d1, and the bishop grabs the rook, capturing on a1. The Grünfeld isn't an opening you pick up casually — which is why fewer top players play it full-time, not because it's bad but because of the vast theory to remember.
The king to c1.
Let's develop our knight to c6.
e4. We just need to develop and get the king out of the centre. Where should this bishop go? Even when we're not up a rook, there's a good square for it in the Grünfeld.

The bishop to e6 — not g4, which does nothing. It's not about developing as far into enemy territory as possible, but about the piece's role: this attacks a2, is centralized, and prevents White's bishop from coming out to c4.
The bishop to b5. We could take the a2 pawn, but up a rook we'd rather prioritise piece play, as you often do in the Grünfeld.
Many good moves here. One approach is to target the c5 pawn, realizing it's a conduit toward his king — so we begin with the rook to c8. The knight to d4 is stronger once it's prepared this way.
The knight to f3 — and we're going for a mating attack, with the knight to d4 next.
The knight to d4 — the bishop can come back to capture it, and note White has the rook to d1 if he wants, but then we take on c5 just in time.
White takes, capturing on d4.
We recapture, capturing on d4, eliminating that bishop.
The rook to d1. If you want to learn the Grünfeld, I'd say at a minimum around 2000 — it's so theoretical and concrete.
The rook takes, capturing on c5 with check.
The king to b1. You might win quick games learning it earlier, but you'd build the wrong habits — that's just my opinion; use your own judgment, and be in charge of your own chess development.
The rook takes, capturing on b5 with check.
The king to c2. Now, we can't save this bishop, which is kind of funny. If we play the rook to b4 to defend it, what does White do?

We play the rook to b4, and White tries a3 — but the rook to a4 wins, or the bishop to b3 with check. The move is the bishop to e5, since the bishop-b5 attacks both the rook and the bishop; probably f6, walk the king over to f7, swing the rook to c8, and win easily.
Against these Pirc/hippo 'unnamed' setups the strategy doesn't change — develop naturally, start with Nc3, and go from there.
notes.teaches: Meet an offbeat, passive system with sound natural development, not a special refutation.

notes.explains: Don't waste a tempo on a4 to stop b5 — you can let the pawn come. Allowing the queenside expansion is harmless; just keep developing with Nf3.
notes.teaches: A queenside pawn push you can ignore isn't worth a defensive tempo — keep developing.

notes.explains: The light bishop always comes to d3 in this line — the standard Austrian Attack setup, then castle.
Qe1 is the flexible maneuver — it commits to nothing but eyes the Qh4 swing, exactly as in the Grand Prix Attack.
notes.teaches: Reroute the queen via e1 toward h4 to build a kingside attack without committing early.

notes.explains: Most players reach automatically for Be3; the stronger move is e5. Since the attack will come on the kingside, half-closing the centre helps — and e5 locks Black's g7-bishop out of the game while cashing in on f4.
notes.teaches: Half-close the centre when you plan to attack on a wing, especially to entomb the enemy fianchetto bishop.

notes.explains: Recapture with the d-pawn, or we drop material — and now the d-file opens onto Black's cramped queen while f6 becomes a glaring hole.
notes.plans: Swing a rook to the d-file and aim a knight at f6.

notes.explains: Ne4 is my favorite kind of move — aggressive and prophylactic at once: it heads for f6 while quietly stopping Nb4. Those double-duty moves are the most annoying to face.
notes.teaches: Prize moves that attack and prevent simultaneously; they give the opponent no counterplay.

notes.explains: c3 kicks the knight and covers d4 — but a move that allows a discovery needs concrete checking, so make sure you've counted every knight jump before you play it.
notes.teaches: Before permitting a discovered attack, calculate all of the discovering piece's landing squares.

notes.explains: When you push a pawn, watch your loose pieces — bring the bishop back to c2 rather than leave it hanging. There's all the time in the world.
notes.teaches: After a pawn push, re-check whether it left one of your own pieces undefended.

notes.explains: g4 chases the knight and grabs space. Nobody should worry about pushing pawns in front of the king here — Black is far too passive to ever exploit it.
notes.teaches: Storming pawns in front of your own king is safe when the opponent has no counterplay to answer it.

notes.explains: h3 supports the advance, and note Black is weak on c5 too — the position is essentially zugzwang-bound; White is winning on strategy alone.
The knockout is all about order: g5 first would hand Black a stronghold on f5, so start with Nf6-check. If Black takes twice, g5 wins the knight; otherwise Qh4 or f5 crashes through.
notes.teaches: In a two-move breakthrough, play the forcing check first so the follow-up pawn push arrives with full effect.

notes.explains: Black has to give up the piece — a full extra minor and every dark square, decisive.
Qf2 sets up Bc5 and coordinates the rooks — patient improvement while up material.

Up a decisive amount there are two winning philosophies: trade into an easy endgame, or use the extra piece to attack. The right answer is a balance — but here, with this dark-square bind, hunting the queen trade with Qh4 would be a crime, prolonging the win forever. Keep attacking.
notes.teaches: Don't trade into an endgame when you have a raging attack; convert with the attack, not against it.

notes.explains: Bc5 politely asks the queen where it intends to live.
Ng5, heading for e4 — the queen starts to feel genuinely uncomfortable with nowhere good to sit.
No rush when you're winning — enjoy the process and simply bring the last piece into the game.
notes.teaches: With a decisive advantage, activate every piece before forcing matters; there's no need to hurry.

notes.explains: The dream is a knight on f6, and the queen guards it — so Bb3 deflects the rook off the d-file, after which Rd1 could trap the queen. Manufacture the threat you can't play directly.
notes.teaches: To reach an outpost the queen defends, first deflect the defender guarding the deflecting move.

notes.explains: So we do trade queens — but in service of the attack: Nf6-check keeps the mate rolling, and the rook finishes faster than the queens could have. Trading queens is only wrong when it abandons the attack.
notes.teaches: A queen trade is fine — even best — when it speeds up the mate rather than dissolving your attack.

notes.explains: The rook swings to d7, the knight and bishop pile in, and mate arrives in a couple of moves.
We open another e4 game.
The knight develops to f3, Black answers with the knight to c6, and we pin with the bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez, our main weapon.
Black plays the knight to f6 — the Berlin.
There are many ways to face the Berlin, but we go straight in — heading for the Berlin endgame, to show it's more than a draw.
Black declines the Berlin endgame with ...d6 — passive, but a legitimate Steinitz Defence.
Previously we'd prepare with c3; now, at a higher level, we play the more topical immediate d4.
Black takes on d4. We open the centre precisely because Black has played passively.
We recapture with the knight.
Black develops the bishop to d7.
We develop the knight to c3, opening things up to press our lead in development.
Black plays the bishop to e7.
Theory says take on c6 with the bishop, keeping our knight strongly centralized.

Black recaptures with the b-pawn, taking a defect into his queenside structure. Now the point: Black wants ...c5 to kick our knight, and we'd love to answer with the knight to f5 — but playing it right now lets Black trade it, and recapturing with a pawn would wreck our kingside and pull a pawn from the centre; b4 would be artificial. We don't need to prevent ...c5 at all — we prepare our response to it. Prophylaxis cuts both ways: you can stop a move, or ready an answer to it. The queen to f3 is best — it improves a piece and readies the knight to f5 the moment ...c5 arrives.
We take White and open e4, Black meets e5.
The knight develops to f3.
Black develops to c6. We're playing the Four Knights Scotch — a great opening for improving players: it brings every piece out on sound principles, not gimmicks.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black completes the knights with ...Nf6.
Now the point: d4, opening the centre — and dangerous if Black plays inaccurately.
Black takes and we recapture with the knight.
Black develops the bishop to c5.
The most principled move is the bishop to e3 — it defends our knight and sets a threat: take on c6, and Black's bishop on c5 falls because the queen behind it hangs.
Black releases the tension with ...Bxd4 — already an inaccuracy, conceding the centre.
We recapture with the bishop, and now we hold the two bishops and a bigger share of the centre.
Black castles. Our priority: finish developing quickly while preserving the bishop pair.
We keep the pair by retreating the bishop to e3 — the aggressive c5 would just invite ...d6; on an open board we want both bishops.

Black plays ...h6 — and that's a hook. A good moment to train your castling intuition: I'd castle queenside, because ...h6 invites g4–g5 to prise it open, and with the bishop pair and more centre, an opposite-side race favours us.
We begin with the flexible queen to d2.
Black tucks the king to h7.
We castle queenside. Note f3 isn't only to stop ...Ng4 — it also props up e4 and prepares g4.
Black plays d6.
We play f3 — unlike h3, it supports the e4-pawn, so it's automatic here: the English-Attack setup of f3, g4 and h4.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
The king to b1 is a fine improving move, but Black has so little counterplay that we simply start the attack with g4.

Black centralises with the knight to e5 — a good move, and now attacking calls for creativity. We must defend f3 — losing it collapses our kingside — while helping the attack, and the queen to g2 does both, landing on the g-file beside the rook to bear down on g7. Then g5 rolls in. And the Shankland question returns: can we play f5 anyway? Yes — f5 traps and wins the queen, and even after a capture the pin from the bishop to d3 decides. The theme throughout: keep asking "what if I do it anyway" instead of recoiling from a threat.
The Queen's Gambit — we offer the c-pawn to deflect Black's center.
The knight to f6 is the Marshall Defense — a cross between a Grünfeld and a Queen's Gambit Declined that simply doesn't work, though White must be precise to prove it.
We take on d5 and Black recaptures with the knight, exactly as the Marshall intends.
The strongest reply is e4, kicking the knight and grabbing a broad pawn center at once.

Now the move you have to know: the bishop to d3. It looks quiet, but the natural knight to c3 is actually a mistake — it walks into e5, when the queen trade with check leaves White scrambling. Bishop to d3 sidesteps all of it and keeps the edge.
teaches: Bd3 over Nc3 to avoid the ...e5 trick

notes.explains: We develop circumspectly with h3, so a bishop to g4 can always be met by f3 — a small luxury we can afford because Black burned tempi shuffling the knight around.
Rather than the passive bishop to e3, we go to g5 — the pawn on d4 is already held by the knight, so we spend the bishop on pressure instead of defense.
teaches: develop for pressure when the center is already held

notes.explains: The simplest plan: go after the fianchetto bishop. The queen to d2 prepares the bishop to h6 — trade that bishop and Black's king weakens and his grip on d4 loosens.
teaches: Qd2 and Bh6 to trade the dark-squared bishop

notes.explains: When Black lunges with c5 we don't take — that would justify his whole setup. We push d5, jamming the door shut and keeping a protected passer.
teaches: push past, don’t capture, to keep the bind

notes.explains: Black recaptures on e5, and note the risk in that: once a fianchettoed bishop ventures off g7, it can struggle to get home, leaving holes and inviting f4.
teaches: a fianchetto bishop that leaves home is at risk

notes.explains: So the bishop to h6 makes him regret it, cutting the bishop off from its return square.
There's no rush and no reason to wait — we take on g7 and strip the king's defender.
The rook belongs on d1: if Black frees himself with e6 and the pawns come off, that rook stacks behind the queen down the d-file.
teaches: place the rook where the file will open

notes.explains: The knight to e2 does double duty — it stops b5 indirectly and reroutes toward the kingside, since it was only biting on granite where it stood.
teaches: reroute the idle knight toward the attack

notes.explains: On to g3, bringing the knight into the coming kingside assault.
Now the gas pedal: f4. We prepared slowly, and this is where we attack fast.
The finish begins with the queen check on c3, driving the king back before the combination.
We crack it open by taking on e6 — Black's passive position simply can't hold everything together.
After the recapture the bishop swings to c4, joining the pile-up on the e6 weakness.
Then f5 lands with tremendous force — the whole position collapses.
The bishop takes on e6 with check, ripping the king open.
Here's the crusher — the knight is pinned, and with king and queen lined up on the same rank the rook check on d7 wins outright.
teaches: the pin plus the rook on the seventh

notes.explains: We collect the queen and the wheels come off.
e6 quietly shores up the d5 pawn, giving the centre a firm second layer of support before anything else develops.

Both sides play this modest pawn move, and it carries a real drawback worth naming: it hems in the queen's bishop. It isn't a mistake — just a conservative way to build, trading a little piece activity for solidity.
c5 strikes back at the centre, refusing to let the position settle into something one-sided. Contesting the middle early is the whole idea.

The centre becomes a little interlocked box of pawns — it looks tangled but it's beautifully balanced, every unit propped up by another. Because nothing can be won by force, neither side wants to be the one to flinch and release the tension.
The tension finally breaks — capturing on c5 is a decision to clarify the centre rather than keep sitting on the standoff.
This little rook-pawn nudge is preparation, not an end in itself — it's clearing the way for a pawn to expand on the queenside with b4.

The point of the earlier rook-pawn move now shows: it discourages a pawn from lunging to b5 to harass the knight, because the answer would be to capture on b5 and rip open the a-file. A small prophylactic move that quietly rules out the opponent's plan.

Why isn't the pawn just hanging for free? Because loose pieces drop off. The move order is everything — capture the knight first, and then the recaptured queen is left a sitting duck: a check springs in from b4, forking and collecting it. Snatch the pawn in the wrong order and the trick evaporates.
We answer e4 with e5, looking for something offbeat.
The knight to f3 — I'd love to play the Elephant Gambit or the Stafford here.
We play the knight to f6, angling for the Stafford.
But the knight to c3 sidesteps it — no Stafford now. You can play d5 here for an interesting game, and the bishop to c5 might transpose to the Stafford.
We try the bishop to c5, Eric Rosen style, hoping to goad a gambit.
He plays the bishop to c4 — so we'll have to play conventionally, but we'll make it interesting.

If we castle and he takes, there's no Stafford left — he's close to castling. So we either play the knight to c6 into a Four Knights, or d6; it doesn't much matter, so we start with d6 to defend the e5 pawn.
White castles. Now, to make it hard for him to develop, how do we add some spice?
The bishop to g4 — because if we play the knight to c6 first, knowing his style he'll play h3 and we'll regret it, so we squeeze this in while we can. He'll probably retreat to e2.
Now we play the knight to c6, threatening the knight to d4.

The bishop to e3. A classic line. The knight to d4 is possible but less strong with the bishop on e3, since he can take with the bishop and keep his structure. Against boring players, keep the tension — give them rope and force decisions.

The classic way to make White decide is to drop the bishop back to b6, avoiding his taking on c5 and ruining our structure — and if he takes now, a takes b6 gives us doubled pawns that don't matter, plus the a-file, which is great.
Make these players think, and they'll do something irrational or panic. h3.
We drop the bishop to h5 — he'll probably contemplate g4 for a while; if he plays it, we consider a sacrifice on g4.
I don't think the time's right for the sac — not enough there — so we keep the bishop. He plays the king to h2, a weird move; maybe planning the rook to g1 and g4.
We just castle — no point doing anything wild.

The queen to d2. Now I see his idea: the king went to h2 so that after the bishop takes f3, g takes f3 keeps his king off the open file, and he can play the rook to g1 and attack down the g-file — even with a ruined structure, he gets the file.
Does that warrant not taking on f3? No — the bishop takes f3, capturing on f3, creates such damage on his kingside that it's worth it, as long as we're careful.

He recaptures, capturing on f3. The weaknesses he's created are permanent, so it's worth it if we manage the open g-file. Two things: start kingside operations, moves like the knight to h5, and balance that with some prophylaxis.
The greater priority is to stake a claim on the kingside so he doesn't run circles over us — so the knight to h5, getting the wheels turning.
The rook to g1 — a pin. Many people reflexively play the king to h8, but that tempo could matter against a skilled attacker. Where's the queen doing more, on f6 or h4? Only one creates a threat.
The queen to f6 — on h4 it does nothing, since we've no light-squared bishop to hit h3; on f6 it's active.
The rook to g4, ignoring the attack on f3 — this guy's legit, gone from passive to aggressive in a snap.
As the Russian expression goes, having said A you must say B — putting the queen on f6 and NOT taking on f3 makes no sense, so the queen takes f3, capturing on f3.

The rook to g1, doubling — now the threats on g7 are serious. One more move and he creates insurmountable threats, probably a sacrifice; g6 doesn't solve it, and he could sack on g6 via the pin. So now's the time.
The king to h8 — the problem is the g-file, not his bishop. The king to h8 is the better move.
The knight to d5 is good — this guy's very legit; I'll play faster. We keep attacking; our king is very safe.
We need spice on the kingside — open files, something to join this lonely queen. So f5 — gutsy play by both of us.
He takes, capturing on f5. With my queen so dominant and the knight on h5 defending g7, I'm optimistic about the attack.
The rook takes, capturing on f5.

The rook to g2 — this seems like capitulation of his attack, which I like; it means he doesn't know what to do and is milking my clock. Now g7 is protected; we want to triple, with the knight to d4 and the rook to f8 coming.
The rook to f8, continuing to pile pieces on the kingside — no need to change strategy.
He takes, capturing on b6 — you have to take.
We recapture, capturing on b6, checking for intermediate moves first — nothing there.
The bishop to e6 — a very advanced idea I'll admit I missed: if we move the rook, he plays the bishop to g4 and wins a piece. So we'll have to sac the exchange.
We sac the exchange with the knight to e7.
After the bishop takes f5 and we recapture with the knight on f5, my worry isn't even the position, it's the clock.
The rook to g5.
The knight to h4.
The rook to g4 — he's blundered back; a small blunder.
Now I want a knight on f3, so we take the rook first, the queen capturing on g4.
He takes on g4, and the knight to f3 comes with check.
The king to g2, and the knight takes, capturing on d2.
He recaptures with the bishop on d2.
We play the knight to f4, check, centralizing it; if he takes, that's a good trade for us — up a pawn.
He takes, capturing on f4.
We recapture, capturing on f4 — a very nice rook on f4, and we're up a pawn.
He plays f3.
Let's get our king out — the king to g8.
a3, and we push b5.
The king to g3.
Our king comes to f7.
The rook to h1.
We play h6.
The rook to h5.
The king to g6 — I want to make things go boom on the other side of the board.
We push c5.
The rook to h1.
The rook to a4.
The rook to e1.
The king to f6.
He offers a rook trade with the rook to e4 — if this is a draw I'll be shocked; let me calculate.
Let's take it — the rook capturing on e4.
He recaptures, capturing on e4.
The king to e6.
The king to h4, and we play g6.
White pushes g5.
We play h5.
The king to g3, and we push d5.
The king to f2.
We push d4.
The king to e2, and we push h4 — this is winning: two passed pawns.
He takes, capturing on d4 — but I've plenty of clock; this is not a draw.
We recapture, capturing on d4 — two connected passers too far from his king.
The king to f2.
We just go h3.
The king to g3.

We push d3 — d2, d1, and it's a queen. A good game by this guy. There's no stalemate: I leave him a pawn, then walk my king around to mate on the other side. A tip: when mating with a couple of seconds left, leave your opponent pawn moves so you never have to worry about stalemate.
The Grünfeld gives White a bajillion tries and none proven to yield an edge, so pick a system that flies under the radar — especially against players still learning the opening.
notes.teaches: Against a heavily-analyzed defense, a sound offbeat system beats fighting the theory head-on.

notes.explains: We take, cxd5 Nxd5, and reach for one of the rarest moves on the board.
Na4 — the Nadanyan move. It looks crazy, but its whole purpose is to prevent the exchange on c3 that the Grünfeld is built on, and to stop the c5 break, keeping White's centre intact.
notes.teaches: A knight to the rim can be justified if it vetoes the opponent's central break.

notes.explains: Ne3 is the point — Black temporarily gives up a knight, but he plans to win it back on a4, since after the coming trades the a4-knight ends up loose.
Here Black slips: the move order must be Bxd2 first, then Qh4-check to fork the king and the a4-knight. Checking on h4 first lets us slot in g3.
notes.teaches: In a forcing tactical sequence, the eliminating capture usually must precede the forking check.

notes.explains: And that's the punishment: after Bxd2 and Kxd2, the queen on h4 still guards nothing of ours — our king recaptures and the queen no longer wins the a4-knight, which we keep defended. Parrot a repertoire one move out of order in these lines and you're simply lost.
notes.teaches: Know why each move order in a sharp line is forced; a single transposition can flip the result.

notes.explains: The king in the centre isn't dangerous — it tucks away on c1. But beware: meeting the b4-check with the knight would drop everything to Qxb2-check, so play Kc1.
notes.teaches: Interposing a piece against a check can hang the b2-pawn with a devastating follow-up — check first.

notes.explains: No shenanigans — just develop, consolidate, and cash the extra piece. Both kings are unsafe and neither side is developed, so calm accuracy wins.
notes.teaches: When you're up material in a messy position, consolidate first; fireworks only give it back.

notes.explains: Retreat the knight to c3 — not e3, which would drop both knights to the queen.
notes.teaches: Before a natural blocking move, check it doesn't leave two of your pieces on one enemy line.

notes.explains: Two ways to convert: force the queen trade with Qd5, or lean on the development lead. With that lead there's no need to trade — keep the pieces on.
notes.teaches: With a lead in development, don't trade queens; use the pieces while the opponent's are asleep.

notes.explains: e4 opens the bishop's diagonal, threatens a pin, and goads Black into castling right into the attack.
notes.plans: Open lines with e4 and lure the king to the kingside.

notes.explains: The key insight: Black lacks his Grünfeld bishop, so the dark squares around his king are chronically weak — and that unlocks a pile of thematic attacking ideas.
notes.teaches: A missing fianchetto bishop leaves the dark squares by the king permanently soft; aim your attack there.

notes.explains: Qh6 with the threat of a crushing Ng5 forces f6 — which in turn weakens the a2-g8 diagonal, so a bishop reaching c4 becomes mate.
notes.teaches: Provoke a defensive pawn move, then attack the new diagonal it just opened.

notes.explains: To land the bishop on c4 we first chase the queen off c6, and Bb5 does it while developing — even if the queen sidesteps, we've simply improved a piece.
notes.teaches: Prefer the queen-chasing move that also develops; it wins either way.

notes.explains: Now the queen no longer guards f6, so take there and bring the knight to g5 — the attack the whole plan was aiming for.
Nd5 is simplest — Qc5-check runs into Kb1, which parries every check and leaves unstoppable mating threats.
Our Sicilian again — we'll test the Accelerated Dragon at this level.
White plays the Alapin, the pawn to c3 — building a big center behind d4 rather than opening the main lines.
Here I'll show a practical, lesser-known try: the immediate d5, striking the center before White is ready.

White pushes e5, trying to move-order us into a French Advance. The escape is that our light-squared bishop isn't shut in yet — we can develop it outside the pawn chain first and reach an improved French.
teaches: dodge the French move-order with the bishop out

notes.explains: The bishop to g4 is the ambitious choice — it pins the knight and leans on the center, challenging White the most. Then e6 gives us a French on steroids, bishop already outside the chain.
teaches: Bg4: the good bishop out before ...e6

notes.explains: White develops to b5. The capture on c6 isn't really a threat, but we'd rather not wreck our queenside pawns if we don't have to.
So the queen to c7 — less exposed than b6, and it leans on the e5-pawn, so we're happy to recapture there if White trades on c6.
teaches: Qc7 to recapture cleanly and hit e5

notes.explains: And that's the point — we take back with the queen, keeping the structure intact and a fine position.
White plays d4 and we've reached exactly that improved French. Rather than a sharp tactical fling that leaves our king behind, we'll keep it simple.
The clean e6 — an intuitive judgment call, no need for tricks when we have a healthy, easy position.
teaches: simple over speculative when you’re comfortable

notes.explains: The Caro-Kann-style route pays off: the knight goes to f5 via e7, pressuring the d4-pawn from its ideal square.
c4 closes the queenside and makes White's rook lift look pointless — a psychologically awkward move to face, even if it eases the pressure on d4.
teaches: close the queenside to freeze the enemy plan

notes.explains: An unconventional idea — the capture on a4, opening the b-file. Normally you'd never crack open the queenside like this, but White is so passive that the open file is all ours, and that a-pawn is now a weakness.
teaches: open the file when the passive side can’t use it

notes.explains: Now we finish development and castle — no need for a defensive a5; White has nothing scary there.
Back to the strong idea: the bishop to a3, which does several things at once and, if the rook steps to a1, drops to b2 with a fork.
teaches: Ba3 with the Bb2 fork tucked behind it

notes.explains: We open e4, and our opponent answers e5 — he plays the Philidor, so this could be a themed run.
The knight to f3.
d6 — the Philidor. In the spirit of dangerous sidelines, I want something against it that isn't the main line but is decent and doesn't need memorizing.
The main move is d4, but a good way to avoid the main lines is the bishop to c4 — Kasparov actually liked this move.
The knight to f6 — I don't think the knight to g5 works here.
We make the modest move d3, transitioning into an Italian where Black has essentially committed to developing this bishop to e7 or g7.
The bishop to e7 — a passive Italian setup. We continue developing.

We can play c3 or the knight to c3 — I like straightforward, so the knight to c3, no theory to remember, just develop with a pleasant position. Black can equalize with accuracy, but openings aren't all about winning out of the gate.
Black castles.
A good idea, as in the Glek, is h3 — preventing the bishop from coming out to g4.

c6. Do we play a4 or a3 in these structures? It doesn't much matter; a4 is fashionable to grab space. I wouldn't play a4 yet — b5 isn't a dangerous threat. If a4, then d5, we drop the bishop back, Black takes on c4, we recapture, and reach an endgame.

I'd rather save the tempo on a3 and castle — because if Black plays d5 now, we play the bishop to b3, and the big difference is: after d5, the bishop to b3, if Black takes on c4 and we recapture, and Black takes our queen, we recapture with the rook.

Our opponent's deciding between d5 and b5 — b5 is best; I don't think d5 is good. The king to h8, prophylactic. Now avoid the bishop to b3 here — never play it in these positions, it blunders a piece to d5 and d4. The knight to g5 is another paper-tiger move — Black just plays the queen to e8.
Remember you can play d4 at some point, but I save it for a rainy day. Now that we've castled, we have time for a4, restricting the b-pawn and preventing b5.
The knight to g8 — he's clearly preparing f5, an advanced plan, but it undevelops the knight. Now Black's pieces are all on the back rank.
When your opponent plays passively, the textbook punishment is to open the centre — so d4 is the perfect opportunity, unless I'm missing something tactical.
f5 — very devious. I need to calculate: if d takes e5, he has f takes e4 and a crazy series of trades I can't evaluate; the rook to e1 feels good but risky. Maybe the bishop takes g8 first.

The bishop takes, capturing on g8 first. The issue: after the trades, if we play the knight takes e4 we run into a d5 fork. So we eliminate the knight first — not to trade bishop for knight, but to remove it — so that when the king recaptures we play d takes e5, f takes e4, and hold the extra pawn with the knight takes e4, up a pawn.
He recaptures with the king on g8. We give up the bishop pair, but he's so poorly developed we may even get the bishop out to g5 later.
d takes e5, capturing on e5.
There's the crazy line where we both take pieces; f takes e4, capturing on e4.
The knight takes, capturing on e4 — I didn't like the alternative, more after the game.
d5, hitting our knight — we should move it back, probably to g3.

The knight to g3, for two reasons: first, more king safety; second, I'm already thinking about knight sallies like the knight to h5. If you play the Ruy or Italian, you know the value of a knight on g3 — a lot of potential energy. And note the bishop takes h3 is not a move, because the knight defends it — but whenever the f-file is open like this, always watch for the bishop takes h3. Black is clearly worse; he missed the bishop takes g8 and has insufficient compensation.

If Black plays the bishop to e6, the natural move is the knight to d4, centralizing and hitting the bishop — but that walks into c5, so it's not desirable yet. He plays the bishop to c5, setting up threats on the diagonal.

We could play the bishop to e3 to trade bishops, at the cost of our structure; or a neutral c3 to prepare b4, where he'd answer a5. I don't like the bishop to g5, which walks into the queen to b6 and a battery on b2. Actually, I think the best move is the bishop to e3.

The bishops trade, and we recapture with the f-pawn, capturing on e3. Yes, our structure is damaged, but there's a perk: the e5 pawn is well protected, and the e3 pawn can later advance to e4 to pressure d5. So these doubled pawns aren't as bad as they look.
I also had to account for the queen to b6, which runs into the queen to d4. The knight to d7 leaves Black with two undeveloped minor pieces stumbling over each other.
Now e4 is very tempting — it runs into the check on b6, but then the king to h2. e4 is begging to be played.
The queen to b6 with check.
The king to h2 — the king to h1 probably doesn't matter.
We have White and open with the pawn to e4, in the spirit of our recent gambits.
The pawn to d4 — another Danish Gambit attempt.
Black plays the knight to c6, declining the gambit — it transposes to a Nimzowitsch setup, and it's not a bad move. As usual, we prefer the centre open.
We capture on e5. The tempting pawn to d5 gains time but closing the centre isn't as good as it looks — better to take on e5 and make the knight move twice.

Black recaptures with the knight on e5. The centralized knight actually helps us — as a standalone piece it's vulnerable: we can chase it with f4, or offer a trade with the knight to f3. The pawn to f4 is okay but exposing, so I prefer the knight to f3 — but first, a more flexible move.
The knight to c3 — flexible: let's see how Black develops before deciding, because if the knight comes to f6, the pawn to f4 gets much stronger.

Black plays the bishop to b4 — good. We're not scared of the capture on c3: we'll castle kingside and don't mind the doubled pawns. And notice both the bishop and the e5-knight are undefended — which points to the queen to d4.
The queen to d4, hitting both loose pieces. The knight to c6 blunders g7, the bishop retreat or the capture on c3 are big wins for us — the only save is the queen to e7.

Black finds the queen to e7. That's usually why the queen to d4 is dubious — but here there's an extenuating factor: the g7-pawn is vulnerable, the c3-knight is pinned, and we can chase the e5-knight with f4.
The pawn to f4. The bishop to f4 would be less effective, since the pawn to f6 holds; the pawn push forces the knight to move.

Black plays the knight to g6 — the point: after the knight to c6 and the capture on g7, the rook hangs, but on g6 the knight defends the rook. The capture on g7 also allows the nasty reply of the queen taking e4.
We take on g7 with check anyway — we can't take the queen because of the pin, and c2 hangs, so it's a mess, but there's an interesting idea I just spotted.
Black plays the queen takes e4 with check — extremely risky for us.

The king to d1 — the exception to not moving the king early. Blocking with the knight buries the bishop, and c2 would hang with a cascade of problems. Instead the king to d1 opens our attack on the queen and, crucially, the e-file — it's a race to land a rook there, and Black can't castle short with our queen on g7.
Black captures on c3.

We recapture with the queen, not the pawn — the pawn recapture is too risky, since the queen could be smoked out by the pawn to g7 and the knight to f5. The queen recapture keeps contact with the rook, and the plan is to bring the knight and bishop out and land a rook on e1.
Black plays the pawn to c6 — a mistake, misjudging the danger. The best was the knight to e7 developing; c6 misses how close we are to a rook reaching e1.
The knight to f3 — don't auto-play the bishop to d3, which hangs a pawn. Play the knight first, and always check for hanging pawns before reasoning from general ideas.
Black plays the pawn to d5, and now we're winning — the knight intercepts the queen.

The bishop to d3 — two threats: the rook to e1, and the capture on g6, a loose piece our queen and rook combine against. That's the reward of keeping the queen in contact with the rook when we recaptured on c3.
Quick review — you play Black, I play White. e4, e5, the knight to f3.
If I go the knight to c3, that's not the move we were just looking at, but I still want you to know it.
d6 is correct.
And if I go h3 — when in doubt, develop your pieces: look for the pieces that haven't been developed yet, and find ways to develop them.
Look through the pieces you haven't developed and develop them; if only one minor piece is left, that's the one — the bishop to e6.

The developing question in the King's Indian is where this knight belongs — c6 or d7. Bringing it to c6 can backfire at a high level, because it invites an annoying pawn thrust to d5 that gains space and kicks the knight around.
So the knight goes to d7 instead — the typical choice, prepping the central break e5 while staying perfectly safe. It doesn't get chased, and it clears the path for the pawn.
c6 does two jobs: it clamps down on the d5 square, and it opens the door to swing the queen out to a5. Small pawn move, two ideas riding on it.

The knight lands on e5, hitting the c4-pawn and leaning on the whole centre. This is the hypermodern bargain — the opponent holds more of the middle, but every one of those pawns is under fire from pieces. The fight will come down to whether that initiative can be beaten back.
Look at the coordination — both knights bearing down on the enemy pawns at once. The pieces are doing the work the pawns usually do.
The rook slides to e8 to pile more pressure on the e-pawn. It also baits a natural-looking f4 push — the kind of move many players fire off automatically, without noticing the drawback it carries.

The enemy knight on d4 is a nuisance — the plan is to compel it out of the picture, and the same move can pile onto the e-pawn and develop a piece all at once. Note the trap to avoid: shoving c5 to hit it is a common mistake, because it badly weakens the d5 square. There's a subtler way to do the job.

The subtle way is the queen to c5, x-raying down onto f2 and threatening to snap the knight off with a fork to follow. Here's the pattern to file away: when the opponent has played g3 but the bishop has abandoned its fianchetto post, the f3 square lights up as a tactical hotspot — a warning bell for your tactical metal detector.
The queen collects the knight, and with the fork lurking behind it there's simply no good answer — the position collapses.
We switch to the queen's pawn.
With c4 we head into Catalan waters — offering the pawn to open the long diagonal.
g3 is the move that defines the Catalan: the bishop heads to the long diagonal, raking across d5 and the queenside.
The Catalan bishop settles on g2, and the whole opening is built around its pressure down that diagonal.
teaches: the g2 bishop is the Catalan’s soul

notes.explains: With a6 Black prepares to grab on c4 and hold the pawn with b5. So we protect the c4-pawn the Catalan way — the queen to c2, which guards it without blocking a single developing piece — and we'll bring a rook to d1 to keep the d4-pawn solid. From here the entire battle turns on one break: Black wants c5, trading his backward pawn and equalizing; we spend the middlegame preventing it. The bishop to g5 discourages it by overloading the piece that guards both f6 and c5, and once c5 is stopped for good we grind down the half-open c-file — that slow squeeze is what makes the Catalan so unpleasant to face.
teaches: Qc2 holds c4 without blocking development
the whole fight is over Black’s ...c5 break
plans: Qc2 + Rd1 to hold the center

notes.explains: We're facing the Caro-Kann. e4, c6.
d6 — a weird combination of moves.
The way to respond is just to develop our pieces. The knight to c3.
The knight to f3.
The bishop to g4 — let's throw in
h3, just to have the ability to push g4 if we want to.
The bishop to h5. The big decision is which side we're going to castle to.
It's tempting to castle queenside, but I'd like to play a little more quietly this game, so we start with the bishop to e2, getting rid of the pin,
the knight to d7 — and we just play quietly with short castling.
Short castling.
The queen to c7 — Black continues to develop decently, but of course we have a nice advantage with our centre.
Where to develop this bishop? Let's bring it out to e3 — I don't want to walk into e5 with tempo.

h6. Because there's no direct confrontation between the two armies, we shouldn't try to punish Black immediately — this is how these systems often succeed: you get over-excited, play something rash like e5, and end up blundering

all of your pieces. So the way we handle this is to make incremental gains, hoping they transform into something more tangible. One easy thing: push a4, grabbing queenside space and preventing Black from expanding with b5.
Not that b5 is scary, but it's a good bonus; and if we drive the pawn up to a5, the b7-pawn becomes backward. But before that, I'd like to address —
actually, no, there's nothing to address, because if Black pushes g4 — it looks scary, like we're opening our king, but we simply respond by moving the knight

to h2 or to d2, and Black loses the g-pawn, because the bishop on h5 is undefended. f6. Every move Black has played in the last five weakens his position; e5 is tempting, but I just spotted a beautiful tactical idea — does anybody see it?
Good chance to pause. Yes — the knight takes g5. Let me explain how I saw it:
the bishop takes e2 — I saw this by evaluating the drawback of Black's previous move;
the knight to e6, and now we
the bishop takes d1,
we take the queen with check
and win the rook in the corner. Incidentally, we could also drop back to e6 — not a bad move — picking up the bishop with total domination; I'm very tempted,
because Black is completely paralysed at the end of that line — it's funny and pretty instructive.
But going back to e6 isn't what I'd do
in a classical game — we take with this rook, because I see a very nice prospect for the other rook.
I'm looking at the backward pawn on b7.
One very typical way to attack it: lift the rook to a3 and park it on b3 — that's why I took with the f-rook.
Black can go the king to f7, but now we
can keep the knight in place with d5 — we do not want to remove this knight, because it would give Black breathing room.
c5. Now we complete our idea with
the rook to b3.
And now, if we're so inclined, there's another tactic with the rook takes b7 and the knight to d8 — but that would involve moving the knight from its dominant post, and there's no rush; Black
is paralysed, we have all the time in the world. How do we improve? Through slow but very decisive queenside expansion.
We start by trading off Black's only developed piece, the knight on d7, by
manoeuvring our knight to b6 — and as a nice bonus this also lets us establish a very powerful rook later on b6,
which creates the possibility of doubling rooks on the b-file and ultimately grabbing the b-pawn in a better version. So if Black plays
the bishop to h6, we're going to respond by
playing f4 — the reason I'm not trading is that I want to make it as difficult as possible for Black to develop this knight.
A high-rated player would play f5 here, but that's a pretty advanced move; you see our opponent is just stagnating.
Now it's time to complete the decisive idea — doubling rooks on the b-file and winning a second
pawn on b7. Are we worried about c4? No, because we can just play the rook to c3.
Black plays f5; let me be accurate here — let's take on f5, grabbing another pawn,
and now I think it's a good idea to reinforce the c4-pawn before proceeding
with our plan. I played a little inaccurately, allowing the knight to d7, and our opponent finds it — but we're up two pawns, and now we have a massive
kingside pawn majority we could push with g4 — let's go for it. Now we're playing on the kingside too, and note that
Black's rook is tied down to the file, so we can push
g5, gaining more.
Now we're going to go the bishop
to d2 and protect — I'm playing very sloppily,
but we are winning.
We can push g — oh, that was another bad move, sorry; I'm suddenly making some mistakes here,
but we're going to
take on g7.
I'm not going to play the bishop to c3; I'll play the rook to e3,
attacking the pawn on e7. Black protects it.
Now it's time to stick the other rook on the outpost — the rook to e6.
Our opponent is finding this game harder to win than against some of the grandmasters I played recently. Let's trade,
the bishop to c3, trading off the
knight; now we're going to go the rook to e3,
forcing either an undesirable rook trade or allowing us to infiltrate with the rook to e7.
Now we take with a pawn in order to be able to play e7. Too many passed pawns — we have three; what we ultimately do is promote one to deflect the rook, then promote the other.
Grabbing the gambit pawn is perfectly fine — that's the Queen's Gambit Accepted, a fully legitimate way to play. Taking here isn't greed, it's theory.
We're Black against a 2050 — this is going to be juicy. The pawn to e4, c5.
d4 — what appears to be the Smith-Morra —
— we take on d4.

The knight to f3 — a slightly odd move order, not bad for White. You could try to keep the pawn with e5, but that's bad: White gets an improved Smith-Morra with c3, and after the trade Black has a gaping weakness on d5.
So essentially play whatever Sicilian you normally play: a Najdorf player goes d6, a Kan player e6 — we're accelerated Dragon players, so the knight to c6.

The knight to c6, and the knight takes d4 with g6 would transpose to the main line — but our opponent insists on a unique style with the bishop to c4, a weird move delaying the knight takes d4. One approach is g6, then after the knight takes d4 the bishop to g7, back to normal territory.
But rather than meekly playing g6, we can punish White for being cute — the knight to f6 is a much better, more testing developing move, hitting the e4-pawn directly, with no real downside.

e5 is the try — but it falls into a well-known tactic. With the king on e1 in the Sicilian, always watch for the check on a5; giving it immediately is wrong, though, since the bishop to d2 then costs us a minor piece, and our queen and knight hang.
That's what our opponent relies on, but a little tactical trickery lets us apply the idea properly: we start by taking on e5, and after the knight takes back —

— but we could take that bishop with the knight rather than the king, avoiding White taking e5 with check. The queen takes d4 — our opponent digs deeper. Two candidates: take the knight to ruin White's kingside structure, or take the bishop for the bishop pair; both are good. The more positional move is the knight takes c4, cashing in for a long-term advantage.
The knight takes c4 — cashing in our chips, grabbing the bishop while we still can, playing methodically.
We open e4, e5, and for the second time in a row we're heading into the Four Knights Scotch.
The knight to f3.
The knight to c6.
The knight to c3 — the Four Knights.
The knight to f6, and we strike with d4 — the Scotch.
Black takes, capturing on d4 — the main line, and at this level people know this opening very well.
Black transposes into a Dutch with f5, but a London player doesn't change course — keep playing the standard London moves.
Think about what f5 costs Black: it weakens the a2-g8 diagonal and makes castling awkward — if we react correctly.
notes.teaches: The Dutch f5 concedes the a2-g8 diagonal; punish it before Black consolidates.

notes.explains: So we break our own routine: Bc4 instead of the usual Bd3 or Be2. This is a schematic opening, but when the opponent deviates you must think outside the setup — Bc4 seizes the diagonal f5 just weakened and slows his castling.
notes.teaches: In a system opening, abandon the automatic move when the opponent's play demands a concrete reaction.

notes.explains: He struggles to play e6, and we keep the Ng5 jump in our pocket — but don't rush it, just finish developing patiently.
notes.teaches: Bank a strong idea for later; complete development before cashing it in.

notes.explains: h3 is a typical London move, reserving the h2 retreat for the bishop.
Now expand on the queenside with c4. Yes, it blunts our own bishop for the moment — but the plan is a later c5, which reopens the diagonal and cranks up the queenside pressure.
notes.teaches: Temporarily blocking your own bishop is fine when a later break reopens it with interest.

notes.explains: Nc3 develops and points us toward the c5 or e4 break — either one gets at the e6-pawn.
notes.plans: Prepare c5 or e4 to open lines against e6.

notes.explains: Rc1 is playing for your future self — not an immediate threat, but the rook wants to be on the c-file long before c5 ever lands.
notes.teaches: Place pieces for the break you'll make later, not only for the threat you can make now.

notes.explains: Here's the deep plan: c5 is much easier with a pawn on b4 first.
notes.plans: Reroute so you can push b4, then break with c5.

notes.explains: But b4 fails right now — the bishop on b3 would have to go to c2, off the diagonal, dropping the c4-knight. The fix, learned from a painful loss: play a3 first, tuck the bishop back to a2, then send the pawn forward.
notes.teaches: When a pawn break needs a square a piece occupies, reroute the piece first, then push.

notes.explains: c5 breaks through. Don't fear him carving out d5 — the square is firmly held by our bishop and knight, so a knight can't settle there.
notes.teaches: A pawn break is safe to make when your pieces already blanket the hole it concedes.

notes.explains: And there's the payoff of reopening the diagonal: Bxe6-check slices straight through, and we simply help ourselves to the free pawns.
notes.teaches: The point of opening a bishop's diagonal is the sacrifice-free tactic waiting at the end of it.

notes.explains: To convert, note Black has no light bishop, so build a queen-and-bishop battery down the light squares — queen in front, since it's the queen that delivers mate on h7. And don't hurry to grab the knight on f6: it isn't going anywhere, Black stays permanently weak on the diagonal, so improve elsewhere and open a file with f4 to pile on.
notes.teaches: Against a king with no light bishop, stack a light-square battery led by the queen at h7, and never rush a capture the target can't flee.

notes.explains: The Scotch starts on familiar ground — the king's-pawn game with knights out. It's less well-known than the Italian, so a prepared player wins a lot of quick games with it.
teaches: the Scotch as a surprise weapon

notes.explains: The purest move order runs through the knight to c3 first, keeping options open before the d4 break.
The pawn to e4, e6 — a French, against David Vest.
d4 — you already know what we play against the French.
d5, and we play e5 — the Advance.
He goes b6 — an alternative to the main move c5; the idea is to get the bishop out to a6.
To slow down, in fact prevent entirely, the bishop to a6, we play c3 —
— a move we normally play in the Advance.
— we just want to develop our pieces nicely, starting with the bishop to d3.
a5. Now let's think about where to put this knight — f3 or e2? If you've watched my French games, you know I have an affinity for e2 —
— the knight to e2, because I like keeping the f-pawn free to charge Black's pawn chain, with f4 and f5 later, since the e6-pawn could get under tremendous pressure.
But first we complete our development — we don't want to rush with f4. The bishop to a6.

Let's castle and do all the nice things, then when we're ready go f4 and try for f5. The queen takes d3, a4 — he's expanding on the queenside without developing, so we press the gas. He could meet f4 with g6, creating kingside weaknesses we could exploit. The knight to h6 stops f5; our idea is the f5 pawn break. In a closed centre nothing happens quickly against good players — you have to be methodical. We could go the knight to g3, but he plays g6; the knight to d2 is patient, but I like a more direct idea to contest f5 — h3, reserving the option of g4.
We take White; Black answers our king's pawn with ...e5.
We develop the knight to f3; Black defends with ...Nc6.
We play the bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez.
Black chases with a6.
We retreat the bishop to a4, keeping the pin.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We castle.
Black develops the bishop to e7.
We play the rook to e1, defending e4.
Black plays b5, gaining time.
We retreat the bishop to b3.
Black plays d6, the closed setup.
We play c3, preparing a later d4 and giving the bishop a bolthole.
Black castles.
We play the modest d3.
Black pins with the bishop to g4.
We develop the knight to d2, heading for the kingside.
Black hits our bishop with ...Na5; we tuck it to c2; and Black expands with ...c5 — the typical Chigorin plan.
We reroute the knight to f1 — the classic Ruy maneuver toward e3.
Black brings the knight back to c6.
We swing the knight to e3.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
We finally strike with d4.
Black takes on d4.
We recapture on d4 — but now Black threatens a fork with ...d5.
Black takes on d4 again.
We recapture with the knight.
Black takes the knight.
We recapture with the queen, centralized on d4.
Black plays ...Nd7.
We jump the knight into d5.
Black takes it off with the bishop.
We recapture with the pawn.
Black plays the bishop to f6, onto a nice diagonal.
We reposition the queen to d3; Black plays g6.
d4 — let's play the knight to f6.
f4 — so this is an attempt at a Stonewall, which has been around a while; White wants to play e3 and c3. There are a couple of things we can do against it: one is d5, controlling the e4-square,

but I don't like playing d5 against the Stonewall. Even if you're not a King's-Indian player, I like the King's-Indian setup against it — you don't have to be a King's-Indian player; White should really meet it with c5, then c-takes and d-takes, to be able to play the King's Indian. So
let's make the standard King's-Indian moves — the bishop to g7.
and castle — the order doesn't matter; we'll play d6, though castling first was a little more flexible.

The bishop to d3. The funny thing is I'm going to allow White to play e4 next, which would be a Pirc up a tempo — I kind of play the Pirc anyway, so I don't mind, and someone who plays d4 and f4 won't be familiar with the Pirc's ideas for White.
So we castle — I'm not afraid of e4.

What's the benefit of the pawn on d6 rather than d5? What idea does d6 prepare? You could play c5, but that's not my favourite — c5 can just be met with c3, much like the London. What we need to prepare is e5 — not immediately, we can't yet — we prepare it with the knight to c6. The point is that when we play e5 we
cause a much bigger explosion in the centre, because we attack both pawns and threaten a fork — so e5 does a lot more than c5 here. Let's get our knight out.

And now we're ready to play e5. You might look at this and say White has three attackers and only two defenders — but if you calculate further, to win the pawn White has to totally ruin his structure,
and we'll win the e5-pawn back very easily. I can show this in more detail after the game, but we can safely play e5 without worrying about losing a pawn.
f-takes-e5.
d-takes-e5.
Our opponent continues to play very fast — the knight to d2. Now we have several options; what's a reasonable follow-up?

The rook to e8 is a pretty inoffensive move we can always throw in, reinforcing the threat of e4, and maybe we play e-takes-d later and open the e-file. Actually, first we should develop our bishop — I know some of you think of the bishop to g4, but then h3 chases it away; the alternate way is b6 and the bishop to b7, fianchettoing the other bishop and aiming at the e4-square. This is a pawn sacrifice — let's see if our opponent figures out how to win it. The knight to g5 is an intimidating-looking move, but is it scary? I don't see what it threatens, so we continue developing; probably the bishop to c4, but then we simply defend the pawn with the rook to e7. The knight to d5 would give up f7 potentially, so be careful — always consider what you're opening and closing when you move a knight. g4 is a mistake. Should we take the knight? Yes — we take on g5, because that exposes an attack on the other knight: after the knight takes and the queen takes g5, White has to recapture our knight with his knight, which takes the pressure off the f-pawn; and one step further, the knight takes e4 is a very natural, strong King's-Indian continuation. Am I afraid of the knight taking f7? I calculated it — if he plays it, f5 chases the knight away, and then e4, or the capture on d4 pushing his pieces back. Now, our opponent is contemplating the knight takes f7 — an intermezzo that attacks the queen, and White has two attackers on our knight over on e4, so wherever our queen goes, even to h4, it appears White can capture the knight with the bishop. But I calculated — wait, maybe I miscalculated; we might have to go into an endgame I don't want. He out-calculated me. I was intending the queen to h4, and what I missed is the smothered-mate idea: after the bishop takes c4, the queen to b3 sets up an unstoppable discovered check against the king and a potential smothered mate. So the knight takes e4 was simply a mistake — I underestimated the knight to f7. So after the capture, since the bishop takes e4 is a big mistake because of the queen to b3, is there an alternative? We have to take the bishop with the queen, offering a queen trade; then he takes on e5, basically everything trades, and it's essentially a dead draw — but we'll try to win that endgame. We panic and bite the bullet, because otherwise the bishop takes c4 and he finds the queen to b3 and we're busted. Now I have to prove my mettle by winning an endgame nearly devoid of chances. The queen to f2, leaving our battery intact — I think this just loses. We can play e-takes-d4, but then there might be the knight to h6 with check, a nasty idea that forces a trade; then we pin the knight. We're not threatening the rook takes f7 — some of you might think we are, but then the queen takes f7 with check — what we're threatening is the bishop from b7 to d5, picking off the knight, which I don't think can be defended. I'm disappointed in my play — maybe fianchettoing the bishop was fundamentally too slow. People in the seventeen-, eighteen-hundred range make this kind of mistake often; there's a psychology name for it, like walking to the wrong floor of a building out of habit. Something even better than the bishop to d5: because after the bishop to d5, the rook to e1 gives us something to deal with — we want to attack the knight without allowing the rook to e1, so the queen to d5. That violates my rule of accomplishing tasks with the lowest-value piece, but it's an exception, because the queen is vulnerable to begin with — so we do two things at once, making the queen safer and attacking and winning the knight. This is a lesson in flexibility: players think they must keep attacking no matter what and rule out all queen trades, and they ignore what's actually going on — that I now have this battery and there's no longer any attack; that inflexibility makes you lose objectivity. Let's snag the queen and convert with discipline. What we shouldn't do is the bishop takes e5 — I don't like giving away the dark-squared bishop, because those with a keen tactical eye see that the bishop to h6 could become a problem, with White creating mate threats on f8. So two options: the rook to f8, trading one pair of rooks; and c5, undermining the knight, which is defended by the pawn — the undermining concept is so important. And after the rook to f1, ask how the position has changed and don't lose sight of the whole board: the a2-pawn is now hanging, so after the trade you can safely take on a2 and start grabbing everything on the queenside. The knight to f3 — he brought the knight back himself, a good move. We have a fancy move available, but there are so many good moves I struggle to verbalise — g5 and then g4. The move I'd play in a classical game is c5. You might say the point was to undermine the knight, which we've done — but I want to get rid of the d-pawn so our queen gets more real estate in the centre: d-takes-c5, the queen takes e5, pinning the rook and threatening to double-capture on f3 because of the pin. That d4-pawn holds us back, so get rid of it and open files — the more files open, the easier it is to convert the extra queen. Our dark-squared bishop isn't good and won't be even after the trade, since there'll be a c3-pawn staring at it, but at least it controls the d4-square. I have a great high-level example of an international master who did exactly this against me — instructive on how chess psychology can be used against people, even to defend bad positions. The rook to e1 — time to grab; pinned. I briefly checked the rook to e8 with check, making sure there's nothing after the king to f7 — anytime you abandon the back rank, always check fast.
