The rook to f1 — b4 is a threat, so we kind of have to take; there's a fancy move, but let's keep it simple and take. After the rook takes f2, I really like the bishop from g7 to e5 idea. The bishop takes h2 — how did I see it? A lot of people passively notice the pin and think, can I attack the rook with the bishop to d4? No, there's a pawn on c3 — and they file it away. I don't stop there: the pin means the king is defending the rook, so it's overloaded, and going after the h2-pawn could be an overloading tactic. The queen takes f2 is also a fork, but just winning the rook is already enough — the point is that high-level players don't just see the tactical phenomenon, they understand how it can be used as a component in a combination. b4 — I saw this; we need to move the queen and defend the bishop, so the queen to e5 or d6; I like the queen to d6, because if the bishop to h6 happens, we can move our bishop back and sacrifice on f8 and keep the bishop; we can also give the queen to g3 with check and win the bishop. Actually the queen to h3 — this is just a fork.

Recapturing with the queen isn't outright terrible, but it's misplaced here. Against a king's-pawn game this early queen sortie is the Center Game — genuinely playable. Against the Sicilian it's just poor, because it hands over a stack of tempi.

Why so many lost tempi? Because it amounts to playing a Scandinavian a move up as the wrong colour — and the Scandinavian is dubious enough that nobody wants it with either colour. Meanwhile the knight leaps out with gain of time, hitting the queen.

There are countless ways to arrange the pieces from here, and the guiding idea is to stay true to the spirit of whatever open-Sicilian repertoire you'd normally play — Dragon players reach for g6, Taimanov and Sveshnikov players for e6, Najdorf players for d6. All of them are valid.
In the spirit of the accelerated fianchetto, the bishop's diagonal comes first whenever there's no concrete reason to deviate — and here there's no downside to it.
The one thing to refuse is a trade of the fianchettoed bishop — swapping that piece off would be a real mistake, so the plan is simply to complete the setup around it.

That little pawn move is conceptually bad — it develops nothing and cramps its own knight. The opponent's development has fallen alarmingly behind, but that changes nothing on this side: just keep bringing pieces out, with a d5 break in the back pocket for when the moment to open the centre arrives.
Keep developing — the knight comes to f6. The trap to avoid is the very error the opponent fell into: dragging the queen out too early.
We open e4, and our opponent plays the Sicilian, c5.
The Alapin move, c3.
We face d5, the direct counter in the centre.
We take, capturing on d5.
The queen recaptures on d5, and we play d4 — a highly theoretical position we've had many times.
The knight to f6, the main move.
We develop our own knight to f3 — all theory. Black is at a major crossroads with four or so worthy options.

The knight to c6 — the natural move if you're seeing this for the first time. Its drawback: the f8-bishop stays locked behind the e7 pawn. The course's best way to punish it exploits exactly that: after d takes c5, Black can't recapture on c5 with the bishop, so the queen must take, handing White tempi. So the move is d takes c5.
We take, capturing on c5 — you might be reluctant, since it lets Black trade queens and drive our king out for a pawn, and you might think c5 is easy to win back, but that's far from true.
The queen takes d1 with check, and our king recaptures on d1 — if he knows the theory, this gets sharp.

a5, a very understandable move preventing b4 — but that doesn't mean we must part with the c5 pawn. We have many ways to cling to it, though not at the cost of our position. The bishop to e3 runs into the knight to g4, ruining our structure; h3 to meet e6 with the bishop to e3 runs into the knight to d5; and a3 with b4 fails to a takes b4, c takes b4, the knight takes b4. So a more indirect approach — a5 weakens the b5 square.

The bishop to b5 has limited value since Black plays e6, so I like the Alapin-esque idea of getting the knight to b5. So the knight to a3 — from b5 the knight eyes c7, and if Black pushes the e-pawn and we play the knight to b5, we can even reach d6, where after Black takes and we recapture, we get the bishop pair and dark-square control; even if Black wins the pawn back, we'd get the better endgame. A nice flexible developing move, waiting for Black to show his cards.
The Smith-Morra — sacrifice the d-pawn for rapid development and open lines against the Sicilian.
Against the solid e6 system, one of Black's better tries, the theoretical move is coming up.

Bc4 — deeply counter-intuitive, since it seems to bite on granite against e6, but the point is hidden: if a knight later lands on d5 and Black takes, the e6-pawn vanishes and the bishop's diagonal blazes open.
notes.teaches: A bishop that looks blunted by a pawn can be aimed at the moment that pawn is forced to disappear.

notes.explains: Rather than hunt for something insane, just castle — put the decision off and trust straightforward development.
notes.teaches: When no forcing idea works, don't force it; a calm developing move keeps the initiative.

notes.explains: Now simple chess with an edge: sling the knight into d5. Probably not objectively sound, but it's a very real practical try.

The knight lunges at the bishop, but this sacrifice isn't preposterous — you should feel intuitively why it works. Black is utterly undeveloped, neither bishop is out, castling is far away, and the e-file is wide open for Re1-check and d6 ideas. In the gambit mindset you don't reflexively defend the attacked bishop — you move it by choice, keeping every threat alive.
notes.teaches: A sacrifice is justified when the defender is undeveloped and the lines against his king are already open.

notes.explains: d4, the knight to f6.
c4, e6 — let's do a Nimzo, sliding into a Queen's Indian.
The knight to c3 — not something we've played often, but it's my second opening after
the King's Indian. The bishop to b4 — the Nimzo pin.
The bishop to d2 — not considered theoretically topical, quite passive, but it's been gaining popularity recently. The Nimzo is a very easy opening
to pick up: you basically just develop your pieces, and then there are a couple of specific setups you should know.
We take on c3 — that's kind of the point of the Nimzo:
we make it harder for White to occupy the centre with e4, by weakening his control of the e4-square, taking that knight off the board. One of the most typical Nimzo setups is:
b6, the bishop to b7, then d6 and the knight to d7 — you create these little holes for your pieces.
The bishop to b7 — one of the most solid setups available in the Nimzo. The move d5 here
would be fine, but not really in the spirit of the Nimzo, so we play in its spirit:
the bishop to e2, and the knight to d7 —
the knight to d7, a very common and very solid setup, because there are no weaknesses.
Now we have to continue improving our position. We placed our pieces where they belong, and now there are a couple of follow-up plans.

One plan is the queen to e7 and then e5; but a more aggressive idea I really like is the knight to e4, a natural move, following up with f5 — the g4-and-f5 idea, ubiquitous across openings. A rook to d1. Now we have the option of subtracting White's bishop from the board: one way is to take the bishop and then reroute the other knight to e4, another classic concept. I don't feel strongly either way — the bishop on c3 does have a bright future, especially if White pushes d5 at some point, so it might be worth taking it, even though our knight on e4 is a strong piece, because we're just replacing one knight with the other; unless he plays the knight to d2, which would be passive but would take the sting out of g4. The queen to c2 — I don't see a reason to refrain from shoving the other knight into the outpost, the knight to d2. That was his idea, and now we need some tactics to preserve this knight on e4. Anybody see how we could create a situation where White can't take on e4? We play the queen to g5, a classic move with a couple of ideas, threatening — and White immediately blunders. After the king to h1, I see a much sexier move than the knight to f2 with check. The most efficient mate: the queen takes e2 wins, the knight to f2 with check wins, but the knight to g3 with check is the fastest — h-takes-g3, the rook to f6 with the rook to h6 to follow. There's no smothered mate, because White can give up an exchange on f2, but despite it being White to move there's nothing he can do — remember this classic mechanism: if White puts a rook on f2, we just take it. That's mate.
We go e4, e5 — and a mouse slip: the bishop to a6 instead of b5. Oh no.
The knight takes a6 — he takes correctly. Rome wasn't built in a day; down a piece, we'll have to unbalance the position and get attacking chances, but first we develop and don't make it worse.

The knight to f3, developing. And funnily, because we sacked the bishop, he can't play the knight to c6 — that may fluster him. d6 is fine here, a Philidor, slightly better than usual since he's up a piece.
d6 — a Philidor. To get attacking chances we'll have to open the position at some point, and not having a light-squared bishop doesn't mean we shouldn't open the centre.

d6 is a bit passive — his bishop is restricted by the pawn, his knight on a6 is on the rim. Even without the bishop, d4 makes sense; we need to plan how to unbalance and create some intrigue to confuse him.

The easiest formula to unbalance is to castle opposite your opponent — he'll castle kingside, so we head for queenside. And don't automatically grab free pawns when down a piece: taking on e5 and trading queens would blunder mate to the rook to d1, and even without mate, trading queens is far too steep a price for one pawn. The bishop to g4 is phenomenal — we need to keep and defend the d4-pawn, best done with another pawn.
The queen to d3 escapes the pin but doesn't defend the pawn. I like c3 — you know this move from all our Ruy Lopez games — building a little pawn chain, keeping our pawns in the centre.
The bishop to e7. Now we develop patiently — nothing crazy like the queen to a4 with nothing developed.
The knight to d2 has the drawback of blocking the bishop, so we change the order and start with the bishop to e3.
Of course we're lost, everything is bad, but we're trying to make the most of the situation.
The knight to d2.

He castles. As I explained, the ideal plan is to move the queen and castle queenside — risky, since c3 already weakened us — but we can't afford any luxury in king safety. The queen to c2 is interesting; I still prefer the queen to e2. Not the queen to b3, which gets vulnerable and too far from a future kingside attack.

Escaping the pin isn't the top priority, but we want the capacity to end it — so we start with h3. If he takes and trades, that's not necessarily good for us, but it eliminates a headache bishop, activates our queen, and prepares castling.

The bishop takes f3 — we accomplish some of what we wanted, eliminating the bishop, and now we have a clear plan of g4, g5, beginning the pawn storm. The g-pawn recapture opening the g-file wouldn't do us too many favors.

The queen recaptures. c5 — we must be very careful; d5 is very bad, closing the centre and untying his hands for a queenside attack with b5, c4, b4, the queen to a5, far faster than us. Keeping the centre open dilutes his attack.
Plus, c5 weakened a lot of squares — he's blunted his own bishop —

— and the knight on a6 can't go to c5 anymore. Keeping the centre open emphasizes the superiority of our pieces; we can play positionally even down a piece. We can castle, but I like the knight to c4 — with one problem.
The knight to c4 lets him slide the queen to d3, incredibly nasty. So I'd risk castling first — the kingside attack plan is still very much available.
The queen to a5 — we have to defend the pawn. A lot of you would play a3 automatically, but —

— you don't want to make any more queenside weaknesses; we've already played c3. So the king to b1 is the automatic response. If he attacks in a focused way he wins, but we bank on him hesitating or getting scared of our attack.
The rook to d8. It's not as easy as when we gave the piece up. What's our plan? I've indicated g4 many times — what's its function?

The pawn storm does two things: first, it removes the knight from f6, the main defender, the gatekeeper; once it's gone we push h5 and try g6. The fundamental purpose is to break open the king's cover; a lesser-known purpose is using the pawns to secure squares for your pieces.
b5 — a move that's good for us, since his rook should have been on b8. We've entered a point of no return; we have to continue the attack and pray we end up faster than he is.
If only we had a light-squared bishop.
We've got to send it — h4, the only way to attack; you don't need to be a GM to make these moves.
He panics, trying to slow the progress of our pawns, but in doing so he creates a pawn hook, making it a lot worse for himself.

We go h5 — this pawn, acting as a hook, lets us open the h-file a lot faster, and all we need is one open file to create serious threats against this king. Not winning yet, but greatly complicated — that's why the rule warns against pushing pawns where you're being attacked. The h-pawn takes g6 would be hasty; what do we play first to prepare it? The threat is stronger than the execution.
We have only one shot to open the h-file, so we play the queen to h3, doubling up first, then take on g6 — a crushing move, though it may seem absurd.

What's wrong with taking and then the queen to h3? He'd play the f-pawn takes g6 and use f7 for his rook to defend the pawn. By keeping things closed until we need to open them, we disallow defences like the rook to f7. He's busted — the h-file massacre is coming whether he likes it or not, and g6 lost him the game; he even trapped his own queen, though that's much less important. A very nice game, only seventeen moves.
The knight to c4. Do we need to take the knight, or react to this move?
No — god forbid, do not take, do not pass go; ignore everything and make sure he isn't threatening checkmate.
The knight takes d2 with check — it's over.
We can take with either piece; the rook takes d2 has more of an elegance to it.
The queen takes h5 — and mate is on the board.
Nice game. On offering a draw over the board, you usually play a move and say 'I offer a draw' —

The Alapin — meeting the Sicilian with the pawn to c3, preparing to build the big centre with d4. Against this, the two moves that fully equalize for Black are the knight to f6 and the pawn to d5; everything else lets White dominate the middle.
Black chooses the knight to f6, hitting e4 — one of the two reputable equalizers, and it leads to sharp, interesting play.
We push the pawn to e5, kicking the knight, which swings to d5 in Alekhine style.
The knight to d5. This is really an Alekhine's Defence with c3 and c5 thrown in — a version that slightly favours Black, because c3 is exactly the square where we'd want our own queenside knight.

So we play the pawn to d4, occupying the centre — that's the whole point of c3. If Black captures, we're heading into Smith-Morra-type waters. And a subtlety: we don't have to recapture at once, because with the knight sitting on d5, capturing on c3 is not a real threat.
Black takes on d4. The main line leaves this pawn alone for the moment — the pinned setup means Black can't just win it.
The knight to f3 — a maximally flexible developing move: it guards the e5-pawn, it's a piece we always want out, and it defers the recapture. Start with the moves you know you'll want anyway.
Black develops the knight to c6, following the main line. Now the moment is right to regain the pawn.
We recapture, the c-pawn taking on d4 — a good moment to release the central tension. From here Black's principled Sicilian tries are the pawn to d6 or e6.

Black fianchettoes with the pawn to g6 — playable, but a touch slow and slightly inaccurate: it's a two-move developing plan, and once the bishop reaches the long diagonal it bites on granite against our d4-and-e5 pawn chain.

We develop the bishop to c4, forcing the knight to decide — and note, if Black ever combines the pawn to e6 with the g6 already played, the dark squares in the centre become badly weak, and our pieces head for d6 and f6.
Black retreats the knight to b6, hitting our bishop.
We keep the bishop on the strong diagonal, dropping it back to b3 — still trained on f7.
We're Black against a 1552, expecting e4 — and we get it.
The knight to f3, the knight to c6.
And we're facing a Scotch — or a Scotch Gambit, depending on what White does here.
We take on d4.
A traditional Scotch. The Four Knights Scotch would include the knight to c3 and the knight to f6; there are many systems against the Scotch.
The two main tries are the knight to f6 and — the one I recommend around 1500 — the bishop to c5: practical, easy to learn, not much theory.

After the bishop to c5 White has a few moves. The bishop to e3 — and here it's vital not to blunder. A lot of people lose by casually developing this knight, because the bishops are x-raying each other: White takes on c6 and then on c5 for a free bishop. So Black has two main replies.

We can drop the bishop back to b6 and anchor it, or develop the queen to f6 — this is our move, the other main line, and it avoids losing a piece: if the knight takes c6, we take on e3 and our queen isn't hanging.
So c3, the main line. The drawback of the queen to f6 is that it takes the f6-square from the knight — but that's not an issue.

Where does the knight go? The knight to e7 — a fine developing move; I like it because it connects the knights. And we shouldn't fear the standoff: if White ever takes on c6 or moves the knight, we take on e3, threatening mate on f2 and forcing a recapture.
White plays the knight takes c6 — actually a mistake. We answer with the bishop takes e3, threatening mate, so the f-pawn recapture is forced, and White's structure is ruined.

The bishop takes e3. White's pawns are wrecked — doubled, and worse, doubled on the e-file where they're most accessible and easiest to target. And after the recapture, the queen to h4 with check becomes a fork once we take back the knight.

After the f-pawn takes e3, the queen to h4 check is a threat once we recapture. What do we take back with? We can make a case for several pieces. Not the queen — that makes no sense. We can take with the b-pawn to keep our structure healthy, or —

— the d-pawn takes c6, which I actually prefer: it opens the bishop's diagonal fastest and streamlines development. I don't care about these doubled pawns — they aren't accessible, they aren't targets. With White's king stuck in the centre, developing quickly is crucial; maybe we win before White even castles. We trade a little structure for speed.

White plays the knight to d2. Against another GM I'd take with the knight and play d6, but here let's have some fun. The knight to d2 defends the e4-pawn, so the queen to h4 no longer makes sense — I'll cover why after the game.
We castle short — flexible, since it's a move we need anyway, whereas we don't yet know where the bishop belongs. In some lines it could go to g4, for instance if White prepared long castling.

White plays the bishop to e2. Important moment: White isn't threatening to castle, which means we keep the queen on f6, and the rook to f1 isn't a real threat — in fact we'd welcome it, since it permanently costs White castling rights.

Now that our bishop won't reach g4, the time has come for the bishop to e6 — developing, unafraid of moves that hit our queen. If the rook to f1, we play the queen to h4 with check and win the h2-pawn.

The bishop to f3 — a great move; White has managed to castle. Now we switch gears from preventing castling to arranging our pieces for the new circumstances. Three jobs: a good square for the knight — e5 is juicy — a good square for the queen, and where to put the rooks.

The queen to g5 — more central than h6, it attacks the e3-pawn and delays castling another move. Next the knight routes to e5, a dominant anchor. Then the rooks: with only one open file, it's crucial we occupy it, so a rook comes to d8 — the more important rook first. I note the alignment of White's queen and our rook in case of the knight to b3, when the bishop to c4 would pin. White plays b3, which weakens c3, and now, using the knight's e5 outpost as an anchor, the rook swings to d3 — total positional domination, every white piece miserable. The knight to c4 tries to break the bind, but we answer with the bishop takes c4 — taking with the bishop, not the knight, so the knight stays on its outpost; if the rook takes d3, the bishop takes d3 and we win everything. Then we calmly collect pawns. Remember diminishing returns: the first pawns matter most, so at some point stop improving and convert. Watch for forks — the knight to d3 combines a fork with deflection along the e-file, hitting a loose piece on e1. For luft I'd prefer g6 and h5 over g6 alone, restricting the f3-bishop further. To finish with a flourish: control the g3-square — a pawn to h4 then h5 does it — and sink the queen to g3 for mate; if White grabs on f7 with check, we sidestep, the king's hiding spot is h6, and White must give up material. An instructive game — twenty-three moves showing how effective clean positional play can be.

The Queen's Gambit Declined is the ideal beginner's opening — a gateway into a whole world of classical play. The traditional developing move is the bishop to e7, but there's a sharper try for a little extra edge, one that looks for all the world like it hangs a pawn.
That try is the knight to d7 — and the point is a trap plenty of players walk straight into. It makes a perfectly sound theoretical move while quietly laying a snare.
Round out the kingside by castling short — get the king safe before committing the rest of the army.

Here's the offbeat gem — the simplifying system. Instead of the usual queenside fianchetto, play the modest c6. Be warned, it looks bad: passive, and it does hem in the light-squared bishop. But there's a method behind the passivity.
Now the paradox pays off — capture on c4. Because the exchange was delayed until the opponent's light bishop had already committed, recapturing it costs them a tempo. Patience turns into a free move.
This is the Jobava London — Bf4 paired with Nc3, a cross between the Veresov and the London, and my main opening.
e6 is already a small inaccuracy, because it opens a square the knight will jump into.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava, an early ...e6 invites the Nb5 leap — watch for it.

notes.explains: Nb5 — a fried-liver-style leap transposed to the other wing. The point isn't to win the rook with a fork; it's to plant a maddening knight that Black can't easily remove.
notes.teaches: A knight jump like Nb5 is worth it for the lasting outpost, not just the tactic behind it.

notes.explains: After Na6 the knight on a6 is stuck out of play, and Black can't kick the b5-knight with a pawn — so we calmly develop the other side.
notes.teaches: Provoke a defender to an offside square, then develop while it languishes.

notes.explains: c3 in true London style, making sure the centre pawn is rock-solid before anything else.
The bishop goes to d3 rather than e2 — both are fine, but d3 is a touch more active.
Careful now: castling immediately would drop a piece to c4, which severs the knight from the bishop's defense.
notes.teaches: Before castling, check the opponent can't fork away the defender of one of your pieces.

notes.explains: Support the knight with a4 — a pawn, because pawns are the best defenders of a piece.
notes.teaches: Whenever possible, prop up an advanced piece with a pawn rather than another piece.

notes.explains: And be ready to give the whole thing up: drop the bishop to c2, don't move the knight, and simply let Black take it — the compensation is real.
notes.teaches: In a gambit-flavored position, offer the piece rather than retreat it; activity is the payment.

notes.explains: The clever b6 pawn sacrifice forces his knight offside to a8, buying us time — his knight now has to trek all the way back into the game.
notes.teaches: Sacrifice a pawn to shove an enemy piece to the corner; the tempi it loses are your compensation.

notes.explains: While his knight is exiled, we complete development and start piling onto the king, combined with pressure down the a-file.
notes.plans: Finish developing, then attack the king and the a-file together.

notes.explains: Ne5 centralizes the knight on its best square while his own knight is still marooned on a8.
g4 launches the attack — we have to use this window before Black reroutes his pieces to the queenside.
notes.teaches: When you're ahead in development, strike before the opponent untangles.

notes.explains: Bring the queen in with Qf3, keep the a-file with Ra1, and prepare e4 to blow the centre open — tighten the noose from every side.
notes.plans: Qf3 and Ra1, then e4 to open lines against the king.

notes.explains: Black plays the Pirc, ceding the center. Played well it's fine, but most players at this level get into trouble fast — so we punish it by strict adherence to opening principles.
teaches: meet an offbeat opening with principled play

notes.explains: We expand the center further with c4, since we're free to grab space here.
The crucial discipline: don't keep over-expanding with f4 — support the center with pieces instead. The knight to c3 develops and reinforces it.
teaches: develop to support the center, don’t over-push

notes.explains: The bishop goes to d3 — and its purpose is forward-looking: it's aimed at the h7 square once the center opens.
teaches: place the bishop for the future attack

notes.explains: Everything's developed — now the hard part most players struggle with: converting a space edge into something real. We expand in the center and attack a flank.
After clearing the tension, the pawn to e5 springs the bishop on d3 to life, opening its fire toward h7.
Black's knight lunges to the rim on h5 — and a knight on the rim is asking to be hunted.
teaches: a rim knight is a target

notes.explains: We trap it with g4. Yes, that's a pawn push in front of our own king — but it's the exception, because it simply wins a knight, and Black has nothing on the kingside to punish it.
teaches: break the rule when it wins material

notes.explains: The knight has no escape — forced back to f6, and we take, opening the f-file.
g5 shoves the bishop, and if it grabs on c3 that only trades off a defender of Black's king — fine by us.
teaches: welcome trades that strip the king’s guards

notes.explains: We snap off the bishop — thank you — removing another piece from around Black's king.
The knight centralizes on e4, heading for the h5 assault. Not Qh5 yet, though — g6 would just stop it; build first.
Another game with Black. e4, e5 — obviously e5.
The queen to h5 — a very common move at the beginner level — attacks the e5-pawn, which you all probably know is a bad idea. The knight to c6, defending.
The bishop to c4 threatens checkmate. How do we defend against scholar's mate? Do not play

the knight to f6 — that doesn't defend against it — and do not move the queen out; we play g6. I'll later explain why not the queen to e7. He brings his queen back to f3 and threatens mate again, so we develop the knight and intercept the queen's control of f7 — and now he can't take the knight, because it's defended. But I find this queen very annoying — can we chase it away? I don't want to deal with the possibility of scholar's mate, so I'm centralising my knight. Aren't I moving the same piece more than once in the opening, against my own advice? Yes, but every rule has exceptions, and he has already played his queen twice, so I can afford to delay my development by a move to get rid of this pesky queen; in an actual classical game I'd play the bishop to g7, but I just want to illustrate. He plays the queen to e3 — and whenever there's a knight landing on d4, it's a royal-family fork. Do we take the rook? No — we look for a better move: we take the queen. Not only are we up a queen, his king has to move away from castling, which is a total disaster. The game is basically over, but let me talk about converting. When you're up a queen, especially with the opponent's king out in the open, you have to open up the centre — only that makes your huge material lead manifest. How? We play d5 — two defenders, two attackers, we can safely proceed. He plays the knight to f3, attacking our pawn; can we develop a piece and defend the pawn at the same time? Yes — the fianchetto, developing the bishop to the long diagonal. Take the knight; and another important piece of advice, when you're up material you still want to develop — a common weakness is to win a queen and then forget to develop and still get mated. He plays d4, doing our bidding: whenever there's a capture, take stock of what has changed — have any files opened, and can we occupy them? Yes — a rook to the e-file, x-raying the king; so we're up a queen, opening the centre, and developing to active squares. Now take the knight — and here's an instructive moment: do you see the pin? Because of the pin, this bishop is immobile, a ghost, so are there pieces or pawns we can take? Count attackers and defenders: the immobile bishop is not a defender, so only the rook defends the pawn, but the queen is another attacker — if the rook takes, we'd take the queen. Can we take on e3? No. So can we move the queen to keep the bishop protected and unpin our own bishop? There are two squares — the queen to g6. Now we're ready to take his bishop with ours, keep trading, and then attack that pawn with our queen to checkmate him. He takes, we take, and he can't take our queen because of the pin — now we're up a queen and a rook. He plays a rook to e1 — very important, involve all your pieces: is any piece doing nothing? A rook — bring it into the game. Careful, though: when you have a piece untouchable due to a pin and he moves his king away from that pin, you have to be careful. I'll just sacrifice my rook for the bishop, because I'm up so much. The queen takes f3, and now I vacuum up the pawns — when you're up this much material you don't need to hunt this pawn, you can go straight for mate: bring the rook. Remember, if the pawn were on g7 we wouldn't, because a rook to e8 would be mate. He plays a rook to e2; I give a check on d1 and checkmate on h1. We could also have taken the rook and the bishop and promoted the c-pawn, but this is a little faster.
With the king already flushed out, the recovery plan is to castle by hand. The king doesn't have to hurry straight back — first complete development, then walk it to safety step by step.

Two routes present themselves: simply retreat the king toward e8, or fianchetto and shepherd the king to f8 by hand. The catch with the fianchetto is a pawn to b3 followed by the bishop swinging to a3 — that diagonal shot freezes the king in place and stops the manual castle.
So play g6 with a contingency in mind — meet b3 with the fianchetto, and if the bishop lunges to a3, just drop the king back to e8. Every setup has its own answer.
The rook goes to e8, not f8 — putting it on f8 would jam the king's own escape route. With the file cleared, the king can march to f8 and onward to g8, and the by-hand castle is done.

All those tempi spent, it's time to hit back in the centre. The opponent's kingside build-up looks imposing but it's flimsy — leave it untouched and it becomes total positional domination, so it has to be challenged.

The pawn storm looks scary but isn't — the setup is rock-solid, and if the h-pawn captures on g6 it's simply recaptured with no damage. Understanding that the structure holds is what lets the counterplay proceed calmly.

Here's the counter-intuitive call: yes, capture again on c4. Most of the time the cautious answer would be to hold off, but not here — it saddles the opponent with an isolated queen's pawn on d4, and the queen immediately leans on it. Opening the centre also pulls the opponent's focus away from the kingside attack. Best of all worlds.

Now bring out the last knight. One plan is the slow route — reroute it toward the blockade square in front of the isolated pawn. The more direct plan is to send it to c6 and trade off the opponent's strong advanced knight as fast as possible.
We open e4, and face the Sicilian.
We play the Alapin, c3.

The knight to c6 is one of the most common responses, but it's already a serious inaccuracy — not quite a mistake if Black follows up correctly, but one more slip and things get disastrously bad within five or six moves.
Our response is obvious: c3 prepared d4, and the knight to c6 doesn't stop it — we have enough defenders — so we grab the centre with d4.
Black takes, capturing on d4. The knight to c6 is misplaced here for a simple reason.

We recapture with a pawn, capturing on d4, threatening to push to d5 — and without a pawn shell to support them, Black's pieces get tossed around with no central footholds and can even be trapped. After d5 and the knight to e5, f4 sends the knight all the way back to g6, and the knight to f6 is even worse: after d5, the knight to e5, f4, the knight to g6, e5, the knight has only g8, since g4 and h5 are covered by our queen. A justified violation of opening principles — moving only pawns, but with tempo.

So we either push our own pawn to d5, grabbing the centre and chasing the knight, or just develop with the knight to c3 and the knight to f3. Black plays d5 — and the instinct is to meet it with e5, but that's inaccurate: unlike the Advance French, where Black's pawn is already on e6 giving the bad French bishop, here Black gets a good French or Caro-Kann, bringing the bishop out to f5 first and only then locking with e6.
So we take, capturing on d5, rather than allow that improved French.
The queen recaptures on d5 — transposing into a line normally reached via a different move order, and this is an isolated-queen-pawn structure.
We're playing the King's Indian — the knight to f6.
The bishop to g5 — the Trompowsky, named after the Brazilian Octavio Trompowsky. There's a misconception that only the knight to e4 works here; actually Black has many ways to equalize.
e6 and even g6 are reasonable, d5 is underrated, even c5 is playable — but I've always played the principled knight to e4.

At a lower level, h4 — the Hodgson variation, a very double-edged move — causes consternation. Its idea is simple: it defends the bishop, and if Black takes on g5, White recaptures with the h-pawn, opening the h-file (Black has the h7 pawn, restricting the rook) and creating a deep-freeze — the g5 pawn making it very hard for Black to ever fix the h7 weakness, since after h6 White takes and damages Black's kingside. So taking the bishop isn't best.

Black has many options; I'll play it simply with d5 — occupy the centre and toss the ball back. h4's drawback, beyond not developing, is that it commits White to an uncertain king: kingside castling is unlikely with the damage, queenside is risky with the knight on e4, and staying central is dubious.

The knight to d2 — he knows his theory. I don't want to take on g5, which plays into White's hands; instead I'll simply drop the knight back to f6 or d6, a symmetrical Queen's-Gambit-Declined-type position.
The knight back to f6. Moving the same piece three times seems wrong, but the centre is closed, so the effect is diminished — and White spent tempi on the weakening h4.

e3. The point of the knight's to-and-fro: we induced h4, provoking a serious kingside weakness, and now develop conventionally. We've been move-ordered into a reverse Queen's Gambit Declined — where White plays c4, we play c5 from the black side, but after c5 we must watch d takes c5.
Since White is developed, after c5, d takes c5, e6, White solidifies with b4 — so we start with the solid e6 and follow with c5 to contest and pressure White's centre.

The knight to e2. Let's play c5 — we can also throw in h6 to force the bishop to commit, but no rush; this pin isn't dangerous, since an easy test is whether the pinned piece is protected by a pawn, and it is.
We play c5, and White takes, capturing on c5.
We recapture with the bishop, capturing on c5 — precisely why we started with e6.
White's knights on e2 and d2 are passive; a3 is a good move, preparing b4. Many would auto-play a5, but not every idea must be prevented — b4 isn't a threat, just an idea; what does b4 actually do?

b4 chases our bishop from c5 — but the bishop is happy to drop to e7, ending the pin. So we develop the knight to c6. And after b4, that pawn becomes a target: we chisel with a5 once White's pawn is on b4 — the base of the chain, or sometimes the tip.
The knight to f4 — a perfect chance for the move I mentioned earlier: the bishop on g5 is now fully deprived of squares.
So it's time for h6, forcing White to trade the bishop for the knight, capturing on f6, letting our queen come to the active f6.
We recapture with the queen, capturing on f6. White has traded the dark-squared bishop, the pride of the Trompowsky — a great position for us.

The queen on f6 attacks b2 and pressures f2 — Black's already better. The knight to h5. We can grab the pawn on b2: people fear the queen getting trapped, but calculate concretely — after the queen takes b2, the rook to b1, our queen defends g7, so we drop it to e5, not c3 where the rook to b3 chases it; the central queen looks vulnerable to f4, but f4 gives up e3 with check.

The queen takes, capturing on b2. After the rook to b1, the queen to e5 — and if White chases with the knight, it severs the connection to the h5-knight, letting us take on h5. So we can safely take b2. Even if e5 were unavailable, taking on a3 would be fine — a king move to f8 isn't the end of the world.
The bishop to e2. We have ways to deal with g7 — g6 is the forcing option, or we simply castle. The king is safest on f8, surrounded by pawn cover; d7 walks into the d-file x-ray.

Castling kills two birds — it develops and protects g7. If I were White I'd contemplate g4 for kingside counterplay, using the uncastled king: the trope where the uncastled side can benefit from the h1-rook if the h-file opens — see Vukovic's Art of Attack.
We have White, open with the pawn to e4, and get e5 — a reply we haven't faced much this run.
The knight to f3.
Black plays the pawn to d6 — the Philidor, a solid, long-standing alternative to the knight to c6. It's not known to be dangerous, but it's sturdy, so it pays to know what to do.
I like the Italian-flavoured approach — the bishop to c4 — and only later d4. It's flexible: you can also play the pawn to d3 and transpose to an Italian structure if you prefer.
The pawn to e4, d5 — the Scandinavian, it's been a while.
We take on d5.
The knight to f6 — an old variation where Black delays the recapture, wanting to take back with the knight. I'll play a line my coach taught me years ago.
You might ask why not c4 defending the pawn — I'll explain after. My coach's line, one of the most reputable, is this check on b5.
The bishop to d7 — developing with tempo. Now the move that might confuse you —
— we drop the bishop back to e2, and Black takes on d5; the point involves the bishop on d7 —
— but e6 is really bad; Black just gives away a pawn.
We take.
Now we're just up a pawn for no compensation. The question is how to structure our development: we can play d4 to occupy the centre, but maybe Black plays c5 —
— so we could develop modestly with the knight to f3, but I think d4 is just more ambitious; I'll show the idea afterward.
The bishop to d6 is some weird move. He doesn't play c5, so we're fine — let's just develop the knight to f3 —
— the knight to f3, and then castle.
We castle, and Black castles.

Up a pawn, no comp. There are always multiple ways to play — one of the best ways to restrict this knight is to push c3, creating a pawn chain and keeping our central pawn well defended. c4 I like a little less, since the centre becomes flimsy and Black could play the bishop to g4.
If we're pushing the c-pawn, I'd prefer c3; or we could start with the bishop to g5, developing and deciding based on what Black does.

The bishop to g4 — exactly my point: if our pawn were on c4, Black would threaten the tactic, the bishop takes f3 and the knight to d4, and because of the standoff between the queens you couldn't recapture the knight.
So it's important here to play c3 and protect the d4-pawn against various shenanigans.

People's reservation about c3 is that it's not clear where to put the knight, but the knight to d2 is a completely legitimate developing move. The queen to d7 is risky — it lets us take on f6 and ruin Black's structure, but the downside is we give up a good bishop, and Black can play the king to h8 and the rook to g8, using the pawn structure to his benefit.
I'm actually not enthralled by the bishop takes f6 — not as slam-dunk as it looks — so we refrain and complete development with the knight to d2, maybe taking a bit later.
Maybe it would have been better to take immediately, who knows. Now his pieces are on pretty good squares.
The rook to e1, continuing to improve our position.
The rook to e6 — the idea is to double on the e-file and pressure our bishop, and the bishop on g4 is quite annoying too. I think I see a tactic; I have to calculate it.
The tactic starts — we take on f6, hoping for the rook to recapture —
— the rook takes f6. If I calculated this correctly, it might win the game.
Anytime you have a standoff between these two bishops, there's a particular move to be aware of — a common idea. Oops, my mouse slipped — I didn't mean the bishop to f1.

My recommendation is the Accelerated Dragon. White surprises with c4 — think of it as an English where White plays c4, we play c5, and White plays e4. Its drawback jumps out: White has created a massive hole on d4 — a square no pawn can ever defend, since the c- and e-pawns have advanced past it.

This gives our knight a potential outpost on d4 — but a hole existing doesn't mean occupy it at once. We start with the knight to c6, not to play the knight to d4 next: it's too early, with nothing else developed.
The knight to f3 would just knock a d4-knight off. It's the long-term weakness that costs White later. We also get a massive diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.
We play g6 — though in a classical game I'd prefer e6 or the knight to f6, since g6 allows White to transition to main lines.
The drawback of g6: it allows d4 — after d4, c takes d4, knight takes d4, we transpose to the Maroczy Bind Accelerated Dragon. Since we're emphasizing openings, I wouldn't mind. White plays d3.
After the bishop to g7, we're flat-out better: great pieces, dominating the dark squares, and White's light bishop is now a big pawn.

The knight to c3. We develop normally. It's self-evidently good to trade our light bishop for White's f3-knight — visualize it gone: our control of d4 increases, and we can contemplate the knight to d4, though White can still trade it with the dark bishop or the c3-knight, both awkward.
The best way to threaten that trade is d6 — a normal developing move I like more than the knight to f6, which I'll delay. White plays the bishop to e3.
We develop the bishop to g4, continuing to clamp d4, trading a piece that controls it — classic positional chess.
The bishop to e2. Do we take on f3 or wait? It doesn't matter — both are good.
I'll eliminate the knight while we can, capturing on f3 — the drawback of waiting is that the knight could move away.
White recaptures, capturing on f3.

The Botvinnik setup: fianchetto the dark bishop, then carve a square for the g8-knight with e6, keeping the bishop unobstructed. The e6 pawn is an asset, controlling d5 and f5 — a toothy central construction.
Bb5-check is the Moscow anti-Sicilian: check, then retreat, steering the game toward a comfortable Ruy-Lopez-style structure instead of a sharp Open Sicilian.
notes.teaches: Bb5+ against the Sicilian sidesteps theory and transposes into familiar Ruy structures.

notes.explains: c3 and then Bc2 — the classic Ruy Lopez retreat, keeping the bishop alive on the b1-h7 diagonal while preparing d4.
notes.teaches: Reroute the Spanish bishop to c2 so it eyes the kingside once the centre opens.

notes.explains: Many players don't know to take twice here, and after Qc7 a4 gives White a pleasant edge.
d5 locks the centre into a full Ruy Lopez structure — space and a clear plan, rather than an early clarifying trade.
notes.teaches: Closing the centre with d5 hands you the space and the standard Spanish maneuvers.

notes.explains: Now the signature Ruy knight tour begins with Nbd2, heading for a better home.
notes.plans: Route the knight Nbd2-f1-e3 toward the kingside.

notes.explains: Ne3 completes the reroute — the knight's ideal square, eyeing f5 and d5.
notes.teaches: The Spanish knight belongs on e3 after the f1 pivot; it hits f5 and supports the centre.

notes.explains: g3 and a follow-up Nh4 clamp down on Black's knight, denying it the active squares it's angling for.
notes.teaches: Use g3 and Nh4 to fence in an enemy knight before it reaches an outpost.

notes.explains: The tactical turn: if the queen grabs e5, Bc3 pins it along the long diagonal, winning back the initiative with tempo.
notes.teaches: A bishop to the long diagonal can pin a queen that ventured onto it, reclaiming the tempo.

notes.explains: Bxg7 then a rook lift and f4 — trade off the strong bishop and roll the central pawns forward.
notes.plans: Swap the fianchetto bishop, lift a rook, and advance the centre.

notes.explains: Slip in b3 first — it opens the queen's diagonal and simply can't hurt before the central break.
notes.teaches: Insert a useful, risk-free improving move before committing to the main break.

notes.explains: e5 finally breaks in the centre, tearing open lines toward the king with the pieces already aimed there.
White tries the bishop to c4 against the Caro-Kann — the hillbilly bishop. It makes little sense here.
Because we hit it with d5, gaining a tempo on the bishop while striking the center.
teaches: d5 hits the c4 bishop with tempo

notes.explains: On the check we block with the bishop to d7 rather than a knight — a small point of principle: don't move one piece repeatedly and trade it for a piece that's only moved once.
teaches: don’t trade a busy piece for a fresh one

notes.explains: Don't fear the knight that lands on b5 — a lone piece on your side of the board is harmless, and you can even gain tempi hitting it later. We just develop.
teaches: a single intruding piece is not a threat

notes.explains: So we develop the knight to c6 as if nothing is going on — because nothing is.
Once White plays c3 the a6 push becomes timely: the knight has lost its retreat, so if it jumps to d4 we take, saddling White with isolated, doubled center pawns — a real positional concession.
teaches: a6 to trap the knight into a bad structure

notes.explains: After the trade White is left with an isolated pawn on d4 — that pawn becomes our target for the rest of the game.
teaches: the isolated d-pawn as a fixed target

notes.explains: The bishop to d6 is an excellent square, eyeing the kingside and supporting our own play.
The knight goes to e7, not f6 — from e7 it can reroute to f5 or c6 to pile onto the d4-pawn.
teaches: Ne7 to reach the attacking squares

notes.explains: With everything ready the plan is to stack pressure on the isolated pawn — a knight and the queen from b6.
The queen to b6 has a bonus: besides hitting d4, it discourages White's dark-squared bishop from developing. That extra benefit is why we move the queen before the knight.
teaches: choose the move order by the extra benefit

notes.explains: The knight swings into f5 — active, and leaning hard on d4.
Rather than cash in on the pawn right away, we open the queenside with a5, prying open files to expose more weaknesses — flexibility over grabbing material too soon.
teaches: open a second front instead of rushing to win a pawn

notes.explains: Now is the moment to take on d4 — we've made a fresh weakness on the queenside, so capturing opens a second front White can't defend everywhere at once.
teaches: time the capture to overload the defense

notes.explains: After trading down, the queen is centralized and we're up two pawns with a passer. The winning method is textbook endgame technique: put the rook behind the passed pawn, bring the king in, and use the extra pawn as a decoy — sacrifice it to drag White's king offside and transition into a won pawn ending where our king marches into his position. Waiting moves and zugzwang do the rest.
teaches: the decoy-pawn transition to a won pawn ending

notes.explains: We take White and open e4; Black replies e6 — the French. This is our opening-focused run: play principled moves and punish typical non-theoretical setups.
We build the big centre with d4.
Black plays the offbeat ...Nc6 rather than the main ...d5. Don't assume a non-theoretical move means you're already winning; just develop soundly.
We simply develop the knight to f3 — an immediate ...d5 is too concrete before we've developed.
Black plays the passive ...d6. We have several ways to punish it; the simplest is the knight to c3, keeping to the spirit of e4 openings rather than grabbing space with c4.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black develops the knight to f6.

The bishop comes to d3 — it props up e4, and once Black castles short we can push e5 and aim the bishop at h7. Combined with the queen coming to e4, that battery threatens mate on h7. Note: even if Black plays ...h6, the square itself stays weak — don't confuse a weak pawn with a weak square.

Black plays ...h6 and we castle. We're unbothered by ...Nb4 — the bishop just steps back and a3 chases it. Black's slow queenside play neglects his kingside, which we punish by opening the centre: Black's d6- and e6-pawns are hooks, and a pawn advance can act like dynamite to blow the centre open.

Black plays ...b6, and we strike with d5 — the thematic dynamiting of the centre, and crucially it opens the e-file straight at Black's king. If Black takes, we have two defenders to his two attackers; we'd play it even as a sacrifice, because that file is the highway to the king — which is exactly why we castled early.
Black captures on d5.
We recapture with the pawn — a major step toward winning.

Black plays ...Nb4. Our objective now is to keep Black's king stuck in the centre — a moving target is hard to hit. We can't stop ...Be7, but a rook to e1 with check pins it, and by piling pressure on the pinned bishop we keep the king glued to the centre as a defender.
First we insert the check on b5 — avoiding a trade and keeping our light-squared bishop, which rakes the light squares that ...b6 weakened.
Black blocks with the bishop to d7.
We take on d7 with check.

Black recaptures with the queen — the best move, though few under 2000 find it. Beyond the open e-file, I'd spotted that the knight on b4 is horribly exposed: a minor piece parked on the opponent's side is easy prey for pawns.
So we shove it away with a3 — a move you'd want regardless; the knight has to retreat to a6, since capturing just loses it.
The knight lands on a6, loose. Remember the acronym: loose pieces drop off — an undefended piece plus a wide-open king is a fork waiting to happen.
And there it is: the queen to e2 with check forks king and knight — we forget the e-file and simply win the knight on a6, a full piece up.
d4, the knight to f6.
c4, g6 — we're going to play the King's Indian Defense.
the knight to c3, the bishop to g7.
The point of the King's Indian, as I've explained many times, is that you basically give
up control of the centre, and in return you develop pieces to attack the centre from a distance. For it to work
properly, you first need to complete your development quickly — the bishop to g5.
So let's castle,
and now the time has come. The knight on f3 defends the pawn on d4 — so what comes to mind for attacking that d4-pawn, directly or indirectly? There are several ways.
You could play the bishop to g4, trading this bishop for the knight and softening up White's defence of the d4-pawn. It's not a typical King's-Indian move, but

it does illustrate one of the key themes. A lot of people would take the knight here, but there's no hurry, because we have the knight pinned — we can take it at a moment of our convenience. So how do we keep pressing on d4
with our pieces, in the spirit of this line — using pieces to pressure the centre from a distance? c5 is possible, striking with the pawn, but let's use our pieces — the knight to c6.
He's castled, simply ignoring the threats we've posed on his centre,
so we can take on d4 — because of the pin he cannot take back, and he's essentially busted;

he's lost the central pawn, and now he makes matters worse by taking on f6. If we were extra fancy here, what would we do? We can take back on f6 with the bishop, but what intermediate move can we also consider? A lot of you get caught here — when you play the knight takes f3, you have to calculate it,

because if you play the knight takes f3 and allow g-takes-f3, that f3-pawn will attack our bishop on g4 and we lose a piece. So believe it or not, we play the bishop takes f3 first; he plays the pawn takes f3,
and now we take on f6, ruining the structure around his king. Now we're also
up a pawn, his kingside is ruined, and we can exploit either factor. One approach a lot of people struggle with is the queenside attack — it's hard for Black to do
anything specific on the kingside yet, but we'll keep it in mind. In terms of activating pieces — the queen to d7.
There was also an idea of pressuring the queenside, but let's go for the
brute-force approach — the queen to h3.
Let me note this down, especially since he's completely ignored the threats. What do we do here?

We win his queen, because there's no stopping checkmate on h2. The bishop to e5 would have been worse — and it's very important to note that in such situations there's often only one correct option, and you have to operate under that assumption.
The queen takes f3 — exactly. He's resigned. First things first: why is the bishop to e5 worse here?

Against the King's Indian around this level the recommendation is the Sämisch, and its signature is the modest pawn to f3. The idea is one you'll have met in the Sicilian — it braces the e4-pawn like a strut, so the big centre can't be undermined.
Resist the urge to lunge d5 too early. Instead develop the dark-squared bishop to e3 — and the deeper plan is the pawn storm with h4, prying open the kingside.
The Sämisch is the one King's Indian line where the king routinely goes long. That's the mainline framework here — castle queenside and hurl the kingside pawns at the enemy king.

So f3 earns its keep two ways: it cements central control, and it slams the door on the knight jump to g4 that would otherwise harass the bishop. That bishop is precious — it isn't traded except for its opposite number.

The opponent has drifted into an accelerated-dragon-style setup, which isn't the best answer to the Sämisch — the position is now simply better for the first player. A quiet queen move consolidates; the tempting retreat to prevent a trade isn't needed, since the trade is perfectly fine.

Now a word on flexibility, the mark of strong play: begin the game with one plan but be ready to stop on a dime — you lined up a layup, and now you pull up for the three. Concretely, a positional edge means you no longer have to force an immediate mate.

That empty-looking rook move hands over the initiative, so castle long and make the intentions plain — go straight for the throat in the classical manner: h4, h5, rip open the h-file and hunt the king.
No reason to delay — push the h-pawn, fully intending to sacrifice it. Feeding that pawn is the entire point of the attack; the open lines are worth far more than the material.

Here's a piece of classical prophylaxis — the king step to b1. After castling long it's a wonderfully healthy move, tucking the king off the exposed c-file so that a rook lift and queenside pressure lose much of their bite. A little insurance before the storm.

A wrinkle: kicking the advanced knight with g4 runs into a nasty leap to g3, hitting the rook and eyeing the bishop. So prepare slowly and attack fast — drop the knight back to b3 instead, easing the central tension, forcing the queen to declare itself, and untying the hands for a single-minded kingside assault.

A crucial habit: a move that failed a moment ago doesn't stay refused forever. Because the queen has repositioned to a vulnerable central square, the whole picture has changed — the same g4 idea is worth a fresh look.

And now it works: after g4 chases the knight to g3, a bishop drops to f4 forking the queen and the knight at once. It's a semi-fake fork — the knight can grab on f1 and hit the queen back — but that never mattered, because the real aim was only to remove the knight and clear the road.

Recall the true objective — not to win material, but to be rid of that knight so the queen is finally free to swing to the h-file and mate. And the queenside remains completely intact, so this side of the attack is miles ahead of anything the opponent has managed.

The queen arrives on h2, and the capture on h7 sets up mate within a couple of moves. The defence can wriggle, but with so many pieces trained on the king it's just a matter of technique — and the enemy queen is marooned uselessly in the centre.

Here's a pattern to bank: the queen would deliver mate on the corner but for a defending bishop — so remove the bishop with a check on h6, and thanks to the pin the mate lands anyway. Clearing the last defender is the whole trick.
We open e4 and meet a French — e6, preparing to challenge our center with d5.
d4, grabbing the full center. This is the heart of the French: our broad pawn duo against Black's coming counterstrike.

d5, and we're at an early crossroads. In earlier speedruns I've recommended the Nimzowitsch Advance — e5, and after c5 you skip the automatic c3 and develop the knight instead, voluntarily giving up the pawn chain and inviting a capture on d4. It's counterintuitive, with a deep positional underpinning, and genuinely dangerous for an unprepared opponent.
But today I'll play the line I'm most comfortable with, the one I've played my whole life — the Tarrasch, the knight to d2.
The knight to d2 is what defines the Tarrasch. It shields e4 without blocking the c-pawn, keeping c3 in reserve to buttress d4.
A quick primer if you don't know the French: against d5 White's most natural, most popular try is a knight to c3.
But a knight to c3 leads to incredibly theoretical waters we don't want to touch with a ten-foot pole, and the Exchange is equally to be avoided. The Tarrasch is the answer.
The Tarrasch straddles the bridge — it isn't drowning in theory, yet it carries real venom that lets you crush an unprepared opponent. Against it Black has two main replies.
e5 gains space and shoves the f6 knight back, locking the center into that Advanced-French shape.
The knight retreats to d7, ready to regroup and to help hit our chain with a later c5 or f6.
The main line is the bishop to d3 — the most natural square, and one that already eyes the h7 pawn for a future kingside strike.
Black plays c5, striking at the base of our chain, the d4 pawn.
And here we do play c3. Don't file this under the Advance variation — this pawn structure shows up across many French lines, and the Advance has very different piece configurations for both sides.
Black develops the knight to c6, and there's actually very little in common between this Tarrasch line and a true Advanced French.
When Black grabs space by pushing the pawn to e4, undermine it at once with f3 rather than let an advanced pawn sit unchallenged.
notes.teaches: Challenge an overextended enemy pawn immediately with a pawn break instead of playing around it.

notes.explains: The Sicilian, aiming for the Accelerated Dragon.

White offers the Wing Gambit with b4 — a third-string gambit with a dubious reputation. Its idea is the usual one: deflect our c-pawn off c5 so White can occupy the center with d4. But here Black is objectively better with accurate play.
teaches: the Wing Gambit idea and its flaw

notes.explains: We accept with the c-pawn, not the knight — taking with the knight would hand White a tempo to play c3 and prop up his center.
teaches: accept with the pawn to deny White c3 with tempo

notes.explains: White plays d4 as expected, and the move on everyone's mind should be d5 — contesting the center before it's too late, and the queen can't even be hit by a knight to c3 because our pawn covers that square.

Here, though, a practical choice — the modest d6. It's probably a shade worse than d5, but it drags a theory-armed opponent onto their own thinking, and it does a fine job stopping White's e-pawn while we've lost almost no development.
teaches: a modest off-theory move to make the opponent think

notes.explains: White pushes past with d5.
The knight swings to e5 to fight for a central pawn of our own; and note the trade is safe — a check on b5 just runs into the bishop to d7, so our queen is never in danger.
teaches: Ne5 for a center pawn, with ...Bd7 covering the check

notes.explains: We open e4 and meet the Caro-Kann — c6.
d4, taking the full center behind the pawn.
Black strikes with d5, questioning our e4 pawn head-on.
f3 — the Fantasy Variation. Instead of the usual moves, we bolster e4 with the f-pawn and dare Black to try to punish the loosened kingside.
Black develops with a knight to d7 — and I'll be honest, I've never seen it here. It isn't a top move; I'd call it an inaccuracy: passive, and it does nothing to contest the center.

So we close it down with e5. I want to give you a broad tour of a closed-center position — a lot of players feel lost when the center locks, as if they're just shuffling pieces. In truth these are some of the richest games in chess, because they force play on the flanks, where the most beautiful and tactical ideas live. Our next job is to reinforce both links of the d4-e5 chain, because Black will attack it with pawns.
c5 hits the base of our chain — a classic French break. Black can also come from the other side with f6, which is exactly why I like f4.
c3, a no-brainer, propping up d4. We absolutely don't want the chain to dissolve this early with no pieces out — that chain is the only thing standing between us and disaster.

The knight belongs on f3; a knight to e2 would be awkward and would bury the light-squared bishop. Black's queen to c7 is a bit pointless — it doesn't even threaten a capture on d4, since we recapture and the c1 bishop is guarded by our own queen. So we keep developing, and the move order is flexible.

I'll bring the bishop to d3 first, since we're lagging in development and haven't moved a minor piece — and it also keeps the knight-to-e2 option alive, which is far more palatable once the bishop is already out.
Black plays e6, and we keep everything as flexible as possible — with the opponent playing so unambitiously, we can leave many developing paths open.
Now f4 — the maximally ambitious, textbook move, grabbing space and taking the fight to the opponent.
Black plays g6. The c1 bishop starts complaining that it's staring at its own pawn, but it has fine squares on e3 or d2 — not every piece has to climb Everest at once.
On e3 the bishop actually does a great job further supporting the chain, which we want rock-solid. But first, the knight to f3 — let's get the pieces we know how to place out.

Black's knight goes to e7, heading for f5 to press d4 in true French fashion. Don't be tempted by g4 to stop it — that's far too cavalier with so little developed. After g4, h5 is a classic response: we can't answer h3, Black captures on g4, and the h1 rook hangs, so g4 hands Black a huge f5 outpost instead of denying one.

So the bishop to e3 — and the subtlety is that when the knight lands on f5, our bishop slides back to f2. Castle first and that retreat to e3 is no longer available; the small developmental detail decides how smoothly the game runs.
The knight comes to f5, and the bishop drops to f2, first overprotecting the d4 pawn and, much later, eyeing a route into Black's position.
A bishop maneuver to h4 and f6 is a common infiltration, especially against a fianchetto with a bishop fianchettoed to g7.
We castle and keep developing. The h5 push is typical for this structure.

h5 does prevent g4, but it creates major dark-square weaknesses — notice the outpost on g5. That doesn't mean we leap there now; a knight to g5 lets Black trade and fill the holes. Later, though, g5 becomes a transit square, and a plan of trading on f5 and swinging the bishop to h4 hands our queen a swarm of juicy kingside outposts. With the center closed we have time — the position simply doesn't change fast.

A knight to a3 is a dead-end after a6, so instead the b1 knight goes to d2 — toward the center, going nowhere in particular yet, a Frankfurt-airport move you never regret. Remember, closed positions offer two broad plans: arrange your pieces to blast the center open, or maneuver on a flank.

Black plays a queen to b6. Here's our plan: rip the whole thing open and bank on our more active pieces handling the chaos better. Not a capture on c5 — that just hands Black space and the e3 square. Instead c4, building a pawn box that guarantees the center will open, perhaps after first eliminating Black's only active piece with a capture on f5.

c4 it is — and we can delay the capture on f5, playing it a little later. And we're not afraid of losing b2: when you've castled on the opposite wing a single b-pawn almost never matters, and here our queenside stays intact — Black can't unravel it the way a b2-then-c3 collapse would.

The queen grabs b2, but it creates no threats and doesn't stop our central agenda. Trying to trap it with a queen to a4 and a rook to b1 fails to a strong resource, and we lack the queenside firepower anyway — so we keep our focus in the center and press to open it.

We start with a move we know is good — capturing on d5. If Black doesn't recapture, the pawn marches to d6 and it's horrific for him, so he'll take back, and then a capture on f5 to wreck his structure is the idea.
Black recaptures on d5, and we should be tempted to grab the knight on f5 — giving up our light-square control hurts, but it's a price well worth paying.
So we capture on f5, taking the knight, while we still can, trading our good bishop to shatter Black's kingside pawns.
Black recaptures with the g-pawn, and now we complete the opening of the center.

We finish it with a capture on c5 — the center is now fully open, so we shift from luxurious positional play to hunting tactics. Black still hasn't developed his queenside, and we've invested a pawn, so we must hit the gas.
Black recaptures on c5. Only a couple of moves stand between him and consolidating that extra pawn, so we accelerate — and a bishop to d4 catches my eye, x-raying the rook.

The bishop to d4 hits the queen, centralizes beautifully, and prepares an e6 discovery against the rook — good as a plan and good as a plain developing move. It also shoos away that b2 queen, which was cramping our coordination.
Black shuffles the queen to a3, but our reply to almost anything here is e6 — and our opponent is defending this fantastically, making us work.
e6 is nearly automatic: without it, Black plants a knight into e6 and keeps the center closed.
Black plays a rook to g8 — and that, I think, is the decisive mistake.
Because now, without a second thought, we capture on f7, dragging the king out into the open.

The king is forced to f7 — f6 was the only survival try. Now the firepower tells: a knight to e5 with check, and lines flow, though a queen grab on h5 with check isn't yet mate because the king slips to d8.
A knight to e5 with check. Black could try the king to g6, using the king itself as a defender, but there's no reason to overcomplicate — the knight to e5 is clean.

The king walks out to e6. This looks like hara-kiri for Black. One pitfall for us is a rook to e1 — there's a knight jump to e4 in reply, and if the king ever steps to d6 a knight to c4 forks king and queen. No need for any of that: the simplest move is to capture the h-pawn, not for the pawn but to route the queen toward f7.

The queen takes h5, Black defends with a rook to f8, and the queen checks from h6 — the whole point being to prevent a bishop to f6. Compare your checks: two similar-looking checks rarely do the same job.
The rook is driven to f6, and remember — even mid-attack you're allowed to win material. Players fixate on delivering mate; here the rook sits under the bishop's x-ray.
A queen to g7 — using the weakness of Black's king to go after his pieces, because a king so exposed forces the defenders onto vulnerable squares.
Black finds the only move, a queen to b4, holding things together; a queen check on g8 and the king to d6 leaves us with a beautiful win to find.

A knight to f3 is what I like — it gives away nothing, prepares a knight to g5, and safely defends the bishop. A resilient defender makes you work, but at most levels the position collapses in a couple of moves.
Crucially, we've sacrificed nothing — it's plus eleven. If Black plays a knight to e4 to take the sting out of a knight to g5, the top computer move is a wonderfully quiet one.
Just a rook to c1 — bringing a piece into the attack and cutting the king off from its escape. These quiet inclusions are the moves people won't make when attacking, yet they decide the game.
Against a bishop to d7 we simply play a rook to c7.
The rook to c7 — its added presence overwhelms Black's defense.
Black tries a rook to d8, and the engine's move is striking.
A knight to f7.
After the rook takes it, a queen to e5 is checkmate — a pretty little concept, everything protected, completely one-sided.
We open e4, and Black plays the knight to c6.
The knight to f3 — if Black plays e5 we transpose to standard lines.
Black plays d6, a version of the Pirc — usually Black plays g6 and transposes, but there's a unique treatment with the bishop to g4.
We grab the centre with d4. Bringing the bishop to g4 is dubious for Black — not losing, but very meh, and White doesn't need much theory to get a big edge.
The bishop to g4. Lots of theory revolves around the move d5 here.
Let's circumvent d5 — why bog down when we can simply develop and target the knight with the bishop to b5?
We take, capturing on c6 with check.

Black recaptures with the b-pawn, capturing on c6. Normally you don't worry about the pawn structure opposite where you'll castle — both castle kingside — but this is an exception: first, White controls the centre, so it's easy to pressure these weak pawns; second, Black is poorly developed.
Until Black completes development, those weak pawns are a real target. We castle.
The rook to b8.
Case in point — h3, to force the bishop to commit.
The bishop takes, capturing on f3.
We recapture with the queen on f3.
Now let's pressure these pawns — we don't have forever; if Black completes kingside development, he's fine. So we act now.
We assault the pawns by sliding the queen to c3. How did I find it? There's a brief moment before the fianchetto completes where the rook is vulnerable.
The rook to b6 — that vulnerable rook is the source of a lot of tactics.
d5, a discovered attack — the knight to f6 is forced.
The knight to f6. Let's not rush d takes c6 — there's the fine alternative the bishop to e3, which lets Black play c5, saving the pawn but granting us big queenside positional gains.
d takes c6 allows the queen to a5 with complications I'd rather avoid — so the bishop to e3.
We play it Benoni style — the knight to d2. Watch: the queen to a3 is coming.
The bishop to g7.
The queen to a3.
Black gets the queen out of the bishop's line of fire, the queen to a8, and now the thematic positional plan — the knight heads for c4.
No hurry — first c3, a move worth noting: it's incredibly effective at restricting the black bishop. Keep it in your pocket.
Black castles.
We deploy the rook to e1.
The knight to d7.
We complete the knight maneuver to c4, applying Russian-schoolboy pressure.
The rook back to b8.
The knight to a5 — spotting an outpost; not necessarily c6 next, but threatening it.
e6. Do we want this exchange? No — we want the d5 pawn to keep clamping.
So we protect it — the rook to d1.
Black opens the e-file for us; we recapture on d5.
Now that d5 is under fire, we could play c4, but a cooler protection is the knight to the outpost first. The knight to f6.
The knight to c6, the outpost.
The rook to b6.
Now c4, removing any knight-takes-d5 undermining. Easy but powerful tactics coming.
The queen to b7. I'm looking at that trapped rook — if the diagonal opens, we win the exchange.
So b4. After c takes b4, the key question is where to move the queen.
When winning the exchange, don't give up too much — not the knight and pawn on c6; the queen would go to e7 with check. The knight to d7.
We take, capturing on c5.
Black recaptures, and we take on c5 with the bishop — knocking on the door of victory, Black's pieces still stuck on the b-file.
The rook to b2. Now Black starts blundering.
The bishop takes on f8 — but watch the f2 pawn: people love the queen to b6 here, so the moment a rook landed on b2 I noted the mate threats on f2.
Black recaptures on f8 — always anticipate where the danger comes from, like defensive driving, treating yourself as the idiot.
The rook to e8.
The queen to b6 — now a large menu of winning options.
One is to plug the diagonal with tempo — c5 — setting up a gorgeous mating construction.
The knight takes on c5. In a bullet game I'd play the rook to b8 skewering the queen — but there's an unstoppable mate.
The knight to e7 would let the king run, so take away the squares first — the queen to c3. That's how you find quiet moves: this would be mate but for the escape square, so can I take it first?
If your opponent isn't threatening anything, the answer is often yes — the queen to c3.
The knight to e7, checkmate — all pieces participating, the knight the hero, having traveled b1, d2, c4, a5, c6, e7 to deliver mate.
e4, e5 — an open game. We've been leaning on the Danish Gambit lately, but let's switch it up.
A knight to c3 — the Vienna. It's a phenomenal opening for anyone below master strength, largely because Black players simply don't study this move.
And a bishop to c5 is already a little inaccurate — the very reaction the Vienna preys on.
The whole idea of the Vienna Gambit is to improve on the King's Gambit: develop the knight first, watch how Black sets up, and only then play f4 — so you're better placed to meet a capture on f4.
And it turns out the bishop on c5 does nothing to stop f4, which a lot of people don't realize.
So f4 anyway. The bishop on c5 doesn't prevent it.
Black takes on f4. This is the hot-button moment, because we have to reckon with a queen check on h4.
A knight to f3 is essential — you can't answer a queen check on h4 with g3 because the f4 pawn just captures it. The knight to f3 covers h4 and is the best move here.
Black plays d6, holding the center — and we still have to keep an eye on that queen check.
And here I play a knight to d4 — a genuine blunder that simply drops the knight. Damage-control time.

Black captures on d4 and we've backed ourselves into a corner — down a knight, with the queen check on h4 still looming. We can't meet g3 with a recapture because both our rook and the pawn would hang.
A queen to f3 begins the recovery: now, if the queen comes to h4 and we answer g3 and the pawns trade, both the rook and the pawn are defended.
Black captures on c3 to trade — but that's already a small win for us, because that bishop was a monster. When you're down a piece, the priority is development.
We recapture with the d-pawn on c3 — the fastest route to quick development. We'll castle long, since the kingside is already wrecked.
Black plays g5 to defend the f4 pawn — another subtle mistake, because we're castling queenside and if his king goes short he'll pay dearly for that advanced pawn.
A bishop to d2, prioritizing development and king safety so we can start attacking. It isn't pretty, but we need to castle as fast as possible.

Castling long is the fastest way to safety. I don't care in the slightest about the a2 pawn — if Black grabs it we play b3 and trap the bishop; when you're down a piece you can't fret over a single pawn.
Black plays a6. Now, the idea I taught last game: when there's a pawn chain, attacking its base can make the whole structure topple.
So h4 — striking the foot of Black's g5-f4 chain. Knock out the base and the whole thing collapses.
We take on g5 to make that foot collapse. I know Black wants a bishop to g4, pinning my queen to the rook, but we're ready to give the exchange to topple his kingside.
Black plays the bishop to g4, and we'll sacrifice another exchange to make his whole kingside cave in.
The queen captures on f4 — we have to preserve the queen while Black grabs the rook.
Black takes our rook, landing on d1, and now we choose what to capture — because something very cool happens here.

After we recapture on f6, Black's bishop is trapped: it retreats to h5, but we've opened the h-file and our rook covers that square. That's the kind of thing that just falls into your lap when you play aggressively and hunt for chances.
Black plays a bishop to c2 — this still isn't better for White if he defends correctly, and he isn't defending badly.
The king recaptures on c2. He's given the bishop for a pawn.

Now we act on our strong f6 pawn — a great anchor for our pieces. The question is what Black wants: he won't castle kingside, since we'd mate him at once, so he'll try to castle queenside via a queen to d7, and we must stop that. A bishop to g4 tempts, but it has a drawback.

So g3 first, preparing a bishop to h3 instead — the difference being that after a bishop to e2 and g4, Black's knight to e5 covers g4; routed through h3, the bishop is far better protected. Same number of moves, better result.
Black plays a knight to e5.
And we go to h3 with the bishop.

Black's knight comes to g6 — but he still can't get his queen out; his pieces are stuck in molasses. He hits our queen, so we move it to a square that keeps the f6 pawn defended — that pawn is a huge bargaining chip.

A queen to f5. Not a queen to e3, which drops the pawn; not to f3, where a knight back to e5 hits it again; and not to g5, where h6 harasses it. f5 also builds a battery — a queen to d7 could be mate.
Black plays c6. We want to open the center, because he's paralyzed and any opening favors us. Here's the thought experiment: if you could remove one of your own pawns, which would it be?
The e-pawn, of course — so paradoxically, rather than a slow rook move first, just play e5 to clear it and free the e-file for the rook.
Black replaces the pawn by capturing on e5. You can sacrifice your rook for his pawn, but never for your own — you have to make him be the one to take it.
A rook to e1, and now we're threatening to capture on e5 with a mating attack.
Black finds a defense with a queen to c7 — so we pile onto the knight, keeping our eyes on the target.
