A bishop to f4, adding an attacker to the knight so we can blast through with a capture on e5.
The king steps to d8.
We take on e5 with the bishop.
Black recaptures on e5.
And now a rook to d1 with check, so the rook can swing into d7.
The rook lands on d7, attacking the queen — it has to move, and the rook will swing to e7.
Black plays a queen to a5.
We begin with a check on e7, forcing the king toward f8 — if it goes to d8 instead, a queen to d7 is mate.
The king goes to f8. Now we just win it normally.
We need to attack f7 while posing as many threats as possible — the queen does that far better from h5 than from d7.
Black tries a queen to d5.

The reason h5 is better: from there the queen also has a check on h6 and a mate on g7. When you have an idea while attacking, develop and sharpen it — this is a forced mate, so we pre-move the queen to g7.
Against this gambit the cleanest reply is simply to accept — take the pawn and make the opponent prove the compensation they don't really have.

Here's a principle for disarming any gambit. Grabbing the second pawn is best by the engine's cold count — there just isn't enough compensation. But in practice the middle path is often wiser: hand the pawn back and, in return, claim a development lead. Stop worrying about clinging to the extra material and just get pieces out.

The developing move that also bites is the knight to c6 — it counterattacks the loose pawn. The natural-looking bishop development isn't as good as it seems, because a pawn thrust to d5 would kick the knight and hand over the e5 outpost.
Insisting on the sacrifice is just a bad decision — so capture on d4. The opponent's centre has caved in and they're simply shedding pawns for nothing; there's no reason to decline the gift.

The knight jump to b5 is pure intimidation — the sort of scary-looking move that concrete calculation keeps you safe from. Ask the obvious question: is there any reason not to just take the knight? The only pause is that the queens could come off and the king lose its castling — but two pawns up, with pieces trading, a king in the centre is a long way from getting mated.

This is a classic trap the opponent falls into — expecting an in-between check followed by a leisurely capture. What they've missed is that a single knight move to d6 does two jobs at once: it saves the knight and blocks the check. Two pawns and a piece to the good, the rest is technique.

Even deep in an endgame, the rule holds: keep developing, don't forget your pieces. So offer the trade of bishops — because when you're up material and a clean path to simplification appears, you take it. Every swap brings the win closer.
The plan is just e6 and the fianchetto — no need to overthink the technique. Grab the pawn back now that the knight has cleared away from its home square.
A touch of class: ask where the enemy knight wants to go — most likely g5 — and quietly deny it with h6. Not strictly necessary, but clinical, snuffing out counterplay before it starts.

A neat realisation about the winning method — the king isn't even needed here. Recognise that the bishop and lone pawn together can't force the issue by themselves, so the plan is to manufacture more.

Roll out a second passer with the kingside pawns, and now two connected passed pawns backed by the bishop are more than enough force to march one home to promotion. Connected passers plus a piece is overwhelming.
The one thing to avoid is the careless push to h2 — that would let the king plant itself in front and blockade the pawns by hand. Keep the king out of the blockade and the pawns keep rolling.
The precise route is to insert the bishop check on e3 first, and only then advance the pawn toward promotion. The check gains the tempo that clears the path cleanly.

The fastest finish is to see that this promotion square is the mating square — under-promote to seal the king's escape and deliver mate, and since there are still spare pawn moves in reserve, there's no stalemate to worry about.

White's recapture leaves doubled pawns on e3 and e4. The old line that doubled pawns are always weaknesses is only half true — here they're dynamic, bracing the centre and enabling a knight to swing via h4 to f5.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns aren't automatically weak; when they control key squares they can be a strength.

notes.explains: g6 is prophylaxis — it takes the f5 square away from White's knight before the attack can even start.
notes.teaches: Spend a quiet pawn move to deny an enemy knight its target outpost.

notes.explains: f5 is the thematic break, prising the position open and handing us the g-file for a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: The f5 lever opens lines toward the king in these closed King's-Indian-style structures.

notes.explains: e4 rams forward, tearing more lines open toward the white king as the attack gathers force.
The king has been chased all the way up to h4 — a monarch this exposed simply gets mated, so drive it down without mercy.
notes.teaches: Once the enemy king is dragged into the open, switch entirely to the hunt.

notes.explains: Rxh3 is checkmate — the king-walk to h4 ends exactly where a king-hunt should.
The Queen's Gambit — and we mix it up.
Attacking has two forms — direct, or indirect, hitting the pieces that defend the target. The bishop to g4 pins the f3-knight, and that knight is a defender of d4.
We take on f3, wrecking White's pawn structure and weakening d4 further.
We play solidly with e6 — defending d5, since a premature capture on c4 would run into the d5 push and let White toss his knight around.
White develops the bishop to f4 — and note the knight jump to b5 is NOT a threat; it can be met several ways, so don't waste a move on a6.
teaches: reassess: Nb5 is not a real threat

notes.explains: Now the capture on c4 works — d5 is no longer a worry — and White will soon be left with a glaring weakness on d4.
Winning the pawn back, we recapture with the queen on d4, forcing the trade — with both white bishops hanging, White has no way to decline.
teaches: the Russian-schoolboy queen trade with hanging bishops

notes.explains: We're not out of the woods with our kingside undeveloped, so priority one is safety — castle short and take the sting out of any b5 tricks.
Even better, we castle long — it makes the king safe AND defends c7 against the bishop, one move doing two jobs.
teaches: a move that does two jobs

notes.explains: The Alapin — the pawn to c3 and then e4 against the Sicilian, and Black replies with the pawn to d5, an impressive choice at this level.
We capture on d5, the queen recaptures, and we play the pawn to d4, gaining the centre with tempo.
Black develops the knight to f6, we play the knight to f3 — a famous, well-studied theoretical position.
Black plays the pawn to e6 — a good move.
The knight to a3 — I've had this against grandmasters in serious games.
Black plays the pawn to a6 — one of the two best moves here.
The knight to c4. Now, how does Black defend the b6-square?

The knight to d7 — defending b6 while developing, and Black's next is likely the pawn to b5, chasing the knight from c4 and preparing the bishop to b7. This is exactly where opening books earn their keep: you look up what the authors recommend.
The bishop to e2 — the book's main line, squeezing the Sicilian.
Black captures on d4.
We recapture with the knight on d4. Now the queen grabbing g2 allows the bishop to f3 with a massive initiative.
After the queen takes g2, the bishop to f3 gives White huge compensation for the pawn.
The pawn to e4, c6 — we're facing the Caro-Kann. How dare he play something I play with Black.
d4. Against the Caro, for a sharp line we could play the Nimzowitsch, but the classic sharp way —
— the traditional, old-school way —
— is the Panov Attack: we take on d5, the Exchange Caro, a gateway to very peaceful lines —
— but the way to make it interesting and tactical, not to suggest the Exchange with the bishop to d3 isn't a great line —
— is c4, immediately contesting the centre. You're trying to get rid of the d5-pawn, and developing with an eye toward pressuring it.
The knight to f6.
The knight to c3, pressuring the pawn.
He takes it, so he relents — and this leads to one of the most well-studied, most famous structures of all time, the IQP.
The bishop takes c4 — the Isolated Queen's Pawn structure. Why is it called that?

Because there's a pawn on d4 and it's isolated — no neighboring pawns, no c-pawn, no e-pawn; we gave both up. Whether the IQP is good or bad depends entirely on the circumstances — that's the magic; it can be the reason you win the game or the reason you lose it. But the bishop to f5 is a mistake — a classic fork, the queen to b3 forking two pawns, and we take one.

The queen to b3, the knight to d7, the queen to b5, e6. We shouldn't go crazy — this is where a lot of people go off a cliff with the knight to b5 and c7; we haven't completed our development, particularly the kingside. Instead of anything rash, let's complete development mindfully — the bishop to f4 prevents the rook to b8, though he's not really threatening it, because we're going to take the a7-pawn.

We take the a7-pawn — careful the queen isn't trapped in a repetition as he chases it with the rook. He plays the rook to b4, hitting the bishop, which isn't scary at all: the bishop moves to b5, a great square protected by the knight, pinning his knight to his king while he's still undeveloped, and the rook on b4 is misplaced, so we threaten a3 to trap it. He plays the bishop to b8, and the queen to b7 is amazing because it pins the rook — a piece of higher value can x-ray a lower one, so if the rook goes to b3 it's undefended, and the knight takes with check exposes the attack on the rook. The queen takes d7 is bad, since the knight is defended by the other knight, and the bishop takes d7 would open the gates for his rook to come back — we want the gates closed. If he castles, we take his rook anyway. He plays the rook to b3, and the knight takes with check — check supersedes, we're not blundering the queen — and we take the rook; his queenside is gone. Now we castle and complete development. He builds a battery on h2, so rather than toy with it, we play g3 — weakening the light squares, yes, but we're up a rook and he has nothing on the kingside to do real damage — and it prepares the bishop to f4; the rule against pushing pawns in front of your king is overrated and needs moderation. The bishop to g4 attacks the knight, but instead of moving it we play the prepared bishop to f4, hitting his queen and getting our last piece out. Then we start trading everything on e5 — no more IQP; it's retired to the beaches. The bishop to f3 is delicate, because the queen to h3 would threaten mate on g2, so we deal with the bishop: the knight on b5 isn't really defending the king, so we drop it back to e2, heading to f4, which limits his queen to g4, and then h3 knocks the queen off its defense of the bishop. He takes, our king is perfectly safe, and we just push the pawn and win.
We answer e4 with c5 — the Sicilian. Pattern recognition comes with patience and enough puzzles; let's walk this line.
White plays the Alapin, c3, and we strike straight back with d5, refusing to let the c3-d4 setup roll over us.
White captures on d5, and instead of the usual queen recapture we play a knight to f6 — an underrated, aggressive gambit line I've had on my radar since I got crushed by it as a junior.
First question: what if White defends the extra pawn with c4? Then we play e6 — we need to dissolve that d5 pawn to unlock our compensation.
So e6, undermining d5. White pretty much has to capture on e6.
White takes on e6 and we recapture with the bishop, reaching a type of position we've seen before — a slightly improved version for White, but still practically unpleasant for him.
White develops the knight to f3, but the position still isn't appealing for him after a knight to c6.
A knight to c6, and our grip on the central squares makes it genuinely hard for White to untangle his pieces.

Where have we seen this? Against an f4 setup the right response is d5, then a capture and a knight to f6 — the same concept — and if White props it with c4, that pawn sticks out like a sore thumb. Same principles, even worse for White.
The pawn to e4, e5.
The knight to f3.
The knight to c6.

The bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez, also known as the Spanish, the most popular opening at the highest levels, around for over 500 years and named after a priest who extolled it in the 1500s. White develops a piece to do something — here the bishop pressures the knight, and since the knight defends the pawn, indirectly White pressures the pawn.
We follow the main line with a6, chasing the bishop away from b5. White must decide: take on c6 — the Exchange Variation — or drop the bishop back to a4.
The bishop takes c6 — a legitimate move. Aren't we blundering a pawn if White then grabs e5? It's actually a trap a lot of beginners miss. Which pawn do we recapture with?
The queen to d4 — to enable that, we have to recapture with the d-pawn. There's a rule to take toward the centre, but it's highly overrated; always weigh the pros and cons.

He knows not to take the pawn, and he castles. Now we have to do something about the e5-pawn, which is hanging — the knight takes e5 is a threat. Many ways to defend it: directly with f6 or the bishop to d6, or indirectly with the bishop to g4, pinning the knight. I'll play the old main line —
— f6, historically considered the most solid response to the Exchange Variation, even though it violates the basic rules of development.
d4. It makes Ben Finegold cringe, and where is the knight going to go —
So the best move, the one I just mentioned, is the bishop to g4 — pinning the knight, since behind it stands the more valuable queen, so the knight can't move.
c3 — also a good move, reinforcing the d4-pawn.
— most people play the bishop to d6, and that's what we play too, for solid, simple chess, though it's not the move I actually play over the board; I'll show that after.
The knight to d2 — our opponent continues developing well, and we should keep developing too.
We need to develop the knight from g8, our last piece preventing castling. The knight to h6 is awkward — you don't usually develop knights to the rim — so the knight to e7.
h3 — he's playing all the top theoretical moves. As a beginner there's a temptation to trade the knight on f3, but —
— there's no need: the bishop was pinning White's knight to the queen, a valuable bishop, so we simply drop it back to h5, preserving the pin. Retreating moves are never inherently bad.
It's perfectly acceptable. As a beginner you might fear g4 chasing that bishop away —
The pawns come off; we simply recapture with the f-pawn, and I think the queen to b3 is the theoretical move.
The knight to c4 — I already don't know the theory here, but it's also very good.

Let's figure out this position. There's no problem — we just castle, and we're not blundering our bishop, because the c7-pawn guards the bishop on d6. By castling we exert more pressure on the knight on f3, still pinning it. But the queen to b3 is a very powerful move: it sets up an x-ray against our king and unpins the knight, which can now move without fear of losing White's queen. Our top priority is to deal with that x-ray, which in many cases leads to a discovered check — White threatens the knight takes d6 with a devastating check.

There's nothing wrong with the opponent's reversed-French idea in itself, but this bishop sortie is a mistake — it develops a bishop before a knight and does nothing to stake a claim in the centre. That leaves the door open to seize the middle with tempo.
So grab the centre with gain of time — d5 both plants a pawn in the middle and slaps the bishop, forcing it to react.

The tempting continuation is to keep grabbing space with another pawn, but centre control is a balance — pawns on one hand, and on the other, not overreaching and not neglecting development. Whole openings exist to lure you into overextending until the pawns crumble. So develop instead: the knight to f6 shores up the centre.

The bishop's ideal home is d6 — it braces the e-pawn, and if the opponent castles short it sets up a later pawn thrust with Greek-gift and attacking ideas. But it can't go there just yet, and knowing why is the key.

The obstacle is a capture on d5 winning the pawn — so play c6 first, defending with a pawn, building a chain, and clearing the way for the bishop. A pawn defended by a pawn is always a healthy structure.

And don't fret that c6 takes the natural square from the other knight — the idea that knights must live on c6 and f6 is beginner's lore. Routing a knight to d7 is no tragedy. Those are the conventional posts, usually the best, but chess is a game of trade-offs; a slightly inferior placement doesn't mean a bad position.

The knight leap to g5 looks aggressive but achieves nothing here — its whole purpose is normally to hit f7, and f7 simply isn't a target in this position. There's a solid way to treat it that doesn't even involve reacting.

Rather than shooing the knight, just castle and ignore it. A piece sitting deep in your half isn't automatically a threat — often it's an asset, a stranded horse with nothing to do. Getting the king safe matters more than swatting at a bluff.

Here the intruder becomes an asset. The opponent's central push is premature with pieces scattered — and holding the h-pawn move in reserve pays off, because the moment the knight is finally kicked, the overextended e4-pawn is left attacked twice and defended only once. Reserving that move for the right moment wins more than playing it on reflex.

Don't overthink the recapture — taking the knight to wreck the structure is double-edged, since it also cracks open a file that could rebound. Just take the pawn simply. The wider lesson: when you're agonising over whether to grab a piece, often the best practical answer is to not take it and find a clean alternative, sparing yourself the time and the second-guessing.

That rook move leaves the king stranded in the centre — and notice the whole queenside is still untouched, which means the queen is boxed in with almost no scope. A trapped king and a smothered queen are exactly the cues to pounce on.

The exploitation is straightforward — the bishop swings to g4 and hits the queen, which has no squares to run to. The opponent is reduced to an ugly retreat or a weakening pawn move just to give it air.

If the pawn shields the queen, capture it — the recapture then robs the knight of its own pawn's support, and everything starts to fall. This is all coming from sensible developing moves, no fireworks required.
The queen falls and the game is over — a whole attack built out of nothing but healthy development and centre control.

This game illustrates how bad f5 is across most openings — it opens the king's diagonal and permanently weakens the kingside. The Dutch is the one exception, and only because White hasn't touched the e-pawn, so that diagonal stays closed; even so, against d4 it's dubious and the Staunton Gambit is no joke.
notes.teaches: f5 is only sound when the e-file diagonal to your king is still closed; otherwise it's a lasting weakness.

notes.explains: So we answer with e4, the Staunton Gambit — a pawn for a big lead in development and open lines against the loosened king.
Nxe5 snaps the pawn, and this is the recurring nightmare of an early f-pawn push: the king is bare to Qh5-check ideas, and a knight sacrifice on e5 opens the floodgates.
notes.teaches: An early ...f5/...f6 invites Nxe5 and Qh5+ — the same king-hunt that refutes the Damiano.

notes.explains: Bc4 looks like it's biting on nothing, but it threatens Nf7 — and Black is so far behind in development that almost any sacrifice lands.
notes.teaches: Against an undeveloped king, aim at f7 and trust that the sacrifices will work.

notes.explains: Nxd5 sacrifices a knight to blow open the h5-e8 line for a check on h5 — with the king this exposed, material is a secondary concern.
notes.teaches: Sacrifice to open the checking line at a stuck king; the initiative outweighs the piece.

notes.explains: Now the motifs cascade: with a knight near the king, g6 fails to the capture; take the pawn rather than the rook to keep the attack; and Be6-check sets up a winning discovery or skewer. The king gets driven to the queenside and hunted down.
notes.teaches: In a king-hunt, prefer the move that keeps the attack flowing over the one that grabs material.

notes.explains: A standard Italian — pieces out, bishop on c4 eyeing f7.
When your opponent is shuffling pawns and you're ahead in development, the rule is to open the center — so we strike with d4.
teaches: open the center when you lead in development

notes.explains: Pushing to d5 instead is the mistake: it closes the center, which cancels out your development lead — a closed position lets the lagging side catch up — and it also shuts in your own bishop.
teaches: a closed center wastes a development lead

notes.explains: I'm in the mood for a Sicilian — e4, c5.
The bishop to c4 — of course not a first-rate move; there's nothing inherently wrong with it, and White can follow up in a variety of ways, like the knight to f3 or c3.
You don't want to commit to a setup too early, so I don't love g6 this early — you want a development move that gives maximum flexibility, and in my view that's the knight to c6, the most open-ended.
f4, transposing into some strange Grand Prix attack, with the bishop having been committed a little too early to c4. So how can
we exploit the premature development of White's bishop to c4? We play e6 — an idea we'd quite possibly play even if the bishop weren't on c4.
The knight to f3.
And we go d5 with tempo — so the bishop looks really, really dumb here.
e-takes-d5, e-takes-d5.

And the bishop to b3. A lot of you would be very tempted to play b5 here — but the problem is that White has ways to defend: you're not going to trap the bishop, because White can play c3 or a3, and I'm not a huge fan of overplaying the queenside like that. It's a lot more important to get your kingside pieces out than to try to trap the bishop and play for gimmicks.
So as unsexy as this move may seem, I like the idea of just developing — the knight to f6.

Now we have a slightly sexier way of developing. Some of you know the rook to e1 is an idea for White, so you could get the bishop out to e7 first, so the rook to e1 isn't a check, and then castle. But to play very ambitiously — remember that just because a move isn't effective in one position doesn't mean you shouldn't consider it in another. When White pushes the f-pawn, one of its main weaknesses is that it creates
vulnerability down the a7-g1 diagonal. So how do I exploit that? I can't play the bishop to c5 with check, but I can play c4, and you might think the intention
is then to get the bishop out to c5 with check — but let's not hurry. You could also play the queen to b6 with check; both moves are fun, but there's a tactic if you take the queen-to-b6 idea

and apply it in a much more dangerous way. This is an amazing tactic — you don't start with the queen to b6, you start with b5, and the idea is that after the bishop takes b5, you fork the bishop and the king with the queen to b6 with check. I didn't even see

this initially — when our opponent castled, at first I saw c4 with the bishop-to-c5 idea, but this is amazing. And now, if you want to take it to the next level, how should we deal with the knight to e5?
This is really cool — we can give the queen to b6 with check and then take on a4; but if you really want to rub it in your opponent's face, we can just take on a4.
The knight takes c6, and the queen to b6 with check first — using the same tactic to pick off the knight.

It's important in such a position not to rest on your laurels — a lot of people win a piece and then get very disoriented. There are essentially two ways to think here: one is to play it very safe, just get your bishop out and castle, and there's nothing wrong with that; but if you want to play for maximum, consider a move like the knight to e4 — the knight to g4 is also very interesting, and then the bishop to c5, with ideas of developing a smothered mate.

Between the knight to e4 and the knight to g4, I like the knight to e4 more, because it also closes the e-file, so White can't defend the f2-square with check — he can still defend f2 with his queen, but not with check — and this arrangement creates all sorts of tactical concepts. The bishop to g4 is an interesting idea: the bishop to g4, the queen takes g4, and we're very close to the queen to g1 with check, and if the rook takes g1 there's mate on f2 — but after the bishop to g4, the queen to g4, the queen to g1, there's the king takes. So you set it up: h5 to prepare the bishop to g4, or, more elegantly, the bishop to c5, which also prepares the bishop to g4 — and I think we win precisely that way. He plays h3 — a good move — but now we can take it to the next level: since we haven't castled yet, we can use that to our advantage with h5, and now the bishop to g4 is a threat, because after h-takes-g4 you recapture with the h-pawn, which is a check against the king, essentially checkmate. And there we go, the bishop to g4 — a total beatdown; that's why you need an opening repertoire at this rating. The queen to e3 is a nice move I honestly didn't see, but let's decline the draw; our instinct here should be to simplify. The moment he played h3, you should have noted that the g3-square is now a weakness — so in your mind, if the queen ever moves away from f3, there's a fork on g3. Combining that observation with this position, the simplest is just to take the queen and then deliver a nice little fork on g3 — we'll be up a rook, and the rest is really easy.

Because the fianchetto setup doesn't immediately challenge the centre, there's no need to rush e6. Instead — exactly as in the Caro-Kann — develop the bishop to f5 first, getting it outside the pawn chain before the e-pawn shuts it in.
Only now does e6 go in, with the light-squared bishop already breathing free air outside the chain. It's an ideal, harmonious structure — everything developed to its best square.
A useful little move — h6 grants the bishop a bolt-hole on h7, so that any lunge at it with a knight to h4 is rendered completely harmless before it ever happens.

The knight to c3 is a familiar inaccuracy at this level — it blocks the c-pawn's path to c4, its most natural challenge to the centre. That leaves the centre as solid as it gets, with the c5 lever held in reserve.
Now castle — and note there's no real threat to the centre: it's defended three times while attacked only twice. Counting the guards against the attackers is what tells you a threat is empty.
And there's the knight lunge — which is precisely why the little luft move went in earlier. The bishop simply steps to h7, unbothered.

The central break is a genuine idea, opening things up. The plainest reply is to swap everything off on e4, which strips away the fianchetto bishop and leaves the enemy king a touch draughty — but there's a sharper sequence worth finding.

The cleverness rests on the fact that the recapturing knight is itself loose. Snap on e4, and after the recapture an in-between capture on h4 wrecks the opponent's pawns while staying a pawn ahead. Order the captures right and the extra material comes with a ruined enemy structure.

There's no obligation to capture on e4 at all — allowing a rook to sit there, ready to swing across for a kingside lift, is unpleasant. Since the bishop isn't truly threatened, a calm recapture keeps everything sound.
The Zen move is the knight to c6 — the tempting pawn advance would just blunder the rook. Same central idea, but a developing move instead of a loosening one.

For the small price of doubled pawns comes an opposite-coloured-bishop middlegame — and those famously favour the attacker, because the defender's bishop can never guard the squares under fire. The knight recapture even forks a pair of pawns as a bonus.
Now the window: the opponent's bishop still isn't out, so the king is under-defended. There's a small chance to strike — pry the centre open at any cost and the lagging development gets punished.

f5 is more forcing than the quieter break — it drives the rook off its square. If it retreats along the file the centre push wins; if it captures, a knight recapture hits it back with a discovered check lurking behind. Every branch keeps a threat attached.
The point that makes it work: the enemy queen is undefended, so the pawn can't be taken. That single loose piece is what powers the whole combination.
And this is exactly why speed matters — the moment the bishop finally develops, the queen is guarded, the discovered attack evaporates, and the tactics are gone. Urgency is the whole idea.
No need for anything fancy — bring the last rook into the game and set up an x-ray against the queen. Quietly improving the idle piece is what converts.

The knight jumps to b3, hitting the rook in the corner. And a safety check first — scan whether the enemy queen can reach a square that hits g7 for a mate threat; it can't, so the plan is clean. Always confirm the opponent has no counter-mate before committing.

The finish looks like a slip — a couple of pieces hang — but sharp vision reveals a forced mate. It begins with the rook, not the queen: if the knight is taken, the queen crashes into e4 for checkmate. Trust the calculation over the material count.
Against a strong opponent, reach for something you're comfortable in — the Jobava London: Nc3 with Bf4, still effective at this level and not deeply known.
We answer with the pedestrian e3, and note Black still has Bf5 or c5 available.
Rather than the g4 sideline, we keep it strictly positional and start with Bd3.
After Bd6 we face a choice, and one option is out: Bxd6 is bad because cxd6 hands Black a broad central pawn mass. Bg3 is the usual retreat.
notes.teaches: Don't trade into a recapture that gifts your opponent a central pawn majority.

notes.explains: But there's nothing to fear if Black takes on f4 — after exf4 the doubled f-pawns actually increase our central control. Think of it as a reverse Maroczy bind, clamping the e5 square.
notes.teaches: Doubled f-pawns from an exf4 recapture bind e5 and boost central control — welcome them, don't avoid them.

notes.explains: Both sides castle and often maneuver around the two bishops staring each other down; Black's ...Bxf4 with a timely c5 is a fine equalizer that strikes at the bind.
Now the heart of London and Jobava play: plant the Pillsbury knight on e5. It's a superb piece in its own right, and it clears a path for the other pieces to join an attack.
notes.teaches: The e5 knight is the London's engine — a dominant outpost that opens lines for the heavy pieces.

notes.explains: The maneuver to know: Qf3, then swing to h3 to bear down on h7. The pawn is guarded by the f6-knight, but that knight is far from invulnerable — and from g3 the queen can x-ray instead.
notes.teaches: Route the queen f3-h3 to pressure h7; then look for ways to remove its knight defender.

notes.explains: The Smith-Morra accepted — we recapture with the knight on c3, trading a pawn for a big lead in development and open lines.
teaches: the Smith-Morra: a pawn for development

notes.explains: The knight to f6 is a very common mistake here — it forgets about White's next move.
e5 kicks the f6-knight and drives it all the way home with tempo.
The bishop to c4 follows, and Black is essentially lost already — badly behind for no reason.
Here's the important point. If Black sets up soundly with d6, what should White actually do?
The answer is: nothing flashy — just castle. There's no need for Bxf7 or taking on d6, which only helps Black untangle. Simply improve, because the tactics defend themselves.
teaches: restraint: castle and let the position work

notes.explains: And if Black grabs with the knight on e5 — that loses the queen.
The check on f7 followed by taking the queen on d8 is the drill: the bishop sacrifice wins the queen outright.
White again — the pawn to e4, e5.
The knight to f3.
The knight to c6 — finally, more main lines.
The knight to c3 —
— the knight to f6, g3 — a main-line Glek.
The bishop to c5, the bishop to g2 — we've faced this before.
The bishop to g2.
The move order isn't essential here — you can start by castling or by playing d3, virtually interchangeable. I'll play d3.
Our opponent plays the bishop to e6 —
— which doesn't really impact what we do; we castle.
The queen to d7. This particular system isn't very common at the top —
— where people generally castle kingside. The rook to e1, the queen to d8, the king to h1.
The bishop back to c8 — both sides castle kingside, and we get a more positional battle.

This may seem scary to less experienced Glek players — you might imagine Black playing the bishop to h3, running the h-pawn down the board, castling queenside, and checkmating us. But there are many ways to fight this, and Black's position has more holes than it looks. The knight to a4 should always be on your radar as long as Black hasn't pushed the a-pawn — that's why top players play a5 or a6. But here I don't love the knight to a4: it does nothing against the bishop to h3, and if we trade on c5 Black clamps down on d4. The knight to g5 I also dislike, because of the bishop to g4, and f3 would be illegal.

The knight to g5 with the bishop to g4 just fails concretely, since Black plays h6 and we've achieved nothing. The move I like, which may surprise you, is the bishop to g5 — largely a positional move.
Our opponent walks right into it, playing the bishop to h3 against everything.
What's the point of the bishop to g5? Very simple — we want the bishop takes f6 —
— completely hamstringing Black's ability to generate any kingside pawn play. Things get much worse — Black is borderline losing.
Notice the king and queen sit on forkable squares, so the move is automatic — the knight to d5 — and suddenly Black is in huge trouble.
Black castles queenside, still playing instantly, but that doesn't make his moves any better.
We could take on h3 and on f6, but that makes no sense — just start by taking on f6, a free pawn.

The queen to e6, the only move. Now we pause: is there a forced win, or do we just drop the knight back to d5 and stabilize? The knight to g5 is bad — the queen takes f6, and after the check the king steps away, leaving that knight awkward. The other option is the bishop takes h3, the queen takes h3, then the knight to g5, nearly trapping the queen with only h6 — but I don't see a clear follow-up, since both knights hang.
I've emphasized the power of a simple move: when a line is very messy, consider avoiding it with a simple alternative — the knight back to d5.
Our opponent completely ignores all the threats we've been creating —
— and walks right into the knight to g5. It worked like a charm, and Black resigns.
I'm going to play b3, the Nimzowitsch-Larsen. e5.
The bishop to b2.
The knight to c6 — the first moment where there are several possible variations. Today I'll play it traditionally. Does anybody know the traditional main line here?
The move is e3 — and as with all hypermodern openings, the point is not to control the centre with pawns, it's to get your pieces out and put immediate pressure on Black's centre.
We got this bishop out to b2 — where does it belong? An obvious question
with an obvious answer: b5, attacking the knight that defends the e5-pawn.

Black can get in big trouble here really quickly if he's not super careful — he could just lose a pawn. The bishop to d6 is a pretty famous line that can end very badly. Notice this opens a potential x-ray on the g7-pawn if we ever capture with the bishop — so if the e-pawn moves or disappears, we may win a lot of material by taking on g7. So the knight to f3 looks really good,

very natural — but Black can actually play f6 and make a pawn chain that makes the e5-pawn very hard to pressure. So we have to use our pawns — this idea occurs in many fianchetto openings: we attack the pawn with our pawn, more immediate pressure than a knight. Black has an unenviable choice: if he takes, after the bishop takes g7 he has a check on h4, but it's not scary, we just move our king and he has no initiative; f6 is considered better but still doesn't solve all his problems — we trade, open the f-file, and the knight to f3 becomes a lot stronger. That's the logic behind f4: you push the pawn out, it's untouchable, and pawns are the best way to pressure other pawns.
The queen to e7 is also possible, but then the knight to f3. The queen to h4 with check,
which obviously we block with g3.
The queen to e7 — I think this is actually the best line for White. Now, do we want to take the pawn? Is that premature?

It's definitely premature to take — that defeats the whole purpose, which is to pressure the pawn by trading it, and it gives Black a get-out-of-jail-free card. So obviously we just develop, the knight to f3.

The bishop to g4, a good move. There are a couple of ways to approach this, but we need to calculate. The first option is to deal with the annoying pin — we can't castle, because e4 becomes a potential problem, and even if Black gives up g7 we don't want to give this knight away — so we can play h3, essentially forcing the bishop to capture the knight, since it would be trapped on h5; the downside is that the knight was pressuring the e5-pawn. What's the second option? Not d3 — he still plays e4; the bishop to e2 is way too passive, and I wouldn't

move this bishop away, it's pressuring the knight. The other move is f-takes-e5. Now, didn't I just say that was a bad move? The situation has changed — it was bad earlier because Black could recapture with the bishop
and take the sting out of our bishop; here it's a lot more complicated, because after f-takes-e5, the bishop takes e5,

we play the bishop takes e5, and he's unable to recapture with the knight — so this carries a lot more weight now that the knight is on f3. Again, just because a move is bad in one position doesn't mean it's bad in another; you have to evaluate and reevaluate captures on every move, because the circumstances may have changed. What should Black do after the bishop takes e5? He should take the knight with the bishop; we respond by taking the bishop, and the queen recaptures — but we've forced him to give away his strongest piece, so White is still slightly better; that's the only move.

The bishop takes f3 immediately — really interesting. One of the most important things in chess is not to assume that two different move orders lead to the same conclusion. When you've calculated something and your opponent makes a different first move, always ask whether this gives you any other options — and even if the answer is no, it's worth thinking about. Here, you don't have to take this bishop; you can take the other bishop, not only attacking the queen but, most importantly, opening up the pressure on g7. So let's calculate: the pawn takes the bishop,

the bishop takes the queen, the pawn takes the queen — and it's in fact a double attack: we're attacking the bishop on d1, and we're threatening that old bishop-takes-g7 idea. But Black has an additional move — the queen to e4 is the most testing, and it may seem White is losing, because Black forks the queen and the rook. Both queens are hanging and the bishop is hanging, so if he takes the pawn we take the bishop,

if he takes the queen we take his queen; and g7 is also hanging — it's good to keep a mental tab of everything that's hanging. After the queen to e4, there are two approaches: move our queen, the queen to c1 — but I don't like it, he takes the rook, and even though we could take on g7 and recover it, I'm really afraid for our king, since we won't be able to castle short. A lot of you have the right general idea — counterattack his vulnerable queen. What about d3? Pawn moves weaken other pawns, and d3 gets mated after the queen takes e3. We could try the bishop to d3, but

as I said, if possible I don't want to move that bishop away from b5, it's an important bishop. Are there any other pieces that could attack Black's queen? Look around — the knight to c3 is a very important resource, counterattacking the queen: the bishop takes d1, the knight takes e4, and now the bishop is hanging, the knight is hanging, and the g7-pawn is hanging, so we don't even have to recapture the bishop — we take on g7, up the exchange. A nice move, but not hard to find if you know what to look for. We could play the in-between d7, but I'm not sure ruining castling is worth giving up this pawn — in an endgame you might see g7 hanging and the pawn threatening to take on c7, and if the queens trade we'll regret d7 and bringing Black's king closer to the centre. He takes e4 — should we take the bishop? We should play the bishop to g7, although taking the bishop would have been amazing too, two pawns up with two great bishops; but we win the exchange here, because Black won't get anything for that rook. The best he can do is the bishop to f3; we move the rook and take on h8 — the bishop takes c2 isn't scary, it's just a pawn — the bishop takes h8, the bishop to f3. Now, what's the sexy move? Castling. Castling is legal when the rook is attacked — it's only illegal when there's a check; people often assume they can't castle when the rook is attacked, but that's not true, and you should, because it coordinates the rooks and the king is very safe. f6 — Black tries to trap our bishop, and to extricate it we need to be creative. First, a good check — the bishop has done its job, so let's give the check and create pressure against the knight. The king probably goes to g6, because going back would sever the connection of the rook and bishop. Now ask what Black's next move will be: the knight to h6, not to g7 because there's a pawn on d6. The drawback of the knight to h6? If we're losing our bishop anyway, we might as well give it up for a pawn — so we can take on f6. Say it's Black to move: the knight to h6, the bishop takes f6, the king takes f6 — then a rook is pinning the bishop on f3, but the pin isn't effective, because a pawn on e4 guards the bishop and our pawns are too far advanced to attack it. But pawns can be dismantled, so the best move is d3, so that after the knight to h6, the bishop takes f6, the king takes f6, we play d-takes-e4 and the bishop is lost. The bishop to d5 might have been even better — I completely missed that — but this isn't a long line; I saw d3 quickly because of the idea of taking on f6, and d3 follows logically, because you have to dismantle the defender of the bishop to win it. We've succeeded in getting the bishop out of f3, so pounce: take the knight, take the pawn, we've extricated our bishop, we're up the exchange, and the game is essentially over. He resigns; it's resignable.
d4, the knight to f6 — the King's Indian Defense.
c4, g6 — because I feel like playing it.
The knight to c3 — very much a King's Indian.
The bishop to g7.
f4 — the Four Pawns Attack, one of the most dangerous and most underrated lines for White; you'll get blown off the board with Black if you don't know virtually all the theory.
We begin by castling.
The knight to f3. Historically I've played two moves here — one is the rare line where Black goes e5 anyway.
e5 — it sounds totally absurd, but it's very possible: an underestimated sideline that throws a lot of players off immediately.
The f-pawn takes e5.
The d-pawn takes e5.
White plays the knight takes e5 — not very advisable. Why? We need to induce weaknesses in White's centre, and a move like the rook to e8 threatens nothing, so —

— we use our pawns: the typical King's Indian move c5. My theoretical knowledge ends here, so now we're on our own. The point of c5 is to force the d4-pawn to move; the knight in the centre is x-rayed by the bishop and vulnerable to the rook to e8 and the knight takes c4, so we must make it undefended at all costs.

d5 is totally reasonable. A fork in the road: to win the pawn back we can take on e4 — the knight takes c4, the knight takes e4, then a check on h4 forces the knight back and we recapture on e5 with a nice position —

— or the traditional idea, the rook to e8, throwing the knight off e5 and building immediate pressure down the e-file. Let's play the rook to e8 and develop massive pressure before White castles kingside.
The knight to f3.
The knight takes e4.
The knight takes e4, the rook takes e4 with check.
The bishop to e2. We've recaptured on e4. White wants to castle kingside next; if he does, our whole e-file strategy has failed, so we must prevent castling at all costs.

We can do it without sacrificing, using our queen: the queen to e8, which is better than e7, where the queen is vulnerable to d6 and to the bishop to g5 with tempo. The queen to e8 prevents castling — if White castles he loses the bishop. His best is probably the king to f2; then we develop the light-squared bishop to g4, and the dark-squared bishop eyes d4.

I wouldn't put the bishop on d4 just yet — the knight on f3 could take it — but one idea is the bishop to g4, trading for the knight, then the other bishop to d4, maybe with check if the king lands on f2. The knight to g5 — an ambitious move chasing the rook off the e-file to guarantee castling. Two options: the rook to d4 with tempo then the bishop to g4, or the rook takes c4 exploiting the pin, winning a pawn but allowing castling.

The rook to d4 is the move if you want to go for checkmate; the rook takes c4 is the materialistic option. We're going for the throat in the spirit of the King's Indian, so the rook to d4. Then the queen to b3: if we play the bishop to g4 prematurely, White has the queen to b3 and e3, throwing our queen off e8 — the battle still revolves around preventing castling. The no-frills option is h6, the knight to f3, then the rook back to e4 to re-establish the pin, and only then the bishop to g4 — less calculation than the bishop to g4 at once. The a5-a4-a3 push putting pressure on b2 is standard but a bit slow; our attention stays on the e-file: prevent castling, drive the king out, induce the king to f2, then go for the throat. If White castles the game simply goes on — our structure is sound. Then the bishop to b3 is a bad panic move, because it lets Black get two pieces for a rook, crushing in the middlegame: we take the knight, achieve our dream of the bishop to d4, prevent castling, and stand up big material. Now the bishop to g4; b2 hangs, but we keep hammering down the e-file. We can take on e2 with a fork. Then the queen to b7, and the quiet knight to d7 opens the connection between our queen and rook to defend it — the bishop takes the rook also wins. If White plays the rook to e1, we have the intermezzo the bishop to e3 with check; then the rook takes d4, choosing the rook that gives us a passed pawn and the check on e3 that ends it.

The defining feature of this anti-hippo setup is to hold the c6 square for a pawn rather than a knight, and pair it with the bishop on d6. The move order is elastic — c6 then the bishop, or the bishop first, or castle in between; it all transposes.
The whole point of c6 is to build a pawn chain, so that when the opponent fianchettoes, the long-diagonal bishop bites on granite — pointing straight into a wall of pawns with nothing to attack.

Now the knight question: rather than blocking the bishop, the knight is routed the long way — to d7 and then around by f8 to g6 — so the bishop's diagonal stays clear. Reaching g6 just needs one preparatory move first.

That preparation is a flexible rook move to e8 — it reinforces the centre and keeps the options open while it's still unclear how the opponent will arrange the kingside. When you don't yet know the plan, make the move that commits to nothing and helps regardless.

The pawn thrust turns this into a hippo on steroids, and it demands care — the natural knight development to d7 would let the knight get trapped by a further pawn push to g5. The earlier rook move wasn't perfectly accurate against this, so a different route is needed.
So the knight takes the odd-looking road out to a6, heading back toward the centre via c7 and later e6. A route around the edge beats a developing square that walks into a trap.

The plan now unfolds in full: throw in a5 to grab queenside space and discourage the opponent from castling long — and if they do go long, the other knight drops back to d7, which is exactly why that square was kept free. The kingside pawns are no cause for fear. Then a knight comes to the fine central c5 square, unbothered by pawn pokes, and the follow-up c7–e6–f4 lands a knight on prime real estate. A knight planted on f4 almost always breeds a tactic — hunt the loose pieces and a jump to d3 appears, winning a pawn, shattering the queenside pawn cover and forcing the king to move all at once. And the finishing lesson: don't play automatically. The obvious recapture is there, but look for the better move — a quiet bishop to g4 wins the queen outright.
The pawn to e4, e5 — a pretty high-rated opponent, which is fine with me.
The bishop to c4 — the Bishop's Opening, intimidating to many; it's the opening where White develops the bishop first.
React no differently than against the Vienna: since White didn't play the knight to f3, we don't need to start with the knight to c6 — we play the knight to f6, exploiting that.
d3 — again, many possible schemes of development.
There's a line with c6, which I won't play; the simplest is just to develop the other knight with the knight to c6.
After the knight to f3 we've transposed into an Italian; with the bishop to c5 it's a full Italian, or we can play the bishop to e7, slightly more passive.
I'll play the bishop to e7 — perfectly viable, and we're playing very solid; some practice in these dry positions.
The knight to c3. We can play d6 or castle — the order really doesn't matter.
Let's go d6 and then castle.
h3, and we castle — the Hungarian Variation: quite passive but extremely solid, no weaknesses, relatively symmetrical.
White's bishops are marginally better placed, but we'll try to neutralize that. We have one undeveloped piece left — would the bishop to e6 be justified? Is that trade something to fear?

In Italian positions, opening the f-file is generally good for the side that controls it, even at the cost of doubled pawns. So the bishop to e6 is rarely a move to refrain from over the bishop takes c6 — never dangerous; after the recapture our doubled e-pawns control important squares, and we get free f-file pressure. The other advantage: if White continues the standoff, we don't have to take on c4 —
— we can actually break through in the centre with d5, gaining space. A tough situation for White — and he takes.
We take, and I already like Black's position here.

One comment: White isn't castled yet — we need to be prepared for castling in either direction. Many good approaches: the queen to e8, aiming for g6 if he castles short; or more ambitiously a6 to prepare a pawn storm if he castles queenside; and if he castles kingside, a6 is still a helpful move.

d5 is probably what I'd play over the board, but for solid style, a6 — flexible, it doesn't hurt to control b5, and if he castles queenside we jump-start our pawn storm with b5. If he castles short, we'll have clear ways to pressure down the file.

a5 would weaken b5. g4 is a blunder — it drops a pawn. Instructive: two ways to win it immediately. The knight on f3 is left undefended — this screams discovery tactic; there are two: the knight takes g4, or the knight takes e4.

After the knight takes g4 and the pawn recaptures, we open the h-file for him — not advisable, since he'll probably castle queenside. Much better to take the centre pawn: we open no avenues on his kingside. He takes, we take the knight on f3.

It's a good idea to make sure your rook doesn't get trapped on f3 — but with the whole f-file, we have nothing to fear, and we're up a pawn. After any pawn trade, ask how the position changed: with the e-pawn gone, the move d5 becomes much stronger.

d5 looks extremely appealing — it sends the knight back, and then d4 might trap the bishop on e3; d5 is our default reaction. The bishop to g5 — d5 still looks great: he'll take the bishop, we recapture with the queen —
— chasing the knight out of the centre. I see no reason to refrain; takes, takes, then we bring the other rook to f8.
Already very depressing for White — the knight to d4 was also great. He takes.
We take, obviously with the queen. This'll go the knight to g5, further exacerbating the situation.
I'd love to reroute the knight to f4, but it's very hard, since e6 is blocked by a pawn. Where does the rook go? A lot of people default to the rook to f8, but don't rush to bring the rook back —

— notice the queen defends the knight; our queen pressures it, and the rook to f4 slices off the connection — the knight is simply trapped. He's got to go h4, giving up another pawn, and White's position collapses.

If he goes h4, another interesting moment. The obvious rook takes g4 opens the g-file — he'd likely castle and seek counterplay, though the g-file alone is unlikely to be enough for two pawns — but an idea is h6 first, kicking the knight, then take on g4, dulling his kingside initiative.
We also have a third approach — we don't have to touch any of that; play the knight to d4, or more incisive, the rook from a8 to f8. The knight to f4 isn't going anywhere.
— then we take c2, a common queen fork at the end of a line, like a famous game. c4 does a whole lot of bad — first, it permanently weakens the d4-square —

— so I love the idea of slamming the knight into d4. We can still play the rook takes f2, nothing wrong with that, but now we can squeeze a lot more by bringing our pieces to dominant squares; pawns don't go backwards, so he can never chase us from d4. We threaten h6 followed by the knight to f3 with a fork. The queen takes g5 is a decent winning endgame, but play to win economically — h6 chases the knight; don't be fancy just to force liquidation, find the most efficient win.
If he castles, we take f2 with a devastating second-rank attack. I like that we still have a pawn on a6 from a past life. The rook to h3 doesn't substantively change anything —
— we can still go h6; in fact the knight is now simply trapped, which is kind of funny. This might be resigns.
The knight takes e6.
We keep the knight on d4 and take with the queen. Resigning is a very good option here.
He takes on d5. We can take g4 or take d5 — it absolutely doesn't matter, as long as we're taking something.
Let's take g4 — that seems more incisive, hitting the rook, and if the rook to g3, we have a nice tactic to finish the game.
The rook to g3. What's important is that the knight is taking a square away from the king —
— that's the second ingredient, with our doubled rooks and queen: the queen takes g3 ends the game, the rook to f1 being checkmate.
He castles — let's just take on f2.
The queen takes f2 — we could have taken the rook, but —
— this simplifies the position.
The Ruy Lopez — Bb5 pins nothing yet but leans on the knight that guards e5, the classic pressure opening.
Here's the endgame reality: even with an extra pawn and a mass of doubled pawns, opposite-coloured bishops make it very hard to win, because the two bishops never fight for the same squares.
notes.teaches: Opposite-coloured-bishop endings are drawish even a pawn up; the bishops can't challenge each other.

notes.explains: The right winning idea in this kind of ending isn't to grind pawns — it's to attack. Pushing g4 and h5 to open the king and play for mate uses the extra piece where a pawn count never will.
notes.teaches: In an opposite-bishop position, convert by attacking the king, not by counting pawns.

notes.explains: So g4 goes in — commit to the attack rather than shuffle, and open lines toward the king while the chance is there.
The Jobava London — the queen's pawn paired with an early knight to c3 and the bishop bound for f4, a sharp, tricky setup.
The bishop comes to f4, and against Black's c5 we hold the center calmly with e3.
Here's the recurring idea worth knowing: the knight to a4, jabbing at the black queen on c5. It nudges the queen around and, in some lines, actually snares it.
The queen is driven to a5, and we can probe again — a maneuver that repeats and, at the right moment, wins the queen outright.

One general warning this line teaches: never lean on a pin alone to keep your queen safe. If the pinning piece can be distracted, the queen is hanging the instant it happens, and you bleed tempi trying to save it.
teaches: don’t rely on a pin to shield the queen

notes.explains: We're playing a strong opponent — let's go e4 this time, and he plays the Modern.
the bishop to g7.
We've already faced the Modern a lot of times — the knight to c3.
My favourite system of development is to develop this bishop to e3,
the point being that we want to keep our centre nicely protected.
a6 prepares b5; a4 here is possible.
There are several ways to play — we could play a4 and stop b5, but we're actually going to allow it. The queen to d2.
b5 is annoying, but not as annoying as it may appear.
We're going to play h4 and start attacking the kingside.
Now, what's the drawback of h5 — he stops us from playing h5 ourselves, but
what's the drawback of this move? First of all, we need f3 to support this pawn. The drawback is that it
weakens g5 — and that's exactly what we're going to exploit: we go the knight to h3 and
the knight to g5, sinking our knight into the weak square he's just created.
Now we need to complete our development,
but we need to do it very carefully, so we're actually going to castle long first, to see how he develops — that helps us understand where to put our bishop.
The queen to e7. What's a good follow-up to castling that I've played a couple of times?
The king can be improved from c1 — a move like the king to b1 is a very good follow-up to

castling long, because the king is just safer there, away from the c-file. Now, what Black is preparing here is c5 — so if we put our bishop on d3 we obstruct our own control of the file and help him play c5, which I don't want. But there's a really cool idea we
could try to apply instead. This knight on c3 can be improved — a typical idea in these positions: we lead the knight to e2, and try to go to
f4, which has its own dangers. He goes c5 sort of automatically, and we
can go the knight to f4 — a very thematic and typical manoeuvre, worth remembering. He can play c-takes-d4 and e5, but I anticipated that; I don't think it actually works.
c-takes-d4, the bishop takes d4. The reason for e5 — I actually
blundered. The bishop to c3 was my idea, because he can't take — but what I blundered was the move b4. The good thing is that because of how I've played it, we can actually sacrifice the piece

and I think we have very legitimate compensation. Let's see if he finds b4 — after the knight to d5 he'll just take on d5 and then take the bishop; he doesn't find b4. We don't actually have to move this knight, but we will.
The d5-square is extremely weak, so we're going to occupy it with our knight and then reoccupy it with our queen.
This opening is absolutely legit. He goes the queen to d7, leaving the knight here. How do we play this position? We should try to find where we can
infiltrate — what are the weak avenues in his position? One thing I see is this diagonal, so we put our bishop here; the bishop has done its job on c3, it was just biting on granite.
Now we improve the position of our bishop and get the rook out of the picture. Two possibilities: we can give a check on c7, but even better perhaps is the knight to b6 and then capturing the pawn on
d6 — the problem is that we trade queens, and I feel we could get more out of this position; but it's fine, a pawn is a pawn.
Let's not overthink it — I'll just take. We still have all the superiorities we had previously — our
pieces are in dominant positions; you can see how passive he is.
He attacks the rook, so we move it back, and we can circle back to d5 with our knight.
We also need to develop the bishops and connect the rooks — he's not actually threatening to take at all, so we have several ways of playing this.
We can go the bishop to e2 — let's complete our development first.
This pawn is very weak — I notice it and think, aha, how can we attack it? Again, it's all about flexibility; there's a certain piece that has already done its job on its square,
so find the move — the bishop to c3, repositioning to attack the pawn. If he plays the knight to d7
and defends, there's a tactic — notice that the king is overloaded, a simple overloading tactic.
What is the tactic?
The knight takes f7.
The king takes, the rook takes d7 — I'm going a little faster because he's really strong and I don't want to lose on time. He simply resigns.
The funny thing: if he goes the king to e6 and tries to chase the rook away from d7, what would White do here?
Not immediately — a lot of people think of the bishop takes e5, which is the right idea, but remember that you can take
the rook, and the rooks defend each other.
e4, and Black tries the Alekhine — a knight to f6, provoking our pawns. Against it White has a knight to c3 or the ambitious e5.
But e5 is the real move — a knight to c3 is unambitious, since Black could answer e5 into a Vienna or d5 into a favorable Scandinavian.
The knight is chased to d5, and now d4.
d4, planting our second central pawn.
Black plays the main d6, striking at our chain — the first crossroads. White can support with a knight to f3, or expand with c4, the start of the most ambitious system: the Four Pawns Attack.
So c4, harassing the knight. The Four Pawns Attack is very dangerous — I'll admit I don't know its theory deeply, since I rarely face it against players my level, but we're going for it.
The knight retreats to b6. Now a capture on d6 is the calmer, positional main line.
But we play something explosive — f4, the Four Pawns Attack proper, considered one of the very best lines: if White knows what he's doing, he's objectively better.
Black captures on e5.
And we recapture toward the center with the f-pawn — not the d-pawn capture on c5, which allows an unfavorable queen trade.

A knight to c6. The plus of this system is a monster center; the minus is delayed development — play carelessly and the center comes under serious fire, and we could lose all three pawns. This is the first moment you simply have to know what to do. A knight to f3 looks like the main move, but it isn't — so how do we defend instead?
A knight to f3 allows a bishop to g4, piling pressure on the knight and the pawn; and d5 would just drop the e5 pawn. A bishop to e3 is the only viable defense.
Black plays a bishop to f5, the main line, and now we can develop normally.
First a knight to c3, simply developing; if Black plays the main e6, we follow with a knight to f3, and the center is successfully defended.

Our center holds. Black can still lash out with a bishop to g4 — such an explosive move that people spend the whole tempo to play it — or the more popular plan of a bishop to b7 and a later f6 to open the center.
A knight to b4 might look scary, but it's harmless because of a rook to c1. Black chooses the bishop to b7, so we complete development — and we have two squares for the bishop.
A bishop to d3 slightly weakens the center by allowing a bishop to g4, so we develop modestly with a bishop to e2. Usually Black now castles and plays f6 to chip at our center.
We castle, Black castles, and f6 is the main move to prise open the center.

Instead Black plays a5, trying to expand on the queenside — but I think it's too slow, so we can already step on the gas. Our center is well defended now, and the move that follows is d5. After d5, a capture, and a recapture, that pawn is defended twice and attacked twice, so Black can't take it with the knight, and the b6 knight will have to move under fire.
d5. The idea isn't a3, which lets Black take the pawn, and a bishop to c4 would drop the bishop to the b6 knight — it's a quieter transformation I'll show on the board.
Black plays a knight to b4 immediately — that doesn't change anything at all.
He keeps a pair of pawns on the board, but we still capture on b6 and follow with d6; White is basically dominating.

Black panics with a capture on d5 — he shouldn't have. We don't need to recapture with the c-pawn; we simply drop the bishop back and we're up a piece. If he takes on c4, a bishop to c4 leaves no compensation.

Where should the bishop go? The safest square, out of reach of a knight to c2, is f2 — nicely protected, and with the file closed it doesn't matter, because we're already up a piece. That's like winning the lottery and complaining the hundred-dollar bills are crumpled.
The game is basically over — down a piece, and look how beautifully our pieces are coordinated in the center. The knight on b4 is no danger; we can always kick it with c6.
Is allowing a knight to c2 dangerous? No — the knight is trapped, so it's totally fine to allow it.
Because we play a rook to c1 and simply capture on c2. Now a capture on d5.
We capture on d5.
We can recapture with the knight, or with the queen — I like the queen recapture, centralizing and offering a trade; it connects the rooks and keeps things open and simple.
Don't overthink these low-level decisions — the knight recapture was perfectly fine too. It's not worth more than ten or fifteen seconds in a rapid game.
We recapture on d5 with the knight.
We're a full piece up with no pawns to complicate things. What's the most clinical path to converting?
Activate — a rook to c1, centralizing on the open file, and the other rook to d1. Black is completely paralyzed.
Black plays a bishop to e4.
We play a rook to d1, defending the knight — no need to move it; he's welcome to trade.
There's a technical threat of a capture on f3 and then on e5, but that's just a pawn — don't fret over every pawn; see the bigger picture.
I like a bishop to b5, attacking the rook — one of many good moves.
A capture on f3 is the one line to calculate — should we take the rook, or recapture on f3? Both win; the point is to check concretely.

We take the rook. If instead we recapture on f3, that same attacked rook takes on e5 — but by taking the rook first, then recapturing with our rook, we stay a piece up, coordinated, and keep the e5 pawn.
The bishop on e8 may look awkward, and Black attacks it, but remember the concept.

Don't be scared of a threat just because it's a threat — threats are only dangerous if you can't stop them or if they achieve something. A piece on a slightly vulnerable square is fine if concrete calculation shows it can't be won.
A bishop to d7 — to stop a rook coming to c8 and keep the rook confined, a thorn in Black's side. Now we finish cleanly.
Better than a meek knight trade: begin with a bishop check on c5, activating the bishop.
The king steps to g8.
And we plant the knight on the weak b6 square, twisting the knife; if a rook to b8, there's a cute follow-up.
A bishop to d6 immobilizes the knight — an easy conversion. After a rook to a6, there's a crushing move: the rook x-rays the bishop.
A bishop to b5 — a back-rank discovery; a bishop to e5 attacking the rook is the simple finish.

The knight lunge to g4 looks intimidating but there's nothing to fear — simply castle. If it grabs on f2 and the bishop recaptures, the trade leaves two pieces for a rook and pawn, and in the middlegame the rooks stay stuck in their corners while the two minor pieces run the board.
The h-pawn move chases the knight and forces a decision. There's no real hurry — a quiet pawn move would also do — but making the opponent commit costs nothing.
The retreat to h6 is an awkward square, and it telegraphs the plan — a quick f5 push, which is close to suicidal with the king still stuck in the centre.

So there's no need to change course — just play the standard d3, completing development while quietly setting up the positional threat of capturing on h6. Playing the system's own moves is exactly the appeal of it.

A subtlety about that capture on h6: it's strong not because it doubles the pawns — pawn structure is routinely overrated — but because the king has castled onto that very wing. Had the opponent kept the king elsewhere, ruining the structure would be far less tempting.
c6 is a poor move on two counts: it robs the knight of its natural c6 square and it fails to defend the e-pawn.
notes.teaches: A pawn move that both blocks your own knight's square and leaves a pawn hanging is doubly bad.

notes.explains: So we simply take on e5, and if Black wants the pawn back he'll have to spend time and moves for it.

Qa5-check regains the pawn but drags the queen out while nothing develops. Block with Nc3, not the tempting Bd2 — Bd2 only shoves the queen toward the pawn it was going to take anyway, and it's an awful square for the bishop.
notes.teaches: Meet a check with a developing move, not one that improves the opponent's plan while misplacing your piece.

notes.explains: Nf3 develops and defends e4; now two pieces are out, the queen is harassed, and Black's knight is stuck with both of its squares blocked by pawns.
notes.teaches: When the opponent burns time on the queen, pile up developed pieces and the edge snowballs.

notes.explains: Ng5 manufactures our own fried liver — it hits the queen and sets up Bc4 against f7. Moving a piece twice is usually wrong, but a lead in development buys you that liberty.
notes.teaches: A big development lead licenses breaking the rules — even moving one piece twice for a concrete attack.

notes.explains: Bc4 trains onto f7 — but be careful: b5 is coming, and a move isn't good just because it makes a threat.
notes.teaches: Don't equate a threatening move with a good move; check the opponent's reply first.

notes.explains: A calculation lesson: Nxf7 forks queen and rook, but grabbing the rook lets Black trap the knight. When a line fails, don't restart from the top — back up to the last move where you had a choice. Taking the rook wasn't forced; Bb3 first keeps the knight defended, then collect the rook. Uncouple your emotions from the calculation.
notes.teaches: When a variation fails, backtrack to the last branching point, not the first move — and judge it analytically, not by taste.

notes.explains: And note Bxf7 is also simply crushing — there was more than one road in.

Up a queen, resist grabbing every scrap — but do take what's literally free. Qh5-check, then a knight sacrifice on g6 rips it open, Qa5-check swings across, and a picture mate follows because the bishop already covers d6.
notes.teaches: With a decisive material lead, take what's free and steer for the clean mate, not extra material.

notes.explains: The knight to f3,
and the knight to c6.
And we're facing the Scotch — d4.
Obviously here we play e-takes-d4, that's what we do, and the Scotch Gambit would be the bishop to c4.
There we go, we're facing the Scotch Gambit. One thing I could do is play a bad line of it for Black and then try to recover. Black has two main approaches — the first is the knight to f6,

which leads to e5 and then Black's move d5, which is what I actually play. The other approach is to cling to the pawn on d4 with the bishop to c5, which is what we'll do — and White's main move is c3.
And that contains a pretty vicious trap, which we're going to fall into deliberately. The correct way here for Black is the knight to f6, with a possible transposition to
the Italian — c-takes-d4, the bishop to b4 with check. What we're going to do instead is something not advised: d-takes-c3.
Now, as our opponent thinks — she knows the correct approach — the bishop takes f7

with check, which forces our king out of its shell, and the bishop on c5 is picked up as the queen swings into the centre with tempo; White is considered clearly better. So that's an instructive blunder. How bad is it? Not as bad as some books have said — Black is by no means losing, but Black is much worse. The first order of business is where to put the king: obviously not g6 or f6, we'd get mated. The real question is e7, e8 or f8 — which is safest, relatively speaking? You might reason: the king to f8 allows White to take on c5 with check, so we don't want that, therefore the king to e7 — and after the queen takes e5 we have a tempo. What can we do with it? We could take on b2 and keep our extra pawn — but that's flawed logic, because although you win a pawn, the bishop comes out to b2 and immediately attacks g7, and Black gets smothered. The point isn't to cling to the extra pawn — it's to make the king as

safe as possible, and so the king to f8 is actually the correct one, relatively the better square. Why? Because after the king to e8 and the pawn to d6, that pawn becomes a hook, and White exploits it by pushing e5 — think five to seven moves ahead and the king could get caught in the crossfire of a vicious attack down the e-file.
On f8 the king is temporarily safe from anything terrible on the e-file for now — does that make sense? So here we go, d6, covering the check and opening up our bishop.
And when your king is weak like this, first and foremost you develop as quickly and as actively as possible, to give yourself a little time you can then use to, for instance, castle
by hand. So what should we start with? The knight to f6 — it hits the pawn on e4, and then the bishop can come out to g4. In such situations you should always be aware of the

eventual plan of castling by hand: the king back up to f7, the rook swung to f8 or e8, and the king tucked back to g8. Unfortunately the immediate king to f7 is bad — why? Because of the knight to g5. So logically, a candidate move: we can play h6 first. You might say, doesn't h6 weaken

the g6-square — can't White play the knight to h4? Yes he can, but then we go the king to f7 and that square is protected. Let's give it a shot with h6 — I'm not developing the light-squared bishop, because castling by hand is the top priority.
If we can squeeze that in, everything else falls into place. Now, a very skilled opponent is going to find a way to deter us from this.

But let's see if she's up to the task. The king to f7 — and another point of not developing the bishop is that if our opponent gives us a queen check on one of these squares, we can cover it with the bishop.

A very important detail, without which this wouldn't work. b3 is not a particularly scary move, and it seems we'll accomplish our first aim. Now, where should we go with the rook — f8 or e8? You could make a case for
both, but the more natural move is the rook to e8, because at least there it's doing something, pressuring the pawn. And our opponent — I like what she's doing — is going to put the bishop on b2,
creating a battery, and that's going to immobilise the knight on f6.
Nonetheless, we've accomplished something very serious — our king is now a

lot safer than it was on f8, but we're still worse. Why? First of all, White has a very nice pawn on e4 that could advance to e5, and the main reason we're worse is this battery — a permanent strain that doesn't let our knight move; and if that knight is eliminated, we face very serious threats along the diagonal. How should we continue? A couple of approaches, but I think the time has come to complete our development. What does that mean? g5 is a candidate, trying to put more stuff on the diagonal — I'll explain after the game why I think it's

a bad move, or at least not the right approach. Instead, the bishop to g4 — we could also play the bishop to e6, but let's play with maximal activity, so the bishop to g4. Someone asked me to explain the king to g8: the point is just to physically get the king as far from harm as possible. When the king lands on f7 it's far more susceptible to all sorts of tactics — the knight to g5, or the centre opening — because it's closer to the centre; the further the king is from the centre, the safer it is, as a rule of thumb. That's why you castle in the first place: it's much harder to open up the kingside and get pieces there than it is to get pieces to the centre. Now, White plays the queen to c2, opening his bishop. The simplest idea is to connect our rooks and get the queen off d8 onto a more active square. There's a little manoeuvre I'm thinking about — where should the queen ultimately go? Be careful, because the queen to d7 allows the bishop to take on f6 and ruin our pawn structure; I'm not sure I want to allow that. So start with the queen to e7, and eventually get the queen to f7 — not g6, f7 — because from f7 the queen controls the knight on f6, controls the f-file, lets the rooks breathe, and physically shields the king. Now you might ask, aren't I worried about e5? I am — it's a worrisome move — but I think we'll survive the impact: we trade, then move the queen aside, and I don't see it being that dangerous. So we'll put the queen on f7, and then how do we keep improving? We can potentially double on the e-file. The knight to d4 is a great move: it gets the knight out of the purview of the bishop, and now that bishop on g4 just looks dumb, shooting into thin air. Then we should probably trade, because otherwise we lose a pawn; some of you are thinking of the knight to e5, but, as I explained last game, a knight on e5 is often unstable and can be chased away with f4 — why allow that? So we take. Now there are issues: if we play the queen to f7, White has a nasty response. Think about type-two undefended pieces and pawns — the pawn on c7 is a type two, protected by the queen, and the queen is overextended, defending the knight and protecting the pawn — so the bishop takes f6 is a positional threat that would force g-takes-f6. So we have to defend the c-pawn: not the rook to c8, we don't want to tie down a whole rook. Can we do it more economically? We could play c5, but I'd argue c5 really weakens the d6-pawn — yes, it's with tempo, but we get a permanent weakness on d6. I think c6 is better, because it makes it far more realistic that we'll be able to play d5; when you're worse and struggling, you don't want to fall in love with tempo moves — c5 is a classic case of one-move-itis, attacking the bishop but creating more permanent weaknesses. I'm not saying c5 is terrible, maybe almost as good, but c6 is a little safer because it creates the possibility of d5 — in fact d5 is almost a threat here, since e-takes-d5 lets us take the rook. The best approach for White is probably f3 or h3 and then activating the knight to c4; the move I'm really worried about is a rook to e3, lifting up to g3. So h3 happens. Now I move the bishop — the bishop to h5 is possible, but it's safer to keep the pieces closer to the centre, clustered so they control more important squares. The knight wants to go to c4; the bishop to d7 looks quite awkward and makes it harder to defend d6, so the bishop to e6 is the most natural, and it also cuts into the pin, which makes it less urgent to move the queen aside. It blocks the battery, yes, but that's not the most important thing — we're not trying to win the e4-pawn, which is perfectly well defended; it makes the rook temporarily a little passive, but we're adopting a defensive posture, controlling as many squares as possible. Now e5, striking in the centre — we have to take that pawn, and then it's a good time to move our queen off e7. The bishop to h5 was fine, but the bishop to b6 is a little safer.
