Queen versus two rooks totally depends on the concrete situation — it can be good, bad, or anything between. The rook takes e5, so we clearly have to move our queen: the queen to d6 attacks the bishop with tempo, but it's further from our king than I'd like — I feel we should stick to our earlier destination and play the queen to f7, where it seems really solid. After a rook to e1 we're still worse, we haven't equalised, but we're making progress, and I feel safer knowing my queen protects the g7-pawn in case the knight is traded off. And notice the opposite-coloured bishops — what does that tell you? In the endgame opposite-coloured bishops are drawish, but in the middlegame they favour the attacker, because intuitively we have nothing to control the dark squares. Now the natural thing is to play the bishop to d5, offering a trade of rooks. Let's calculate: the bishop to d5, the rook takes, the rook takes back, the queen takes — and at the end White has the bishop taking f6, but then g-takes-f6, and because so many pieces are traded I'm far less concerned about the pawn structure; White also has the bishop taking a7, but calculate one move further and Black has a check, on e1 or the queen to e2, and the combination of opposite-coloured bishops with our activity should give sufficient compensation for a draw. Someone asks, can't we take with the knight? You can, but you yield the e-file, and I really don't want to give the opponent full control of it — if the rook ever infiltrates to e7 we're toast. So we're expecting the rook takes, a trade of rooks and an endgame. The queen to f5 puts on more pressure but isn't as scary as it looks — we should discharge the tension by trading, the best method of dealing with pressure and a dubious position. We can trade immediately, the rook takes e5, or some propose the knight to d7 forcing a queen trade — but the knight to d7 doesn't work concretely: after queen-takes-queen and king recaptures, once the rooks come off on e8 the g7-pawn hangs, because our knight is no longer covering it. So take on e5 first, and then the knight to d7 makes more sense, forcing the queen trade, and in the endgame White's control of the e-file matters far less. The endgame is still slightly worse for us, because White's bishop is a little better — it pressures both pawns and White has the e-file — but we're close to equalising. Move order is super important: don't assume different move orders transpose, because frequently they don't, and that's where problems happen. Now what? The rook to f3 is no problem, our bishop controls that square. Ideally we solve the problem of our pawns on dark squares that the bishop pressures: we could play a6, but let's go full attack mode with a5, creating pressure on White's queenside — a5, a4, maybe open the a-file and one day attack that b3-pawn. Then g4 — the move I was worried about, because it forces a trade: the knight to d6 would be a nasty threat winning the b7-pawn, which is unallowable, so we have to take that knight. The bishop takes g7 — there was the rook to g8, which I missed — but the bishop takes g7, and here we had the rook to g8 in response. Now a very interesting endgame, bishop versus knight. We could contemplate a4, but White answers b4 and it doesn't accomplish much. I don't like c5 or b5 — pushing pawns just creates further weaknesses, and remember White is threatening the bishop takes g7 — so we could push the g-pawn, but I like the knight to f6: the rook to e8 loses a pawn, and the knight to f6 offers a trade that's good for us, with the knight used as a shield from the bishop's pressure on g7. A rook to f4 might worry you because White can follow with the bishop taking f6 — but remember that in the endgame pawn structure works differently: doubled pawns on f6 and h6 would be unthinkable in the middlegame with the king so weak, but in the endgame they're totally fine, even better than consecutive pawns, because the king can defend both from a single square. So we take with the king, not g-takes-f6, and I think we've fully equalised — it took twenty-nine moves — into an equal, drawish endgame. How to play it? First, activate the rook: it's sitting doing nothing, so bring it to d8 and potentially to d5. The other idea is to push our pawns — b5, c5, c4, to create a passer — but if we push too fast they become weak and White wins them, so we could also play g5 to slow White's pawns. Let's try b5, an ambitious move that weakens the c6-square but might pay off. Does the queenside majority mean we're better? No — both sides have a three-versus-two majority, so any pawn endgame depends directly on king placement and who creates a passer faster. A draw is offered; let's play on. The move c5 is very interesting but risky: whenever three pawns are arranged with none defending the other, moves that carve out squares become dangerous — White has the move a4. Our opponent goes a rook to e3. If we play c4 it's premature, because after the exchanges and a rook to c3 our pawn becomes more of a weakness than a strength, so instead let's play g5 to slow White's pawns, or the rook to d4, though that lets White infiltrate to e8. I'll start with g5, which helps in the event of a pawn endgame by slowing the creation of a passer. Now we have to play the rook to d5 to defend the pawn, and potentially h5 and h4 — a deep freeze, where two pawns hold three. The king comes to e3; our opponent wants the king to e4, but that's not dangerous because we have a check on e5. This might be a good moment for h5, but I also like centralising our king. The problem is we can't move our rook and we'd like to: b4 is bad, because it disqualifies us from ever making a passer on the queenside; a rook move blunders the pawn, so we have to defend c5 with the king to d6. Maybe the pawn endgame is winning for White — I don't rule that out, it's very close and I'm too lazy to calculate it exactly. But calculating the pawn race carefully — the h-pawn and the a-pawn queening, king and pawn against king — it turns out we win: we promote and hold the new queen, and this would only be a draw if White's king could reach b8, which it cannot. In fact the move f4 for White actually loses. A really cool endgame. And as a closing thought — there are a lot of underrated, strong players out there; be careful about jumping to cheating accusations on the basis of a few good moves, and act on evidence you can check.
White plays the Torre Attack — the bishop to g5, the same spirit as the London but with the bishop on g5 instead of f4.
White develops the bishop to c4, a slightly unusual choice — normally it goes to d3 or e2 in the Torre.
We keep the King's-Indian character with d6, not d5 — d5 would drift into Grünfeld territory. The beauty of the KID is you barely change your moves for what White does.
The KID has two pawn breaks — c5 and e5 — and the whole point of the Torre's bishop on g5 is to discourage e5 with a nasty pin. So we don't rush into it; we finish developing first.
teaches: the c5 and e5 breaks; beware the pin on e5

notes.explains: We fianchetto the light-squared bishop to b7 rather than g4 — a bishop developed to g4 has no retreat, and h3 would simply trap it.
teaches: fianchetto to keep the bishop safe

notes.explains: The bishop settles on b7, raking down the long diagonal.
We meet White's queenside expansion with a5 of our own, freezing his a-pawn.
teaches: a5 to stop the a4-a5 push

notes.explains: The knight develops to d7, not c6, so it doesn't block our fianchetto bishop. From here the plan is clear: break the pin with g5 and h5 when needed, pile pieces onto the kingside — the queen to f6 and beyond — and eventually launch the e5 and f5-f4 pawn storm, opening the h-file at White's king and overloading the f3-knight.
teaches: Nd7 keeps the bishop’s diagonal open
accumulate on the kingside, then storm
plans: open the h-file, overload the f3-knight

notes.explains: We take Black and answer with the Sicilian, c5.
White develops the knight to f3 and we bring ours to c6.
White plays c3 — the Alapin. But this move order, with the knights already out, denies us the line I usually recommend.
We take the risk with e5 — objectively White is a touch better with precise play, but it's hard to prove, and I want to test our improvisation in fresh territory.

White strikes with d4. Our ...e5 is risky mainly because it leaves a hole on d5 — but as in the Najdorf's ...e5 structures, that square can be well covered by our minor pieces, so it's far from the end of the world.
So we take on d4.
The centre pawns are swapped off.

White recaptures with the knight. This is essentially a Scotch, only with the c-pawns already gone — which slightly favours White, because our d6-square is tender: if we try the bishop to c5, as I like against a normal Scotch, White gets the extra shot of the knight to f5, exploiting d6.
So instead the knight to f6 — now White has no time for the knight to f5, because the e4-pawn hangs. We reach a Scotch-like game, a shade worse for us but very playable.

White develops the knight to c3 and we've transposed into a Four Knights Scotch. The main move is the bishop to b4, pressuring e4 — there's also the sharp ...Nxe4 — but let's keep it straightforward with the bishop to b4.
The pawn to e4, e5 — the move most people actually play.
The knight to f3.
The knight to c6. I like to showcase different openings and how to play them.
d4 — the Scotch, the one opening among my recommendations that I suggest to beginners.
Black takes on d4.
We recapture on d4. The Scotch teaches you to play with all your pieces, because d4 opens up the centre.

When the centre is closed you have a crutch; open, it teaches active development and punishes your mistakes. d6 is passive — not terrible, but it opens one bishop while blocking the dark-squared bishop, which can now only come to e7.
The knight to c3. Now we develop the bishops — where does this bishop go?
The knight to f6. Two squares to consider: b5 and c4. I like the bishop to b5 less — surprising, since people love pins, but the problem is Black unpins with the bishop to d7 —
— and then that pin is empty. Instead, the bishop to c4 is quite a bit better, mounting sustained pressure on the f7-pawn.

Chess is gradual — we're not threatening to take f7 yet, just applying long-term pressure and setting up an attack. Black plays g6 to fianchetto. We have an even sexier move — the bishop to g5, but let me explain the logic. Notice the queens are in a standoff: two pieces facing each other with more than one piece between them. If the position opens, they'll face each other directly. Black's queen is defended by the knight and the king. Can I decoy the king off its defence of the queen?

The bishop takes f7 — but not immediately; only if the queens end up staring at each other. First, can I remove the knight on c6? Let's take it. Then the only thing preventing the bishop takes f7 is the d6-pawn.
The b-pawn recaptures, and to the rescue comes another decoy sacrifice — e5, attacking the knight; if he doesn't take, that pawn wreaks havoc.

If he does take, we play the bishop takes f7, distracting the king from the queen. He didn't have to take the bishop, but his position would be ruined regardless. Black plays d5, counter-attacking the bishop. Should we take the knight —

— actually there's a better way: the bishop to g5. Conceptually we should take the knight — it opens the position when the opponent is behind in development — but we take it with the bishop, which forks. If he takes our bishop we take his knight, or we can take his queen first —
This position resembles a Maróczy bind — I've played it a couple of times over the board with Black; Black is solid here but slightly worse. The difference from the Danish is that
c-takes-d4.
Black hasn't moved his e-pawn, he's played the c-pawn instead,
so you don't play the bishop to c4 — that Sicilian-Danish idea is no longer as effective, because Black's central pawns are intact.
We answer the king's pawn with the knight to f6 — the Alekhine, a rare but sound choice.
White chases with e5 and our knight hops to d5.
White expands with c4.
We retreat the knight to b6.
White plays d4, taking the centre in a measured way.
We strike back with d6.
White captures on d6 — one of the two main lines.

We recapture with the c-pawn on d6 — my recommendation for Alekhine beginners, because it teaches you to handle an imbalanced structure: White gets a queenside pawn majority, we get a kingside majority.
White develops the knight to c3. Our light-squared bishop will struggle to get out, so we'll fianchetto.
We play g6, preparing the fianchetto.
The bishop settles on g7.

We continue naturally with the knight to c6, and the plan writes itself: press White's two central pawns. It resembles a Dragon but far calmer — both sides castle short and nobody's getting mated soon. It's hard to play at club level for two reasons: you're a touch cramped, so accuracy matters, and you must know how to meet a wide range of White setups.

And there it is — the Maróczy Bind, the very thing most people who avoid the Accelerated Dragon are afraid of, and rightly so. It's both a variation and a structure: pawns planted on e4 and c4, both trained on the d5 square. That's the bind — it makes the freeing break to d5, the whole point of the Dragon, virtually impossible, leaving black cramped.

Here's the dangerous, under-the-radar answer: instead of the automatic fianchetto, start with the knight to f6, delaying the bishop. It immediately puts the question to the e4-pawn and hands black real chances to fight for the initiative rather than just sit passively.

A tactical footnote that makes it sound: if the opponent captures on c6 and pushes to e5 to boot the knight, there's a queen check on a5 that scoops the e-pawn back. The whole idea holds together on concrete tactics.

Now the step that startles the uninitiated — capture on d4, dragging the queen out into the centre. It looks reckless, inviting the knight to be pinned with a menacing central push, but it works out concretely for black.

It's important not to fianchetto here, since that would walk into the central push — so insert d6 instead. It frees the bishop and, just as importantly, jams the advance of the enemy e-pawn. If it pushes anyway, it's simply captured; and even if the queens come off at the cost of castling rights, that trade isn't worth a whole pawn to the opponent.
The Austrian Attack — f4 alongside e4 and d4 for a big pawn centre.
The mindset: don't rush a kingside attack. Bank on the centre and develop each piece to support it, so you never overextend and bite off more than you can chew.
notes.teaches: In broad-centre systems, develop to reinforce the centre first; the attack comes only once it's secure.

notes.explains: Bc4 would be the natural-looking mistake — it runs into Nxe4 and d5, blasting the centre apart. So the bishop goes to d3 instead, quietly buttressing e4. Not every piece has to climb Everest.
notes.teaches: Place a piece to defend your centre even if the square looks passive; the flashy square can hang tactically.

notes.explains: Because everything is healthily placed, we can expand further with e5.
An instructive recapture choice: fxe5 opens the f-bishop and lets us storm the h-pawn for mate, but in a serious game dxe5 is better — it opens the d-file so a rook can x-ray the queen painfully.
notes.teaches: Pick the recapture that opens the file your pieces want, not just the one that looks natural.

notes.explains: Develop the bishop to f4, placed precisely so it over-protects the e5-pawn — exactly the point behind taking with the d-pawn.
notes.teaches: Post your bishop where it guards your advanced pawn, tying your development to your structure.

notes.explains: When Black tries c5 to break the chain, the principle is to capture toward the centre — but our central grip is so strong we can often just push past and ignore the poke.
notes.teaches: With an overwhelming centre you can sometimes brush aside a flank break instead of resolving it.

notes.explains: Qd2 piles on and hits the knight; the greedy Qxb2 in reply just loses a piece.
The queen grabbed b2 and attacks our rook, so first things first — Rb1 gets it out of the fork.

Here's the key move: before winning the knight on h6, ask whether we can preemptively defend our own c3-knight with tempo, so Black's knight can't wriggle free. Rb3 does exactly that — it shields c3 and hits the queen at once.
notes.teaches: Before cashing a win, secure your loose piece with tempo so the opponent gets no escape and no fork.

notes.explains: Now Bxh6 collects the piece cleanly — the rook guards c3, so there's no Nxc3-check fork to save Black.
Ne4 forces the issue: the queens x-ray each other through the knight, and Black must also defend the g3-bishop, so he's overloaded — either trade queens down a rook or lose the bishop.
notes.teaches: A knight that both unmasks a queen trade and attacks a second piece overloads the defender.

notes.explains: Against the bishop on c4, we blunt it and build with e6.
A useful rule of thumb: don't commit both e6 and g6 in the same setup — pick one, or you weaken too many squares at once.
teaches: don’t play e6 and g6 together

notes.explains: White pins with the bishop to g5.
We answer with d5, staking out the center and taking the sting out of that pin in one move.
teaches: d5 hits the pin and grabs the center

notes.explains: To deal with the pin we don't rush the bishop to g4 — we develop the light bishop by fianchetto and castle, keeping it safe from being harassed.
teaches: fianchetto rather than expose the bishop

notes.explains: The bishop to e6 relieves the pressure on d5 and gets our last piece into play.
A strong plan is the b5 break — and the way to prepare a pawn move is usually another pawn move, so a6 comes first.
teaches: prepare a pawn break with a pawn

notes.explains: The break with c4 goes further — it can trap White's light-squared bishop entirely.
teaches: the c4 lever to trap the bishop

notes.explains: We have White against a strong opponent — the pawn to e4, met by e5.
The knight to f3.
Black plays the knight to c6. At these higher ratings there's a dilemma — play the recommended Four Knights Scotch, or reach for the main repertoire against a strong player.
The knight to c3 — the Four Knights Scotch, still a powerful weapon at most levels.
Black develops the knight to f6.
The pawn to d4 — heading for the Belgrade Gambit.
Black takes on d4. This is the Belgrade — I've played it in semi-competitive games and it's far more dangerous than its reputation, dismissed as unsound since the 1970s.
The knight to d5 — the Belgrade Gambit, instead of the mainline recapture. A surprise weapon to spring on a strong player.

Black plays the pawn to h6 — a reasonable move preventing the bishop to g5, one of White's main Belgrade ideas to pressure the f6-knight. The old original Belgrade doesn't come close to equalizing, but engine analysis livens it up — here I found the bishop to d3, where the classic players instead recaptured with the bishop to f4.

The bishop to d3, then a plan of repositioning to g5. If Black plays the pawn to d6, take the knight and reroute the bishop to b5 to regain d4. The bishop to c5 is possible but risky — the queenside storm with a3 and b4 can force it to lose contact with the d-pawn while opening a fianchetto square for us; and long-term, the h6 weakness invites a sacrifice on h6 once Black castles.

Black plays the pawn to d6. The key idea: the knight takes d5 is almost always in White's favour, because recapturing on d5 kicks the c6-knight and risks the d4-pawn — and if Black takes on d5 too early, a rook to e1 massacres him down the e-file. So the line goes the knight takes f6, the queen recaptures, then the bishop to b5.
The bishop to b5. If Black grabs the e4-pawn I'm not scared at all — we just castle with a huge development lead. So I like the bishop to b5 immediately.
One last game — let's play a Sicilian. e4, c5.
The bishop to c4, the knight to c6.
This guy is playing very weird chess — b3, wasting time trying to
fianchetto his bishop, which doesn't make too much sense. Let's just develop our knights,
and then you know the drill in such positions —
the best thing to do is to play e6 and prepare the move d5.
And he's already lost a bishop, because his bishop only has one square, and that
results in the loss of a bishop and the loss of the game — e-takes-d5, e-takes-d5, a tactical pattern most of you are probably aware of.
The bishop to b5 — the fianchetto doesn't make sense; it's just weird to develop bishops this way, and there's the chess principle, knights before bishops,
which he's violating. The queen to a5 with check —
we're going to force him to develop his knight, and what do we do with it?
d4 — exactly, winning the knight.

The bishop takes c6, b-takes-c6 — we don't care about that; he's got to give up a pawn for the knight, and we're just going to be up a full piece for no compensation. This stuff people will try to do to you; we can play the bishop to e7 or the bishop to b6, it doesn't matter, as long as we cover the check — and he doesn't even get a pawn for the knight. Now a trick question: can we castle here? Don't get caught — it is actually possible to castle, because after the queen takes c7 we play the rook to e8 and pin the king. Sometimes our brain tells us something is impossible, but before concluding that, ask what happens if we do it anyway — that awakens the possibility of finding something like this. So we're up a full piece, and there's nothing else to really talk about — we can just go about trading as many pieces as possible. His queen, over on e3, is very clearly vulnerable; we can attack it by shifting the knight over to d5, opening a channel between the bishops, or we can take the knight and start trading pieces, ruining his structure. The game is essentially over — we take all the pieces, up a knight, his kingside completely ruined, and we approach fifteen hundred. These triple pawns remind me of a famous game. Now we win another piece — we take the knight, removing the defender from the bishop, and we're up two pieces; the rest you know the drill: put a rook to e8, and don't forget to deploy the remainder of our pieces.
We play the Accelerated Dragon, hoping for an open Sicilian — praying for d4.
The knight to c6.
The bishop to b5 — the Rossolimo, like a Ruy Lopez against the Sicilian, the favorite of top players for over a decade.
As Accelerated Dragon players we play g6 — there are two main ways to meet the Rossolimo.
The opponent is walking into trouble — if the bishop gets taken, a capture on h5 leads to a forced mate in two. The whole ragged pawn adventure is backfiring.
The mate gets parried, but the pawn is still there for the taking — two pawns up now, and the enemy king dragged out into the open. It's hard to ask for more out of the first few moves.

Care is needed with the bishop's retreat: the opponent wants to capture on d4, and recapturing with the queen would leave the far-flung bishop hanging. So the bishop drops to e3, adding a second defender to d4 — now the pawn can be retaken by a pawn and the bishop kept.
Watch the developing move — the natural knight to f3 would be an outright blunder. The knight belongs on c3, because from there it threatens a leap to c5 that's very nearly mate.

That bishop has become a nuisance, so tuck it back to e2 and out of harm's way. It's a quiet, unspectacular square — but it's perfectly fine to park a piece passively when there's a concrete reason, and being two pawns up against an exposed king is reason enough.

Now an instructive question — which way to castle? Because the opponent has already stripped away the pawns in front of one wing, castling toward it would hand them a ready-made attack and justify the whole gambit. So the king goes the other way, castling long.

Before castling long, shoo the advanced knight away — but only as castling prep, since otherwise there'd be a fork winning a pawn. The knight itself isn't doing anything; removing it is purely about clearing the way to safety.

A guiding priority: it matters far less to wreck the opponent's pawns in general than to wreck the shelter around their king. Capturing here would only open a file that helps them attack, so it's declined.

The moment has come to open the centre — and the key is what not to do: resist locking it with a pawn push. Simply capture, prying the d-file open. Restraint over the tempting advance is the whole point.

The recapture weakens a key square, and now a tactic is waiting. Notice the relationship — the rook and queen stand on one line in an x-ray. Whenever that pattern appears, hunt for a discovery: if the front piece steps aside and a certain pawn were gone, the queen falls.

The move that makes both wishes come true at once is the knight capture on e5 — it removes the shielding pawn and unmasks the line in a single stroke. If it's recaptured, a discovered check crashes through.
And the discovered check on g5 ends it — not merely winning the queen but delivering mate in the process. Tactical awareness is exactly what makes these hidden shots easy to spot.

There's an even faster finish than grabbing the queen — a bishop check first, planting a piece on f7 to seal the king's flight square, and then the rook delivers mate. Blocking the escape before cashing in is the cleaner path.
We take Black and answer the king's pawn with the Sicilian.
White develops the knight to f3. As a gateway Sicilian for improving players the accelerated dragon is the recommendation, but nearing the top of the run we reach for the Sicilian we know best.
We play d6 — and note we're not even facing the Open Sicilian here.
White plays the bishop to b5 with check — the Moscow, also called the Canal Attack.
We block the check with the knight to d7.
White plays a4 — a recent fashion, ultra-positional, straight from a course; many who follow it reach the middlegame with no plan.
We develop the knight to f6, forcing White to decide how to defend e4. Inducing the knight to c3 is a plus: it stops White from setting up c3 and d4 in the quiet, Alapin-like manner.

White plays the knight to c3. We're happy to transpose into an Open Sicilian structure once d4 arrives. Why not ...e5 to stop d4? It's positionally dubious — it weakens the d5-square, and we actually welcome d4.
We play e6 — the Scheveningen structure, pawns on e6 and d6 rather than the ...e5 you see in other lines.
White castles. White could instead keep the centre closed with a modest c3 or d3.
We continue developing with the bishop to e7. Against a quiet d3 we could even strike with ...d5 ourselves.

White plays d4 — exactly the Scheveningen we wanted. Why not kick with ...a6 first? The b5-bishop is no real nuisance and the d7-knight is our best-defended piece, so we save ...a6 for a rainy day when it truly counts.
We release the tension and take on d4.
White recaptures with the queen on d4 — a queen rather than a knight in the centre, and with the rare bishop on b5, an unusual flavour of Open Sicilian.

We castle, completing kingside development. On the surface White looks better — more space, the d6-pawn a target — but the position is deceptively robust. If White ever tries the bishop to f4, then ...e5 would fork it and win a piece; and Black's pieces all guard one another, so d6 is far harder to reach than it appears.
White plays the rook to d1, piling on d6 — the best move. We can delay ...a6 one move more.
We play the queen to c7, completing the setup — it x-rays the c2-pawn, adds a defender to d6, and stands ready to jump to c5.
The pawn to e4, c5 — the Alapin, against a very strong 2198, our strongest opponent to date.
c3 — let's see how the Alapin fares against a high-caliber player; I vehemently disagree that it's only good at beginner-to-intermediate level. It's a dangerous weapon all the way to GM.
e6 — a flexible move, one tier behind the two main moves, d5 and the knight to f6.

The traditional response is d5. To play it, Black has to be okay allowing e5, an Advanced French — but since I don't play the Advanced and never have, most Sicilian players are really bluffing White into e5, and often neither side knows what to do.

The more Alapin-esque way is to take on d5, and Black is at an early crossroads: recapture with the queen, transposing, or keep the e6 spirit with the pawn — and you can already see the IQP structure forming.

If Black recaptures with the pawn and White later takes on c5, Black recaptures and has an isolated pawn on d5 — the classic isolated queen's pawn. One good thing about c3: after we take on c5 and he recaptures, that c3-pawn slows the d5-pawn and controls the square in front of it, the most important thing against the IQP — controlling the square matters more than occupying it. Taking on c5 immediately is decent but not best; ideally, as in the Queen's Gambit, you wait for Black to move the dark-squared bishop first, then take on c5 to cost him a tempo.
Black plays the bishop, and then it takes on c5, so we've gained a tempo. The best and most recommended move is the bishop to b5 with check, developing with tempo —
— and asking Black another difficult question.
Instead we develop and wait for a more opportune moment — the moment Black develops his bishop is a very good time to take on c5. The knight to f3.

So far, standard, well-known theory. The bishop to d6 — funnily, we can delay the pawn takes c5 one more move by castling, since Black can't resolve the central tension, but I'll stick to the traditional way.
Traditionally you take on c5 the moment Black develops his bishop —
— the bishop takes c5, and we've earned a tempo, since Black made an extra move with his bishop.

Now we castle and get our king out of the centre. The next big question is where Black develops his knight — e7 or f6. Against the knight to f6, I like the bishop to g5, pinning it; but if the knight goes to e7, the bishop to g5 makes less sense.

The knight to f6 — the bishop to g5 walks into f6, and here f6 isn't so weakening we'd want to spend tempi inducing it. Important IQP ideas: the check on e1 is tempting, but Black covers with the bishop and the f2-pawn becomes a major problem — the queen to b6, or the bishop takes f2 forking king and bishop — so keep the rook on f1 to solidify f2. Two questions: where the bishop goes, which is g5, and what to do with the knight — in these structures the knight often goes to b3, hits the bishop, and heads for the blockade square.
There really aren't other options for the knight; the real decision is the order. I like starting with the bishop to g5, restricting the knight and immediately setting up a pin.
The bishop to e6. The drawback of playing the knight to d2 first —
— is that the bishop would be temporarily blocked in by the knight.
So this seems a more harmonious way of developing. The bishop to e6 follows — I don't love it; Black delays castling, giving us options like the immediate knight to e4, pressuring his minor pieces —

— but I don't want too many adventurous moves; I want to play traditionally to highlight our IQP technique. The knight to d2. White is slightly better — not because Black has an IQP, since you can't make categorical assertions about the isolated queen's pawn; it depends on the placement of the other pieces.
This resembles the bad-IQP case more than the good, because Black's piece activity isn't impressive — he's pinned along the diagonal, and the bishop on e6 is a passive observer tied to the pawn.
And as we play the knight to b3, we achieve complete control of the square in front of the pawn —

— so the IQP is no longer a moving target; it'll saddle Black for as long as it sits on d5. Now we make marginal improving moves. Avoid the queen to d2, which runs into the knight to e4 and bad trades. The low-hanging fruit is a knight to d4 — controlling the square matters most, but occupying it isn't bad either; the knight to c4 is also on an ideal square, pressuring his minors.

The knight to d4 — I prefer the knight from b3, keeping the other knight on the kingside where it supports our king. Now we threaten to win a pawn by taking twice on c6; if the knight takes d4, we recapture with the knight.

Black's in a little trouble — hard to move, since moving the queen off d8 allows the bishop takes f6, spoiling the structure. The bishop to d7 is a good 2100 move, keeping the tension and protecting the knight. Black threatens the knight takes d4 with tactics, and the bishop takes d7 there loses a piece to the capture on f3. So we can change the nature of our advantage from an IQP to something more dynamic — my instinct is an unnatural move.

The bishop takes c6 — it transforms our advantage from a strictly positional one into an actual initiative based on superior piece activity. Two minuses: we give up the bishop pair, and, more importantly, we allow the b-pawn recapture, after which the d5-pawn is no longer isolated.

The b-pawn takes c6 — the hanging-pawn structure: pawns on c6 and d5 with no b- or e-pawn, a self-sufficient island. Think of it as the isolated pawn shifting from the d-file to the c-file: c6 is now essentially isolated, since d5 can't go backwards to defend it.

So c6 is the biggest weakness, attacked directly by the knight to e5. But the knight to e5 has other threats: taking on c6, or taking on d7 and then f6 to ruin Black's kingside structure; the bishop takes f6 also works, since the queen can't recapture. Black struggles to cover everything; the bishop takes d4 gives us a huge advantage — Black is borderline lost if he gives up the dark-squared bishop. His pieces are passive; ours are all on optimal squares.

The queen to e8 was a smart proposal, unpinning and hitting the knight. Black plays c5, which I expected, but it fails tactically to a beautiful sequence I saw when playing the bishop takes c6. Your instinct is to move the knight from d4, but the bishop takes f6 is available — the queen still can't recapture, and the knight takes d7 comes with a fork. After the bishop takes f6, the pawn recaptures, we take the bishop on d7 and claim a small edge on Black's damaged kingside — though he could tuck the king to h8 and use the g-file. There's a specific tactical line, but I need a little more time; there's a detail I missed, which may force me off my intended path.

So we resort to the straightforward path — take on f6, take on d7, and claim a small advantage based on the weak hanging pawns and the weak king. The bishop takes f6; we have to play faster given the clock.

The queen takes f6 would lose on the spot. The g-pawn recaptures. The knight to c6 here fails tactically to the bishop takes c6, the knight takes c6, and the queen to e8 — ultra-advanced tactics I'll show after the game.
The knight takes d7 — you either see these tactical details or you don't; a lot of top-level chess boils down to spotting them.
The queen recaptures. Now we have to move our knight and figure out where it belongs.

The knight to f3 I don't like, because it'd be restricted by the f6-pawn — so the knight to c2, keeping the diagonal open for the queen and able to reroute to e3 to keep harassing the d5-pawn, one of Black's main weaknesses, along with f6. White's better, not as big as I'd hoped, but only one side is having fun. The queen to f3 targets d5 and f6 and defends g2, nipping any g-file pressure in the bud, a good response to the king to h8. On Black's d4: a passed pawn is double-edged, still isolated after the trade, and we take on d4 and play the queen to f3 with tempo. The queen to f5 for Black is an impulsive blunder walking into the knight to e3 fork.

I like positions where both sides have only one minor piece — very instructive. It's not really good-knight-versus-bad-bishop, since his bishop activates with c4, but the bigger problem is all the pawn weaknesses and the flimsy king. The rook to d8 makes the king even more uncomfortable; I'd start with the queen to f3, forcing Black to contend with the threat of the queen takes f6. If Black throws in d4 anyway, after the trades I'd seriously consider not taking on f6, since it lets the d-pawn run with d3, but White's still good; the rook to d1 also works. The queen to d6 protects f6, but now the knight reaches f5 with tempo, so the knight to e3 gets even more tempting.

The queen to f3, the queen to d6. Both the rook to d1 — the measured Russian-schoolboy approach, later lifting to the kingside via d3 — and the knight to e3 are good; the knight to e3 is super juicy, since the knight to f5 with the queen to g4 and g7 could lead to checkmate very quickly. My guess is the king to h8 in response; we start with the knight to e3. The bishop to c7 is a one-move threat, met simply by g3, keeping the tension — don't give an empty check on g4, which only helps Black reach h8, and definitely don't trade queens.
Simple, effective chess in the Italian — d3 and castle, quiet but perfect for illustrating principles.
c3 is typical theory: it quietly prepares the d4 break, the backbone of the modern Italian.
notes.teaches: In the Italian, c3 sets up d4 — the central lever the whole system revolves around.

notes.explains: This is the modern main-line Italian with Nbd2, hugely popular now.
Retreat the bishop to b3 — off the b5-a6 chase, but still glaring down the a2-g8 diagonal at f7.
notes.teaches: Reroute the Italian bishop to b3 so it keeps eyeing f7 while dodging the pawn kicks.

notes.explains: Now the Ruy-Lopez knight tour: Nd2-f1 and onward, angling the knight toward the powerful f5 square. We don't jump in at once — the bishop guards it — but the threat looms.
notes.teaches: Reroute the knight via f1 to g3, targeting f5; the threat pressures even before you land it.

notes.explains: When Ng4 pokes at us, the second point of c3 arrives: d4 intercepts the bishop with tempo. That's the Italian's resilience — the same pawn that prepared the break also parries the threat.
notes.teaches: A prepared d4 in the Italian both opens the centre and answers threats with tempo.

notes.explains: And Black hands us the whole centre — after h3 chases the knight, we're simply better with a free hand.
Complete development — Be3 is the thematic Italian square, since e4 is untouchable on tactics, though Bf4 keeps it simple here.
notes.teaches: In the Italian, Be3 is normal because the e4-pawn is defended by tactics, not just pieces.

notes.explains: Bb7 gives up control of f5, and notice Black's king is genuinely weak — every piece is clustered on the queenside, so the kingside is bare.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces all huddle on one wing, his king on the other is ripe for attack.

notes.explains: Rather than jump to f5 and give up a pawn, prepare the Bxh6 sacrifice with Qd2 — so the queen lands on h6 after the trade. Prepare slowly, attack fast. The knights that quietly hold the centre now stand ready to switch to attack.
notes.teaches: Prepare a sacrifice fully first; then the attack is a few easy moves, not a desperate lunge.

notes.explains: Bxh6 tears the king's cover apart.
With the king wide open, Nf5 is crushing — there's no defense to the mate, so Black has to shed his queen.
notes.teaches: Once the shelter is gone, a knight to f5 with the queen behind it is usually decisive.

notes.explains: The pawn to e4, e5 — a 1674, a pretty high-rated opponent.
The knight to f3.
d6 — a Philidor. Two good moves here, and they often transpose into each other.
The way to punish the Philidor — not that it has a bad reputation, but the way to get an advantage — is to strike in the centre with d4.
Black takes on d4.
The knight takes d4, and we have better control of the centre.
The knight to f6, the knight to c3 — a good position.
Multiple good setups: one is the bishop to f4 and the queen to d2, but there's a setup that flies under the radar and is extremely nasty for Black —
— fianchetto the bishop, g3.
g3, the bishop to g2.
The idea is that the bishop collaborates with the pawn and makes it very difficult for Black to free himself in the centre with d5.

I like getting my bishop into the fianchetto. c5 — a classic move, but I think a mistake: a positional error, creating a backward pawn on d6, already weak, and correspondingly a very weak square on d5. Now, where should the knight go? An important decision — we shouldn't just throw it on a random square.
The knight to f5 allows the bishop takes f5, a trade I'm not sure benefits us, so I like the knight to e2, from where it can go to f4 —
— and control the d5-square, a better square than b3. Do we need to rush the knight to f4 right now? No —
— first it makes sense to complete our development; let's castle.
And it would also make sense to play h3. The bishop to g4 — we're not too worried about the bishop takes c2, that's not scary.
If we were worried we could play f3, but I don't particularly want to — let's play h3 to chase the bishop away.
If the bishop takes on e2, what should we recapture with? Both pieces can, but I like one more than the other — these are high-level positional decisions a 1700 should start learning to make.
I like taking with the knight; taking with the queen walks into the knight to d4 with tempo, a little unpleasant. And we still don't allow d5 — three defenders on that square to only two attackers.
The queen to b6. A really good setup is not only to reroute the knight to f4 but also to restrict the c6-knight as much as possible.
How do we restrict that knight? A concept I've talked about many times — with this pawn arrangement we play c3, controlling the knight's advance squares.

The knight to e5 is kind of aimless; we could play f4, but that would deprive the knight of that square, so f4 is too hasty. We'd like to develop the bishop to e3 or g5, but we can't yet, because we dropped the b2-pawn. Instead of b3, we play the harmonious queen to c2, which defends b2 and prepares to connect the rooks — it prepares the rook to d1, reinforcing our control of d5, and a rook on d1 is better than a queen there, getting the queen out of the way and freeing the bishop. The knight to c4 is pointless — it prevents our bishop, but b3 chases it whenever we want, so no rush; let's improve first with the rook to d1, then play b3, tired of that knight. Now develop the bishop — not to g5 to trade for the f6-knight and give up our dark-squared bishop, imprudent since we'd be left with a bad light-squared bishop, but the bishop to e3, x-raying the queen. The queen to c6, and a good chance to reinforce control of d5 — not just the knight to f4, but c4, using our pawns to clamp the square, and the knight gets a nicer path through c3 that doesn't interfere with the f-pawn; we're not afraid of weakening d4, since a bishop and a rook guard it. The knight to b4, we move the queen to e2, and to increase central pressure the g4 and g5 plan is interesting, but let's be Russian-school and double rooks, the rook to d2 and d1, staying flexible, no pawns pushed. Black doubles rooks and then resigns — I think he thought I'd moved the rook off a1, leaving a2 hanging.
We take White; Black answers with the French, ...e6.
We build the centre with d4.
Black challenges with d5.
We push e5 — the Advance.
Black strikes at the base with c5.
Instead of the natural c3, we gambit the centre and just develop — the knight to f3.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We keep developing with the bishop to d3, inviting Black to grab the pawn.
Black plays the queen to b6, eyeing the pawns.
We castle — the point is to keep the e5-pawn that clamps Black, and to develop fast.
Black develops the bishop to d7 rather than taking on d4.
We overprotect e5 with the rook to e1.
Black plays ...Nh6, the knight heading for f5.
We play the awkward-looking knight to c3, eyeing the Nb5–d6 route.
Black plays a6.
The thematic leap — the knight to a4, hitting the queen on b6.
Black tucks the queen to a7.
Our knight takes on c5; Black recaptures with the bishop.
We take that bishop with the d-pawn; Black recaptures with the queen — and we've traded off Black's important dark-squared bishop, keeping the two bishops.
We solidify d4 with c3.
Black reroutes the knight back to g8 — very slow.
We develop the bishop to e3.
Black plays the queen to a5.
We gain a tempo with b4.
Black retreats the queen to c7.
The dark-squared bishop slides to c5, controlling the key diagonal and eyeing d6.
Black develops the knight to e7.
The bishop parks on d6, right in Black's gut.
Black plays the queen to c8.
The knight jumps to g5, going for Qh5 and a kingside mating attack.
Black plays the knight to g6.
White opens d4 and we answer with a knight to f6, heading for a King's Indian setup.
White grabs the center with c4.
We fianchetto with g6 — another King's Indian.
And White plays the modest e3.
We complete the fianchetto with a bishop to g7.
White adds b3 — a double-fianchetto setup.
So the first step is to play all the standard King's Indian moves. We castle.

White plays a bishop to b2, and now the big decision I discussed last game: the traditional King's Indian is to prepare d6 and e5, but the modern understanding is that against some setups it's more efficient to play Benoni-style with c5, or even Grünfeld-style with d5. Stay flexible about which pawn break you choose. Against this setup a case can be made for either c5 or preparing e5.

The c5 break tempts, since it would create a bishop standoff with White's king still in the center — but I also want to show the classic King's Indian way, so let's play d6 and carry out the e5 break even with White's bishop already on b2.
White plays a knight to c3, trying to discourage e5 — but the great thing about the King's Indian is you can usually force that break anyway. Still, this changes my thinking a little.

The problem with e5 now is that it allows a queen trade, and I want more than an endgame. So because White played the knight to c3, I like c5 a lot more — after White's standard d5, we have a tactic: a knight to e4, exposing the bishop on b2 and grabbing the bishop pair.
White develops a knight to f3. We're going to pressure White's center, but carefully.

A knight to c6 right now would let White push d5 with tempo, so we reserve it and start with a queen to a5 — a very challenging move, already setting up the knight-to-e4 idea while we play on the queenside.
White plays a bishop to d3, which stops the knight to e4 — but since the bishop didn't go to e2, we now have a bishop-to-g4 idea for the right moment.
And the right moment isn't yet — the whole point of the queen to a5 was to enable a knight to c6, because now we have a tactic against d5.
White pushes d5, and our pieces come together — we're piling serious pressure on d4. A knight to e4 is the thematic idea, but there's a better execution.

Since we're moving the knight anyway, we grab the pawn with a knight capture on d5 — just winning a pawn. It's easy to calculate: a recapture on d5, and then a bishop to c3 with check trades the bishops and leaves White in shambles.
White recaptures on d5.
The bishop takes on c3 with check — and it's very important that it's a check.
White's position collapses. He can't play a queen to d2, a common reflexive blunder here, because it drops the rook on a1 — a bit of whole-board awareness.
White bites the bullet with the king to e2, but it brings little relief. A common mistake is to win a pawn and rest on your laurels — dropping back or trading knights — but we have a better way.

Don't forget our knight is hanging, but we don't want to stop at one pawn while White's position is collapsing. The instinctive move is a knight to b4 — it hits the pawn, pressures the bishop, and sits very stably.
White is lost. After a rook to c1, we have a really pretty move.
You might expect a knight capture on d5, but I prefer a capture on a2 — it also hits the rook, and if White takes our queen we recapture with a fork.
White takes and walks right into it, and we win — up a ton of material.
The rest is easy: we have a big queenside majority and the extra exchange.
The next step is to open files for our rooks.

A bishop to g4 trading minor pieces is fine, but to win efficiently I want to open a rook's file. Playing a5 immediately creates a weak square on b5 for White's bishop — pedantic here, but let's start with a bishop to d7 to make the a5-a4 push smoother.
Now we play a5 — f5 is worse, because pushing to f4 lets White keep things locked up.
White plays a bishop to c2.
Obviously we push b5.
And a4, creating a passed pawn and opening the b-file.
We'll occupy the b-file with our other rook.
White plays a knight to d2.
If White aims for c4, that's no problem — a bishop to b5 pins and pressures the knight.
It doesn't win the knight, but it trades it off, letting our pawn inch forward.
Just trading — I'm playing quickly here.
Everything is simple now — we want to push the pawn toward a2.
A rook to b4, forcing the bishop back.
And a rook to b2, tying the bishop down; if it moves again, a2.
The bishop moves, we push to a2, and it's easy.
People are taught to trade pieces, so they'd give up the a-pawn — but that takes longer to convert, and there's no reason to give it up.
The easier win is to chase the bishop with the other rook, a rook to a4, and push the c-pawn.
This is dull for advanced players, but c3, c2...
The last step is just to get this rook to b1.
A rook to b4.
We don't care what our opponent is doing.
And the pawn promotes.
We recapture on g6.
And our opponent resigns — a simple game. The big blunder came on move nineteen, but it happened because we chose the right pawn break.
White plays the bishop to c4 — popular below master level because players default to their anti-e5 Italian moves. Against this Sicilian setup it's ineffective, and the reason is one word: e6.
e6 completely blunts the c4 bishop and makes it look silly — and a later d5 can come with tempo.
To punish the bishop fully we strike with d5, seizing the center with tempo.
The light-squared bishop's placement dictates our whole development. We can't lead with the dark bishop — it would drop d5 — so we bring the g8-knight out first.
teaches: let the key piece decide the move order

notes.explains: The knight to f6 is natural — the knight to e7 would just block in the dark-squared bishop. Don't rediscover the wheel; put the pieces on normal squares.
c4 is White's first real error — a weakening move that pretends to fight for the center but only helps us.
We take on c4, and though it opens White's bishop, it leaves him with a backward pawn on d2 and an open d-file to lean on — and we get the open-center game the Sicilian wants.
teaches: open the center; saddle White with a backward d-pawn

notes.explains: The bishop goes to its most active square, d6 — and it's safe, because if White tries to fix the weakness with d4, everything trades and the bishop check on b4 picks up his queen.
teaches: Bd6 works: the Bb4+ trade-down motif

notes.explains: White plays d3, and now we combine development with prophylaxis.
h6 stops White's bishop from reaching g5 — quiet, Petrosian-style prophylaxis. And there's no fear of a sac on h6 with White so undeveloped.

The bishop to g4 pins, and it's especially juicy because the pawn on d3 denies White the Be2 unpin — the pin simply sticks. Now we threaten the knight into d4 or e5, either of which lets us capture on f3 and wreck White's kingside pawns.
teaches: a pin White can’t break, then Nd4/Ne5 to smash f3

notes.explains: We take White; Black plays the Modern with ...g6.
We grab the centre with d4; Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7.
We play c3, a solid Advance-French-like setup.
Black plays e6.
We develop the bishop to d3.
Black plays d5.
We lock the chain with e5.
Black develops the knight to e7.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black strikes with c5.
We castle.
Black closes with ...c4.
We retreat the bishop to c2.
Black castles.
We play the rook to e1.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We develop the knight to d2.
Black develops the bishop to d7; we reroute the knight to f1.
Black plants the knight on f5.
We develop the bishop to g5, hitting the queen.
Black challenges with f6.
We take on f6; Black recaptures with the bishop.
We take the bishop on f6.
Black recaptures with the queen.
We reroute the knight to e3.
Black expands with b5.
We jump the knight to g4, hitting the queen.
Black tucks the queen to g7.
We bring the queen to d2.
Black plays h5, stopping Ng4.
We plant a knight on e5.
Black takes on e5.
We recapture with the knight.
Black plays the bishop to e8.
We double on the e-file with the rook to e2.
Black plays the knight to h6.
We play h4, prying at the kingside.
Black plays ...Ng4.
We take the knight on g4.
Black recaptures with the h-pawn; we sacrifice on e6, ripping open the king.
Black returns the bishop to d7.
The rook grabs on g6.
We've been playing d4 religiously — d4, and a Queen's Gambit.
He declines with c6 — the Slav; I don't think we've faced it, or maybe once.
introduce you to it. We can reach it through c-takes-d5, or through the knight to c3 — that's the Boor variation. Take on d5.
c-takes-d5 — the pure way of reaching this position.
Now we play the knight to c3. Whether we can play this line hinges on Black playing the main move, the knight to f6; if he plays the knight to c6, we have a second, also very dangerous idea.

The knight to f6. This is the Exchange Slav — following main-line theory it results in a very colourless position, a lot of pre-arranged draws; after the knight to f3 and the knight to c6 you get a symmetrical position that draws about seventy-five percent of the time. But recently people have started playing the Exchange Slav for a win — this line has been around for decades, informally named after a master who championed it, and it's the move f3.

If you're seeing this for the first time, this move should feel crazy — it violates essentially all principles of development. But that's exactly why it contains so much venom: people don't realise how dangerous Black's position can get, and how fast. Black has several ways to equalise, but the vast majority of players below 2200, and even 2000s, get completely lost in the complications. The idea of f3 should be obvious — to occupy the centre with e4 — but that's only the tip of the iceberg. Most people here play the knight to c6, which isn't necessarily bad, but really lets us carry out the main idea. It's not played at the highest level, because strong players know how to neutralise f3 — I'll show that after the game — and the critical move is not the bishop to f5. I'm not a specialist in the Boor, so our opponent might make a move I don't know.
The knight to c6 — so we ignore it and

continue with our plan, e4. Here you start to understand the main idea. It may seem d-takes-e4 wins a pawn — d-takes-e4, f-takes-e4, Black has two attackers on d4 and White only one defender, so the queen takes d4 wins a central pawn and offers a queen trade. But the point is that after d-takes-e4, you play d5 — an intermezzo a lot of players miss — leading to a very

dangerous position for Black: we play d5, force the knight off c6, and only then recapture on e4, getting a major pawn mass. But all of that is moot, because Black has played e5 — I don't know this move, which probably means it's not correct, but we'll think on our feet. Logically, White's choices are limited to really one move; it doesn't make much sense to
take on d5 — if we play e-takes-d5, at the very least Black takes the pawn on d4, establishing a knight in the centre. So the only reasonable move is d-takes-e5.

The knight takes e5 — a critical moment. A couple of candidate moves jump out. The most obvious is e-takes-d5, winning a pawn — but the drawback is that our development isn't great, the main flaw of the Boor. After e-takes-d5 I'm worried about the bishop to c5, developing to a really nice square, preventing us from castling. So set e-takes-d5 aside. Noticing this knight configuration should lead to a typical, universal idea: play f4 to chase one knight away, then e5 to drive the wedge and chase the other, creating a central pawn chain — that looks a lot more appealing than taking on d5. So I think f4 is correct. Why not develop the bishop while doing the same? Because

the bishop to f4 — if the knight drops back to g6, the bishop on f4 will be hanging; doing it with the pawn is generally safer. Let's go f4 — I'm confident it's best, which probably means it's wrong, but at least it makes logical sense. The bishop to g4 isn't dangerous, that's just one-move-itis.

The bishop to g4 simply creates a one-move threat against the queen, which we parry a million ways — the queen to b3 or the queen to a4 with check. Now, the fact that he's played the knight to c6 increases the appeal of taking on d5, because now it comes with tempo. After e-takes-d5, probably the knight to b4; but there's another interesting option, and a way to trade queens by force — even after the trade, though, our king could be a sitting duck. The main deterrent to e5 is the counter d4: after e5, d4, we take the knight on f6, Black takes on c3, we trade queens with the queen takes d8 with check, the knight to d8, b-takes-c3, g-takes-f6 — evaluate that endgame: both sides have a pawn deficiency, but Black's kingside pawns are worse than our queenside ones, and White has a small
initiative — we can quickly get the bishop to b5 with check, and it seems easier for us to castle than for Black. So I think e5 is the wisest continuation.

what's so scary about this position, beyond Black's lead in development. Maybe there's a crazy idea leaving that knight where it is and playing the bishop to c5, accelerating development. But the knight to g4 is on the board — and I'm beginning to see why we might be in trouble. What I underestimated is that after the queen takes d5, Black has the weird-looking queen to b6, and suddenly our queen is left stranded in the centre and Black threatens a devastating check on f2 — he gets his pieces out so quickly. So we need to amend our strategy: develop at all costs, accelerate before worrying about the d5-pawn. How can we supercharge development? Can we develop with tempo, attacking a piece?

We can play the bishop to e2. The crazy thing is that the bishop to e2 doesn't actually carry a threat, because even if we take on g4, Black responds with the queen to h4 with check, forking the king and the bishop — but that leads to a queen trade, and after g3, the queen takes g4, a queen trade should be in White's favour, since we're behind in development. On the other hand, giving up our light-squared bishop is problematic given how many weak light squares we have. The move I'm most worried about is the advanced bishop to c5,

because he'd have to sense that the bishop takes g4 meets the queen to h4 with check, and just continue developing as if nothing's the matter. The bishop to c5 is very, very dangerous. Let me spell out why the bishop takes g4 is so unappetising: the bishop takes g4, the queen to h4 with check, g3, the queen takes g4 — the queens are off, but our king is still devastatingly weak, and Black can swing the knight into d4, too many threats, and we don't get to complete our development. So the best move here might be the queen takes d5 — the trickiest move you can play: we take a pawn, attack the bishop, and after the queen takes d5, the knight takes d5, we're also threatening a fork on c7. Black has the knight to f2, but that's bad, because we

take the bishop and then trap the knight on h1. If Black plays the queen takes d5 first and then the knight to f2, we both essentially take each other's rooks and then both try to get our knights out of the corner. The bishop to f2 with check — I was not expecting that move.

The bishop check — okay, I'll bite, the king to f1. We're pretty close to getting mated here, but I think the king is safe for the time being. The bishop to f2 might have been a mistake, unless there's a ridiculous follow-up like the knight to e3 with check — but after g3 with check we can already take on e3 and trade queens, White probably still worse but defensible. The other problem of putting minor pieces so close to the king is the contact, so the bishop takes g4 has become a serious threat; the bishop on f2 is a type-two undefended piece, defended by one piece that's also under fire. The queen to h4 is possible, but then we develop with tempo, the knight to f3. The queen to b6 might be best — it protects the bishop and builds a battery threatening the bishop takes g1 and the queen to f2.

After the queen to b6, we'll have to find a way to defend the f2-square with another piece — but let's cross that bridge when we get there. Our opponent's already getting really low on time, which is good.

I think we have to go the knight to h3 — I don't see another move; we develop the knight, but most importantly we defend the f2-square, taking the sting out of any bishop move Black could come up with.

This bishop out to c4 is the Italian-style idea against the Sicilian — but it simply doesn't work the same way here. The clean reply is e6, blunting the bishop's diagonal and quietly readying a central break.
We take White; Black meets our king's pawn with ...e5.
We build the centre with d4.
Black takes on d4.
We offer c3 — the Danish Gambit.
Black takes on c3, accepting.
We develop the bishop to c4 — the heart of the Danish.
Black plays the queen to e7 — targeting our pawn, but with nothing else developed it's a poor way to do it, and it blocks in his own bishop.
We recapture on c3 with the knight — two pieces out already, and that queen on e7 is a liability.
Black plays c6.
We develop the knight to f3. If ...d5 comes, so much the better — with our lead in development we want the centre opened.
Black plays h6 — you can't abandon development like this; it will backfire in a few moves.
We simply castle — no need for wild sacrifices; completing development already does us a huge favour.
Black plays d6, the lesser evil. Now for a little creativity — rather than the murky e5 break with a sacrifice on d5, notice the queen and king sitting on the same file.
We slide the rook to e1 — queen and king share the e-file. The e4-pawn is in the way for now, but this sets up the knight to d5.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
The knight leaps to d5 — not really a sacrifice, since ...cxd5 is met by exd5, reopening lines and prying open the e-file.
Black takes the knight, a pawn landing on d5.
We recapture on d5, and now the bishop on e6 is attacked — once it falls the whole position caves in.
Black finally develops the knight to f6 — but here developing is the decisive mistake.
We take the bishop, our pawn landing on e6.
Black tries the knight to e4.
We simply take it with the rook.
Black plays f6.
The knight swings to h4, eyeing the juicy light squares — g6 is coming.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We drop the knight into g6, heading straight for the rook.
Black plays the queen to c7; the knight crashes in and takes the rook — up a rook and a piece, it's time for Black to resign.
The Ruy Lopez — the bishop to b5, pinning the defender of e5.
Black grabs space with b5. It's the Norwegian idea, and it's inaccurate — it sends the bishop where it wanted to go anyway while Black is still undeveloped.
teaches: ...b5 loses time when Black is behind

notes.explains: The bishop retreats to b3 — its ideal square — and Black's pieces are still at home.
The rule when your opponent is underdeveloped: open the center as fast as possible. So we strike with d4 to shred it open.
teaches: open the center against a lagging opponent

notes.explains: Now the knight to g5 is strong — with the center tense it still targets f7, and a defensive d5 plunges Black into a lost race to castle. This is the revisit-the-move method: a move that didn't work a moment ago can be exactly right once the circumstances change.
teaches: revisit a move when the position shifts

notes.explains: The clean intermezzo is the bishop taking on f7 — a free pawn that drags the king into the open — rather than the knight capture, which would only trade queens.
teaches: Bxf7+: win a pawn and expose the king

notes.explains: We follow with f3, defending the queen with tempo and forcing the enemy bishop to declare itself.
Black's bishop to h5 actually helps us — our bishop was stranded on f7, and this hands us a free tempo to snap it off.
Now we close the center with d5 — normally wrong with the enemy king exposed, but here for one concrete purpose: to plant a knight on e6, then reopen the position with f4 to even greater effect.
teaches: a purposeful center-close to win the e6 outpost
plans: Ne6 outpost, then f4 to reopen the f-file

notes.explains: The knight settles on e6 — an absolute monster of an outpost, right in the heart of Black's position.
We castle to prepare f4 methodically — the king gets safe and the rook is ready for the f-file that's about to open.
Black's c6 is no worry: the pawn on e4 defends d5, so a capture there doesn't win anything — it just opens the e-file for us.
teaches: the pawn chain holds; the capture only helps us

notes.explains: f4 reopens the center and pries open the f-file straight at the exposed king.
The cleanest finish — the knight takes with a threat on the queen, then collects on h5: now we're up a piece AND still attacking, the best kind of insurance if the attack ever stalls.
teaches: convert into a material lead while keeping the attack

notes.explains: White plays a knight to c3 — the Vienna.
And we answer with the traditional knight to f6. This is still very much theory.

f4 — the Vienna Gambit, hugely popular lately thanks to Levy's course and a wave of content. Every e5 player needs to know how to meet it. People confuse it with the King's Gambit, but the difference is the two knights already out on c3 and f6 — which means accepting the gambit is terrible, because White shoves the pawn to e5 and our knight has to slink back to g8.
So Black has only one good move: counter-strike in the center with d5. It fits the classic rule — when your opponent is pushing pawns on the flank and loosening his king, you hit back in the center.
White captures on e5.
And we recapture with a knight on e4 — common, well-known theory. Now White has two tries.
A knight to f3 is the old move.
We make a developing move and keep the knight on e4 — no trading on c3 unless forced. A bishop to c5 is a fine choice: it threatens a knight fork on f2 and guards that square.
This might look dumb, since we walk right into d4, letting White grab the center with tempo and chase the bishop — but there's a catch.

d4 exposes the a5-e1 diagonal, so we swing the bishop to b4. Yes, moving a piece twice breaks a rule, but White gave us license by pushing so many pawns — here quality of development beats speed. Now we pressure the knight from two directions and threaten a capture on c3 that would fork the king and rook, forcing White to defend.

A bishop to d2 is White's best, but then we capture it with our knight, keeping the bishop pair and continuing to press the center with a later c5. To my knowledge this is the best way to equalize against the knight-f3 Vienna.

We eliminate the bishop and White recaptures with the queen. Now several solid options: a bishop to g4, a bishop to e6, or c5 against d4. I want to keep it solid, and I especially don't want a bishop to f5, because a bishop to d3 trades off our light-squared bishop — and I want to preserve the bishop pair, a genuine asset.
So the light-squared bishop develops to e6 — solid, completing our development quietly, with c5 still available down the line.

Where should the bishop go? Most would drop it to a5 to keep the pin, but that's an inaccuracy — White plays b4, and after the bishop retreats to b6 it's hemmed in by White's pawns, and, crucially, c5 becomes nearly impossible.
So we drop the bishop back to e7 instead, keeping c5 alive. White can still push b4, but now it comes without tempo — so it carries no threat, and we can undermine it with our own pawns.
The classic undermining move is a5 against a b4 push.
Let's continue developing — we castle.

White castles, and we have a major choice. We can play c5, which I've praised, but we can also aim for the other break most people are reluctant to try: f6. The reason is that White's e5 pawn hangs over us like the sword of Damocles, clamping our pieces and cutting communication between the flanks.

The best way to prepare f6 is to develop the knight — but to d7, not c6, so we keep c5 in reserve and the knight covers f6. It slightly loosens d5, but White can't pile on it, and we can always defend with c6.
We could build a little pawn chain with c6 if needed, so d5 is no worry. White plays a knight to d1.
White is probably rerouting the knight to e3, but that doesn't stop f6 — now is the perfect moment to push it and undermine e5. If White doesn't capture, we take on e5 ourselves.

White recaptures on f6, but that leaves the e5 pawn isolated — it loses the support of d4. Between the recaptures, a rook to f6 is awkward, so it's a knight or bishop capture: the knight recapture heads for the fine central e4 square, and though it allows a knight to g5, that's harmless — we drop the bishop to d7 and chase with h6.

So we recapture on f6 with the knight — the clearest path to a good position, always seeking the best square for a piece. Don't suffer from one-move-itis, fearing a move just because it makes a threat: moves aren't good simply because they threaten something.
White plays a knight to f2 — a good move; the position is fairly balanced. In these quiet, symmetric structures the best strategy is to find pieces that can be improved.
Our bishop can be repositioned from e7 to d6 — a better square, controlling more, discouraging a knight to e5, and clearing the e-file for a rook.
White mirrors with a bishop to d3. It's equal. We coordinate our rooks: a queen to d7, then a rook to e8, centralizing everything.
A queen to d7 — it defends the e6 bishop, so a rook to e1 no longer carries a threat and we can safely bring our own rook to e8. I've soured on c5, since White just meets it with c3.
White plays a rook to e1.
We do the same, a rook to e8 — totally equal. This is where 1700-level players often start to go wrong, unable to keep the tension without weakening.
White plays c3. Do we have a long-term plan? Not really — plans are overrated.

We play c6 to protect d5 and open the c7 square for our queen, so if a knight comes to g5 we needn't take it — we drop the queen aside. In open-center positions like this it's hard to form a plan, and you don't need one yet: both sides improve pieces until the confrontation comes.
White plays a bishop to c2 — a fine move eyeing a knight to d3. Our light-squared bishop is clearly worse than White's, so I want to trade it off.
A bishop to f5 — trading our worst piece for White's better one, and starting a direct confrontation: the rooks stare at each other and tension builds, fertile ground for tactics.
We recapture on e8 with the rook — the queen recapture would just drop the bishop. The pawn structure is dead symmetrical with the e-file open, so this will be a tough position to squeeze.
White captures on f5.
We recapture with the queen. These boring positions are exactly the ones you must learn to play without doing anything dumb — squeezing equal positions is an inevitable skill.

White plays a rook to e1, posing a decision: trade rooks, decline with a rook to f8 (which cedes the open file), or the option I like — block with a knight to e4, creating tactical tension. What bothers me is a queen to d3, hitting the undefended rook on e8.

We take the risk with a knight to e4, betting on a blunder. The key move behind everything is a rook to e6 — it solves our one problem, keeping the knight on e4 safe by guarding e8, and it prepares a rook lift to h6, because the bishop already eyes h2 and if the f3 knight ever moves, h2 becomes a fatal weakness. After White's c4 I first looked at a clearance sacrifice, a bishop capture on h2, but the combination needs setting up. So we play g5, aiming to push g4 — that both weakens f2 and, by forcing the f3 knight away, weakens h2; and White's king is nearly out of defenders, so opening our own kingside is safe when nobody's around to exploit it. After g4 the f3 knight is paralyzed, because moving it drops the f2 knight, and White's king is in serious trouble. The finish: a bishop capture on h2 forces the king there, then g3 forks king and knight; after the pawns trade we lift a rook to h6, and a rook to h1 is mate that White can do nothing about, since the f2 pawn is defended twice. It's objectively winning — pick the simple win over the beautiful one.

A framing note before the theory: if you already have an answer to the London that makes you comfortable — a central strike, a fianchetto, whatever — keep playing it. What follows are proposals, not a demand to tear up a repertoire that already makes you happy.

The opponent has a handful of tries against the early c-pawn break: an immediate capture, which is rare and simply not good; the ambitious central push to d5; the modest c3; and the topical e3. Knowing which is which is half the battle.
Standard Accelerated Dragon theory — the fianchetto is set and Black is fully mobilized.
The move here is simply to castle and complete development before doing anything committal.
a5 is the point: it grabs queenside space and, more importantly, prepares a4.
notes.plans: Follow with a4 to harass White's pieces and undermine e4.

notes.explains: a4 distracts one of the two pieces guarding e4 — and if the resulting trade favors us, we snap off the central e4-pawn in return for our flank pawn.
notes.teaches: Chase away a defender of the enemy centre; swapping a wing pawn for a central pawn is a good bargain.

notes.explains: The main line runs into Nb5 and Bb6, hitting our queen and rook and handing White the initiative — but in exchange we've pocketed the central pawn, a fair trade.
notes.teaches: Accept a temporary initiative against you when the compensation is a permanent central pawn.

notes.explains: d6 shores up the position; next we round up the offside knight with Nf6 and untangle.
notes.plans: Reclaim the knight with Nf6 and consolidate the extra centre pawn.

notes.explains: First, move the rook out of the attack with Ra6 before anything else — safety before ambition.
After the trades, occupy the centre with d5, defend it with a rook, reinforce with e6, and reroute the c6-knight via a5 to the fine c4 square.
notes.plans: Build the centre with d5/e6 and improve the knight toward c4.

notes.explains: We open with the queen's pawn. Black's e6 offers a French transposition, but as a d4 player we're under no obligation to oblige.
teaches: e6 has transpositional potential, not a French requirement

notes.explains: Black tries a strange b5 — a Benko-flavored pawn sacrifice that isn't really a known line.
We just take the pawn. Against an obscure gambit, don't agonize over why — simply grab the material and develop.
teaches: accept and develop against an unknown gambit

notes.explains: The knight to c3 is the flexible choice — it protects the extra b5-pawn and keeps e4 in reserve.
teaches: develop while guarding the extra pawn

notes.explains: The bishop to f4 leans on the c7-pawn — and our pawn on b5 clamps that backward pawn in place, so any ...c6 just liquidates into us staying a pawn up.
teaches: fix and pressure the backward c7 pawn

notes.explains: e3 and the bishop to d3 give us ideal development — everything on its best square, a clean pawn to the good.
A little prophylaxis: h3, taking the sting out of any ...Nh5. We can easily afford it, given how passively Black has played.
teaches: you can afford a quiet move against passive play

notes.explains: The knight centralizes on e5, clamping down on Black's whole position.

Black's knight to c6 looks like the best knight in the world — pawn-supported and central — but it can be undermined by ...a6 or a bishop to b7, so it's not as good as it looks. A tempting move isn't automatically a good one.
The trap: the bishop to e5. After the trade, the knight on f6 has lost its d7 retreat — the queen's knight took it — and it's trapped, because the e4 square is guarded twice and attacked only once.
teaches: trap the knight by taking its retreat square

notes.explains: Up two clean pawns, the winning plan is simple technique: make a passed pawn on the queenside, give away nothing to counterplay on the kingside, and march it home. One elegant finish is to stalemate the enemy king with your own, then feed it just enough pawns to keep it in moves until you promote.
teaches: convert two pawns up: passer + no counterplay

notes.explains: We're going to play d4 and a London System. d4, d5, the bishop to f4.
e3 — let's play a couple of Londons.
the knight to c6.
We're going to play the knight to c3 here and transpose into the Jobava London — I've done that several times now.
c-takes-d4.
e-takes-d4.
You already know the drill — this knight can potentially go to b5, but we don't want the knight to b5 here. Why is the knight to b5 innocuous after the bishop to f5?
He played the bishop to f5 correctly because of a specific move — not the queen to a5, because of c3, but the rook to c8; it's not actually the check that matters. The knight to f3.
So now we basically want control over this diagonal.

What's blocking the bishop to b5 from being a check? The knight on c6. How do we get rid of it? We slam our knight into e5 — one of the key ideas of the Jobava. Now, this bishop on f5 is actually in more trouble than it appears, and the idea that exploits its hidden vulnerability is g4 and h4. And

it's not that Black loses the bishop, but he may have to play h6, and if the bishop is on g6 and the knight on e5, then the knight takes g6 forces f-takes-g6, which is tremendously awkward. We're spoiled for choice — let's see how

this works, g4. I had a really cool over-the-board game exactly like this where I beat a 2500. There's a lot to unpack, but everybody should see the bishop is being attacked. Black has a complicating intermediate move that seems to offer a solution: the knight takes e5. After the knight takes e5, d-takes-e5, both the knight and the bishop are hanging, but Black plays the knight takes g4 — and at the very end of that line, don't forget the main idea of g5: the bishop to b5 with check is devastating, because there's nothing to block that diagonal, and the king has to move out to e7.
That's just absolutely devastating — when the king moves out to e7 in the opening, that's generally not a good sign. Now of course we play the typical f3, attacking
the bishop, forcing it back to g6. I'll show everything after the game.
The bishop to g6, then h4 — that's the bottom line — and here we go, h5.
Now we play the knight takes g6. How do we exploit the fact that the g6-pawn is weak?
The bishop to d3 is correct, attacking the pawn — and of course the knight takes d4 is not possible now.
The knight takes d4 isn't really a threat, because the bishop takes g6 with check exposes the attack on the knight. So how do we arrange our pieces here to increase
the pressure — while not losing sight of the fact that we haven't completed our development? We're going to go g5 here, which isn't an intuitive move — why close down the position?
It may appear White is the one attacking; the reason I'm doing this is to give myself a little time that I'll use to prepare castling long.
So we go the queen to d2 — remember, the knight takes d4 isn't worrisome, I can just ignore that move entirely.
Can I ignore this and castle here, or do we need to deal with it and take the bishop? Yes,
no — that's why we put the queen on d2. Now we castle long.
the knight to e7.
