We bring the rook into the game — the final piece comes in.
the knight to f5.
Let's get rid of the knight, and now a very typical winning move — this move crushes when we have a pawn on g5 and the e6-pawn is

weak, very thematic, and this should be automatic to you in many of these positions. Boom goes the dynamite — g6 with check, isolating the king; the king is the second-worst defender after the queen, because it can be easily attacked and a check must be dealt with by definition. If the king tries to cling to the pawn with the king to f6 or e7, your tactical detector should be on high alert.
And the king stepping into the same diagonal as the queen should also catch your attention. Now we play the rook takes e6.
The bishop takes f4, the queen recaptures — this is also something that should alert our metal detectors,
because a mate on e8 is actually very likely, and we already have distraction sacrifices that help create the possibility. The rook to h6.
The idea is of course to double the rooks.
Now we don't need to overthink things — all we need to do is simply collect the
harvest, as they say in Russian. Let's take on d5 — no need to do anything outlandish in such a position.

We simply want to improve our pieces until an opportunity to win presents itself naturally. How do we win this? Play gradually rather than doing anything crazy. Let's think logically: how do we get our rook to e8? The number-one item on the wish list is

to get a rook to e8, and we know we should employ the least valuable piece for the task. You're making the mistake of employing the queen, but we can employ the knight — the knight to c7 — and the reason this is better than the queen to e3 is that we actually win Black's queen; involving the queen isn't good, because ultimately we'd capture with the queen and offer a queen trade, and we want to win the queen, not trade it. The queen to f5 doesn't work — close, but no. A rook immediately would be insane — he'd just take. g7 with check, and he resigns.

The knight to c3 is a springboard into many systems — you'll know it as the Grand Prix introduction, but it's also a sly move order, because next move the other knight can come out and transpose straight back into an Open Sicilian. So how you answer it depends entirely on which Sicilian you play.

The underrated reply is an early a6 — most reach for a knight or a central pawn, but a6 makes wonderful sense for a Najdorf player and is a fine way to meet the Closed Sicilian and the Grand Prix alike.
The whole point of a6 is a quick b5 — grabbing queenside space early and, just as importantly, handing the light-squared bishop a natural home on the long diagonal.

Now the classic Sicilian setup: the central pawns settle on d6 and e6, a Scheveningen-style shell that controls a cluster of key squares. It looks passive but it's the heart and soul of the opening — and the knight can come out to f6 without fear, since the central break just runs into a loose bishop.
d6 gives maximum flexibility and, crucially, opens a d7 square for the other knight — in these structures it belongs there rather than on c6, where it would clumsily block the fianchettoed bishop.

This is the moment for the queen to c7, and it's played for layered reasons: it connects the rooks, and paired with the knight on d7 it double-guards e5 — smothering the central break that would otherwise be so dangerous. It's simply a better home than the back rank.

You'll feel the kinship with a hedgehog or hippo here — the d6-and-e6 pawns give that flavour, though it's really its own animal. And a castling caution: going long is risky, since those queenside pawns are hooks the opponent can lever open; short is safer, though long is never off the table.

A deliberately provocative move — h5 to stop the kingside pawn expansion, keeping the king parked in the centre for now. It's risky, but the aim is to be as annoying as possible and see how the opponent reacts.

When the opponent props the centre with c3, the thing to notice is that it has quietly weakened d3. And here's the key insight — you don't only attack a weak pawn with pieces, you undermine it with your own pawns. That points toward a c-pawn thrust to c4.
But capture on c3 first — playing the thrust immediately would leave the advanced b-pawn hanging. A small preparatory recapture, and then the undermining pawn goes in with a clear conscience.

Now the pawn arrives and the centre creaks. See how the minor pieces suddenly make sense — the queen guards the pawn, the bishop and knight both rake e4, and where they were biting on granite before, d3 is now a glaring weakness. That's the danger of shrinking your own pawn chain: the fewer links, the easier it is to undermine.

Don't snatch the weak pawn on reflex — the move is a knight to c5, bringing a piece into the attack and piling on d3, now genuinely threatening the capture. If the pawn advances to dodge, the central capture on e4 forces matters.

And a permission worth hearing: you're allowed not to castle at all. When the centre is closed and both wings look dangerous, keeping the king in the middle can be the lesser evil — the only real cost is that the rooks stay disconnected, which is rarely mission-critical.

The centre bursts open, and now it's pure order of operations. Trade on g2 first — that eliminates the bishop headache, and if the opponent grabs the knight the rook is simply captured with an extra exchange in hand. Clear the simplest question before weighing the harder one.

Of the remaining captures, the pawn recapture keeps the centre intact and stays a pawn up, and the pawn mass shields the king while the opponent's own shelter is far more exposed with the g-file about to open.

Recapturing toward the centre with the pawn is counter-intuitive but correct — in the Sicilian, keeping pawns pristine is rarely the priority. Shifting a pawn onto the f-file actually improves the structure: more pawns mean a safer king, it pries open the g-file as a direct road to the enemy king, and the front doubled pawn becomes a free battering ram to push while the one behind guards home. And it sets up the e4 outpost, the crown of the whole plan.

The pawn to d5 does three jobs at once — it cements the monster knight, springs the queen to life, and adds a third attacker to the target. And once you're this far ahead, remember the value of simplification: trading eliminates calculation, and don't fret about conceding a passed rook-pawn — it's a marathon from promotion while the centre steamrolls. In the technical phase, a pawn can even be used to cut the enemy bishop off a key square near the queening line.
The Nimzo-Indian — Black pins the c3-knight to fight for the centre.
f3 is the Sämisch, and its whole idea is simple: build toward e4.
notes.teaches: The Sämisch f3 exists for one reason — to prepare the e4 break.

notes.explains: a3 chases the bishop, and after it takes on c3 we get the Sämisch structure. The entire game now revolves around one question: can White get e4 in under the right conditions?
notes.teaches: In the Sämisch, everything hinges on whether White can achieve e4 safely.

notes.explains: So every move aims at e4 as fast as possible — and first the kingside must develop and castle, so the king isn't caught in the centre when the position bursts open.
notes.teaches: Before a central break, tuck your king away so opening the position doesn't expose it.

notes.explains: c4 is a mistake for Black — it releases the tension, and the d4-pawn now sits better protected, so White can aim everything at e4. Keeping the tension would have made e4 far harder to prepare.
notes.teaches: Don't resolve a central tension when it only frees your opponent to complete his own break.

notes.explains: Ng3 goes in before e4 — the knight is bound for the strong f5 square, and preparing e4 patiently makes it land far harder. Be a good Russian schoolboy: castle first.
notes.teaches: Improve your pieces to their attacking squares before the break; a prepared push hits twice as hard.

notes.explains: Now e4 — the break the whole setup was built for — and we steamroll the kingside.
e5 rams forward, locking Black's knight out and seizing a huge space advantage.
The pawn storm rolls with f4 and f5 — and en passant is worth it here, even though it hurts to part with the pawn mass. You have to transform an advantage at some point; kill your darlings.
notes.teaches: Convert a space advantage into concrete gains when the chance comes; don't cling to a pretty pawn chain.

notes.explains: f6-check pries the king's cover open and drags more pieces into the attack.
And the pin is deadly precisely because no pawn protects the pinned knight — so we simply pile up on it, win the piece, and transform into a won endgame a piece up.
notes.teaches: A pin is fatal when no pawn defends the pinned piece; stack attackers and collect it.

notes.explains: Against the French we play the Tarrasch — the knight to d2 rather than c3. The whole point is that it leaves the c-pawn free to come to c3 and reinforce the center.
teaches: Nd2 keeps c3 for the pawn chain

notes.explains: We grab space with e5, an Advance-style pawn chain that Black must attack.
And there's the payoff — c3 buttresses the d4-pawn, the very reason the knight went to d2 instead of c3.
The bishop takes its most active diagonal, d3, aimed at the kingside.
Black plays f6 — a famous mistake. It opens the very diagonal our queen wants, the road to h5.

The knight to g5 is the key blow — a distracting sacrifice that also attacks e6, so Black can't both meet that threat and stop the queen reaching h5. And he can't castle out of it, because his own bishop blocks the king's escape.
teaches: a distraction sac to force the queen to h5

notes.explains: White develops the knight to f3, hitting our pawn.
We defend with a knight to c6.
A bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez.
We head for the main line with a6, questioning the bishop.
White retreats to a4.
And we develop the knight to f6, hitting e4.
White castles — Morphy's move, the main line ever since. The main reply isn't a bishop to c5.
A bishop to c5 is the Møller and a bishop to b5-side is the Archangel; the main move is the modest bishop to e7.
White plays a rook to e1 — and now it actually poses a threat.
You might think it's time for d6, but first we throw in the very useful b5 — grabbing queenside space and forcing the bishop back.
White retreats to b3. Now e5 is no longer hanging, so d6 isn't forced — the main move d6 just opens the bishop, but we can also play the Marshall Gambit.
We castle, going for the Marshall — not moving the d-pawn, hoping to play d5 in one fell swoop. If White plays c3, we can choose the Marshall with d5 or transpose back to the main line with d6.
White plays c3.
So we play the Marshall Gambit — d5, sacrificing a pawn for a raging initiative.
White captures on d5.
We recapture with the knight on d5.
White grabs on e5 — the gambit is that we've sacrificed it.
We take on e5, and White recaptures with the rook.
Our knight on d5 is hanging, so we have to deal with that threat.
The best move is to defend the knight with a pawn — c6. Defending a piece with a pawn is generally the way forward.
White plays d4. Now we need to chase the rook off e5 — it's in our way — while aiming our pieces at White's king.
So a bishop to d6, chasing the rook knowing that once it moves, our pieces are trained on the white king.
The rook retreats, and we bring the queen into the attack with a queen to h4.

White plays g3, and the queen sinks into h3. This is all theory — I'm rusty on it, and White looks out of book too. Our compensation is clear: a development lead and Swiss-cheese light squares around White's king. If his bishop could reach g2, Black would have nothing — but it can't, so those weak light squares are a lasting problem. The immediate threat is a bishop to g4, hitting the queen.
White plays a knight to d2 — not a main line, sensible but awkward.
Now the bishop can't move, and it does nothing against a bishop to g4 — so let's play it and see where his queen goes.
White plays f3, tremendously weakening — and the moment it's played you should start looking for the typical tactic.

So a bishop capture on g3. If White grabs the light-squared bishop instead he gets mated — a queen to h2, the king to f1, a queen to f2 — so he essentially has to take, and then a queen recapture on g3 gives at least perpetual, though I believe we have more.
White plays a knight to f1 — not testing. A big mistake when sacrificing is forgetting you can simply win material.
A bishop capture on e1 — the rook just hangs! We take it, go up the exchange, and the attack rolls on. Black is winning.
White recaptures on g4.
We could retreat the bishop to h4, but that's plain — a rook to e8 does more, defending the bishop and bringing the rook toward e4 to hit g4, potentially crushing.
White captures on d5.
We recapture on d5. The only reason I put the a-rook on e8 was a possible f5 to open the file — otherwise it doesn't much matter.
White plays a bishop to f4. The f5 idea looks really nice here.
So let's play f5, trying to open the f-file. If White answers g5, we get a passed f-pawn that can later push to f4 and accelerate the attack.
White plays a bishop to e5 — a good move. In such positions it's less about exact moves than following a consistent strategy with healthy attacking moves.
White intercepts with a bishop to h4, so our bishop is attacked and must move — but that's no issue; if we open the file, the game ends fast.
White captures on f5.

We recapture, and the f-file is ours with a million threats — a rook to f2 hitting the queen and threatening mate on g2. Its only drawback is that White can give up material to survive a little longer, so a rook to f8 doubling might finish faster. But if you see a move that wins the queen and you know how to convert, just do it — don't rule out a win because it takes a few extra moves.
You get into trouble when you dismiss options just because they feel slow.
We throw in a rook check on f8 to reposition the rook onto the open file.
The king goes to g1. Now the plan is to eliminate White's defensive resource.

We want to stop White from blocking a check with a piece on g5, so we push the h-pawn to take that square under control — White is totally paralyzed — and then lift a rook to g5 to force the king out.
White plays a rook to d1. The classic mistake would be to reflexively push the h-pawn — but keep your eyes peeled for faster wins, like a queen to g4 winning the rook.
We have Black and answer the king's-pawn with e5.
White plays the pawn to f4 — the King's Gambit. There's an incredibly rare reply here, not the capture on f4, not d5, not the bishop to c5.
The pawn to c6 — it looks completely insane, one of the rarest lines against the King's Gambit.
White develops the knight to f3. The pawn to c6 is a waiting move on steroids — a souped-up Caro-Kann where White has badly weakened his kingside with f4.
The pawn to d5 — the whole point of c6, now that we've waited for the knight to commit to f3.
White captures on d5, walking right into it.
The pawn to e4 — the f3-knight, far from productive, is now vulnerable. We recover the pawn and get a monster centre with White's king very weak.
White jumps the knight to e5.
We recapture on d5 — Black is in very good shape.
White gives a check with the bishop to b5 — how should we cover it?
The knight to d7, not to c6 — and we hope White castles, a very common oversight.
White castles — the oversight, leaving loose pieces.
The queen to b6 with check! With f4 played, White is weak on the diagonal, and this wins the bishop and the game.
White plays the pawn to d4.
We take the bishop — we could have captured en passant first, but it doesn't matter.
White plays the knight to c3, keeping the centre closed. We're up a piece; now consolidate.
The queen to a5 — the correct square, holding on to the pawn rather than the queen to d3.
White plays the bishop to d2, x-raying the queen and threatening the knight to take e4 — not the knight to d5, which the queen would just capture.
We cover the pin with the bishop to b4, preparing to remove the c3-knight.
White plays a3 and we take on c3 — the simplest.
White recaptures on c3.
Now we can safely retreat the queen to b6 — the d5-pawn no longer hangs, and we're up a full piece.
White plays the bishop to b4, resiliently — but it won't be enough.
We develop the knight to f6, completing development before worrying about dislodging the bishop.
White plays the pawn to c4. We must be careful — the goal is to castle short, which solves all our problems.
We can't castle yet because of the b4-bishop, so we push the pawn to a5 to kick it out.
White takes on d7. Which piece do we recapture with? Keep the prize in mind — castling — so we deny the bishop the c5-diagonal.
We recapture with the knight on d7 — it covers c5. Taking with the bishop, also winning, would let White's bishop park on c5 and delay our castling.

The bishop out to b5 is slightly offbeat — normally the c-pawn goes first in the London. And here's a deep positional idea: a queen check to a5 doesn't win the bishop, but at this level you play moves that induce a move you want. The whole London rests on d4 being a fortress, and it's rock-solid only once c3 supports it.

So the check induces a knight to c3, which permanently denies the c-pawn that support — and d4 flips from a strength into a weakness. As a bonus the queen stands beautifully active, and there's nothing wrong with leaning on the bishop while you're at it.

Stay active — e6 now would be too passive with development lagging, inviting a central knight leap. The move is a bishop to g4, pinning the knight that props up d4 while developing a piece. Restrain and develop in one stroke.
The bishops come off, and the recapture toward the centre leaves a compact, healthy pawn structure — the kind of solid shell that's a pleasure to play from.

There's a choice of resolving the centre now or playing e6 first — and the guiding rule when unsure is keep the tension. Let the opponent be the one to decide whether to capture; carrying that question is always more of a headache for them than for you.

Take on the knight, or retreat the bishop? The deciding question is whether the opponent would realistically lash out with a weakening kingside pawn push — and the answer is no, there's no reason to fear it. So hold the tension and drop the bishop back.

That pawn thrust weakens the shelter in front of the king. The central knight jump looks intimidating but it's surface-level — it merely hits the loose pawn, which just needs careful defending, sidestepping the tempting queen move that runs into a knight fork.

Now a principle to bank — the rule of piece value: carry out any task with the least valuable piece that can do it. So a rook drops back to defend the pawn. It isn't glamorous, but pieces have to do the dirty work sometimes, and there's nothing wrong with that.

Now it's time to take stock — keep the king in the centre for the moment, and set the priority: to make the open h-file pay, the defending bishop has to be eliminated so the advanced pawn behind it loses its guard.

The obvious knight jump fails to concrete calculation — a trade sequence leaves a pawn hanging with a fork and the queen crashing in. But failing on one move doesn't kill the plan; it only rules out that one route.

So modify rather than abandon — the knight to h5 instead. It temporarily clogs the h-file, but piece placement is temporary while the long-term priority of prying that file open is permanent. Don't confuse a short-term blemish with a real problem.

The knight loops back around, and now the advanced enemy pawn simply can't be held. Distinguishing the temporary from the permanent is the whole art here — you can't make an omelette without cracking a few eggs.
Double the rooks and never surrender the file — a pawn to the good, heavy pressure down the h-file, and every positional trump. Now it's just a matter of precise conversion.
The queens and a pair of rooks come off into a knight endgame a clean pawn up — and now the plan is to open a second front, rolling the queenside pawns forward starting with a5.

A move that looks dreadful — b3, deliberately closing the position — but its purpose is to fix the weakness so it can be targeted. Locking the pawn in place is what makes it a permanent target rather than a runner.

And the point is revealed: the opponent can't stop the knight from reaching d3, and with the weakness now fixed it can't be defended either. One quiet preparatory move set up the decisive infiltration.
We play e5 again, staying with classical openings.
White develops a knight to f3.
We answer a knight to c6.
A knight to c3 — the Four Knights, not my favorite to face.
We develop the knight to f6.
And White throws in a knight capture on e5 — the Halloween Gambit, actually not a bad line and under-covered in books.
We accept, recapturing on e5. We'll play a variation that dodges most of the theory.

White plays d4. The engine's best is to keep the extra piece — retreat the knight to c6, meet e5 with a knight tucked back to g8, and White lacks full compensation — but I'm out of my depth there and suspect our opponent has analyzed it.
So we play a knight to g6 — not to keep the piece, but to give it back.
White pushes e5. The good thing about facing a gambit when you're unsure is that you can always hand the piece back and cash in on development instead.
We don't even move the f6 knight — a bishop to b4 develops as if nothing's the matter.
White captures on f6.

We recapture with the queen. I can't believe Black could be worse here — and gambit players hate a line where you sacrifice the piece back and drain the life out of the position. We'll play a solid, positional style, aiming a later queen to e6 to open lines toward f2.
A classic standoff of queens — you don't want to be the one to release the tension and help your opponent develop, so we won't take on e2; we develop and castle instead.
We recapture on e6 with the d-pawn — it opens the d-file and gives our light-squared bishop air, whereas the f-pawn recapture would leave that bishop boxed in behind pawns on d7 and e6.
White castles long.
A bishop to d7. The position is completely equal — we win it by patience, developing our pieces first.
White plays a3.
We trade on c3 — most people wouldn't, but this has a lot of venom.
White recaptures on c3, and now he's left without a knight in this type of position.
A bishop to c6, onto the long diagonal — the point is that White's bishop on c3 is a bad piece, and we'll launch a campaign against it.
White plays a rook to g1.
A rook to d8. Our plan is to pile on the d4 pawn — double the rooks and reroute the knight to f5, and before long d4 becomes a sitting duck.
White plays g3.
We start doubling with a rook to d7. We'll speed up, since our opponent is playing fast and confidently, but the pressure keeps building.
White plays a bishop to h3. Still equal — and knowing how to outplay strong players from such positions is an essential skill.
A rook to d8, completing the doubling — I don't see what the bishop threatens, so we continue the plan.
White plays a rook to e1.
Now it's time to reroute the knight to e7, heading for d5 or f5.
White plays f4. A knight to d5 might run into f5, so we think carefully.

A very good move is h5, stopping g4 and making it impossible for White to push f5 — a light-square blockade. It looks passive, but it freezes White's pawns; then g6 makes his kingside pawns immobile, and a capture on e6 is nothing to fear since we recapture and White loses his light-squared bishop. Our structure is watertight.
White plays b3. What I want is the c6 square for the knight — it would press d4 even harder. A knight to d5 is a dead end; c6 is the dream.
A bishop to f3 would allow a rook to d3 with tempo, so instead we build a home for the bishop with b6 and drop it back to b7, freeing the knight to reach c6.
White plays c4 — this also lets us push c5 if needed.
We play a knight to c6. White was almost lost but survives with a rook to e4 — very fortunate for him.
White plays a rook to e4. Maybe repeating and rerouting the knight to f5 is a better approach — and d5 could be unpleasant.
A rook to d6. Maybe the h5-and-g6 plan was a mistake, since it weakened the dark squares — I underestimated that, and now we have to spin our way out.
I'm quite concerned about d5 here — I'd totally forgotten it was an idea. We have to be careful not to get mated, but we have resources.
A knight to a5 was my initial idea, and against this very strong player, let's play it.
White plays a bishop to f6. There's a back-rank idea, so we always have to keep a rook guarding the eighth rank, which really limits us. We need to calculate carefully here.
We have to play the capture on d5.
White captures on d8.
We recapture on e4.
White takes on d6.
We recapture on d6. The good thing is that our knight on a5 is a monster, hitting b3.
White plays a king to c2. The knight on a5 gives us a tempo — we can push toward promotion, bring the king to f8, or play the f5 I like, which solidifies the whole pawn chain.
We play a king to f8 — the drawback is a bishop to f6, but it's better than nothing.
White plays a bishop to f6 — incredible tactics for White.
We bring the king closer with a king to e8.
And if the king comes to c3, we'll play d5.
We're playing for a win a pawn up, but White's bishops are strong and he has a lot of time — this will be a real challenge.
A knight back to c6 — now I'm concerned about b5.
White plays a4.
Let's play e3 — inducing b5 has an upside: it fixes the pawns on light squares, so if the king moves away we can play a bishop to b3.
White plays b5. I wouldn't say I'm in trouble — probably equal, but hard to win with Black despite our extra passed pawn on e3.
A knight to e7. If White now plays the king to d4 or d3, we have a bishop to b3. What worries me is a5, a high-level move to shatter our queenside.
White plays a bishop to e5, also very strong, eyeing b8.
It's time for e2 and a bishop to b3 — a bailout.
White plays a king to d2. We can try a bishop to c4, an ambitious try.
We play a bishop to b3. If White plays a bishop to b8 and takes, we can't win — but I see no alternative.
Very well played by my opponent. Let's try a knight to d5.
There are still tricks, but the problem is a bishop to g2 — one more trick up my sleeve.
He plays perfectly right up to the last, then blunders a piece — but this is far from over.
White plays a king to f3.
I apologize for the sparse explanation — I really need to focus to win this.
Even up a piece it's hard — the pawn on b5 ties us down.
h3 is another mistake, because we drop back to e7 attacking the bishop.
We'll take on h3 next and be up a full piece — but I have no time, so it's a tall order.
White plays f6 with check.
It should be a bishop to f5 — we complete that anyway.
Maybe not the cleanest way I'm playing this, but a knight to f6, heading for e4.
We go here to stop the pawn.
The point is that after b7 we stop it with a king to c7.
Now we take on g3 and simply push the h-pawn home.

This guy is clearly legit — an amazingly played game. I'm honestly not proud of my level of play: a couple of misjudgments and flat-out misses, which makes it instructive because I can explain what I missed.
Nf6, the Two Knights, is a very practical intermediate choice — the Fried Liver isn't as scary as its reputation, and there's less tricky theory than after Bc5.
notes.teaches: The Two Knights is a sound practical weapon; the Fried Liver is more bark than bite.

notes.explains: Playing principled chess, we grab on e4 into the Max Lange — the tamer d6 keeps it out of theory but leaves the bishop passive on e7.
The knight is attacked, so d5 defends it, and for a moment Black looks two pawns up and dominant — but this is the Max Lange, and it's all theory.

The century-old point: Nc3 can't be taken — the knight is pinned, and capturing with the pawn drops the queen — so the queen must move, and White recaptures with heavy e-file pressure. The whole line is objectively equal.
notes.teaches: In the Max Lange, White's compensation is the e-file pin, not an advantage — it's dead level with accurate play.

notes.explains: Qh5 is a safe square and x-rays the knight on f3 — never a bad thing in these positions.
notes.teaches: Park the queen where it's safe and quietly x-rays an enemy piece.

notes.explains: The calculation that decides it: after a queen trade, the d4-knight would be guarded only by the rook on e4 — and rooks and queens are terrible defenders, being so easy to chase. So Be7, then f5 shoves the rook along the fourth rank and g5 again, until White must give up the exchange.
notes.teaches: Rooks and queens defend pieces poorly; attack the piece they guard and chase the clumsy defender off.

notes.explains: Qd5 centralizes the queen, hits the rook, and adds a second defender to d4 all at once.
notes.teaches: Prefer the centralizing move that defends and attacks in the same breath.

notes.explains: White opens on the flank with the g3 fianchetto, and the knight-and-d5 setup transposes toward Grünfeld territory.
teaches: flank openings transpose into main structures

notes.explains: We fianchetto in turn with g6, heading for a Grünfeld.
With d4 White steers into the symmetrical Grünfeld fianchetto — a deeply theoretical line. Black can grab the pawn with dxc4 or hold the center with c6; both are heavily played and sound.
We haven't faced the English yet — I'm going to play it in principled fashion. c4, e5, playing the
Reversed Sicilian. As you might know, we play the Alapin Sicilian with White against the Sicilian, and the Reversed Alapin is a very viable system against the English —
and it's quite theoretical, very popular in recent times.
The bishop to g2.

Meeting the c-pawn with e6 heads for a Queen's Gambit Declined structure — and there's a hidden bonus: as a QGD player you barely need to study the English at all, which slashes the amount of theory you have to carry.

Capturing on d5 this early is simply a bad move — it releases the central tension prematurely, hands over better control of the middle, and is completely toothless. It's a sign the opening's ideas aren't fully understood.
There's no single right way to develop, but a fine plan is the bishop to d6 followed, London-style, by c6 — a compact, harmonious shell that's easy to handle in any move order.

Now the question of the light-squared bishop. It wants the good diagonal, but a pawn move to prepare it would weaken the kingside — so instead insert a flexible move first, a rook to e8. It's a square the rook is simply happy on, and it quietly rules out an annoying central knight leap. When unsure, play the move you know can't hurt.

Here's the elegant way to get the bishop to its diagonal without the weakening pawn push: develop to g4, then swing it around via h5 toward g6 — no hurry, it's happy where it sits. And a strategic point on the queenside: most players would automatically stop the pawn expansion, but you can allow it and then freeze the pawn in place, which isn't good for the opponent at all. Then a rook-pawn nudge puts the question to the pinning bishop. If it retreats to a square where a pawn is its lone defender, watch for an overload — one pawn guarding two things at once is a defender stretched too thin. And the meta-lesson of the finish: the hallmark of the great attackers is knowing when to just play simple. Don't chase the brilliancy prize and leave points on the table — a clean pawn grab ends it, and even then order of operations matters: the right capture sequence leaves the opponent unable to recapture in any legal way.
The whole idea is to pile pressure on the d4-pawn immediately — dawdle and you're lost in five moves.
notes.teaches: In the Chigorin, every move must add pressure to d4; slow development loses on the spot.

notes.explains: e5 is the only move — the decisive central strike that makes the opening work.

Against e3 — a passive try — we develop actively with Bg4, adding another attacker to d4. And the key detail to remember: if White plays Nc3, we have Bb4 to neutralize it; without that resource the whole line collapses.
notes.teaches: The Chigorin hangs on the ...Bb4 pin to answer Nc3; know it or the opening falls apart.

notes.explains: Castle long and look at the pressure crashing down on d4 — this really is a good Scandinavian, where the queen goes to h5 instead of a5.
Qh5 is the thematic square: once White castles, Bd6 piles onto h2 for a quick mating attack — and the b4-bishop has done its job, since d5 is no longer a threat.
notes.teaches: Steer the queen to h5 to prepare a bishop-and-queen battery against h2.

notes.explains: White's d5 is bold but bad — he's simply not developed enough to hold it. Nf6 wins the pawn, since dxc6 fails to the pin.
notes.teaches: A pawn thrust unsupported by development is a target, not a threat — win it.

notes.explains: Take the pawn — no calculation needed, just see the pin and the loose rook. Then Bxf3 is the instructive move: strategically it hands over our fine bishop, but tactically it's justified, clearing the e-file to hit the uncastled king with Qe5-check hitting the king and the knight. Chess is a constant interplay between the strategic and the concrete.
notes.teaches: Trade your good bishop when a temporary tactical feature — like an uncastled king on an open file — outweighs the long-term loss.

notes.explains: Black takes the gambit pawn on c4. Main lines are worth learning precisely because an opponent who doesn't know them often just loses out of the opening.

We recover the pawn while developing — the knight to f3, not a queen check on a4. Winning the pawn back is only half the job; you have to develop while doing it, and dragging the queen out early achieves nothing.
teaches: recover the pawn with a developing move, not the queen

notes.explains: e3 is the positional route, opening the bishop to recapture — cleaner here than the knight to c3.
We take the pawn back with the bishop on c4, raking toward f7.
Black hits back with c5, and after the exchange we reach the classic isolated-queen-pawn structure — the same battleground you get from the Queen's Gambit Declined.
teaches: the IQP structure from the QGA

notes.explains: Let's play one more blitz game. e4, c5, the knight to f3.
He's playing the Sicilian; we're going to play the Open Sicilian, which I've been doing.
He plays e5 — the Kalashnikov variation, a pretty common Sicilian; Black strikes in the centre immediately, but the drawbacks are pretty evident.
The drawbacks are that it weakens two squares, principally d6 and d5, and we have to manoeuvre our pieces to exploit them — so the knight to b5 is the main line here.
d6, and then we're going to bring up the
other knight in order to access d5.
and the other weak square that's been created. This is all theory, by the way.
This is all theory, and we've
transposed into what's called the Sveshnikov. Now, what we don't want is for our knight to be easily dislodged from d5.
We want to keep this knight on d5, but what's preventing us is his knight on f6 — so we're going to develop our bishop to eliminate it.
the bishop to e7, the bishop takes f6.
I'm sort of trying to explain why the theory is theory. This knight on a3 everybody should notice is very misplaced — it has no prospects, so
what we're going to do is give this knight some prospects — manoeuvre it somewhere civilised — so we go c3 in order to deploy
this knight through c2; it's not ideal, but at least our knight is now doing something. This is the main line of the Sveshnikov; so far he's been playing all the theoretical moves, kudos to him.

Now, note that c4 is also a move here, but it would weaken the d4-square, though c4 is theoretical too. The other thing to notice is that there's a pawn on b5 sticking out like a sore thumb — how do we go about undermining or exploiting its weakness?

It's a very typical idea, you'll see it in the Ruy Lopez and many openings — we go a4 to break up this pawn and also deploy the rook via the a-file; it's always nice when a piece already participates without you having to move it.

He takes, and we'll take with the queen, and the queen ably performs the task previously fulfilled by the knight. Maybe I should have supported my knight by playing the knight to e3 — that's another way.
He's also given our bishop a very nice square — where can our bishop now go to support the knight?
We were waiting for the square to open up for the bishop — development is not something that should always be rushed; it's a priority, but make sure you're giving your pieces good squares first.

Now he's given up a pawn on a6 — I think we'll just snag that one; that's a free pawn in my book. There's a little pressure down the a-file to be careful of, particularly because this rook is unprotected, but

what I'm seeing is that I can later move my bishop back to b5, and that bishop will simultaneously defend the rook on a4 — so while it's something to keep an eye on, it's not something to be overly concerned about. He takes, we take; he could have taken with the rook, but I don't see a point in shying away from this tension, and even if he attacks the bishop again, we have many ways to defend it — we can defend it with our queen, dropping the queen back to lend additional support. He's good, not going down without a fight, but you can see the cracks beginning to show. Now is a great time to show why we deployed the knight to c2: there's a move I call a glue move — a move that glues together all the disparate parts of White's position; it stops the queen from attacking b2, lends further support to the bishop, and just glues everything together nicely. That's the knight to b4. Note that b2 was hanging — f2 isn't hanging, because it's protected by the king. Now we have time for simple prophylaxis: where's his knight going? To f4, obviously — how do we prevent it? By going g3. A good observation is that the d5-square is also free, but we don't want to rush a knight there, because the knight on b4 is fulfilling the crucial role of defending b2. He goes back, and now we complete our development by castling. He plays f5 — a lot of people would worry about him opening the file, but understand the drawback of pushing the f-pawn when castled: you weaken the diagonal, so this check on c4 might be very strong in a couple of moves. Let's take on f5, and if he takes back, we make a discovered check and his knight is lost. He can't recapture on f5 — well, he did, but this knight is defended by the rook, and that rook also defends the other rook, so it's overloaded, and by giving the check we expose the tension of the rooks. Boom and boom — we're up a knight and a pawn, and we're winning. The most important moment in the game was g3 — it frustrated him, he got impatient trying to create counterplay, and he fell apart very quickly. Let's capture the knight, and now, notice, the bishop and the queen can combine in a battery threatening checkmate, and his bishop on f6 is going to be lost as well, because to defend against it he has to give it up. He runs, we take; how do we keep harassing the king after it moves to f7? Notice the knight to d5 could be a fork. The bishop to c4 or the bishop to g6 are both good. Our goal is to get the king onto e7, a forkable square, so we assess all the checks we can make, including retreating moves — people often miss retreating moves, and they're the glue that makes an attack run. The bishop to g6 cuts the king off from f7; the queen to h3 forces the king onto e7, literally the only move, and that king walks right into the fork with the knight — we win the queen and the game. We didn't do anything extraordinary: we played the theoretical moves and he collapsed quite quickly.

The early queen sortie is the amateur try — and rather than the automatic developing move, there's a way to maximise the advantage: the knight jumps to e5. It isn't quite a fork, since the bishop can escape, but it grabs the bishop pair early and drives the queen onto a horribly exposed square.

Now expand and put that uncontested light-squared bishop to work. Prefer e6 over the natural pawn move for two reasons: it readies a central break — one you won't rush, since opening the centre just for its own sake is unwise — and the bishop is destined for the fianchetto anyway, so it won't get trapped behind the pawns.

Against the central push there's a nifty device to blunt the opponent's dark-square grip — the simple central knight move is fine, but the pawn to d5 is stronger, and if a queen check comes it can be met by a block or by dropping the knight home to d7.

No reason to trade queens with such a lead in the centre and in development. And when the queen's escape route gets closed off, file it away — start hunting for ways to exploit its vulnerability for queenside gains, and, if the opponent is careless, to trap it outright.
Turn the queen's awkwardness into space — a rook-pawn nudge to a6 chases it, and then b5 does double duty: it builds an imposing pawn mass and prepares the fianchetto onto a gorgeous long diagonal.

When the opponent pushes back on the queenside, the sharpest reply is the immediate fianchetto — and it isn't even a sacrifice. Playing Benko-style, if the b-pawn is grabbed the bishop swings to a6 to press the weak d3-pawn, and without calculating a step further you can trust that there's full compensation, most likely more.
It's not even necessary to go that route — a queen check on a5 forks the king and the loose pawn. Turning the opponent's own aggression into a tactic is the cleanest path.
Nc3 is the doorway to the anti-Sicilians — the Grand Prix with f4, the Closed with g3, or a transposition straight back into an Open Sicilian.
notes.teaches: Nc3 keeps every anti-Sicilian and the Open Sicilian in White's back pocket.

notes.explains: As Accelerated Dragon players we answer Nc6 — though a Najdorf player should avoid it here, since White can move-order you into a system you don't play.
notes.teaches: Match your move-two choice to the Open Sicilian you actually play, or risk being transposed out of your book.

notes.explains: Bb5 is a faceless anti-Sicilian — it looks like a Rossolimo but is inferior, because d4 is left unguarded: the knight that would defend it never comes to f3.
notes.teaches: Bb5 without a knight developed to f3 concedes d4; that missing guard is the flaw to exploit.

notes.explains: The principled reply is Nd4 — the same motif you'd use against a Trompowsky bishop: the knight becomes a monster in the centre and hits the bishop at once.
notes.teaches: Meet a pinning bishop by leaping the knight to d4, gaining a central monster and attacking the bishop.

notes.explains: We swap the knight for the bishop. Now a6 is the human instinct, but it's worth questioning your instincts — the b5-knight isn't dangerous on its own, so d6 or Nf6 hitting the loose e4-pawn are real options too.
notes.teaches: Don't play the automatic pawn-kick reflexively; a stray enemy knight often isn't worth the tempo.

notes.explains: Even after cxd4 this stays an anti-Sicilian — White has no light-squared bishop, so it's a different animal from a Najdorf. Our one problem is that we're badly behind in development.
notes.teaches: Read the position by what's missing: no light bishop means it's not a real Open Sicilian.

notes.explains: Nf6 would run into e5, so we head that off — sometimes you accept a small positional concession rather than get crushed while undeveloped.
notes.teaches: Concede a little structurally to prevent a central break that would punish your lack of development.

notes.explains: h6 stops Bg5 — the Smyslov idea of trading the knight and then planting one on d5. We have to keep a knight available to contest that square.
notes.teaches: Prevent the trade that would surrender d5; contesting the outpost is worth a pawn move.

notes.explains: Now we finally develop with Nf6; if Bb6, Qd7 is a fine, if slightly awkward, answer, and the queen can reroute to c6 later to free the bishop.

Under pressure the queen must go to e6 — the only square that keeps e5 defended, since otherwise Nxe5 crashes in. Conducting an initiative cleanly is one of the hardest skills in chess, and it cuts both ways.
notes.teaches: When defending, find the one square that holds your key point; sustaining an attack is hard even for the attacker.

notes.explains: We occupy the center with d5. The formula against any flank opening is simple: take a sound chunk of the center and back it with pieces — it's not a race to cram in the most pawns.
So we develop the knight to f6 instead of shoving more pawns forward and biting off more than we can chew.
Then the c6 setup — a pawn to c6 with a specific purpose.

White fianchettoes, and the bishop on g2 immediately bites on granite: it stares at the d5-pawn, which our pawn chain defends beautifully, so the bishop is nearly useless. The knight will develop via d7 and reroute f8-g6 rather than block it.
teaches: blunt the fianchetto bishop with the c6/d5 wall

notes.explains: a5 clamps the queenside, making White's textbook b4-c4 hippo expansion very hard to organize.
teaches: a5 to stop the b4-c4 plan

notes.explains: White's knight to c3 is out of step with the hippo setup — it just invites us to grab more space.
So we play d4, seizing space and asking the knight awkward questions — the very reason we put the pawn on c6.
teaches: d4 to gain space and harass the knight

notes.explains: The knight to a4 is a natural-looking reaction in many openings, but here it's a classic blunder.
The punish is b5 — trapping the knight on a4. This resource is a genuine blind spot that even strong players miss on both sides of the board.
Let's do one more ten-minute game, White. e4 — great, so we get to play a Fantasy variation of the Caro.
d5. This hasn't been my only recommendation against the Caro — I've also been advocating e-takes-d5 — but I kind of miss the Fantasy,
so let's do it, f3.
d-takes-e4.
f-takes-e4. I feel like a lot of people have been demonstrating pretty good theoretical knowledge in the Fantasy,
but not yet at this level; I think people start showing good knowledge around 2200, and below that the Fantasy is still basically a forced win for White.
Our response is d5.

So Black is trying to play this kind of Benoni style, but because he's lacking in development, if we play carefully we can put Black in very serious trouble — though we can also get into serious trouble ourselves if we're not careful. Now, because our f-pawn is gone, we have to look at this position through a very specific lens: we have to remember that the f-pawn is gone, and that bears consequences — so the queen to h4 with check is always in play in these situations. A similar opening where this is a thing is the Four Knights, the a-line — if White plays it, as I'll show you after the game, you always have to watch out for a check on h4, just like last game. So we don't actually need to play c4, which I assume is a lot of people's instinctive response, because Black isn't attacking this pawn — just the knight to f3. And in general, our biggest advantage here as White is not the fact that we have a pawn on d5.
We want to play aggressively — the Sicilian, c5.
White develops a knight to f3.
We play d6, heading for the Najdorf — my childhood opening, the Sicilian I know best.
But White plays c3 — the anti-climactic delayed Alapin.
The move here is a knight to f6, hitting e4.
White pushes e5 — a move I've seen before, and I know for a fact it isn't good.
We capture on e5.
And recapture with the knight. The annoying thing is White's knight on e5 as a launching pad against f7, so our first job is to remove it efficiently.
A queen to c7 would let White support the knight with d4, so the best way is with another knight — a knight to d7. It looks awkward, but once you know why, it's completely natural.
White captures on d7.
We recapture with the bishop — and from d7 it can swing to c6, onto the long diagonal.

This is a bad opening for White, struggling for equality. He plays a bishop to c4. We have two priorities: improve that d7 bishop toward c6, and complete our kingside development — best done with e6, making the c4 bishop bite on granite, rather than g6.
A bishop to c6 first, because it hits g2 and forces White's hand.
White is basically forced to castle.
And now e6, completing our development. Playing the bishop to c6 first also means that if White plays d4 and we capture, he can't recapture with the queen and keep his structure intact.
White plays a knight to a3, clearly aiming for b5.
We play a6, mainly to prevent a bishop to b5.
White plays a bishop to b3 — very strange play, opening c4 for the knight, though I'm not sure why that's dangerous.
We play b5, continuing to restrict White's minor pieces — I like it a lot; look how much it cramps his pieces.
White plays a knight to c2. Amazingly this doesn't blunder a piece, because after c4 there's a knight to d4 counterattacking the bishop on c6 — I don't think White even saw it.
A different approach is called for — let's set up a Greek gift. A bishop to d6 develops, aims at h2, and completes what we'd left undone. When in doubt, default to reasonable moves.
White plays c4. I sense we're on the cusp of a tactic. The Greek gift — a bishop capture on h2, the king takes, a knight to g4 with check — doesn't work yet, because the queen on d1 covers g4.
Can we set it up? The move h5 is tremendously effective — it anchors the g4 square, preparing both the Greek gift sacrifice and a straight knight to g4.

White plays d4. If we sacrifice on h2 and jump to g4, White intends a king to g3, and I'm not sure we have enough firepower — for some reason it's hard to play against his moves. I keep calculating the Greek gift.
A compromise — we capture on c4 first.
And now the knight to g4.
White plays h3 — I'm getting outplayed a little here.
A queen to c7 — the position stays complicated.
White plays a knight to e3.
I have a really sick idea — a bishop check on h2.
After the king to h1, if you've done your tactics you'll know the idea — a bishop to g1.
The bishop tucks into g1, threatening mate on h2 from two different sources.
White captures on g4.
We recapture on g4 with the h-pawn — and if White takes the bishop on g1, we play a capture on h3.
We take on h3. If White plays g3, we mate with h2; anything else, we capture on g2 — I didn't see a defense.
White plays d5 — complicated, but this has to be good for us.
We capture on g2 — this will take a lot of precision to win.
White recaptures on g2.
We give the obvious check — a queen to h2.
After the king to f3 we have several ways to continue — asking which pieces aren't yet in the attack.
A rook to d8 is the typical thought, but I have a better idea — a rook check on h3, which looks counterproductive.
Why help the king toward h2? White plays king to e2.
The idea is that after a capture on d5, we've lured the king to e2 for a reason.
A bishop capture on d5 would meet a bishop check on b5 — the c4 bishop is stuck and retreats to d3, a good move. Now it's critical to activate our a8 rook.
A king to d7 walks into a fork with a bishop check on f5, so we play a king to f8 — tucking the king safely and preparing to bring the rook in via e8.
White plays a king to d2. Nobody canceled the plan of activating the rook.
A rook to e8 — a good piece on an open file, period, even if it isn't doing anything obvious. That 'not doing anything' idea is misleading.
White plays a king to c2. A bishop check on a4 is tempting.
It's ineffective directly because of b3, so we start with c4 to set it up.
White plays a bishop to f5.
And now the bishop check on a4 — now we're winning.
White interposes with b3.
We capture on b3 with check.
White plays a king to b1 — that makes it easy for us.
We capture on a2 with check — it's a free queen, and there was absolutely nothing White could have done.
White recaptures on a2. A good game, though I'm unhappy with how I attacked — I'll check the bishop-to-g1 idea with the engine.
Now how do we actually win? It's important not to rest on your laurels or lose on time.
We've got the b-file as the vehicle toward White's king, and the rook was hanging anyway, so a rook check on b3.
If the king goes to a1, notice a queen check on e5 picks up the f5 bishop. White plays a rook to b2, defending as best he can.
We can simplify.
We capture on f2.
Given the clock, the prudent choice is to simplify.
White plays a rook to e1. If you've found a winning strategy, follow it through — a rook to c1 to trade, russian-schoolboy style.
A rook to c1 — we don't even have to take immediately.
We just start pushing the g-pawn, with plenty of squares for our king; if the bishop moves anywhere it gets forked. White resigns.
We have White, open with the pawn to e4, and get e5.
The knight to f3.
Black plays the pawn to d6 — the Philidor again, becoming quite a trend this run.
Both the pawn to d4 and the bishop to c4 are good — this time the bishop to c4.
Black develops the bishop to e7 — again, these moves are interchangeable.
Let's play principled chess with the pawn to d4.
Black takes on d4. A subtlety: once the bishop is already on c4, recapturing with the queen is a touch incongruent — it's not bad, just awkward.

So the knight recaptures on d4. The reason to avoid the queen recapture: after it, you'd want the bishop to b5 in a single move to answer the knight to c6 and pin, keeping the queen safe — but with the bishop already committed to c4, that costs a tempo.
Black develops the knight to f6.
The knight to c3. With a bishop on c4 like this, the tactical alarm bells should be ringing.
Black plays the pawn to c5 — a typical mistake at this level, though the center fork trick with the knight taking e4 always has to be calculated.
The clue that it's not a knight move leaves one logical option — the bishop to b5 with check, a trick you can also use in the Sicilian.

Black blocks with the bishop to d7. The point is simple: generate the f5-square for the knight and trade off the light-squared bishops — once the knight lands on f5, it hits all of Black's weak spots at once.
So the knight to f5 immediately, rather than trading on d7 first.
That f-pawn move is one of the very worst available here — the same Damiano-style error that's bad even after a normal knight development. It fatally weakens the king's diagonal.
Resist the tempting immediate check, which would just be met by a pawn move — capture on e5 first. Order of operations turns a near-loss for the opponent into a lost one.

The queen has strayed into a trap, and the way to free it is to lean on the fact that it pins a piece — a bishop to h6 exploits the pin and essentially forces the queens off. Use the very pin that looks awkward as the lever that saves the piece.
Don't grab the material in the corner in a hurry — it isn't going anywhere. Cover the intervening check, develop a knight, and shore up the pawn first; the loose piece can be collected at leisure.
With a winning material edge, just keep improving — advancing another pawn into the centre and letting the position play itself. No need for anything fancy when you're up a rook.

The knight lunge eyes the f2 square, and there are two ways to defend — a rook step or a knight to the edge. Prefer the rook, because you never want a knight consigned to the rim purely to babysit a pawn; the intruder can be shooed away by a pawn later.

A principle worth repeating: when the opponent has a piece parked in your half, you don't always need to rush to chase it — first understand what it's actually doing. It can be evicted in good time; meanwhile just keep developing.
Now the pawn push to e5 forks the two knights at once, cashing the accumulated advantage into more material.
Capture on d6 — the point is that it nets two pieces for a rook, converting the pressure into a clean, decisive material lead.
Notice the discipline even in the endgame — every rook and minor piece gets brought into the game. No coasting; activate the whole army and finish cleanly.
We take White and face the Caro-Kann.
We build the centre with d4.
Black challenges with d5.

We play f3 — the Fantasy Variation. It's the kryptonite of most Caro-Kann players: less studied than the mainline trifecta, and so sharp that Black can't get away with just improvising standard Caro moves.
Black takes on e4.
We recapture on e4, and Black plays ...e5, the main line. Note we must not grab with our own pawn on e5 — ...Qh4 with check would then pick off the e4-pawn — so we prioritise development.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black pins with the bishop to g4, the best move.
We bring the bishop to c4. In past games the shot on f7 has been overlooked by unprepared opponents.
Black correctly plays the knight to d7, guarding against the f7 sacrifice.
We castle kingside — a big appeal of the Fantasy: the semi-open f-file that fuels the attack.
Black develops the knight to f6. Now we must shore up the centre, because once Black is developed ...exd4 grows nasty.
We play c3 to buttress the centre — the b1-knight can develop via d2 later. And a capture on e5 doesn't work: Black would take our f3-knight first, and then the centre just evaporates.
Black develops the bishop to d6. As a rule, get the bishop out before the knight, so one piece doesn't block another.
We develop the bishop to g5, its one good square.
Black plays ...h6, and this is about where most club players leave theory.
We retreat to h4, provoking ...g5.
Black plays ...g5.
We drop the bishop to g3 — and remember, ...Nxe4 is never a real problem, because the check on f7 always answers it.

Black plays the queen to e7, solidifying e5 and preparing to castle queenside — an opposite-wing race, with Black storming ...h5–h4 while we can advance a4–a5 or swing the queen to b3 or a4 to worry his weak queenside pawns.
First we complete development with the knight to d2.

Black castles queenside. Before pawn-storming, apply the best-case-scenario test: even if a4–a5–a6 all worked, Black just plays ...b5 and we've wasted three tempi for an unexploitable weakness — so we attack with pieces instead, starting with the queen to a4, and don't forget the standing weakness on f7.
We take and recapture exd4, leaving a unique doubled-pawn shape — a false Ruy Lopez that stands entirely on its own.

The Vienna Gambit — the knight to c3, then f4, offering the f-pawn. We're sacrificing for two things: a bigger center with d4, and the open f-file, which will hand our rook a battering-ram file against f7 once we castle.
teaches: the Vienna Gambit: center + the f-file

notes.explains: The passive d6 declines the gambit — it blocks in the bishop and simply hands us everything we wanted.
The Ruy-style bishop to b5 is the best move — immediate pressure on the e5-pawn, a Spanish on steroids.
Don't go pawn-hunting: grabbing on c6 and e5 doesn't even win a pawn — it runs into a queen check on d4 forking king and knight. The Vienna is about development and attack, not the material.
teaches: develop and attack, don’t chase the pawn

notes.explains: With the king safe we bring the bishop to c4, trained on f7 with a sacrifice in the air.
We take on e6, weakening his structure — a clean, simple trade on our own terms.
The aggressive path — the knight to g5, going straight at the weak e-pawn.
d4 comes with tempo, kicking the knight off e5, and it's a phenomenal position for us.
The key break is d5 — not e5, which just drops a pawn and invites a queen trade. d5 carves out a stronghold on e6 for the knight.
teaches: d5 to make the e6 outpost

notes.explains: The knight lands on e6, an absolute monster — it paralyzes Black, who can't even castle, and it's propped up by a pawn chain, immune to being undermined.
teaches: the e6 knight paralyzes the position

notes.explains: The bishop to g5 hits the knight on f6, and Black's whole position is on the verge of collapse.
And the fastest finish: the knight takes on d5. After the queen recaptures on e6, the knight check on c7 forks king and queen.
We take White and open d4; Black plays ...Nf6.
We claim space with c4.
Black fianchettoes with ...g6; we develop the knight to c3.
Black completes the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
We develop the bishop to e3.
Black castles.
We play h3, taking the g4-square.
Black strikes with c5.
We take on c5.
Black develops ...Na6, eyeing the c5-pawn.
We fianchetto with g3.
Black plays the queen to a5.
We play a3.
Black jumps the knight to e4.
We drop the bishop to d2.
Black takes our knight on c3.
We recapture with the b-pawn.
Black grabs on c5 with the knight.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black replays ...Ne4.
We play the rook to c1.
Black snatches on a3 with the queen.
We complete the fianchetto with the bishop to g2.
Black plays d6.
We castle.
Black takes our bishop, capturing on d2.
We recapture with the queen.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
We centralize the knight on d4.
Black snatches on c4 with the bishop.
We grab on b7.
Black plays the rook to b8.
We reroute the rook to a1.
Black plays the queen to c5.
We play the bishop to a6, offering a trade.
Black takes the bishop on a6.
We recapture with the rook.
Black doubles rooks with ...Rfc8.
We play the rook to c1.
Black takes our knight, capturing on d4.
We play e3, hitting the bishop.
Black plays the queen to c4.
We bring the rook to a1.
Black plays the bishop to c5.
We tuck the king to h2.
Black plays h5.
We play the rook to d1; Black pushes a5; we swing the rook to b1; Black trades on b1.
We recapture with the rook.
Black pushes d5; we infiltrate with the rook to b7.
Black plays ...Bd6; we grab on e7 with the rook; Black recaptures with the bishop.
We offer the queen trade on d4; Black takes.
We recapture with the pawn; Black pushes the passed a-pawn.
The move order has drifted into something unorthodox — but the guiding decision is simply to treat it like a Pirc, leaning on the familiar dark-squared fianchetto and flexible pawn breaks.
The point of the exchange sequence is to win the bishop pair — two bishops in an increasingly open position is a lasting asset well worth the small concession.

An honest strategic moment — the easy, natural moves are all played, and now the position demands a real plan, a concrete maneuver. This is exactly the hard part, where drifting on autopilot starts to get squeezed positionally.
A committal call: the rook-pawn move is undesirable because it leaves the queen nearly boxed in — but it goes in anyway, accepting the awkwardness as the lesser evil under pressure.
In the ending the safe resource is a bishop trade steering into a draw — the practical honesty of recognising when a position no longer offers a winning try, even when you'd rather press.
f3 is the Sämisch — it props up a future e4. In true King's Indian spirit we don't fight it; we just fianchetto and let White build the centre.
notes.teaches: Against the Sämisch, don't contest e4 directly — fianchetto and prepare to strike the centre later.

notes.explains: d6 stops e5, and then we castle and finish development.
Bd3 is an instructive inaccuracy — and it goes to the heart of why the King's Indian is so annoying: White carelessly severs the queen from the d4-pawn, leaving it weak.
notes.teaches: Watch for the moment White's own move disconnects the defense of his centre pawn — that's your target.

notes.explains: Normally we'd hit d4 with a pawn, but c5 or e5 here just lets White push d5. So Nc6 is the move — attack the pawn with a piece instead.
notes.teaches: When a pawn break lets the opponent lock the centre, pressure the target with a piece rather than a pawn.

notes.explains: Nd7 is the subtle reroute — it brings the g7-bishop to life, and remember, bad bishops defend good pawns. Now e5 comes with real force.
notes.teaches: Reroute a knight to unblock your fianchetto bishop before you strike in the centre.

notes.explains: Now e5 strikes at d4, and if White pushes d5, the central square opens for our pieces.
Nd4 is the payoff — the bishop supports the square and the knight plants itself on the finest central outpost.
notes.teaches: Occupy the outpost your bishop already supports; it can never be dislodged by a pawn.

notes.explains: The knight tour continues to c5 — look at the pressure these two knights pour onto White's position.
When the knight is attacked by a third piece, don't defend it — let White spend time capturing it while we coordinate and strike. f5 fires up the attack.
notes.teaches: Rather than passively defend an attacked piece, let it go for tempo and open your own attack.

notes.explains: Bh6 is a blunder — a type-two piece, defended only once. Combine that with the diagonal f3 weakened: once the f6-knight steps aside, the queen swings to h4, and the bishop falls with the game.
notes.teaches: After f3, remember the queen's route to h4; unmask it by moving the f6-knight to snap off a loose piece.

notes.explains: Against the French we play our Tarrasch — the knight to d2.
Black captures on e4 — the Rubinstein French, a solid but passive choice.
The knight to f6 here is inaccurate, because it forces Black to wreck his own pawn structure at once.
After we take with check and he recaptures with the g-pawn, Black's kingside pawns are shattered — doubled and weak.
The bishop comes to d3, and the plan is to root out Black's bishop — his only good piece.
teaches: target the opponent’s one strong piece

notes.explains: The bishop on b7 is that piece. We contest it — but there's a subtlety worth knowing: if we grab with the bishop on a6, after the recapture Black can leave a loose piece that a queen check on a4 forks against king and knight. Beyond that, we're happy to give a pawn for the initiative here: with Black's king stranded in the center and the board wide open, the bishop to f4 keeps the rook-lift avenue open, and we attack down the half-open g-file.
teaches: pawn for initiative against a stuck king

notes.explains: We have the Black pieces against a good player. As promised, I'm going into my main repertoire. d4, the knight to f6.
The knight to c3 — we might be facing a Jobava London here.
The knight to c3 is the introductory move; I'll oblige with d5, and this is going to be a very interesting twist.

Of course the bishop to f4 isn't the only move, and we are indeed facing the Jobava London — I'm now Black against my own opening, but I won't hold back, I'll give my honest recommendations. What you should understand about the Black side of the Jobava is that there are seven or eight equalising lines — it's impossible to say that e6 is worse than the bishop to f5, or a6 worse than e6; all the typical moves here, other than the knight to c6, which blunders the knight to b5, are approximately equivalent in objective strength. 'Best' is relative — each line leads to a different type of position, and whichever you play, you have to know it well, because almost every move is good. Even the relatively rare c6 is quite decent. The move that's probably easiest for most people to understand, because it's also the most forcing —
and you could call it the most principled — is the direct central strike, c5. You're basically trying to punish White directly for bringing the knight out to c3.
In the traditional London, how is c5 often met? With the move c3, to reinforce the d4-pawn. So you're trying to highlight

the most forcing line, and currently considered the most reputable within c5 — take on e4 with the knight, to force the knights off the board before White plays d-takes-c5. So the knight takes e4; White of course
will recapture on e4, the only feasible move. Take note that the knight to b5 is not dangerous as long

Capturing on c6 is already a slight error — it opens the b-file for the second player and, just as usefully, clears the way to prepare the central break to d5. A trade that helps the defender is no trade to make.
The fianchettoed bishop must not be traded — resist by developing the knight to f6. And note the pawn move to e5 would be poor, since it hands over the d6 square as a lasting hole.
There it is again — that f-pawn move is one of the most weakening moves on the board, yet players toss it in reflexively. There's a good reason the old advice is simply never to play it.
The bishop out to c4 walks straight into the break you should be playing on autopilot — a pawn to d5, seizing the centre and opening lines while the opponent is still sorting out development.

The first order of business is to stop the opponent from castling and keep the king stranded in the centre — a queen to b6 does it. It may not prevent castling forever, but every tempo spent chasing the queen away is a tempo spent expanding in the centre, so even if the king eventually tucks away, it does so into a hot mess.

Expand — but with the right pawn. The natural central push would close the queen's diagonal and actually help the opponent castle. The move is e5 instead, keeping the diagonal live and the pressure on.

Now a crushing quiet move — a knight to g4. It's found by reading the opponent's intention: they want a bishop to e3 so they can finally castle. The knight leap stops that while feeding the attack, and the fianchettoed bishop rakes into b2. If the knight is challenged, a queen check on f2 leads to mate.

This is where intuition earns its keep. You don't need to see the exact mating sequence — one glance at the opponent's tangled pieces tells you it's there, and it's either checkmate or catastrophic material loss. Intuition is trusting that judgment instead of burning your whole clock trying to calculate it to the end.

Don't forget the other route — sometimes the simplest conversion is just to win a heap of material, a kind of insurance. If the attack ever misfires, you're still up a rook. When a full rook is on offer, take it, even if a mate might be lurking; the safe path is nothing to be ashamed of.
Against the Vienna, Nf6 is more accurate than Nc6.
White's passive d3 invites the principled reply — d5. Count the defenders: everything trades off, and that exchange on d5 favors Black. When White plays passively, strike the centre.
notes.teaches: Answer a passive setup by breaking in the centre where the exchanges work in your favor.

notes.explains: Nc6, and resist taking on c3 — the doubled pawns don't really hurt White, and releasing the tension only strengthens his grip on the central squares.
notes.teaches: Don't inflict doubled pawns that actually reinforce the opponent's centre.

notes.explains: More advanced isn't always better — Bg4 lets White set up the Nxe5 tactic. The dark bishop's primary job is simply to let you castle, so Be7 is perfect.
notes.teaches: Develop the dark-squared bishop to castle, not to the most forward square available.

notes.explains: By the same logic Be6 reinforces the knight and stops Ng5 — bishops posted on safe, invulnerable squares.
notes.teaches: Place your pieces on unassailable squares that defend each other, not on ambitious but loose ones.

notes.explains: a5 prevents b4 — if White got that in, b5 would follow and our e5-pawn could grow weak.
notes.teaches: A little a-pawn move can pre-empt an enemy pawn expansion that would loosen your centre.

notes.explains: f6 stops Ng5 and shores up e5. When is f6 safe rather than weakening? Case by case — here White has no light bishop for that diagonal, so it weakens nothing.
notes.teaches: f6 is safe when the opponent can't exploit the diagonal it opens; judge it position by position.

notes.explains: Now be concrete: h4 weakened g4, and the queen on d7 backs up a bishop there, while White's queen is off d1 so there's no Nxe5 trick. The very Bg4 I rejected earlier is now excellent — circumstances changed.
notes.teaches: A move that's bad in one position can be strong once the concrete factors around it change.

notes.explains: Reinforce e5 with Bf6, not Bd6 which would drop the knight. Defend with the least valuable piece and keep your rooks free for bigger jobs.
notes.teaches: Accomplish a defensive task with your cheapest adequate piece; save the rooks and queen for real work.

notes.explains: Rae8 completes the coordination — every piece is now working — and only then do we think about pressing with f4 or e4. No hurry.
notes.teaches: Finish coordinating all your pieces before you commit to the breakthrough.

notes.explains: Now press the gas: f4 begins cracking White's kingside. It concedes the e4 square, but you can't make an omelet without breaking eggs — the attack is worth it.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are fully coordinated, launch the break even at the cost of a square.

notes.explains: Don't fear retreating a long-range piece — the bishop on d8 eyes h4 exactly as it did from f6, and it clears the f-file for the rook. How far a move retreats says nothing about whether it's good.
notes.teaches: Retreat bishops and queens freely; long-range pieces attack just as well from behind and can unblock your own lines.

notes.explains: Nf5 keeps the knight pressing the kingside, eyeing a Bxh4 sacrifice and a rook lift.
We're higher-rated here, so a bit faster — and we answer e4 with the Sicilian, c5.
White plays d4.
We capture on d4.
c3 — the Smith-Morra Gambit. I have a new line to show, excellent from a practical standpoint and very rare.
It's the move d5 — exceedingly rare, but I won a Title Tuesday game with it against a strong IM who knew all the theory and still got into trouble.
White grabs with the queen on d4 — not the move.
So a knight to f6, avoiding the queen trade — and if e5, a knight to c6 is fine.
We play a knight to c6, hitting the queen.
White plays a bishop to b5, and precision is required — dropping a knight into e4 can get it trapped after f3.
So a knight back to d7 — yes, we give up d5, but it's solid.
White plays a knight to f3, and we win the queen with a knight capture on d4 — White simply blundered.
White recaptures on d4 — a piece for the queen.
We play e6.
White castles.
We play a6.
White retreats to a4, and the rest is easy conversion — we're up a queen for a piece.
We play b5.
We just grab the pawn in the center.
White plays f4.
A knight to c4, centralizing.
We bring the knight around to d6.
I shouldn't have allowed the knight to c6, but it doesn't matter.
A queen to c7 — a slight loss of discipline.
White captures on e7.
We recapture with the queen.
Don't over-finesse the placement — just get your pieces out.
Like a rook to c8. Now identify the biggest target.
White plays a knight to e5.
Trade pieces when it doesn't harm your position — a knight to e4, hitting the pawn and encouraging a trade.
White plays a rook to f3.
The knight on e5 is active, so let's chase it with f6.
White plays a knight to g4 — and we have a tactic. A keen tactical eye and well-developed pattern recognition are what let you finish efficiently.
White plays the King's Gambit — f4, offering the pawn to rip open the center at the cost of weakening his own kingside.
We take the pawn, then play d5. The point is simple: f4 weakened White's kingside, and the principle is to open the center to exploit that weakness.
teaches: ...d5 to open the center against f4

notes.explains: We don't recapture d5 with the queen — that would allow a knight to c3 kicking it and boosting White's development. The knight to f6 takes it instead, keeping the queen safe and even lending support to our f4-pawn.
teaches: recapture with the knight, keep the queen safe

notes.explains: The knight recaptures on d5, comfortably ahead.
The bishop to c4 can't touch the knight.
The bishop to e7 looks passive, but it's perfectly fine — we're up a pawn, so there's no need to develop aggressively.
teaches: solid development is enough when ahead

notes.explains: Here's the key theme — transforming the advantage. We're happy to give the pawn back for lasting positional pluses, and that's exactly why the King's Gambit isn't the terror it was once thought to be: Black can hand the pawn back and get compensation.
teaches: give the pawn back for positional gains

notes.explains: The bishop to e6 blunts the annoying bishop on c4 — killing its x-ray on our knight and its pressure on f7.
The far-sighted move is the knight to c6.

After the trade we recapture with the b-pawn. The doubled c-pawns look ugly but are a bargaining chip — they roll forward one after the other to contest the center, and they can be undoubled later with c5 and a queen recapture on d4.
teaches: doubled pawns as a dynamic bargaining chip

notes.explains: Let's play one game. There have been a lot of requests to play d4, so we're going to stick with d4 for a couple of games. c6 — this
offers us the possibility of transposing to a Caro-Kann, but we're going to stick with d4, so we play c4 and
transpose into a Slav. This is the first time we
face the Slav, I think, in all of our speedruns. The knight to f3 is the main line — we
develop both of our knights, standard fare here.
The knight to c3. Here Black has a major fork in the road —
a couple of possible variations, of which a6 is one.

I don't know much about a6, since I don't really play the Slav with White that much, but one thing I've always played here is the move g3, a very Catalan kind of style — I'm a big fan of playing g3 in the Slav; I think it leads to very dynamic positions.

Of course this is a pawn sacrifice, so Black can take on c4, and we will not try particularly hard to win that pawn back immediately, so you have to be ready to play sacrificial lines. The bishop to g4 is quite dubious — why? Generally in these positions the bishop to g4 walks right into the knight to e5.
The knight to e5 — so we centralise our knight.

And of course you should also be aware of the move queen to b3, which in many cases comes with great effect. But before we do any of that, we should probably develop our bishop to g2 — but then Black plays e6 and solidifies his position. So the other option is to play the immediate queen to b3 and go for Black's throat. I actually like the look of the queen to b3, hoping for b5 here. What some players do in these positions is play a very weird b6 — that has to be inaccurate; it just looks really ugly and weakens the queenside, though it's not losing. When you play d4, you've got to be ready to play long games. So here's what we're going to do: try to open the centre as quickly as we possibly can — so let's start by taking on d5 and finally completing our development.
The standard way to meet the bishop out to c4 is e6, blunting its diagonal — but develop the knight first, keeping the move order flexible before committing the pawn.
The knight comes to f6, and this is actually the most accurate move — it hits the centre and sets up a tactical resource that's about to appear.

Here's the cool device — the centre-fork trick: capture on e4, and the follow-up of grabbing the bishop and striking with d5 tears down the opponent's grip on the centre. A theme that recurs across many openings.
exd5 gives us the Carlsbad structure — a subtly imbalanced formation, named for the city where it appeared in the great early-1900s tournaments, with a lifetime of ideas inside it.
notes.teaches: The QGD exchange leads to the Carlsbad, one of the richest positional structures in chess.

notes.explains: The first Carlsbad move is c6, reinforcing the d5-pawn that anchors the whole structure.
notes.teaches: Prop up d5 with c6 first; it's the foundation of Black's Carlsbad setup.

notes.explains: Be7 breaks the pin — the dark bishop's usual square here, though d6 is possible — and h6 can go in any time but isn't obligatory. Then castle, and start the key Carlsbad maneuver: Nbd7 to guard the f6-knight against Bxf6, then Re8 and Nf8, from where the knight both heads to g6 or e6 and defends h7.
