notes.teaches: The Carlsbad knight tour is Nbd7-f8-g6/e6; from f8 it also shields h7 against the bishop sac.

notes.explains: A concept that runs through these lines: trapping the light-squared bishop with g4, then h4-h5. Forced to a square where a pawn recaptures it, the defender's structure shatters — the resulting weak pawns and open files decide the game. The same overload idea keeps recurring.
Playing a slower game is a new experience for me. My opponent opens with e4; I'm going to open with e5, which is
my main move, and the most popular chess move — the King's Pawn Game. He goes the knight to f3.
I'm going to go the knight to c6, just defending the pawn — standard fare.
He plays the bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez opening, also called the Spanish Game — and the idea of this move is that he's indirectly putting pressure on the pawn on e5.

You might say this bishop has nothing to do with that pawn — but it does, because the knight on c6 is defending the pawn, and White's bishop is potentially threatening to take that knight. So I'm going to play a6.
This might seem to merely invite my fate, because he can take on c6 and then capture my pawn — but after the game I'll talk about why that's not as effective as it might seem.

He drops his bishop back correctly, and in turn I will simply develop my knight and pressure his pawn on e4. Now, once again, I'm not really attacking the pawn on e4 — the reason is that I haven't completed my development.

When you haven't completed your development, especially your kingside — I haven't developed my bishop, haven't castled — you want to be very careful about grabbing pawns. It's a moot point now, because he's brought his knight out and defended the pawn.
I'm a little annoyed by the pressure the bishop is exerting on the knight, so I'm going to go b5 and chase his bishop away.

This will allow me to develop my pieces in a harmonious fashion. A lot of beginners just choose the first square that comes to mind for a piece, not realising that every development square has its strengths and weaknesses. What I'm trying to do

is find the most active development square for each piece. For this bishop, I'm asking where it can develop most actively and control the most central squares — and that square is c5, because it also contests the weakest square on the board, f2, which could be a precursor to a potential attack I could load up with a move like the knight to g4.

I anticipate my opponent will just continue his own development by castling — still theory, common fare. He does castle as anticipated. Now I'm looking at this bishop on c8, and where I'd really like it is g4, to pin the knight to the queen — pins are a huge asset. I could also fianchetto, placing one of my bishops on the long diagonal,

but there it would be blocked by my own knight — I want to open the diagonal, so I prepare to put the bishop on g4, still completely normal. What my opponent could do here is play h3 to stop my bishop from coming to g4 — this is called prophylaxis, an intimidating-sounding term that really just means stopping the threats posed by your opponent.
He plays d3.
And he does allow my bishop to access this very active development square. Notice how I've positioned all of my pieces on optimal squares — this bishop lining itself up on the king,
this bishop pinning the queen. He chases my bishop away. Now, a lot of beginners have a tendency, when they see a capture, to go for it — here I can
capture the knight, but that would defeat the whole purpose of what this bishop is doing, which is essentially immobilising that knight on f3 — so I'm just going to drop the bishop back to h5.
He pins my own knight — he liked that idea. So this is a very interesting situation that's now arisen.

I'm annoyed by the pin, and I'm sure he's annoyed by his pin too — the question is who can get rid of their pin first, and I think that's going to be me; I'll do the same thing he did and chase his bishop away,
and tempt him into taking my knight. He drops his bishop back.

And here what I'm going to do is just say goodbye to that — I play the move g5, attacking the bishop, which has to drop back to g3. Now you might look at g5 and say, wait, you're pushing pawns out on your kingside, aren't you about to castle short, and won't your king be very weak? The answer to all of those is undoubtedly yes — but after the game I'll unpack why this is in fact justified in many cases; the better you become at chess, the better you become at strategically violating opening principles. He's left his bishop on h4, so I'm just going to grab it — and he hasn't gotten rid of the pin either. What have I gained with this capture? First, a bishop, a pretty big deal; but I've also gained access to the g-file — and when you're thinking about your opponent's king, you want to think about avenues to access it.

A practical lesson: when you sense the opponent is steering into a line they know and you don't, you can sidestep the sharpest theory with a quiet move, accepting a slightly worse position in exchange for not being blown off the board. The principled tries here are the knight to f6 or clinging to the pawn with a bishop to c5.
So opt for solid, even slightly passive chess — the bishop to e7, which also rules out an annoying knight lunge and lets development finish in peace.

Here's a famous trap to know: grabbing the offered pawn is a blunder, because a queen leap to d5 threatens mate on f7 with no good defence — the only try drops a piece. So the pawn can't be taken, which leaves the standard menu of choices: ignore, accept, hand the pawn back on your own terms, or, failing all else, resign.
The choice here is to give the pawn back on favourable terms — a modest d3, denying the opponent a dominant pawn centre by forcing the capture rather than letting them build.

The queen sortie to b3 is genuinely nasty, because the target pawn simply can't be held. The known antidote is a knight to a5, prising the queen away from the defence of the bishop and untangling by concrete means.

The tempting queen move to d5, keeping it lined up with the bishop, is actually a mistake — a pawn to c6 both attacks the queen and defends the knight in one move, and the queen is driven off with tempo. One move answering two threats.

Even after a surprise resource, don't hit the panic button — just identify the real issue. The danger is a discovered check, and a knight to f6 interposes between the queen and bishop, which is cleaner than the bishop block that would allow a capture.

Development stays the priority. When the knight lunges in defending the bishop, stay logical — but before kicking it, do the discipline: look for the opponent's checks and rule out any weird mating sequence. Only once it's confirmed safe do you proceed.

The concrete central push counterattacks the knight — and it simplifies the position rather than complicating it, because the reply is forced: capture the knight, then recapture, with no room to do things any other way.

Now spot the standing feature — the opponent still hasn't castled. A queen check on e7 probes to see the reaction, and the whole plan revolves around exploiting that stranded king before it finds shelter.
A knight to c4 barges in, and the reason it can't simply be pinned against the king is that the pinning bishop is itself pinned. Slowly the initiative changes hands.
Here's the shot to see — the enemy bishop and queen sit a knight's move apart, so a knight to e5 forks the pair. Whenever two pieces stand a knight's-distance apart, the fork should light up.

A recurring truth about strong lower-rated opponents: they're excellent in the opening and rattle off good tactical moves, but keep your composure and they'll lose theirs first. Sometimes winning is just outlasting them in the calculation.

A queen to e5 induces a weakening pawn move in front of the king — and this is a lovely example of not needing a pawn storm. The open file has already been handed over, so pushing pawns would be counterproductive; the attack flows down the file as it is.
Offer the queen trade — it may feel tame, but when you can play fast and accurately in the resulting endgame, simplifying into a won ending is exactly the right practical choice.

Converting the ending is a matter of order: centralise the king, bring the rooks to the open files, and identify the wing where a passed pawn can be made — that passer is ultimately what wins. Keep one eye always on knight forks, and the finish is a rook lift that dislodges the blockading knight so the pawn can promote.
White's d4 tries to punish the missing knight on c6, but Nf6 is a fully sound answer — we analyzed exactly this before.
The critical resource to remember: if White plays e5, Nc6 hits the queen with tempo and Black is completely fine — a Dragon-like position where White is at most a shade better.
notes.teaches: In the g6 Sicilian, meet an early e5 with Nc6, gaining the tempo that equalizes.

notes.explains: The Jobava London — the queen's pawn paired with the knight to c3, headed for an early bishop to f4.
Against a likely French player we grab the center with e4 — so if you take up the Jobava, be ready to play the French from the White side too.
teaches: Jobava can transpose to a French

notes.explains: Black steers back with d5, the standard Jobava structure.
Let's play something very aggressive. e4, e5 — let's play a Vienna.
A good old-fashioned Vienna Gambit, with the knight to c3 and f4. If he goes the knight to f6, of course — let's see how the Vienna holds up at this level.

The bishop to b4 — this move kind of takes the fun out of the position; it's not a great move, sort of a Trompowsky inverted to the other side of the board. A lot of you might be tempted by the knight to d5, as in a Trompowsky, but the problem is that the bishop drops back to c5 and the knight on d5 isn't stable — Black chases it with c6. So instead of that reactionary move, we have a couple of other interesting options.
One is to just play this as if it were a Vienna — play f4 — because I don't really see how the bishop on b4 impacts the effectiveness of f4. Let's keep the spirit of the Vienna.
e-takes-f4. Now, a common misconception is that we follow this up with the immediate d4 — we do not. That's a big mistake in almost all of

these positions, because it allows the nasty check on h4. Same with the bishop to c4 — we don't want to allow the check on h4. We start by developing the knight to f3, a crucial component of the Vienna: you don't play d4 without the knight to f3 first, to prevent the queen to h4.

He goes h6. His intentions are nakedly obvious — he wants to play g5 and build a pawn chain, not letting us win the f4-pawn back. At this level it's not enough to memorise theory; you have to be flexible and adjust to how your opponent plays. Normally you'd play d4 to win the pawn back, but here d4 walks right into his plan — d4, g5 — and I'm not sure what we gain, so we prioritise minor-piece development and punish him for not developing.

Some propose h4, but as I'll show after the game, h4 is way too weakening — it burns all the bridges and weakens the g3-square, which is significant. Let's play the calm bishop to c4 and see how he arranges his pieces.

The knight to f6 is an excellent move. I wouldn't say we're clearly better — the position is complex. I like e5, and I also like the simple castle short; when in doubt, just develop. There's a small tactical issue with d3: it opens the pin and justifies the bishop on b4 — after d3, Black plays d5 with nice development, e-takes-d5, the knight takes d5, and this knight can't capture because it's pinned.
So if we go e5, Black most probably plays d5. Instead of any of that, we just castle — as Hikaru would say, just castle.
And if he castles, then e5 becomes a much more effective move.

e5. What's the difference here? If he goes d5, the difference is that we're castled — we don't have to worry about king safety anymore. The simplest for White: we don't take en passant, we take the knight, then take on g7, ruining his pawn structure permanently, and then go after the f4-pawn.
He's got a pretty big decision — whether to go for that or move the knight. The knight to h7 is a really passive move. How should we follow up?
The Scotch is one of the oldest openings there is — the whole idea is to contest the centre at once and open lines for the bishop. It's principled, but it comes with a catch.

The downside is that the knight has moved twice already — and that's dangerous, because it lets the other side develop pieces while attacking them at the same time. That's developing with tempo, and the bishop to c5 does exactly that.
Rather than recapture, bring the queen to f6 — and crucially don't grab the knight. It's an in-between move, and the knight isn't going anywhere while the opponent scrambles to defend.

That f-pawn defence weakens the king. Recapture with the d-pawn, because it opens the diagonal for the bishop — a reminder that when choosing between recaptures, pick the one that also serves your development.

Develop the knight — and notice the opponent simply can't castle. That's why the f-pawn move is so reviled: it opened the diagonal, and with the bishop already glaring down it, tucking the king to safety becomes a nightmare.

The bishop move blunders a piece, and it teaches the single biggest beginner affliction — tunnel vision. The opponent saw only that they were attacking a pawn and never noticed the queen eyeing the bishop. Most mistakes at the improving level are exactly this narrowing of view.
Now the theme of the whole game — converting a material advantage. Being up material is only half the job; turning it into a win with clean, purposeful play is the skill worth drilling.

A pawn just advanced — so run the check: whenever a pawn moves it leaves weaknesses in its wake. Two pawns are now loose, and when you see a good capture, look for a better one: taking on b2 not only grabs the pawn but also hits the rook in the corner, which can't escape.

And a pattern to file away: if the opponent tries to x-ray-defend the rook, the queen and king end up on the same diagonal — so always look for a pin whenever the queen and king line up like that. It happens astonishingly often.
The rook is simply collected — now up a rook and a piece, hitting the knight, and the opponent still can't castle. That inability to get the king safe is what ultimately sinks them.

Before pressing on, evacuate the queen so it doesn't get stranded in the corner — retreating it to e5, where it also pins a pawn against the king. Rescue the far-flung piece before it becomes a liability.
We have Black against a strong player and answer the king's-pawn with c5 — the Sicilian.
White develops the knight to f3.
The knight to c6, heading for a mainline Accelerated Dragon.
White strikes with the pawn to d4 — the Open Sicilian.
We capture on d4.
White recaptures with the knight — music to my ears.
The pawn to g6, the Accelerated Dragon fianchetto — only our second of the whole run.
White plays the knight to c3 — the other main line, as opposed to the Maroczy Bind with c4.
The bishop to g7, developing and pressuring the d4-knight down the long diagonal.
White develops the bishop to e3 — the main line.
So we keep it uniquely Accelerated by developing the knight to f6 first — not pushing any central pawns yet, maybe not for several more moves.

White plays the queen to d2 — a not-especially-good sideline; the main is the bishop to c4. In any Dragon setup, once the queen leaves d1, consider the knight to g4: trading it for White's dark-squared bishop leaves our Dragon bishop uncontested. After the knight to g4 the bishop can't move — it would drop the twice-attacked d4-knight — though White can take on c6 and shift the bishop to d4.
We castle. And we don't play d6, which would let White transition to the Dragon with f3 — keeping the pawn on d7 means we can later strike with d5 in one move.

White castles queenside. Now the king and queen are aligned, so we recalculate the knight to g4: if White takes c6 and plays the bishop to d4, we have the bishop to h6, pinning the queen. White blocks with f4 — but then the pawn to e5 is winning.
The knight to g4 — hitting the f4-pawn, threatening the capture on f4, and attacking the d4-bishop: a simple double attack that costs White at least a piece.
White takes on c6.

We recapture with the b-pawn, ruining White's structure and opening the b-file — with White castled queenside that often spells immediate doom. The queen to b6 hits f2, which the g4-knight also attacks; the pawn to e5 chasing the bishop is another plan.
White plays the bishop to d4.
We respond instantly with the bishop to h6, pinning the queen.
White plays the pawn to f4, walking right into the losing line.

The pawn to e5 — the crusher. With the queen pinned, the f4-pawn can't move, so it's as if it isn't there and e5 wins. White's best is to take on e5 and decline the recapture, down a full piece. Then the attack is decisive: the c3-pawn becomes a battering ram shattering White's queenside cover, the queen to b6 threatens mate in one plus a check on e3, and the lobster-pincer mate with the queen reaching a3 finishes it — first opening the centre with d5 so the king finds no relief, and connecting the rooks with the bishop to g4 to bring a rook to d8.
The Modern is the Pirc's cousin — g6 and Bg7, often transposing, the hypermodern way to hand White the centre and shoot at it later.
White just castled — and that quietly hangs the e4-pawn.
So take it: Nxe4, a free pawn with no reason to decline. The lesson is to never autopilot against an unusual opening — your opponent did, and dropped a pawn for nothing.
notes.teaches: Don't play on autopilot against offbeat openings; check for free material every move.

notes.explains: Now react accurately: d5 cements the knight on its e4 outpost.
notes.teaches: Support a well-placed knight with a pawn rather than leaving it to be kicked.

notes.explains: Answer the check by building a pawn chain with c6 rather than blocking with a piece.

Here's the key: not Bf5, which runs into the nasty Nh4 hitting the bishop and toppling the whole construction. Instead f5 — the Pillsbury knight. Pawns are the best defenders of a piece, and now the e4-knight is a rock.
notes.teaches: Anchor an advanced knight with a pawn, not a piece; a pawn-defended outpost can't be dislodged.

notes.explains: Just castle and develop — and don't take the g5-knight, which would defeat the whole purpose of the knight on e4.
notes.teaches: Don't trade off the piece whose only job is to support your dominant outpost.

notes.explains: Now the strike: the knight on e4 is a type-two piece, and the queen already x-rays it through the pawn — so push the pawn to e5, occupying the centre while keeping the knight supported. If White replies f3, we take on d4 with devastating consequences to his loose king.
notes.teaches: When your queen x-rays your own advanced knight through a pawn, advance that pawn to gain the centre with tempo.

notes.explains: Black tries the bishop to c5 — it looks too good to be true, seeming to stop our d4. If it really worked, everyone would play it.
But it has a flaw — the fork trick, the knight snapping on e5.
...Bxf2+ is the classic mistake at this level.
The king takes, and material is dead level.
We collect the pawn back on e5. The exposed king looks disastrous — but it's an illusion: Black has thrown away several tempi AND the dark-squared bishop for it.
teaches: open king is fine when the opponent overpaid for it

notes.explains: So we take the center with d4, cashing in the tempi Black handed us.
The queen check is nothing to fear.
The king simply steps to g1 — perfectly safe behind its pawns.
teaches: the king is safe on g1

notes.explains: We develop quietly with the bishop to e3 — better than a knight to f5, which just chases the queen back to where it wanted to go anyway.
teaches: don’t make a move that helps the enemy queen

notes.explains: With our development lead we play ambitiously — the bishop to c4 — and a careless ...d6 here would even drop the queen.
The queen-trap: the bishop to g5, and it works precisely because the bishop on c4 already covers the queen's only escape square. Play tricky moves that are good in their own right AND carry a trap.
teaches: the Bg5 queen-trap, guarded by Bc4

notes.explains: h4 does two jobs at once — it threatens h5 to win another piece, and it finds a job for the rook.
teaches: a move that does two things

notes.explains: The sacrifice on h6 tears the king's cover apart, and the pieces come home with interest.
We take White and face the Caro-Kann.
We build the centre with d4; Black plays ...d5.
We take on d5.
Black recaptures with the c-pawn.
We play c4 — the Panov Attack.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
We pin the knight with the bishop to g5.
Black plays the queen to a5.
We take on f6.
Black recaptures with the e-pawn.
We grab queenside space with c5.
Black fianchettoes with ...g6.
We develop the bishop to d3.
Black completes the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
We castle and Black castles.
We play a3, preparing b4.
Black plays the bishop to g4.
We expand with b4.
Black retreats the queen to d8.
We reroute the bishop to e2.
Black plays f5.
We play the rook to b1.
Black plays the rook to e8.
We bring the queen to d2.
Black plays a6.
We double on the e-file, the rook to e1.
Black plays the queen to d7.
We reroute the bishop to d1.
Black doubles rooks with ...Rad8.
We tuck the king to h1.
Black lifts the rook to e6.
We play h3.
Black retreats the bishop to h5.
We play g3.
Black takes our knight, capturing on f3 with check.
We recapture with the bishop; Black grabs on d4 with the knight.
We fianchetto the bishop to g2.
Black lifts the rook to e4.
We snap the rook on e4 with the knight; Black recaptures with the f-pawn.
We play the rook to d1.
Black plays f5.
We tuck the king to h2.
Black centralizes the bishop on e5.
We play f3.
Black plays the queen to c7.
We step the king to g1.
Black reroutes the knight to e6.
Another Pirc. e4, d6.
d4, c6 — it is a line, but we don't

have to do anything particularly different from what we normally do. I'm tempted to play the knight to d5, since this guy will probably pre-move — the knight to c3, the queen to c7. How should we continue our development?
There are several approaches here — we can choose to occupy more of the centre with f4, but let's play the calm move with the knight to f3. e5.
And now of course we develop this bishop to c4, and we're going to dismantle the hell out of this line.
Now the bishop to g4 pins our knight, and by pinning it he's exerting indirect pressure on the d4-pawn. So where should we put this bishop with an eye toward that?
The bishop to f7 doesn't work because of the queen takes f7 — he thinks he's cool, but we're going to show him he's not. This is why you shouldn't be afraid of

these kinds of players who do all this stuff really fast. Now, here's an interesting question: which side do we castle? We can actually castle queenside — that would be risky — but before we decide, I'm annoyed as hell about this pin: how can we dispose of it without moving the bishop to a passive square? h3 and g4.

Now, what would h3 and g4 mean in terms of where we castle? We basically commit to castling queenside — but that's okay, because he's developed so poorly that it's fine for us to telegraph it; he's not going to checkmate us, he doesn't have anything.
Let's get rid of the pin.
And since we've decided to castle queenside, let's castle queenside — the queen to e2, castle — and then we're going to start attacking on the kingside, even though he's not castled.

That doesn't matter — it doesn't mean we can't attack on the kingside. The queen to e2, so the rook is the star of the show on the d-file. Do we need to defend this square? I'd say no, probably not — we can just castle, and if he takes, I'll show why that's fine. We're ahead in development, so the immediate association you should make is to open up the centre — so the first step is to open it up a little more so we can better exploit our lead. Now, what should we capture here? This is not an obvious answer at all — there are actually three plausible captures, all with a compelling case. We can take f7, luring the king onto f7, sacrificing our bishop to try to mate him; we can also play e-takes-d7. Let's do it, punish him, get our hands dirty, since his whole queenside is undeveloped.

This is a Scotch where the queen's knight was never committed — an odd but pleasant version, with the bishop already leaning on the centre. The most ambitious choice isn't a quiet developing move but to castle: it keeps a central break in reserve for the right moment, and it readies a rook to pile onto the weak e-pawn.
Press the luck — the rook swings to e8 to attack the weak pawn. If the opponent props it with the f-pawn, that's a huge concession, weakening the diagonal and inviting a central strike.

When the bishop pins to defend the pawn indirectly and then retreats, the real question is whether to grab the pawn with a further push that weakens the king — so weigh it concretely. The verdict is yes: it's a valuable central pawn, and the calculation holds up, because after the dust settles the enemy knight hangs and the king is still stuck in the centre, tied up, buying the time to consolidate. That's the judgement: a concrete line, not a general rule, decides it.

A tactic to watch for in the resulting position — a knight leap to f5 becomes possible precisely because the central pawn hasn't moved yet, so that square isn't yet under control. Always check which squares your own un-played pawns are leaving open.

Don't snatch the bishop — the recapture would open a file and hand the opponent pressure. Instead the knight captures on c3, and the in-between check doesn't work because the king simply steps up and wins the piece back. Calculate the zwischenzug one step further before trusting it.

The queen to f6 does triple duty — attacking, defending, and eyeing threats at once. And if the opponent lunges the queen out, the central pawn advances to shove the knight back, and the position is officially consolidated.

Rather than the automatic pawn move, develop as incisively as possible — with threats. The knight to c6 piles onto the enemy knight immediately, and if it's captured, a recapture leaves a piece hanging. Develop while harassing, not just developing.

When there's a choice of recaptures, take with the knight rather than the queen — keeping the dark-squared bishop, because bishops guard weak squares better than knights do. Grabbing with the queen would tempt a trade but creates no threat and lets a pawn fall.

Only now, once the pressure has done its work, is it time for the modest pawn to d6 — the king is still a touch airy, so a couple of consolidating moves finish the job and leave an excellent position.

When the bishop attacks the pawn, the passive rook retreat ties a heavy piece to defence — better is a pawn to c6, building a chain so the bishop just bites on granite, with a further central expansion to follow.
Against Owen's b6, resist f3 — that's weakening and violates the don't-block-your-own-pieces rule; it belongs against g6, not here. Simply play Nc3 first.
notes.teaches: Don't reach for f3 by reflex against ...b6; develop naturally with Nc3.

notes.explains: Black wants Bb4, so we neutralize it with Bd3 rather than committing a3.
Ne2 is the key — the g1-knight goes to e2 so that after a3 and Bxc3, we recapture with the other knight, keeping our pawn structure whole and the e4-pawn firmly defended.
notes.teaches: Reroute so a knight can recapture on c3, avoiding doubled pawns and keeping e4 solid.

notes.explains: After the trades we own the two bishops and stand solidly better; castling is simplest, but Bg5 is the more ambitious, annoying try.
Bg5 threatens e5, and its bite grows the less developed Black is — he has fewer resources to meet the break.
notes.teaches: A pin that threatens a central break is most dangerous against an underdeveloped opponent.

notes.explains: d6 doesn't solve the threat, so e5 crashes through and White is already winning.
The bigger takeaway: don't play these offbeat sidelines as Black until you're nearly a master, and never as a main opening — meanwhile you rack up points with a good setup ready against them.
notes.teaches: Have a prepared setup against dubious sidelines; you score heavily against players who overuse them.

notes.explains: Now don't get greedy for minor pieces — go for mate. The pieces fall into place: open the g-file, get the queen to h5. Bxf6 forces the pawn recapture, then Rxg2-check and Qh5, and Qxh6 is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: When a mating net is available, aim for checkmate, not the maximum material.

notes.explains: Black answers with c5, the Sicilian.
Black fianchettoes with g6, and White replies c3 — the Alapin idea, preparing to seize the centre with d4.
teaches: c3 prepares d4 against the fianchetto Sicilian

notes.explains: The bishop comes to g7, glaring down the long diagonal.
White builds the full centre with d4, and after the trades holds a broad pawn duo.
Black hits back with d5, but White snaps it off — and pockets a clean pawn in the process.
teaches: A premature ...d5 can simply drop a pawn to the exd5 break

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to f6 to chase the extra pawn, and White props it up with the bishop to c4 — the setup White knows and trusts.
Black's bishop shuffles to d7, a passive post, and the engine already reads White better than a pawn up: extra material and the freer game.
The knight develops to c3, reinforcing the extra d5-pawn, and Black castles.
White nudges the bishop back to b3 — out of harm's way, still guarding d5 — and castles. Everything is defended and the pawn stands.
teaches: Retreat the bishop to keep it defending the key pawn

notes.explains: White begins rerouting the knight from c3 toward the kingside, while Black rolls the queenside pawns forward.
teaches: Reroute a knight toward the action rather than leave it passive

notes.explains: The knight reaches f4 — an aggressive square eyeing e6, g6, and the d5 support — as Black keeps pushing on the flank.
White centralizes the rook to e1, stacking force behind the passed pawn.
And the knight lands on e5 — a monster outpost the pawns can't touch. The evaluation leaps: White is now winning by a clear margin, the whole board bending toward that central knight.
teaches: A knight on e5 backed by a passed pawn is a decisive trump
plans: Push the passed d-pawn behind it

notes.explains: The passed pawn drives to d6, splitting Black's camp in two and freezing his pieces — the engine now sees it as good as won.
teaches: A passed pawn on the sixth cramps and divides the defense

notes.explains: The pawn to g4 attacks the bishop on f5 and simply wins it — with two knights swarming, the tactics all fall White's way.
The knights crash through, White collects material, and the position is overwhelming.

This is the starting position of the Jobava London — what you'll get 75 to 80 percent of the time. d4, the knight to f6, the knight to c3; most people know to play d5 here, otherwise Black risks getting move-ordered into a French or a Pirc, so a lot of people go g6 or
pre-move, and then White plays e4. d5, the bishop to f4.

g6 is on the board — the line most King's-Indian and Grünfeld players end up choosing, because it's essentially a Grünfeld setup: d5, the knight to f6, and g6, except our pawn isn't on c4, which leads to a fundamentally different, incredibly tactical game. When we prepared the course, we concluded the most testing setup against g6 involves quickly pushing the h-pawn up the board.
It sounds gimmicky, but it poses very serious practical problems — strong players have beaten top players with this setup over the board, so it's legitimately annoying. e3.
the bishop to g7.
After e3 we immediately start running the h-pawn up the board with h4.
If you're not experienced with this idea, which recurs in several openings, I'll show you some examples.
Now we respond by continuing our development — the knight to f3.

It appears the kingside is completely frozen after Black castles — that there will never be any attacking chances — but that's not true. Sooner than you might think, we'll be able to play the typical g4, to force Black's pawn off h5 and then push our own pawn to h5, a common attacking technique you see in Sicilian Dragons: open as many files and diagonals as possible and let the pieces infiltrate. There are a couple of options — the knight to b5, or

the knight to e5 — but we settled on a move that prepares long castling, the queen to d2, which is ultimately where we'll castle; with a pawn on h4, in the g6 lines you castle queenside 95 percent of the time.

You get a fascinating opposite-side-castling game, and our claim is that White's attack is simply more effective — though the game might also be decided by a battle in the centre, which seems likely given the last move, c5. c5 is typical in queen's-pawn openings and particularly sensible here because we have a knight on c3; in the regular London you often meet c5 with c3, and here we can't solidify quite as effectively, but there's a major
benefit to developing the knight to c3: the knight aims at the d5-pawn, and very often c5 is simply met with d-takes-c5, which is exactly what we do.

We take this pawn. You might say aren't we giving away central control — to an extent, but the d5-pawn is now under very serious fire, and we can capture it. The knight to d7. Our opponent seems very confident — this is a lot more theory than most people at this level reproduce. I'm pretty sure we can take the other pawn, but then Black takes and plays the bishop takes b2 — let me think. We could play the knight takes d5, but then the knight takes d5, the queen takes d5, and the bishop takes b2, and after we move our rook, Black drops the bishop back to c3 — I'm not enthralled. b4 runs into the knight to e4, losing at least the exchange on a1. d-takes-e5 might have been wrong, but let's make the most of it; even allowing the knight to take c5 is fine — Black isn't winning. One typical setup involves

moving this knight away from f3 — playing the knight to e5 — and then putting the pawn up to f3 to prepare the idea I mentioned. Let's play the knight to e5; I assume he'll take on c5, the only sensible move.
He probably has my course — c5 is definitely analysed; there are just so many lines that I often get confused.

The knight takes c5, and our knight is nicely positioned in the centre. Now the second component: f3, played for two reasons. The most important is preparing an eventual g4 and h4-h5; the second is positional — controlling the e4-square, not permitting either of Black's knights to jump into e4, which would be very unpleasant. We restrict the knights' mobility, and yes, Black has superior central control, but that's not necessarily good, because the d5-pawn is a serious target, and by castling queenside we add an attacker on it.

The position is incredibly sharp, and we've found that people struggle in unconventional Jobava positions where the usual principles don't apply — one of the biggest perks of playing it. The bishop to f5. In many of these lines this is met with g4, h-takes-g4, and h5, a risky idea we could try; the alternative is to play it safe, castle queenside, continue our development, and go after the d5-pawn. The bishop to e2 is a candidate to prepare g4, but it's a little passive — we often don't need it, because we're happy to sacrifice the g4-pawn, which opens up the files.

As much as the tacticians want us to play g4, I think it's way premature — it might work, but this isn't what I want to promote; I don't want to make gimmicky trap-setting moves unless we're losing. So let's castle. We're threatening the knight takes d5, and we'll take that pawn if given the chance. It's a little dangerous, because this bishop is x-raying the b2-pawn, and the knight on e5 isn't supported by a pawn, so it's vulnerable — we have to react carefully. If Black plays the queen to b6, probably the best move, it creates no immediate threat but aims at b2, so once our knights leave e5 and c3, we must be especially careful about mate on b2. With opposite-side castling, you always have to identify the short-term threats and understand how each move affects the long-term tactical patterns, so you can nip things in the bud before you blunder them.

It's risky, what we're doing, but it's fun and teaches you a lot about tactical positions, and it's just not easy for Black to play this structure. The bishop to e6 is a bit passive — music to my ears, because it doesn't accentuate the queenside attack, essentially loses a move, and takes the e6-square away from the knight, which could have dropped back there. So this increases the appeal of g4, which is now very tempting — still incredibly double-edged, but with our king shepherded to safety it's a good time to consider it. We just smash through on the kingside, the kind of move a GM plays without calculating many variations, because in this line g4 and h5 just works, opening a bunch of files — and our queen from d2 gets direct access to the h-

file, so when the h-file opens, the queen to h2 could create an unstoppable mate threat on h7. We could still play positionally with the king to b1, but let's go for it and play in the spirit of the Jobava — g4. Hopefully Black takes; he could also ignore it, which might be best. I actually would not take on g4 with Black — an advanced decision — realising Black is stable on the kingside for now: we're not threatening anything, g5 isn't really a threat, and g-takes-h5 isn't a threat because the knight recaptures.

The queen to a5 — very impressive play so far, but it might be inaccurate, because it walks into a lot of tactics. The queen to a5 doesn't do anything immediately, but it pressures the a2-pawn, which is annoying, because we don't want our knight to be the only piece standing between us and checkmate — we want to be safer than that.

There's a move that caters to the defensive needs of the position, one you should automatically consider any time you castle — the king to b1. As it turns out, it also poses a hidden tactical threat, which increases its appeal.

Another recurring theme: when the queens are in a standoff on this diagonal, there's the idea of the knight takes d5, a classic discovery concept. He missed it — but it's not as simple as it seems: after the knight takes d5, Black can't take the knight or he loses the queen, so he plays the queen takes d2; we take the queen, and Black takes on d5 and is up a piece — but the rub is that after the knight takes d5, the queen takes d2, we can go and take the pawn on e7, an intermediate move, and only after the king moves do we recapture the queen — up two pawns. The knight on e7 is virtually trapped, and Black could try the rook to e8, but my intuition says we'll be able to evacuate it, maybe with g5.

The d5-square is open for our knight; it doesn't seem Black can win the knight cleanly, but it's a little dicey — let's take the plunge; I'd be beyond impressed if he saw all this and found a way to trap the knight.

So this is an important point. The queen takes d2, and now the knight takes f6 is a very common blunder, because Black actually recaptures with the pawn, and then the pawn attacks our knight on e5 — you're assuming Black
has to recapture with the bishop, and then everything is chill — but no, Black takes back with a pawn and we lose our knight. So instead, the knight takes e7 with check.

Another important tactical detail, in our favour, is that the rook is on f8 — I'll explain why after the game. Funnily, we could also play the knight takes g6 and cash in the knight for a bunch of pawns, but there's no need now.
Let's recapture the queen — and of course this rook is also hanging.

Don't forget that when a lot of exchanges happen, it's a very common time to blunder, because people forget to update their perception of the board — the rook on c8 is a piece that would often be blundered. The rook to d8 is the most testing move. The downside of taking on d8 is that Black then threatens checkmate on c1, forcing us to burn a tempo moving the bishop, and I don't see a great spot for it; but I have an idea — take on d8, then the bishop to h3, he attacks the knight with the rook to e8, and I go g5. I don't like the knight takes g6, because after the recapture and king move a rook hangs and we gain nothing. Let's go for my idea — we're short of time. There's also the rook to d4, a collinear move: putting a piece on an intermediate square of the same file when two pieces stare at each other.

The rook to d4 looks very interesting, because then the knight takes g6 becomes a serious threat. It has to be calculated — a head-spinning line with crazy tactics — but let's take the plunge, the rook to d4, an extremely complicated position, and we're short of time, so I might have to put on my GM hat.
The knight takes g6 is still possible as an emergency bailout, but h5 is very attractive to me — it feels like we emerge ahead in the resulting pandemonium.
Maybe I'm miscalculating — I'm largely using intuition, but h5 feels like the move. If the knight takes on h5, we play the pawn takes g4;

the knight takes h5, and the knight is pinned — we win it. He played this instantly, so maybe I'm missing something — let me think. f-takes-g4: as much as is going on, everything is protected for the time being, the bishop on f4 is untouchable because the knight is pinned,

the rook we took was protected by the pawn, and the knight on e7 isn't being attacked, so it's safe. I don't see it — I think we can just play f-takes-g4. Now not only are we threatening to take the knight, but when we do, we're also threatening the follow-up h-takes-g6, essentially checkmate with the rook on h1 opening up. The bishop takes g4 here loses on the spot.
I think Black is lost, but what would we do after the bishop takes g4? Let's avoid tunnel vision. The bishop takes c5 doesn't help at all,

Then when the king moves — f6 — let's try to be very precise, because we can take literally anything we want now; this is the fun part. The simplest option is the knight takes g6 with check, because on top of everything it also wins the rook in the corner. Less accurate is g-takes-h5, because then Black plays f-takes-e5 and the king runs to f6, so it's not mate. And the bishop takes f6 with check might be even stronger — I just realised it exists, because the knight is pinned, and if the rook takes, we take d8 with check
and then recapture the knight. The bishop to f6 or the knight to g6 — literally take your pick, it's totally winning either way; but let's play elegantly, in the spirit of the Jobava.
Total feast — the rook takes f6.
The rook takes d8 with check, and then of course we pick up the knight; and it's very
important that the bishop is protected in the final

position — this bishop is defended by the rook. The rest is a matter of technique. It's impressive that our knight ends up where it started, on e7, perfectly safe, and now we can evacuate it through d5 — another, sexier way would be to evacuate it through g8 using some tactics.

I'm trying to find the fastest win, a mate, but I don't see one, so let's just play it simple — the knight to d5, plain vanilla, just get the knight out of the danger zone. Not everything has to be tactically crazy; play simple chess, especially when you're up material.
And now our knight is manoeuvring to f4, where it's on a perfectly defended square pressuring h5. The rook to f5.
the knight to f4.

We're going to eliminate Black's last passed pawn — this is completely resignable. I always say, when you reach these positions, there are five or seven equally good moves, so how you convert is a matter of taste.
I like to go for checkmate and more material — some people emphasise trading, like the bishop to d3, but I want to deliver the check on g1, because I want to hunt this king down.
Maybe unsuccessfully, but this move feels right. The bishop to d3 — I don't see a mating pattern here, unfortunately.
We could play b3 if you're paranoid, but there's no back-rank threat right now — Black has no pieces left to deliver the back-rank mate. Let's give another check.
The king to e7.
And now I'm going to slide the rook over to h6, putting the rook behind the pawn,
maybe the rook to h7 to follow, then bring the bishop out — something's going to give.
The knight to e4 aligns the knight and the rook, so without further thinking, let's go the bishop to d3 and force exchanges.
The knight to d2 with check, obviously going
to c1, in order to attack the knight
simultaneously. Now again we have a choice: we can play the bishop takes f5 and simplify, or, if we want to win more material — all of Black's pieces, which is what I want to do —
we go the rook to g3. The one thing I'd recommend is that you don't automatically just trade — sometimes, if you can win a minor piece, that's better.
Black has the knight to h4, but then we go the rook to h3. This isn't a trade — I'm saying we could have taken on f5 and traded the rooks, which is a form of trade, but

The cleanest way to meet this gambit is to decline it — accepting the pawn is playable but dangerous, since the defender has to know a great deal to survive, which is exactly the fight the gambiteer wants.
The best declining move is the knight to f6 — developing and counterattacking the central pawn at once, which forces the opponent into a tamer, transposed structure rather than the sharp main lines.

Since the opponent declined to push the centre, now the pawn can be safely taken — and it's a superior version, because the bishop parked on d3 is passive, staring into its own pawn instead of raking toward the king. That single misplacement drains most of the activity the gambit is supposed to buy.

The tempting central push would weaken the d5 square, letting the opponent trade off a knight and plant a piece on the outpost. So begin with a flexible developing move, the knight to c6, with a modest pawn move to follow.

The pawn to d6 stops the central advance — and note how much friendlier this is than a real Morra, where the attacking bishop and an open file give the aggressor real chances. Here, everything is under control.

There's the eternal debate between the restrained and the fianchetto setups — and the deciding factor is urgency. With no pressure on development, there's time to optimise the bishop onto the long diagonal, since the central break isn't available to the opponent anyway.

The pin doesn't actually threaten the knight, so there's no need to react to it — the real question is whether to insert a rook-pawn move. Follow the logic: castling invites the standard plan of trading off the fianchettoed bishop, which would leave lasting holes around the king.

That bishop is the strongest piece on the board, so preserve it — the rook-pawn nudge, played while the rook is still home, shoos the bishop off the key diagonal. Then castling becomes safe, with the trade-off idea defused.

And here's the resource that makes the whole plan hold together — a king step to h7. It shores up the weakened pawn, and without it the earlier rook-pawn move simply wouldn't work. The king is perfectly safe there, screened by its own pawn chain.

Don't lash out with the central push, which would blunt the fianchettoed bishop and weaken d5 again. Instead solve the other bishop's development by bringing it to e6 — usually a square to avoid, but when the bishop isn't hemmed in it's an excellent, centralising post that controls the key square.

In a solid position like this, don't force matters — improve in measured steps. When you're unsure how to make progress, tap the pool of reasonable improving moves rather than freezing up. A rook to c8 activates the piece and contests the file — not every move has to climb Mount Everest.

A lovely little regrouping — a knight back to d7. It lifts the knight toward e5 or c5, reopens the bishop's diagonal, covers a central square, and readies the knight for an outpost. Small, substantive actions that quietly make the whole position healthier.

As the opponent reroutes a knight toward an outpost, adapt — one knight jump risks a pawn, so instead the knight leaps to e5. It seems to block the bishop again, but only for a moment: from e5 it either takes an important bishop or hops on to a dominant square.

When there's a choice of recaptures, make the positionally conscious one — take with the bishop, not the queen. Recapturing with the queen would allow a rook to the open file with tempo; keeping the file uncontested is worth more than the small material nicety.

A concept many players miss — an exposed queen isn't only something to attack with pieces or try to trap; it can be 'attacked' by your own queen to force a trade you actually want. Up a pawn and craving the open file, offering that swap hits the bishop and the queen at once, forcing the exchange into total queenside domination for the endgame.
In the queen endgame the extra passed pawn on d6 should win, but Black is angling for a perpetual — so the task is to avoid the draw with precise checks that walk his king out of the checking net.
notes.teaches: Convert a queen-and-passer ending by using checks to march the enemy king out of perpetual range.

notes.explains: g4-check is the precise finish — the king has been driven into the open and the checks finally connect to force the win.
We're White against the Scandinavian: the pawn to e4, d5, we take on d5, and instead of recapturing with the queen Black plays the knight to f6.
The bishop to b5 with check — the line I like. It's just a matter of knowing the patterns.
Black blocks with the knight from b8 to d7.
d5 completes the transposition to a Queen's Gambit Declined.
The traditional QGD — White pins with the bishop to g5.
The tricky main-line knight to d7, which also lays a trap that strong players have fallen into.
The queen to c2 is inaccurate — it leaves the d4-pawn unattended, and the principled c5 break pounces on exactly that weakness.
d4, and the knight to f6 — Black declines to fight for the centre with a pawn, planning to let White build it and then strike back. The makings of a King's Indian.
The knight to c3, the classical set-up — White is happy to take the whole centre and dare Black to challenge it.
d6 — the King's Indian in earnest. Black cedes space on purpose, banking on a later …e5 or …c5 break to hit the centre from the side.
e4, and White has the broad pawn centre the opening invites. The whole game is now a question: can Black crack it before White uses it?
g6, preparing the fianchetto — the dark-squared bishop is the soul of this defence, and it belongs on the long diagonal aiming straight through the centre at White's queenside.
The bishop to e2, a calm, classical developing square.
The bishop settles on g7 and White brings the knight to f3 — both sides just developing, the tension still coiled.
Black castles, tucking the king behind the fianchetto — one of the safest shelters in all of chess.
White castles too. A textbook classical King's Indian; now the plans diverge — White expands, Black looks for a break.
The bishop to g4, pinning the f3-knight. Black would love to trade it off, because that knight is the natural defender of White's centre.
The bishop to e3, developing and eyeing the dark squares.
The knight to c6, piling a second attacker onto d4 and White's centre.
d5 — White answers the pressure by pushing past, grabbing space and kicking the knight. This is the main King's Indian tension: a big White pawn chain versus Black's piece pressure.
The bishop takes on f3 and White recaptures with the bishop — Black cashes in the pin, trading off a key defender of the light squares.
The knight swings to e5, the classic King's Indian outpost, and White retreats the bishop to e2 to keep it. A beautiful square: central, secure, hard to dislodge.
c6 — the thematic break. Black chips at the base of White's pawn chain to open lines on the queenside.
a4 — White grabs queenside space of its own and takes b5 away from Black. The two sides are now racing on opposite wings.
The tension resolves on d5 — the pawns come off and the position opens a touch, both recaptures the engine's top choice.
The knight reroutes toward d7, unclogging and eyeing c5 and e5. Still all main-road stuff; the engine can't separate the sides.
a5, clamping down — White fixes the queenside and cramps Black's play there.
a6, shoring up b5 and keeping the structure intact.

The bishop to d4, offering to trade the dark-squared bishops. It's a slight concession — the engine would rather reroute the knight to a4 — but trading Black's proud g7-bishop is a reasonable positional aim.
The rook comes to c8, onto the half-open c-file — the natural home for a King's Indian rook once the c-file opens.
The queen to d2, connecting the rooks and supporting the dark-squared plans.
The knight to c5, a strong central post eyeing the queenside light squares.
The bishop to f3, defending the centre and reinforcing d5. The position is balanced and rich — both sides fully developed, no weaknesses yet.

And here's the slip. The knight steps back to d7 — but it pulls a guard off c5, and the engine's needle lurches almost four points toward White. The right idea was to keep the pieces coordinated, not to loosen the knights.
White pounces the way the engine demands: the bishop takes on g7, stripping away the fianchetto — and the follow-up b4 will hit the loose knight. White is suddenly winning.
Black recaptures with the king. The dark squares around it are now permanently tender, and White should be collecting material.
But the favour is returned. The rook to e1 instead of b4 — and the winning pawn-fork on c5 simply evaporates. A blitz game between two very fast players; the advantage sloshes back and forth.
Black seizes the reprieve — the knight back to f6, re-covering the light squares and climbing back to level. Crisis survived.
The queen to d4, centralising and pressuring the dark squares.
The knight to d7, calmly holding everything together.
The bishop drops to e2, a quiet regroup.
The queen to c7, eyeing the open c-file and the loose queenside.
The bishop to f1 — passive, the engine would rather reroute more actively, but the position is roughly balanced.
The rooks come to e8, contesting the centre file.
h3, a useful little luft, taking g4 away from Black's pieces.
The queen to c5, offering to trade queens into a comfortable position.
The queen to d2, sidestepping the trade for now.
The knight returns to e5 — that outpost again, the heart of Black's play.
The rook to a4, defending along the fourth rank and keeping an eye on the queenside.
h5, grabbing a little kingside space — slightly loosening, but the position stays roughly level.
The king to h1, a prudent tuck out of any back-rank or diagonal ideas.
e6 — Black strikes at the centre, prying open lines against White's slightly awkward pieces.
White takes on e6 — but the engine calls it an error; a quiet move like f4 was stronger, and now Black's rooks come alive on the open file.
The rook recaptures on e6, seizing the file.
The rook to d1 — again the engine prefers f4; White keeps missing the most testing continuation as the clock bites.
The rooks double on the e-file — Black is building real pressure down the centre now.
The queen to d4, trying to hold the fort — but it's an inaccuracy; the engine wanted to force matters instead.
The knight to c6, hitting the queen and gaining a tempo for the coming break.
The queen to d2 — and now the eval tips to Black. Small errors have accumulated, and White's position is quietly worse.
d5 — Black plants the pawn in the centre and takes over. This is the payoff of all that pressure: a mobile centre against a passive White army.
The bishop to d3, trying to blunt the coming push.
The pawn storms on to d4 and the knight is driven to e2 — Black's centre knifes forward, and it's Black firmly in control now, on the board and on the clock.
The c-pawn thrust turns this into a Maróczy Bind out of the Accelerated Dragon — the classic cramping structure, and familiar territory for a player who lives in these positions.
A rook to e8 is a natural move here, quietly preparing the central break — but it has to be handled with care, since the centre can bite back before it's fully prepared.
The central pawn advance to e6 is a serious error, because it invites a knight to b5 hitting the weakened dark squares. A single loosening move can hand the initiative straight over.
The way to stay in the fight is a pawn to d4, striking the bishop — it concedes the exchange, but keeps the position alive and full of play rather than passively worse.
Against a passive e3, just occupy the centre — this becomes a reverse French with an extra tempo for us.
notes.teaches: Meet a passive first move by planting pawns in the centre and playing for the extra tempo.

notes.explains: When White plays d4, close the centre with e4 — a clean introduction to how to handle a locked structure.
notes.teaches: Lock the centre with e4 to steer into a closed game you control.

notes.explains: Bb5-check is an empty check — block it with c6, which also props up the centre and gives us a nice pawn chain and a small edge.
notes.teaches: Answer a harmless check with a move that also reinforces your own structure.

notes.explains: Develop the bishop to d6, not b4 — d6 supports the centre and eyes the kingside.
Don't take the g4-bishop, which would let White's queen out to hit g7 — instead f5 simply chases it back while extending our pawn chain.
notes.teaches: Repel a bishop with a pawn rather than trade it into your opponent's attacking plan.

notes.explains: The open game — both sides stake a claim in the centre with the king's pawns.
White develops the knight and then pins with the bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez, leaning on the knight that guards e5.
teaches: The Ruy Lopez pressures the e5-defender via Bb5

notes.explains: Black plays the knight to f6 and puts the question with a6; the bishop retreats along the diagonal to a4, keeping the pin alive, and White plays the modest d3 — a quiet, modern Ruy.
Black gains space and shoves the bishop with b5.
The bishop tucks back to b3, still eyeing the a2-g8 diagonal and the f7-square; both sides finish the kingside and castle.
teaches: The b3-bishop trains on f7 in the closed Ruy

notes.explains: Black bolsters the centre with d6 — the classic closed Ruy structure.
White plays h3, making luft and denying Black the ...Bg4 pin.
teaches: h3 prevents the ...Bg4 pin before it can land

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to e6, offering to trade off White's strong light-squared bishop.
White obliges and takes on e6.

Black recaptures with the f-pawn — a double-edged choice: it hands Black a half-open f-file for the rook, but it also leaves doubled, isolated e-pawns. White brings the knight to c3 and points at the soft d5-square.
teaches: Recapturing ...fxe6 trades a half-open file for doubled e-pawns

notes.explains: The knight hops to g5, probing the weakened e6 and f7 squares.
Black answers by planting the knight on d4 — a proud central outpost right in White's half.
teaches: A knight on d4 is a powerful central outpost

notes.explains: White challenges it immediately with the knight to e2, offering to swap off the intruder.
The knights come off, and Black recaptures to leave a pawn wedged on d4.
White plays c3 to chip at that wedge and open lines against it.
teaches: Undermine an advanced enemy pawn with a pawn lever

notes.explains: After the trade White rebuilds a c3-d3 pawn chain, and the structure settles.
White expands in the centre with d4, claiming space and opening the position for the better-placed pieces.
The queen slides to d2, coordinating the pieces — and the engine now reads a clear pull for White, the small edges finally adding up.
teaches: Accumulated small edges become a real advantage
plans: Coordinate the queen and rooks on the central files

notes.explains: This is the highest-rated person we've faced thus far, and I'm going to switch back to e4 after a couple of d4 games — let's see how our openings hold up at a high level. e4, c5.
I'm going to play the Smith-Morra, which is kind of a scary prospect,
because I don't know the Smith-Morra well enough to justify playing it at this level — but if Black demonstrates superior knowledge, so be it. c-takes-d4, c3.
I'm actually happy to see the knight to f6, because this transposes the game into an
Alapin Sicilian — the move here is e5. Most Smith-Morra players are disappointed when they see the Declined Morra with the knight to f6.
The early c-pawn advance isn't great — it permanently weakens the d4 square, and that hole can be occupied straight away by developing a knight toward it.
Develop as if this were an Accelerated Dragon — the fianchetto with g6 and the bishop to g7 controls the d4 square with even greater force. Everything is aimed at that one weakness.

The knight-development question has a subtle answer: the natural square would block the bishop's grip on d4, so route the knight to e7 instead. It looks odd, but it's a very typical set-up that keeps the bishop's control of the key square intact.
Now cash in that control — the knight leaps into the d4 outpost, a permanent monster in the heart of the position, soon to be reinforced by its partner so the two knights guard each other.
Before adding any spice, finish the basics — castle and get the king safe. Don't jump the gun on an attack until development is complete.

One way forward is to break with f5 and open the position — the logic being the classic one: with better-placed pieces, especially that dominant knight, it's often the moment to open lines. It's risky in front of your own king, but the piece superiority justifies it.
The opponent's kingside pawn push has handed over a hook — a fixed target to lever against. The plan is to attack it, capturing to open lines and prise the shelter apart.
The queen swings to h4 to pile onto that weak pawn — bringing the heaviest piece to bear exactly where the opponent overextended.
As the opponent shoves pawns further forward, they only overextend — the pawns become harder and harder to defend. The way to punish it is a central strike to shatter what's left of the defences.

No need for fireworks — the calm capture wins a free pawn, and it rolls forward to send the defending bishop back, clearing the way for the queen to infiltrate. Simplicity beats a speculative sacrifice when the position is already winning.

Recapture with the knight — and even though it allows the outpost knight to be traded off, look at the dark squares laid bare around the enemy king. The exchange rips open the very colour complex the attack needs.
With the king boxed into the corner and no escape, the threat of the queen to h4 is essentially mate in two. The collapse came purely from pushing too many pawns in front of the king.
Against the Fried Liver, Na5 is the only move — the Polerio, giving back a pawn for the bishop pair and a lasting initiative.
notes.teaches: Meet the Fried Liver with Na5, trading a pawn for the bishop pair and long-term pressure.

notes.explains: Recapture with the pawn, bxc6, not the knight — it hits the bishop and pushes it back with tempo, which is the whole engine of Black's initiative here.
notes.teaches: Recapture with the pawn that gains a tempo on an enemy piece, keeping the initiative rolling.

notes.explains: The compensation is hard to see — our pawns are ruined and the a5-knight looks offside — but it's real: White's g5-knight is stranded and his pieces are undeveloped. We have to keep the pressure on before he untangles.
notes.teaches: Compensation for a pawn lives in the opponent's loose pieces and lost time, not in your own pretty structure.

notes.explains: We answer e4 with c5 — the Sicilian, our fighting reply.
d4 already. This is an anti-Sicilian move — the entry point into the Smith-Morra Gambit, where White throws a pawn at us to rip the position open.
We take, capturing on d4. Now White has a choice — recapture, or slip into an open Sicilian with a knight to f3.
c3 — the true Morra pawn offer. Here there's almost an ideological choice: grab the pawn and play right into a Morra player's dream, or refuse it and take the fun out of White's whole setup.
The knight to f6 is that refusal. We won't touch the c3 pawn — that's exactly what Morra specialists want. Instead we hit e4 and steer the game somewhere White is far less prepared for.
e5 lunges forward, kicking our knight. This is the transposition we were after — the pawn structure is now an Alapin, not a gambit.

The knight settles on d5, and we've reached an Alapin Sicilian by force. This is the whole point: instead of memorizing forcing Morra theory where one slip loses in five moves, we've reached a much safer, more understandable structure.

White recaptures on d4, rebuilding the center. The beauty of this whole line is that you can play it without fear — you don't have to know it to the same razor's-edge depth the accepted Morra demands.
d6 immediately, chipping away at White's advanced center. We start questioning that e5 spearhead right away rather than letting White sit comfortably.
A knight to f3 develops and props up e5. Now we have several tries — we could grab on e5 — but the cleanest is the main road.

The knight to c6 is the main, principled continuation, piling on d4 and finishing our development. Against the standard bishop to c4 there's a rare line — one Sam Shankland showed me — that really tests how deep our opponent's theory runs.
But White plays the bishop to d3 instead of c4. The pause before it tells us they're already out of book — this is just a developing move, nothing special, and crucially it doesn't do what c4 would.

So we develop the bishop to g4, eyeing the f3 knight. If White does bail out by capturing on d6, we recapture with the queen and land an ideal isolated-queen's-pawn setup, with our knight already planted on the blockading square in front of that pawn.

White does go queen to b3, we chop on f3, White recaptures with the g-pawn, and we commit to e6. Now the sharp line is queen takes b7, knight takes d4, and the check on b5 has to be reckoned with — we capture the bishop, White checks with the queen from b5, and the point I'd missed at first is that we don't have to run the king to e7; we simply block with the queen to d7, and the resulting endgame favors us because White's pawn structure is a wreck. In the game White actually declines the b7 pawn, which makes our path obvious — keep striking at the center with a capture on e5 while White still can't finish developing. The safe alternatives, a rook to b8 or the queen to d7, were both excellent; honestly the queen to d7 would have been far easier to handle. But we're playing maximally principled, trusting the complications, because our lead in development is enormous and White's whole position is on the verge of collapse.

Our knight is hanging and can't move — a retreat walks into a bishop check on b5 that's mating, and the knight on c6 will be under crushing fire. So the near-automatic move is the bishop check on b4, played essentially without further calculation, because it can only help us: it opens the door to castle kingside — a safety valve, a worst-case escape. Even in the grimmest scenario we could sacrifice the knight on c6, throw a rook to c8 with tempo, and dream of infiltrating on c1 after a knight takes c3. That's all brainstorming, not forced yet.

White blocks with the bishop to d2. The first question I ask is simply: can we castle? If yes, most of our problems dissolve and we never have to shuffle the king to f8. And there's a gorgeous resource lurking — after we castle and White grabs on c6, a rook to c8 sets up a rook lift to c1 with check that isn't a blunder, because the blocking bishop on d2 is pinned. When the king steps to e2 we scoop the rook on h1, and even if White interposes by capturing our bishop, we have one more blow: the knight swings to f4 with a nasty check and then collects the d-pawn with the queen. It all works because White's queenside has never developed.

So we castle — the answer was yes. This is why we did the hard thinking in the opening's first ten moves: now the play is straightforward, and White is simply lost if the calculation holds. Once a queen takes c6 fails to that rook lift, White's position caves in; his queen goes from greatest asset to greatest liability — stranded offside on the queenside, unable to rejoin the game or defend the loose points scattered across the board. White can't even castle safely: a capture on d2 with a queen check on g5 rakes in the minor pieces, and our knight leaping to f4 hits g2 with mate ideas.

White tries a rook to g1. Now we shift from sharp tactics to simple technique. Our knight isn't really hanging — we can leave it on c6 — but why would we, when it has a dream square on d4? After the knight lands on d4 we've checked the ideas: if White captures our bishop, we recapture, and should the queen take on b4 our knight jumps to f3 forking the king and rook while unmasking a discovered hit on the d3 bishop. White can't hold everything together.

We take on d4, and there's nothing to fear — a bishop lunge to h6 at g7 is simply illegal, and there are no pieces near our king for White to attack. The one thing to avoid is pushing the f-pawn, which would allow a lateral back-rank mate. White's best try to stave off the doom is a bishop to e4, since it guards the sore f3 pawn; there's no easy way to hold f3 otherwise. Meanwhile we can pile up on the queenside with a rook to b8 or even set about trapping that stranded queen with a quiet a5.
White does defend with the bishop to e4. Now we just maximize — and the straightforward path is a rook to b8, bringing our last piece into the attack with tempo against the offside queen.

The rook swings to b8. From here it's take the bishop, take the b2 pawn, and our rook roars into the attack while White's queen is hopelessly stranded on a7 — it did its job snatching b7 and a7, but now it can't get home. When you sense the win is close, don't hunt only for mate: look for the move that wins material outright. A knight to c3 is the cleanest, hitting the rook and preparing tactics down the file. There are a dozen winning tries — a queen to h4, a knight to f4 — but the discipline is to choose simple, healthy moves and never blow it chasing a brilliancy: a flashy queen check that lets the king slip out can hand back the whole advantage. White is completely cooked and resigns.
White plays the Alapin — the pawn to c3 — preparing to build the center with d4.
The bishop to d3 isn't a great move — it blocks in his own other bishop.
So we grab the center ourselves with d5.
White's e5 attacks our knight.
The knight jumps to g4 — dodging forward and going straight after the e5-pawn.
White pins with the bishop to b5.
We unpin with the bishop to d7, freeing the knight to move again.
Now the tactic: the knight takes on e5, winning the pawn — because the bishop on b5 is hanging and our knight is double-parked, covering both captures at once.
teaches: the double-parked knight wins the pawn

notes.explains: After the bishop check on d7 the recapturing knight collects everything, and we come out a clean center pawn up.
White tries to pry open the f-file with f4, heading for f5.
g6 takes the sting out of f5 — since pawns capture diagonally, it quietly adds a defender to that square, so any push there just gets taken.
teaches: pawns defend diagonally: g6 covers f5

notes.explains: We fianchetto the bishop to g7, onto the board's longest diagonal.
The knight reroutes to f6, heading for a dream central outpost.
We have White against the French — the pawn to e4, met by e6.
The pawn to d4, grabbing the centre.
Black challenges with d5.
The pawn to e5 — the Advance Variation.
Black strikes with the pawn to c5. The normal move now is c3, but we've been playing this differently.
The odd-looking knight to f3 — accelerating development instead of the usual c3.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We keep avoiding c3 and simply develop — the bishop to d3. Not the bishop to b5, a very common mistake here I'll explain later.
Black captures on d4.
We castle, just developing our pieces.

Black plays the pawn to f6, a main line. The whole zen of this system is full control over the e5-square: lose it and Black's pawns start rumbling up the board. So we must NOT just take on f6 and give up that control.
The rook to e1 — either that or the bishop to f4 to reinforce control of e5; we choose the rook.
Black captures on e5.
We recapture with the knight on e5, maintaining our grip on the square.
Black develops the knight to f6. Now, how to develop the bishop while keeping control of e5 — the pin with the bishop to g5?
Don't get distracted by the one-move pin — the goal is further control of e5, not the pin. So the bishop to f4: it looks a little lame, but positionally it's the better decision.
Black plays the bishop to d6. We need even more control of the square — the whole battle is about preserving that e5-knight. The queen to e2 would defend it, true.
But better to combine two things: develop the last knight to a square that also defends e5 — the knight to d2, heading for f3.
Black castles.

The knight to f3. Watch the x-ray — our bishop is undefended, so mind discoveries like the knight to g4; not dangerous, but the prophylactic bishop to g3 when time permits keeps it safe and off the rook's file. It's the London principle: control the central square and we have full compensation for the pawn — lose it and there's hell to pay. The queen to d2 walks into a skewer and the knight to g4, so the queen to e2 may be better.

Black plays the knight to e4. I'm not worried about the knight to h5 — I'd just retreat the bishop; enough pieces cover e5, which is exactly why we rerouted the knight to f3. Options now: the bishop to g3 pretending nothing's wrong, or a more direct approach.
The direct way: capture on c6. The recapture with the b-pawn is forced, since the queen hangs — and now we take on d6.
Black recaptures on d6 with the queen — surprising; I expected the knight, in which case we'd have brought the other knight to e5.
We take the knight, the bishop landing on e4.
Black recaptures on e4. A common mistake here would be to pre-move — never pre-move unless you're 100% sure; always take a couple of seconds to check you're not missing something.

Because the rook capture would let Black play c5, opening a massive diagonal for the bishop — no good. Instead the queen takes d4, hitting the queen: after a trade, Black's pawn structure is in shambles, so his failure to recapture correctly was a real mistake.
The pawn to e4, c5.
c3 — I was selfishly hoping for the elephant, and we get it.
e6 — a second-tier move, considered by most to be the third-best option.
Black plays d5, and we have a totally viable alternative, recommended in the elephant bible I've been using.
We take the pawn on d5 — White is considered slightly better in the resulting position.
Black recaptures with the queen, which transposes to a position that could also arise from the main move d5.
— is to develop the knight to f3, a move we know we want to play.

Black plays the knight to f6. I love facing this, because my recommendation is rather sexy — a dangerous move that can win fast against imprecision, though a quick win shouldn't be your only goal; there's nothing wrong with tricky lines that don't sacrifice objective quality.
The knight to a3 — rare, incredibly dangerous, and even against Black's best moves you're seriously fighting for an advantage. A typical Alapin developing move.

The knight is heading for b5, and what makes that strong in the elephant is Black's queen sitting on the forkable d5-square — the knight to b5 threatens the knight to c7. But that's not its only path; our opponent correctly plays a6.
Once a6 is played, a different forkable square opens — b6 — so the knight goes to c4.

The queen to d8 — what we mostly face. Let's keep developing. b5 in itself isn't dangerous: the knight has a lovely parking spot on e5, and the a6-b5 structure can be hit with a4, chipping at Black's pawn chain — attacking an unsupported chain with your own pawns is incredibly effective. So we're not afraid of b5; we develop, starting on the side we'll castle.
Between e2 and d3, the bishop to d3 is the more active square, since Black will probably castle kingside one day and we want to aim at h7.

The bishop to e7. Another byproduct of the bishop to d3: we can take on c5 with tempo, forcing that dark-squared bishop to move twice — a common Queen's-Gambit-Declined trick, waiting for a piece to develop and then capturing a pawn it must recapture.
We castle, getting our king out of the centre first — and again not spending a tempo on a4.

Black castles. Black's position is more dangerous than it seems. Our superiority is on the kingside: the bishop aims at h7, the knight can leap to g5, the queen can later reach h5 — the makings of a Greek-gift attack — while Black is undeveloped, the c8-bishop hemmed in by its own e6-pawn. With a development lead, the prescription is to open the centre, so rather than d5, which drops the pawn, we take on c5 and open the d-file.
We take on c5, opening the centre, to press on Black before he completes development.

Now, how to get a rook to d1 — and where does the queen go? Not c2: a battery with the queen behind the bishop is toothless, only hitting h7 while the queen is hamstrung. The queen belongs in front, so we play the queen to e2 — keeping the queen to e4 in our pocket for when the knight is forced off f6, likely by the bishop to g5, and a queen in the centre is strong anyway. Then the knight to d7, and we play the rook to d1, x-raying the queen and adding central pressure; the queen to c7, and we bring the bishop to g5, pressing the f6-knight, with the maneuver to h4 and g3 in reserve. Black plays b5; the knight goes to e5 as planned — a knight on d7 doesn't change that — and after the trade on e5 we threaten the bishop takes f6, forcing a pawn recapture and opening mating chances with the queen to g4, h5 or e4. Our pressure reaches its apex, but Black defends well, so we convert: we trade knights on d7, giving up the bishop pair, then the classic bishop takes h7 with check — forcing the king to a checkable square, then the queen to d3 forks the knight — winning a pawn into a slightly better, probably drawable endgame; the bishop to h4 was the alternative, but the sac is the natural payoff to our middlegame. Remember that h7-sac idea works for both colors. Black keeps queens on with the queen to b6; our queen becomes the most vulnerable piece, since the bishop to d5 and a rook to a7 would trap it, so we retreat the queen to d2, guarding f2 — unafraid of the bishop takes f3, because Black has no pieces left to exploit the opened g-file, while we get the king to h1 and the rook to g1 for a furious attack. f6 forces our bishop to decide: we retreat it to e3, simplifying — up a pawn, simplification is our friend, and an isolated pawn in an endgame is nothing.
