The knight is temporarily tied down by Black's battery — the knight to d4 would get mated on g2 — so we play the knight to e1 and f3 to blunt it, then reroute back through d3, and stack rooks on the only open file rather than trade it away; the piece-threshold rule says: up a piece, simplify hard; up a pawn, simplify but never at the cost of the open file. We eye the knight to c5 as an outpost, supported by b4, and prepare it with the rook to c1. Then Black plays the queen to c4 — positionally fine but a tactical blunder: with our rooks stacked behind the knight, moving it is a discovered attack, and the queen to c4 abandons the defence of the rook that had come to d6. So the knight takes e5, and it works only because that rook and its partner on the back rank are both undefended; if Black takes our rook we recapture rather than grabbing the queen, which would cost too much. We win the second pawn, trade rooks, and keep the knight safe with the knight to c3 — not the knight to g6, which drops to the queen check and a fork. The winning plan: trade queens if a good chance comes, create a passed pawn and push it — start with b3, pry the black queen off d5, then push c4. Bring the king to f2 and to d4, watching that a pawn can't dislodge the king from defending the knight, and finally the knight back to b4 defends everything; we make the passer with a4 and c4, and Black resigns.
We try another Alekhine — a knight to f6, hoping White commits with e5 rather than a quiet knight to c3.
White plays e5.
And the idea: a knight to d5 — the ultimate hypermodern opening, where you refuse to touch your center for a few moves and try to get White to overextend.
White plays a bishop to c4 — a move, but not the best; we'll cover the theory later.
A knight to b6 — where this knight belongs in the Alekhine — attacking the bishop, so it retreats and loses a tempo.
A bishop to e2 is passive. Our strategy doesn't change: White's e5 pawn is a hook we'll use to contest the center while developing.
The most accurate move is d6, saying we want to remove that e5 pawn — and if we do, White has no central control left.
White plays d4 to fight for the center. Now a knight to c6 makes sense — the way to stop your pieces being trampled by pawns is to combine piece moves with pawn moves, so the pawns act as anchors.
Is d5 a problem before we play the knight to c6? Look carefully — no, because d5 loses control of e5 and drops a pawn.
White plays a knight to f3. Now we transform the position — a bishop to g4 is obvious, but in the spirit of positional chess we take on e5 into an endgame.
We capture on e5.
If White recaptures with the knight, a knight to d4 wins a pawn; he takes with the pawn instead.

We trade queens, and now that e5 pawn becomes a huge weakness — that's the whole point of the Alekhine: White has more central control, but he'll likely lose that pawn or wreck his pieces defending it.
How do we pressure e5? First its defender, the knight — a bishop to g4.

Critical moment: don't just grab on f3 and e5, because it drops the b7 pawn — and even if it didn't, giving up that g4 bishop isn't clearly worth a pawn. The threat is stronger than the execution: keeping him tortured by the weak pawn beats winning it and relieving him.
So we castle long, defending b7, keeping pressure on the bishop and mobilizing our knight. Now we threaten to take on f3, but we could also just keep pressing with e6.
White plays a knight to d2 — a bit of a panic; a knight to g5 would have dropped the bishop to two attackers.
We win a piece — take the bishop, which also pins the rook, rather than traveling to g4.
We take the pawn on e5 — otherwise a knight to a3 could defend.
White plays a knight to c3. Now we just play e6.
e6, to get our bishop out.
White plays a knight to e4, untangling. We could take the rook, but I like just developing — trading on your own terms forces the opponent into uncomfortable decisions.
A bishop to e7 is fine — its main job here is to connect the rooks; it restricts the e4 knight and controls g5. Not every piece has to climb Everest at once.
White plays a bishop to f4, also controlling d8, and attacks our knight — we can move it with tempo.
A knight to g6, in Alekhine spirit — and it sets a trap: a bishop to g3 loses a piece.
White sees it and plays a bishop to e3 — little relief. That e4 knight has been a recurring theme: a central piece still vulnerable to pawns.
So f5, attacking the e4 knight — it has no good squares; the ones near it touch our e7 bishop, and its only defender is the bishop, a vulnerable undefended piece we can dislodge from e3.
If White retreats the knight to d2 it only grows more passive — a big win for us. We trade the rooks and recapture.
White found a creative solution — a knight to c5, attacking c6, so if f4 he has a knight capture on e6 counterattacking our rook. We have to calculate.
Two pieces for a rook with no other rook pair usually favors the rook, but here the minors are super active, so we go for it — also to show how to play with this common imbalance.
White captures on e6 — he's playing very well.
We recapture on e3.
The king recaptures on f2. Now, to be surgical...
...a bishop check on c5, improving the bishop first — an intermediate move.
You're always hunting for intermediate moves, which can be tactical or positional — like improving the bishop before taking the knight.
A rook check on d1.
The king goes to e7 — the only good square.
White made a small error bringing his king backward — you shouldn't do that in the endgame — and he trades the knights.
We recapture on d5.
We recapture with the rook, reaching bishop and knight against rook with equal pawns — a great imbalance.
White attacks the bishop; we drop it back to d6 to attack the pawn. In these situations piece activity decides everything.
White plays c4.
A bishop capture on h2 nets a free pawn — and if he relies on a rook to h5, we have a sexy idea.
A rook to h5 forks the bishop and pawn — and how do we punish it?
A rook in the corner looks invincible, but it isn't — a bishop to f4 threatens to trap it. Rooks can be caught by minor pieces.
White grabs on h7.

A bishop to h6 — the rook is trapped: the knight covers its escape, the bishop covers the h-file, and our king will walk to g8 to finish it. He can try to ram the pawn, but there's no time — that's jail.
Don't free the rook by moving carelessly — the king walk is a brutal idea.
It's over — he has to take the bishop.
Now we're up a full knight.
A knight check on e5 to win the pawn.
Bring the knight back, and there are many ways to win.
We bring the king up, he gives us access to the pawn, and we push — had he defended, I'd just create a passer and distract his king. He resigns.
It seems contradictory, but you don't play b3 to occupy most of the centre — you do it to attack the centre with pieces. b3, d6 is fine, nothing wrong with that move, provided
he accompanies it with e5. The bishop to b2.

e5 is a legitimate way to play. But h5 is obviously completely unhinged — and funnily, a5 in this position is a legitimate line grandmasters have played, and I've faced it over the board; the idea is to undermine the pawn chain with a4, though I think White is probably slightly better, and the best move against a5 is actually c4, which isn't easy to play unless you've analysed it.
The critical decision after the pin is to capture — and once the pawn recaptures, the freeing break to c5 is available, striking back at the bind before it clamps down.

Conceding the bishop pair here is worth weighing honestly — the resulting position is only slightly worse for the second player, and never as frightening as it looks. Solid and a shade passive is a perfectly playable bargain.
The pawn break to b5 injects life into the queenside — a committal try to crack the bind open, though it invites a sharp scramble where the central push in reply can turn dangerous.
The bishop capture on d4 is the topical shot — the kind of central exchange that reshapes the whole position in a stroke, easy to overlook until it lands.
We open with the pawn to e4, met by c5 — the Sicilian.
The pawn to c3 — the Alapin, our opening. It's given us better or winning positions out of the opening in nearly every game at this level.
Black develops the knight to c6 — a viable move, and what people often play, but if Black isn't careful it can already drift into an inaccuracy.
The pawn to d4, striking at the centre.
Black takes on d4.
We recapture on d4. Now Black basically has to play d5 — it's the only route to a viable position; every other move hands us control of the centre and an amazing game.

A lot of people play d6 here when they aren't familiar with the theory, but White is simply better: our centre is fully intact, we have the c3-square for a knight, and it's a very pleasant position. Which knight to develop first? It hardly matters — the knight to f3 and the knight to c3 are both fine.

I like the knight to c3 first, because the knight to f3 would allow the bishop to g4 — why give Black extra options when it isn't necessary. And it's often good to follow with h3 and then the knight to f3, keeping that bishop off g4; its only other squares are passive.
So h3 is a good attempt to restrict the bishop and essentially force it to the far more passive d7 — I think it's very accurate here.
The pawn to h3 — just restricting that bishop as much as we can.
Black plays g6, heading for the fianchetto.
And now we continue developing with the knight to f3.

Black fianchettoes with the bishop to g7. Is d5 good for us? Positionally no — it opens the g7-bishop, so you'd push it only with a concrete follow-up, like rerouting the dark-squared bishop to d4 to disarm that bishop. Playable, but I prefer simpler chess — no need to worry about overextending the centre yet. I like the bishop to e3; I don't like the bishop to f4, for two reasons.

The bishop to e3. The bishop to f4 bites on granite against d6 and is vulnerable — Black hits it with e5 or the knight to h5. On e3 the bishop reinforces the centre and is very safe; that's the second point of h3, since we've also stopped the knight to g4. Black is cramped and uncomfortable, without control of the centre.

The second reason c4 is wrong: we'd walk into b5, and the bishop there is vulnerable, just like on f4. So I much prefer the bishop to d3 — the bishops reinforce the centre pawns and give us the freedom to operate on both wings without our centre collapsing.
Black plays b5, and no action is required from us. b4 is no threat — the knight drops to e2, and pushing further just overextends Black.
There's a proposal for e5, but I don't get it: Black takes, the knight goes back to d7, and a pawn pushed to e5 becomes a weakness. No need to reinvent the wheel — we complete development and castle.

Black develops the bishop to b7. We have several ways to handle this. Many propose the queen to d2, eyeing the bishop to h6 to trade the fianchettoed bishop, but I prefer to play on the queenside — an idea that shows up often in the Ruy Lopez.

The pawn to a4. Rather than the immediate knight maneuver, we provoke Black into damaging his queenside: a4 invites b4, then we route the knight toward g3, and a black pawn stuck on b4 becomes a lasting headache. If Black answers a5, that leaves a hole on b5 for our bishop and dries up his counterplay, freeing us for the kingside. We're expecting b4 — taking on a4 would just leave a6 weak.
Black plays the knight to a7 — whoa.
So we take — a free pawn. After a4 takes b5 we could also play the knight takes b5; e4 hangs in that line, but so does the a7-knight.

Black recaptures with a6 takes b5. The funny thing is we have something even better than the knight takes b5. Ninety-five percent of people would just grab it — knight takes b5, knight takes b5, bishop takes b5 with check, Black covers with the knight and limits the damage to a pawn. But the a7-knight is tremendously vulnerable — a loose, undefended piece pressured by the rook. Not e5, which would hand Black the d5-square.

The move is d5. It does two big things: it blunts the b7-bishop — yes it opens our other bishop, but that's a worthy price — and above all it piles onto the knight, which now has no good squares. Remember, when you push a pawn in the centre you often give away a square in return, but here it's worth it.

Black plays b4. I didn't ask you to find a response, but it matters. The obvious approach is to take on a7 then on c3 — that wins a pawn — but there's a much better move: the queen to a4 with check. It doesn't just win the pawn, it may win the game, because Black's minor pieces all end up hanging. There's also the creative knight to c6, covering the check and hitting the queen, but it doesn't work.

So the queen to b3, Black defends with the knight to d7, and the queen captures on b4 — grabbing the pawn while attacking both queenside minor pieces at once. The queen to b8 looks like Black's only defence, and it's a disaster for him.

Black finds the queen to b8 — a disaster, but good defending; even at this level people find resourceful moves. What's the priority? Stopping Black from castling — keep his king in the centre and we win faster. The immediate queen to a4 walks into a discovered attack with the knight to c8; the bishop to b5 to pin the d7-knight is the right idea but wrong execution, since it gives up our valuable light-squared bishop — we want that bishop to sit and pin, not be traded.
So the bishop takes a7 and then the bishop to b5 is very viable, but I prefer the knight to b5 — forcing a trade.

Black takes, and our bishop lands on b5 — the ideal version: we prevent castling and the bishop is unassailable. Black can try to contest it tactically with the bishop to a6, but I believe we're fine.

The bishop to a6 is Black's best, but he plays the queen to c7 — understandable, protecting the knight and preparing to castle, but the queen is incredibly vulnerable here. We can chase it with the rook to c1, but there's a much prettier tactical sequence.
The bishop to b6 — using the pin. If the queen takes the bishop, we take on d7 and win the queen. It forces the queen back, and then the rook to c1 is decisive.

After the queen to b8 the best move is to capture the knight and transform the advantage — we take on d7, drag the king into the open, then check on b5, and it essentially leads to mate. When you have a pin, always consider taking the pinned piece.
The bishop takes on d7 — the fastest path to checkmate.
The king recaptures. Now it wants to retreat to e8, so we stop it and force it onto the c-file, where the rook checkmates it.
We play another Caro-Kann — c6.
White plays d4 and we answer d5, challenging e4.
White plays a knight to d2. If you want to get better, embrace positions that make you uncomfortable — you never improve at what you avoid.
We capture on e4, heading for the Tartakower — a line I've played a lot in blitz.
White recaptures on e4. The main line for Black is a bishop to f5, and a knight to d7 is the old main line.
But we play a knight to f6 — old-fashioned wisdom calls it bad because we voluntarily ruin our structure, but strong players including Magnus have taken it up.
White captures on f6.
And we recapture with the e-pawn — the Tartakower. Recapturing with the g-pawn instead is the Bronstein, considered too weakening.
White plays a knight to f3. Magnus lost to Duda from here but had a great position — the e-file recapture opens our bishop's diagonal.
So a very natural bishop to d6.
White develops a bishop to d3.
We castle — another natural developing move.
White castles, which is already inaccurate, because it allows us a very nasty move that's hard to meet.
A bishop to g4, pinning the knight. Meeting it with h3 and g4 is tremendously weakening, and retreating the bishop to e2 is far too passive — so this causes White real problems.
In the Caro-Kann there's often a pawn on c6, so this knight develops to d7.
Black's plan now revolves around improving that d7 knight, which isn't well placed.
First we drop the bishop to h5.
This is a Ruy-Lopez-style plan: a rook to e8, a knight to f8, and then to g6 or e6; the secondary idea is to centralize the knight via b6 and d5.
Let's play a rook to e8 — a good move regardless, putting the rook on a semi-open file.
White plays a bishop to g4 — a creative idea I've never seen; it gives us a choice.
We play a bishop to g6, keeping the tension — and it threatens f5, which would trap White's bishop, while pointing toward the pawn-box structure I love.
White has to play a knight to h4 to hold the balance, since we threatened f5. After a knight capture on g6 we recapture with the h-pawn and get the pawn box.
We keep improving with a knight to b6 — a bit more active, maybe heading to d5. Another idea is to drop the bishop to c7 and prepare a queen to d6.
White captures on g6.

We recapture on g6 — the pawn cube. After a bishop to c7 and a queen to d6, if White plays g3 to block the battery, a rook capture on e3 works because his f2 pawn is overloaded, guarding both g3 and the bishop.
White plays b3 — but a rook capture on e3 wins, since f2 is overloaded. So delaying a knight to d5 is a good idea.
A bishop to c7 — and delaying a knight to d5 matters, because if we jump there and he retreats the bishop, we lose this tactic.
White plays c4, and we play a queen to d6 — he's already basically losing.
If White plays g3, we capture on e3; if f4, we capture on e3 anyway. This was not boring — you can score many nice attacking wins in the Tartakower.

White finds a queen to e2 — a super move, the only way to stay alive. When attacking, be flexible about converting: a stubborn rook capture on g3 lets his king drop back since h2 is no longer accessible, so we retreat the rook, aware his next move is c5 to win the piece back.
So a rook to e4, preparing to grab as many pawns as possible if he plays c5 — then a capture on d4 leaves us two pawns up and winning even in an opposite-colored-bishop endgame.
White plays a bishop to f3 — not resilient.
We just capture on d4, and now it's over even faster — kudos to him for the queen to e2, but the bishop to f3 blunders.
White plays a queen to e2. A rook to e8 would be nice but the square is undefended; he's no longer threatening c5, so we have a free hand.
A queen to d7 prepares the cube, and the knight on b6 is annoying since it blocks d5 — so we bring it back to d7 to centralize. Don't overthink these; there are a million good moves.
White plays a rook to d1. Taking the rook is bad, because he recaptures and pins our knight.

A bishop to b6 — how to trade on our terms. Assume his rook takes on d4: we want the bishop to land there, centralizing and threatening a capture on g3, then a knight to e5. No need to be fancy with a rook to h4.
White plays a king to g2, seeing it — again, we don't have to take his rook; let him improve our position.
Now we centralize the knight with a knight to e5, and then a rook to d8 controls the d-file.
White's bishop to e4 and our rook to d8 — a good moment to study how the pawn structure shapes both sides' plans.
White plays a rook to c1, sidestepping to keep pieces on.
A rook to d2 almost traps the queen and forces it back to e1 — easy play. We could play f5 first, but it's not necessary.
White plays a queen to e1 — like a snake shedding its skin.
We centralize with a queen to d4, piling on the f-pawn — no need to play f5.
White plays c5.
Can we take it? Yes — after a rook capture on c5 and a queen recapture, our rooks are doubled on the d-file so our d2 rook is defended. He resigns.
White opens with the Nimzo-Larsen — b3 and Bb2, fianchettoing to bombard the centre and the long diagonal from afar.
Into the endgame, follow the rules — an active king never hurts, so march it toward the centre and the action.
notes.teaches: Centralize and activate the king in the endgame; it's a fighting piece once the queens are off.

notes.explains: Place your pawns on the opposite colour to your bishop, so the bishop covers the squares the pawns can't — leave them on the bishop's colour and they become permanent weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Keep pawns off your own bishop's colour so the two cover complementary squares.

notes.explains: And with the king too active to be dislodged, the defense holds as a fortress — a structure the opponent simply can't break, no matter the material.
notes.teaches: A fortress plus an active king can draw even down material when there's no way in.

notes.explains: White tries a Bg5 line against our King's Indian.
White builds a huge pawn front. That's the hypermodern bargain — we cede the center on purpose, attack it from a distance with our pieces, and only claim the center ourselves when WE are ready.
teaches: hypermodern: cede the center, then strike it

notes.explains: Now the strike — c5. It looks like White is winning, but Black is already better: White has overextended, his pieces are uncoordinated, and when we hit the center we mean business.
teaches: strike when the big center is overextended

notes.explains: White pushes e5, attacking our knight.
The key move order — we take on d4 first.
White grabs the knight with the pawn on f6...
...but we recapture, and now we're a pawn up, attacking two pieces at once with an open avenue straight at his king.
We recapture with the bishop, keeping our King's-Indian bishop alive — taking with the queen would allow a knight to f5 harassing it.
teaches: keep the queen for better duties

notes.explains: The rook to e8 piles onto the knight on e4.
And we win it with check, the rook capturing on e4.
The queen to e7 kills two birds — it stops him from castling AND builds pressure down the e-file toward e5.
The rook to e3 attacks the queen, and then — never forget pawns as attackers...
...the pawn crashes in to d3 and wins the bishop; castling comes too late to save him.
teaches: pawns are full participants in the attack

notes.explains: Another Caro-Kann. e4, c6.
The knight to f3 this time,
which doesn't change what we do. d5.
e5 — and because he's played the knight to f3, he's given us the extra option of bringing the bishop out to g4,
which is generally not possible, because the queen controls that square. Is it worth it? I think so — the bishop to g4 seems like a great improvement, even over the bishop to f5.
The bishop to e2.
e6 — the fact that he's playing this passively doesn't alter our plan.
d4. What now? Remember, the knight to d7 is possible but not
strictly necessary — instead we can go c5 and then the knight
to c6, the optimal way of developing. What's the thematic move now?
We take — it's time, because we've virtually destroyed his pawn chain, and we could take on d4 immediately,
but the classy move is to play the knight to c6, withholding the capture and letting him
do the taking, trading on our own terms.
d-takes-c5,
and look how our bishop has developed — his e5-pawn is still very weak, and we're going to win it.
In fact he doesn't put up any resistance —
we just take it.
The bishop to e2. What do we do now? The queen to a5 was fine,
so we don't have to reinvent the wheel — the knight to f6.
He wants b4, and because we're playing this very positionally,
we could play a5 here and stop it, but we don't actually need to, because b4 is not dangerous — we can just move our bishop.
And another thing players at this level don't always factor in are squares — I've talked about weak squares. What square does this weaken, and where should our bishop go now?
We can put it on d6 or b6, both good — I like d6, look at this juicy square.

Had he played the bishop to b2, he wouldn't be attacking our knight, and we'd have a more aggressive plan of building a battery. But in the name of positional chess, how do we increase our control of the c4-square? The rook to c8 — but before that, let me improve the queenside: this pawn sticks out like a sore thumb, and when I see this construction I immediately think of undermining.

When you undermine, you try to break down this pawn structure — it's very vulnerable because he hasn't completed his development. He's in a lose-lose spot: if he plays b5, that creates another hole on c5, and his whole position starts to crumble.
And if he goes c3, he pays the price for not having developed the knight — his rook is undefended, a-takes-b4, c-takes-b4, the bishop takes b4. He takes, and now we can bring the
queen out, and perhaps even bring the other rook to c8, so the a8-rook is now fulfilling a pretty important role.

The bishop to d2. Where should our queen go? Every one of these decisions may seem insignificant, but keep your eyes on the prize: we want to increase our hold on c4 and potentially pressure the pawn — so the queen to c7.

I did kind of overlook the knight to c3, which aims for b5 — not an issue, but I didn't realise it comes with tempo, and I really don't want to part with this bishop, because it's the instrument that lets us attack the pawn, the glue guy. The rook to a5 isn't effective, because he still plays the knight to b5, defended by that bishop. So are we busted? No — we take the opposite perspective: instead of physically stopping the knight to b5, take the sting out of it, by moving one of these two pieces so the knight to b5 doesn't act as a soft fork —
preferably without ruining the placement of the pieces, maybe even improving it. The bishop to e7 would worsen the bishop, but the bishop to c5 would not.
The other move I thought of was the queen to e7 or c6 — and you see how effective this thinking is: we just go the queen to c6, we're good, our bishop is still great, and
this knight is now dangling on b5, doing absolutely nothing. He supports it with a4 — and when a move like that is made, I consider its drawbacks: what squares does it no longer control?
Sorry, I meant that the knight to b5 relinquishes control of certain squares. The knight to e4, centralising.
The bishop to e3. I said we don't want to part with our bishop — that was then, this is now, and the
circumstances have changed: he's offering us a much better deal — we can ruin his structure, weaken his king, create an isolated pawn, and get rid of his dark-squared bishop. I'm fine with that.
f-takes-e3. Some of you might be thinking of moves like the knight to g3 — we don't need to decide that yet, we
can make a general improving move: the knight to c3, trading his strongest piece for our strongest — a fantastic move,
because we've also got the other centralised knight, so he's only got one good piece and we've got a bunch.

Is the queen attacking the pawn? No, we're not concerned about it — again, the worst-case-scenario test: even if we allowed him to do everything he wanted, how could he possibly have enough firepower to attack this pawn?

He's just giving us the pawn. We can go the queen to e3 and take with the pawn — but I like taking with the pawn, because it creates a far-advanced passer and opens the d-file, which we're definitely going to control.
Open files are overrated — I'll talk about that. Which rook do we go to d8 with?
The rook on f8 lends some support to f1, so why risk it? Let's go with the a-rook.

Now there's a distinction between things you know are going to happen and things you're doing just to be safe — this is a safety move; probably nothing would have happened if we'd used the f-rook, but I want this rook to supervise, for abundance of caution.

He attacks the queen. Where should we go? We can offer a queen trade, but if we're offering one, do it actively — the queen to d2, take our queen, but you'll be making our rook incredibly active. We could also have gone the queen to c5 with check.
It attacks the bishop, and now we need to start thinking about how to improve the position further.
the rook takes d2 — we have a bunch of extra pawns, most of them
on the kingside, so we should consider pushing them. We can't push e3, nor do we need to — we could snag a third pawn, but we don't even need to; let's get down to business.
A rook lift is possible, but we can play more directly — we have a bunch of these pawns, and at some point you just start pushing them; look how our knight is right in
the centre, completely dominating over the bishop. f4. Now, you don't just want to put your head down and go crazy willy-nilly — you want to exercise a tremendous degree of caution.

What is the idea of the rook to c3, where is the rook potentially going? Let's play this without giving him any chances at all — maybe to c5, and I don't want this knight to leave e5. Prophylaxis; these moves drive your opponent crazy.
He can go to c7, but that one rook in isolation is going to accomplish nothing —
what's it even going to threaten? This comes in way too late. What can we do now? We could just keep pushing.

And which of these should we keep pushing? You're thinking of defending the pawn, but look how far advanced these are — f3, the game is over, because we're just going to take this pawn; we're actually going for checkmate, not necessarily only promotion.
He takes — that's a good move.
Now we take, and now we need one final manoeuvre to
win the game. Now, we don't want to move the knight, because if we do, we drop the e4-pawn —
not a disaster. So how do we prevent that? f5, simple, making sure this isn't mate — the king to f7.
And now this rook — we notice that his king is out of squares, so our mating patterns
begin to activate. He blunders and just gives us this — the rook to h5 would have been the idea.
The funny thing is, this is a good way to practice the don't-move-the-attacked-piece question — a lot of people have the instinct of moving the knight, but

my instinct is not to move the knight, but to first check whether I can play the rook to h5 anyway — and I can, and it's not hard to calculate: the rook to d7, the king to e6, and mate is unstoppable.
the rook takes d7 with check —
bringing the game closer to the centre, making sure there is no stalemate, because he's got pawn moves at his disposal.
the rook to b7 — and the game is over.

Against the early f-pawn thrust, the antidote is the immediate central break to d5 — and that's exactly why this move order isn't recommended; a genuine Grand Prix player would develop the knight first.
Don't recapture with the queen — instead develop the knight to f6, aiming to win the pawn back on your own terms rather than being dictated to.

The opponent defends the extra pawn, but that's no cause for alarm — the point is that the d4 square is now badly weakened. So switch into gambit mode: play e6, force the trade, and emerge with enormous compensation for the pawn. It's a well-known line every Sicilian player should carry.

The compensation, in one breath: huge central control anchored on d4, an enemy pawn stuck out like a sore thumb, a wretched bishop hemmed in behind its own pawns biting on granite, and an opponent's king with no safe haven, since the advanced pawn leaves castling short far from a cure. Spending a tempo on a rook-pawn move here is playing with fire when nothing is developed.
So develop with tempo — the bishop to d6, coming out with a hit on the weak pawn. Every developing move should also pose a threat when the opponent is this far behind.
The opponent ignores the threat, so simply grab the free pawn — it also unmasks a diagonal that can spell real trouble for the enemy king. Winning a pawn and opening a line in one is worth it.

Castle long for the adventurous game — the rook lands on the file already x-raying the queen and threatening a capture on c4, and above all it reinforces control of the key d4 square. Hold that square and everything is comfortable; now it's time to move in for the kill.

Don't rush the central knight jump — the move to reach for is the knight to g4, generating threats at the king with a capture on h2 looming and the knight eyeing an infiltration square. The storm clouds gather fast.

Here's the mating mechanism — the queen would mate on h2 but for the knight guarding it, and it can't leap over its own bishop. So distract the knight by planting a piece on d4 purely for tactics, not as an outpost; once it's captured, a bishop check on e3 forces the issue and the queen crashes into h2 for mate in two.
Against the e6 Sicilian and Nc6 we're into Taimanov territory — a flexible Paulsen-family setup.
White has countless setups here; the g3 fianchetto is a matter of taste — the bishop stays out of the way and rakes the centre from g2.
notes.teaches: The g3 fianchetto against the Taimanov keeps the bishop safe while it pressures the centre.

notes.explains: After castling, make a plan: the c1-bishop still needs a home, and the f1-rook wants e1 to x-ray Black's king down the file.
notes.plans: Reposition the rook to e1 and find the right square for the dark bishop.

notes.explains: The dark bishop is awkward everywhere — Bf4 runs into Nxd4 and e5, Bg5 is kicked by h6, Bd2 hangs the knight. When you're unsure where a piece belongs, one answer is not to develop it there at all. We fianchettoed one bishop — why not the other? b3.
notes.teaches: When no good square exists for a bishop, consider a second fianchetto rather than forcing a bad developing move.

notes.explains: And here's the payoff of the double fianchetto — the moment Black plays Bg7 the bishop is undefended, and with both knights gone the two bishops would stare each other down. That's the seed of a discovery.
notes.teaches: Two undefended bishops facing each other down a diagonal signal a discovered-attack tactic.

notes.explains: Ndb5 is the precise execution — sacrifice just one knight, not both, and exploit Black's queen. After axb5, Nxb5 hits the queen, and then Bxg7 tears the king open. The move order is everything; the other knight to b5 would let Black decline.
notes.teaches: In a knight sacrifice, choose the piece and order that also attacks the queen, denying the defender a decline.

notes.explains: The Carlsbad is defined by this early trade on d5 — instead of the traditional Bg5 main line with the pawn left on c4, we release the tension right away.

After Black recaptures we reach the Carlsbad structure: White's e-pawn against Black's c-pawn, with everything else symmetric. That small imbalance is what generates rich positional — and often sharply tactical — middlegame play.
We handle it like a normal Queen's Gambit Declined — the bishop to g5, e3, the standard moves — and let the structure dictate the game later.

Starting with the queen to c2 stops an annoying bishop to f5. When Black develops to the inaccurate d6 rather than e7, we go for the classic plan: install the Pillsbury Knight on e5, braced by the d4-pawn and a pawn to f4 — a construction many players simply can't handle. If Black challenges it, f5 nets a full minor piece for two pawns, and with our two bishops raking an open board we castle queenside and grind, seizing the only open file.
teaches: the Pillsbury Knight plan in the Carlsbad
plans: Ne5 braced by d4 and f4
f5 to win the bishop, then two bishops vs pawns

notes.explains: You played perfectly — for the home stretch, let's go. e4, c5.
This is a Sicilian — the knight to f3.
The line I told you to play here is to push d4 next — you want to open it up; it's literally called the Open Sicilian.
c-takes-d4, the knight recaptures on d4.
Now you don't want to react to this — if he takes your knight, you can simply recapture with the queen, so you can just develop normally.
The knight to c3. Now, your bishops — where do they belong?
f4 for one bishop — but you mean the light-squared bishop.
The dark-squared bishop is more active than f4 — and f4 blunders a fork to e5 — so you can put it on g5.
If he goes e5 — think about his knight on f6; he's actually weakened himself.
If you take the knight on f6, notice that he has to ruin his entire pawn structure by recapturing with the pawn — so I would.
Now I would immediately prepare to castle queenside, because you're going to attack him on the kingside, and you want to tuck your king away.
Your queen is defending the knight, so you want to keep it on the d-file — I'd put it on d2, and prevent Black's ideas.
Now he's attacking your knight — how can you defend it?
Where can you put it? The knight to b3 would be good, because it stops him from taking the pawn on b2 — a low-key move, but a good one.
And look at his queen on b6 — you can attack that queen in the future, but complete your development first.
So now I'm castling queenside, and then to attack the queen it's bringing the knight over to a4.
So he takes this first —
do you take back with the c-pawn? Yes, the c-pawn is good, keeping the a-pawn where it closes up the a-file.
Whoa — he takes on b3?
That came out of nowhere — a-takes-b3.
The confidence with which that was played! The knight to b4.
But let's not relax — you have some developing to do. The bishop to b5 with check.
Now you have a fork — let's practice that thing I tortured you with previously: what are the undefended pieces and pawns, and how can you attack two of them at once?
The undefended pawns: d6 is defended by the bishop, but f6 is completely undefended, and the knight is ready — forks. The queen to d4.
That was really the mistake he made — but careful, there's a trap hiding under the surface.

Now you can take the pawn — the queen takes f6 with check — but if he moves his king out, you actually can't take the rook, and that's the entire point of his variation. What if he covers with the bishop?

The king to c7. So you can't take the rook, because of a check on h6 — so do the next best thing, take the stuff that you can take. He'll probably go the king to b6, and then you have a sexy move: a check on a4 with the knight — and I want you to tell me why we're not blundering the bishop. He might think you blundered it. Then it's checkmate — c4, even sexier than the mate I had in mind, because you dropped the piece back; the knight from the rim is defending b6.

The Danish begins when the opponent thrusts into the centre, prepared to shed pawns for speed. Recapturing with the queen instead would be the Center Game, which is largely frowned upon — the true gambit lies down a sharper road.
In the Rossolimo, recapture with dxc6, not the b-pawn — it opens the bishop's diagonal and, crucially, boosts our grip on the d-file and the d4 square.
notes.teaches: Recapture dxc6 in the Rossolimo to open the bishop and dominate d4.

notes.explains: e5 seizes control of d4. It looks like it entombs the g7-bishop, but remember — bad bishops defend good pawns; that bishop's job now is to hold the centre.
notes.teaches: A blocked bishop is fine when it shores up a strong pawn chain; that's a bad bishop doing good work.

notes.explains: a5 stops White's queenside expansion, and the knight develops to e7, not f6, which would simply drop the e5-pawn.
notes.teaches: Route the knight to e7 rather than f6 when f6 would undermine your own centre pawn.

notes.explains: Qc7 shores up the e5-pawn, and there's a King's-Indian flavor here — the main plan is a kingside break with f5.
notes.plans: Prepare the f5 break for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Our position is a bit flimsy, so finish developing before launching — f5 now, with the rooks disconnected, would be premature. And a key idea when up a pawn: don't cling to it. Give it back with interest at the right moment to gain something bigger.
notes.teaches: Complete development before the break, and return an extra pawn when doing so wins you more than it costs.

notes.explains: Ra6 is the simple answer — attack the knight and threaten to win it.
Slide the rook to d8 — out of the pin and onto a file where it x-rays the enemy queen.
notes.teaches: Free a pinned rook onto a file where it does new work, like x-raying the queen.

notes.explains: Kh7 preemptively guards h6, so that when Be3 comes it doesn't hit the pawn with tempo — buying us the free move we need.
notes.teaches: A prophylactic king move can rob the opponent's next attack of the tempo it relied on.

notes.explains: Qc8 does double duty — it supports the bishop on e6 and preempts Nxe6, which would have crippled our pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Find the multi-purpose defensive move that both supports a piece and forestalls a damaging trade.

notes.explains: Now to trap the bishop, c5 first — it protects the b4-pawn and incidentally threatens Nc6, tightening the net.
notes.teaches: Before springing a trap, secure the pawn the tactic depends on so nothing hangs in return.

notes.explains: We've been playing the Danish Gambit almost exclusively — if it ain't broke, don't fix it. d4, e5, e4.
e-takes-d4.
d-takes-c3.
The bishop to c4.
c-takes-b2.
The bishop takes b2.
The bishop to b2, c6 — I think we faced this once; the motivation is to prepare d5, but the d5-square is well defended by three of our pieces, so we respond to
this move in a very unremarkable way — we need to complete our development, since we don't have enough out to mount any serious threats against the king. The knight to f3.

The bishop to b4 with check, a good move — which begs the question, do we cover with the knight to c3, the knight to d2, or move the king? In the Danish you can sometimes move the king. The move we can rule out is the knight to c3 — it may look most natural, but it covers up the bishop, and we want this bishop attacking g7, one of the appealing things about the Danish. So that leaves the king to f1

or the knight to d2 — I'm pretty indifferent, both make sense, but I want to castle and not move the king around, so let's go the knight to d2. Actually I have a feeling the king to f1 is the theoretical move here, but I'm not playing theory, just the most natural moves. He could play d5, but g7 is hanging, so the bishop takes g7 would win the rook — so d5 isn't
justified. f6 — not the greatest move; he's blunting the bishop, but look at the weaknesses he's creating on his kingside; the first thing I see is the knight on g8, targeted by the bishop —

a type-two undefended piece. So there's a very natural move that doesn't win a piece but creates further difficulties for him: the queen to b3, stacking the bishop and the queen. I'd have preferred this battery flipped,

then we'd be threatening checkmate, but this is good enough — he has to take. A lot of people would grab instinctively with the knight, and we will take with the knight — but I'll point out that the king takes wouldn't be stupid either: the king in the centre isn't great, but he's got no pieces out, and there's something to be said for opening the e-file quickly and slamming e5. But something

gives me the creeps about that move. I'll take with the knight, because we're not in a hurry to put a rook anywhere — he's not castling anytime soon; two of our pieces stop his king from castling, so this is justified
in the sense that we tuck our king away on the kingside — and sometimes playing the simplest chess is the most reliable kind. The knight to h6; let's castle.
He can go d5, we take on d5; he can't castle there, and we take everything on c6 — he'll play a Danish Gambit of his own, the difference being he'll lose a bunch of his pieces.

The queen to e7. He's not threatening to castle, so ask what his idea is: I think it's to bring the knight back to f7 and then castle, so we don't have forever. A lot of you say the rook to f1, and I like it, but there's an important question to ask: do we need the rook to f1?

When you're preparing a move, allocate a couple of seconds to whether you even need the preparatory move — can you eliminate the middleman? Those with sharp tactical vision see that you don't: you can play e5 straight away, f-takes-e5, take with the bishop, and if he takes that bishop, his queen gets skewered with the rook to e1.

So just ask, do I need the middleman — sometimes yes, sometimes no. f5, but that leaves us with a beautiful pawn on e5, which can't be captured even without the bishop on b2 — it's a pin. The bishop to a3 is a great move now: you can think of the bishop on b2 as having done its job.

It's a superfluous bishop now — its role was to help prepare e5, and now that e5 is played and doesn't need protection, this bishop can seek greener pastures, particularly because the bishop on a3 covers the f8-square and makes it even harder for him to castle.
It would be amazing to put the knight on d6. c5 is a great move — this guy is good — but I do see a way to get the knight onto that unbelievably juicy outpost, even better than a kebab.
The bishop to d5.
Why d5? Because we want the bishop to remain on this diagonal, and now the knight can go to c4.
The king to d8.
Let's not eat quite yet —

Why is that even a good thing — don't we want a pawn to support the knight? In principle yes, but the queen takes e5 works in our benefit, because it opens up the position further, and the side with more active pieces generally benefits — so we want him to take. He plays b6, very solid. I see taking the knight on c6, which doesn't lead anywhere after d-takes-c6 — but imagine a rook on d1 x-raying his king; then we could step aside with the knight and win his queen. Which rook to d1? If we put this rook on d1, it restricts the other from coming to e1; he'll probably play the king to c7.

You want to escape the pin, and if he does, we might want this other rook to come to c1, to once again re-pin the king — so the rook to d1, and if he takes on e5, we take his knight with a devastating discovery. The consideration is simple: when deciding which rook to put on a square, look at what the other rook will be doing.
That sometimes requires a prediction — I predicted he'd go the king to c7, and then we'd put the other rook on c1. He does.
They don't call me the prophet for nothing.
And we have once again x-rayed the king. Now this is where things get very tactical and tricky.

We're going to step aside with the knight — I'm making this quickly to not lose on time — and this puts him in a very difficult situation: if he goes the king back to d8, that's why we put the rook there, and we take his

knight, a free knight, and that's winning. If he goes the king to b8, then the queen — and this is elegant, all three of our major pieces have taken a turn x-raying the king; if this pawn were gone from b6, we'd have a devastating discovery. So what move comes to mind here?

This guy is definitely not an easy opponent. I like the bishop takes c5, blasting open the pathways to his king and threatening the bishop to d6. He has to take, and it's still not easy for us to win — in fact we might want to hold off on the discovered check until we get all of our pieces into the attack.
Not an easy game, not an easy opponent, but we're keeping our foot on the gas pedal, and at some point, if you stay calm, something will come up. We're going to take with the rook.
Here we're just going to take, no rush — we create another x-ray against this queen, and hopefully this is the final straw that leads him to collapse.

The bishop to b7, a good move. There's a line I'm calculating that potentially leads to a beautiful win, but I want to make sure I'm not screwing it up — oh, there's a defense there; let me focus and find a win.
I think the knight to d6 is the move here.

This is the Jobava London — the knight to c3 paired with the bishop on f4. It looks innocuous, hardly an attacking weapon, but that's an illusion: it's a genuinely aggressive system, and players who underestimate its potential get burned.

The pawn to c5 is already a slip. It tries to punish the early knight development — in a normal London you'd prop the centre with a pawn — but committing the knight to c3 has a hidden virtue: it puts immediate pressure on the d5 pawn, which changes everything.

Because of that pressure, a capture on c5 becomes available — a move you'd never make in the traditional London. It intensifies the heat on d5 and makes winning the pawn back surprisingly awkward for the opponent without falling behind.

The natural knight development is the common online choice but it's wrong here — the accurate move is the rook-pawn to a3, with the obvious idea of following up with b4 to cement the extra pawn on c5. Preparation before consolidation.

The opponent grabs the centre and eyes winning the pawn back with interest — but there's a catch. Instead of meekly retreating the bishop, plant it on g5, and the power of the early knight shines: now there's a threat to swap on f6 and capture on d5, knocking out a key central pawn while keeping the extra material.
The opponent has to waste a tempo defending, which is exactly the opening to secure the c5 pawn with b4 — the whole reason the rook-pawn went to a3 earlier. A full pawn up, and for no compensation.

Develop modestly to e2, not the more natural square, which would walk into a fork. And appreciate the extra pawn — it's not just any pawn; sitting on e3 it's a speed bump, restricting the opponent's central break and choking the squares their pieces want.

The queen shift to e8 is tricky — it lays a trap. Snatch on d5 too soon and the alignment of the opponent's bishop with the rook in the corner springs a discovered attack on the knight, winning the pawn back with interest. Just stay up the pawn and don't take the bait.

And a genuine surprise — a knight leap to e4 that's easy to miss. It forces a sequence leaving one side with a rook and two pawns against two minor pieces, a fascinating material imbalance to navigate.

The formula against a troll opening: develop your pieces, blast open the centre, then go for mate. Don't lunge with Qh5-check or Bc4-check — they run into g6 and e6. Start with the most flexible developing move, Nc3.
notes.teaches: Punish an offbeat opening by developing first; premature checks just hand the opponent the moves he wanted.

notes.explains: Bc4 is better than Bd3 here — it loads up the d5 break to blast the centre, and d5 is dangerous because Black's queen sits undefended on the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: Aim the bishop at the break that opens lines onto an undefended enemy queen.

notes.explains: d5 is really a positional threat that Black himself wants to play — so we push it first, staking the larger claim in the centre.
notes.teaches: Pre-empt a break your opponent is angling for by making it yourself with more support.

notes.explains: Keep expectations realistic: these troll openings don't lose by force — the evaluation is plus two, not plus six. Aim for a solid middlegame edge and don't excoriate yourself for not mating in five.
notes.teaches: A bad opening is a lasting edge, not a forced win; play for a healthy advantage, not a quick knockout.

notes.explains: Ne2, not Nf3 — it connects the knights, defuses Bxc3 against our structure, and eyes f4 to lean on the soft e6-pawn.
notes.teaches: Develop the knight to e2 when it keeps your structure intact and reroutes toward the weak pawn.

notes.explains: Castle, but keep an eye on e5 and d6 — the one thing we must never allow is Black closing the centre, because a locked centre lets him move the same piece five times without cost.
notes.teaches: Keep the centre open against a passive setup; a closed centre erases your development lead.

notes.explains: dxe6 wins the chronically soft e6-pawn — the first concrete gain.
After the main-line exchanges we have three good replies — the bishop to f5, the knight to d7, or the knight to f6.
The knight to f6 is the Tartakower — it accepts a slightly damaged pawn structure in return for solid, active piece play. Once the least popular of the three, it's now among the most popular.
White's f3 is premature — it weakens the king far too early.
We develop with the bishop to f5, pressuring the knight. No need to rush to punish f3 — it's not a race, and White pays for it later.
White's bishop to c4 tempts us to capture on e4, but taking there is risky — it opens the f-file and hands White real compensation. So we simply keep developing.
teaches: don’t grab a pawn that opens a file at you

notes.explains: The knight to d7 is the ideal Caro-Kann arrangement — some players are allergic to the square, but this knight pair is excellent here.
The knight to g5 threatens mate.
Which is the perfect moment for e6, blunting the bishop.
We recapture toward the center and, as a bonus, open the c-file for a future rook.
White pins with the bishop to b5.
And the shot — the queen check on a5 wins the undefended bishop, exploiting the loose bishop and the uncastled king together. Keep your eyes peeled for this tactic; it's missed at every level.
teaches: Qa5+ forking the loose bishop and the king

notes.explains: He resigns — good game. Let's look at the game. e4, c5.
the knight to c6.
the knight to c3.
The best way for White to handle the situation is to play g3 and transpose into
what's called the Closed Sicilian — the point of the Closed is that you don't play d4, that's why it's closed; the centre remains
There's no need to rush the shutting-out move — nothing is threatened on f7 yet — so develop the knight first, keeping the options open before committing the pawn.

Against offbeat play the recipe is to follow principles to the letter — just develop, and there's only so much harm the opponent can do. The knight comes to f6, and the central push is already denied, since that square is guarded — which is exactly why the other knight came out first.
The centre-fork trick is available — capturing in the centre and regaining the piece with a pawn break — but here it's premature and leads to needless complications. A calmer path is better.
So play e6 instead, quietly preparing to expand with the central break. The fork trick doesn't vanish — it stays in reserve, ready depending on how the opponent develops.

Against a second-rate opening, play principled chess and punish it — the pawn to d5 grabs the centre and takes the fight to the opponent, rather than drifting. Seize the initiative when the opening invites it.

Priority now is kingside development, since the king is still central and the opponent is signalling a quick castle. But there's a subtlety — they also intend a central push, and sleepwalking into the recapture would leave an isolated queen's pawn, with the opponent controlling the square in front of it and that bishop suddenly justified. Meeting the push yourself is an option, though it too has a real cost, opening that bishop's diagonal.
We meet the king's-pawn opening with the Sicilian and settle in for a quiet, principled game.

The queen's knight to c3 is a rare guest here. The rule of thumb against it: play the same line you'd choose in the open Sicilian, because White can still slide the king's knight out and push the d-pawn to transpose straight back into one. A Najdorf player answers with d6, a Taimanov or Kan player with e6 — pick the matching setup or you risk getting move-ordered into a line you don't actually play. For an Accelerated Dragon there's an underrated try that dodges a mountain of theory.

The immediate g6 flies under the radar. It sidesteps all the Nc6, Bb5 Rossolimo-style theory you'd otherwise have to know, and it's perfectly sound — a bishop sortie to b5 makes no sense against this move order.

White transposes into the Grand Prix Attack. It shares the DNA of the Closed Sicilian, but where the Closed version fianchettoes and plays positionally, the Grand Prix goes for the throat — the light-squared bishop swings to c4, often after a check on b5, to lean on the f7-square. It's a genuinely scary weapon against a less experienced Sicilian player.
We complete the fianchetto, exactly the setup we'd want whether we'd started with the knight or with g6.
Against the knight coming to f3 we assemble the structure regarded as Black's best answer to the Grand Prix — and it doubles as a recipe against the Closed Sicilian too.
First things first, develop. The queen's knight to c6 is the most flexible start — it commits to no pawn move yet and simply waits to see where White's pieces go.

Now the bishop on b5 tells us more about White's plan. The key is what to avoid: don't reach for e6. After e6, White snaps the knight and rams the pawn to e5, leaving Black riddled with dark-square holes on d6, f6 and c5 — a miserable version to defend.

Instead the immediate knight to d4 flies under the radar. It's the same motif you meet in the Trompowsky: a bishop parked on b5 is simply loose, vulnerable to a knight leaping into d4. We ask the bishop a question right away.

White castles and turns the tables — daring us to take the bishop. We're delighted to. That light-squared bishop, once it lands on c4 bearing down on f7, is the Grand Prix's main attacker, the bishop from hell in these positions. Off it comes.
So we capture, eliminating the bishop before it can do any damage.

White recaptures and we hit our second decision. The instinct against a knight on b5 is to shove it back with a6 — but resist. The knight isn't threatening c7 or d7; it's just sitting there, undefended and harmless. Save a6 for a rainy day, because playing it now only invites the knight back to c3 where it clamps the d5-square. Leave it be and finish our development.

If we develop the king's knight to f6 immediately, White gets to push e5 and jam a pawn into our position. So we prep with d6 first — the classic Sicilian move, staking out the central squares and taking e5 off the table.
Black's a6 is a nothing move here. Don't fear ...b5, and resist the instinct to play a4 — that would only weaken the b4 square and do more harm than good.
teaches: don’t weaken b4 answering a harmless ...a6

notes.explains: We just keep developing with the bishop to g2, the Glek's fianchetto.
When Black pins with the bishop to b4, don't reflexively play d3 — Black isn't actually winning a pawn. We simply castle.
teaches: don’t defend a pawn that isn’t really hanging

notes.explains: And when the trade comes, recapture with the d-pawn — opening lines for our pieces.
Black confidently grabs on e4 — and there's a standard tactic that wins the pawn straight back.
The knight takes on e5 — a discovered attack, unveiling the bishop on g2 down the long diagonal at the knight on e4.
After the recapture we take on e4 and win the pawn back, emerging with the two bishops.
White is much better here — the bishop pair, Black's king stuck in the center, and tremendous piece mobility.
teaches: bishop pair + central king = a big edge

notes.explains: f4 chases the knight — but play it only with a clear follow-up in mind, since it does loosen our own position a touch.
teaches: commit to f4 only with a plan

notes.explains: Black's knight to c4 is a bad move — it lands loose and can be targeted from many directions.
The quiet queen to e2 might just win on the spot — it attacks the knight AND sets up a devastating discovered check with the bishop taking on b7, which nets the rook in the corner.
teaches: Qe2: attack the knight, prep the Bxb7 discovery

notes.explains: The bishop takes on b7 and wins the exchange.

c4 — a move that's probably not on most people's radar; you may have faced it but don't know much about it. It looks very ugly, because it creates a massive hole on d4, but be careful about assuming moves like these lose — they definitely don't, and if White follows up accurately, c4 is a pretty legitimate sideline that can contain some venom.
Our follow-up is pretty obvious — we start with the knight to c6, really clamping down on the d4-square. One

thing we should avoid with Black is to play e5 — we shouldn't just mirror White's setup. As often, we have a choice of pawn structures; experienced Sicilian players will be inclined to play g6, the standard way, fianchettoing the bishop and increasing our control of d4 — but that's not the only
viable setup; we could also play e6 and try to carry out the d5 pawn break quickly. Let's go g6 and play more conventionally.
You don't have to be a Dragon player to play g6 —
fianchettoing the bishop here should make sense independent of what Sicilian you play against the Open Sicilian.

Now we have a secondary choice of where to develop the g8-knight: the obvious square is f6, but its drawback is somewhat decreasing our clamp on d4. So we could instead carry out the Botvinnik setup: e6 and the knight to e7,
where the knight and bishop cooperate nicely and the bishop stays unobstructed on the long diagonal. Both setups are fine; it's a good idea to start with d6, making the moves we know we need.

The bishop to e2 — White plays standard developing moves. Before choosing a square for our knight, it's a good idea to initiate a favourable trade. Our whole play revolves around constantly increasing our control of the d4-square — and it's more important to control a square than to occupy it. How do we increase control? Two ways: add attackers, or remove defenders.

That second method is what people often forget — they think of moves like the queen to b6 or e5, but the knight on f3 can also be dealt with by the bishop to g4, which is the move we play, of course intending to take on f3.
You might say aren't we giving up the bishop pair, making two moves with the same piece in the opening? True, but because the centre is closed,
and because we have a bigger priority here that supersedes these general opening rules —
we won't have any problems with our development, and our king won't get stuck in the centre, so it should be obvious we won't get punished for this small
opening violation. Now we finish up the Botvinnik setup — e6, and we'll put the knight on e7 — and our pieces will be really harmonious. Another thing you might notice
is that we're combining the moves e6 and g6 in the Sicilian, which on previous speedruns I've called one of the cardinal

sins of the Sicilian — but again, this is a completely different scenario; I was referring to situations where the centre is open and White can access the d6-square. This isn't one of those; the centre is completely closed, so that principle doesn't apply at all.
the bishop to g5.
Let's go h6 and see where this bishop

wants to park itself. The bishop to h4, and now we have an interesting dilemma — because we have a nice positional advantage and a clamp on d4, there are many good ways to play, so if your intuition suggests a different move than mine, that doesn't make your idea bad. The way I play this may strike you as a little loose or risky, but hopefully I'll show
that it's in fact not risky at all, and it isn't even tactical — it's motivated by positional considerations, not a desire to just checkmate our opponent. The move is g5.
We're not trying to go h5 and build a pawn storm — that would be nice, but we can't. The point of g5
is to carve out the g6-square for our knight, and notice how we're playing on the dark squares.
The bishop to h5 — fine, maybe White wants to take on g6, but that's not really a tactical threat, maybe a positional one, and we have several ways
to deal with it — we can put this knight on f4, or play the knight to e5. I like the knight to f4; we're trying to get the perfect material imbalance,
opposite-coloured bishops, to really emphasise White's dark-square weakness. The knight to b5 — not sure what it does; we can play a6 to push it back, or take on b2, though that's not
really in the spirit of the position — I don't see why we'd go pawn-grabbing; a6 is safer, simpler, and probably just better. So a6, and the knight simply has to go back to c3.
increasing our bind over the centre. The bishop takes f4.
Our opponent plays an intermezzo; we take back on f4, of course — we don't want to take the
We're Black, playing the Caro. c4 — the first time we see this move; White is clearly preparing to grab the d5-square as soon as possible.

But we still play d5 — very likely to transpose into the Panov Attack after the pawns trade and d4; White can also grab twice. Both variations likely lead to the same structure — the classic isolated queen's pawn.
The pawns trade on d5 — probably an IQP; the fact that he's thinking tells me he's maybe not too familiar with the Caro. Takes, takes, and e5.

e5 is definitely not the way, for many reasons — one is that it gives us an ideal French. We'd normally bring the bishop to f5 and then e6, but no rush; we could also develop the knight to c6. There's the idea of d4, to prevent White's d4 and sever the connection between the d- and e-pawns —
— which also gives the bishop a nice square on c4, but let's not be too adventurous — the knight to c6 and the bishop to f5; no reason to refuse an ideal French setup handed to us like this.

The bishop to f5 — French players are completely in paradise: an Advanced French with the bishop on f5. One semi-drawback: in the French we'd have pawns fixed at c5 and c3, and here we've traded on d4 so the knight has a natural square on c3, but the bishop outside the pawn chain is no contest.
The knight to c3. Black has a very comfortable position — I don't think Black is better, it's still equal, but White is the one who has to be careful his pawn chain doesn't collapse.

Of course we play e6. Even with White’s pawn advanced to c3, there's also one advanced to c5 — they cancel; the presence of c5 and c3 doesn't make d4 any weaker or stronger, just one more attacker and defender, but Black holds the power, deciding when to take on d4, and White's queen's knight lacks the c3-square. g4 is interesting but not dangerous — we'd meet it with h5, and White overextends further.

The knight to f3 — he's a bit out of his depth, which is why the Caro or French can be effective at this level: not that they haven't seen it, just perhaps less well studied. Why not the knight to b4, threatening the knight to c2? Because the knight to b4 exposes the king to a check on b5 —

— we don't want to bring the king up, so the queen to b6, just like in the French, putting significant pressure on the d4-pawn; the queen to a4 is the same concept, also forcing the knight back. Unlike the French, our bishop is on f5.

The one drawback, if you can call it that: we'll have to be creative developing the g8-knight, since in the French it often goes to f5, but the bishop is there. Two or three ways — the knight to h6, leaving room for the dark-squared bishop, then castle; or the knight to h6 or e7 and then a maneuver to vacate the f5-square for the knight. We'll do the bishop to g6 and the knight to f5.
I like starting with either e7 or the knight to h6. With the knight to h6, you should be curious why I'm not afraid of the bishop takes h6 — I hope he takes, so I can demonstrate.

As I showed in my own game against a Peruvian grandmaster, it's not dangerous, because his dark-squared bishop is a very important defensive piece — without it the d4-pawn is much harder to defend and his position looser. The knight to a4 — fine; we can go the queen to a5 with check, but then the bishop to d2; the bishop to b4 with check looks good, but he just plays the bishop to d2, and trading dark-squared bishops isn't good for us.
It's good if he trades his dark-squared bishop for our knight, but I want to keep a bishop. No need for anything crazy — just drop the queen back to c7.
He castles.
Let's begin by developing our bishop to e7.
The bishop to d2.
Now complete our regrouping — the bishop to g6, and then the knight to f5.
a3, and the knight to f5 — everything is in perfect place; our knight has a home, our bishop has a home, all our pieces are developed except our king. We're going to castle —

— and then embark on the middlegame. I have to compliment my opponent — he's handling this very well; not better for us, but a very comfortable position. Do we take on e3? No, for two reasons: that bishop isn't going anywhere, it'll be there for us to take later —

— and why open the f-file for him, or eliminate a knight that's putting the d4-pawn under significant pressure? Instead let's begin by castling, the most flexible move. A very typical French idea follows —
— the pressure has reached its apex; how do we take it to the next level? The move is f6.
f6, opening up the centre — there are some subtleties, but let's keep things simple.
The knight to b5, attacking the queen. Where should we go?

We can go to b8, that's okay, but I like dragging the queen back to b6 — it pins the knight to the pawn and reinforces the pressure on d4; after the pawns take on f6 and the bishop recaptures, look how many of our pieces will be trained on that d4-pawn, his position close to collapsing. If he doesn't take, we play a6, or remember we can still take the bishop and then the pawn — that's why we held off.

So we hold that over his head. A very funny subtlety I just realized: after a6 and the knight to c3, is the knight takes b2 possible? I missed this at first — after a6, the knight to c3, taking, there's the pattern the knight to a4, and the rook to b1 blunders the knight on c3 —

The knight on b5 is hanging — that's why it's so important to note all the undefended pieces; forgetting a piece hangs at the end of a line is one of the most common causes of miscalculation. Doesn't that give White an attack on the queen? No — the bishop is gone, and if White takes with the d-pawn, we take his bishop on e3 and his position collapses.
We recapture on d5 with the queen. It's centralised but carries no real threat, so the priority is speed — e6 or the knight to f6, and just develop.
e6 is chosen partly to open the door for the bishop to g4 later.

The bishop swings to g5, eyeing the knight on f6, and there's a knight-to-d5 idea in the air. The queen has to find a square and the f6-knight needs support — h6 covers the g5 bishop's pressure without loosening the structure the way f5 would.

The opponent trolls with a quiet e3 and d3 — a Hippo-style setup where White fianchettoes both bishops and tucks the knights back toward e2 and d2. It's worth knowing a sustainable way to punish these off-beat systems, because a lot of players either get scared or start stumbling against them.
Since White is handing us the centre, we grab it — the principled e5.
And we grab more with d5, taking a big share of the middle.

The preferred setup refrains from the knight to c6. Instead c6 builds a solid pawn chain, and the queen's knight reroutes Ruy-Lopez style via d7 and f8 to g6. Against such unambitious play, we have all the time in the world to improve.
teaches: the c6 chain and knight reroute

notes.explains: The bishop to d6 complements c6 beautifully — London-style. It defends the e5-pawn while the pawn defends d5, giving us a super-compact, well-placed centre.
Castle kingside — never queenside here, that's far too adventurous. And note White's h3 is already a slight weakness; if g3 follows, it only creates another target on that wing.
teaches: castle kingside, note the h3 weakness

notes.explains: Temper your expectations against these setups. I've seen countless games where one side plays an offbeat system and the other charges straight for the throat and loses — White isn't doing anything to lose the game. Be patient, get every piece out, and accept that breaking such a setup down takes time; it can't be done in the opening.
A typical queenside idea is to advance the a-pawn to poke and prod — and if White answers b4, we chip in with c5. With a closed centre, don't rule out moving the same pawn twice; there's no hurry.

Leave the light-squared bishop at home for now — a bishop to f5 walks into a g4 or e3-e4 expansion, and a bishop to e6 invites a knight jump to g5. We want to keep that bishop, because a key middlegame plan is pressuring the h3-pawn. So develop the knight to d7 instead.
teaches: keep the light bishop for the h3 plan

notes.explains: The rook to e8 overprotects the e5-pawn — a good move in its own right — while we continue rerouting the knight toward g6.

If White's queen slides to e2, it signals a flirtation with castling queenside — a near-suicidal plan into our setup. So we play a5, telling the opponent: don't you dare castle into this, because we'll be ready to make mincemeat of that king.
White clamps with the Maroczy Bind — c4 — the most testing system against the Accelerated Dragon, gripping the d5 square.
We choose a rarer setup with d6 rather than the usual immediate fianchetto — a slightly dangerous, less-charted system.
The knight to f6 transposes us back into the main line.
We develop the bishop to d7.
Then reroute it to c6 — a good, solid square that eyes the long diagonal.
Now the queenside plan: a5 and a4, clamping down so the queen can swing to a5 and start attacking. That's the Accelerated Dragon's formula against the Bind — grab space on the queenside.
White's knight to d5 is a strong move, planting itself on the Bind's key square.
We take it with the bishop.
White recaptures on d5. Now the key question — which bishops to trade. We want White's dark-squared bishop gone; his light-squared bishop is the bad one, hemmed in by pawns on its own color.
teaches: trade off the good bishop, leave him the bad one

notes.explains: White plays f4, expanding preemptively on the kingside.
We give up the fianchetto bishop with the check on d4 — a real concession, but with so few pieces left he can't get at our king, and this trade was the whole point of the plan.
teaches: a concession that fits the plan

notes.explains: A ten-minute game. e4, e6 — the French. Those of you who've watched a while know what I do against the French.
d4 — the variation someone introduced me to, and we're going to play it again.
Actually, no — White plays a6. That's not a move you see every day, but believe it or not, a6 is a move.

When you face such moves, there's nothing in particular you should do — you should simply develop your pieces. The knight to f3 seems reasonable, not the knight to c3, because we want to be able to play c3

when the moment is right. c5 — Black is trying to transpose the game into a Sicilian; if we play the knight to c3 here, Black takes on d4 and we transpose. But of course we're not going to play the knight to c3; we're going
to punish Black for all these pawn moves — we play principled chess and push the pawn down to d5, almost a Benoni structure, except Black has lost a bunch of tempo on weird pawn moves.
The knight to f6 — a reasonable move.
But we defend the pawn — the knight to c3.

d6 is a good move — I was really hoping he'd take on d5, which would be wrong. There are multiple ways to play this with White; don't feel White is winning, just solidly better. Now we have a positional approach and a more tactical one — we can take on e6 and keep the centre open, White is definitely better, and given our lead in development it makes sense to go after him.
The other approach is the positional move a4, preventing Black's main idea, b5 — largely a matter of taste, but with White I feel we should go for a more principled approach. Take on e6.

The bishop takes e6. Now what? Of course we can develop with the bishop to f4 or g5, but I'm hinting at principled play — this might not be the best thing, but I feel like playing ambitiously and really trying to punish Black. e5, d-takes-e5 leads to an endgame we don't want. We want a move that's often extremely superficial, one I've discouraged in many positions, but here has a specific aim.

The knight to g5 — its very specific aim is to destroy Black's pawn structure and get rid of the bishop on e6. We want to take the bishop, then get our bishop out to c4 and hit him where it hurts, on that e6-pawn; and if the bishop moves away, the bishop to c4 is totally crushing, that threat against f7 incredibly nasty. The knight to g5 might not be best — as Black here I'd simply develop with the knight to c6, not h6, since we want to take the bishop anyway, and h6 weakens the diagonal. The bishop to g4 isn't dangerous — we go f3, or the bishop to e2, trading the light-squared bishops and getting nice control of the d5-square. Black's best is the knight to c6; b5 could be considered but it's dangerous to keep not developing.
I'd go the knight to c6 here, and then the knight takes c6, f-takes-c6, the bishop to c4, and White is better but the game isn't over. Instead he blunders a piece — the knight to g4
walks right into the knight takes e6, and we win the knight; I think he had internet problems that distracted him. This type of play often works, so at this level don't be afraid

queen takes g4. He plays the knight to f2. Let's try to be accurate — a lot of people would just instantly grab this. We have a choice: we can play the knight takes d8 and simplify into an endgame up a piece; the king takes f2; but there's a third move I think

is even more accurate. Not the queen to f3 — though I like the queen to f3 too, because then we can take on f2 with the queen and preserve the right to castle — I like the queen to h5, pinning the pawn and going for the throat: we're pinning the pawn, still attacking the knight, and attacking the queen; and after the queen to f6, rather than the knight to c7 with check, which isn't the most accurate though still completely winning, there's a very typical concept that wins on the spot — g5; and of course if the queen to e6, the knight to c7
We settle into a Philidor-like structure — quiet, positional, no rush.
Now we work out the plan. The standard idea in this kind of structure is c3, challenging the opponent's central pawn before committing anywhere else.
We retool the position, rerouting the bishop back to a more civilised square where it actually does something.
Ask who benefits from a bishop trade here — it's us, because both of our bishops are passive. Swapping the poor pieces off is a small win.
The plan is to make the bishop better; right now it just bites on our own pawns.
The opponent's centre had been biting on granite — solidly held — but this advance changes the picture.
Now the bishop has a future and can breathe. But new problems arrive at the same time: the advanced pawn is weak, and the opponent's knight has become a monster.
teaches: weighing the trade-offs of a break

notes.explains: First, king safety — tuck the king to h2, out of the danger zone, and solidify before doing anything ambitious.
We're White — the pawn to e4, c6, the Caro-Kann. There are so many good lines against it.
d4. We could play the Nimzowitsch, but that's a little too cheap — let's play the Fantasy, which doesn't get nearly enough love.
d5 — the Fantasy has a shoddy reputation —
f3 — undeservedly, because played well it's a very dangerous line, and Caro players just don't like to face it.

The idea of the Fantasy is obvious: maintain the centre, yield no control, and keep the light-squared bishop at bay — the Advance's problem is that it lets that bishop out to f5 — while not prematurely defining the pawn structure. h5 — I've never seen that; it's totally off-base.
The knight to c3. White's scheme is simple: develop the bishop, generally to e3, and castle short or long depending on Black's setup —
— and if he continues this way, we'll probably go long to exploit these shenanigans. The knight to f6 is just bad.
Here the knight on f6 is very vulnerable, so e5 is clearly right — this isn't like playing the Advance; Black is almost busted.
The knight to h7 — this is not the way to play the Caro. Had he played the knight to d7, we'd play e6, a typical gambit. f4 is possible but we don't need it yet — we have something far better.
The bishop to d3 — not f4 — stopping him from coming out to f5; now his bishop has nowhere good to go, and if we want we can follow with a4, the knight to f3, and so on.
The bishop to d7. Now the time has arrived —
— to figure out where the knight goes: f4 and the knight to f3 is the natural way to continue, reinforcing our centre. An amazing position — look how passive he is.
The h5-pawn adds to his passivity. He plays the bishop to g4 — no need to panic and drop the bishop back to e2; not every pin is dangerous, particularly this one.
