So we simply play the knight to f3 and follow it up with h3 — no need to change how we play at all.

He keeps making moves with the same piece and will pay the price. The queen to b6. The key question: can we play h3, or must we first defend the d4-pawn? A cool trap: after h3, the bishop takes f3, the queen takes f3, there's the queen takes d4 — painful to give up the central pawn, but see the bigger picture; your development lead gives full compensation. And there's a very cool idea here.
I'll play a move and let someone decode the idea — a3.
He plays e6.
Now h3, pretending to blunder the pawn —
— the bishop takes f3, the queen takes f3.
The idea is to trap the queen — he bites, the queen takes d4, and here comes the queen trap with the bishop to e3. It works like a charm.

There's a cool application of this in the Sicilian, where I originally learned the idea. The knight to g5 — he won't go gentle into that good night. A lot of players out of happiness just grab the knight, satisfied to be up a piece — don't settle for good enough; find the best idea.

Do we have to take the knight and let his queen out? Is he actually doing anything with this move? No — the queen back to e2 is simplest, and his queen is still very much trapped. Kudos to Black for the knight to g5, a nice defensive resource.
He started to think, but a little too late — now he gives up the queen.
The queen takes e3.
The knight to e4. It doesn't matter — we're up a queen — but let's be precise: should we take with the knight or the bishop?
We should take with the bishop, because d6 is a huge weakness, and the knight is the piece best equipped to exploit it — so we sack the bishop back.
You might say he has a dark-squared bishop that defends d6 —
— but that doesn't mean the square isn't a weakness; we can still slam a knight onto d6, and that trade is desirable since we're up a queen.
Clearly we should castle — always compare and contrast. The knight is much better equipped than a bishop to exploit these weaknesses; a bishop on e4 would just bite on granite.
Understanding how the position has changed: we can play the knight to g5 to go after the pawn, or the knight to d6, but the simplest —
— is to take what's hanging: the queen takes a7, which wins on the spot.
The bishop to e7 — many ways to finish straight away. There's one really cool idea —
— we could put a knight on d6, but we could also put a rook on d6, using the knight; I really hope he plays f5 so we can demonstrate the finale.
The king to c7. Even up a queen, I have a nice idea cooked up — it doesn't quite do it; I'll show you after.
One idea was just doubling rooks, putting insurmountable pressure on his knight.
The knight to b6. In such positions, looking for mate, always look at the squares — the queen eyes the b7-pawn —
— a potential mating square, so the knight to c5 stems naturally from that; and as soon as his knight leaves d7 he relinquishes control of squares, accelerating the search for mate. It's over.
He'll probably play the rook to b8, and then he's going to lose.
He takes instead, and it's checkmate on b7. Let's analyze quickly and call it a night.

The recommended weapons against the double king-pawn are the Vienna and the Four Knights Scotch. The Four Knights sounds like the most boring, mundane development there is — but it's an incredibly dangerous weapon at every level under 2000, and fully legitimate above it too.

The knight jumps to d4 — a move designed to scare a beginner: 'a knight is charging into the centre!' Look at it calmly and you'll see it just wanders in with nothing behind it. It might be some trick gambit, but we don't buy the bluff.
teaches: not fearing a lone central knight

notes.explains: If you were nervous you could ignore it entirely and keep developing with the bishop to c4. But there's nothing to calculate: we simply capture on e5, because the other side has only one piece out — a real trick can't exist when your opponent hasn't developed.

We're not satisfied with just the pawn. The Soviet-schoolboy move is to retreat the knight to f3 and smoke the intruder out of d4. Grabbing with the bishop to c4 instead invites a tricky queen-to-e7 line where White is actually much better but there's real theory to know. The point to hold onto: a knight sitting in the centre isn't automatically good — this one lacks an anchor and is easy to harass.

The real threat is the queen coming to e7 — it would chase the knight back and let Black regain the pawn on e4 at the same time. So we double back to f3, killing two birds: the knight retreats to safety.
And this also contests the knight sitting on d4.
The opponent obligingly captures on d4 and hangs the piece in one move. The game is effectively already over.

Now convert clinically. A beginner is tempted by the bishop check on b5, developing with tempo — but it's a mistake: it allows c6, and the Nxc6 tactic only trades two minor pieces for a rook and two pawns. Still winning, but there's no reason to give material back.
teaches: not every check with tempo is good

notes.explains: By process of elimination the knight drops back to b3: b5 walks into a6, e2 blocks the bishop — b3 keeps everything flowing so we can develop rapidly and actively.

The pawn on e4 is annoying, hanging over the position and cramping us. Playing d3 liquidates it, makes the minor pieces easier to coordinate, and opens the dark-squared bishop toward an eventual post on g5.

The queen-and-king alignment on the e-file is a liability, not a strength: if we seize the d-file the king has no squares, and since the c5-pawn is already committed, a future bishop check on b5 can no longer be met by c6. That's the move this is quietly setting up.

We take back on e4 to control the d-file and keep the b5-check threat alive. The knight-takes discovery looks scary but it's a paper tiger — even without the winning check, we'd simply take and force a queen trade.
The bishop is untouchable — the e4-pawn is pinned to the queen — so the bishop check on b5 just develops with tempo, and then we castle.
When you're up a piece there are usually four or five roughly equal moves in every position; defending e4 with f3 is a perfectly fine working move. The bishop check is just a touch more to the point.
We trade the bishops off and, crucially, force Black to recapture with the knight — clearing the way to plant our own knight on a beautiful d5 stronghold.

Queens come off, but a queen trade is no licence to abandon principle — development still comes first. Castling queenside is the plan here: no risk left, and it drops the rook straight onto the open d-file.
The bishop to g5 would walk into f6 or h6, so it goes to f4 instead — invulnerable there, and covering d6 to make it harder for Black to untangle.
Whenever a pawn is pushed, get in the habit of asking which squares just opened. Here the push hands us a juicy central outpost for the knight on d4.
Black replies c5, the Sicilian.
White pins with the bishop on b5 against the knight — the Rossolimo, a positional anti-Sicilian that swaps sharp theory for a small, controlled centre. The knight comes to f3 behind it.
teaches: The Rossolimo (Bb5 vs Nc6) is a positional anti-Sicilian

notes.explains: Black plays e6, building a compact, flexible pawn shell.
White castles, and Black tucks the second knight on e7 — a modest square that keeps the option of rerouting to g6 or d5.
c3 — the heart of the Rossolimo plan: prepare d4 and claim the centre without ever committing to the sharp lines.
teaches: c3 prepares the d4 central break in the Rossolimo

notes.explains: Black grabs queenside space with a6 and b5, and rather than let the bishop be harassed off the board White nurses it back — first to d3, then c2, keeping it on the long light diagonal aimed at the kingside.
teaches: Retreat the bishop to preserve it rather than let pawns chase it down

notes.explains: Black fianchettoes with the bishop to b7, leaning on the e4-pawn along the long diagonal.
a3 quietly forbids b5-b4, denying Black the tempo and keeping the queenside clamped.
teaches: a3 takes the b4 break away from Black

notes.explains: Black strikes in the centre with d5, challenging the e4-pawn head-on.
White meets it with d4, and the centre locks into full tension.
After the trades White recaptures with the bishop to e4 — beautifully placed, raking down the long diagonal at Black's bishop on b7 and eyeing the kingside.
Black sends the knight to the rim on a5, and the engine's needle jumps White's way: a knight on the edge of the board defends nothing and attacks little.
teaches: A knight on the rim is offside — it defends nothing and attacks little

notes.explains: White trades the light-squared bishops, and Black is forced to recapture with the knight, leaving it stranded and passive on b7.
teaches: Trade to leave the opponent\u2019s piece passive

notes.explains: The knight develops to c3, hitting the d5-square and joining the fight for the centre.
Black centralizes with the knight to d5 — active-looking, but White is already clearly on top, and the engine wants the outpost.

White plants the knight on e5 — a dominant central outpost the pawns can't chase away. The engine now reads it near a full pawn for White: the offside a5-b7 detour has left Black a passive game against a commanding centre.
teaches: A knight on e5 that can\u2019t be evicted is a lasting positional trump
plans: Anchor the knight on the e5 outpost
Press the space and the better-placed pieces

notes.explains: Our first 1500 — once again playing the basics, the classics. e4, e5.
The King's Gambit — nice, because I can remind you of my King's-Gambit system, an incredibly rare move
that scores incredibly well. c6 — what the hell are we doing? This looks like the worst move in the position, and that's exactly the point: c6 is like the Caro-Kann against the King's Gambit.
Why do you play c6 in the Caro-Kann? To prepare d5 — that's the whole point: we wait for the knight to f3,
and then we strike with d5. If he takes on d5, we can push e4 — that's why
most of the time I end up getting better positions with the Black pieces. d3. Now, the actual objective evaluation of c6 is that Black is slightly worse, but only if

The answer is yes, of course we should — because after d-takes-e4, d-takes-e4, we can trade queens and force the king onto d1, an incredibly undesirable square. Take on e4. It's possible he'll take on e5 with the knight, probably the best move.

If d-takes-e4 happens, that endgame is better for us — the king on d1 is really vulnerable even though there are no queens on the board. The knight takes e5. Now, f6 is impossible because of the queen to h5 with check — an important thing to note — and we shouldn't rush to take on d3 and help White develop.
So we trade on our own terms, and do it while developing our pieces — the knight to f6, developing; if he wants to take on e4, be my guest, we'll trade queens and recapture

with the knight. You might say aren't we worried about the knight on e5? It's annoying, but what is it actually attacking? Not really anything — we'll deal with it later with the knight to d7. The knight to c3, and we have several options: we can take on d3 and follow with the bishop to c5, preventing White from castling and keeping the king in the centre — we'd love the bishop to c5 immediately, but it gives up a pawn. The other approach is the bishop to b4, developing, pinning the knight, and taking the sting out of d-takes-d4.

The bishop to b4 is the more positional approach — we'll probably end up taking his knight on c3 and damaging his pawn structure. Let's go the bishop to b4, playing more positionally; I'm expecting a3, the instinctual response,

which is maybe even the best move. The Falkbeer Counter-Gambit is one of the most overrated systems against the King's Gambit — it sounds cool, but it's actually just bad. The bishop to d2, a good move, our opponent's playing well — it unpins the knight and

reinforces the attack on e4, essentially forcing us to trade on d3 — but now that we've developed most of our pieces, we're fine taking on d3, because we can castle next move; and my point is that the pawn on f4 will, in the long run, be a weakness.
In the short run it looks good, like it supports the knight, but once White castles kingside, my claim is that this pawn will end up causing trouble. The bishop takes d3. Now let's castle.

And on the next move, after he castles, we need to deal with the knight on e5 — try to trade it, ideally, by going the knight to d7; this is more important than developing the bishop, so I wouldn't play the bishop to e6, I'd immediately go the knight to d7 and address the knight before he solidifies it. The queen to f3 is another very good move; he wants to castle queenside, but that doesn't change what we do — the knight to d7, and obviously we recapture with the bishop, developing a piece. This is a blunder, and I've seen people blunder like this all the time: when you castle and swing the queen to f3, your rook and queen end up on the same diagonal, a very common blunder — so it's skewer time, the bishop to g4 wins the exchange, a massive material win, and our position is essentially winning. People forget to visualise the position after they castle. The queen to g3, the bishop takes d1. Now the technical stage: make priorities as always — what haven't we finished? Getting our pieces into the game. Don't rush to move the queen — there are two bishops on the d-file, so when he moves the bishop from d2, then we move our queen. The rook to e8, getting our rook on the open file. At this level, be very concrete; I'm not afraid of anything on the d-file, because you can't move two bishops at the same time, so nothing can happen as long as he keeps both there — but I make a mental note to move my queen the moment a bishop moves; it can go to c7 or a5, depending. The queen to f3. Again, multiple approaches — less about the exact move, more about the general approach: we want to trade pieces. There's a move that initiates a bunch of trades — the knight takes d5, the bishop takes d2 with check, the rook takes d2; we don't recapture with the queen, which walks into the discovery, we take with a pawn — and if we reach that moment, we have an even better move than pawn-takes-d5. If he doesn't take on d5, some of you might worry about the h7-pawn and the queen to h5 or h3, but that's not worrisome, because you can always play g6 — White doesn't have sufficient material on the kingside; never just be afraid of a mate threat. The knight takes d5, the bishop takes c2 with check, and after the rook takes d2, another lesson in not playing automatically — he plays the king takes d2, probably seeing that after the rook takes d2 there's the rook to e1 with check, forcing a rook trade, and then the queen takes d5. We can take with either piece, but in the interest of playing consecutively, having initiated this campaign to trade, I keep to our strategy; this won't be the easiest endgame, White is well coordinated and we'll have a weak pawn on d5, but we'll make it happen. The queen to h3 makes our job easier — I like the queens off; it threatens h7 because pinned pieces protect. Now, h6 or g6? Both are fine, but one is more accurate: when making luft with a bishop on d3, h6 often doesn't accomplish it, because the bishop controls h7, so I much prefer g6, shutting the bishop down entirely — and I'm not worried about weakening my dark squares, because White has no dark-squared bishop to occupy them. Now a very nasty queen move: I understood White is probably intending the king to c1, so, rather than pushing the a-pawn, the queen to a5 is a great move that wins the a-pawn — in fact the queen to a5 with check is superior to the queen to d4. The queen takes a2. The idea of a5, a4 is a good follow-up. Before that, it makes sense to bring a piece in — the rook to a8, getting the final piece into the action, and it creates a hidden threat of forced checkmate that starts with a quiet, deadly move: the queen to a1 is almost mate — it would be mate if the d2-square were controlled, and we can control it with either rook, but the bishop on d3 is blocking the rook, which is how the rook to e2 comes to mind, not immediately because White checks, but after a move like the queen to h6, the rook to e2 controls d2, forcing the bishop takes e2, and then the queen to a1 is just mate. There's another pretty mating sequence starting with the queen to a1 with check. f-takes is very weakening, opening the diagonal for the bishop, and loses to the bishop to c4 with check. We can pre-move the queen to a1 — there's literally nothing White can do.

Here comes a famous concession — capturing on c3 and giving up the fianchettoed bishop. At first sight it looks reckless, surrendering a prized piece and tearing a hole on the long diagonal — unthinkable to a beginner — yet the structural damage it inflicts on the opponent more than justifies it.
And the supposed dark-square weakness can't actually be exploited, because the knight hops out to f6 to cover the sensitive squares. The trade is all upside once the defence is properly arranged.

Even a bishop swung out to h6 achieves nothing here — it just sits there, doing no real work, while the opponent's shattered pawns quietly begin to collapse. Menacing placement without a threat behind it is empty.

The lasting point of the whole exchange is that the opponent's central pawn is badly weakened, left leaning on a single defending bishop — and it's never healthy to have a piece chained to a pawn. Meanwhile a knight is already routing toward c5, where it will pile onto that very pawn.

The whole plan with an extra queen is: develop normally first, then open the centre — because in a closed position the queen just sits there doing nothing; only open lines let that material advantage speak. A few running principles from the lesson. When a pawn is attacked, the queen is the worst defender — it's the easiest piece to chase — so defend the pawn with something modest, even a knight to the rim on a3, and keep the queen free. Learn the material threshold: up a queen, shedding a pawn or two to open lines is fine, but giving up a whole piece to open a file is only worth it if you forcibly deliver mate down it — otherwise the open file is a mansion in a ghost town. Treat undefended pieces as the pressure points on the map. And when two of your pieces are attacked at once, run the checklist: can one move to defend the other; if not, can one move away and capture or attack something in return. Then activate the idle pieces and finish with a forced mate.
teaches: open the centre to use the extra queen
the queen is the worst defender
material threshold when up a queen

notes.explains: But here's the correction. Sacrificing a piece to open a file isn't worth it unless you're actively mating on it — the king simply won't stay in the centre, it castles to the other wing, and then the file you opened is worthless, like owning a mansion in a ghost town.
teaches: open lines only mean something with a target

notes.explains: Black accepts the gambit, taking on c4.
The ambitious e4 — the most popular modern choice, staking out a beautiful pawn center. Black's whole task now is to attack these two pawns as fast as possible.
We push e5 rather than the old knight to c3, which would let Black equalize comfortably with ...e5.
We recover the pawn with the bishop on c4.
The whole battle now revolves around the d5 square — if White seizes it, Black is in trouble almost instantly. The bishop to f5 looks natural, but the knight to b6 was more accurate.
teaches: the fight for the d5 square

notes.explains: Nineteen-eighty-two, the highest rated we've faced by far — let's put my money where my mouth is and go very positional against this guy. d4, and out comes e5, the Englund Gambit.
We obviously accept it — d takes e5. Black's whole idea is to make a mess and hope we don't know the refutation.
Black plays the knight to c6, hitting the extra pawn, and we simply defend it with the knight to f3.
Now there are two main tries. The queen to e7 is the tricky one, and the Englund is one of those openings where if you don't know the antidote you can get into real trouble.
The so-called trap is to go the bishop to f4 or the bishop to g5 — both essentially transpose into the same overall picture. We go the bishop to f4, defending the pawn and staying developed.
And here's how bad it can look: the queen to b4 with check. Yet if you know the theory, you realize Black is so underdeveloped that all of this activity is going to backfire.
We block with the bishop to d2, calmly interposing and inviting Black to overreach.

The queen grabs on b2, attacking the rook in the corner. Now comes the actual trap: the very tempting move is the bishop to c3, thinking, let me attack the queen — but that's exactly what Black wants.

Because after the bishop to c3, the bishop swoops into b4, pinning our bishop to the king, and that creates very problematic consequences for us. So we sidestep the whole thing and develop the knight to c3 instead — same square, but no pin, and the queen is still in mortal danger deep in our camp.
Black tries the bishop to b4 anyway — this is the famous queen-sacrifice line the strong analysts have looked at.
We answer with the rook to b1, kicking the queen and daring Black to give it up. This is where Black's whole gambit stands or falls.

The queen to a3 isn't challenging at all. The critical way — the line the theory recommends — is the queen takes c3, a genuine queen sacrifice; I'll show you how that goes after the game, but the point is Black is grabbing pieces to justify parting with the queen.
Excellent move here: the knight to d5, immediately going after the c7-pawn and the bishop on b4. You don't want to dilly-dally — you go straight for the throat.
If Black tries the queen to a5, we just take the bishop — it's attacked, and there's no good way to keep everything defended once we start collecting on b4.
So the knight takes on b4. Whatever piece ends up sitting on b4 is going to be an issue, because Black would love to play c5 and win it back, so we have to be precise about which piece recaptures.
Black recaptures — the knight takes on b4. Taking back with the rook instead would have been bad, because our d5-knight was also hanging to the queen; the recapture order matters.
Now takes takes — and I'd like to recapture with the bishop, taking on b4 to prevent Black from castling and keeping that king stuck in the center.
Black snatches our edge pawn, the queen taking on a2. Now, how do we continue? Very often players get over-creative here or too fancy — you don't need either.
You simply follow the rules of development: complete your development. We push e4, opening the diagonal so this light-squared bishop can finally come out.
Black will try to dislodge the bishop from that strong diagonal, which is completely understandable — the knight to h6, heading for f5.

Some of you are thinking about the knight to g5, but generally speaking I want to orient my pieces toward the center, so I bring the knight to d4 — a beautiful central square, eyeing b5 among other things.
From d4 the knight can jump to b5 and do all sorts of damage; it's not just parked there. Black plays b6, making a little room.
Now the point: that queen on a2 needs an escape square, so we think methodically about trapping it — can we cover the b2-square so it has nowhere to run? The queen to c1 starts building that net.

One piece of advice: if you're up a queen in a position like this, don't lose on time trying to force the trap. If you don't win the queen outright, that's no tragedy — you're already winning. Black lunges with the queen to a4, still hunting for air.
Black is trying to escape, but notice the queen has literally no prospects. We have a very simple move, the bishop to b5, calmly sending the queen back and tightening the noose.

Count the net: it takes one, two, three, four, five pieces to trap a man's queen — and here they all coordinate. Black resigns, but of course we'd have finished by rounding the queen up; the queen to a2, the rook to a1, and it's caught.
Same story on the other wing — the queen to a4, the rook back to b1, and the queen simply runs out of squares. The hunt is a matter of technique once every escape is covered.
We take White and face the French.
We build the centre with d4.
Black plays d5; we lock the chain with e5 — the Advance.
Black strikes at the base with c5.
Instead of c3 we play the odd-looking knight to f3, which has brought a lot of success.
Black plays the queen to b6, the usual try.
We develop the bishop to d3 — unfazed by ...cxd4.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We take on c5.
Black recaptures with the bishop.
We castle — reaching the same structure as if Black had taken on d4, but without sacrificing the pawn.
Black develops the knight to e7.
We develop the knight to c3, eyeing Na4 to trade off Black's good dark-squared bishop.
Black plays the queen to c7.
We swing the knight to b5, aiming to sink into d6.
Black returns the queen to b6.
The knight leaps to d6 with check — d6 is uncovered, so no sacrifice is needed.
Black takes the knight with the bishop; we recapture with the e-pawn, planting a monster on d6.
Black develops the knight to g6.
We play the rook to e1, keeping options and x-raying e6.
Black plays ...Nb4, hitting our bishop.
We take the knight first, so the bishop can then come to f4.
Black recaptures with the h-pawn; we plant the bishop on f4, cementing d6 — with no dark-squared bishop, Black can't challenge it.
Black castles — opening himself to an attack down the h-file.
We play the prophylactic knight to g5 — it prevents ...f6 and eyes the kingside.
Black develops the bishop to d7.
We lift the rook to e3, swinging it toward the king.
Black brings the rook to c8.

Capturing on d6 is better than letting the bishop develop, because however the opponent recaptures — pawn or bishop — they're saddled with a backward, sickly pawn. Choose the exchange that leaves the enemy structure worst.

A successful opening is no licence to get arrogant — just keep developing. The knight comes to c3, and a modest pawn to e3 is preferred over the bolder advance, out of caution that the enemy queen could otherwise swing to e7 and x-ray down the file.
A Scandinavian. It isn't a bad opening in itself, but at this level it's genuinely hard to play well.
The queen's knight to c3 is the move — developing with tempo by hitting the exposed queen.
We could develop a knight, but occupy the centre first with d4, so the other side never gets in e5 or c5.
We could shove the pawn to d5, but let's stay principled: the knight to f3 defends the pawn while developing.
Now it's actually time to bend our own rules. That queen's knight has hopped around so many times, and the other side still hasn't moved a single central pawn — a clear drawback we can pounce on.
So d5 punishes it. Can the pawn be taken? Count: two attackers, two defenders — so no, the capture doesn't win it.
A lot of players miscount here. The subtlety: a knight is an attacker, but the instant it captures the pawn it stops being one — that's why the count comes out in our favour.
teaches: the capturing piece leaves the count

notes.explains: The pawn to e4, c6 — the Caro-Kann. We haven't faced it too many times.
d4. There are countless setups against the Caro; what matters more than which you pick is that you know it well.
f3 — the Fantasy Variation, the line we played the one time we faced the Caro. Let's see how it holds up here.
Black takes on e4. The Fantasy doesn't have the greatest reputation, in my opinion very undeservedly — it's incredibly tricky and can lead to quick wins against imprecise play.
We recapture on e4.
e5 — the main line, a classic idea. You don't want to take on e5, because of the super-nasty check on h4.
And you don't play c3, which doesn't stop that check either — so, almost Vienna-style, the knight to f3. The Fantasy is very annoying for Caro players who like a quiet positional game.
The bishop to g4 — the main move, pinning the knight. Again we don't take on e5: that allows the queen trade and Black wins the pawn back.

The correct move is the bishop to c4, aiming at f7 — threatening the bishop takes f7 and the knight takes e5, the classic idea. If Black takes the knight, you take back with a massive attack on f7; the bishop takes f3 is terrible. Black has to be very precise — reminds me of Tal.
The knight to f6 — immediately a blunder. This is exactly why you choose lines based on what your opponent won't like to face.

The point Black missed: after the knight takes e5 with check, the bishop is attacked by two pieces and defended by only one, so the bishop takes f7 with check is crushing. The move was the knight to d7.
The king takes on f7 — you had to know the knight to d7 to cover the e5-square.
The knight takes e5 with check.
The king to g8.

The knight takes g4 — now we're two pawns up, the king in shambles, completely winning eight moves in. It could become one pawn if the knight takes c4, but we have mating ideas on the a2-to-g8 diagonal.

The knight to d7 — as good a move as any, and it leaves our centre intact. We can choose between the materialistic knight to c3 protecting e4, or simply castling; we care far more about the open f-file and activating quickly. There's also c3 threatening the queen to b3, but that over-relies on a gimmick and under-emphasizes development.

The knight to c3 — probably simpler, keeping the two extra pawns; we'll castle next. Don't fall for one-move-itis: seeing a cool mating pattern, getting excited, and not asking whether your opponent can stop the threat.
The bishop to b4.
Now of course we castle, not fearing the bishop takes c3 and the knight takes d4 — because without the dark-squared bishop, Black's dark squares will also be really weak.
The queen to c7. Time to step on the gas. Some of you are contemplating the bishop to f4 —

— but I don't like it, since it blocks the f-file. The best is e5: the idea is to dislodge the knight from f6 — you control that square, so after it takes, we recapture and threaten the queen to e6 checkmate, with nothing able to block the rook; our centre evicts Black's last remaining defender.
Black's bishop to c5 walks straight into the center fork trick.
The knight takes on e5 — the center fork trick, a theme that recurs across many openings, and your reaction should be automatic.
The bishop to d6 is the ONLY move that keeps Black's bishop pair and a viable position — everything else loses quickly or is much worse.
teaches: ...Bd6 is forced to keep the bishops

notes.explains: After the trades White is clearly better — three pieces clamp the d5 square, and the bishop on e5 is an awkward, vulnerable piece.
teaches: d5 control + a loose enemy bishop

notes.explains: The accurate move isn't the flashy one — the quiet bishop to d3. Not f4, which lets ...Bxc3 and ...d6 turn that pawn into a liability and hampers our own Bg5; and not Bc4, which leaves e4 loose.
We castle — and there's no Greek gift here, since the g4 square is covered.
The conventional bishop to g5 — better than dropping the knight to e2, which would surrender our grip on d5.
After ...h6 we retreat to h4, and that h6-pawn becomes a hook we'll use later to push f4 open.
teaches: a pawn hook to lever open the kingside

notes.explains: The vanilla queen to d2 coordinates the rooks and links the queen to the knight — now ...Bxc3 is completely harmless.
Black's knight to g4 makes no sense — we just chase it with h3. The knight to h2 is the road to hell: we move the rook and the knight is trapped.
We happily collect the knight.

The simplest finish — not g3, which would trap our own bishop after ...g5, but the bishop to g3: a piece up, we shed a pawn to remove Black's only developed minor, keep the king safe, and grab the semi-open f-file.
teaches: don’t be greedy — simplify when ahead

notes.explains: Let's unpack this. The bishop to g7 is the Modern, and the move I'm interested in — c3 — is definitely not the most popular; most people just develop the knight.
The mainstream choice is the knight to c3, the natural developing move that grabs a share of the center.

The kingside fianchetto ushers in the Glek System — a practical way to sidestep the symmetrical defences and steer the game into quieter, less-charted positional territory where understanding matters more than memory.
As the opponent readies queenside expansion, the prophylactic pawn to c3 stops the pawn break before it starts, and then the rooks come into the game — restrain the plan first, activate second.
Let's play the Budapest. Compared with other offbeat lines it's on the reputable side — not a gimmick you play just for a cheap trick, but a legitimate gambit.
Two ways to chase the pawn back: the knight to e4 is very speculative — essentially trash — while the reputable try is the knight to g4, which goes straight after the gambit pawn.

As with every gambit, the currency is development and initiative: bring pieces out fast, push White into passivity, then turn to a kingside attack. Committing the queen to e7 straight away would be too awkward.
The knight to c6 is the move, simply pressing to win the pawn back — and after the bishop comes to f4, there's an interesting check on b4 waiting.
The bishop to c5 is tempting but less effective than it looks — e3 blunts it. The bishop to b4 with check is the real try, because it carries a trap.
So we develop with tempo, giving check.
White usually blocks with the queen's knight to d2 — and that's exactly the setup for a smothered mate.
We play the queen to e7, and White typically continues a3 — after which a very pretty tactic wins the pawn back.
Look at what the queen is doing: it x-rays down toward the king. If the e5-pawn were to vanish and a knight were to land on d3, that would be checkmate.
So the knight captures on e5 — threatening that smothered mate. Someone at this level really shouldn't miss it.
But he grabs the bishop on b4 instead, walking straight into it — one of the appeals of these gambits is that eventually someone does.
The knight to d3 — smothered mate. Exactly what the line was built for.
Black's passive e6-and-c6 hybrid concedes the initiative. We don't change our plan for weird moves — after the exchanges, look how nicely our knights sit.
teaches: don’t be intimidated by an offbeat setup

notes.explains: The bishop belongs on d3, not c4 — on c4 it would just bite on granite against Black's pawn wall.
teaches: Bd3 over Bc4 against this structure

notes.explains: The key principle — the least-valuable piece does the job. So we defend the center with the pawn to c3, not the bishop, building a solid chain, and Black's dark-squared bishop is left weak.
teaches: defend with the pawn, not the piece

notes.explains: We castle, and now a mating idea is in the air.
The Greek Gift needs the g5 square under control first, and h4 does exactly that — the essential preparatory move.
teaches: prepare the Greek Gift by covering g5

notes.explains: The Greek Gift itself — the bishop takes on h7 with check.
The king is forced to take.
The knight arrives on g5 with check.
The king runs to g6 — and here's why h4 mattered: had the king taken the knight, the h-pawn recaptures and rips the h-file wide open for the queen and rook to deliver mate.
teaches: the h4 pawn opens the h-file after ...Kxg5

notes.explains: We're White against a lower-rated opponent, so let's play very aggressively — we still haven't had the chance to unveil a legitimate Danish Gambit. e4, e5.
d4 — the Danish, offering the center to blow the position open.
Instead of grabbing, he plays the knight to c6. So what do we do here?

My favorite move: d takes e5. The short reason is that it clarifies the center — the knight to f3 would just transpose into a Scotch, but I think capturing is best, both to open things up and because the knight that recaptures on e5 will be awkwardly placed.
The knight recaptures on e5, and this knight is really not well placed — it's exposed to a whole series of tempo-gaining attacks.
We develop naturally with the knight to c3, getting a piece out and keeping options open.
Black offers a trade with the knight to f6 — a non-committal move; we don't have to decide about trading yet.
f4 — you give an exoskeleton to your position. When you only develop pieces without supporting pawns, those pieces float; the pawn advance both kicks the e5-knight and gives the center a spine.
The knight retreats to c6, and now the advance is associated with a very strong follow-up: e5, chasing the f6-knight back.
He has to go all the way back to g8, losing a ton of tempo, and his position already looks grim.
We bring the other knight out, the knight to f3, developing with gain of time.
His best try is d6, striking at our advanced e5-pawn.

Here's a tip: once your pieces are out and the opponent's king is stuck, a queen trade doesn't kill your attack — a lot of your attackers aren't the queen. The bishop to b5 pressures the pinned defender and steers toward exactly that.
A queen trade would have cost him his castling rights and left his king a sitting duck, so instead he plays the bishop to d7, breaking the pin.
We castle — the king still has a nice pawn shell, and the fact that we advanced the f-pawn doesn't spoil it. He replies d takes e5.
We recapture, f takes e5, and he's done us a big favor by opening the f-file straight at his king.
Now his king is going to be in real trouble. He gives a check with the bishop to c5.
We tuck the king to h1, out of the checks and ready to attack.
It looks like Black will finish developing before we do — the knight to e7 — but that doesn't matter, because we're about to whip up a very quick attack on that king.
What active moves can we play? The first thing my mind's eye sees is that loose bishop on c5 — so the knight to e4 jumps in, hitting it.
Black slides the bishop to f5, and we take the bishop — the knight captures on c5, winning the bishop pair and staying on top.
Black plays a6, poking at our bishop.
The bishop simply drops back to c4, and we're basically winning.
He offers the queen trade, queen takes on d1, and we recapture with the rook. This raises a very contentious question — is it good to trade when you're up material?
Black finally castles into safety.
My take: don't feel you HAVE to simplify just because you're ahead. A lot of blunders come from ignoring the other features of the position. We calmly play c3.
Black brings a rook to d8, contesting the file.
Don't go blind to attacking chances just because you're trying to simplify — the bishop to g5 eyes the dark squares.
Black slips the bishop to c2.
I do have a clean chance to trade rooks, so why not — the rook takes on d8 with check. We give up the d-file, no big deal.
Black recaptures on d8.
It's an endgame and we can snap off another pawn — the knight takes on b7, a free pawn.
Black tries the rook to d1 with check; we trade it off. A word of caution I've shared: don't chase too many extra pawns when you're already up a stack of pieces.
But if there are free pawns with no consequences, absolutely take them: the bishop comes to d3, bishops are traded, Black plays h6, and the bishop scoops up on a6 — more material for nothing.
Now we simplify: Black shuffles the knight to c8, our bishop comes to f6, the knight reroutes to e7, and the bishop takes on e7, peeling off another defender.
Black recaptures with the knight on e7.
The knight comes to c5, centralizing and supporting the passed e-pawn.
Black jumps the knight to f5, trying to blockade.
We push the passed pawn to e6 — it's about to become a monster.
Black lunges with the knight to e3. We'll just retreat our bishop and then win this pawn — the game is over, we're up a piece.
e7 is correct — the pawn is one step from queening.
Black tries the knight to g4, but there's nothing left; he resigns.

Against the Ponziani, the thematic counter is to strike in the centre with d5 — the whole point is that the queen's knight can no longer develop to its best square. Most players continue with a routine pawn move, but there's a little-known gambit that not only unsettles the opponent but objectively equalises: developing the bishop, which looks like it hangs the pawn and does, yet it prepares to trade off the opponent's only developed piece and seize a massive lead in development. That lead is compounded because the queen's knight struggles to get out at all, and the plan sets up a discovery — a knight leap into the centre that forces the queen to retreat, after which the trade lands and the kingside develops with tempo. The queen is left awkward and vulnerable, and the whole game becomes a hymn to active piece play: keep the extra central pawn alive as an anchor and outpost, aim a bishop behind it as stored-up potential energy, and pursue the kingside attack with a pawn break, exploiting any hook the opponent hands over. Above all, learn to win in simple fashion — you have to master not sacrificing before you can sacrifice well.
e4, and the Scandinavian — d5.
We know how to play against the Scandinavian — we take it, and we've got
the knight to c3 coming. The queen recaptures on d5.
The knight to c3, hitting the queen.

The queen to d8 — the Bartholomew setup, a move that's gained popularity recently, a very solid system. The best way to play against it is very straightforward chess: first we should occupy the centre
with our pawn, and then develop naturally and actively. What does that mean? We start with d4, of course, then the knight to f3, the bishop to c4,
and so on — the knight to f3.
h6 — that's already bad, completely unnecessary movement. We can try to punish it by playing in a very principled manner.
We should start with the bishop to c4, aiming at the f7-pawn. g5 here is an interesting move too, but I like the bishop to c4 — develop the bishop, aim at the pawn; and if he plays a loose move,
this is flirting with disaster. Why? The bishop to f5 without e6 — now we're
aiming at f7. We should definitely play the knight to e5 — and look, this is serious. e6,

this is serious, let me think. There are multiple tempting moves here, and I'm going to teach you a really cool tactical idea. Not g4 — g4 isn't dangerous for Black, don't succumb to one-move-itis; g4 and the bishop to h7 does nothing. The move I'm debating is the queen to f3, but maybe we should just be Russian and disciplined and castle and forget everything crazy. The queen to h5 is interesting, but he plays g6, and I don't really understand the follow-up. I'll go on record and say the queen to f3 is a mistake, but I'll play it anyway, in the hopes he allows the tactic. He can take on d4, and after the queen takes d4 I had a cool follow-up in mind — but he allows the tactic. What tactic? To find it you break it into parts: first, you detect the pressure we're putting on f7; second, you note that if the king lands on f7 the pawn on e6 becomes pinned — therefore the knight takes f7, the king takes f7, and the queen takes f5. Tactics are pretty logical when you think about it: now we win a pawn, the king is in shambles, and we're completely winning. This concept exists in many openings, not just this one — I can show you fifteen examples of this knight-takes-f7, queen-takes-f5 business. I know it's scary, because our queen seems to hang and we depend on a tenuous pin, but remember: if you get scared, you can always move the queen back — he can't break the pin and take the queen at the same time — and the bishop is completely safe on c4, it can even drop back to b3. When I do a tactic like this, file it away, even write it down or photograph it, and keep a running record of interesting tactical ideas, because before you know it you'll get a chance to apply it. Now, the queen to d6 is a tilt move that walks right into a developing move with tempo — get the bishop out with tempo again, and now we don't need to move our queen at all, the bishop is perfectly capable of defending it. Then we castle and try to put a rook on e1 and smash through on e6; this is already essentially resignable, and what makes it worse is that Black can never drop his king back to g8, because that blunders the pawn on e6. The queen to e7. Where should we castle? It really doesn't matter — kingside or queenside is essentially the same — but since we're in an attacking mood, I'll castle queenside. Why not g4 for Black? g6 is the only way to stay alive, and not for long. Where should our queen go? Think of the queen as a supporting actress: people are always tempted by the queen to e5 here, but that's counterproductive — putting your queen on the front lines is like sending Napoleon himself to fight in the trenches; you want your general behind the lines directing traffic. The queen to e5 walks right into the knight to d7, a developing move that forces us to move the queen again — we want to keep the queen back, still pressuring the e6-pawn but invulnerable. If you want more on this, I wrote a chess.com article a couple of years ago literally called 'The Queen, a Supporting Actress,' full of attacks where the queen was kept behind rather than in the thick of it. The king to g7 is very impatient and blunders the e6-pawn — thank you very much, we gladly take the free pawn, and Black's position collapses; the bishop to e5 is a great follow-up, pinning the knight to the king, and a rook to e1 is great too — anything is winning. Yasser is the originator of this concept; he's the one who told me about it. Black is totally busted. We can play the bishop to e5, because in the event of a trade our rook gets free, but in the interest of disciplined attacking chess let's get our final rook into the game. He sets up an x-ray against our queen — but really, it doesn't matter how you play here as long as you make decent attacking moves. Once the queen goes to d8, the first thing that catches my eye is that x-ray — I'm obsessed with x-rays, they're valuable and can be exploited, but only if we get rid of the d-pawn, and we absolutely can: we push d5, a typical attacking motif, and if Black plays c5, which I expect, we shove the pawn all the way to d6 to entomb the bishop forever. It's an x-ray because the rook is staring at the queen through a bunch of pieces. He takes on d5 — the bishop to e5 was just as strong, everything is winning. When you're this far ahead there are often four or five winning attacking continuations; don't obsess over which one you or I chose, because chances are the other move is winning too — it's a matter of taste, though of course sometimes a move really is wrong. The knight takes, we take back with the rook, completely crushing, just demolition. The bishop to b7 — we can take any piece and win, but since the two knights defend each other, the best is to take the knight and then take the other knight with the rook, because if he recaptures with his knight we take the queen. Take the queen — elementary. We can bring the queen to e6; the bishop to b5 to trade the last bishops is good; a rook to e6, or the rook takes f6, all fine — anything wins, it's trap city, you could be deep Stockfish and you're losing. The simplest is the bishop to e5, trading off the last defender of the king, and the point is that we want to get a rook to the seventh rank, the fastest path to mate — which is what we do now: a rook to e7 with check. I'm playing quickly because it's so winning that at this level you should be comfortable converting these. The simplest is to keep the rook on the seventh, the rook to h7, and then the queen takes h6 is the immediate mate threat; the other idea is the queen to a3 followed by the queen to e7, infiltrating the seventh rank. The position is completely resignable, so now we go for our secondary idea, getting the queen to e7 with checkmate along the seventh — and, by the way, use the whole board, not fixating on two files: even the empty queenside is a springboard to swing your heavy pieces over to the king.

castling — and castling really is the mature approach to the position, but I wanted to show you this tactical idea, after which it's game over. To prove the point that it appears across openings, here's a game from 1996, a Caro-Kann Panov: the bishop to f5, and Black plays the capture, which is bad — e6 is the move here — the knight to f3, the knight to e5, the queen to f3, played perfectly, the bishop to d6, then f5, and here White plays the knight to e4, the very move we wanted, then the knight to g5 with check; and beautifully, the queen takes c6 with check, and White simply castles out of the pin — the point being a rook to e6 hitting the f5-fork, and White went on to win the game.
We take White and face the Sicilian.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black plays d6; we open with d4.
Black takes on d4; we recapture with the knight.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black plays the ...e5 Sicilian.
We give the check on b5.
Black blocks with the bishop to d7.
We trade on d7 with check.
Black recaptures with the knight; we jump the knight into f5.
Black plays the queen to b6, eyeing b2.
We castle.
Black plays the rook to d8.
We pin with the bishop to g5; Black greedily grabs on b2.
We plant the knight on d5 — a huge threat.
Black takes it off.
We recapture with the queen, centralized on d5.
Black plays the rook to c8.
The knight crashes on d6 with check.
Black takes with the bishop; we recapture with the queen; Black tries ...f6.
We check with the queen on e6.
Black's king goes to d8; we bring a rook to d1.
Black plays the queen to b5.
We swing the rook to d5.
Black plays the queen to a4.
We double rooks, the other one to d1.
Black's king walks to c7.
We check on d6.
Black returns to d8.
The queen sacrifices itself on d7 with check.
Black recaptures with the queen; our rook takes on d7 with check.
Black's king steps to e8.
We reroute the bishop to c1.
Black plays the rook to g8.
The bishop swings to a3.
Black plays the rook to c3.
We check with the rook on e7.
Black's king goes to f8.
The rook delivers mate on d8.
The other side plays the Pirc — d6 and g6. It gets a bad rap for a simple reason: it hands us the full centre without a fight.

White's key strategy in the Pirc is to castle queenside and storm the kingside — you can't launch a pawn avalanche at the wing where your own king lives. So we clear the path for the king to c1 by lining the bishop and queen up on e3 and d2.

That battery has a bonus: the bishop can swing to h6 and forcibly trade off the fianchettoed bishop — Black's strongest piece, the one that supervises his whole defence. No need to rush the swap, though.
Now start the attack — h4. Take the hammer to Black's position; without ripping open files and avenues on the kingside, we never reach his king.
The knight jumps to h5, so g4 chases it out — we don't want it sitting there.
The whole aim is to pry open the h-file, the artery to the king. Rather than sac immediately, we play f3 to defend the g4-pawn — patience first, elimination later.

How to handle the centre? Since we're attacking on the wing, we want it closed — so d5 slams it shut. A closed centre buys the time to focus everything on the kingside; an open one splits your attention.
teaches: close the centre when attacking the wing

notes.explains: With the centre shut we transition straight back to the plan — h5, prising open the kingside.
He plays g5 to keep things closed, but the queen takes on g5 and it's simply winning — it threatens mate, and his only defence of the bishop drops the queen.
We recapture with the queen rather than the rook. The rook would have won a second piece, but keeping the queens on lets us keep taking the hammer to him.
He trades the dark-squared bishops to slow the attack, but we're still up a full piece.
Now, fresh blood — don't forget to finish developing. Castle, then reroute the knight toward f5 to lever open the g-file.
This is the maneuver: the knight to f5 either forces a trade that opens the g-file, or dislodges the queen — and then a rook lands on that file with crushing effect.
teaches: knight maneuver to open a file

notes.explains: Even after a queen trade it doesn't matter — the attack has done its work and it's still mate in a couple of moves.
So how should Black have defended? The Pirc doesn't lose — but castling this early is already inaccurate by modern theory, because it walks straight into the bishop-to-h6 and h4-h5 assault.
We take Black and play the Caro-Kann, c6.
White plays the unusual e5 — rare, but not terrible. We can't play ...d5 now, and White could later push d4 into an Advance Caro.
To leave White no advantage at all, we hit the pawn at once with d6, simply trading it off — the simplest response.
White captures on d6.
We recapture — the position is dead equal.
White plays d4. It's a bone-dry, equal position — White isn't fighting for anything, and sometimes you just accept that.
We can play ...d5 now or later; first we develop the knight to f6.
White plays c3. After ...d5 we reach a symmetrical structure where we're effectively playing the white side, a tempo up.
So we push d5, opening a path for the bishop to d6.
White pins with the bishop to g5. There's no single right answer here — but learning to handle dry positions well matters.
The simplest is the bishop to e7, breaking the pin.
White develops the knight to f3. With the pin gone we can play ambitiously — the knight to e4 centralizes and forces White to resolve the tension — or castle first; it hardly matters.
We choose the knight to e4, introducing an asymmetry — ...Bg4 would just be met by the bishop to e2 and stay too symmetrical.
White retreats the bishop to f4 — a surprise; I expected the trade on e7.
We don't change our plan and simply castle.
White develops the bishop to d3. Notice we held our own bishop back to see where his went — a subtle posturing, making the opponent show his cards first.

We play the bishop to g4 — no need to defend the e4-knight, our pawn supports it. This makes White waste a tempo retreating to e2, a small annoyance. The plan is patient: the knight comes to d7, pinning White's f3-knight to the queen, and we build pressure inch by inch.
White castles. You can't do everything at once — you pile on pressure by degrees, and small problems eventually coalesce into big ones.

We complete development with the knight to d7, keeping ...f5 in reserve. When White loses patience with the queen to b3, the point of ...Bg4 pays off — we take on f3. Even a b7-pawn sacrifice would be worth it, but we needn't: the knight to d6 defends b7, and if White grabs both, his king is stripped bare. A mating tip: drive the king in first with a queen check on g5 — before the tempting queen to h4 — then the queen to f4 sets up the battery and mate; the check first stops the defender making luft with the rook.
A deliberate handicap experiment — Black jettisons the dark-squared bishop on a3. The point isn't the sacrifice; it's what you do once you're a piece down.

The first and most important lesson when you're down material: do NOT spiral. Players blunder a piece and then, out of a false sense of necessity, throw away rook after rook pretending it was all planned. Instead, keep your remaining pieces, play sound chess, and make your opponent earn the win.
teaches: don’t compound a blunder — play on soundly

notes.explains: And a real resource even here — we can tempt White to trade on f6 and recapture with a pawn. The doubled pawns look ugly but are a blessing in disguise: they hand us dark-square control and open lines toward White's slightly loose setup.
teaches: recapture toward the center for dark-square control

notes.explains: We're Black, and against d4 out comes the knight to f6 — let's go.
The bishop to f4 — the London System, one of White's most popular setups.
We're going to test our opponent on a London line I've used myself, one a lot of people still don't know. It starts with c5, hitting the center immediately.
White props things up with e3.
We take on d4, forcing the issue.
After White recaptures, we quickly fire off the queen to b6 — the very tricky line, and inexperienced London players hate it because it hits both b2 and d4.

He plays the knight to c3. If you know the first thing about this line you don't rush that — the theoretically good try for White is different, something Rosen has analyzed — but a natural developer reaches for the knight to c3.

And here's the point: we play d6, deliberately luring that knight to stay on c3. London players do not like having their knight committed to c3 — it clogs the natural pawn setup London players lean on.
White shores up b2 with the rook to b1.
Now the fianchetto should feel natural: g6. If you play e6 instead you block in your own light-squared bishop, so we let it breathe on the long diagonal.
White brings out the knight to f3; we complete the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
White develops the bishop to e2; we castle.
White castles too — a normal-looking middlegame, but our queen sortie has already made White slightly uncomfortable.

There are a couple of viable setups. One is to trade this bishop for White's knight and then post the knight on c6 pressuring d4 — but I don't love parting with the bishop, so I play the bishop to f5, eyeing c2.
White plays h3. A tempting move here is the knight to h4, but that's succumbing to one-move-itis — chasing a single idea while ignoring the rest of the board.
We develop the knight to c6, piling onto d4.
White lashes out with d5 — a committal push London players usually dislike, but he goes for it, kicking our knight.
The knight jumps into b4 — and this is the whole point of the bishop on f5: together they gang up on c2 and win a tempo.
White defends with the knight back to e1, an ugly, passive square. Most players in the 1700-1800 range would shuffle the rook toward c1, which is even more passive.
We bring the rook to c8, stacking up on the c-file.
White plays a3, poking our knight on b4.

We retreat the knight to a6, planning to redeploy it to c5 — and one point I want to make through this game is that people become terrified of a move like the knight to a6 when there's no reason to fear it.
White develops the bishop to e3, hitting our queen.
We slide the queen to a5 — and honestly this drops a pawn; I completely forgot it was hanging. I should have brought the other rook over instead, a clean improving move rather than this.
The bishop out to c4 is a different way to handle the Alekhine — prioritising rapid piece development over grabbing the centre with pawns. It carries a sacrificial idea against f7 to stay alert for.
Wary of a trap, prop the centralised knight with a pawn — passive, but rock-solid. There's real merit in openings where you sit slightly worse yet remain almost impossible to break down.
Develop the knight to attack the advanced pawn and force the opponent to make a decision — and when it's exchanged, recapture with the bishop, keeping the structure harmonious.
Allowing the opponent a broad centre is fine here, because the compensation is superb piece placement. Then capturing on e5 clears the diagonal for the bishop to come to life.

Where does the bishop belong — e7 or c5? It's a trick question. The answer is e7, because developing to c5 would concede the g5 square to an enemy piece, handing over exactly the outpost you don't want to give.
The opponent's bishop move is inexplicable, and the simple capture wins by force — a reminder that a single careless developing move can lose on the spot.
It's a Scandinavian, just dressed up with an early a6 — not that bad, but our strategy doesn't change. We capture and treat it like a normal Scandi.
With the d-pawn already advanced we simply develop the knight to c3, gaining a tempo on the exposed queen — exactly as in the main Scandinavian.
One subtlety: Black's idea may be b5. You can always meet b5 with a4, softening the queenside pawns — or develop the bishop to c4 first, before b5 ever arrives.
The bishop to c4 develops and lays a trap: if Black grabs space with b5, there's a crushing tactic waiting — a very common mistake at this level.

The knight to c6 is a touch odd because it invites d5. But d5 isn't as good as it looks — it blocks the very bishop we just developed, and pushing the pawn weakens a square the knight can hop into on e5. Better to just keep developing.
teaches: do not push into your own bishop

notes.explains: So the knight comes to f3. Note that a bishop sortie to g4 here would be a blunder — the sacrifice on f7 with check refutes it, and it must be that capture first, not the knight jump, which only draws.
So we crash on f7 with check. The king loses castling rights and the whole kingside is wrecked — well worth it, even though the d4-pawn will hang at the very end, so this isn't the usual clean win.
The knight comes to g5 with check, driving the exposed king.

Queen and knight are the strongest attacking tandem in chess, so the usual 'let the queen support from behind' rule bends here. The queen to e6 is the move — it eyes a landing on f7. We even allow the knight to grab d4 with tempo; it doesn't matter, the queen is going to f7 regardless.

After the king runs to d7, Black threatens to grab on c2. Do we bend over backwards to defend it? Absolutely not — the cleanest, most elegant move is to castle, straight out of the fork, preparing the rook to d1. The c2-grab then simply loses to a rook check on d1 with a skewer. When you do play the rook to d1, watch the weak back rank for discoveries, but the knight-to-e2 check is harmless — the king steps to f1, hitting the queen, and it's over. And when converting, keep completing development — the Russian-school habit of bringing every piece in, even when you're up a queen — then the back-rank mating net with the bishop on b6 finishes it.
The Nimzowitsch-Larsen — b3 and the bishop to b2. It's a hypermodern opening: instead of building our own center, we attack the opponent's from a distance with our pieces.
e3 is the old main line — pure hypermodern, with all our pressure aimed at the enemy center rather than our own.
The bishop to b5 hits the knight and threatens to win the e5-pawn.
The queen to e7 defends, but at a real cost — it makes Black's kingside bishop much harder to develop.
teaches: Qe7 defends but blocks his own development

notes.explains: The knight goes to e2, not f3 — f3 would invite ...e4 with tempo, and we want to leave that pawn on the operating table. The e2 square also prepares a second plan.
We take the knight. Even though e5 is no longer attacked directly, we can pile straight back onto it — Black is already in trouble just six moves in.
The pawn to f4 pries at e5 — d4 would only block in our own bishop and hand Black the ...e4 push.
teaches: f4, not d4, to open the bishop and hit e5

notes.explains: Black pushes e4.
The knight takes the awkward route — first to a3, the Frankfurt airport, on its way toward the center.
teaches: reroute via the rim toward the center

notes.explains: Then to c4 — ugly, but imagine how good it'll look once it reaches e5. No rush, though: the threat is stronger than its execution.
teaches: the threat is stronger than the execution

notes.explains: Black castles long — so we have opposite-side castling, a straight race of attacks.
Our attack starts with a4, heading for b4 and b5 to blast open his queenside pawn cover — and in opposite-side castling you simply have to get on with it.
teaches: a4-b4-b5 to crack the castled king

notes.explains: The point I keep coming back to is never to fall in love with a particular piece. One more game — we face a fianchetto, e4 and g6.
We stake out the center with d4.

Black tries d5 — not a move that's typically studied or theoretical. It's not terrible, but Black falls behind in development and in space, and there are two ways to meet it: push e5 for a big center, or capture.
We take, e takes d5, opening the position while Black is underdeveloped.
Black recaptures with the queen on d5, pulling the queen out early — always risky.
Now just follow basic principles: the knight to c3, exactly like the Scandinavian, developing with tempo against the queen.
Black digs a deeper hole with the queen to e6 with check — a really bad move: it blocks in the bishop and stumbles the queen into the crossfire.
I block the check with the bishop to e3. Several moves are roughly equal here, but I have a specific plan in mind that I'll detail after the game.
Black fianchettoes with the bishop to g7. Meanwhile I'm already picturing where I want to castle — queenside — and where the attack goes: the kingside.
The queen comes to d2, connecting the plan: it eyes the h6-square and prepares to castle long.
Black develops the knight to f6.
I follow through on the concept and castle queenside, anticipating that Black castles kingside — opposite-side castling means a pawn-storm race.
Black castles kingside, right into the teeth of where I want to attack.
I take the middle ground and develop the knight to f3 before committing the h-pawn.
Black plays b6, preparing to fianchetto the other bishop.
One option is the bishop to h6, offering the trade of dark-squared bishops; another is h4, though h4 often meets h5 and stalls.
Black continues the fianchetto with the bishop to b7.
You don't automatically have to take on g7 in these positions, but here I will — the bishop takes on g7.
Black recaptures with the king on g7, and now those dark squares around his king are permanently tender.
The knight leaps to e5. We don't have to restrict ourselves to the kingside; we can play in the center and against Black's queen — exactly what I'm doing.
Black develops the knight to a6 — no reason not to bring it out toward c5.
I complete development with the bishop to c4, and now Black's queen doesn't have many good squares.
I'm anticipating the queen to d6 — probably the only reasonable retreat for Black.
I play the quiet f3. Where is the attack headed? To the b-file eventually — and I'm also watching that the knight to b5 could, under the right circumstances, trap the queen.
Black plays c6, taking the b5-square away from my knight.
Now h4 — this is the moment in every attack where you press the gas pedal down.
Black grabs space of his own with b5.
h5 — when the attack is overwhelming enough you start sacrificing without agonizing over every line.
Black takes, the knight capturing on h5.
Recapturing on h5 with the rook is playable but not most accurate — I think g4 is far more straightforward, keeping our rook for bigger things while trapping the knight.
The knight scurries back to f6.
The queen swings to h6 with check — Black is making it very easy for us.
Black tucks the king to g8.
Now the final, important step: we need to deflect that f6-knight, and the most clinical way is with another knight — the knight to e4.
Black tries the rook to d8, seeking counterplay on the d-file.
My mouse slipped to the queen on f4, but it doesn't change anything — I'm still totally winning.
We take White; Black plays the Alekhine with ...Nf6.
We push e5, kicking the knight.
Black hops the knight to d5.
We build the centre with d4.
Black challenges with d6.
We chase the knight with c4.
Black retreats the knight to b6.
We play f4 — the Four Pawns Attack.
Black takes on e5.
We recapture with the f-pawn.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We develop the bishop to e3.
Black develops the bishop to f5.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black plays ...e6; we develop the knight to f3.
Black develops the bishop to e7.
We develop the bishop to e2.
Black challenges with ...f6; we castle, and Black castles.
We take on f6.
Black recaptures with the bishop.
We bring the queen to d2.
Black plays the bishop to g4.
We centralize the rook to d1.
Black plays the queen to e7.
We jump the knight to e4.
Black takes our knight, capturing on f3.
We recapture with the rook.
Black plays h6.
We double rooks on the f-file.
Black plays the rook to d8.
The knight takes on f6 with check.
Black recaptures with the rook.
We take back on f6.
Black recaptures with the g-pawn.
We lift the rook to f3.
Black plants the knight on e5.
We swing the rook to g3 with check.
Black's king goes to h8.
The bishop grabs on h6.
Black plays the knight to f7.
The bishop checks on g7.
Black's king steps to h7.
We check with the bishop on d3.
Black blocks with f5.
We swing the queen to f4.
Black plays the knight to d6.
The queen crashes in with check on h6.
We have White against the Caro-Kann — the pawn to e4, met by c6.
The pawn to d4, taking the centre.
Black challenges with d5.
The pawn to f3 — the Fantasy Variation, my official recommendation: the most fun line against the Caro by a country mile.
Black takes on e4, giving up the centre.
We recapture on e4. Capturing there only makes sense in the context of one specific follow-up.

Against the pawn to e5 we don't take and don't play d5 — both allow the queen to h4 — instead the knight to f3, sacrificing d4 for quick development. But Black plays the knight to f6, a developing move that isn't the main line and invites e5, like a souped-up Alekhine. The knight to c3 would let Black revert with the pawn to e5, so we go the other way.
The pawn to e5 — if we mishandle this, the knight leaps to g4 threatening a fork on f2 and to win e5 back with interest, so e5 is near-automatic.

Black retreats the knight to d5. We've bitten off a big centre with only pawns, so the pawn to c4 is tempting but risky — pushing more pawns invites overextension. Still, c4 chases the annoying d5-knight, and Black's one central break is the pawn to c5; if we ever meet that with c3, the d5-knight becomes unassailable.
So the pawn to c4 — I flip-flopped, but it works, provided we follow up with accurate development.

Black retreats the knight to b6. The knight to b4 would be no danger — a3 chases it. And the pawn to c5 is simply met by d5, making our centre even more imposing while the c4-pawn stays protected by the bishop. This transposes toward the Four Pawns Alekhine, where you develop the queen's knight first — otherwise the bishop to g4 pins the king's knight.
So the knight to c3 — the most accurate, waiting for Black's bishop before committing the king's knight.
Black develops the bishop to f5 — exactly the cat-and-mouse we wanted, the bishop out first.
Now we can safely play the knight to f3.
Black plays the pawn to e6 — and still not threatening c5, because we always have d5 in response; that's why developing the knight to c3 promptly mattered.

The bishop to e2 — not d3, which would encourage the bishop to g4. Then we castle and bring the other bishop to e3 to solidify. The centre is our main industry; we check for the c5 break every single turn, since we need d5 to answer it — then the queen to d2, a rook to d1, even b3 Alekhine-style to reinforce c4.
Black develops the bishop to e7 — and it really does look like a Four Pawns Alekhine.
We castle — an inferior version of that Alekhine for Black.
Black castles. As White we have everything we could ask for.
We complete development with the bishop to e3 — the bishop to f4 was a viable alternative, but for now we overprotect d4, the linchpin of the whole structure, in Nimzowitsch's sense.

Black plays the pawn to a5, grabbing queenside space — but it loosens the b6-knight, so d5 gains appeal. We avoid a4, which would leave a hole on b4 for Black's knight; if the pawn reaches a3 we just play b3, a move we wanted anyway. So we keep improving flexibly and decide where the queen belongs.

The queen to e1 — heading for g3 and a kingside attack down the semi-open f-file. It allows c5, but Black is so poorly developed that the rook to d1 answers it, and d1 is a better home than the queen there, since the rook x-rays the black queen.
Black plays the knight to a6, rerouting — and we'll make that hard.
The pawn to a3 — no downside, and it locks the knight in place on a6.
Black plays the queen to c7. The c5 break is still serious, but after the rook to d1 we either push d5 or Black trades on d4 into a central massacre.
The rook to d1 — protect the centre before anything else.
Black plays the rook to d8. The c5 break still isn't a threat, because we can meet it with d5.

The queen to g3, completing the maneuver. Why is c5 and d5 bad for Black? The pawn travels to d6, forking the queen and bishop and trapping the e7-bishop. Players under 1800 struggle under strain, and Black is very cramped with a storm brewing on the kingside.

Black plays the rook to d7, preparing to double. Now the d6-square is a major weakness — it'd be a dream to plant a knight there, so we manoeuvre toward it with the knight to g5 or d2. The knight to g5 lets Black trade the important dark-squared bishop, but after the recapture we threaten the bishop to f6 and stop Black doubling.
So the knight to g5 — the more adventurous choice, packing a slightly bigger punch.
Black plays the rook to d8 — a lot of players would reflexively play h6 here. There's a juicy rook sacrifice available, but in time pressure we just complete the maneuver with the knight to e4.
The knight to e4, heading for d6. The knight to d6 looks like it drops a pawn, but at the end of the line the pawn to c5 forks the b6-knight and whatever sits on d6.
So the pawn to c5 first, establishing the stronghold before infiltrating d6 — and Black meets us head-on with the pawn to c5.

The tempting knight to f6 with check fails to the bishop taking f6 and the recapture, winning our queen, with a fork on d4 at the end. So instead the pawn to d5 — the move we've prepared all game. The point: the f5-bishop is loose, so if Black takes on d5, the rook takes f5.
Black plays the bishop takes e4, correctly — and we don't automatically recapture.

The pawn to d6 — a beautiful in-between move, shoving the pawn to fork the minor piece and the queen while the e4-bishop still hangs. It gets very dicey for Black; the bishop takes d6 is the only grandmaster-level try, meeting the recapture with the queen to c6.
Black finds the bishop takes d6. But after the queen to c6 we play the pawn takes e7, and Black can't recapture, because the d8-rook would hang with mate once the queen has left.
We recapture on d6. Black's defence is resilient, but we're winning anyway.
Black plays the rook takes d6 — the losing move.
Just the knight takes e4 — always look for hanging pieces first. The knight to b5 is even stronger, but I want my bishop.
Black plays the knight to c8. The downside is that Black gets three pawns for the piece, so conversion won't be trivial.
Let's play utilitarian — the knight captures on d6, taking the rook, the no-calculation move that ends the game.
Black plays the queen to e7. That knight on a6 was dead the entire game — the c5 break was a dead end with a pawn in the way.
The rook takes f7 — simple. It matters that our d1-rook is protected by the bishop; otherwise Black could take on f7 and then on d1 with check and recapture, winning material.

The modest pawn to e3 is the Colle — a very solid opening, but the reply doesn't change one bit: just play the Queen's Gambit Declined setup no matter how the opponent arranges the pieces. Let their choice be the one that has to adapt.

Notice what jumps out — the opponent hasn't developed a single kingside piece, and the standard punishment for that is to open the centre. It isn't easy here, since the direct breaks are covered, so rather than the slow preparation there's a sharper way to make the key break possible.
That way is to undermine the pawn with a5 — a typical response in countless openings, hitting the base of the queenside advance. Even if it's captured, the freeing break becomes available anyway.
The opponent's move drops the pawn — so capture, but take the hanging rook first, since it's the piece under attack. Resolve the loose material before collecting the winnings.

Facing the bishop, most instincts say you must trade — but there are ways to swap on your own terms or even decline. Keeping the tension with the queen out, ready to trade but demanding the queen reach an active square, is one option; the knight development has the downside of blocking a pawn.

The best move is the central break c5 — it carries two ideas at once. If it's captured we can't recapture immediately, since the bishop x-rays through, but the break's real gift is that it opens a path for another piece to join in.

That other piece is the queen, swinging to a5 to pin the bishop — now capturing on the queenside would lose the queen, so the opponent's retreat is absolutely forced. The break didn't win the pawn; it opened the line that wins the game.

A perfect illustration of not assuming you must trade — the bishop is simply taken, keeping the queens on the board because the enemy king is stuck in the centre and the other bishop can barely develop. Keeping the strongest pieces on multiplies the winning chances.

The king is stranded, so open the centre as fast as possible — the d-file is the avenue of attack, the pathway that leads straight to the king. Identify that main file or diagonal early, because you simply cannot attack without open lines.
When a knight parks itself on a strong central square, the first instinct should be — can it be kicked? Here the pawn push to e5 does exactly that, evicting it before the rook swings in with check.

The best development comes with check — the bishop to f5, hitting the exposed king. It's almost mate, forcing the only defence, and the whole point is that the threats against the king vastly outweigh a hanging bishop of one's own.

Recapture in the centre with the knight, unmasking a devastating discovered check — and if the opponent trades, the bishop finishes it. The material left hanging elsewhere is irrelevant next to a forced mate.

A piece of attacking wisdom — be wary of checks delivered right up against the enemy king. A rook check at close quarters lets the king sidestep and suddenly ties your own knight to the very rook you just planted. The king is a pesky defender, so attacking from a distance is often stronger than crowding your pieces next to it, where they can get loose.
And the clean finish is the queen check on b4, the king driven to the corner, and a rook to the back rank delivers mate — the simplest, most accurate path home.
We take White and face the Sicilian.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We play the bishop to b5 — the Rossolimo.
Black chases with a6.
We take on c6.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn.

Below about 1500 almost nobody plays the open Sicilian. The knight to c3 is the gateway to all the anti-Sicilians — the Closed Sicilian, the Grand Prix with an early f-pawn push, and the bishop-to-b5 lines.

We answer with the knight to c6. The reason is move-order safety: White could still play the king's knight and steer us into a Sicilian we don't play, and this keeps our accelerated-Dragon transposition available.
The bishop to b5, the Rossolimo idea — a Ruy Lopez against the Sicilian, and the recommendation in a lot of anti-Sicilian books.

The book move against the bishop is the knight to d4, mirroring the Trompowsky motif on the other wing. But to dodge theory we play the immediate g6, simply setting up the accelerated-Dragon structure against this slightly different move order.

After g6, White takes on c6. Recapturing with the b-pawn damages the structure visually, but look at the compensation: the bishop pair, the half-open b-file, early access to the d5-break, and solid central control. A fine practical bargain — theory calls White a touch better, but this dodges a mountain of preparation.
d4, c6, e4 — another Caro-Kann.

d5, the pawns trade on d5, and the knight to c3 — an inaccuracy, not huge, but after it White is basically fighting for equality.
