The knight to c3 blocks the c2-pawn, and with a pawn on d4, that pawn in effect becomes isolated, since the knight blocks its only pawn defense. c4 is the Panov Attack, a legitimate line, but the more solid line I recommend to beginners is the bishop to d3 and then c3, to protect the pawn with another pawn.
Then White's knight can develop eventually via d2. The knight to c6.
The knight to f3.
The knight to f6, developing.
The bishop to b5, the bishop to g4 — this is where you should ask questions if you have them.
And the queen to d3 is a good move. Now, if White had played h3, here's an instructive question —
— should we take on f3, or drop the bishop back to h5?
We take Black and face d4, replying with the knight to f6.
White claims space with c4.
We start the fianchetto with g6.
White develops the knight to f3.
We complete the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
White plays the offbeat bishop to f4, delaying the queenside knight.
We castle — the most flexible move, forcing White to commit first.
White develops the knight to c3.
We choose a King's Indian setup with d6 — very effective against the f4-bishop.
White props the bishop with e3.
We play c6 — preparing queenside expansion and grabbing central space, without blocking the b8-knight's usual route to d7.
White develops the bishop to e2.
We play a6, preparing ...b5 — the a6, b5, c6 pawn triangle.
White plays the queen to d2.
We expand with b5, just in time.
White stops ...b4 with a3.
We fianchetto the bishop to b7.
White castles.
We complete development with ...Nbd7, discouraging c5.
White makes a waiting move, h3.
We discharge the tension, taking on c4.
White recaptures with the bishop.
We push c5 — opening the bishop and threatening ...Bxf3 to wreck White's structure.
White closes with d5 — a Benoni structure.
We hit the bishop with ...Nb6, pressuring d5 and forcing it to a poor square.
White retreats the bishop to a2.
We push c4, slicing the bishop from the pawn and vacating c5 as an outpost.
White plays e4.
The Nimzowitsch Sicilian — the knight to f6 on move two. It flies under the radar and looks dubious, but it's a semi-legitimate line worth knowing.
The reason it looks shaky is e5, hitting the knight — but this simply transposes into an improved Alapin, with the extra pawn on c5 working in our favor.
White plays c4, Alapin-style, to kick the knight.
The knight tucks back to c7, ready to reroute through e6 to contest the center — and our pawn on c5 discourages White from playing d4.
We develop the knight to c6, contesting White's centralized knight on d4.
And in my part of town, this is called a free pawn — the knight takes on e5. Unlike the Smith-Morra, both sides have developed evenly, so White has no real compensation for it.
teaches: a free pawn with no Morra-style compensation

notes.explains: g6 does double duty — it defends the knight on e5 and prepares the fianchetto, so even a bishop to f4 with tempo can't stop us.
teaches: ...g6 defends e5 and enables the fianchetto

notes.explains: We fianchetto the bishop to g7.
And complete development with d6 — solid, typical Sicilian play, a healthy pawn up.
We play the Sicilian, c5, on our main repertoire.
White plays c3 — the Alapin.
Here I go for my official recommendation for Black — d5, immediately striking the center.
White captures on d5.
We recapture with a knight to f6 — our opponent wasn't expecting it and pre-moved d4.
We capture on d4 and White recaptures, funneling into an isolated-queen's-pawn structure.
We take on d5 with the knight — and it's not a good version of the IQP for White, because we already have the dream: a blockading knight on d5.
White develops a knight to f3.
We develop a knight to c6. Black isn't much better — after a knight to c3 this often transposes into main-line Caro-Kann theory — but it's a pleasant position with that blockading knight.
White plays a knight to c3. A bishop to g4 would transpose into a Caro line where a queen to b3 liquidates into an equal endgame; e6 keeps more pieces on.
So we play e6, keeping the purity of the IQP and avoiding the drawish bishop-g4 line.
Against a strong opponent we answer the king's-pawn with c5 — the Sicilian, heading for the Accelerated Dragon.
White develops the knight to f3.
The knight to c6.
White strikes with d4 and we take on d4.
White recaptures with the knight, and we fianchetto with the pawn to g6.
White develops the knight to c3.
The bishop to g7, onto the long diagonal.
White plays the bishop to e3, and we develop the knight to f6.
White plays the bishop to e2 — a peaceful line. It's not bad, but it lets Black equalize.
We castle.
White castles. There's a specific reason White usually puts the bishop on c4 in the Accelerated — to stop the freeing break we're about to make.
The pawn to d5! We exploit the drawback of White's setup — and in the Accelerated, if you get a good version of d5 in, you solve all your opening problems.
White captures on d5. Our pieces are active and it's equal — White isn't worse with accuracy, but can drift worse if careless.
The knight recaptures on d5 — well-known theory.
White takes on c6.
We recapture with the b-pawn.

White plays the bishop to d4, and it's equal — so we must manufacture winning chances. One option is the knight takes c3, forcing a pawn recapture that ruins White's queenside, though both structures suffer. A more circumspect idea is the bishop takes d4, the queen recaptures, then the queen to b6, forcing a queen trade on our terms to fix the structure — though that may just draw.
We choose the knight takes c3 — it creates more imbalance and is the simpler move.
White recaptures with the bishop, also wanting to trade bishops.
That's fine — we take, ruining White's pawn structure.
White plays the queen takes d8 — not a good move: it hands us the d-file and plays for a draw.
We recapture on d8, and White recaptures the bishop. He's playing for a draw — now we devise a strategy to play for the win.
The rook to d2 is tempting but not as good as it looks — the bishop to d3 would trap it. Instead the bishop to f5, developing with tempo and hitting c2.
White plays the bishop to f3.

We calculate: the bishop takes c2, and if the bishop takes c6, the rook to c8 skewers the bishop and the pawn. We absolutely take — and a bonus is that White can no longer swing a rook to b1 or to d1, so our bishop is superb.
White plays the rook to e1. Our bishop is so strong we protect it at all costs, unless White chases it away properly.
We play the pawn to e6, defending it — the king to f8 was also fine and it barely matters.
Facing an eighteen-eighty-something. e4, c5 — and another Smith-Morra, just like the last game started; let's hope for a different result.
d4, throwing the pawn into the fray.
Black grabs it, c takes d4.
c3 — the true Smith-Morra, offering a second pawn for a big lead in development.
Black accepts with d takes c3, and we recapture, the knight to c3 — a fully accepted Morra.
Black plays e6. The guideline here is that you generally want the knight to f3 before the bishop to c4 in most of these positions.
So we develop the knight to f3 first, staying as flexible as possible and waiting for Black to commit to a setup before we do.
Black plays a6, heading into a main-line structure.
Now the bishop to c4 — you don't want it drifting to f4 where the e5-break could hit it with tempo. On c4 it's perfectly placed.
Black develops the bishop to e7. Our bishop on c4 is what makes the position tick — it quietly supports the knight that later jumps to d5.
We castle, tucking the king away and finishing development ahead of schedule.
A game of Fischer's — he was ahead of his time, playing openings unpopular in his day and understanding them very well. The pawn to d3, e6, then e4.
d5 — a very familiar King's Indian Attack setup.
The knight to d2.
The knight to f6, and Fischer plays g3 first — the order doesn't really matter.

This has become a reversed Nimzo-Indian, and the pin needs answering. A queen move handles it, but remember the rule — when a lesser piece can do the job, use it rather than the queen. Not every piece needs to be doing heavy work.
To free the other bishop, avoid the fianchetto route — it would allow a capture that ruins the pawn structure in an unpleasant way. The modest pawn to e6 is the sounder path.
The bishop belongs on d6, the more active square — pointing toward the kingside rather than sitting passively.

Now a subtle idea — the knight retreats to d7 to force the strong enemy knight off its central square. It looks like it hangs a pawn, but there's a point: if the pawn is taken, it rips open a file that hands over massive attacking chances.

This beats the routine queen move, where the opponent could cement the knight with a pawn to f4. They play the pawn thrust anyway, but now the knight can simply be taken — and the queen gains access to the very square that thrust just opened up.

Whenever the position transforms substantially, stop and ask the same question — how has it changed? The queen swings to g5 to occupy the newly opened lines. Re-evaluating after every big shift is what keeps you finding the right plan.
The opponent slips — so grab the pawn with check, then survey the whole board before deciding the next capture. Take stock before you strike again.
Capturing in the centre is right because it destroys the opponent's pawn chain — dismantling the structure that was holding everything together.

The winning method is patient improvement — finish development and castle, overprotect the sensitive f7 pawn by swinging the queen back, blunt the long-diagonal bishop with a pawn, and open some air on the kingside with a pawn break. Then, since the opponent has vacated a file, double the rooks on it, centralise the queen, and tuck the king to safety before pushing. Small, purposeful moves, each leaving the position healthier, until the advantage becomes decisive.
We play the Sicilian, c5, our real opening.
White develops a knight to f3 and we play d6, heading toward Najdorf waters.
White plays c3 — the delayed Alapin, a relatively harmless anti-Sicilian, but dangerous against an unprepared opponent, like any anti-Sicilian.
The first step is a knight to f6, of course.
White plays h3. One appeal of this line for beginners: a knight grab on e4 loses to a queen check on a4, forking the knight and king — the most commonly missed opening fork. h3 is a sideline.
The main move here is a knight to c6.

White plays a bishop to d3 — the Copc system, a weird-looking move until you see the follow-up: he wants to drop the bishop back to c2 and control the center with d4. I'll choose a setup that's less theoretical, even if it's slightly worse.
We play g6 — a Dragon setup. I've played this against Magnus in blitz: allow d4, then attack the center from a distance.
White plays a bishop to c2.
We fianchetto with a bishop to g7.
White castles, allowing us to play e5 — another interesting setup. Which setup you choose as Black is largely a matter of taste.
I like e5, clamping d4 — it strongly discourages d4, and if White plays it anyway, a series of trades reopens our g7 bishop to lord over the long diagonal.

White plays a rook to e1. Don't think of the g7 bishop alone — the bishop and the e5 pawn are a unit exerting control over d4, the key square. The d5 hole is real, but White can't easily occupy it, since our knight guards it.
The drawbacks are real, but the benefits outweigh them here, and we have nice central control.
White commits to d4.
We capture on d4 — that's the whole point.
We take twice — with the pawn, not the knight, which is too committal; then we can decide between grabbing on e4 or a neutral move like a rook to e8.
We recapture on d4 with the pawn — the whole zen of the setup was to take this way if he pushed d4.

White recaptures on d4. d6 is a weakness, but we have real strengths: a development lead, White's undeveloped queenside, our monster g7 bishop, and the e4 pawn as a target for our rook — a structure I know well from the Ruy Lopez.

A rook to e8, keeping the tension. To beat a higher-rated player who knows the fundamentals, force them into hard decisions — which often means quiet improving moves that pass the ball back, not forcing the action, especially in time pressure.
White plays a knight to f3 — a bishop to a4 would be a feeble one-move threat. Now d5 is the direct attempt to erase our biggest weakness.
So d5. The complications peak — either the center opens and our superior bishop and White's undeveloped queenside tell, or White pushes on and we've exploited his lack of development.
White captures on d5. Very important not to fall asleep and play a knight capture on d5 — that loses a piece.
First we take on e1 — a rook capture threatens the exchange on e8 with the queen overloaded — then, depending on how White recaptures, we take on d5.
White recaptures with the queen on e1 — the natural choice, keeping the knight developed — again forcing an unpleasant decision.

We recapture on d5 with the knight — a queen recapture walks into a knight to c3 with tempo. Centralizing, we discourage a knight to c3, and the knight has b4 and d3 in its future. Black has a small edge, and open-center positions are hard for anyone.
White plays a bishop to b3 — a good square. We develop our bishop: a bishop to b6 walks into a knight to g5, so a bishop to f5.
A bishop to f5. The queen isn't overloaded — against a bishop to g5 we move the queen to d7, which also lets a rook come to e8.

White plays a knight to a3, working around the obstacles. The only way to develop the bishop with tempo is a bishop to g5, else b2 hangs — so we want to take the sting out of it with a queen to d7, off the bishop's line.
A queen to d7 — the most natural, getting the queen out of the bishop's fire.
White plays a queen to d1, attacking the knight. A bishop capture on d5 would play into our hands — an unassailable queen on d5, and without that bishop White's position comes unstuck.
A knight to b4 protecting the other knight and preparing a knight to d3 — I'd like to keep the queens on to preserve pressure, though the endgame also looks nasty for White.
I think the queen to d1 was a mistake — only a bishop to g5 held the balance.
White's queen drops back to d1 and we plant the knight on b4 — White is stuck, hamstrung by the weak pawn on b2.
White is stuck because of the b2 pawn — nothing moves. He plays a knight to d4, trying to eliminate our g7 bishop, which anchors our whole position.

White sandwiches with a bishop to d3, which actually attacks the knight — the knight is Atlas holding up the world, ripe for an overload, but I don't see one, and a bishop capture on d5 just runs into a queen recapture.
White plays a knight to c2. First question: what's his threat? A bishop capture on d5 is the real problem to defuse.
So a rook to c8, activating our last piece and pressuring the c2 knight — the c-file is where the party is.
White captures on b4.
We recapture on b4 — the knight still protects the bishop, and White still has the problem knight on d4.
White plays a3 — a panicky reaction. There are crazy complications, and I've found an interesting idea.
A bishop capture on d4 — counterintuitive, but I've calculated a winning line.
King's Indian or Nimzo-Indian? The Nimzo flies under the radar and is a superb positional choice.
Let's play positionally — e6, heading for the Nimzo.

One misconception: the Nimzo proper is only the knight to c3 met by the bishop to b4. Against anything else we shift to a Queen's-Indian or Bogo setup. White's e3 is passive but solid — it does box in his own bishop, and the ideal companion here is the Queen's-Indian plan with b6.
teaches: when it is really the Nimzo

notes.explains: Why not check on b4 now? The bishop check is most effective specifically against the knight once it commits to c3; here White just interposes on d2 and we lose the structure-wrecking capture. So b6 instead — d5 transposing into a favourable Queen's Gambit Declined was also fine.
We fianchetto the bishop, and note the lovely control it gives us over the e4-square.

Now d5 to stake out the centre — a chance to explain the pawn as an extension of the bishop. It looks like d5 buries our own bishop, and it does restrict it for the moment. But the aim is control of central squares: if we later plant a piece on e4 and recapture with a pawn, the bishop ends up defending that pawn — and we can always take on c4 to reopen the diagonal. No rush; complete development first.
teaches: the pawn as an extension of the bishop

notes.explains: The bishop belongs on d6 — now both bishops are trained on White's king, so make a mental note to watch for tactics as the game opens.
teaches: point the bishops at the king

notes.explains: We've got very nice central control. White's e4 break isn't a threat — we outnumber it three defenders to two attackers.
The queen's knight goes to d7, never c6 — c6 would block our own c-pawn and hem the bishop in further. And a6 is often useful to take the sting out of a knight jump to b5.

Here's the strategic engine of the position. Rather than the passive a6, we answer the knight-to-b5 threat with c5, turning up the temperature in the centre — and if the knight does jump to b5 we simply tuck the bishop back to b8, keeping it on its beautiful diagonal. Recapture with the pawn to preserve our central integrity, and now a d4 break can open that bishop with devastating effect — this is potential energy, the bishop coiled behind its own pawn. The calculation lesson runs through everything that follows: don't cash in too soon. Grabbing on f3 was more complicated than it looked, so keep every piece maximally active and hunt for a real knockout instead. There's a Greek-gift sacrifice in the air — the bishop crashing on h2, the knight to g4, and a queen infiltration exploiting an undefended f2 — and an all-hands-on-deck effort where even the sleepy knight must join. Control the e2-square so the king can never make its dash to safety, and the net closes with a rook to e2 and mate. The theme is converting potential energy into kinetic: often the simplest continuation is strongest because it keeps all your trumps.
teaches: bring every piece into the attack

notes.explains: The Danish Gambit — d4 and e4, offering pawns to blast the position open for lightning-fast development.

A warning the whole title is built on — never play ...f6 in these open positions. The Damiano refutation runs on it: after ...f6 White has a queen check on h5, and the pawn stuck on e5 gets forked by the queen, hitting king and rook at once — a sacrifice as old as the 17th century.
We offer the second pawn with c3, and Black grabs it.
The bishop swings to c4, raking straight at f7.
And the second Danish bishop lands on b2 — now both bishops cut clear across the board at Black's king, the whole point of the double pawn sacrifice.
Black's bishop check on b4 is the computer's best try, though the theory runs deep and Black must be very accurate to hold — which shouldn't stop you playing the gambit at all.
A ten-minute game, and we're climbing — rated sixteen-seventy-three now. Black plays d6, which could be a Pirc or a Caro depending on what follows.
We grab the full center with d4.
d6 and c6 — this flexible system exists; Black usually follows with the knight to f6 to transpose into some kind of Pirc.
Our strategy is no different from usual — the knight to c3, developing and holding the center.
Black plays g6, and now it's a Pirc with an early c6, a perfectly viable continuation.
How to arrange our pieces? There's no single right answer — the bishop to b3, the bishop to c4 — but I like f4, planning the knight to f3, especially against this early c6.
Black fianchettoes with the bishop to g7, and we bring the knight to f3, supporting the big center.
Black develops the other bishop to g4, pinning our knight on f3 — double-bishop development aiming at our center.
We develop with an eye toward defending d4 and that pinned knight — the bishop to e3.
Black plays the queen to b6, a theoretical thrust hitting b2 and pressuring d4.
The theoretical reply, as far as I remember, is the queen to d2 — now if Black snatches on b2, we're ready to meet it.
Black takes on f3, and we recapture with the g-pawn. Yes, we have doubled pawns, but it's really no big deal — it opens the g-file straight at Black's kingside, which could benefit us.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We castle queenside. Not h4 yet — that's too early, since we don't even know where Black is going to castle.
Black castles kingside, and now we can start thinking about a kingside attack.
h4 is a great move here, but it's not the only way to shatter Black's king position — we can also use the f-pawn and play f5 first, prying it open so h4 lands even harder later.
Black plays the queen to c7.
Now h4, cranking up maximal pressure on the g6-pawn.
Black seeks counterplay with b5.
We push h5, and notice I'm completely ignoring Black's queenside — his attack there simply isn't fast enough.
Black plays b4, poking our knight.
Where should the knight go? It doesn't have many squares, but the knight to e2 is ideal — it's rerouting toward f4.
Black develops the knight to d7. It temporarily blocks in a bishop, but that's only temporary — pieces will reshuffle.
We take, h takes g6, also eyeing the e6-square that gets weak once the f7-pawn is pried away.
Black recaptures on g6, and we take again with the f-pawn.
Black recaptures once more, and the knight completes its journey to f4 — a beautiful, devastating outpost right next to the king.
Black's king crawls to f7 with literally no squares, and our queen is ready to pour into the attack.

A neat move-order trick — sometimes lead with the bishop to e7. It quietly prevents an early pin, and if the opponent develops the knight, the reply keeps you out of the more annoying lines of the opening. Small orderings can dodge a lot of theory.

The cool treatment is a pawn to c6 and then repositioning the bishop from e7 across to d6. It looks like a waste of tempi, but it's the setup strong players favour — offering to trade the dark-squared bishops, which helps the defender, since that bishop is often awkward with no good parking spot.

You might object that no pieces are being developed — how can that be safe? It's all down to the state of the centre. With a solid pawn chain and a closed middle, the opponent can't break with the central push while their own king is stuck there, so you can afford several moves with one piece. Don't be a slave to the rule — judge the position intuitively.

A subtlety in the knight order — develop to d7 before f6, because leading with the other knight would invite a central leap into e5. Deny that outpost first, then bring the second knight out. And if the queen probes the b-pawn, defend with a rook: yes, the rook is tied to defence, but the queen is equally tied to the attack — a happy trade of duties.

Don't rush the central knight jump — but keep the key motif in mind: if it's exchanged, recapture with the pawn to pry open d5 for the other knight. Timing that break is what turns a solid position into an initiative.

Now is the perfect moment for the knight to e4, because after the exchange and pawn recapture the enemy knight can no longer retreat to its home square, and the piece stranded on the rim starts to find itself in real trouble.

There's a choice of approaches, and the positional one is to route a knight to d5 — a semi-outpost in the heart of the board. Resist the central break, which would only open lines for the opponent; keeping the centre closed is where the advantage lives.

What is the centralised knight actually doing? Nothing specific — and that's fine. It occupies a central square, radiates control across the board, prevents the opponent's pawn expansion, and stands ready to spring to f4. Think about what a piece does, but don't box yourself in by demanding a single concrete task.
As the opponent prepares to expand, the near-automatic response is a5, meeting the advance head-on and keeping the queenside from opening on the enemy's terms.

There's a way to prevent the pawn break for good — a pawn to a4, so that any advance is met by a capture that hangs a rook. No rush to play it, though, since the break isn't yet a threat; first swing a rook toward the kingside, and keep the freeze in reserve.

Pushing the enemy knight back takes real care — the immediate pawn thrust would only hand it a counter-outpost. So play the shielding pawn first to shut off that square, then the rook-pawn to chase the knight into the corner, and only then advance the f-pawn to blow the position open. One pawn stops the knight, the other does the pushing.

The traditional plan is to prepare the pawn break with a rook behind it. Toss in the queenside freeze first so the opponent gets no counterplay — there's never a formula for how much a wing pawn is worth, but denying counterchances before attacking is the safe order.

And the break lands at last — after all the patience, the knight that waited so long on its central square becomes the hero of the attack, and the pressure down the newly opened lines is about to make something collapse.
It starts as the Petrov — the knight to f6, the Russian Game, one of the most solid, peaceful openings there is.
In the real Petrov Black recaptures with d6. The Stafford instead comes from a completely different, far trickier idea.
White's c3 is already a mistake — it blocks the knight's own natural c3 square, leaving that knight with no good home.
teaches: c3 robs White’s knight of its square

notes.explains: We just keep developing the knight to f6 — we can't win a pawn yet, everything is defended twice over.
White's f3 is a very common mistake — it props up the pawn but creates lasting weaknesses around his king.
We strike with d5 — the power of the Sicilian, opening the center to exploit exactly those weaknesses.
Keep the tension. Instead of rushing to resolve it, we simply castle and keep developing — the benefit comes later.
teaches: maintain the tension, don’t resolve it

notes.explains: The pawn-winning capture is the knight taking on d4 — not dxe4, which would allow the intermezzo Nxc6 first.
teaches: choose the capture with no zwischenzug

notes.explains: Then dxe4, exposing our attack on d4.
And here's exactly why we play the Accelerated Dragon — the bishop crashes in with the check on d4, winning the pawn cleanly.
We complete development with the bishop to e6 — its only square, since d7 is unavailable.
The Sicilian — c5 and a knight to c6.
Into the Accelerated Dragon fianchetto with g6. The Maroczy Bind is White's c4 setup, named after Géza Maróczy, the Hungarian who first developed it.

c4 — the Maroczy Bind, the biggest reason the Accelerated Dragon isn't more popular at GM level. At lower levels it isn't scary: it demands very positional play, and Black has tricky responses most players under 2200 don't know — miss them and White's center can collapse.
A knight to f6 — tricky.
Our opponent falls into the first trap, capturing on c6.
We recapture with the b-pawn.
White plays the tempting e5 — but remember the resource.
A queen check on a5 — don't forget this trap; it's super important.
We win that central pawn and Black is simply a healthy pawn up.
White plays a bishop to e2; we develop the bishop to g7.
A bishop to g7, and we can castle and advance d5 — the queen can always drop to c7, a Scandinavian-style envelope.
We castle, content to sit on the extra pawn.
White plays a rook to e1.
The easy way to guarantee safety is a queen to c7.
Over a thousand this time — let's go. e4, e5.
d4 — the Danish Gambit. We still haven't managed to get one accepted; nobody seems willing to grab the pawn.
Sure enough, Black declines and develops the knight to c6 instead.
I haven't given you much choice — it's not the knight to f3 here, it's d takes e5, clarifying the center.
Black recaptures, the knight to e5. It looks like we're letting Black plant a knight in the center, but that knight has no stable home — it'll have to move again.
We play an inoffensive developing move, the knight to c3, and see how Black arranges his pieces before we commit to f4.
Black develops the knight to f6.
Now f4 — both knights are stuck in no man's land, so we just push and kick them around.
The e5-knight has to retreat, and it goes back to c6 — the jump to g4 would be a disaster.
e5, and now the f6-knight has only one reasonable square.
It's forced all the way back to g8. We have a big center, a big development lead, and Black's king is slightly loosened.
We finish developing with the knight to f3 — no need for anything crazy.
d6 is exactly what Black should do, challenging our center — and these players are starting to play a bit better.
The bishop to c4 is tempting, but the move is the bishop to b5, pinning the knight.
Black breaks the pin with the bishop to d7.
We don't have to do anything fancy — just castle, and look at that f-file, where the disaster is going to unfold for Black.
Black takes on e5, and we recapture with the f-pawn — no reason to take with the knight and trade off pieces that help Black defend.
Black plays the queen to e7, but he's in huge trouble: the e5-pawn cramps him and the open f-file is disastrous.
The knight leaps to d5, threatening the knight to c7 — a devastating fork of the king and rook.
Black checks with the queen to c5. Players are much better at spotting a tactical pattern than at calculating it deeply.
They get attracted to grabbing the bishop — so we block the check with the bishop to e3, hitting the queen.
He finds the best defense, the knight to d4, trying to unpin himself with tempo.
We take on d7 with the bishop, check.
Black recaptures with the king. There are several options — the queen takes d4, simply up a piece in the endgame.
But there's a subtlety: from f2 the bishop could get hit by the knight to f5, then the bishop to d4 walks into the knight to e3 unpinning with check — you have to see that trap before it bites.

Which system to use against the London depends entirely on what you already play against the two main queenside openings — a Queen's Gambit player answers with the central pawn, a King's Indian or Grünfeld player fianchettoes, a Benoni player strikes with the c-pawn. Reach for the setup you already know, and the least flexible choice is the passive one.

The move that really challenges the London is c5 — it lets the opponent capture, which is ambitious and mainstream, and immediately contests the centre, essentially playing it like a Queen's Gambit a move down. Confrontation, not accommodation.

Keep the tension and develop the knight to c6 — now grabbing the pawn is far less appealing, because a central push with tempo regains it at once. That resource is part of the reason the knight went there.
The queen swings to b6, pressing the pawn and setting up the tension between the queens. This is the move that leads to a structure many opponents in this range struggle to handle.

Should you trade the queens? No — that would let the opponent recapture with a pawn, and the resulting semi-open file matters enormously; you want to be the side controlling it. So instead encourage the trade on your own terms with the pawn to c4.

The typical plan hinges on a detail — the enemy rook in the corner is undefended, so there's a standoff between the rooks. Exploit it to steamroll the queenside with b5, which also supports the advanced c-pawn and threatens to break through, the follow-up knight capture being untouchable because taking it would drop the hanging rook.
We meet the Spanish bishop with the knight to f6 — the Berlin Variation, rock-solid.

Grabbing the free pawn is the theoretical main line, but the ambitious try is the knight to d4 — attacking the bishop and planting a pawn there. A little dubious, but it brings an edge worth experimenting with.
When the trade comes, take the bishop, not the knight — that light-squared bishop is one of White's most important pieces, and recapturing sends his knight to an awkward square.
Don't be tempted by the loose pawn — our own pawn on e5 is hanging and we're undeveloped. Priority one is defending e5 with d6, then developing as fast as possible.
You don't always have to fling the bishops out to g4 and b4 — the bishop to d7, and later to e7, is a perfectly solid, unimposing way to develop.
Deal with the central tension. Not every trade is a winning trade — some are just maintenance: here it's trade a pawn or lose a pawn.
Don't rush c5 — it strips the d6-pawn of its neighbour's protection, leaving it defensible only by a piece. The queen sitting on d4 is annoying but doing little; just keep developing.
The bishop comes to e7 and we castle. This is a kind of chess to learn: unimposing but solid, no weaknesses, the two bishops, and no clear plan for the opponent to break through.
With everything developed, make a maintenance move — bring the idle piece in. The rook to e8 is exactly it.
Now improve the passive bishop onto a more open diagonal, leaning on White's pawn — not threatening to take it yet, simply bettering the piece.
White pushes and we attend to the tension — take the pawn. Whether he heads for an endgame is his call; either way we're fine, with the two bishops.
Here's the lesson: the right move is often the one you least want to play — a trade. Take the queen, and watch what it does — the recapturing rook abandons its defence of the back rank.
Now the knight on e5 is immobilised — moving it hangs a back-rank mate. The bishop to d6, protected by a pawn, piles on it, and here you see the payoff of not having pushed the c-pawn earlier.
A threat needs a purpose beyond the threat itself — if the piece just retreats and nobody has gained, the move accomplished nothing.
Another way to pile on the frozen knight — the knight to g4, while the bishop cuts the defending rook off from the far side.
teaches: stacking pressure on a pinned piece

notes.explains: He finds the one defence, guarding the back rank. But we switch targets: the bishop to c5 skewers the rook against the f2-pawn — and he can't recapture, because that knight is still frozen.
Exploiting the pinned knight again, the bishop takes on f2 with check and simply wins the pawn — and don't overpress hunting for more when there's nothing more there.
Drop the bishop back to safety and look for a fresh attack — with every piece trained on his king, he's not safe even with the queens off.
His blunder relinquishes a key square, and the knight jumps in with check, forking his pieces.
Winning the rook, and the rook swings back for a clean back-rank checkmate.
White pushes e5, and we settle into a favorable French-type structure.
The key move order — the bishop to f5 FIRST, outside the pawn chain, and only THEN e6. Play e6 first and it simply transposes into an ordinary French.
teaches: develop the bishop before locking it with ...e6

notes.explains: We develop the knight to c6, in no hurry to play e6.
White pins with the bishop to b5, eyeing the doubling of our c-pawns.
The elegant answer is the queen to b6 — it prepares to recapture on c6 with a piece, keeping our pawn structure intact.
teaches: Qb6 to recapture with a piece

notes.explains: So we recapture with the queen, structure preserved and everything groovy.
And now e6, completing the French-style setup.
The knight-development puzzle has a nice solution — the knight to h6 and the bishop to e7, rather than a fianchetto that would only bite on granite against e5.
The Gurgenidze-style h5 — it grabs space, prepares the knight to h6, and takes away White's g4 break.
So the knight comes to h6.
Then the reshuffle — the bishop to g6 and the knight into f5, a monster square. If White tries g4, we just open the h-file at his exposed king.
White's knight to d2 is a blunder — we gladly snap off the loose central pawn, the bishop landing on d3.
Black answers the king's-pawn with the pawn to c6 — the Caro-Kann.
We grab the centre with the pawn to d4.

Black contests it with d5, attacking our e4-pawn — so we must deal with that. Options include the knight to c3, the pawn to e5 for the Advance, capturing on d5, or the line that flies under the radar.
The pawn to f3 — the Fantasy Variation. It defends the e4-pawn and preserves our big pawn centre.
Black captures on e4 — not a mistake, but it has to be followed up correctly.
We recapture on e4 — a pawn trade leaving us two pawns in the centre.

Black follows up correctly with the pawn to e5. It looks like we can just take, but never forget development in the opening: after taking on e5, the queen to h4 is a fork — check on the king while hitting the e4-pawn at the same time.
So we prevent the queen coming to h4 not by pushing a pawn but by developing — the knight to f3.
Black develops the bishop to g4. Taking on e5 is still bad — not for a check, but because it allows a queen trade that drags our king into the centre.
The bishop to c4 — the most active square, aiming straight at f7, the weakest square on the board.
Black plays the knight to d7. A very sharp opening — we have sacrifices ready on f7.
We castle, continuing development. Notice both the c4-bishop and the f1-rook aim at f7 — only our own knight is in the way, and it's easy to move, after which f7 comes under heavy fire.
Black plays the bishop to d6 — a mistake, because it fails to defend f7, which is guarded only by the king, and the king is a poor defender.

The bishop takes f7 with check — a sacrifice, giving a bishop for a pawn to crack open the king. If the king recaptures, moving the knight is a discovered check that wins the bishop back; the best try is the king to e7, though Black is still losing.

Black plays the king to f8 — the umbrella method, hiding behind our bishop. We can't win with a discovered check yet, so we step back and retreat the bishop — but with a distracting move that forces a reaction.
The bishop to e6 — sacrificing again: if Black takes it, his king lands directly in the rook's line of fire. He can defend by capturing the knight, but he's still in big trouble.
Black plays the knight to f6, covering the rook — but forgetting the g4-bishop.
We take on g4, winning a piece — and if Black recaptures, he exposes himself to a discovered check again.
Black recaptures with the knight on g4. Now notice the king and queen sit a knight's move apart — so picture a knight landing on the square that forks them and wins the queen.
The knight to g5 with check — the fast route to that fork. If the king moves, it loses the knight and mate follows.
Black covers the check with the knight to f6.
The knight to e6 with check — the fork, winning the queen, and the game is basically over.
Black plays the king to e7. Losing the queen for nothing ends the game.
We take the queen, and after the recapture we're up a full queen for a piece. Now just complete development — but first make sure the d4-pawn is well protected.
The pawn to c3, supporting d4 with a pawn chain to keep the centre intact.
Black contests the file with the rook. Our centre is safe — now we complete development, since the bishop and knight are still on their home squares.
The bishop to g5 — developing with a pin on the f6-knight. A pin means the knight can't move without exposing its king. Next we'll develop the knight to d2 and maybe c4.

Black plays the pawn to h6. When you're up material, a good rule is to trade pieces — like taking a deal to remove ten players from each side when the opponent is already a man down: one against zero is easy.
So we trade the bishop for the knight, following the trade-when-ahead principle.
Black recaptures with the knight on f6.
The knight to d2 — developing the last piece and protecting the pawn so his knight can't take it.
Black plays the pawn to g5 — which doesn't do much, but it creates a weak square: one that can no longer be defended by pawns. The f5-square is now weak.
The rook to f5 — occupying that outpost, a piece planted on a weak square, and attacking the e5-pawn to bait a capture on d4.
We take White and face the Sicilian.
We play the Bishop's Opening against the Sicilian — the bishop to c4.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We develop the knight to f3.

We play a3.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We play d3.
Black strikes with d5.
We take on d5; Black recaptures with the e-pawn.
We pin with the bishop to b5.
Black checks with ...Qa5.
We block with the knight to c3.
Black pushes d4, hitting the knight.
We take on c6 with check.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn.
We play b4, hitting the queen.
Black takes on b4.
We jump the knight to e4.
Black grabs on e4 with the knight.
We recapture with the pawn.
Black takes on a3 with check.
We block with the queen to d2.
Black pins with ...Bb4.
We grab on a3 with the rook.
Black takes our queen, capturing on d2 with check.
We recapture with the knight.
Black plays the queen to c5.
We castle; Black grabs on c2 with the queen.
We reroute the knight to f3.
Black plays c5.
We develop the bishop to f4.
Black castles.
We play the rook to e1.
Black develops the bishop to b7.
We plant the knight on e5.
Black plays the rook to e8.
We lift the rook to g3.
Black snatches on e4.
We play h3.
Black retreats the bishop to g6.
We swing the rook to c1.
Black takes our rook, capturing on c1 with check.
We recapture with the bishop; Black takes our knight on e5 with the rook.
We play the bishop to f4.
Black checks with the rook on e1.
We tuck the king to h2.
Black pushes the passed d-pawn.
We interpose the rook on e3.
Black takes our rook on e3.
We recapture with the bishop; Black pushes the passed c-pawn.
We step the king to g1.
Black pushes c3; we walk the king to f1; Black rolls the pawn to d2.
Our king comes to e2; Black plays the rook to d8.
Our king steps to d1; Black's pawn crashes to c2 with check.
Another game — a ten-plus-five. I want to keep hammering a narrow set of key concepts rather than sprawling across openings; the focus here isn't really theory. e4, c5.
c3 — the Alapin, preparing to build a big center with d4.
d5 is correct and in fact main-line theory.
We capture, e takes d5.
Black recaptures with the queen on d5, pulled out early — but here it's fine.
d4, challenging the center. And Black doesn't need to rush the queen away, because it's well placed for the moment.
Black takes, c takes d4.

We recapture and Black develops the knight to c6. A word of warning: people have a tendency to release the tension — if there's a trade available, they grab it — but sometimes you should resist clarifying the position.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black pins with the bishop to g4.
Here's the trick: the bishop to e2. You might think Black can just win the d4-pawn — but that's not the whole story, because the queen becomes a loosely-defended piece and White gets tactics.
Black plays e6, shoring up.
Now we reap the reward and develop the knight to c3, hitting the queen with tempo.
Black tries the bishop to b4 — it may look fancy, but it's not that good. What should White do to break the pin?
We castle — the passive bishop to d2 is unnecessary; castling is the move.
Now we can develop the light-squared bishop toward a3, and if Black doesn't castle in time, that king in the center will have a very bad time. Black plays the queen to d7.
d5, a thematic pawn thrust I played almost without calculating, dislodging the knight on c6.
Black takes on c3.
Resist the automatic recapture — consider the options. d5 takes c6, and now Black loses either his queen or his bishop.
Black trades queens on d1 and we recapture with the rook — and now two of Black's pieces are hanging at once.
Black retreats the bishop to a5, but he simply doesn't have the firepower to contain our passed pawn on the queenside.
The pawn storms forward, c takes b7, one step from queening.
Black throws the rook to b8 to blockade the pawn.
One key mistake people make is taking their foot off the gas — instead let's defend the pawn with tempo, the bishop to a6.
Black takes on f3 and we recapture with the g-pawn, and Black develops the knight to f6.
The bishop to f4 — this just wins on the spot, hitting the blockading rook.
Black plays the knight to d7 — he has to move the rook, and then we promote the pawn.
Taking on b8 with the bishop is good, no doubt — let's not overthink it, keep it simple.
Black recaptures with the knight on b8.
The rook to c1 — could you propose an alternative? This is a clear second-nature move, aiming the rook at c8.
Black shuffles the king to e7.
We plant the rook on c8, and it's goodbye — no matter what Black does.
Black tries the rook to e8, staying on the back rank.
Now something cool: the bishop to b5, continuing to harass his rook.
Black slides the rook to f8.
The rook to d7, a beautiful check.
We force the knight to take, and after we recapture the red carpet is unrolled — the pawn is about to promote.
The modest pawn to e3 braces the centre — and crucially, don't capture on c5. Holding the tension is part of the Jobava's venom.

And the trap springs — a knight to b5, with the threat of a fork on c7 that has no good answer short of an awkward king move. This is exactly why the Jobava is so appealing: strong players walk right into it.

When the opponent counterattacks the knight, don't overthink it — the simplest path is to note that the d-pawn is weak and just retreat the knight to c3, hitting the enemy knight. If it moves, the pawn falls, and the opponent is left two pawns down.

After the queens come off, don't rush — develop with tempo. Castling long with check is the classic device, gaining a free move while the king tucks away and leaving a full, healthy extra pawn for the endgame.
Choose the recapture that doesn't help the opponent — taking toward the centre would only assist their development. Never do your opponent's work for them; keep their pieces cramped.
The Modern — Black fianchettoes the bishop at once, often transposing into a Pirc.
He plays the Gurgenidze system, a cross between the Caro-Kann and the Modern, preparing to strike with d5.
There are many ways to meet it, but an underestimated one is to develop the bishop to c4 immediately — the point is to take d5 away from him.
And here's the common mistake: he props up d5 with e6, not noticing the very subtle reply that cements the weakness he's just created.
That reply is e5 — a move that permanently cements the dark-square weaknesses, straight out of a famous game that shaped how I see these positions.
He's forced to push d5, and we snap it off en passant.
Look at the wreckage: his bishop is passive, he's saddled with a weakness on d6, and he's dragged the queen out early instead of developing — a badly cramped position that's hard to untangle.
By jumping the knight to d5 he surrenders control of a gorgeous central square — so we slam our own knight into e4, eyeing the d6-hole.
We could play the modest c3, but let's be ambitious with the bishop to g5, trying to induce f6 — a horribly weakening move.
He pins himself. His position is desperately passive, so we lay it on by centralising the knight on e5 — look at the disparity in piece activity.
Keep a running wish list, updated every move — the ideas you'd love to play if only they were possible. Here, after a rook-pawn nudge, the queen swings to f3 and his knight is simply lost.
Black plays d6 — a delayed Philidor. It transposes into Philidor waters, where d4 is the natural break.
After the exchanges our queen recaptures on d4, and Black's setup is already passive — White is comfortably better.
Black offers the queen trade with the queen to f6.
We decline it and find the RIGHT square — the queen to e3. It looks awkward, but from there it oversees everything, and the plan is to castle long quickly and punish Black's undeveloped pieces.
teaches: decline the trade to a purposeful square

notes.explains: Temporary versus permanent: we castle queenside fast. The awkward bishop is a temporary problem that resolves itself — getting the king safe and the rooks working is what matters.
teaches: distinguish temporary problems from permanent ones

notes.explains: Black plays b6, completely unconcerned.
We pounce on that weakness with the bishop to a6, aiming to follow with Bb7 and win the pawn.
Then a spicy idea — the bishop to b5, preparing to plant the knight on d5.
The knight to d5 works because the c-pawn is pinned by the bishop on b7 — sounds strange, but it's pinned, so the jump is fully sound.
The queen is forced back to d8.
And now e5, the classic method of tearing the center apart — with Black utterly undeveloped, it's overwhelming.
teaches: e5 to blow open the center

notes.explains: The queen crashes in on e5 with check, and the game is over.
We get White again against a strong opponent, and another Sicilian — c5.
We play the Alapin, c3.
Black challenges with d5.
We capture on d5.

Black plays a knight to f6 — the line I recommend for Black, actually. The point is to recapture with the knight; and c4 is no solution, because Black answers e6, and after the trade gets a monopoly over the central squares and full compensation for the pawn.
So we start with a bishop check on b5 — a natural move that poses real problems and tests our opponent.
Black plays a knight to d7 — the correct reply.

We strike with d4. If a knight capture on d5, we take on c5 with a discovered attack, since the pawn can't be recaptured — the knight is pinned. If Black captures on d4, we recapture with the queen, shielded by the d5 pawn like an umbrella, and unless Black is precise he ends up a pawn down for nothing.

Black plays a6. A bishop to a4 would be too stubborn, enabling b5 and gifting Black the fianchetto square — the point is to use the pawn as a bargaining chip for a development lead, not to cling to it.
So we drop the bishop back to e2 — not d3, which would sever the queen's contact with the d5 pawn. It's the same idea as the Portuguese Scandinavian: check on b5, then retreat all the way to e2.
The game opens with e4, and the plan is to bring the knight to f3, developing naturally toward the center.
The tension builds — but White is already up a whole queen from an early blunder, so the heavy lifting is done. From here it's just about clean conversion.
White castles. With an extra queen in the bank, the recipe is simple: occupy the center, keep developing, stop any threats, and nothing bad can happen.
Black lifts the rook to g8. The thing to watch when you're this far ahead is not overpressing and handing back material.
White develops the bishop to f4, eyeing the dark squares.
Black plays g5, forking the bishop and the knight — but it's fine, you only give back one piece, no need to panic; White is still up a queen for a piece.
If you're moving the bishop anyway, trade as much as you can while ahead — the bishop to e3.
Black grabs the knight, g takes h4, but White remains up a queen for that piece — plenty to win with.
White trades bishops on c5 and Black recaptures with the pawn — the key word being that White should win this.
The knight jumps to b5, hitting the c7-pawn.
A good move, forcing the king to d8 to defend c7. Now it's time to put that extra queen to work.
The queen comes to d2 eyeing c7, Black lifts the rook to g6, and the queen swings to f4 — setting up a fork.
Black plays e5 to defend c7, which he can't afford to lose to the queen — but it steers White straight toward other loose material.
There's a free pawn to be had right now — the queen takes on h4.
Black plays a6. At a stronger level, simply hoovering up free material like this is exactly how you win — the little pawns matter now in a way they didn't before.
The knight retreats to c3.
Black plays the knight to d4, creating a threat — your job is to spot it: from d4 the knight eyes an unpleasant check on f3.
So White tucks the king to h1, sidestepping the f3 check idea entirely.
Black plays c6.
There's a hanging pawn to collect — the bishop grabs it, taking on f7.
Black plays the king to e7, completely lost — the pieces are falling one after another.
The bishop takes the rook, capturing on g6 — another piece in the bag.
Black recaptures, h takes g6.
Now revisit opening the position — with all these extra pieces, you need open files to exploit them, so White plays f4.
Black takes, e takes f4.
e5 — find the crushing moves. These weaknesses are temporary, so exploit them efficiently and go after the knight.
Black defends with the bishop to e6, but White is winning the knight; the rest is easy mopping up.
The queen takes the knight with check, capturing on f6 — a free check that grabs a piece.
Black steps the king to d7.
The queen to g7 with check, and from there White can rake in the g6- and f4-pawns.
Black flees with the king to c8 as his position crumbles.
The queen to f8 with check — and now the rook falls, because Black can't protect it.
Black tries the king to c7, but the rook is lost next move — a clean tactical progression to finish.
The pawn to d6 is the Deferred Steinitz, quietly creating a threat to snap off the central pawn. There are several ways to respond, and the choice reveals how you like to handle a passive opponent.

The way to punish passive play is to strike immediately in the centre and open the position — and in the Ruy Lopez that means the central break to d4, recapturing with the knight. Meet quiet development with a jolt in the middle.

A moment where players often go wrong — there's no need to grab the knight on c6 straight away. Just keep developing, bringing the knight out; and if the opponent trades in the centre, recapture and swing the queen to a fine central post. Patience over a premature exchange.

When the moment comes to take, the choice of recapture is a trap for the unwary — standard principle says preserve the bishop in an open position, yet taking with the knight is actually worse, because the opponent recaptures with tempo and forces the bishop to move. The general rule bows to the concrete point.

Look hard at the surviving knight — it has real prospects, eyeing a leap to f5, so prepare that jump without fear of moving the queen. And there's more: with the queen x-raying and the knight pressing a loose enemy pawn, a central push wrecks the opponent's structure, leaving isolated, weak pawns everywhere. Don't trade queens — keep the queen active, pressing the backward pawn, and steer toward an endgame where the guiding question is who owns the passed pawns. Making a passer of your own, and denying the opponent one, is the compass for the whole ending.
The pawn to e4, e6 — the French.
d4 — let's play the main line.
We've been playing e5 exclusively; I want to vary it up a little.
Let me introduce the Tarrasch — the knight to d2, what I actually play myself.
The knight to f6. The point of the knight on d2 instead of c3 — which should jump out if you've never played this — is that you block in your own bishop —
— why? Because you can meet c5 with c3 and keep your centre intact. e5.
The knight to d7.
The bishop to d3.
c5, and we meet it with c3, keeping our centre intact. In a way you get the best of all worlds: you develop your pieces and keep the centre —
— with the other knight responsible for defending d4. The knight to c6. For many decades the knight to e2 was considered automatic here —
— and the knight to f3, which looks more natural, was thought inferior; yet we're going to play it. That changed about 25 years ago —

— when computers came and people figured out that the knight to f3 is perhaps more testing than the knight to e2. The queen to b6 is the classical old line — the reason old-timers thought the knight to f3 was bad.

The old worry: you have a hard time defending d4. But computers asked an interesting question — what if you don't defend d4 at all, simply sacrifice the pawn, and in return get a lead in development —
— more space —
— we recapture on d4 —
— and a clamp on the centre with the pawn on e5. Black goes for the line and takes on d4.
We take on d4.
The queen takes d4. Now, without our next move, White's entire position would collapse — the bishop is hanging and the pawn is hanging —
— so we play the knight to f3.

The knight to f3 forces the queen back, and the main move here is the queen to b6. This isn't the only French line where you give up the d-pawn — the Milner-Barry is another — but you must follow up very accurately or Black consolidates and we get nothing. White's best is the queen to a4, stopping the knight from coming to c5 and preparing to swing to g4. So the queen to g4, attacking g7 — Black can't castle, since that runs into the bishop to h6 winning the exchange, and if g6, we put the bishop on h6 anyway, with serious control of the dark squares. The bishop to f8 is a serious concession. Nothing happens fast here; White mounts a slow campaign, massaging the weak dark squares, getting the rooks in, a rook to e1 to overprotect e5. Moving the bishop back to e3 would be a tempo move, but I like the queen to f4 — b2 is hanging, but we're happy to sacrifice it; in these lines you must be ready to give up two or even three pawns to keep control, and the knight to g5, hitting f7, is a real threat. We keep the tension to get the queen to h6 and prevent castling. The queen to d8. Now a perfect chance to bring pieces in — the rook to c1 stops the knight to c5, confining it to d7, and controls the only open file; if the queen to e7, we infiltrate to c7. A cool idea against an opponent with all his pawns on one color: chip at the pawn shell with h4 and h5, since g6 is our primary target — if we play h5 and Black ignores it, we take on g6 with devastating effect. The knight to c5 — now tactics: calculate the h-pawn takes g6; if the bishop is taken, we have the pawn to g7 and then the queen to h7, forking the knight and rook, re-establishing material at worst. The queen to a3 heads into d6, the mouth of madness, and the queen to e7 is an elementary blunder — the rook to c7 wins the queen, with mate to follow. A nice technical game showing the power of this line; don't get tunnel vision on checkmate — you can use the king's weakness to win material — though here the rook takes c8 and the queen to d6 with check is mate in three.

The queen-to-b3 versus queen-to-b6 standoff is standard — it mostly turns up in d4-based openings, so in the London system you get it very often. For instance, one of the main lines of the London runs the bishop to f4,
the knight to f6, e3, and then e6 — this can happen through
the knight to f6 and e3,
and e6,
various move orders, but the bottom line is c5, c3, the knight to c6, the knight to d2 — so here,
c5, staking out the centre,
c3 and the knight to c6,
the knight to d2. For example, the queen to b6 is a very standard
way to play, and White responds often with the queen to b3, and
you get this exact standoff, where Black doesn't want to be the one to
take on b3. The a-pawn recaptures. And as you can confirm with
A Sicilian, and we go for the Open with the knight to f3 and d4.
He's already erred — d6 here is not how you play the Sicilian; you're meant to capture on d4 first.
Why is d6 a mistake? It lets us expand in the centre with d5 and kick the knight, and now it has nowhere good to go — a retreat to e5 wrecks his structure this early.

After the trades a lot of players reach for the knight to c3, but that's a positional error once the position transforms like this. Develop with purpose: his pawn on e5 is weak, so the question is how to bring a piece to bear on it.
Don't play c4 yet — reserve that square for the knight. The knight belongs on c4, not f3, where a bishop pin would annoy us.
teaches: reserve the square for the knight

notes.explains: This is what purposeful development means — at this level you can't just put pieces on the same squares every game; you reinforce the plan of landing the knight on its best square.
teaches: develop to a plan, not by rote

notes.explains: So we prop the pawn up with c4 — which does mean the knight now has to go to f3 instead; our development has to react dynamically to what the position needs.
He castles and we can grab the weak pawn — though personally I'd have castled first, for reasons I'll explain after the game.
Rather than trade, drop the knight back. Beyond the extra pawn we have a space advantage, and with more space you want to keep pieces on — no reason to ease his defence with a trade.
teaches: keep pieces on when you have space

notes.explains: That knight on f3 is excellent — it pressures the e5-pawn and ties his knight to its defence, which in turn keeps his bishop bottled up.
Many plans exist; one is a queenside expansion. But first, h3 — prophylaxis before anything else, taking a bishop-to-g4 pin off the table.
To prepare the b4 push we play a3 first — at this level the plans we run are no longer one-move plans; they take two or three moves, and that's fine.

His queen crashes in to complete the bishop sacrifice. Why not be scared? Because it's actually harmless — but to refute it cleanly we make an escape route for the king and note he has no threat beyond a check on g4.
The rook to e1 does two jobs: it opens a path for the king toward the centre — safer here since the centre is closed — and it prepares to reroute the bishop to g2.

The knight jump looks like it prepares mate, and that's what frightens people — but the knight on f3 already guards h2, so there's no mate. At this level the margins are narrow; don't fear phantom threats.

To swing the rook to h3 we must move the knight — most players won't, fearing the check on h2. But that's exactly why the rook went to e1 earlier: it takes the sting out of that check, so we just slide the king.
The rook lands on h3 and his position begins to collapse — the queen is chased off, and once it moves the h-pawn falls, opening our own file for the attack.
Now his position is weak enough that we open the board — taking on f5 lets our pieces stream in toward a decisive attack.
White plays the Bowdler Attack — the bishop to c4. It's remarkably common below 1600, but genuinely not a good move against the Sicilian.
The first step is e6 — it blunts the bishop, leaving it biting on granite, and prepares the freeing d5 break.
And remember, the knight to f6 is perfectly safe here — no need to fear e5, which we'd meet with d5 or a knight jump to g4 hitting the pawn.
White plays the quiet d3.
And we reap the reward of not committing d6 early — d5 in one fell swoop, grabbing the center and solving all our opening problems at once.
teaches: ...d5 in one move solves the opening

notes.explains: White pins with the bishop to b5. We have a pleasant choice — force a slightly better endgame with dxe4, or simply keep developing.
We choose the fun game — the bishop to e7. No need to force the trade with a6; White may well capture on c6 anyway.
White pounces with the knight to e5, but it's not scary — there's no real horsepower behind the attack.

We defend the knight the strategic way — the queen to c7, not the bishop to d7 which would surrender the bishop pair; and if a bishop comes to f4, we unpin by shifting our bishop to d6. One habit to keep with a hanging queen: before moving it, look for an intermezzo like dxe4, and always check the opponent can't reply with a queen-check desperado.
teaches: look for the intermezzo before moving a hanging queen

notes.explains: Finally we get White — and we're going to play the mainline, d4 and c4, grabbing the big classical center.
Black strikes with c5 — he's steering into the Benoni.
d5, clamping down and gaining space in the center.
Black plays d6 immediately, which is a bit inaccurate — a little passive; not terrible, but passive.
How should White expand? The typical Benoni move, of course, is e4, building the full pawn center — and comparing move orders is exactly what reveals why d6 was slightly off.
Comparison often yields wisdom about a position you'd otherwise miss. Black develops the bishop to e7.
The bishop to d3 is the right square, anticipating that Black will probably capture on d5 — and even if he doesn't, it's well placed there.
Black plays the knight to d7. There's no need for us to take on c5 — that trade doesn't especially help White.
You could play f4 immediately to grab a pawn, but I don't like that — playing positionally, we simply develop the knight to f3.
Black is cramped, and we're going to squeeze the life out of him. He tries the knight to g4.
No need to go out of our way to stop it — we just castle, because if you calculate a bit further you'll see it resolves in our favor.
Black plays the knight to e5. There's a misconception about pieces in the center — you can't assume a central piece is automatically strong.
The real question is how easily you can chase it, and we'll be able to hit it with f4 — so we take, the knight capturing on e5.
Black recaptures on e5. That knight is good for a couple of moves, but then f4 comes.
Be careful not to automatically drop the bishop to c2 — that would blunder the pawn. The bishop to e2 is precise, and then we hit with a nice f4 with tempo.
Black plays the bishop to f6.
I don't see a reason not to play f4 — let's go.
The pawn to e4, c5 — a Sicilian.
c3 — once again we go for the Alapin.
d5 — one of the two main lines.
We take on d5.
d4. Now Black generally plays the knight to f6 or the knight to c6, the two main moves.
The knight to c6. As often in the Alapin, there's tension between the c5 and c3 pawns, and it's usually not a good idea for Black to take on d4 prematurely —

— because it opens the c3-square for White's knight. The knight to c6, the knight to f3 — there's the bishop to g4, the knight to f6, e6; many possible moves, but under 2000 a lot of people don't know the theory, and the queen on d5 is both a strength and a weakness — controlling a lot of squares, but incredibly vulnerable if we can get a bishop to c4.

The bishop to g4. A couple of moves here: the bishop to b2 is what most people think of, but there's a more dangerous move if Black doesn't know the theory — it kills two birds, guarding against the bishop takes f3, which would ruin our structure —

— the knight to d2, the same idea as the knight to a3 but reinforcing the knight on f3. Now we've lost the queen's connection to the d4-pawn — can't Black just take on d4 and win a pawn? He can, but that's exactly why we play the knight to d2: we sacrifice the pawn for very rapid development. After the pawn takes d4, the idea isn't just to recapture — against almost all of Black's moves except the bishop takes f3, it's the bishop to c4, developing with tempo, and then the queen to b3, since b7 and f7 are vulnerable. Yes, it blocks the bishop, a drawback, but we prioritize developing our other pieces.
The knight to f6 — that doesn't fundamentally change what we want to do.
So the bishop to c4, following our plan, hitting the queen.

The bishop takes f3, as I expected, and now a very interesting decision. The queen takes f3 allows a queen trade, which neutralizes our initiative, so I'd consider the pawn recapture on f3 — risky, but later the queen to b3 hits both pawns — or a third move, the queen to b3, ignoring the bishop entirely; the key is that Black's queen can't escape with check, since a4 is controlled by the knight, b5 by the pawn, and e6 by the bishop. After the queen moves, we take on f7 with check or take the bishop on f3, recapturing with the knight, preserving the queens with a tremendous initiative, since his king is nowhere near castling. The knight to a5 is the only move to stay in the game — we give a check, the queen to b5 rather than a4, since the queen to a4 leaves our queen undefended after the queen to d7, whereas after the queen to b5 with the queen covering, we take on f3 and stay a little better. But he plays the unexpected queen to c6, a mistake, because now the bishop to b5 is a far more serious threat, so we play the queen takes a5 — checking first that there are no e-file checks leading to mate, and there aren't — taking the knight with the threat of the bishop to b5. He plays b6, and the important follow-up is the queen to a6, preserving the bishop-to-b5 threat. Panic creeps in at this level when players see their queen threatened, so they stop resisting. The simplest win: our queen is defended by the bishop, so we just take Black's bishop on f3, emerging up a piece — game over in twelve moves. Then the bishop to b5 with check keeps the king in the centre, and even in the endgame the knight to e5 or g5 hits f7.
This is Owen's Defence — and whatever system you choose, the one constant is that the central pawn must be defended. The simplest way is the knight to c3, doing exactly that while developing.

The subtle choice is to develop the knight to e2 rather than its natural square, in order to connect the knights — so that if one is traded for the other, the pawn structure stays intact. The real concern isn't the trade; it's the central pawn turning into a weakness.
A rook-pawn to a3 forces the opponent to capture, handing over the bishop pair — and two bishops are an asset well worth the little tempo. Put the question and collect the pieces.

Once the opponent castles, don't reflexively lunge the bishop, which would allow a knight to interpose and shove it back. Instead swing the queen to g4 — anticipating a kingside attack, that probing move is remarkably hard to meet. Then apply whole-board awareness: after forcing the enemy queen back, notice a pawn on the far wing left undefended, and pile onto it with a knight that can't be chased off — a classic idea in cramped positions where the defender simply can't marshal a defence in time. A pawn up, take the foot off the gas and make general improving moves — a rook to the open file, preparing a lift, and chasing the intruding knight with a pawn. And keep looking for checks and for the drawback of every enemy pawn push, since advancing a pawn weakens a diagonal a bishop check can exploit. The one caution learned the hard way: don't get so intoxicated by combinations that you start playing unobjectively — the cleanest mate is often the quiet rook infiltration, not the flashiest try.
We set up a King's Indian.
The whole point of the King's Indian is to prepare the e5 break; one way to support it is routing the knight to d7.
And here's the typical King's Indian tactic — we play e5. He can't safely grab the pawn, as the post-game will show.
teaches: the e5 break is tactically sound

notes.explains: Because his king is stuck in the middle, opening lines lets us exploit it.
Now the concrete point: his e4-pawn is pinned, so it can't move — which sets up a way to win it.
teaches: a pinned pawn is a target

notes.explains: The move is d5 — and if he castles here, he simply gets forked.
teaches: d5 to win the pinned pawn

notes.explains: He pushes to e5, a good practical try, but the pawn is now very weak — so how do we round it up?

We reposition the knight to go after it. Important distinction: the knight isn't moving because it's attacked, it's moving to win the pawn. He'll get to castle, but he's down a crucial central pawn and our bishop will be a monster.
teaches: move with a purpose, not in reaction

notes.explains: Don't give away the King's-Indian fianchetto bishop lightly — it guards the holes you created with g6, so you'd only part with it for a lot of material. And note the capture on f3 doesn't win a piece, because the recapturing knight defends the bishop.
So we play c5 to chase the bishop onto a square where our own bishop can take it — his best is to give up a bishop himself, leaving our fianchettoed bishop uncontested, exactly what we want.
His bishop comes off and ours is now uncontested and dominant on the long diagonal — up a pawn with a great position out of the opening.
Take the other bishop too, so we have the two bishops against two knights on an open board — an ideal imbalance.
Most would swing the bishop to g4 for a pin, but f5 is far better — instead of a vague pin, the bishop does something specific: it hits a weak pawn that his passive position can barely defend.
Up two pawns, run the winning checklist. First item: can we make a passed pawn? Being up pawns, we should be able to — and bishops are far better than knights at escorting passers.
We already have a passer on the d-file, but the c-file one is better — because our bishops control exactly the squares c3 and c2 that the pawn needs, rolling out the red carpet in front of it.
teaches: create the passer your pieces support

notes.explains: The pawn advances with tempo, and then the bishop controls the promotion square while the pawn queens — knights are hopeless at stopping passers.
An immediate push would let him give up a rook for the pawn to drag things out. Instead the patient rook to c8 brings the last piece in — we're not settling for an exchange, we want the whole queen.
Now a tactical shot — the pawn to c2, which looks like a blunder but isn't; there's a tactic behind allowing the capture.
Black meets the king-pawn with c5 — the Sicilian, the great fighting reply when Black wants an unbalanced game rather than a symmetrical one.
teaches: The Sicilian unbalances the game from move one

notes.explains: White develops the knight to f3, the natural Open Sicilian move-order — but he has a quieter idea in mind than d4.
There it is — the bishop checks from b5, the Moscow Variation. White sidesteps the sharp theory of the Open Sicilian and steers for a calmer, positional game.
teaches: Bb5+ is the Moscow — a positional anti-Sicilian

notes.explains: Black has three ways to block the check, and the choice is a statement of intent. Dropping the bishop to d7 offers a trade and the peaceful road; the knight to d7, the combative one — it keeps the pieces on and plays for a win. Black takes the fighting square.
teaches: How you meet Bb5+ chooses between a peaceful and a fighting game

notes.explains: White simply castles, tucking the king away and keeping the tension. The engine calls the position dead level — a classic, slow Moscow middlegame is brewing.
Black develops the knight to f6, hitting the centre and completing the kingside pieces.
The rook lifts to e1, backing the e-pawn and readying the centre. Nothing forcing — both sides are just improving, and the balance holds.
Black nudges the pawn to a6, putting the question to the bishop and gaining a little queenside space in the bargain.
teaches: ...a6 questions the bishop and claims queenside space

notes.explains: Rather than trade on d7 or sidle to a4, the bishop retreats all the way to f1. It keeps the bishop pair and stays flexible — and here the engine even gives Black the whisper of an edge, exactly the sort of slow pull Black was fighting for.
teaches: Retreat to keep a flexible bishop rather than trade it off

notes.explains: e4, c5 — the Sicilian.
The bishop to c4 — and it's surprising how many people still play these relatively obscure anti-Sicilians.
We've faced this many times, and the response is simply to develop — there's nothing special White threatens. The knight to f6.
White props the bishop up with d3.
We continue developing, the knight to c6.
White plays c3. Now a very important point — there's a trap lurking here if Black isn't careful.
You can handle this properly with a fianchetto and g6, but the line I like is e6, preparing to immobilize that c4-bishop.
White castles.
We develop the bishop to e7, planning the bishop to b7 and castling — and White will often drop the bishop back to b3, just like in an Italian or a Ruy.
When that happens, we often want to play b5 to gain queenside space. White develops the bishop to e3.
Let's castle and complete our kingside development.
White plays the knight to d2. Our light-squared bishop is a little boxed in, true, but it'll find a nice square in time.
How to play? There's something macho about d5 in this position — we're not messing around, striking in the center at once.
White captures, e takes d5.
We recapture with the knight on d5 — the plan being b6 and the bishop to b7, keeping contact against White's d3-pawn.
If White opens with d4 we still go b6. White plays the knight to e4.
b6, for two reasons: it defends the c5-pawn and it prepares to develop the light-squared bishop to b7.
White pins with the bishop to b5, and we develop the bishop to b7, defending the knight — Black is comfortably better here.
Everything is so compact, every piece coordinating — and here White blunders with the knight to g5, losing on the spot.
We refute it: the knight captures the bishop, taking on e3.
White recaptures, and we take the knight on g5 — and note the queen to h5 is ineffective because of h6.
White takes back, the knight capturing on g5.
The queen takes on g5, and Black is simply up a piece.
White lashes out with e4.
The rook to d8, getting the last piece into the game and paving the way for the rook to d2.

The consistent recommendation against the Italian bishop is the knight to f6, which invites the sharp Fried Liver — a line you simply must know. And a central pawn thrust is a serious sideline of its own, transposing into the Scotch Gambit that also has to be prepared.

In the Scotch Gambit the knight can hop away, but the move you have to know, considered by far the most reputable, is the central strike to d5 — hitting back in the middle rather than retreating passively.

Tradition held that the forward knight retreat was practically the only move, but a popular modern alternative is to drop the knight all the way home to d7. It looks like nothing special, yet it neatly covers the pin — the central capture no longer works, since the pawn can be taken or the knight grabbed and the position held with a pawn move.

Don't waste a tempo shooing the bishop — it's likely to capture of its own accord anyway. Develop the bishop to e7, deliberately keeping the c-square free so the pawn can later expand there once the exchanges happen.

Note that capturing the advanced pawn fails, because a recapture leaves you pinned. The right way to break the pin isn't the reflexive rook-pawn move but castling — an unpin that also completes development. Solve two problems with one move.

The most oppressive feature of the position is the advanced enemy pawn hanging over everything, cutting the arteries and denying the pieces access to the sixth rank. So the idea is to challenge it directly with f6 and try to remove it at all costs. A knight retreat to reinforce the queenside is the quieter alternative.

The practical decision is to plant the knight on e5 — if the opponent captures twice there, the castled king is stripped of defenders, and with the bishops activated and the f-file thrown open there are real attacking chances. Sometimes the soundest choice is the one that maximises practical trouble for the opponent.
Owen's Defence is a second-rate opening — combative, but no matter how White sets up, Black ends up worse for handing over the centre like this.
Against the bishop on d3, Black's main move is the knight to f6; the bishop to e7 is passive. The active square for that bishop is b4.
The open Sicilian — d4, opening the center to punish Black for pushing pawns instead of developing his pieces.
teaches: open the center against passive play

notes.explains: The bishop to c4 — the Bobby Fischer variation, trained on f7.
Black's e5 is a poor positional move — it permanently weakens the d5 square.
We retreat the knight — any square is fine, and f3 is its natural home.
Now the plan crystallizes: to install a knight on d5 we first remove its defender — the bishop to g5, pressuring the knight on f6.
We take the knight, freeing the outpost.
And plant the knight on d5 — a dominant central outpost. Often the threat is stronger than the execution, but here there's every reason to go straight in.
The knight reroutes to d2, on its way to prepare the f4 break.
