One preparation before f4 — the pawn to c3, blunting Black's dark-squared bishop so f4 won't drop b2, and covering the d4 square so his knight can't use it.
teaches: prep f4: blunt the bishop and cover d4 first

notes.explains: Now f4, prying open the f-file toward f7 in true Fischer style.
A strong opponent, and he's legit. e4, c5.
The knight to f3.
Black develops the knight to c6.
c3 — the Alapin, preparing d4.
e5 is a bad move — it weakens the d5-square and the long diagonal.
d4 just hands White an advantage, opening the center against Black's loose setup.
The tension is released, c takes d4 and we recapture.
He pushes d5 himself — clearly some kind of preparation.
We take on d5 and Black recaptures with the queen, pulling it into the open early.
The usual follow-up: the knight to c3, hitting the queen with tempo.
Black pins with the bishop to b4.
The bishop to d2 — we unpin ourselves and, in doing so, keep pressure on his queen.
Black trades on c3 and we recapture — now we have the two bishops.
Black develops the knight to e7.
d takes e5 — that's a free pawn; I'm not sure what Black is doing.
Black tries the bishop to g4.
Let's just develop with the bishop to e2 — we're up a pawn and clearly better.
Black lunges with the queen to e4.
We keep developing and castle.
Black brings the rook to d8, and we play the queen to e1 to maintain contact with our e5-pawn.
Black plants the knight on d5 — he's very active here.
The bishop to d1, getting it out of the way and defended by the queen — a tough opponent, so I focus.
He takes the queen on e1.
We recapture, which lightens the load — now it's an endgame where I have weak pawns scattered around but I'm up a pawn.
Black takes on c3 and we recapture with the b-pawn — weak pawns, yes, but up a pawn, so this should be winnable.
Black castles.
h3, making luft and controlling g4.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
The bishop to c2 — or maybe b3 is the better square.
A little maneuvering dance — the rook to d1, the bishop to b3, rooks reshuffling, the bishop back to d1.
The bishops shuffle b3-c2 and back, contesting the light squares.
Black plants the rook on d3, deep in our position.
The rook to c1, defending the pawn.
Black plays a6 — he's much worse, but he's completely legit, playing very accurately.
We look to improve, and it'd be nice to trade off that active rook — the knight to g5.
Bishops come off on b3 and we recapture, giving us doubled pawns — a trip to the orthodontist.
Black plays h6, poking the knight.
The knight back to f3.
Black doubles rooks with the rook to d8.
Let's step the king out of the way to h2.
Black plays a5, pushing his queenside majority.
We push e6, and Black answers with the rook to e8.
e takes f7 with check and Black recaptures with the king — a strong move that pries his king out.
The rook to d1, contesting the file.
Black opposes with the rook to d8.
Rooks come off on d3 and we tuck the king to g1, planning to march it to e2.
Black plays the king to e8, and we begin the king walk with the king to f1.
Black centralizes the rook to d5.
The king to e2, bringing it into the endgame.
Black plays the king to f7.
The knight to d2, rerouting toward e4.
Black plays the king to f6.
The knight to e4 with check.

Recapture the pawn with the knight — the tempting central push has a drawback while the bishop sits on c4, because a counter-thrust to d5 hits that bishop and frees the defender's game. Once the knight recaptures, that push becomes a genuine threat of your own.

The entire point of the gambit is a lead in development, and it demands speed — let the opponent castle and consolidate and you're simply a pawn down for nothing. Step on the gas before the king finds shelter.

When calculating, always start with the simplest move — if it already leads to a good position, you save time and dodge mistakes. Here the straightforward captures win the queen, and the far-advanced passed pawn becomes a huge endgame asset: it ties down a rook, keeps the enemy king weak, and lets you castle long with check. A pawn like that is worth more than it looks.

The opponent's hope, that recapturing wins the piece back via a fork on the king and rook, fails — the fork is simply parried by interposing the bishop. So the central pawn can be safely collected, and it's just a clean piece to the good.

Here's the crucial follow-up to the interposition — with the e-file open, the queen steps to e2, pinning the enemy king to its queen and forcing the trade that wins. Whenever a file opens toward the kings, always look for a check on the second or seventh rank; it changes everything.

The enemy queen can't move until the king steps off the open file, so you dictate the terms — force the opponent to capture your queen, which lets your king come to the centre, exactly where it belongs in an endgame. Trading on your own terms turns the pin into an advantage.

A nice concrete question — castle short or long? The answer is long. It may look risky with the queenside pawns gone, but with the queens off and the opponent undeveloped the king is in zero danger, and castling long automatically springs the rook into the game. Far more efficient than a slow rook move.

Before the check, insert the bishop to b4 first — denying the king its escape to f8. Not playing the obvious move immediately, and surveying all the options, is what makes the follow-up so much more efficient.

It isn't mate — the opponent can always block a check with the bishop — so simply win as much material as possible, snapping off the rook with check. When there's no forced mate, take the practical, decisive material rather than hunting a marginally prettier line.
This is the Jobava London — d4 and the knight to c3, then the bishop to f4. Same position by either move order.
Back in the ring against a 1580 — and we answer the king-pawn with the Sicilian.
He picks the Alapin, the quiet c3 move. Its whole idea is to build the big center with d4 next. Our job is to preempt that — don't let him roll his pawns to d4 and e4 unchallenged.
The tempting reply is e5, and it's playable — but pushing that pawn leaves the d5-square permanently soft. I'd rather not gift a hole on a central square, so we strike with d5 instead.
teaches: Advancing a pawn concedes the square behind it

notes.explains: He answers e5 anyway, still angling to follow with d4 and grab space.
So we jam the door shut with d4 of our own, wedging a pawn into his position before he can get there first.
teaches: Contest the center directly with a wedge

notes.explains: After the trade our pawn sits wedged deep in his half, cramping him and denying the natural central setup he wanted.
The bishop swings out to b5 to pin our knight. We've met this pin a hundred times — the only question is how we choose to break it.
We just quietly unpin with the bishop to d7. Not every piece needs to be doing something heroic — a modest developing move that solves the pin is plenty.
teaches: A quiet unpin is often enough — pieces need not all attack

notes.explains: d3 here is a very typical mistake, and it's black to play and win. Two alarms should ring: first, loose pieces lie all around, and loose pieces drop off.

Second: the moment a pawn moves near the king, look at the diagonal it just opened. The check on a5 does both jobs at once — it rakes that fresh diagonal and forks the loose bishop, winning a piece outright, because our wedge pawn covers c3 so the knight can't block.
teaches: A pawn move near the king opens diagonals to exploit
Combine a check with an attack on a loose piece

notes.explains: We scoop up the bishop. A whole piece to the good, and the game is essentially decided.
We grab the central pawn on d3 — though honestly we should have taken on b2, which would have snagged the rook in the corner too. I got greedy for the juicy pawn.
Here's the rule I hammer on: when you win a stack of material, don't forget to develop. Get your pieces out and coordinated instead of gorging on more pawns.
Now a lesson on converting. Trades are good when you're up material — but only take them when they fall in your lap. Never wreck your position just to force one.
teaches: Trade when ahead, but only when it comes for free

notes.explains: His queen lands on d6 and it's actually trappable — Qc5 would hunt it — but there's something even cleaner.
The knight jumps to f5, hitting the queen and forcing the trade back on our terms. The extra material carries the game.
Into the endgame, and the same rules hold: consolidate first. We recapture and keep everything tidy.
teaches: Consolidate before converting in the endgame

notes.explains: The bishop redeploys to c6, its most active diagonal, doing real work rather than sitting home.
teaches: Put pieces on their most active squares

notes.explains: King to e7 — in the endgame the king is a fighter. No need to castle; walking it toward the center improves the coordination between our pieces.
teaches: Centralize the king in the endgame

notes.explains: Careful: dropping the bishop to b7 would run into a nasty rook check on c7. We sidestep to d7 instead, which also forces the rook trade.
teaches: Check for tactical replies before developing

notes.explains: Now the textbook conversion: pick a wing, make a passed pawn, and use the extra bishop to keep dislodging his blockading rook until it has to give way — then push the pawn home. And with a winning position, watch for stalemate before you finish.
plans: Create a passed pawn and escort it
Use the extra piece to evict the blockader

notes.explains: Another White game — e4, e5.
The knight to f3, and we continue developing as Black brings out the knight to c6.
We continue with the Four Knights, heading for the Scotch — it's performed very well for us so far.
d4 — the Scotch break. We still haven't faced the main line, which is the bishop to b4 or the bishop to c5.
Black takes and we recapture with the knight on d4. Most players below 1500 tend to grab the knight here.
Black takes the knight on d4 — but that's not a good move, as we've discussed several times.
We recapture with the queen, which enters the center. Now a lot of players reflexively want to play c5 to attack it, thinking they gain something.
Instead Black plays d6. Note the bishop to b5 with check would be an empty gesture, because c6 just kicks it and we've gained nothing.
So the bishop goes to c4, and Black develops the bishop to e7.
White castles.
Black castles. Now the other bishop is a trickier question.
I don't like the bishop to d2 — it's passive and blocks the d-file, where we'll want a rook. So b3, planning to fianchetto.
We answer the king's-pawn with c5 — the Sicilian, heading for the Accelerated Dragon.
White develops the knight to f3.
The knight to c6 — reinforcing the concepts of the Accelerated.
White strikes with d4 and we take on d4. The Accelerated is the gateway Sicilian: not too theoretical, easy to learn, built on simple development moves.
White recaptures with the knight, and we fianchetto with the pawn to g6 — a setup that leads to really strong positions if White isn't careful.
White develops the bishop to e3.
The bishop to g7 — the fianchetto, applying immediate pressure on White's centre down the long diagonal.

White plays the pawn to c3 — already a mediocre move. It reinforces the knight and takes some sting out of our bishop, but it doesn't develop anything, it robs White's own knight of the c3-square, and it leads to very passive development.
So the knight to f6 — no need to reinvent the wheel: knight out, castle, then d5, often without even needing d6.
White plays the bishop to b5 — and simply blunders a pawn.
No reason not to take — the knight captures on e4, and the mediocre opening is already bearing fruit.
White takes on c6 — moving the bishop twice to grab a knight that only moved once. Both recaptures are reasonable, but I like to prioritize piece activity over pawn structure.
We recapture with the d-pawn on c6 — up a pawn, it opens a line for the queen and frees our light-squared bishop onto a juicier diagonal. And we keep the two bishops as a unit.
White castles.
We castle too. The e4-knight is perfectly placed — undefended, but there's no way for White to fork it, and everything else is covered.

White plays the knight to d2. We could trade knights, but for spice we keep them on: White's d2-knight is passive with no prospects, while ours is central and flexible — we can even retreat it to f6 and reroute to g4 or d5.

So the knight goes back to f6 — a retreat in name only, redeploying toward an outpost on d5 or the strong g4-square, and keeping pieces on makes it harder for White to breathe. White jumps the knight to c4, where it feels a touch loose — the queen to c7 or d5 comes to mind.
We play the queen to c7, keeping the tension. This is a universal, very safe construction — the c6-pawn guards against knight jumps to b5 and d5, and the queen sits comfortably.
White plays the queen to f3, intending the bishop to f4 to hit our queen — something we can cut across with a bit of calculation.
The knight to d5 — centralizing and stopping the bishop to f4; the knight to g4 was also good. Now we're ready to push our central pawns.

White plays a rook to d1. We don't take the bishop — our central knight is a monster, defended by the pawn and blanketing the position. The theme is keeping the tension, not trading unless forced, and it's time to start the kingside plan of e5, f5, and e4. The pawn to h5 threatening the bishop to g4 is met simply by h3, so it's not worth the weakening.
So the pawn to e5 — kicking the d4-knight, with f5 and then e4 or f4 to ram our pawns down the board. Notice how vulnerable White's queen is compared to ours.

White retreats the knight to b3, and we push the pawn to f5. White's pieces are like unanchored bowling pins — we just keep rolling them back with our pawns, while our own pieces are well anchored, either far away or protected by a pawn.

The reply c5 against the king's-pawn — the Sicilian. Today's choice is the Accelerated Dragon, a fast, clean setup and one of the friendliest gateways into the whole Sicilian family: less theory, clearly defined ideas, quick development.
White develops the king's knight to f3, the standard move against the Sicilian, eyeing the centre.
The queenside knight to c6 — the Accelerated move order. The plan from here is simple: trade in the centre, fianchetto, and get pieces out with tempo.
White strikes with the pawn to d4, the central break every Open Sicilian is built on.
We capture on d4, conceding a share of the centre for quick development and an open c-file to lean on later.
White recaptures with the knight, reaching the classic Open Sicilian structure.
Now the fianchetto — the pawn to g6, clearing the way for the bishop onto the long diagonal. Getting that bishop out fast is the whole point of the Accelerated.
White develops the queenside knight to c3, guarding e4 and looking toward d5.
The bishop settles on g7, aimed straight down the long diagonal at White's centre and queenside. Rapid, natural development is the accelerated dragon's calling card.
White develops the dark-squared bishop to e3, a natural square that supports the knight and readies queenside castling.
Our king's knight comes to f6, hitting e4 and finishing minor-piece development. Depending on White's next setup, we'll castle, play d6, or in some lines even strike with d5.
The bishop to c4 — a sharp Sozin-flavoured try that stares down f7. We simply carry on developing.
We castle, and note what we're deliberately NOT doing: pushing the pawn to d6 yet. Holding it back preserves maximum flexibility for what comes next.

The knight steps back to e2 — a poor choice, because it abandons the strong central d4-square and does nothing active. And here's a reflex worth burning in: whenever White keeps a bishop on e3, always keep one eye on it. There is a way to challenge White at once. We could play the calm d6 — perfectly fine — but if we want to be maximally testing, a sharper idea is waiting.
The knight jumps to g4, leaping at the bishop on e3. If the bishop moves, we get to hit f2 and b2 at the same time — and with the c-pawn already traded off, that double attack has real teeth.
White slides the bishop to g5 rather than the tempting retreat to d4, which would just drop the bishop. Now the second pattern to know is armed: the queen sortie.
The queen swings out to b6, forking the pawns on f2 and b2. It carries risk — our light-squared bishop still isn't out — but the pressure should tell.
White castles, choosing to hold f2 and let the other pawn go. A garden-variety double attack: one of the two pawns is going to fall.
We capture on b2. The key question before ever taking like this is always the same — can the queen be trapped? Here, no chance.

White chases with the rook to b1, and the queen simply steps to a3. That's the whole safety net: from b2 the queen had a3, and beyond it a5 and c5 — too many routes to be caught in a single move. That is exactly the check to run before snatching a pawn: list the queen's escapes, and ask whether any one move takes them all away.

White's best try — the knight leaps to d5, generating real pressure, so we must stay careful. Even so, it's hard to see much for the pawn; our position is solid. To consolidate we want the queen back — either to c5, or to d6. But the queen-to-d6 has to be calculated: it steps off the a3-e7 diagonal, dropping the guard on e7, and then the knight crashes in with a check on e7, forking the king and the knight on c6 — losing material. So d6 is out, and c5 is the safe route.

The knight comes back into the centre to e5 — retreating from a loose square, hitting the bishop, and centralising, all at once. And crucially the queen still guards e7 for now: if White probes with a rook to b3, the c5-square is always waiting for the queen.

White tucks the bishop back to b3, out of harm's way. Now we diagnose what's blocking full consolidation. We'd love to play d6 to free the light-squared bishop — but d6 cuts the queen's defence of e7 and drops that pawn. So d6 has to wait.

Instead we start kicking. Trying to fianchetto with b6 wouldn't cure the real disease — White's two strong pieces on d5 and g5. We need to chase at least one away, maybe both later with a well-timed e6. The pawn to h6 first — the most flexible poke, keeping options open depending on where the bishop runs.
The bishop retreats to h4, staying on the pin — and where it lands decides our next step.
We keep coming — the pawn to g5, chasing the bishop away entirely. This unburdens our position and lets us consolidate on our own terms.

The bishop drops to g3. Now d6 finally works — e7 is covered well enough. We could also try e6, but combining g6 and e6 leaves too many dark-square holes, so there's no rush to chase the d5-knight yet.

So the pawn to d6 at last — solid and freeing. And if White tries the knight to c7, there's simply no follow-up: the rook steps to b8 and nothing comes of it. That jump only bites if a rook were sitting on e8, which it isn't.
White plays the correct plan — the pawn to h4, prying open our king. This won't be an easy game.
We finally develop the light-squared bishop to g4. Honest admission: White's h4 is stronger than it first looks — this was underestimated.
White centralises the queen to d2 — a good move. Now we've got an interesting resource: the queen to a5, trying to force the queens off.

The queen to a5, offering the trade. There's a tactical wrinkle — White has the check on e7 — but calculate one step further: after the knight takes e7 with check, the king steps to h7, and now we hit two things at once, White's queen and the checking knight, so the queens come off. We hand back the extra pawn, but the mating danger evaporates.
White declines and lifts the queen to e3 — music to the ears, because now the check on e7 no longer bites: that knight is tied to defending White's own queen, so the moment it moves, the queen falls.
So the queen to c5, again pressing for the exchange and eyeing White's queen.
White sidesteps to d2. No matter — our queen is beautifully centralised while White's is tied to the knight. That means we can get on with the plan: e6.
The pawn to e6, kicking the d5-knight. A strange, tense structure — the pawn-grab has led to a real fight, and if the knight retreats to e3 there's a very pretty resource waiting.
The knight goes to e3. And here's that resource — not a gimmick, it genuinely does something.

The bishop drops in to f3! It's untouchable thanks to the fork, and the point is plain: we're hitting the e4-pawn. With such a strong knight on e5 backing the operation, that pawn is hard to hold — normally a capture on c5 would break the pin, but the other knight just recaptures and the bishop stays immune.
White grabs on g5.
We have to recapture on g5 — otherwise our whole kingside is shattered.
White captures our centralised knight, the bishop landing on e5.
We recapture on e5 with the other knight — all according to plan.
The knight to g3, a good defensive try. Suddenly our f3-bishop could become a liability — if White's queen ever steps aside, the bishop can be taken. Time to think about shoring it up.

The pawn to g4 — solidifying the bishop, and more than that, preparing to sacrifice it: if White captures on f3, our knight recaptures and gets anchored by this very pawn. The deeper idea is to bring the dark-squared bishop to h6 and crank up the pressure.
White finds a very strong move — the queen to c1. And now our f3-bishop really is trapped.
We carry on with the plan — the bishop to h6, pinning the knight and pouring heat onto White's position. The f3-bishop is lost, so we roll with it and turn it into fuel.
White takes the bishop, a pawn recapturing on f3.

And now the instructive choice — most players would recapture with the knight, but we take with the pawn. This f3-pawn is a far more dangerous attacker: it jams White's position and becomes an anchor point for mating ideas. We're down a piece for two pawns, but White's king is the one in danger.
White unpins with the queen to e1. We have many ways to improve.
The king to h7 — stepping off the g-file so the rook can pour down it into the attack.

White cracks under the pressure — the knight to c4, which simply hangs itself. But the beautiful point is that we don't need to take it. The first thing to notice isn't the loose knight — it's that White's pawn on f2 is now pinned, so it no longer guards the knight.
So the in-between move — the rook to g8, threatening the crushing capture on g3 with check. Once that knight vanishes, White's king stands utterly alone.
White's king shuffles to h2. We keep our eyes on the bigger prize, not the loose knight on c4.
The knight to g4 with check — crushing.

The king to h3. Now don't drown in the sea of winning moves — plan properly. The real target is getting the queen over to the kingside, ideally to h6. What's in the way? Our own bishop. So move the bishop first.
But we don't bury the bishop uselessly — the bishop to f4 keeps it in the attack while clearing the queen's route via g5 to h6.
White pushes the pawn to e5. And here we spot an even faster finish — the knight crashes in on f2 with check.
The knight takes on f2 with check and the game is essentially over. A rook lift to g5 was also winning, but this is the cleanest.

Against the Modern, which cedes the centre, a brute-force approach really tests the opponent's understanding — they've pushed out a lot of pawns and created targets, so the plan is to storm the h-file and start attacking one of them directly.
The rook-pawn advance in reply is already a mistake — ask which square it weakens. That hole invites the bishop out with a threat, and the whole thing sets off a chain reaction in your favour.

Accept the bishop trade — and look at the damage: the opponent's dark squares are terribly weak, hollowed out by their own pawn advances. Trading off the defender of those squares is exactly what you want.

Cement control of those dark squares with the central pawn to e5, seizing the key square for good — but don't get carried away. Combining a positional grip with actual piece development is what turns an advantage into a win.

Develop with tempo — the queen to d2 does three jobs at once: it prepares castling long, it hits an enemy piece, and it eyes a later swing to the attack. The best developing moves come with a threat attached.

Now the knight heads for its dream outpost on f6 — shielded by a pawn chain that's extremely hard to break, each pawn propping up the next. A protected knight on that square is the backbone of the whole attack.

The opponent finds a strong move that was underestimated — and part of mastery is reacting to the unforeseen and admitting when a plan hasn't worked. So bring the knight back rather than stubbornly pressing on. A coach's phrase for it is simply 'saying sorry' — retreating gracefully beats clinging to a flawed idea.

To keep the attack going you need more pieces, and there's a standard mechanism — the rook lift or doubling. Doubling the rooks on the open file piles onto the enemy knight, clearing the way to plant your own knight back on its outpost. Bring the reserves to the front.

A clean finish through an in-between move — the knight leaps in, and if it's captured, don't grab the rook at once. Insert the pawn recapture with check first, then collect the rook, harvesting the maximum material. That's how you find intermediate moves: pause and ask how to get the most, rather than snatching the first thing on offer.

Even with queens off, the attack lives — bring the last piece in with the knight to g5, hitting a pawn that's pinned and can't be defended. The endgame doesn't extinguish an attack; it just needs the final piece.

A closing maxim for endgames — do not hurry. There's a strong temptation to rush both on the clock and in your ideas, but often the most effective way to convert is simply to keep improving your position one patient step at a time.
The bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez, the Spanish. At the top level this is the most popular move, and one I play myself with White.

We don't need to chase the bishop; it isn't doing much. But note the principle of proximity — the closer things happen to your king, the more attentive you must be. If the bishop had pinned a knight near your king, then h6 would be the move.

He captures unprovoked, so you actually saved a tempo by never playing a6. The recapture opens the b-file, and don't fret the doubled pawn — one doubled pawn is nothing, and you've got the two bishops.
teaches: doubled pawns for the bishop pair

notes.explains: Don't trade the bishops here — that would open the f-file for HIM. Drop the bishop back to b6 instead, so that if he takes it, YOU get to open the a-file for your rook.
teaches: open files for you, not him

notes.explains: Now develop the bishop to its most active square, g4, setting the pin. If he shoves a pawn at it he only weakens himself, and we simply hold the pin.

Keep developing and hold the pin. It's a tough position for him — the pin, your piece coordination — and because he's already given up his light-squared bishop, that pin is very hard for him to break.
teaches: a pin is stronger once the defender’s bishop is gone

notes.explains: He pins you back, so chase it with h6 — because now if he pushes his bishop's pawn you can't be taken by his knight, which is itself pinned. Your pin is better than his.
The pawn pushes to g5, excommunicating his bishop from the game.

This is great practice for finding moves in unclear positions. The plan is to open the f-file with f5, and g4 prepares it — and by recapturing on g4 with the knight rather than the bishop, you keep your pin intact. Best of both worlds.
With the file about to open, push f5 — and don't fall into thinking attacks happen in two moves. You often spend a long time just accumulating pieces before it breaks.
And sometimes you play a quiet, near-empty move to bide your time while the tension holds — knowing when to wait is its own skill.

Decide your queen's ideal square first — where it sits most harmoniously with the rook. To f6, then it can slide to g6, and you slowly bring both rooks to bear. And keep in reserve that the bishop eyes f2: not now, but the moment his defender moves or you sacrifice for it, that becomes real.
teaches: place the queen relative to the rook

notes.explains: The pawn to e4, c5 — our favorite Alapin Sicilian.
c3 — the elephant. Let's see how it holds up at a 2000-plus level.
The knight to f6 — one of the two main responses; we haven't faced it as much.
e5 — a great chance to review the theory of this line and show some new, exciting analysis.

After the knight to d5 we're already in the weeds: two fundamentally different ways to play the Alapin. The traditional one is d4 here; Black takes, and White needn't recapture, since the d-pawn taking c3 isn't a threat — the queen x-rays the knight. So the main line is d4, the pawn takes d4, and the knight to f3 is an important inclusion —

— but recently elephant experts embarked on a different, more tactical approach: start with the knight to f3. It often transposes — Black plays the knight to c6, you'd think White must play d4, and after the pawns trade it's the main line. But after the knight to c6 there's a second approach —

— which I'd like to introduce. Black could also play d6 or e6 — those are the three main moves; the knight to c6 is on the board. Do you know the move I'm implying? It may seem natural, but on closer look it may seem a serious positional mistake.
The bishop to c4 — bringing it out straight away, hitting the knight on d5 and forcing it back to b6, or Black supports it with e6, a popular but, I think, not very good line.
I'm really hoping for e6 — those positions are fun for White — but so are the main lines after the knight to b6, when we drop the bishop back to b3.
The bishop to b3. Why did I say the bishop to c4 may seem a serious positional mistake? Because we're actually encouraging a very scary-looking move —
— our opponent didn't play it, and that's c4. c4 is scary because after we play d4 later, Black takes en passant and breaks up our chain, seemingly losing our e5-pawn; I'll show the theory.
— because if we don't, Black gets an ideal setup by bringing the bishop out to g4. So without question we take en passant, keeping the diagonal open for our bishop.
The queen recaptures. We might be attracted to the immediate d4, but that's not the point of this line — the point is to quickly develop and go after the b6-knight.
How do we go after the b6-knight? A very important idea that lights the fire on the queenside — but first things first, get the king out of the centre. And realize the bishop to g4 —
— is an incredibly common blunder in this position.
First we trade bishops on e6, to buy ourselves a couple of tempi —
— making it difficult for Black to develop his kingside: he'd love to play e6 next, but he has to move the queen away first, and that costs tempi we use to develop rapid play on the queenside.

The idea, not d4, is to go after the knight on b6 with a4 — universally applied in many positions — shoving the pawn toward a5. It may look like a one-move threat with plenty of retreats, but the point is to push all the way to a6, creating long-term light-square weaknesses; the pawn on a7 becomes a long-term weakness once our pawn reaches a6 and fixes it. If Black plays a5, the knight loses its defender and b5 becomes a gaping weakness for our knight; at the right moment we play d4 and blast the centre. The rook to e1 is tempting, but the queen on e6 is actually a good thing — it hampers Black's development — so the rook to e1 would only help him by forcing the queen back.
The queen to d7 — instructive how tempting moves are often bad here. He abides by the clear strategy of kingside development.
So no time to waste — we continue the queenside campaign with a5; still theory, the queen to d7 being the main line, and don't worry, we're going to play d4.
The knight to d5. We need to complete the queenside picture; we do not want to allow Black to play a6 himself, because then our a5-pawn becomes a very serious liability —

— a liability because the knight on c6 aims at it. We want to freeze the queenside on our terms, so we throw in a6, inducing b6. The weak light squares may seem inaccessible without a light-squared bishop, but the queen also moves diagonally and will be the vehicle to exploit them. I'm anticipating b6.

If Black doesn't play b6, we take on b7 and shatter his queenside; if the b-pawn takes a6, same idea, inviting our rook to a super-active square. b6 is played. We must be very accurate — if we fall asleep, Black plays e6 and the bishop to e7 — so we combine queenside play with keeping Black frozen, making it as hard as possible to develop his bishop.

We want Black frozen on the kingside, unable to protect the weak squares and the a7-pawn. It's the perfect, maybe last, opportunity to strike with d4, opening the centre without forcing Black to take. If Black takes on d4 —

— we recapture with the knight, and if he takes again, with the queen; our queen recapturing on d4 sits centrally, supported by c3, aiming at the g7-pawn, making it hard for the bishop to come out. e6 is on the board — impressive handling. I think the move is the knight to a3... actually c4 is tempting, but it allows the knight to b4, breaking our chain. There's also e5 — I think the move is actually e5, a hard move to explain.

e5 — inviting a knight trade and changing the pawn structure from a potential isolated-queen-pawn to a structure where the pawn lords over Black from e5, controlling f6 and d6; Black would love the dark-squared bishop on f6 and f6 for the knight. After the knight trade the d-file opens, and White, more active with better pawns and more space, is better placed to exploit it.
There's also a very important idea without which this wouldn't work: after the trade on e5 —
— I'm assuming our opponent plays the bishop to b7. Knowing typical elephant ideas really helps.
What's a very typical way to meet the bishop to e7 here? It should be largely automatic —

The knight to a3 — the more flexible approach, since we don't know exactly where the queen belongs; we can always play the queen to g4. The knight is ready to drop into b5 the moment the black queen leaves the seventh rank, when the knight to b5 is potentially devastating. That's why we leave the rook on a1 — to support the pawn once we take on a7. b5 stops the knight to b5, but it also adds further strain to the queenside.

The bishop to e7 virtually forces our hand — the queen to g4, using it to induce kingside weaknesses. We're starting to squeeze Black: castles, the bishop to h6 loses the exchange; forcing kingside weaknesses gives Black weaknesses on both sides, and we keep pressing toward the knight to b5. Watch the e5-pawn, now without a defender; watch our a6-pawn; watch out for the knight back to c7. Don't get fixated on the knight to b5 — sometimes the knight to c4 and d6 is more worthwhile after the dark-bishop trade — and c4 on demand chases the knight and opens b5, though then the knight drops to c7 and a6 hangs. On my opponent's turn I discuss general ideas — the Kotov, Russian-school approach: calculate concrete variations on your turn, and build conceptual wisdom about the position while your opponent thinks.

The queen to g4, the bishop back to f8 — a clear sign our opponent is in full backpedal mode. There's a crazy tactical sequence: the rook to d1 pins the queen and threatens c4, but Black drops the knight back to f6, and if we take, our rooks aren't coordinated, so the queen takes d1 is mate; but after the rook to d1, the knight to f6, we trade queens, our back rank is weak so we can't take a7, yet we trade rooks on d8, the knight finally gets into b5, and Black loses a7. The rook to d1 is very juicy, threatening c4 not to win the knight but to force that winning endgame. The bishop to g5 is a second candidate, just as good — only careful of f6, which buys Black a tempo and encourages us to give up the e5-pawn.
We play the Sicilian, c5.
White plays a knight to c3. Which reply depends on your Sicilian: Najdorf players play d6, Accelerated Dragon players play a knight to c6.
So a knight to c6, since we're playing the Accelerated Dragon here.
White plays a knight to f3 — we proceed expecting d4 next.
As Accelerated Dragon players, it's easy — we play g6, and if d4 comes we take and transpose straight into an Accelerated Dragon.
White plays d4.
We capture on d4.
And we fianchetto the bishop to g7 — our first Accelerated Dragon.

White plays a bishop to e3. The zen of this opening is to delay d6 — playing it early lets White transpose into the sharp mainline Dragon, and by holding off we deny White comfortable queenside castling.
So we develop the knight to f6 first, keeping the option to play d5 in one fell swoop.

White plays a3 — a sideline I've never seen, essentially a waste of time since we're not putting anything on b4. But we can't play d5 yet: before castling, a bishop to b5 pins our knight and threatens a capture on c6 and a bishop fork on e6.
So we castle kingside first — the rule of thumb is only play d5 after castling. Now we're ready to open the center and punish White for delaying.
White plays a bishop to c4 — and here's the center fork trick, a ubiquitous idea you cannot play the Accelerated without knowing. The precondition is a bishop on c4 (or, for Black, on c5).
We play a knight capture on e4 anyway — it looks like a blunder, but with the trick in hand it isn't.
White recaptures on e4, and we meet it with d5.
d5 re-forks the knight and bishop — that's where the name comes from — and we win the piece back. White can give the piece for a pawn, but here it isn't even easy for him to regain it.
If White plays a knight capture on c6...
...we recapture with the pawn, protecting d5 with our new c6 pawn — and White really pays for a3, because normally this arises with White already castled; keeping the king in the center burns him.

White plays a knight to g3. A very bad move now would be a bishop capture on b2 — we've already sacrificed a piece, so after we grab the rook White recaptures with the queen and we're left with rook and two pawns for two pieces, usually worse, and we've given up our precious fianchetto bishop.
So we simply recapture on c4 — now we're up a pawn.
White trades queens into an endgame.
We recapture on d8 — we'll still need good technique to finish in style.

White plays c3, closing off our bishop. With queens off, our king is safe — so no need to rush the c8 bishop out; the bigger fish is the b2 pawn. Our pawn on c4 deep-freezes it: b2 is backward with no path forward, a huge weakness on an open file.
So a rook to b8 — a move that begs to be played, needing no calculation. And a7 can't be taken.
White plays a rook to b1 — but a loose piece drops off, because the rooks aren't coordinated.
The move that ends it is a bishop capture on c3 with check.
A must-win game against a strong junior. I take the mainline Open Sicilian with the knight to f3, and he steers toward his pet setup.
He answers e6 — the flexible move-order that keeps both the Kan and the Taimanov on the table.
Earlier in the event I met this with c3, the Alapin, and won a nice game — but he'll have spent the break preparing exactly that.
We open e4 and face the Scandinavian — d5, and after we take, the Portuguese variation with a knight to f6.
There are good lines here — the one thing not to do, unless you play the Panov, is c4. I always recommend a bishop check on b5 — a nasty little check.
It forces Black to put a piece on d7, which is awkward by definition.
My coach's easy line: drop the bishop back to e2 — low-maintenance, not the sharpest, but a nice little edge.
Black recaptures on d5.
And we play d4, building a pawn center.
Black replies with a knight to c6 — a very sloppy move.
So we use our pawns to stake a claim in the center, starting with c4 — pretty automatic.
Black plays a knight to f6.
The ambitious move is to push d5 — not very committal, so why not?
Black plays a knight to e5. Now be careful — a bishop to f4 lets the knight drop to g6 with tempo.
The deeper approach is a knight to f3, developing.
Black plays a knight to g6. My idea was that after a trade on f3, Black can't easily play e6 — the b7 pawn would hang — making it hard for Black to develop.
Whenever a knight lands on g6 like this, one idea should automatically occur to you — and it's very powerful here since Black is so cramped: shove the pawn to h5.
Black plays h6 — but Black should have played h5.
And we literally win the knight, trapped on g6.
Two trapped pieces like this show the importance of a space advantage.
We recapture on h5, and Black plays e6 — now the choice: keep pieces on for mate, or trade down. We'll trade.
We capture on e6.
Black recaptures on e6; we're low on time, so we trade queens.
A queen capture on d8.
Black recaptures on d8 — the boring but effective method.
We develop a knight to c3.
Black plays a bishop to b4 — the pin isn't scary at all.
A bishop to e3 — no need to rush a3, and we don't care about the doubled pawns; we're up a piece.
Black plays b6. Now I want to improve our king — the a1 rook is out of the game.
We'd love to castle long, but the rook is on the d-file, so a knight to d4 — stable, and it clears the way to castle queenside and, if needed, eliminate the e6 bishop.
Black plays a bishop to d7.
We castle queenside, which also opens a knight jump to d5 if Black doesn't trade.
Black trades on c3 — completely winning for us.
We recapture on c3. Where does the knight go? We keep encouraging trades.
A knight to f5, hitting g7 — if Black takes, we trade rooks and recapture on f5.
Black captures on f5.
We trade rooks and recapture on f5, left with the extra minor piece.
Black plays a king to e7.
Following the plan to its conclusion, a bishop to h5 prepares to trade the last minor pieces.
Don't be dogmatic about trading everything — if the attack on the enemy king is a slam dunk, take it.
We capture on g6.
Black recaptures, and a rook to d5 is totally winning — but stay flexible; trading isn't always the easiest path.
Black pushes h5.
It's an endgame, so first bring the king up.
Our opponent is doing nothing of substance on the kingside.
We just trade pawns with a4.
The pawns come off on h3.
Now we hunt Black's weak kingside pawns.
The easiest way is to go after the base of the pawn chain — a rook to d8 and then a8.
Black plays a6.
So a rook to b8, picking up the pawn.
Black plays a rook to h4.
We take on b6 with check.
Black plays a king to d7.
A king to d3 is clinical — why give up pawns when we can just defend them?
We take on a6 and can swing the rook over to g6.
Black plays a rook to h5.
We push a5 — no need to grab more pawns, we can just promote.
Black plays a king to b8.
We take on g7 to cut off the king, and I expect resignation.
Now take another pawn, capturing on c5 — the one thing to watch in these scenarios is stalemate.
Black plays a king to a8.
A bishop to b6 — as long as the king has b8 and a8...
Black plays a rook to f8.
We push c5 — and it's a good idea not to push a7, which is what causes last-second stalemates.
Black checks on f3.
Don't stalemate the enemy king unless you absolutely have to.
Black plays a rook to f8. Watch how I convert this.
It occurs to me I can play a rook to d7, then d8, and trade the rooks.
Black plays a king to b8.
As long as the king is cornered that's good — but don't overdo it by stalemating unless you've calculated to mate.
We trade the rooks and promote the pawns with checkmate.
We push c6.
Let's move the bishop back to b6 — Black has a g-pawn, so no stalemate worry.
Black has the g-pawn move available, so we're safe.
We promote to a knight — checkmate. A straightforward game, because Black blundered a piece in the opening.
The pawn to e4, c5 — another chance to play the elephant.
c3 — the elephant. So far it's brought us tremendous success, almost invariably clearly better or straight-up winning positions out of the opening.
Black strikes with d5.
We take on d5, and Black recaptures with the queen — most people play one of the two main moves here, d5 or the knight to f6.
d4. Previously, facing this, our opponent played the knight to c6.
The c-pawn takes d4 — one of several viable tries, but an incredibly risky line.
We recapture on d4. Conceptually it's an inaccuracy, because now the knight gets the c3-square to chase the queen off d5 and, ultimately, to set the d-pawn in motion.
The knight to c6, following our last Alapin game; after the knight to f3 our opponent played the bishop to g4, and we may follow that game a while.

The knight to f3 — Black attacks the d4-pawn and we must defend it. The main alternative is e5; there's also the bishop to g4, and e6, after which Black is clearly worse once we play the knight to c3.

In that earlier game, against the bishop to g4 White shouldn't play the obvious bishop to e2 but go directly the knight to c3, then push d5, already winning; the testing line was the bishop to g4, the knight to c3, and the bishop takes f3. But our opponent plays g6 — and as extreme as it sounds, Black is already almost lost.

The knight to c3 — developing with tempo, the whole point, which is why Black should have kept the pawns on c5 and c3; that version would have been incomparably better. Once the queen moves, unless to e6 with check which we block, we pre-move d5. In fact g6 makes it worse: if Black can't fianchetto, the queen to d4 hits the rook in the corner and stops the bishop to g7.
We play the Caro-Kann — solid chess with Black — c6.
White plays a knight to f3.
We play d5, challenging e4.
White captures on d5 — a weird Exchange Caro; the knight-f3 move order is a little inflexible.
We recapture on d5.
The Exchange Caro — not much going on; Black simply develops.
The one thing to understand: the c8 bishop often lacks a good home, so it's worth developing it early — a knight to c6 first, then a bishop to g4.
White plays c3 — fine. We can develop in any order.
The drawback of a bishop to g4 right now is a queen to b3 hitting b7 — so I'll develop the knight to f6 first.
White plays a bishop to b5 — not common, but fine; we're very comfortable as Black.
A bishop to g4 — we're not afraid of the pin, since the pawn defends the knight and the only way to pile on it is a knight to e5.
White plays a queen to d3, unpinning. In the Exchange Caro you often give this bishop for the knight, so you can develop without it getting stuck behind the pawns.
So a bishop capture on f3 — it seems odd to go g4 then take, but eliminating the piece that would be trapped behind the pawns is the right way to play these structures.
White recaptures, and we play e6.
White castles. The bishop can go to b7 or d6 — d6 is more active but allows a bishop to g5 pinning; e7 is more passive but takes the sting out of it.
We play h6 first to stop a bishop to g5, then aim for a bishop to d6 — I don't like delaying the bishop long, but our position is solid enough.
White plays a knight to d2 and we develop the bishop to d6.
White captures on c6.
We recapture with the b-pawn — taking on c6 wasn't necessary for White.
White plays a knight to b3, eyeing the c5 outpost, which it reaches if the bishops are traded — so White wants a bishop to f4 to offer that trade.
So a queen to c7 — a healthy, typical Caro move that prevents a bishop to f4, denying that bishop a good square.
White plays g3. But notice a subtle drawback of our queen move: the g7 pawn is now overloaded, so castling would allow the thematic bishop capture on h6 — so we delay castling.
We play a5, aiming for a4 to chase the knight; and if it goes to c5 while our bishop is still here, we simply take.
White plays a knight to c5.
We happily take, ruining his pawn structure.
White recaptures on c5. We still shouldn't castle because of the bishop capture on h6.
Now is the time for a knight to e4.
White plays a rook to e1. We can support the knight with f5.
We castle first — I'm not too concerned about an exchange sacrifice.
White plays b4. We don't take on b4, which would repair his structure — and he isn't threatening to take on a5.
We play f5, cementing the knight — the most flexible move.
White plays a queen to h5, moving off the c3 pawn. We can't take c3 immediately because of a capture on e6.
So a queen to e5, piling on c3 and pinning the f-pawn to the rook.
White plays f3.
And we play a queen capture on c3, attacking both rooks.
White finds a bishop capture on h6 — an unexpected counterattack, defending his rooks and counterstriking.
We just take on h6 with the pawn.
White plays a queen to g6 with check — extremely strong.
We have to block with a queen to g7.
We head into an endgame still better for Black — trading down, keeping our strong pawn chain.
The queens come off on e4 and we keep a very strong pawn chain.
White's position collapses — he blunders another pawn.
A rook to b3 is very underrated — now we're winning with the pawn chain.
A rook to b7 defends the pawn. His c5 pawn is isolated, so a rook to a5 or b5 attacks it.
A rook to b5 has the advantage of a defended square.
We take on a3, forcing the trade, then grab another pawn.
We recapture on a3.

We take on c5 and start pushing our pawns. He's super resilient, so we win the long way: bring the king around to c3 and prepare to promote. If we want to be fancy, we can sacrifice two pawns to force a rook trade into a winning king-and-pawn endgame — promote to a queen forcing the rook onto the king's file, a rook check, and roll out the red carpet with the king to b2, then push the c-pawn home.
A twenty-four-thirty-nine opponent. e4, and Black replies d5 — the Scandinavian.
Black recaptures with the queen, and the move is the knight to c3, hitting it with tempo.
The queen to d8 is one of the possible retreats.
The move here is of course d4, seizing the center, and Black develops the knight to f6.
The knight to f3, developing.
Black plays c6, and we bring the bishop out to c4, seeking the most active squares for our pieces.
b5 is already pretty weird.
The bishop steps back to b3.
I'm not sure what b5 achieves other than creating weaknesses. Black plays e6.
Let's complete our development and castle.
Black develops the bishop to e7. Now, where does the queen's bishop belong in these positions?
In my view the most active square is f4 — the bishop to f4 is a good move.
Black castles, and we slam the knight into e5 — and the bishop does a nice job keeping that knight stable.
Black plays the knight to d5. White is slightly better, and this is one of those moments where you just keep the tension.
So we drop the bishop back to g3, maintaining everything.
Black takes on c3, seemingly ruining my pawn structure.
We recapture, b takes c3 — and I'll explain during the game why this doubled structure isn't actually a problem.
On one hand it's doubled, but on the other we have a big mass of central pawns all defending each other. Black plays a5 and we answer a4.
Black plays the bishop to a6, creating an x-ray against my rook. How should we respond?
Simply the rook to e1 — and now you should immediately notice how loose Black's pawns on e6 and f7 are.
Black plays c5.
The knight takes on f7 — I play it pretty intuitively, because at the very least it's a rook for two pieces, and it hits the queen while stripping the defender of e6.
Black recaptures with the rook, and now the bishop takes on e6 — the defender is gone and the attack crashes through.
Black plays the bishop to b7. Notice the rook in the corner is undefended, which means our threats are just getting started.
The Smith-Morra — we offer the c-pawn to rip the centre open.
He sets up with e6, the most popular and honestly the most annoying reply to face.

Here's the counter-intuitive move: the bishop to c4. It looks like it violates development, but it isn't as passive as it appears — it supports a future knight sacrifice on d5, and if the e6-pawn ever collapses, this bishop is beautifully poised to wreak havoc. Pure potential energy.

We retreat the bishop to b3 and reach the edge of theory — from here we're on our own. The core idea to hold in mind is the knight sacrifice on d5, shoving it into the centre to blow up the e6-pawn and open the e-file.

With Black's whole kingside undeveloped, this is the moment for the knight to d5 — and we can play it almost without calculation, because if it's taken we get tremendous play down the e-file. Some sacrifices are so typical you can trust them intuitively. The knight disrupts his coordination, and a bishop to e3 and b6 even sets up a fork on c7.

Notice his king is boxed in with no squares — file that away. Now develop our last minor piece: the bishop to g5 pins and piles on, while the bishop to e3 would close the e-file and make a recapture on d5 more palatable for him.
Both are fine — a matter of taste. We choose the long-term move, the bishop to g5, and if he ever meets it with f6, a bishop sacrifice there becomes very interesting.

After h6 and the bishop to h4, we're hoping for g5 — because then the knight to f6 is checkmate, a smothered mate with the king boxed in. The only reason the knight to f6 isn't already mate is that the g7-pawn still covers that square.
He plays g5, and the knight to f6 is smothered mate. That's what happens when you pile long-term pressure on an undeveloped position — it collapses.
One last game against a 1600 who trots out the Scandinavian, meeting our king-pawn with an immediate central strike.
He recaptures with the queen, and this is the whole problem with the Scandi: the queen is out early and about to become a target.
teaches: Scandinavian: the early queen is exposed to tempo

notes.explains: The knight to c3 is the best move — it develops a piece and gains a free tempo by hitting the queen.
teaches: Develop with tempo against the exposed queen

notes.explains: He retreats all the way home to d8, so we've already gained ground for nothing.
We seize the full center with d4 — space and a big development lead, exactly the dream against a passive Scandinavian.
teaches: Occupy the center when ahead in development

notes.explains: He just shuffles pawns with b5, doing nothing for his development. There's no special reply needed — we simply keep bringing pieces out.
teaches: Answer aimless pawn moves by continuing development

notes.explains: So the bishop goes to d3, a simple, natural post aiming at his kingside.
We centralize the knight on e5, a powerful outpost right in the heart of his camp.
teaches: A knight on e5 is a dominant central outpost

notes.explains: And the bishop develops to g5, pinning his knight. Nothing fancy yet — just getting every piece to a good square, fast, while he flounders.

Now the queen swings to f3 to pile on the pressure. I'm deliberately leaving the d4-pawn hanging: he's so underdeveloped that if the queen grabs it, she'll be hunted down and the lost tempo will cost him far more than a pawn.
teaches: A development lead is worth more than a pawn
plans: Offer d4 as bait — the greedy queen becomes a target

notes.explains: We open e4 and face a French — e6.
We play d4, taking the full center.
Black plays d5 and we answer the Tarrasch knight to d2.
Black captures on e4 — the Rubinstein French.
We recapture on e4.
Black plays a knight to d7 — the Rubinstein, incredibly solid and hard to break down. The classical setup with a bishop to d3 promises little, so I'll play one of the more enterprising modern lines.
We start with a knight to f3, the entry point to all of this.
This is the tabia — almost everyone plays a knight to f3.
We capture on f6.
Black recaptures. From this tabia White has five or six setups — a bishop to d3 is classical but the least promising.

I'll play c3 — a move with a very good reputation among top GMs. It looks purely positional, reinforcing the pawn, but a big point is that a queen check on a4 is a major idea while the king sits on e8: White develops on the a4-e8 diagonal and pressures Black before he completes development.
Black plays c5. The main moves for us are a knight to e5 or a bishop to e3.

A bishop to e3 — a developing move that pressures c5 and threatens to win a pawn with a capture on c5. If Black takes on d4 we recapture with the bishop, and the structure resembles an Alapin Sicilian, where a bishop in the center can be very powerful.

Black plays a knight to d5. A capture on c5 now runs into a knight capture on e3: even with queens off, Black recaptures the pawn and leaves us a poor structure plus the bishop pair — so the c5 capture is out. And a bishop check on b5 is ineffective, since Black just plays a bishop to d7.

So this is the moment for a knight to e5 — centralizing, and preparing a bishop check on b5 and a queen check on a4, against which a bishop to d7 no longer works: we take on d7, and the bishop to b5 wins the queen.

Black plays a6, preventing a bishop to b5 and taking the sting out of a queen check on a4. Our options: a capture on c5, though Black gets away with a knight capture on e3; or just a normal move like a bishop to d3, since a knight capture on e3 doesn't scare us — d4 stays secured and after castling we hit f7 while the d3 bishop eyes h7.
I'm leaning toward capturing on c5 — an interesting endgame if Black takes on c3.
Black captures on e3.
We trade queens on d8.

Black recaptures and we take on e3 — and concretely we threaten a knight capture on f7, which is why this whole thing works: Black has to waste a tempo shuffling the king back to defend it. Our e3 pawn is weak but Black lacks the firepower to attack it, and we're not just keeping the extra pawn — we're playing to keep Black's bishops passive with b4.
Black plays a king to e8.
We play b4, building the pawn chain to keep the dark-squared bishop at bay. Now, optimal squares: e5 is a good temporary spot for the knight, but a knight to c4 heads for the b6 outpost.
Black plays a bishop to e7, aiming for a bishop to f6 — a threat we must address.
We start with a knight to c4 — removing the knight from e5 so a bishop to f6 won't come with tempo, and we'd play this move anyway.

Black plays a bishop to f6. This c5-b4-c3 construction is superb at winding down Black's queenside counterplay. I'll hold off a knight check on d6 — keeping the knight on c4 keeps its options open, like potential versus kinetic energy.
We play a king to d2 to secure c3 — the typical advice is not to tie a heavy piece to a menial task, so a rook to c1 would waste it; the king belongs on c2, defending c3 and off the d-file.
Black plays a king to e7. A rook check on d8 isn't scary, since we shift the king to c2 — what we really watch is how Black develops the c8 bishop.
So a bishop to e2, to meet a bishop to d7 with a bishop to f3 and beat Black to the long diagonal — these endgames hinge on who reaches a square first.
The king slides to c2. Against a bishop to d7 and a threatened check on a4, a prophylactic a4 stops the bishop reaching b5 and a4, and if a bishop to c6, we play a bishop to f3, disarming it.
Black plays a bishop to d7. His bishop on f6 is a terrible piece — it only stares at a well-defended pawn — a lesson in understanding what a piece actually does.
We play a4 as planned — it stops the bishop's checks and lets us later push b5 and advance our majority.
A bishop to f3, disarming Black's light-squared bishop. We've disarmed both bishops; now the final stage is converting the extra pawn.
When you're holding your opponent's pieces back like this, be careful not to accidentally give up a square.
We recapture on f3.
A rook to d1 to contest the d-file — Black's last source of activity.
Black plays g6 — paralyzed and low on time, reduced to waiting moves.
The key is not to hurry — a king to b3, bringing the king toward c4 and a future b5.
Once the knight leaves c4 we can bring the king to c4 and prepare b5 — inching the king closer while Black shuffles waiting moves.
A rook to d6 — a classic idea, occupying the file to prepare doubling.
The rooks trade on d6.
We recapture with the knight, pressuring the clock.
Black plays a rook to c7.
We bring the other rook to d1 — the whole point of our approach, controlling the d-file.
I'll play h3 to restrict Black's pawns and stop any g4 activity — there's no hurry.
We don't allow any activity with g4 — no hurry, Black isn't threatening to take on d6. The king to c4 is interesting; converting this is annoyingly not elementary — the hardest part of the game.
A knight to e4, to freeze Black's kingside pawns so I can convert my majority without worrying about a Black passer.
Black plays f6.
A king to c4 — slightly risky, opening a rook trade, but the rook trade is winning. If Black plays a rook to d7...
Black plays a rook to d7 — pushing the b-pawn only helps us; b5 should win.
After the rook trade, a tactic wins another pawn.
f4 — knocking the bishop off e5, then a capture on f6 with check, and coming around to take on h5.
Black's bishop drops back to e5 to dominate the knight.
We extricate the knight by maneuvering the king to e4 to dislodge the bishop — the winning idea.
We take on h5.
Black threatens a king to g6. Do we rush the king to e4, or do we have a tempo to fix the queenside?
We play c4 first — an extra tempo — and only after a king to g6 do we play king to e4.
Black plays a king to g6.
We play king to e4. The magic: after a nasty bishop to c3 attacking b4, a knight to f4 comes with check.
The knight to f4 with check extricates the knight, and we win.
We play b5 — too many passers; we could even sacrifice the knight, but no need.
Black plays a bishop to b4.
We play c6 to create an outside passer on a6.
Black captures on c6.
We take on a6 — a passed pawn should be as far from the enemy pieces as possible.
Corner pawns are the hardest to stop — a knight to d3, and the rest is obvious.
A bishop to a7 — we head for c6 to dislodge it and push a7.

A knight to e5, the final nail — a knight to c6 and a7 are coming. That's how we convert. The Rubinstein French is named for Akiba Rubinstein, but it was actually first played in 1861 by Ignatz Kolisch, one of the top opening experts of the 1860s.
We're White, hoping for another Danish — d4, e5, e4, building a broad center.
Black plays the knight to c6, declining the gambit. It's fine, not a terrible move.
We want to open the center as much as possible — the more open it is, the more chances to attack — so we take, d takes e5.
Black recaptures, the knight to e5. Some of you are eyeing f4, but that knight is genuinely well centralized, so let's develop first.
The knight to c3 — developing flexibly and keeping our options open.
Black plays d6 — and that's what flexible development gets you: we waited, and now he's shown us he'll castle short.
Once Black castles short, we'll have carte blanche to storm our pawns. The bishop to e3.
The bishop to g4 is a common slight mistake — it lets us shore up the e4-pawn.
f3 — a move I know causes confusion, because didn't I just warn that pushing the f-pawn creates weakness?
But things have changed: because we're about to castle long, f3 turns from a liability into a huge asset, covering e4 and building the chain. Black plays the bishop to h5.
The queen to d2, connecting the plan and preparing to castle queenside.
Black plays c5 without developing a piece — and now the d5-square becomes a very juicy outpost for us.
We castle long — now it's easy to operate, because we don't have to worry about our own king.
Black develops the knight to f6.
By the book we'd hold off, but let's go — g4, offering the pawn and prying open lines.
Black takes on g4 with the bishop.
We recapture with the f-pawn, Black takes back with the knight — and now, and only now, we've won a piece.
Time to develop the bishop with tempo — the bishop to b5 with check.
If Black knew what was good he'd block with the knight, but instead he plays the king to e7 — and this is going to get juicy.
The knight to d5 with check, driving the king forward.
Black plays the king to e6, marching into the open — exactly where a lot of players get confused.
The right piece for a hunt like this is a screwdriver piece, a knight that can wiggle in around the edges — the knight to h3, and Black grabs on e3.
And that knight arrives on f4 — checkmate.

The knight lunge threatens a fork on f7, so the reply is the central break d5, interposing to block the bishop's aim. And the key rule to remember — if the pawn captures, do not recapture it with the knight.

Once a piece up, the whole plan is patience and then opening the position so the extra piece is felt. Don't rush to grab the enemy knight — keep developing and let the opponent be the one to decide and to commit, since forcing choices saves you time and invites their mistakes. Finish the kingside first for king safety, then peel the position open: recapture toward the centre to free the f-pawn, push it to f5, and blow the file open. Bring the queen into the attack as an extra force, and when your pieces outnumber the defenders of a target, take with the knight to keep the bishop as your strongest attacker. And don't tunnel-vision the kingside — a queen check from the far wing swings in to finish, the move most people miss because they only look where the king sits.
We answer the king's pawn with d5, heading into a Scandinavian.
White grabs space by shoving the pawn to e5 — but this is already too ambitious.

We hurry the light-squared bishop out to f5 before the centre locks; White builds with d4, and we settle the pawn on e6. It's a French Advance where our "bad" bishop is already free and outside the chain.
White spends a move on a3.
We hit the base of the chain with c5 in one fell swoop — no wasted tempo on c6.
White props up the centre with c3.
We develop the knight to c6, leaning on d4.
White plays h3, denying our bishop the g4 square.
We swing the queen to b6, piling onto d4 and glaring at b2.
White develops the knight to f3, guarding d4.
We choose this moment to capture on d4 — there's a concrete point coming.
White recaptures on d4 with the c-pawn.
Here's the idea — the bishop snaps off the knight, capturing on b1.
White must recapture on b1 with the rook, and now the bishop swings back to grab the pawn, capturing on a3.
White develops the bishop to d3, reinforcing so that b4 could win our loose bishop.
We keep the bishop working and give check from b4.
White blocks with the bishop on d2. Little rule: when a piece is defended only tactically, deal with it every move — don't let the threat build.
Rather than trade, we develop the king's knight to e7, keeping f5 and g6 in reach.
White castles kingside.
We swap first, capturing on d2.
White recaptures with the queen on d2.
Now we castle into safety — and note White's queen can't reach h4 or h5, so there's no Greek-gift on our king.
White lifts the f-rook to e1.
We reroute the knight to g6 — a solid blocker on the bishop's diagonal, full of potential energy, dreaming of f4.
White throws in h4, aiming to chase the knight with h5.
We've out-calculated him — the knight captures on d4.
White recaptures with the knight, and we take back on d4 with the queen.
White lunges h5, going after our g6-knight.
We slide the queen to f4, using the g6-knight as its shield.
White retreats the queen to c2, rebuilding pressure on h7.
We bring the a-rook to c8, deliberately keeping the f-rook home to shelter the king.
The opponent throws in an unusual bishop-to-a6 — a positional sacrifice, aiming either to wreck our structure or to drag our knight off the centre. Odd, but genuinely sensible.
We recapture, but this will be hard to come back from — we've given up our light-squared bishop, the one that so often fuels a kingside attack, so attacking chances will be scarce.
When you're down material, your first aim is to create difficulties — keep as many pieces on the board as you can and generate complications, so your opponent gets a chance to go wrong.

Best is to steer into a Ponziani with c3, preparing a quick d4 to fight for the centre — and perhaps to throw an unprepared opponent off. It's worth a bishop for two tempi and a fresh problem to solve.

Don't defend the e-pawn passively with a rook or d3 — play d4, right in the Ponziani spirit. The point: if he captures, we push on to e5, a common gambit motif; and a knight grab on e4 is harmless, met by taking on e5 or by d5.

The bishop to d6 almost hands the piece back and hands us a big lead in development, because it blocks in his other bishop. The tactical idea is to trade twice on e5, then f4 to shove the bishop back, then e5 — though it doesn't quite win a piece because of a bishop check on c5 and a knight jump to e4. So keeping the tension with the bishop to g5 is the sober alternative.
teaches: the f4 tactic and its flaw

notes.explains: We answer the king-pawn with the Sicilian and head for the Najdorf, my main opening from 1600 all the way to 2500.
For the 1400-1500 crowd I'd recommend the Accelerated Dragon, but here we go for the Najdorf itself, starting with the little d6.
He opens with d4, the Open Sicilian, and after the trades we reach the tabiya.

Now the move that defines it: a6, the Najdorf. Its simple purpose is to take the b5-square away — no bishop or knight check on b5 — and to prepare a later b7-b5, grabbing queenside space, an idea that runs through almost every Sicilian.
He chooses f3, the English Attack — the signal that he's going to castle long and storm my king with his pawns.
teaches: English Attack: f3 prepares queenside castling and a kingside pawn storm

notes.explains: And here's the move I grew up on: e5, kicking the knight. The downside is obvious — it weakens the d6-pawn and gouges a permanent hole on d5. The pawn and the square in front of it go weak together, as they so often do.
teaches: A pawn push weakens the square in front of it
...e5 in the Najdorf concedes d5 for dynamic play

notes.explains: He retreats the knight to b3. What Black gets for that weak pawn and weak square is dynamic, concrete counterplay — that's exactly why the Sicilian is so sharp and theoretical.
First we solve our light-squared bishop, developing it to e6 to lend cover to d5, so he can't just plant a knight there and blockade.
teaches: Cover the weak square before the opponent occupies it

notes.explains: He pins with the bishop to g5 — not actually the main move; Be3 is. And that misplaced bishop is going to cost him dearly, because it sits right where his own g-pawn wants to go.
We simply unpin by developing the bishop to e7. Note we avoid h6: that pawn would become a hook his g-pawn could latch onto once we castle short, so we keep our kingside pawns intact.
teaches: Don\u2019t create a pawn hook in front of your king

notes.explains: The queen-knight reroutes to d7, where the two knights defend one another — the classic Najdorf configuration.
teaches: The b8-knight belongs on d7 in this structure

notes.explains: He castles queenside; we castle short. Opposite wings — now the race is on, each side storming the other's king.
teaches: Opposite-side castling means a pawn-storm race

notes.explains: He starts the storm with h4, intending g4-g5 to pry my king open. We answer on the other flank.
This is where a6 pays off: we counterattack with b5, and both sides are charging on opposite sides of the board. My follow-up is b4, a5, a4.
teaches: Race the opponent\u2019s attack with your own — tempo is everything

notes.explains: We push b4, hitting his knight — and watch how much time that stranded g5-bishop costs him: it blocks his g-pawn, so the storm he wanted in one move now takes several.
teaches: A misplaced bishop that blocks your own pawn storm loses crucial tempi

notes.explains: He drops the knight into d5. We don't let it marinate on such a fine square.
And we take with the bishop, not the knight — because recapturing with the knight lets him take back and trap our e6-bishop, while his g5-bishop stays defended by the h-pawn.
teaches: Choose the recapture that doesn\u2019t leave a piece trapped

notes.explains: After he recaptures, that d5-pawn is like a dental filling: it closes the center and walls off our weak d6-pawn from the d-file, sealing the very weakness he was pressuring.
teaches: A closed center can neutralize your own structural weakness

notes.explains: With the center shut, we roll on with a5 and a4 — pure, sharp Najdorf, which fits my style like a glove.
He tucks the king toward safety, but we're a step ahead in the race. Now we bring in the beef — pawns alone won't break through; the pieces have to join.
teaches: A pawn storm needs pieces behind it to break through

notes.explains: The queen swings to b6, sidestepping while it connects the rooks and clears the way for a rook to c8.
Now b3 — we sacrifice a pawn to blast open the files around his king.
teaches: Sacrifice pawns to open lines toward the enemy king

notes.explains: We crash through on b3, opening the b-file, and prepare a frontal assault against the exposed king.
The exchange sacrifice on a2 — cutting the legs out from under his knight and ripping the a-file wide open.

Ra8+ chases the king, then we scoop the knight back with the queen. And the key lesson: sacrifices live on a sliding scale — an exchange sac is nothing like a queen sac. Even if the attack fizzles we're only down the exchange, so there's no reason to be scared.
teaches: Sacrifices exist on a sliding scale — risk the exchange freely

notes.explains: Look how many attackers we have. Even the d7-knight, seemingly outside the zone, comes roaring in with Nc5. The Najdorf poses very human problems that are hard to defend at the board.
plans: Bring the d7-knight in via c5
Pile every piece onto the open king

notes.explains: He plays Qc3 to trade queens, but that lifts the defender off his d1-rook.
teaches: Beware trades that undefend a piece

notes.explains: We collect on d5 — up a piece, his position collapsing. The game is over.
We know we're facing the Sicilian — c5.
We play c3 — the Alapin, which I recommend to every beginner; it's positionally very healthy.
Black plays e6, contesting the center.
We play d4.
Black plays d5 — now a choice: e5 into an Advance French, or capture.
We go the traditional Alapin way and capture on d5, letting Black choose how to recapture.
Black recaptures with the pawn — this heads toward an isolated-queen's-pawn structure, since we'll eventually take on c5 and leave Black an isolated d5 pawn. No rush to take c5 yet — develop first.
A knight to f3. The rule of thumb is to wait for Black to develop the dark-squared bishop and only then capture on c5, to make him lose a tempo.
Then a bishop check on b5 and castle, taking on c5 only when the f8 bishop moves.
A bishop check on b5, developing with tempo. Trades favor the side playing against the IQP — the more pieces come off, the weaker the pawn.
Black blocks with a bishop to d7.
A retreat with b6 isn't scary — Black avoids the IQP but at the cost of development.
We trade on d7, then castle.
Black recaptures and we castle — the main line; White is slightly better, a chance to show fundamentals.
Black plays a bishop to e7. He's positioned the knight so that after a capture on c5 he can retake with the knight — but we still want the IQP, even without winning the tempo.
We capture on c5.
Black takes with the bishop on c5 — a bad move. The three good bishop squares were e3, f4, and g5. Now there's a rook check on e1, and I suspect he's planning a knight to e4 in reply.
A rook check on e1. If a knight to e4, Black loses contact with the d5 pawn and we play a queen capture on d5 — after a bishop capture on f2 with check, keep calculating.
So a knight to e4, a queen capture on d5, a bishop capture on f2 with check — but we move the king to f1, Black takes the rook, and we assess.
It's going to be two pieces for a rook.
The king steps to f1 — very good for us.
Black takes on e1 and we play a queen capture on e4 with check — then trade queens and pick up the bishop, two pieces for a rook.
Black interposes a queen to e7.
We take the queen.
Black recaptures and we take the bishop with the king. Our knight is perfectly placed on f3, and we have two pieces for a rook — a material advantage we should convert.
Black plays a rook to e8. Two things to watch: a hole on d3 the knight wants, and the e-file under Black's control.

A bishop to e3, preventing a knight to c5 — and I'm not worried about the pin, because if the king moves we answer king to f2, getting out and defending the bishop. Concrete calculation supersedes a vague worry about a temporary pin.
The plan: king to f2, a knight to d2, then a knight to c4, and bring the rook in — once all our pieces are active, Black struggles to hold.
Black plays a knight to e5.
We trade. The key rule for two-pieces-versus-a-rook: the extra pair of rooks favors the side with the pieces.
We recapture on e5. The rooks let us keep the minors anchored, defending against side-to-side rook moves.
We develop the knight to d2.
Black plays a rook to e8. We can't move the bishop because of a rook to e2 — so a knight to c4 is the aim.
A rook to e1, bringing the rook in, ready to play a knight to f3 and chase the rook off e5.
Black plays f5, threatening f4.
But a knight to f3 comes with tempo, so we don't worry about f4.
A rook to b5. Instructive moment — a lot of people play b3 automatically, but see the bigger picture: b3 isn't the only way to defend the pawn.
I like b4, creating an anchor point for the bishop to reach c5.
Black plays b6 — the rook is almost trapped; if our pawn were on a3 we'd play c4. I have a clever move: a4 would trap the rook if not for a rook to d5.
So a rook to d1, guarding the d5 square and threatening a4 — I don't think Black has a defense.
Black plays f4 in desperation, giving up a pawn to open the rook's path.
We take on f4 — another pawn to the good, ready to infiltrate with a rook to d7.
Black plays a rook to f5.
A bishop to g3 — it truly doesn't matter which; this keeps the bishop solid and guards g5.
We're White. e4 — not refuted, but not quite as strong as it used to be.
The knight to f3.
Black plays the knight to c6, and we go into the Ruy Lopez, the bishop to b5.
He plays the knight to d4 — that's the Bird Defense.
The idea is to attack our bishop, so naturally we take the knight.
Black recaptures, e takes d4. The key is not to change our strategy just because he played a weird line.
We play as we normally would — complete our development and castle.
Black plays the bishop to c5, and now that pawn on d4 is genuinely annoying.
d3 — we need a way to develop the queen's knight, since the knight to c3 is blocked by that pawn.
The plan is the knight to d2 and then f3. Black plays the queen to h4 — there are some traps to be aware of.
The coast is mostly clear — he's not threatening mate — so the knight to d2.
Black plays c6. Where to put the bishop? We don't even have to move it immediately.
The bishop to c4 — better than a4, because at least here it's doing something.
Black plays d6, and now the bishop is biting on granite — my favorite expression.
Now we complete the maneuver, the knight to f3.
Black plays the queen to h5, and I'm about to do something that might make people roll their eyes.
I'm actually going to head for an endgame — the knight to g5, hitting f7 and eyeing the queen.
Black plays the king to e7, and here's the point: we don't take the queen, we have the intermediate move, the bishop takes on f7 — then the queens come off on d1 and we recapture with the rook.
Black plays h6, thinking he's won a piece — if we move the knight he takes the bishop, but I've foreseen this; it's fine.
The bishop takes on g8, grabbing the knight.
