Black recaptures on g8 and we play the knight to f3. This isn't hugely better for us — his pieces are active — but it's an endgame, so that activity matters less.
Black pins with the bishop to g4. I don't love the pin, but I don't want to waste time with h3.
So I move the rook to e1, out of the way — if he takes the knight he simply doesn't have enough for the piece.
Black plays g5, grabbing space.
We tuck the knight to d2 — isn't that passive?
Black doubles with the rook to f8.
In the endgame the rules are slightly different — with no queens, his 'attack' isn't scary, so we casually develop, the knight to b3.
Black plays the bishop to b6, and we play the bishop to d2, paving the way to develop.
Black retreats the bishop to c7. What I'm eyeing here is the e5-break.
e5 — that's the idea.
Black takes, d takes e5, thinking we blundered a pawn.
But his king and rook are on the same diagonal — always be alert to that — and we exploit it with the bishop to b4, check.
Black plays the king to d7 and we take on f8 — winning the exchange.
Black recaptures. Now that knight on b3 has done its job — where's a good square for it?
The knight to c5 with check.
Black plays the king to c8.
The knight to e4 — a beautiful, unassailable square. He can trade his bishop for it, but that's good for us; we're up the exchange.
Black plays b6 and we play f3, supporting the knight.
Black develops the bishop to e6, and we bring a rook to e2 — the plan is to double the rooks.
Black plays the bishop to d5, and we finish doubling with the rook to e1.
Black takes on e4 and we recapture with the rook — he's doing a lot of our work for us.
Black plays the king to d7. When you're up the exchange you have to make the rooks count, and rooks love open positions.
So h4, starting to pry open lines for the rooks.
Black plays c5 and we take on g5.
Black recaptures and we step the king to f2, getting it into the game.
Black offers the rook to f4 — great, he's helping us trade everything.
We take on f4.
Black recaptures, g takes f4.
Now we complete the plan of getting a rook to the seventh — the rook to h1.
Black plays the king to c6 and the rook swings to h7, onto the seventh rank.
Black plays a6. Now we need to involve the king.
g4 — an even more elegant plan than marching the king around the other way.
Black takes with check and we recapture with the king on g3.
Black plays e4 with check.
The rook takes on c7 with check — transforming the advantage, giving back the exchange to reach a winning pawn endgame.
Black recaptures the rook and we take on e4.
The kings maneuver, and we're winning because we're up a pawn and have a protected passer — basically a king-and-pawn endgame.
e5, fixing the passer.
Black pushes b5.
The king to e4, centralizing.
Black plays a5.
b3 — placing our pawns as bumpers to stop his pawns and exhaust his moves.
Black plays a4.
We take, b takes a4, to accelerate things.
Black recaptures and we play a3 — now he's in zugzwang, where every move harms his position.
He has no choice but to move the king back, since his only pawn move gives one up.
The king to d5, keeping the squeeze on.
Black plays the king to e7.
The king takes on c5, cashing in the pawn.
The kings shuffle and we take on d4 — coming around to collect all the pawns.
Black plays the king to e7.
The king to d5.
Black plays the king to d7.
We simply advance the pawns with d4 — no need to go around.
Black plays the king to e7 and we push e6.
Black plays the king to f6 and we play the king to d6, escorting the pawn.
Black plays the king to f5 and we push e7 — the red carpet is rolled out.
We underpromote to a rook with check to avoid stalemate — the rook to e5 is the first move of a mate in two.
Black plays the king to c4 and the rook to c5 with check seals it.
d4 — I have to play my main repertoire; can't dilly-dally here.
The bishop to g7 — the King's Indian.

g3 — our opponent trots out the Fianchetto Variation, one of the most reputable and positionally dangerous responses: White fianchettoes the kingside bishop and castles. We haven't committed to a King's Indian yet — we commit by pushing d6; we could also play it Grünfeld or Grünfeld-Slav style with c6 and d5.
The c6-and-d5 line does equalize, no doubt, but it's more fun and more in the spirit of my repertoire to play a traditional King's Indian.
The bishop to g2.
— which is why we play d6, reaching a very wide theoretical crossroads.

Black has a million setups against the Fianchetto, broadly three categories: setups preparing e5 — the most traditional, which we play here; setups with c5, more Benoni-flavored, which Gawain Jones recommends; and systems with neither immediately, like c6, the bishop to f5, or the knight to c6 and a6, the Panov.
So many decent variations, but we choose the one I've played the longest — the knight to d7.
The knight to d7, quickly pushing e5. White castles.

White's main response is to strike back in the centre with e4. Here I've played two lines: the first is the pawn takes d4, trading immediately, then the knight to c5 — a Maroczy-bind-like construction with pawns on e4 and c4, resembling an Accelerated Dragon where Black is cramped and White has a big space advantage —

— but Black applies long-lasting pressure to White's centre, which can collapse if mishandled. In this game I'll play a second, older line I used to play over the board up to IM level and still play almost exclusively in blitz — c6, an incredibly tricky line.
h3 — this line often slips through the cracks of even very experienced Fianchetto players.
The point of the line is to bring the queen out to a5. Our opponent already shows very good knowledge of this system.
The bishop to e3.

— so this is the last chance to exchange the pawns before White closes. White's at a further crossroads: the bishop takes d4, or the more traditional knight takes d4. Most of the time White doesn't even have the bishop-takes-d4 option, so less-experienced players auto-recapture with the knight. Run it through the computer and White is better, but he has to show tremendous precision, as in most King's Indian lines, and in a rapid game Black has a lot of easy moves and threats — and you know what happens in a King's Indian when Black gets the initiative.
We face a knight to f3 and answer, of course, with a knight to f6.
White plays d4 — another King's Indian is coming.
We fianchetto with g6.
White plays c3 — a move with no independent value, the gateway to the London, the Torre, or a fianchetto setup.
We play a bishop to g7 and wait for White to show his cards.
A bishop to g5 — the Torre Attack, essentially a London but with the bishop on g5 instead of f4, which completely alters the character of the game.
We castle. Because the bishop is on g5, treating this like a London is innocuous for White.
We keep the King's Indian spirit and push d6.

Now h4 — not a move I've faced, and it looks scary if you don't know it. Against h4 there are three options: ignore it and allow h5; push h5 ourselves to freeze the kingside; or push the pawn one square.
We choose the third — h6, encouraging White to hand us the bishop pair, then we push h5.
White captures on f6.
We recapture and White pushes h5.
And now the point of h6: we push g5, and the kingside is essentially frozen.
White plays a knight to d2. The drawback of what we did is the light squares.
One interesting move probably not on your radar: we push d5, restricting the knight and preventing it from jumping to e4.
A knight to g4 isn't scary, just annoying since it hits two pieces — so we bring the bishop back to g7.
White plays a queen to e2. Now we attack White's center — e5 wouldn't make sense here.
So we play the other break, c5 — because after e5, White just takes and we'd shuffle the bishop repeatedly.
White castles queenside — right into a massive attack. The queenside is never safe for White's king, but punishing it takes patience, not a hasty sacrifice.
A queen to a5 looks good, but the white king could evacuate to b1 and a1 — so first a bishop to f5, fixing the king on c1.
White plays a rook to e1. It's harder to shoot at a moving target — by fixing the king, we stop it fleeing to a1, and now a queen to a5 is much more effective.
A queen to a5 — mate is incoming very soon.
White plays a3. The immediate threat is a queen capture on a2.
We capture on d4 — not a bishop capture on d4, which is a blunder.
White recaptures on d4.
Patience is the crucial element — we set everything up by bringing the rook to c8, threatening a rook capture on c3.
The threatened rook capture on c3 leads to a quick mate: rook takes c3, the recapture, queen takes c3, king to d1, then a bishop check on c2 forces the king to e2, and a queen to d3 is mate.
We play the rook sacrifice on c3 with check.
White recaptures and we check with the queen on c3.
The king goes to d1 — the bishop to c2 is the key move.
A bishop check on c2 — if the king goes to c1, we play a bishop to d3 and a queen to c2.
The king is forced to e2 — a classic pattern to know.
And a queen to d3 is checkmate.

In the Accepted there are two fundamentally different roads — the solid one built around a modest pawn move, or the aggressive central grab with e4. The big centre isn't the only move, or even the main one, but it's considered the most testing.
The rook-pawn move is odd — it just lets the pawn be recaptured, and in this line every tempo matters. Facing passive play, there's nothing exotic to do; simply develop the pieces cleanly.

Follow your instincts — capturing would only invite a queen trade, so the obvious move is to push to d5, grabbing more of the centre and building tension. If it's exchanged, a knight lands on a beautiful central outpost.

A very instructive moment — many players see the knight tension and assume they must react, breaking the position or lunging the queen out. It's a false alarm: nothing is actually threatened. A capture is met by recapturing with the bishop, which is just as good, and grabbing the central pawn would be catastrophic, opening the file for a rook and a decisive pin. So develop as if nothing happened, because nothing did.

The opponent blunders — spot the standoff, the two queens facing off with the king tied to defending its own. Distract that defender with the classic bishop check on f7, and the queen falls. A queen guarded by only one piece is always susceptible to exactly this kind of shot.

Do run the safety check first — after the king takes, make sure there's no in-between check that saves the defender. Here that resource is blocked by the opponent's own pawn, so the queen is simply won and the game with it.
Against the queen's-pawn opening we play the Queen's Gambit Declined — the rite of passage for most improving players.
The QGD has two ideas. First, a serious claim in the centre — the pawn on d5, solidly defended by the pawn on e6. Second, quick, effective kingside development without giving up our pieces' activity.
The bishop on e7 looks passive, but look carefully — it's the very piece that lets us expand our central claim, because it can support another pawn push.
That push, c5, creates central tension — complex, favouring neither side. This is what makes queen's-pawn openings a positional battle: the fight is in the centre, not a race to mate.
He plays the strong bishop to g5, pinning our knight — and the real meaning of that pin is that our d5-pawn loses one of its key defenders.
So we add a defender to d5 with the bishop to e6. Playing against a queen's-pawn opening you sometimes have to bite the bullet — a defensive move like this isn't passive weakness, it's sound.
Because our bishop now guards d5, he can't recapture there with the queen — only with the knight. He does, and that's a mistake: he never stops to weigh the consequences.
Here's the drawback — there's no need to take back the knight; we simply grab on b2 at once.
Now the theme: the queen is the worst defender of all. His queen on d1 is the only thing guarding the rook on a1, so we must drive it off that square.
teaches: the queen is the worst defender

notes.explains: The bishop check on b4 does it — practically mate but for the knight interposition, and after it his position is on the verge of collapse.
We take on d2, forcing the queen to move — recapture and we take the rook, decline and it's mate. A rock and a hard place.
1681 with the black pieces. Against d4 we develop the knight and get ready for something adventurous.
In a celebratory mood, so we roll out the Budapest Gambit — an underrated, rarely-seen sideline. A great second string once you're around 1700: not bad, a little offbeat, and one you know well.
teaches: Keep an offbeat sideline you know well alongside your main opening

notes.explains: We toss the e5-pawn onto the board and hope he grabs it. Players in this range are often uneasy facing these second-tier openings, which works in our favor.
He pushes d5 instead of taking — not a great try. It hands us exactly what we want, because advancing that pawn gives up control of the c5-square.
teaches: Advancing a pawn concedes the square beside it

notes.explains: So we make a natural developing move that also pounces on that hole: the bishop to c5, a lovely nook, with d6 to follow and later c6 to chip at his center.
teaches: Occupy the square your opponent just weakened

notes.explains: We anchor the bishop with d6 and open the other bishop's diagonal. The position's equal — he's not worse, but he's posing us no problems. Note Bg5 here would be a tactical blunder to Bxf2+.

He plays e4, and this is already dubious: it weakens the d4-square as a future knight outpost, fully opens the diagonal for our bishop pressuring f2, and takes away his own e3 to relieve that pressure.
teaches: e4 here weakens d4 and bares the a7-g1 diagonal

notes.explains: The move that leaps out is Ng4 — superficial-looking, but genuinely hard to meet. It piles onto f2, and his only defense is an awkward one.
teaches: Hunt the f2 weak point with ...Ng4

notes.explains: He's forced into the ugly knight to h3. A rule for these d4 positions: the moment that knight leaves f6, think about pushing the f-pawn to f5 to blast open the f-file.
teaches: When the knight leaves f6, consider ...f5 to open the f-file

notes.explains: But first the ideal setup — we want a rook on f8 backing the f-pawn before we push f5, so we simply castle and complete development.
teaches: Prepare ...f5 by first placing a rook on f8

notes.explains: On the recap: his f3 could have been met by the strong positional knight to e3, forking into his camp and forcing a decision.
After knight to e3 he essentially has to give up his bishop for it.
And now his structure is grim — our dark-squared bishop is unopposed, raking both long diagonals and dominating a fistful of key squares. A miserable position for White.
teaches: An unopposed bishop that controls both diagonals is a lasting edge

notes.explains: A pretty high-rated opponent at seventeen-ninety-three — let's see how our repertoire fares. e4, c5.
d4 — we've been playing the Smith-Morra exclusively.
Black takes and we offer the gambit pawn with c3 — the Morra gets more exciting at this level, because people tend to accept and play conventionally.
Black accepts, d takes c3, and we recapture with the knight on c3 — a big lead in development for the pawn.
Black develops the knight to c6.
The knight to f3, developing the other knight.
Black plays e6 — one of many possible systems.
The bishop goes to c4 regardless — it's an exception to the usual rule, because from c4 it supports a knight sacrifice on d5 and makes it hard for Black to play d5.
Black develops the bishop to c5.
The big-picture rule is to develop your kingside and castle quickly — so we castle.
Black plays a6, which is quite inaccurate — the d6-square is very important, and it becomes hard for him to ever push d6.
The bishop to f4, clamping down on that d6-square.
Black plays the knight to e7, contesting d6.
A logical plan is a bishop on d6, so we push e5, seizing space and squeezing the square.
Black castles.
The knight shifts to e4, adding another attacker to d6 — look at the control we've built over that square.
Black retreats the bishop to a7.
Now we switch gears and keep improving — the queen to d2.
Black plays the knight to g6 — not scary. The bishop to g5 would hit the queen, but keep the bigger picture in mind.
We're trying to keep our e5-pawn well defended, so we calmly drop the bishop to g3.
Black plays b5 — and the knight on g6 is actually quite misplaced, with an h4-h5 idea to exploit it.
The bishop steps back to b3, out of harm's way.
Black plays the queen to b6 — I don't like that move at all for him.
The only thing Black might be preparing is the knight to d4, so we bring the rook to d1 to prevent it and get into the game.
Black plays the bishop to b8 — and good thing we tucked our bishop to b3 earlier.
Now everything is in place and we can start attacking — the queen to g5, with knight checks on f6 also worth considering.

This is the Four Knights Scotch — a simpler, less theoretical cousin of the main Scotch, and a fine vehicle for illustrating basic opening principles. The centre has been opened, and now the ideas do the talking rather than memorised theory.

The pin puts the centre under real pressure with a threat to win the central pawn, and the natural retreat would just drop a piece. So the first job is to relieve that pressure by trading off the knight, which then lets the central pawn be reinforced.

The opponent doubles the queenside pawns, but in return comes the dark-squared bishop, a valuable piece for the coming middlegame. This opening is a lovely demonstration that doubled, isolated queenside pawns matter far less than people fear.

Defend the central pawn with the bishop — and yes, it stares blankly at its own pawn for now, but the maxim holds: bad bishops defend good pawns. Later, when the pawn advances, that same bishop becomes an absolute beast. Resist the tempting pin that only ends up looking silly.
The immediate central advance is possible, but the low-key, disciplined choice is to castle first and put the fundamentals in order. Get the house in order before launching anything.

There's a small window — the opponent's bishop is undeveloped, the position is clamped, and pieces are aimed at the king, so put the attacking hat on. Rather than the queen sortie that lets the centre be undermined, the queen to h5 is stronger: it sets up a sacrifice on the weakened square and brings the heaviest piece toward the king. And don't fret over the loose pawn — you're going for mate, so let the opponent waste moves grabbing it.
Now the mindset shifts — a piece to the good, simply develop and defend, with no need whatsoever to give back any material. When you're winning, don't complicate; consolidate.
Convert with natural moves — a rook to the only open file, taking care not to bury one rook behind the other. A vulnerable pawn is no concern while nothing real attacks it.

And don't rush to trade queens to convert — keeping the queens on doesn't make the win any harder. In fact, up a piece, the cleanest path is often to go straight for mate: lift the rook into the attack and turn the extra material directly into a decisive assault on the king.

Crucially, don't recapture the weak point with the bishop, which would give up the queen — take with the queen instead. It's not a mere trade, because once the queens come off, the pawn shielding the king simply can't be held, and the game is over.

Making luft doesn't have to be the reflexive rook-pawn move — here a different pawn push serves two purposes at once, both parrying an annoying rook lunge and preparing to anchor a piece. In the endgame especially, if another luft move accomplishes something extra, don't be afraid to play it.

And a satisfying finish — the rook that sat out the entire game finally activates down the open file and reaps all the rewards. The piece that waited out the war emerges at the end and takes all the credit.
We take Black and play the Sicilian, c5.
We continue with d6, heading for the Najdorf.
The centre opens — we take on d4, White recaptures with the knight, and we develop to f6: a mainline Najdorf at last.
White develops the knight to c3 and we play the Najdorf move, a6.
White plays the early f3 — the English Attack.
We strike in the centre with e5.
White retreats the knight to b3. In the English Attack White typically follows with the bishop to e3, the queen to d2, castles long, and storms the kingside with pawns.
We develop the bishop to e6.
White develops the bishop to e3.
We play the bishop to e7. Normally this is the classic opposite-wing race — Black on the queenside, White on the kingside.
But White chooses the modest bishop to e2 — not dangerous; combining f3 with kingside castling is slightly weakening, though far from fatal.
White castles short.
We castle too.
We develop the knight to d7 — the customary Najdorf square; the knight rarely goes to c6 here, for positional reasons.
With a6 we reach the Najdorf Variation.
The bishop to f4 here is simply a blunder dressed up as theory — there's nothing sophisticated about it.
The refutation is just the pawn to e5, hitting the bishop and winning material — a simple pawn move, no genius required.
The retreat and the whole 'sacrifice' amount to nothing — Black is simply up a piece with no compensation for White whatsoever.

And the real lesson underneath the joke: bluffing is genuine — strong players will sometimes play a bad move with total confidence, hoping you won't trust yourself to refute it. Don't refrain from the winning move just because a titled opponent played the position calmly.
teaches: don’t be bluffed out of the refutation

notes.explains: e5 is a strong move here — it grabs central space and cramps his position.
teaches: Claim space in the center when you can hold it

notes.explains: The knight swings to a4, hitting the c5-pawn — that was the plan, to win it or chase it.
Careful — his knight is now attacking your e5-pawn. Think about how to defend it.
You push d4 — very good. The best way to defend a pawn is with another pawn.
teaches: The best way to defend a pawn is with another pawn

notes.explains: Now watch for his b5: it would fork two of your pieces at once. There's a piece you need to tuck out of the way first.
teaches: Sidestep a pawn fork before it lands

notes.explains: The bishop steps back so that b5 no longer forks anything.
Against d4, Black lashes out with e5 — the Englund Gambit. Don't pre-move something like c4 or the bishop to f4, because e5 comes as a cold shower.
We accept the pawn, d takes e5, and reach the first big crossroads.
Black has three or four popular tries, but the main move by a country mile is the knight to c6, developing and hitting the pawn.
To which of course we respond the knight to f3, holding the extra pawn.
The line that's the subject of most videos is the queen to e7 — this will be our main line, but first there are other moves to consider.
We dive into a Sicilian — c5.
White plays d4.
We capture on d4.
And White recaptures with the queen — a center-game against the Sicilian, an offbeat line we still face at this level.
We don't waste time — a knight to c6. The plan is to expand with e6 and d5, though a fianchetto is also possible depending on where White puts the queen.
White retreats the queen to d1. Our setup depends entirely on where the queen goes.
Even some GMs try this setup with more venom than it appears — titled players go a queen to e3, hiding behind the pawn.

The Four Knights Scotch is ideal for practising the fundamentals of getting every piece out — but it's no beginner's toy: it's popular at the very top and genuinely dangerous for the defender who isn't precise with the theory.

The bishop to c5 is a well-known inaccuracy, and the way to punish it is to snatch the central pawn without fear. The reply people dread, a bishop sacrifice with check, isn't merely harmless here — it's essentially losing for the defender.
The bishop retreat to b6 is also poor, because the defender won't even get a pawn back for the fork. A concession that hands over material for nothing is no way to meet the trick.

Now a fancy option that lays a trap — whenever there's a standoff between the queens and the kings are still uncastled, and the opponent's pieces are underdeveloped, look for it. The key is that the enemy queen is guarded only by its king. So develop the bishop to c4, and a capture invites a sacrifice on f7 that distracts the king and wins the queen.

And the one detail to verify when running this combination — make sure your own king isn't exposed to an in-between check that turns the tables. Here it's fine, but confirming there's no such resource is exactly the discipline these tactics demand.
A crossroads: a Grünfeld player must seize this moment to play d5, because if you castle White develops the queen's knight to c3 and takes d5 away, forcing you into a King's Indian.
We commit to a King's Indian, putting the pawn on d6 rather than d5 — even after the knight to c3 prevents d5, that's fine, it's what we want.
The point of routing the knight to d7 was to prepare e5, which we now play, striking at the centre.
The flexible c6 is a common multipurpose King's Indian move — it controls squares and, semi-tactically, opens the d8-a5 diagonal for the queen.

And there's the idea — the queen to a5. It's not that a5 itself is special; it's a safe jumping-off point, very hard to attack and out of the other pieces' way, from which the queen can swing to b4 to hit c4 or drop back as needed. White's sharpest reply is the queen to c2 — the instinctive bishop to d2 actually cuts White's own queen's contact with d4.
teaches: the queen as a flexible hub

notes.explains: Now discharge the central tension with the capture on d4 — wait too long and White closes the centre, leaving our rook biting on granite.
Recapturing with the queen would walk it into a discovery, so the knight recapture is the natural, sound choice.
The rook to e8 is flexible and full of tactical venom, leaning on the e4-pawn — revealing less than jumping the knight out immediately.

The knight jumps to e5, its main King's Indian post — the c5-square is awkward here with the queen on a5. This c4-and-e4 structure is a Maróczy-like bind: White has a big space advantage, and a King's Indian player must be willing to sit in cramped positions.

The King's Indian is an anti-engine opening — engines love White's space and overrate the edge, but the positions are hard to play practically. Since d5 will never happen, we nibble around the edges instead: a6 is a low-risk move preparing b5 to chew at the c4-pawn. Nothing happens fast here; it's a long maneuvering battle where you accumulate weaknesses, hedgehog-style, until something gives.
teaches: create weaknesses for the long run

notes.explains: When White plays the queen to d2, spot the forkable squares — his queen and king now sit on a fork pattern, and our own queen is in an undefended standoff to watch. The f3-square is the target.

So c5 chases the knight — positionally committal, weakening d5, but in the service of a tactic: once the knight moves, the bishop takes on h3, winning a pawn and, crucially, deflecting White's fianchetto bishop to crack open the centre.
teaches: commit a pawn for a tactic

notes.explains: The bishop crashes on h3 — untouchable, because the knight jumps to f3 with check, forking king and queen and winning the queen for two minor pieces. A classic textbook deflection sacrifice: even if White declines, we've traded off the fianchetto bishop that holds his centre together.
Black trots out the St. George — a6 and b5, a queenside fianchetto setup. The mirror version with h6 and g5 would be far worse, since it just shreds the kingside.
Six thousand viewers — let's go. e4, e5.
The knight to f3 and the knight to c6.
He plays c3 — the Ponziani, a genuinely dangerous opening; White wants to build a big center.
There are several ways to meet it, but I go for f5 — a very sharp move. Yes, it exposes my king, but I'm banking on the counterplay.
White plays d4.
I take, f takes e4, which lessens the immediate risk of my king being blown open.
White grabs on e5. Now his queen wants to come to h5 and do damage, so I have to develop fast.
The knight to f6, developing quickly — this is theory.
White plays the bishop to c4, threatening a fork. How do we deal with it?
We play d5, blocking the bishop. The bishop to b5 is theory here.
Instead he plays the bishop to b3, a bit passive.
We don't want to take the e5-knight — if we do, he recaptures and piles pressure on us. So the bishop to d6, dislodging the knight.
White takes on c6.
We recapture, b takes c6 — doubled pawns, but a solid pawn chain; that's not the end of the world.
White castles.
We castle too. Now the Greek Gift sacrifice does NOT work here — I'll show exactly why.
White plays the bishop to g5.
We involve the queen with the queen to e8, a very typical idea; White plays the knight to d2.
Let me demonstrate the Greek Gift — the bishop takes on h2 with check. I wouldn't play it in a real game here, but watch.
White takes the bishop, king takes on h2.
The knight to g4 with check — this isn't as simple as it looks; White has defensive resources.
The king to g1.
The queen to h5 — not attacking the bishop, but heading to h2.
White plays f3, but there's no way to stop the mate except giving up the queen.
The queen to h2 — checkmate. Well earned.

This is the Advance French, chosen deliberately to practise closed positions — thriving in them is a genuine skill few players are comfortable with. The first job is the modest pawn to c3, building and bracing the pawn chain.

The way to understand a closed position is to zero in on what the battle revolves around — here it's the d-pawn at the head of the chain. Whoever controls that fight wins: hold it and you keep a big space advantage and easy development; lose it and the whole structure collapses.

Against the pressure on the chain comes an odd-looking rook-pawn move to a3 — and its purpose is to prepare b4, shoving the enemy pawn away and keeping the chain intact. Prophylaxis that also gains space.

Yes, it's two pawn moves and no piece development — but preserving the health of the pawn chain is exactly that important. And it isn't wasted: the queenside expansion also readies a further push to kick a knight, and opens the door to a fianchetto. Several gains from one plan.

Develop the bishop to d3 — and the square is chosen by seeing a tactic. It looks like the central pawn hangs, but it doesn't: after the exchanges a check springs in on the exposed diagonal, exploiting a standoff to win the queen. Always confirm the pawn is really loose before fearing for it.

Castle now — the pin-check resource is still available, so the pawn is safe. And notice the deeper point: don't develop the other bishop yet. Make the moves you know you must, wait for the opponent to reveal their plan, and only then place the discretionary pieces. That posturing over who commits first is a genuine grandmaster sub-battle.

Recall the recurring idea — reroute the knight around to c5, targeting the weak enemy pawn. Same weak pawn, same maneuver, just a different transit square; and even the outpost itself is a fine square in its own right.
He plays the Modern with g6 — we take the whole centre.
The bishop to e3 — the 150-attack setup, rather than the f4 Austrian. With the centre in hand, we develop our pieces so they actually lend it support.
Don't rush the queen to d2 — it allows the annoying knight to g4 hitting the bishop. So f3 first, ruling out that jump and preparing the queen move, since we're castling long anyway.
The queen to d2 does two jobs: it readies queenside castling, and it sets up the bishop swinging to h6 to trade off his fianchettoed bishop.
Top priority is eliminating his strongest piece, the fianchetto bishop — and he correctly counters in the centre with c5.
Now d5 is fine here. Normally it would be a mistake because it opens his bishop's long diagonal — but since that bishop is about to come off the board, we don't care.
teaches: a trade justifies a committal push

notes.explains: Don't take the bishop yet — squeeze more first. The attacking idea is to blast open the h-file with h4 and h5, straight at his king. We don't even bother stopping his queenside expansion; we go for the throat.
Now the bishop comes off on g7 — the timing of that trade is the key to the whole attack.
And here's the point — rather than move the attacked knight, we sacrifice it, capturing on g6 to rip the h-file and the king's cover wide open.
The queen swings to h6 with check, and we've built a beautiful attacking battery — he's hanging by a thread.
With the knight attacked, reroute it toward a lovely central home on e3 — not to g2, which would bury our bishop.
Think about the knight's destination, not the next move — it's a two-move maneuver to g5, a gorgeous square pressuring h7 and hitting e6, more stable than f4.
Black meets the king-pawn with c5, the Sicilian.
We stay with our workhorse, c3 — the Alapin. In my view it's the single best Sicilian to face for anyone under 1900: no theory arms race, just a sound center and a game you understand.
teaches: The c3 Sicilian is the most practical anti-Sicilian below 1900

notes.explains: He plays e6, a very common reply at this level.
And we plant the center with d4.
Taking on d4 already drifts. It doesn't hand us the full center — he can still hit back with d5 — but it does give us one thing for free that he had no need to concede.
We recapture, and now the c3-square is reserved for the knight. If he plays d5 to contest, we've essentially reached a comfortable French with an extra tempo.
teaches: ...cxd4 cxd4 gives White a French-style center a tempo up

notes.explains: He develops the knight to f6 instead. A lot of people itch to push e5 here, Alapin-style — but there's no reason to give up the d5-square: after e5 the knight simply drops into d5 and sits on that hole for the rest of the game. So we hold the pawn back.
teaches: Don\u2019t push a pawn if it hands the enemy knight a permanent outpost

notes.explains: We bring the knight to c3. The pin with Bb4 that's coming looks scary to some of you — it isn't, and I'll show you exactly why.

There's the pin. Now the wrong ways to break it, because they're instructive. f3 is out of the question — never weaken your king like that in the opening. And Bg5 is the trap people fall into: after Bg5, Black plays h6, and if the bishop just slides to h4, then g5 chases it and — here's the sting — the e4-pawn hangs the moment the bishop steps off the a8-h1 watch. Defending a pawn with a counter-pin that can be kicked is a flimsy way to hold it.
teaches: A counter-pin is a bad defense if the pinning piece can be chased
Never play f3 in the opening

notes.explains: So the clean move is the bishop to d3 — develop, eye the kingside, and keep the position sound.

He develops the knight to c6. We could just take his bishop, sure — but why surrender our dark-squared bishop and spend two moves doing it? We'd rather keep developing. The knight to f3 is next; Ne2 was also perfectly reasonable.
teaches: Don\u2019t trade off a good bishop just to break a pin

notes.explains: Knight to f3 — and I'm already smelling a Greek gift on h7. That's contingent on him playing d5, castling, and tucking a knight into d7, but the picture is forming.
plans: Watch for the Bxh7+ Greek gift once he castles

notes.explains: He plays d5. Crucially, we do NOT take it: capturing lets him recapture with the knight and saddle us with an isolated queen pawn under a blockade — exactly what we don't want.
teaches: Avoid a capture that leaves you an isolated, blockaded pawn

notes.explains: The move is to push e5 — grab the space, shut the door, and clamp him. This should be clear to everyone.

He jumps the knight into e4. Now the adventurous, instructive choice: we castle and simply offer the c3-knight, prioritizing development. It's the very same idea as a main-line Italian. Retreating with Bd2 to save the knight would be wrong — I want to keep the dark-squared bishop to guard d4 with Be3 later. Qc2 is the clinical, everything-holds move; but in this house we take the tactical road.
teaches: Sacrifice a pawn for a lead in development when the attack is real

notes.explains: We castle and keep that dark-squared bishop, because our d4-pawn lives on a dark square and I want to be able to defend it with Be3 down the road.
teaches: Keep the bishop that guards your weak-colored squares

notes.explains: He grabs on c3. If you've played the main-line Italian, this whole structure — the doubled c-pawns, the open b-file, the bishop pair — should feel like home.
We recapture toward the center.

And the bishop takes on c3. Rb1 isn't even forced here — Ba3 is a genuinely strong alternative, sacking the exchange to keep his king stuck in the middle and dominate the dark squares. But Rb1 is the trickier, more testing move.

So Rb1. And here's the lesson from last game: if he tries the knight fork on d4, remember that a forking knight can just return to c6 and block the fork — the immediate queen check is the popular wrong answer for exactly that reason.
teaches: A forked knight can often retreat to block the fork

notes.explains: He does grab on d4. We take the knight first — remove the defender — and only then does the check pick up the piece cleanly.
teaches: Eliminate the defender before you cash the fork

notes.explains: We collect the bishop.

The point of checking on a4 first is that I get to keep this bishop rather than trade it — once he castles short, that bishop is aimed straight at his king. And with his knight gone, the Greek gift is off the table, so there's no downside.
teaches: Choose the recapture that keeps your attacking bishop

notes.explains: No reason I can see not to take on b7 — a perfectly juicy free pawn. You don't need to go hunting for a knockout when material is simply offered; take what's given and don't overreach. And note the rook on b7 isn't misplaced at all — it's excellent there.
teaches: When you\u2019re up material, take what\u2019s given before forcing matters

notes.explains: He hits the rook with the bishop to c6. Now, where to retreat — and you want to squeeze the most out of a retreat, not just flop back to b1. Grabbing on a7 first is completely fine.
teaches: Squeeze value out of a forced retreat

notes.explains: But we've had our fill of queenside pawns — time to attack. The rook lifts to b3, and once the bishop clears d3 this rook swings across to the kingside. Look how bare his king is: there's nothing around it.
teaches: A rook lift transfers the attack to the other wing
plans: Swing it to the kingside for the attack

notes.explains: He counterattacks the queen with Qa5. Fine — now we've got all manner of ideas against that stripped-bare king.
The Greek gift — bishop takes h7. It's not as clear-cut as people think, but it is winning, and it's worth seeing why.
He takes the bishop.

Here's the careful part: everyone wants Qh4 then Rh3 for immediate mate — and it does NOT mate, because f6 opens an escape hatch for the king. So we start with the queen check on h4, a flexible entry that keeps every option alive.
teaches: Check the king\u2019s escape square before committing to the mating net
Qh4+ first keeps the attack flexible

notes.explains: The king scurries back to g8.

And the constructive idea: don't only look at the open files — look at the semi-open ones too. That g7-pawn is pitiful cover, so the rook to g3 sets up Qf6, sets up Bh6, and keeps the sacrifice on g7 firmly on the table.
teaches: Attack down a semi-open file where the pawn cover is thin

notes.explains: A Black game — the knight to f3, and we answer d5, so no Philidor this time.
And e4 — the Lisitsin Gambit, also called the Tennison.
We're supposed to take the pawn, d takes e4.
The knight to g5 — a good case study in how to react to a gambit you've maybe never seen.
The knight threatens to grab the pawn and pressures f7, so our first priority is to develop — the knight to f6.
No need to panic; White plays d3. Keep in the back of your mind that you can always give the pawn back and trade into an endgame — the last thing a gambit player wants.
Just make a developing move and don't touch his knight — let him waste time. The knight to c6.
You're using the psychology of gambit players against them. White plays the knight to c3.
Keep developing — the bishop to g4 is very effective; if he plays f3, we take and open up his position.
f3, and we take, e takes f3.
White recaptures with the g-pawn — look at his structure now: the bishop undeveloped, the king exposed, and we keep our extra pawn.
We step the bishop back to f5, no problem.
White plays the bishop to h3.
We take on h3.
White recaptures. Here it makes sense to play conservatively rather than grabbing more space.
Let's build a solid structure — e6.
White develops the bishop to f4.
The bishop to c5, stopping him from castling.
White plays the knight to b5, eyeing c7.
Now, that knight left c3, so it no longer covers d5 — the knight to d5 is a great square, and it defends the c7-pawn.
White plays the bishop to g3.
That b5-knight is on my nerves — a6, get off my back and go back to c3.
White retreats the knight to c3.
Think about his weak squares — his pawn on f3 leaves holes — so the knight to e3 is more aggressive than the queen to f6.
White plays the queen to d2; he can't take our knight because of the fork.
The knight to d4 — the great thing about a knight here is that it prevents him from castling either way; his king is stuck.
White plays the rook to c1, but he's overwhelmed with threats.
The knight takes on f3 with check — goodbye queen.
White plays the king to e2, and we take the queen, capturing on d2.
White recaptures with the king.
We castle.
White plays the knight to e4.
The bishop to b6, tucking it safely.
White plays the rook to g1.
The knight to c4 with check — winning the exchange.

Against this slightly offbeat English setup, just develop and identify the target — the d4 square is weak, and the whole plan revolves around planting a knight there. A weak square is an invitation to occupy it.
The route to that square begins with the bishop pin to g4, tying down the knight that guards it. Set up the occupation before playing it.

Crucially, don't rush to trade the bishop for the knight — keep that capture in your pocket as an option, to be played only when the moment is exactly right. Holding a threat in reserve is often stronger than executing it.

First eliminate the annoying enemy knight, then plant your own on d4 to shatter the kingside pawn structure. And there's a bonus — removing the knight from f6 opens up a powerful pawn break in the future.

Here's a fine judgement call — normally you'd take the knight and keep your own established in the centre, but because the coming pawn break is so strong, take the bishop instead. Then castle and ram the f-pawn through, piling pressure on the pinned knight, exploiting the kingside weaknesses the opponent created to stop it.

Before launching the sacrifice, crack open the centre — a pawn break there is essential, because while the opponent's pawns hold the middle it's hard to get anything going. Unpin the king, connect the rooks with a queen move that keeps the f-rook home for the break, and prepare the pawn advances. Once the enemy queen strays from the defence, sacrifice a piece to blow the king open, trusting the two rooks and queen to be more than enough force.
White meets the Sicilian with c3 — the Alapin, aiming to build a big pawn centre with an early d4.
Black rushes and walks into a disaster — playing the same setup against every opening is a classic rookie mistake, and here d5 forks its way to a winning position.
The upshot is a pawn for a piece — down material, but far from over; the side that's up has to play really well to actually convert it.
When you're down material, the key is: don't shuffle your king. Trading is your friend — interposing the bishop to block the check is completely fine, no need to fear the swap.
The bishop takes with check, and now the basic tactic appears — the queen to a4, forking and winning the enemy queen.
It gets missed — a 500-level tactic, take the bishop, win the queen. That's exactly what happens when you don't do your puzzles.
If it ain't broke — we roll out the Danish/Center Game again, opening with d4 against the king-pawn.
He meets it with knight f6, an uncommon and not-great try that counterattacks our e4-pawn — but that knight is about to go wandering into trouble in my position.
We snap off e5 first, opening lines.

He grabs on e4. Here's the key idea: a knight can be centralized and still deeply vulnerable if no pawns or pieces support it — that's exactly this knight. Don't be reactive: Qe2 lets it drop to c5 and boxes in your bishop, and f3 walks into the Qh4+ then Nxg3 pattern.
teaches: A centralized knight without support is a target, not a strength
Don\u2019t react to a loose knight — find the opponent\u2019s other weaknesses

notes.explains: Instead we ignore the knight and hit the real weak spot: f7. The bishop to c4 pressures f7 and, since the knight is undefended, sets up forks that hit both at once.
teaches: Target f7 early; combine pressure on it with the loose knight

notes.explains: The queen to h4 — a delayed response that forks the knight and swings at the king together. Careful though: the tempting g3 loses, because the queen x-rays our own c4-bishop, so after g3 Nxg3 the queen slides over and wins the undefended bishop.
teaches: Watch for a discovered attack when your queen and a loose bishop share a line

notes.explains: We reposition the queen to f3, keeping the heat on f7 — a near-mate threat that deters his discoveries and buys us time. When you have a strong card, hold it and play it when it hits hardest.
teaches: Exercise restraint — play your strong move when it lands with most force
plans: Bring the queen into the queenside pressure next

notes.explains: e4, e5, the knight to f3.
Black plays d6 — the Philidor, which we've seen a lot.
We know the move is d4, opening up the center.
Black takes and we recapture with the knight on d4.
Black develops the bishop to e7, and we bring out the knight to c3 — just natural development.
Black plays the knight to f6, and we develop the bishop to c4.
Black castles here, which is actually inaccurate — there's a specific idea to be aware of.
We tuck the bishop away to b3 so that idea isn't a thing.
Black plays the knight to d7.
And now we can very safely castle.
Black puts the knight on e5 — a bit weird, since we can just challenge it.
f4, chasing the knight away in a manner conducive to our kingside attack.
The knight goes back to d7.
Now we decide about the f-file — the knight to f3.
Black plays the knight to c5.
Let's not play e5 immediately, which would allow the queen trade. First the queen to e1 — it kills two birds: preparing e5 and rerouting the queen to a strong attacking post.
Black plays the bishop to g4.
Now we can go e5.
Black takes, d takes e5.
We recapture, f takes e5 — see how methodically we're playing.
Black plays the knight to h5.
Never forget about development — we still have a whole side to finish. The bishop to e3.
Black plays the knight to e6.
The rook to d1; his pieces are scattered, the knight stranded on the rim.
Black plays the queen to e8 and doesn't even take our bishop.
We keep tightening the screw — the knight to d5, centralizing.
Black plays c6. The knight to d5 was a bit impulsive, but Black is so passive we can afford it.
The knight goes back to c3 — it's okay to admit a mistake in chess.
Black pins with the bishop to b4.
Now h3 to break the pin — remember the principle for judging whether a pin is dangerous.
Black takes on f3.
We recapture with the rook on f3.
Black plays the rook to d8.
We look at that knight on h5 — g4, going after it.
Black plays f5.
The rook takes on d8, to drag the queen off e8 so it no longer defends the knight on e6.
Black plays the queen to e7, we take on h5, the queen takes on d8, and the bishop takes on e6 with check — we're up two pieces.
Black plays the king to h8.
We're up two pieces; he gives more, and we carefully collect — the bishop to g5, f4, the bishop takes on f4.
Black tries the bishop to c5 with check, thinking it forks us — but it's an empty check.
We simply step the king to g2. Now we win by centralizing and going after his king.
Black plays the queen to e7, and we develop the bishop to c4.
Black plays b5 and we reposition the bishop to d3 — with no light-squared bishop for Black, this battery is unstoppable.
Black plays g6 to prevent it, which is incredibly exposing; then the knight to e4, b4, the queen to e2 — closing in.

Against the Philidor, apply basic principles — the modest pawn to d6 is passive, closing in the bishop and developing nothing. The logical response is to open the centre with the pawn to d4, punishing the passivity with lines.

Passive development leaves the defender short of resources against a quick onslaught — and in the opening, always associate an onslaught with the f7 square, the only accessible weak point. So the bishop swings to c4, aiming straight at it for a fast kill.

Developing the knight to f6 is a mistake — the knight jump to g5 leaves the defence in real trouble, and a central break wins a pawn outright. It's the Fried Liver pattern, but an even worse version for the defender because they're so passive.

A check on b5 is the precise move, since the natural block isn't available — and if the bishop interposes, capturing wins a tempo. In a position built on a development lead, every extra tempo is gold.

The opponent hasn't castled — and any time your opponent's king is stuck in the centre, the alarm bells for tactics should ring. An uncastled king by definition means a heightened chance of a combination.

Here's the common pattern to bank — if the enemy queen lands on the open central file, a rook to e1 wins it. Combining that with the exposed king yields the pawn thrust to e6, which forces a capture, and the recapture keeps the tactic alive because the queen can't take without walking into the rook.
Against the Philidor — the opponent stakes out the centre with d6 and e5.
Black invites the Modern — fianchettoing the bishop to g7 and handing White a big pawn centre on purpose, planning to chip away at it from the flanks.
teaches: The Modern cedes the center to counterattack it later

notes.explains: Black stakes out the small centre with d6, keeping everything flexible.
White develops the knight to c3, building the broad e4-d4 wall.
Black begins the queenside expansion with a6, preparing b5 to strike at White's centre from the wing.
teaches: ...a6 and ...b5 hit the center from the flank in the Modern

notes.explains: White pins with the bishop to g5, eyeing the dark squares.
Black grabs space with b5, and the counterattack is under way.
The second bishop comes to b7 on the long diagonal, leaning directly on the e4-pawn — the whole hypermodern idea in one move.
teaches: The b7-bishop pressures the center along the long diagonal

notes.explains: White lunges with e5 to break the tension, and after the trade on d6 the position cracks open.
White centralizes the knight on e4, and the middlegame is sharp — White's space against Black's piece pressure, with the engine giving White a real pull.
White castles and completes development, the broad centre and freer pieces worth a clear edge.
Black keeps fighting with the queen to b6, hitting b2 and probing for counterplay under the pressure — the defensive resourcefulness that separates classes of player.
teaches: Keep creating threats even in a worse position

notes.explains: White offers to trade the strong dark-squared bishop with Bh6, aiming to strip the shield off Black's king.
The bishops come off, and Black recaptures with the king — the position simplifies but Black holds it together.
White breaks with c4 to prise the position open, and the pawns come off around the centre.
And here the tables turn: Black captures on e4 and the material swings his way — White's pieces have overreached, and the GM pounces on the loose ones.
teaches: Punish overextended pieces by winning the loose material

notes.explains: White grabs on a6 to try to muddy it, but it only loses more — Black emerges clearly up material, the whole assessment flipped.
teaches: A desperate grab in a lost position usually just loses more

notes.explains: Black steers toward the queens coming off — with a material lead, every trade brings the win closer.
teaches: Trade pieces when you\u2019re ahead in material

notes.explains: The knight centralizes on d5, a commanding blockading square, as Black settles into the technical conversion.
The extra material and the active pieces do the rest — this is the GM's edge over the IM: absorb the early pressure, then convert cleanly once the chance comes.
teaches: Defend soundly, then convert without hurry once ahead

notes.explains: Let's start with d4, and Black fianchettoes with g6.
c4 is the correct, principled move, grabbing more of the center.
Black completes the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
And now we play e4 — the key difference to understand.
The knight leap to g5 is the Fried Liver Attack — one of the most common variations at every level, and especially among improving players. It's the branching point where the Traxler lurks.

Don't take opening shortcuts. You could slot into a Queen's-Gambit-Declined shape, but the principled move that really challenges the English is e5 — think of this whole opening as a reversed Closed Sicilian.
The bishop check on b4 leads to rich positional battles, but the simpler, more approachable move is to develop the knight to f6 — flexible, committing to nothing yet.

We play the principled d5, reaching a reversed Accelerated Dragon — an Accelerated Dragon with White a tempo up. The danger for our side is that if you just put pieces on natural squares without a thought, you drift into serious positional pressure.

Now the whole opening battle revolves around one thing: stopping the d4 break. So the knight drops back to b6, keeping its clamp on d4 — and we avoid Be6, which, down a tempo, would let White strike with d4 at once.
We go for the King's Indian from the very start, fianchettoing the bishop on the long diagonal.
teaches: KID: fianchetto and aim the g7-bishop at the center

notes.explains: He pins with the bishop to g5, the Smyslov-style sideline. It doesn't change our plan.
We simply play d6 to start, keeping the classical King's Indian structure.
We castle and keep it as simple as possible — there's nothing fancy needed against this setup.
Now c5, contesting the center and trying to open the long diagonal for our fianchettoed bishop.
teaches: ...c5 is one of the two KID central breaks

notes.explains: We complete development with the bishop to f5. It's not exactly what I'd play in a classical game, but it's an easy, sound setup.
Here we start with g5, chasing the bishop back, planning to plant the knight on e4 next.
And the knight jumps to e4 — this trade is extremely common in King's Indian positions.
We trade on e4.
He pushes d5. Two things we've achieved: we've cleared the path for our dark-squared bishop, now a monster on the long diagonal, and we've loosened White's grip on the center.
teaches: Trading on e4 frees the KID bishop and loosens White\u2019s center

notes.explains: The knight reroutes back — Na5 would run into b4, so instead it heads around toward d7.
teaches: Reroute a knight the long way to avoid being kicked

notes.explains: His attack on b7 is a false alarm — we can ignore it — and now we begin operations on the queenside.
We start with a6, preparing the b5 break to prise open the queenside.
teaches: ...a6 and ...b5 open the queenside in these structures

notes.explains: The rook lifts to b8, keeping the pressure down the b-file, and our knight eyes the e5 outpost.
We recapture toward the center with the f-pawn — deliberately opening the f-file, because both our rooks and that pawn are lining up for an attack down toward f2.
teaches: Recapture toward the center to open a file for attack
plans: Stack the rooks for an attack on the second rank

notes.explains: The queen finally joins with Qa5 — the one piece that wasn't working — and it hits the knight from a fine square.

There are a million wins, but the cleanest forces the queen trade with the knight to b6. Whenever one of your pieces makes contact with an enemy piece, automatically consider the idea — it's central to consistent tactical vision.
teaches: When pieces make contact, always check the tactic

notes.explains: We simplify and grab the central d5-pawn — up material with a winning position. Game over.
We go Sicilian — c5.
White plays a knight to f3. Past 2100 I'm reverting to my real repertoire, the Najdorf.
We play d6.
White plays d4 — the open Sicilian, the main line.
We take on d4 and White recaptures with the knight.
We develop the knight to f6 — and here there's a major fork in the road.

White almost always plays a knight to c3. Now Black chooses: the Najdorf is most popular, then a knight to c6 (Rauzer/Classical), g6 (Dragon), e6 (Scheveningen), the obscure bishop to d7, or the Keres with an immediate e5.
We play the Najdorf, a6 — named for Miguel Najdorf, who breathed the most life into it.
White plays f3 — the theory here is far too vast for any one video, so I'll stick to what we face.
That other move is e5, immediately hitting the knight — leading to a fundamentally different type of position.
White plays a knight to b3. For now, just recognize this is known opening theory.
After e5 we must secure the d5 square — the main drawback of every e5 Najdorf — so a bishop to e6, guarding d5 and preventing a bishop to c4.
White plays a bishop to e3.
We continue with a bishop to e7. Typically White plays a queen to d2, preparing to castle long.
A queen to d2 — and the fascination of the Najdorf is opposite-side castling: Black attacks on the queenside, White on the kingside.
We castle kingside.
White castles long. The main move by a mile is a knight to d7, but I play a much more obscure line — successful for a year in blitz, and even top players are clueless against it.
The move is a5 — it may seem awkward since a6 usually prepares b5, but a5 is the idea I want.
White plays a bishop to b5, one of the best moves — its point is to stop a4 kicking the knight to the awful a1 square.
The drawback of b5 is vulnerability to Black's queenside knight — so a knight to a6, a move you wouldn't find at first sight.
White plays a king to b1 — a good move.

We follow with a knight to c7, posing White a dilemma — here White must know four or five moves of obscure theory or end up much worse. The main move is a bishop to b6, pinning the knight to the queen.
White plays a bishop to b6.
We unpin with a queen to b8, shifting off d8 and renewing the threat of a knight capture on b5.
White plays a bishop to a4. Two options: push d5, or a rook to a6 to kick the bishop — after a rook to a6, if the bishop retreats to e3, b5 traps it and wins.

I go for d5 — exciting and in the spirit of the position. It opens our dark-squared bishop, and though White has more attackers, our queen being among the primary attackers overrides that after the exchanges.
White can win the pawn by first capturing on c7 to remove a defender, then grabbing it — but we'd have a rook to d8 to recover it.
White recaptures on d5 with the knight.
We recapture with the knight — a bishop recapture wouldn't come with tempo. Our aim remains to drive the bishop off b6: if White plays a bishop to f2, then b5 ends the game.
White plays a queen to f2. We shouldn't rush to grab the bishop, because the queen replaces it and is hard to shift from b6 — the whole reason for a5 was to guarantee a rook to a6.
So a rook to a6, hitting the bishop. The lines here are incredibly complex — one inaccuracy loses.
The bishop drops to c5.
We push b5.
White captures on e7, dodging the minefields beautifully.
We recapture on e7 with the knight.
Welcome to the Opening Lab — the King's Gambit, the father of all gambits. e4, e5, f4, offering the pawn to seize the center.
We accept, e takes f4.
The immediate d4 has long been known to be dubious.
Because it allows the very natural queen to h4 with check.
White can't play g3, so the king is forced out to e2 — no fun at all.
The best continuation is to strike the center with d5, sacrificing the pawn to develop fast.
White takes, e takes d5.
The bishop to g4 with check — and note this doesn't win White's queen because of the knight to f3.
White interposes the knight to f3.
Now aim for rapid development to mate the king on e2 — the knight to d7. Notice Black is the one sacrificing a pawn.
If White grabs it, the bishop takes on f4.
The bishop takes on f3 with check — White can't recapture with a pawn.
White has to take with the king.
We avoid the immediate queen to h5 because of g4, and start with the bishop to d6.
White takes on d6.
Now the queen to h5 with check — White has to play g4.
White plays g4.
The queen travels and takes on d5 with check.
After the king to f2, the one thing to remember is not to take the rook.
Grabbing the rook on h1 would be bad — after the queen to e2 with check, Black's own king gets exposed and the queen could get trapped.
We play the Sicilian — c5.
White plays a knight to f3.
We play d6.
White plays d4 and we capture on d4.
White recaptures with the knight and we develop a knight to f6.
White plays a bishop to d3 — a move that's gotten more popular. Its point is to reserve c4 for a Maroczy-style clamp. We're not tied to the Najdorf; stay flexible.
We take White and face the Caro-Kann.
We build the centre with d4.
Black challenges with d5.
We play f3 — the Fantasy Variation, sharp and tactical, and far less studied than the mainlines.
Black plays e6 — the most reputable reply — and we treat it like a French. Note the threat: ...dxe4 and then ...Qh4 with check.
We defend while developing — the knight to c3 reinforces e4 and takes the sting out of ...Qh4, which would now meet g3.
Black pins with the bishop to b4 — the main move, just like the Winawer French.
We try a3 — a pawn sacrifice, forcing the bishop to decide.
Black takes on c3 with check.
We recapture with the b-pawn onto c3. Black has given up the dark-squared bishop, leaving a position riddled with dark-square weaknesses on d6 and e7.
Black grabs on e4.
The computer move — not a bishop but the knight to h3. It prepares fxe4 to win the pawn back, and a check on h4 is now harmless because Nf2 would cover e4.
Black plays the theory move to a5, the queen eyeing the c3-pawn.
We fianchetto to b2 rather than d2 — d2 would run into ...e3, deflecting the bishop and forcing our king to move. On b2 it looks bad now, but c4 and d5 later give it real potential energy.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We take back on e4.
Black recaptures with the knight — dubious, I think.
We develop the bishop to d3, hitting the knight and preparing to castle. If ...Nxc3, then Qd2 would pin and win it, since the a5-queen is undefended.
Black drops the knight back to f6.
We castle — king to safety, and more importantly the rook lands on the semi-open f-file, a hallmark of the Fantasy.
Black plays the slow b6, preparing to fianchetto — but we're a couple of moves from smashing open the kingside.
On theme, we push c4 — investing a tempo to free the b2-bishop and prepare d5.
Black connects the knights with ...Nbd7, taking the sting out of d5.
We bring the queen into the attack with Qf3; Black develops the bishop to b7; and the queen slides to g3 — its real destination, bearing down the g-file at g7 and clear of the rook.
Black castles queenside, conceding g7 — not an easy thing to do, but the grandmaster choice.
We take the free pawn — even in attack, material matters; the queen crashes into g7.
Black swings the rook to g8, hitting the queen.
The queen slips out to f7, grabbing a second pawn; Black answers with the quiet rook to e8 — a high-level defensive resource.
